paragraphs: SECTION I

The sage Vālmiki asked Nārada—a legendary sage known for his wisdom and deep knowledge of the Vedas—a question: “Is there anyone alive today who has every good quality? Someone who’s strong, knows right from wrong, is grateful, truthful, and sticks to his word? Someone whose character makes him worthy, who cares for everyone, is smart, understands society, and knows how to make people happy? Who’s good-looking, controls himself and his anger, is charming and never holds a grudge, and so powerful that even the gods fear him in battle? I really want to hear about such a person. You, Maharshi, can surely tell me if anyone like this exists.” Hearing this, Nārada—who knows everything happening in all the worlds—answered eagerly, “Listen carefully. The qualities you listed are rare, but there is someone who has them all. He comes from the Ikshwāku dynasty and is called Rāma. Rāma is calm, incredibly strong, radiant, patient, controls his senses, intelligent, knows morality, speaks beautifully, graceful, a destroyer of enemies, and has a sturdy, impressive build—broad shoulders, strong arms, a thick neck, and a wide chest. He’s a master archer and has arms that reach his knees, a striking face and forehead, and perfect physical strength and symmetry. His skin is cool in tone, his chest is well-developed, and his eyes are large and expressive. He’s marked by luck and good omens, knows his duties, keeps his promises, always looks out for his people, and is famous for his achievements. Rāma is knowledgeable, pure in mind and body, respects elders, understands himself, and is as wise as Prajāpati. He’s prosperous, protective, destroys enemies, supports everyone, maintains order, and helps those who follow him. He’s an expert in the Vedas and attached sciences, a top-notch archer, has a sharp memory, quickly figures out the truth, and is loved by all. He’s never blamed, never defeated, perceptive, skilled in every subject, and respected by the good, like rivers flow to the ocean. He deserves honor, treats everyone the same, and always inspires new feelings in people. He makes his mother Kaushalya proud, is as deep as the ocean, as patient as the Himalayas, has the strength of Vishnu, the beauty of the Moon, the fury of fire when angry, the forgiveness of the Earth, the generosity of Kubera (the god of wealth), and the honesty of Dharma himself.

“Wanting to make his people happy, King Daśaratha, out of deep love, decided to make his eldest son Rāma co-ruler. Rāma was brave, full of virtues, and always thought about others’ well-being. But when preparations for the ceremony began, Queen Kaikeyi—who had been promised two wishes earlier—asked for Rāma to be exiled and for her son Bharata to be crowned instead. Because he’d promised, King Daśaratha felt he had no choice and sent his favorite son Rāma away. Rāma, obeying his father and wanting to please Kaikeyi, left for the forest. On the night before Rāma left, his brother Lakshmana—gentle and loyal—chose to go with him out of love. And just like the star Rohini follows the moon, Rāma’s beloved wife Sītā, a princess from Janaka’s family and a symbol of goodness, insisted on going too. As they left, Daśaratha and the people of Ayodhya followed them for a while. Rāma met the noble king of the Nishādas, Guha, and, with Guha, Lakshmana, and Sītā, sent his charioteer back home on the banks of the Ganges at Sringaverapura. They traveled from forest to forest, crossed many rivers, and, following the sage Bharadwāja’s advice, reached Chitrakuta, where they built a beautiful home and lived happily. For a while, their days were peaceful, almost like those of gods. But after Rāma reached Chitrakuta, King Daśaratha died of heartbreak. After Daśaratha’s death, the powerful Bharata was asked by the priests, led by Vasistha, to be king, but he refused. Instead, he went to find Rāma in the forest to convince him to come back. When Bharata found Rāma, he begged him respectfully to return. Rāma told Bharata, “You are king now too,” but Rāma, always generous, kept his promise to their father and refused the throne. Instead, he gave Bharata his sandals as a symbol of authority, even as Bharata begged him to return. Disappointed but respectful, Bharata touched Rāma’s feet and went back to Nandigrāma, ruling there and waiting for Rāma’s return. Once Bharata left, and as more citizens and others came looking for him, Rāma decided to go deeper into the Dandaka forest. There, Rāma, the lotus-eyed hero, killed the demon Virādha and met sages like Sarabhanga, Sutikshna, Agastya, and Agastya’s brother. Following Agastya’s advice, Rāma gratefully received Indra’s bow, an endless supply of arrows, a sword, and a magic quiver. While Rāma was living in the forest, a group of sages came to him, asking for his help to rid the forest of demons and evil spirits. In front of these fiery ascetics, Rāma promised to defeat the demons in battle. While living there, the demoness Surpanakhā—who could change her shape—was punished and disfigured. Not long after, stirred up by Surpanakhā, Rāma fought and killed the demons Khara, Trishira, and Dushana, along with their followers. In that battle, Rāma killed fourteen thousand demons. When Rāvaṇa heard that his relatives had been wiped out, he was furious and went to the demon Māricha for help. Māricha tried hard to talk him out of it, warning Rāvaṇa not to fight Rāma, but Rāvaṇa wouldn’t listen.

“Māricha said, ‘You really shouldn’t fight someone that powerful, Rāvaṇa. Please, let me be!’ But Rāvaṇa, driven by fate, ignored him. Together, they went to the forest where Rāma and Lakshmana were living. Using Māricha’s magic, they lured Rāma and Lakshmana away and Rāvaṇa kidnapped Sītā, killing the vulture Jatāyu who tried to stop him. When Rāma found the dying Jatāyu and learned that Sītā had been taken, he was overwhelmed with grief. After cremating Jatāyu, Rāma kept searching for Sītā and encountered a terrifying demon named Kāvandha. Rāma killed Kāvandha, burned his body, and Kāvandha’s spirit was freed. The demon’s soul told Rāma, ‘Go see the wise hermit woman, Shabari—she knows all the ways of righteousness.’ Rāma, full of energy, went to Shabari, who honored him, and then, on the banks of the Pampa river, met Hanumān. Following Hanumān’s advice, Rāma met Sugriva, the monkey king, and told him everything, especially about losing Sītā. Sugriva was moved and, in front of fire, made a friendship pact with Rāma. Sugriva, still sad about his own troubles with his brother Vāli, told Rāma the whole story. Rāma promised to kill Vāli. Sugriva, worried about Vāli’s strength, showed Rāma the massive skeleton of the demon Dundubhi to prove how strong Vāli was. Rāma, smiling, flicked the skeleton with his toe and sent it flying nearly ninety miles. Then, with a single arrow, he pierced seven palm trees, a hill, and even the underworld, to convince Sugriva of his power. Convinced, Sugriva led Rāma to the cave of Kishkindha. When they arrived, Sugriva roared loudly to challenge Vāli. Hearing the challenge, Vāli came out, and after getting permission from his wife Tāra, faced Sugriva in battle. Rāma killed Vāli with a single arrow. At Sugriva’s request, Rāma made him king. Sugriva gathered all the monkeys from different lands and sent them out to search for Sītā. With help from the vulture Sampāti, Hanumān crossed the ocean—one hundred yojanas wide—to reach the city of Lanka ruled by Rāvaṇa. There, Hanumān found Sītā in the Ashoka grove, lost in thought. He secretly gave her Rāma’s ring and told her about the friendship between Rāma and Sugriva, cheering her up. Hanumān then destroyed the palace gates, killed five generals and seven princes, and defeated the heroic Aksha. He was eventually captured by Indrajit, but because of a blessing from Brahma, Hanumān was unharmed. He forgave the demons who bound him, then set fire to the city of Lanka—except the place where Sītā was held—and returned quickly to tell Rāma the good news. Hanumān met Rāma, circled him in respect, and said, ‘I’ve really seen Sītā.’ With Sugriva, Rāma marched to the ocean’s edge and shot arrows into the sea, making it boil. The ocean god appeared and, following his advice, Nala built a bridge to Lanka. Rāma crossed the bridge, attacked Lanka, and killed Rāvaṇa in battle. Rāma rescued Sītā, but felt deeply ashamed that she had lived in another man’s house for so long, and harshly questioned her in front of everyone. Unable to bear it, Sītā entered a burning fire. But the fire god Agni proved Sītā’s innocence, and Rāma was overjoyed and praised by all the gods. Because of Rāma’s actions, the whole universe—gods, sages, and all beings—were pleased. Rāma crowned Vibhīṣaṇa, Rāvaṇa’s brother, king of Lanka, and finally felt at peace. The gods granted Rāma a wish, so he brought back to life all the monkeys who had died in battle. Surrounded by friends, Rāma returned to Ayodhya on the flying chariot Pushpaka. He stopped at the hermitage of Bharadwāja, sent Hanumān ahead to Bharata, then, with Sugriva, flew to Nandigrāma. At Nandigrāma, Rāma and his brothers cut off their matted hair, reclaimed Sītā, and took back the throne. Rāma, son of Daśaratha and lord of Ayodhya, ruled his happy people like a father. During his reign, everyone would be content, healthy, righteous, and free of anxiety and disease. No parent would ever have to see their child die; women would always be faithful, never widowed. No one would fear fires, floods, storms, or fevers. There would be no hunger or theft, and cities and lands would be rich and full of crops and wealth. Life would be as joyful as the Golden Age. Rāma would perform a hundred horse sacrifices, give away countless cows and endless riches to Brahmins, and establish a hundred royal families, making sure each caste followed its duties. After ruling for 11,000 years, Rāma would leave for the world of Brahma. Anyone who reads this sacred, sin-destroying, and rewarding story of Rāma—equal in holiness to the Vedas—will be freed of all sins. Whoever reads this Rāmāyana will enjoy a long life and be honored in heaven with their children and family. A Brahmin who reads it becomes eloquent; a Kshatriya gains land and power; a Vaishya becomes wealthy; and a Shudra achieves greatness.”
SECTION II

After hearing Nārada’s words, Vālmiki, who was wise and skilled in speech, honored the great sage along with his own students. Once Nārada had been respectfully received and given permission to leave, he took off for the heavens. When Nārada was gone, Vālmiki made his way to the banks of the Tamasā river, not far from the Ganges (Jahnavi). When he got there, he noticed a clean, mud-free spot and turned to his disciple, saying, “Hey Bharadwāja, look at this clean and beautiful spot. The water here is clear and pleasant, just like the minds of good people. Set down your water pot, and hand me my bark garment. I want to bathe here in the Tamasā—it's the nicest place.” Bharadwāja, always eager to serve his teacher, quickly brought Vālmiki his bark. With his garment in hand, Vālmiki wandered along, taking in the wide forest. Not far off, he spotted a pair of Krauncha birds (cranes), singing sweetly and moving around together in peace. Suddenly, out of nowhere, a cruel hunter picked out the male bird for no reason and shot him down right in front of Vālmiki. The dying bird fell to the ground, bloodied, while his mate cried out in heartbreak, mourning her partner with desperate, sorrowful cries, grief-stricken at losing her copper-crested mate, who had been proudly showing his feathers. Seeing the bird killed so senselessly, Vālmiki was deeply disturbed and saddened. Realizing how wrong the hunter’s act was, Vālmiki, full of pity as he watched the grieving crane, spoke out: “Hey hunter, because you killed one of this loving pair, you’ll never find happiness!” Right after saying these words, he wondered to himself, “What did I just say, moved by the bird’s pain?” Turning this over in his mind, the wise sage said to his disciple, “What I just spoke came out in equal lines and rhythm—it could be sung to music. Let it be known as a shloka, born from my sorrow.” Bharadwāja, pleased, agreed. Vālmiki felt satisfied. After bathing at the holy spot, Vālmiki walked back, still thinking about how the poem had come out of him. Bharadwāja, humble and learned, followed behind, carrying the water pot.

When Vālmiki and his student returned to the hermitage, Vālmiki kept thinking about the verse, even while chatting about other things. Then, hoping to visit the great sage, the god Brahmā himself—creator of everything and shining with four faces—appeared. As soon as Vālmiki saw Brahmā, he quickly got up, amazed, and stood before him with folded hands. Bowing low, Vālmiki offered water to wash Brahmā’s feet and brought other items of welcome. Brahmā sat on a seat of honor and asked kindly about Vālmiki’s well-being, then invited him to sit too. Sitting in front of the Grandfather of the world, Vālmiki kept thinking about the strange lines he had spoken.

Vālmiki’s mind replayed the scene: “How awful was that cruel hunter’s act, killing the innocent and singing Krauncha bird for no reason!” Still upset for the grieving female, Vālmiki found himself silently repeating the verse. Then Brahmā smiled and spoke: “Vālmiki, the verses you just created will become famous—don’t doubt it. I inspired you to say them. Now, I want you, greatest of sages, to write the full story of Rāma. Tell the world everything about Rāma—the wise, righteous, and remarkable Rāma. Tell everything you know, and even what you don’t yet know—about Rāma, Lakshmana, Sītā (Videha’s daughter), and the Rākshasas. I’ll make sure even things Nārada didn’t tell you will be revealed to you. Every word you write will be true. So, write this beautiful story of Rāma in verse. As long as mountains and seas exist, your Rāmāyana will be remembered. And as long as your Rāmāyana is known, you’ll live in this world and in mine.” With that, Brahmā disappeared. Vālmiki and his students were amazed. The students began reciting the verses again and again, feeling joy. In awe, they said, “These verses, perfectly measured and made up of four lines, have real emotion and now stand as a true shloka. Now our teacher plans to write the whole Rāmāyana in this style.”

The great sage Vālmiki, famous for his kindness and wisdom, went on to compose hundreds of beautifully crafted verses, telling the story of Rāma’s family. Listen to this epic tale of the greatest of the Raghus, and the defeat of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, set down by Vālmiki with careful structure and clear, moving language.
SECTION III

After hearing the whole story of the wise Rāma—a story that brings spiritual merit, success, pleasure, and even the promise of liberation—Vālmiki wanted to understand it even more deeply. He sat facing east on a seat made of kusa grass, sipped water as tradition required, and started meditating on the story using his yogic powers. Through his meditation, he could see Rāma, Lakshmana, Sitā, and Daçarātha with his wives in the palace, all laughing, talking, and living their lives just as they had in reality. He witnessed everything that Rāma, ever true to his word, went through alongside his wife. Like holding an amla fruit in his hand, Vālmiki could see the entire past and future of Rāma’s life thanks to his spiritual insight. After truly seeing it all through deep contemplation, the generous sage decided to write down Rāma’s enchanting story. Following what the powerful sage Nārada had told him, Vālmiki composed the tale of the Raghu dynasty—a story full of wisdom, delight, and depth, as vast and rich as the ocean, and captivating to both ear and mind. He included every important detail: Rāma’s birth, his incredible strength, his kindness, popularity, patience, virtue, honesty, and his amazing interactions with Viswāmitra; the marriage of Jānaki (Sitā); the breaking of the great bow; Rāma’s confrontation with Paraśurāma; the noble traits of Daçarātha’s son; Rāma’s planned coronation; Kaikeyi’s jealousy; the cancellation of Rāma’s coronation and his exile; the king’s heartbreak, mourning, and death; the grief of the people and Rāma sending them back to Ayodhyā; news from the king of the Nishādas; the charioteer’s return; crossing the Ganges; Rāma’s meeting with Bharadwāja; arriving at Chitrakuta as Bharadwāja advised; building a home there and living for a while; Bharata’s arrival and attempt to persuade Rāma to return; Rāma offering rites to his father’s spirit; the installation of Rāma’s sandals; Bharata living at Nandigrāma; Rāma’s journey to Dandaka and killing Virādha; meeting Sarabhanga and Sutikshna; Sitā’s friendship with Anusuyā, who gifted her fine clothes and ornaments; Rāma’s meeting with Agastya and receiving a powerful bow; the story of Surpanakhā and her mutilation; defeating Khara and Tricira; Rāvana’s plotting; the death of Māricha and the kidnapping of Sitā; Rāma’s grief and the death of the king of vultures (Jatayu); Rāma’s encounter with the demon Kabandha and his arrival at Pampā; meeting the hermitess Savari and living on forest food; Rāma’s grief at Pampā and meeting Hanumān; traveling to Rishyamukha and meeting Sugriva; earning Sugriva’s trust and forming a friendship; the fight between Vāli and Sugriva; the defeat of Vāli and Sugriva’s coronation; Tārā’s mourning; Rāma and Sugriva planning the search for Sitā; Rāma’s stay during the rainy season; his growing frustration; gathering the monkey army; sending messengers in all directions; Sugriva assigning search zones to the monkeys; Rāma giving Hanumān his ring; Jāmbavān’s discovery of the cave; the monkeys fasting at the ocean’s shore; Hanumān meeting Sampāti; Hanumān climbing the mountain and leaping over the ocean; being greeted by Maināka at the Ocean’s request; encountering the demoness Sinhikā and defeating her; seeing Lankā at night and sneaking in; figuring out how to survive in enemy territory; visiting the tavern; exploring the royal chambers; seeing Rāvana and his flying chariot, Pushpaka; reaching the Asoka grove and finding Sitā; Hanumān giving Sitā Rāma’s ring and talking with her; the demonesses roaring at Sitā; Trijata’s prophetic dream; Sitā giving Hanumān her jewel; Hanumān breaking trees; the demonesses fleeing and the slaves being killed; Hanumān being captured; his terrifying roar as he burns down Lankā; his leap back over the ocean; forcefully taking honey; Hanumān comforting Rāma and giving him Sitā’s jewel; Rāma negotiating with the Ocean; Nāla building the bridge; the army crossing the sea; laying siege to Lankā at night; Rāma meeting Bibhishana; Bibhishana sharing Rāvana’s weaknesses; the deaths of Kumbhakarna and Meghanāda; Rāvana’s defeat and Sitā’s rescue; Bibhishana’s coronation; seeing the Pushpaka chariot; Rāma’s return to Ayodhyā and meeting Bharadwāja; Hanumān traveling ahead; Rāma meeting Bharata; Rāma’s coronation; disbanding the army; Rāma pleasing his people and banishing Sitā—and everything else about Rāma’s earthly life, even the things that had not yet happened—were all included by the great sage in the final part of his epic.
SECTION IV

After Rāma had reclaimed his throne, the revered sage Vālmiki wrote the complete story of Rāma’s life. He crafted it in beautiful verse, rich with meaning, and recited a total of twenty-four thousand slokas. The epic was divided into five hundred sections and organized into six main books, plus the Uttara Kanda. When Vālmiki finished writing—even including events that were still to come—he wondered who should present this epic to the world. As he was thinking about this, Kusi and Lava (sometimes spelled Kusha and Lava), dressed like the sons of sages, entered and respectfully touched his feet. Vālmiki saw that Kusi and Lava, the noble brothers, were deeply moral, living in the hermitage, and blessed with beautiful singing voices. They were quick learners, skilled at understanding poetry, and had excellent memories. Vālmiki taught them how to interpret the Vedas, then, after they completed their Vedic studies, he taught them the entire Ramayana—detailing Sita’s story and the fall of the demon Ravana (Paulastya’s descendant). These brothers, graceful as Gandharvas, also excelled at music and dance. They understood musical notes and rhythms and began to sing the poem, which was arranged in three tempos and seven notes, performed with string instruments. The poem expressed love, sadness, humor, anger, terror, and heroism. Fully grasping the elements of drama, and gifted with smooth, melodious voices, the brothers—who looked so much like Rāma that they seemed like his reflections—memorized the whole epic. Concentrated and focused, Kusi and Lava performed the Ramayana as they had learned it, reciting and singing before gatherings of sages, Brahmins, and other good people.

One day, these remarkable and virtuous brothers performed their poem before an assembly of pure-hearted sages. The music moved the ascetics so deeply that tears filled their eyes, and they cried out, “Amazing! Bravo!” Filled with admiration, the holy men praised Kusi and Lava’s performance: “What beautiful music! What sweet verses! Even though these events happened long ago, it feels like we’re witnessing them now.” The brothers sang in perfect harmony and high pitch, blending their voices with the music’s notes and captivating everyone. The sages, proud of their discipline, continued to applaud them as they sang. Some in the audience, delighted by the performance, gave them gifts: a water pitcher, a bark robe, a dark deer skin, a sacred thread, a kamandalu (water pot), a belt made of sacred grass, a vrishi (staff), and a kaupina (loincloth). Others gave an axe, a red cloth, thread for tying hair, twine for bundling wood, a sacrificial pot, firewood, or a seat made of fig wood. Some called out “Swasti!” (blessings), others wished them long life, and all the ascetics offered their heartfelt blessings. The sages said, “This story is wonderful! And your singing is so skillful and moving—it delights our ears and hearts and will inspire poets for generations.” The brothers, now famous, were seen one day by Rāma, Bharata’s elder brother, as they sang in a street of Ayodhyā lined with a few stalls. Drawn to their performance, Rāma invited Kusi and Lava to his palace, honoring them as they deserved. He sat on a throne of gleaming gold, surrounded by his brothers and counselors, and admired the brothers’ handsome appearance and modesty. Turning to Lakshmana, Bharata, and Satrughna, he said, “Listen to this story, composed with great skill and meaning, sung by these inspired performers.” With Rāma’s order, the brothers began to sing. Their music sent shivers down the listeners’ spines and captivated every heart, their voices as clear and moving as a Vina. The entire hall was enchanted by their song. Rāma remarked, “Although these two look like ascetics devoted to penance, they also have the marks of royalty. And besides, the story they sing brings honor to my name. So listen carefully to this important history!” At Rāma’s command, Kusi and Lava continued their chanting in the traditional Marga style. Rāma, sitting at the center of his court, was completely absorbed by the music, eager to see his own story live on forever.
SECTION V

The epic of the Ramayana tells the story of a legendary line of kings, starting with Prajapati and founded by Ikshwaku, who ruled over the earth like no other rulers before them. Among their descendants was Sagara, famous for digging the ocean, who was once followed by his sixty thousand sons on a great journey. Now, we will recount the entire history of that dynasty from its beginning. Please listen carefully and with open minds to this story, which brings virtue, wisdom, and joy.

On the banks of the Sarayu River, there was a rich and thriving land called Kosala, known for its abundance of crops and wealth. The people there lived happy lives. Its capital city was Ayodhya, renowned among men, and said to have been founded by Manu himself, the greatest of men. This impressive and beautiful city stretched twelve yojanas long and ten yojanas wide, with wide, well-planned roads running through it. The streets, scattered with flower petals and sprinkled with water, looked especially lovely. King Dasharatha, who ruled from Ayodhya, brought prosperity to many kingdoms and was as powerful as the king of the gods. The city had strong doors and gates, neat rows of shops, all kinds of weapons and tools, and was home to every type of craftsman. It was filled with poets and historians who praised the city’s greatness. Magnificent buildings rose above the city, topped with flags and guarded by hundreds of powerful weapons called Sataghnis. There were theaters for women, lush gardens, and mango groves, all enclosed by sturdy walls. A deep moat surrounded Ayodhya, making it impossible for friend or enemy to enter easily. The city was full of elephants, horses, cows, camels, and donkeys. Kings from neighboring lands came to pay tribute, and merchants from distant countries filled the markets. Palaces shone like mountains covered in jewels, and there were beautiful places for the royal women to enjoy themselves—Ayodhya was as splendid as Indra’s heavenly city, Amaravati. The city was a dazzling sight, shining with gold decorations, crowded with courtesans, overflowing with treasures, and filled with royal halls. Rice and grain were plentiful, and the water was as sweet as sugarcane juice. The air echoed with the sounds of drums, stringed instruments, and songs. This city was the finest place on earth, almost like a flying palace won by the Siddhas through intense meditation, and was full of the best people. King Dasharatha filled Ayodhya with thousands of expert warriors—Maharathas—who were quick, skilled, and strong enough to fight and kill wild lions, tigers, and boars in the forest. Yet these warriors would never attack anyone who was helpless, abandoned, hiding, or running away. Most of all, the city was home to excellent Brahmanas, who kept the sacred fires burning, were wise, generous, truthful, and deeply spiritual—true experts in the Vedas and Vedangas, and as noble as great sages.
SECTION VI

In the great city of Ayodhyā lived King Daçarātha, a ruler deeply knowledgeable in the Vedas. He had every resource at his command, was wise and powerful, and beloved by both city dwellers and villagers. Born into the Ikshwāku dynasty, Daçarātha was a master charioteer (“Athiratha”), performed grand sacrifices, and strictly followed his royal duties. He had remarkable self-control, like a great sage, and his reputation spread across all three worlds. As a king, he was strong, destroyed his enemies, had loyal friends, and kept his senses in check. Daçarātha’s wealth and treasures matched those of gods like Indra (Sakra) and Kubera (Vaisravana), and he protected his people just as Manu, the legendary lawgiver, had done before him. Like Indra ruling over Amarāvati, Daçarātha governed Ayodhyā with unwavering commitment to duty, prosperity, and happiness, making it the finest of cities.

The people of Ayodhyā were happy, virtuous, well-educated, and content with what they had. Greed was unknown, and truthfulness was a common trait. In this exceptional city, everyone enjoyed plenty—no one lacked food, money, or possessions. Every household was well-stocked with horses, cattle, grain, and wealth. Nowhere in Ayodhyā would you find people obsessed with desire, unattractive, dishonest, uneducated, or without faith. Both men and women had good character, self-control, and cheerful spirits. Their work and behavior were pure, resembling that of holy sages. They wore earrings, tiaras, and garlands, and truly enjoyed life’s pleasures. Personal cleanliness was important; people bathed and perfumed themselves, ate clean food, gave generously, wore jewelry like armlets (Angadas), necklaces (Nishkas), and other ornaments, all while keeping their passions in check.

No one in Ayodhyā neglected the sacred fire or skipped religious rituals. There were no mean-spirited, thieving, or dishonest people, and everyone came from respectable families. The Brāhmanas (priests and scholars), calm and self-disciplined, were devoted to their duties: giving charity, studying the scriptures, and accepting gifts thoughtfully. None of them was faithless, dishonest, uneducated, critical of others, or incompetent. Every Brāhmana was thoroughly trained in the Vedas and Vedāngas, practiced vows, gave generously, and was neither timid, insane, nor troubled.

Every man and woman in Ayodhyā was graceful and attractive, and all showed respect to their king. The four social classes flourished, led by the Brāhmanas. People honored the gods and their guests, showed gratitude, were generous, brave, and capable. Most people lived long lives, stayed true to their duties, and lived surrounded by children, grandchildren, and spouses. The Kshatriyas (warriors) respected the Brāhmanas, the Vaicyas (merchants) followed the Kshatriyas, and the Sudras (workers) faithfully served the other three classes.

The city was expertly managed by Daçarātha, the best of the Ikshwāku line, just as the wise Manu had ruled before. Like a lion-filled mountain cave, Ayodhyā was packed with fierce, well-trained warriors, disciplined and highly educated. The city was famous for its extraordinary horses, imported from places like Kāmvoja, Vāhlika, Vanāyu, and the banks of the Sindhu river—horses as fine as Indra’s own. There were also powerful elephants from the Vindhya and Himavat mountains, strong and massive as hills. These included the Bhadra, Mandra, and Mriga breeds, as well as mixed breeds, all superior and as impressive as Airavata, the legendary elephant. The elephants also came from famous bloodlines like Mahāpadma, Anjana, and Vāmana, each as mighty as a mountain.

Ayodhyā itself stretched for over two yojanas (a considerable distance), truly living up to its name—“the unconquerable.” King Daçarātha, powerful and respected, ruled firmly, protecting the city just as the Moon influences the stars. Like Indra, Daçarātha governed Ayodhyā with its strong gates and locks, impressive buildings, and thriving crowds, making it a truly magnificent city.
SECTION VII

After hearing the request from the greatest of the gods, Vishnu—the one who knows everyone’s hearts—even though he already knew how Rāvana would be defeated, spoke gently to the gods: “Tell me, gods, how should I destroy Rāvana, the king of the Rākshasas? What’s the best way for me to take down this enemy of the sages?” The gods replied to Vishnu, who never ages or weakens, “Take on a human form and fight Rāvana in battle! For a long time, he performed intense penances until Brahmā, the creator, was pleased with him. Brahmā gave Rāvana a boon: that no creature except man could harm him. When the boon was given, Rāvana didn’t even consider humans a threat. Now, proud because of Brahmā’s gift, Rāvana terrorizes the three worlds and kidnaps women by force. That’s why we believe only a man can end him.” After hearing the gods’ words, Vishnu decided to be born as the son of King Daçarātha. At that time, King Daçarātha, powerful and undefeated in battle, was desperately hoping for sons and was performing a special sacrifice to gain children. Having made his decision, Vishnu bowed to Brahmā and then disappeared, honored by the gods and great sages.

At that moment, from the sacrificial fire that King Daçarātha had lit for his ceremony, a huge and powerful being emerged, holding a large golden bowl with a silver lid. The bowl was filled with divine Pāyasa (a kind of sweet rice pudding), shining like creation itself. This being was massive, covered in dark skin and wearing a red robe, with a fierce face, hair like a lion’s mane, and an impressive beard and head of hair. He was decorated with heavenly jewelry, looked as strong as a mountain, and glowed like the sun or fire. He stared straight at Daçarātha and spoke: “O King, I am a messenger sent by Prajāpati.” Hearing this, Daçarātha pressed his palms together in respect and asked, “Lord, you are welcome here. How can I serve you?” The messenger replied, “O King, because you have honored the gods, you have earned this today. Take this sacred Pāyasa, prepared by the gods, which will grant you sons, health, and prosperity. Give it to your worthy wives and tell them to eat it. Through them, you will have the sons you have wished for.” Daçarātha said, “So be it,” and joyfully placed the golden bowl on his head. He bowed to the divine messenger and, overcome with happiness, walked around him again and again in respect. With the Pāyasa in his hands, Daçarātha felt as lucky as a poor man who suddenly becomes rich. The radiant messenger, having finished his task, vanished on the spot. The king’s palace glowed with happiness, like the night sky brightened by the autumn moon.

Then Daçarātha went to his wives’ quarters and spoke to Kausalya: “Take this Pāyasa—it will help you bear a son.” He gave her a portion, then gave a quarter of it to Sumitrā. Next, he gave Kaikeyi an equal share of what was left. After thinking for a moment, he gave the last portion to Sumitrā again. In this way, the king divided the divine Pāyasa among all his wives. The queens were overjoyed and felt deeply honored to receive it. After each of the king’s wives ate her share, they soon became pregnant and later gave birth to children who shone like fire or the sun. Seeing his wives expecting children, Daçarātha’s heart was filled with joy—just as Indra, king of the gods, feels when worshipped by the Siddhas and sages.
SECTION XVII

After Vishnu agreed to be born as the son of the great king, Brahma (the self-born Lord) spoke to the gods. He said, “To help the brave Vishnu—who always keeps his promises and works for the good of us all—you should create powerful beings. Make them able to change shape, skilled in illusions, courageous, fast as the wind, wise about right and wrong, intelligent, and as strong as Vishnu himself. They must be impossible to kill, know all about war and peace, have excellent bodies, able to resist any weapon, and look like immortals. Take the best Apsaras, Gandharbis, Yakshis, Panagis, Rikshis, Vidyadharis, Kinnaris, and Vanaris, and from their bodies, create sons in the form of monkeys.” Brahma added, “Earlier, I created the great bear Jambavan, who appeared from my mouth when I yawned.”

Hearing Brahma’s command, the gods started creating sons in monkey-shapes. Holy sages, Siddhas, Vidyadharas, Uragas, and Charanas also produced strong sons who would become forest wanderers. Indra created Vali, the greatest of monkeys, as his son—Vali was as mighty as the Mahendra mountain. The Sun god had Sugriva as his son. Brihaspati fathered Tara, a powerful and intelligent monkey. Kubera, the god of wealth, had the handsome Gandhamadana. Vishwakarma, the divine craftsman, created Nala. Agni, the fire god, had Nila, who shone like fire and was even more energetic, powerful, and famous than Agni himself. The beautiful Ashwins (twin gods) had Mainda and Dvivida. Varuna fathered Sushena. Parjanya fathered Sarava, who was extremely strong. The Wind god had Hanuman as his son—Hanuman had a body as tough as diamond, could move as fast as Garuda (the legendary eagle), and was the smartest and most powerful of all the monkeys.

Suddenly, thousands of mighty bears, monkeys, and Gopuchchhas (tail-monkeys) appeared. They had incredible strength, could change their forms, and had bodies as massive as elephants or mountains. All of them were meant to help defeat Ravana, the Ten-headed demon king. Each son of the gods looked and acted like his divine father. Some Golangulas (another monkey clan) were even stronger than the gods themselves. Gods, great sages, Gandharvas, Tarkshyas, famous Yakshas, Nagas, Kimpurushas, Siddhas, Vidyadharas, Uragas, and more all created thousands of monkeys through Rikshis and Kinnaris. The main Apsaras, Vidyadharis, daughters of the Nagas, and Gandharbis gave birth (through the Charanas) to heroic monkeys with huge bodies, who roamed the forests eating fruit and roots.

All these monkeys were incredibly strong and could change shape or travel anywhere they wanted. They were as bold and fierce as lions and tigers, both in attitude and strength. They could fight using rocks and even throw mountains. They fought with their claws and teeth and were skilled with any weapon. They could move entire mountains, crush massive trees, and even trouble the ocean with their force. They could split the earth with a kick, swim across the sea, leap into the sky, and catch clouds. They could subdue wild forest elephants and make birds fall from the sky with their roars. In this way, millions of powerful leaders of monkey-herds came into being, able to take any form. These mighty monkeys became the chiefs of the main monkey-herds, and they, in turn, fathered more heroic monkeys—future leaders themselves.

Some of these monkeys lived on the peaks of the Rikshavana mountain, while others made their homes on different mountains and in forests. All the leaders of the monkey-herds stuck together—especially around the brothers Sugriva (son of the Sun god) and Vali (son of Indra), and also with Nala, Nila, Hanuman, and other top monkey chiefs. With the strength of Garuda and expert fighting skills, they roamed about, defeating lions, tigers, and giant serpents (Uragas). Vali, with his massive arms and unmatched strength, protected the Rikshas, Gopuchchhas, and monkeys with his power.

The earth—covered in mountains, forests, and oceans—became crowded with these heroic monkey-lords, each living in different places, marked by their unique features, looking like clouds or mountain peaks, and possessing terrifying strength and appearances. All of this happened so they could be ready to help Rama when the time came.
SECTION XVIII

After King Dasaratha’s grand horse-sacrifice was finished, the gods accepted their offerings and returned to their own realms. Dasaratha, having completed all the rituals, went back to his palace with his entourage. The visiting kings were honored by Dasaratha and, full of joy, returned to their own lands after paying their respects to the sage Rishyashringa. The royal armies, dressed in shining clothes, looked impressive as they headed home. Once the visiting kings had left, Dasaratha entered his palace again, led by the foremost of priests. Rishyashringa, honored and accompanied by his wife Shanta, left with the king’s blessings. Now that his purpose was achieved, Dasaratha settled into palace life, eagerly awaiting the birth of sons.

Six seasons passed after the sacrifice. Then, in the twelfth month, on the ninth day under the Punarvasu star, when the Sun, Moon, Saturn, Jupiter, and Venus were aligned in Aries, Capricorn, Libra, Cancer, and Pisces, and as Jupiter rose with the Moon in Cancer, Kausalya gave birth to Rama—the future lord of the world, adored by all, descended from Ikshvaku, and blessed with divine features. He was half the essence of Vishnu, known for his righteousness, rosy eyes, powerful arms, red lower lip, and voice like a drum. After Rama’s birth, Kausalya glowed with pride, just like Aditi after bearing Indra. Soon after, Kaikeyi had a son, Bharata, who was virtuous and held a quarter of Vishnu’s essence. Then Sumitra gave birth to twins: Lakshmana and Shatrughna, both heroic and skilled in weapons, each carrying a quarter of Vishnu’s power. Bharata was born under the Pushya star with the Sun in Pisces, while Sumitra’s twins were born under the Aslesha star with the Sun in Cancer.

So, four noble sons were born to the king—handsome, virtuous, and as radiant as the stars. In celebration, the Gandharvas sang, the Apsaras danced, celestial drums sounded, and flowers rained down from the sky. The people of Ayodhya held grand festivals. The streets filled with entertainers and dancers, glittering with jewels and echoing with music. Dasaratha gave generous gifts to bards, historians, and singers, and donated thousands of cows to Brahmins.

On the eleventh day after their births, the king held the naming ceremony for his sons. Sage Vasishtha, full of joy, gave them their names: the eldest was Rama, Kaikeyi’s son was Bharata, and Sumitra’s sons were Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Dasaratha fed Brahmins and both country and city folk, and gave away many jewels. This was how he celebrated his sons’ births. Among the princes, Rama—like a comet in the sky—was especially loved by his father and admired by all, almost as if he were the creator himself. All four brothers mastered the Vedas, were brave, cared for others, and possessed many virtues. Rama, especially, was a paragon of truth and purity, and desired by all like the full moon. He could ride elephants and horses and was skilled with chariots. He constantly trained in weaponry and always served his father. From a young age, Lakshmana was deeply attached to Rama, following him everywhere and putting Rama’s needs above his own. Lakshmana wouldn’t sleep or eat treats unless Rama did so with him. Whenever Rama went hunting on horseback, Lakshmana followed, bow in hand, ready to protect him. Likewise, Shatrughna grew inseparable from Bharata, loving him as much as his own life.

Because of his exceptional sons, Dasaratha felt overwhelming joy, like Brahma rejoicing over the gods. As the princes grew in wisdom, virtue, modesty, and fame, Dasaratha became prouder and happier, like the lord of creation himself. The brothers kept up their Vedic studies, mastered archery, and always looked after their father.

One day, as the wise King Dasaratha sat with his priests and friends, thinking about his sons’ marriages, the powerful sage Vishwamitra arrived. Wanting to see the king, Vishwamitra told the palace guards, “Tell the king that I, son of Gadhi and descendant of the Kusika line, am here.” The guards rushed to the king’s chambers and told Dasaratha of the sage’s arrival. Delighted, Dasaratha gathered his priests and hurried out to welcome Vishwamitra, just as Indra would greet his teacher Brihaspati. The king greeted the radiant sage with the traditional offering of water. Vishwamitra accepted the greeting and asked Dasaratha about his wellbeing and the wellbeing of his kingdom. The sage asked about the treasury, the provinces, and whether Dasaratha’s friends were at peace. He inquired, “Are your commanders obedient, have you defeated your enemies, and are you performing your duties to gods and men?” Vishwamitra also greeted Vasishtha and the other sages, showing them respect. After being welcomed properly, the guests entered the palace and took their seats according to rank. Dasaratha, overjoyed, honored Vishwamitra and said, “Your visit is like finding nectar, or rain after a drought, like a child to one who has none, or the recovery of a lost treasure—truly, it is a moment of great happiness for me. Sage, you are most welcome. Tell me your heart’s desire. What can I do to please you? You are worthy of my best service, and I am lucky to have you here. My life feels fulfilled because of your visit. Just seeing you makes this day auspicious. First, you earned the title of Rajarshi through your penance, and now you are a Brahmarshi. You deserve every honor from me. Your visit is truly special, and seeing you makes me feel blessed. Please tell me your wish and the reason for your visit. I want nothing more than to serve you. Don’t hesitate; I will do everything you ask. Your presence brings me fortune and merit.” Hearing these sincere and heartfelt words, the great sage Vishwamitra, virtuous and accomplished in every way, felt deeply pleased.
SECTION XIX

When King Dasaratha heard these shocking words, he was stunned. The powerful sage Viswamitra, clearly moved, replied, “O greatest of kings, descended from a famous line and guided by Vasishtha, only you could respond this way. Now, please consider carefully what I’m about to ask, and stand by your promise. I am preparing for an important sacrifice, following all the rituals. But two Rakshasas—Maricha and Suvahu—who can change their forms at will, have made it their mission to ruin the ceremony. Just as the sacrifice is about to be completed, these two, skilled in battle and full of strength, throw flesh and blood onto the altar, spoiling everything. When they disrupt the ritual like this, all my hard work is wasted, and I was so disheartened that I left my country. I can’t use my anger against them, because it’s not right for someone performing a sacred ritual to curse others. That's why, O king, I ask you to let your eldest son, the brave Rama, come with me. With his great strength and his legendary side-locks, Rama—protected by me—has the divine power to defeat those Rakshasas. I promise I will bless him in many ways, and he will earn the respect of all three worlds. When they face Rama, Maricha and Suvahu won’t be able to stand against him. No one else can defeat them. Their arrogance has led them to their doom, and truly, they are no match for Rama. Don’t let your fatherly love hold you back. Rama only needs to stay with me for ten nights, just to destroy those enemies of my sacrifice. Believe me, you can already count those Rakshasas as dead. I know exactly how powerful Rama is, and Vasishtha and these other sages do too. If you wish for virtue and lasting fame, then grant me Rama. And, Kākutstha (that’s you, descendant of Kakutstha), if your advisors and the Brahmanas led by Vasishtha agree, then please send Rama with me. That is my only request—and after all, he’s old enough now. So, let your lotus-eyed son Rama go with me for these ten days of the sacrifice. Please make sure he leaves in time for the ceremony, and don’t let yourself be overtaken by sadness. Good luck to you—don’t grieve.”

After saying all this, Viswamitra, strong in both mind and body, fell silent. King Dasaratha listened to these words, which were full of both righteousness and self-interest, but they filled him with overwhelming sorrow. He shook with grief and confusion. Trying to regain his composure, Dasaratha stood up, but anxiety and fear weighed him down. The sage’s words pierced his heart and mind, and the great king sat stricken with sorrow, shaking where he sat.
SECTION XX

When Viswāmitra finished speaking, King Daśaratha was so shocked that he couldn’t react at first. Once he regained his composure, he said, “My son Rāma (Ram) is barely sixteen years old. I just don’t think he’s ready to fight Rākshasas (demons) in battle. I am the king of this entire Akshaukini army. Let me take my soldiers and fight the night-stalking demons myself. My men are brave, well-trained, and skilled with weapons—they can handle the Rākshasas. Please, don’t take Rāma. I’ll go myself, leading the army from the front, and fight the night-rangers as long as I am alive. That way, your sacrifice will be protected and nothing will get in the way. So let me go instead; there’s no need to take Rāma. He’s still young, inexperienced, and doesn’t really understand his own strength yet. He hasn’t learned the art of war, and he’s not skilled in battle. He’s no match for the Rākshasas, who are treacherous fighters. Honestly, I wouldn’t survive a moment if you took Rāma away from me. So please, don’t ask for him. If you really must take Rāma, then at least take me and my fourfold army along with you! O son of Kuçika, I’m sixty thousand years old, and after all those years of struggle, I finally have Rāma—please, don’t take him from me now. Of my four sons, Rāma is my firstborn and the one I love most—he’s the most virtuous too. That’s why I can’t let you take him. Tell me: what kind of power do these Rākshasas have? Who are they? What do they look like? Who protects them? How could Rāma, or my army, or even I myself possibly defeat these cunning demon warriors in battle? Please, great sage, tell me—if they’re as strong as you say, how could I ever hope to fight them?”

Hearing all this, Viswāmitra replied, “There is a Rākshasa named Rāvana, born from the Pulastya lineage. He received a boon from Brahmā, and now he stands against all three worlds, supported by countless Rākshasas. He’s incredibly strong and powerful. I’ve also heard that this lord of the Rākshasas is the brother of Vacravana and the son of the sage Vicravan. Rāvana himself doesn’t usually disturb the sacrifices, but he sends two powerful Rākshasas—Mārich and Suvāhu—to ruin the rituals on his orders.”

After hearing this, the king answered, “I can’t stand up to someone so wicked in battle. So, please, wise sage, protect my son! I am a man of little fortune, and you are my guide and my hope. Even the gods, demons, gandharvas, birds, and snakes can’t face Rāvana in battle—so how could a human? He drains even the strongest of their power in a fight. I can’t fight him or his forces. And, great sage, even if you take my son or my army, you won’t be able to defeat him. How can I give you my son, who is still so young and innocent, and knows nothing of war? I simply can’t do it. The sons of Sunda and Upasunda are like Death itself on the battlefield—they’re the ones ruining your sacrifice. That’s why I can’t let you take Rāma. Mārich and Suvāhu are both powerful and skilled with weapons. But if you insist, I’ll go to face them with my friends. If you won’t accept this, then please, I beg you, let it go!”

When Daśaratha finished speaking, Kuçika’s son, the great sage Viswāmitra, was overcome with anger. His fury burned like a blazing fire fed by ghee and wood.
SECTION XXI

When Daçarātha finished speaking, his voice trembling with emotion, Viçwāmitra (Kuçika’s son) grew furious. He glared at the king and said, “You made me a promise, but now you’re trying to back out. That’s not worthy of a descendant of Raghu, and it could bring ruin to your family. If you really think you’re doing the right thing, fine—I’ll just go back to where I came from. O descendant of Kākuthstha, if you’re going to break your word, then enjoy your life surrounded by your friends.” As Viçwāmitra’s anger grew, the whole earth seemed to shake. Even the gods were afraid.

Just then, Vasishtha, the wise and calm sage known for his strict discipline, stepped in. Realizing that the whole world was on edge, he spoke to Daçarātha: “You were born into the Ikshwāku line, and you’re the very picture of virtue. You’re patient, lucky, and you always follow your vows—you shouldn’t give up on what’s right. The world knows the descendants of Raghu as righteous. Don’t stop keeping your promises now; it would be wrong. If you say, ‘I’ll do it,’ but then don’t follow through, all the good you’ve done—digging wells, performing sacrifices—will mean nothing. So, you need to let Rāma go.

Whether or not he’s skilled in weapons, the Rākshasas can’t touch him as long as Kuçika’s son protects him, just like fire can’t burn nectar. Rāma is the living embodiment of virtue and the best among warriors. He outshines everyone in knowledge and is the model of spiritual discipline. He knows all the weapons in the three worlds—those that move and those that don’t—but no one else knows this about him, and they never will. Not the gods, not the sages, not the immortals, not the Rākshasas, not even the top Gandharvas, Yakshas, Kinnaras, or the powerful serpent spirits.

Back when Kuçika’s son ruled his kingdom, Shiva gave him the legendary weapons known as the sons of Kricācwa. These weapons were actually the children of Prajāpati’s daughters—each one dazzling and terrifying in a different way. Two daughters of Daksha, Jayā and Suprabhā, created a hundred brilliant weapons. Thanks to a boon, Jayā had fifty sons with unimaginable strength who could turn invisible and wipe out armies of demons. Suprabhā had fifty sons called Sanhāras—unstoppable, deadly weapons. Kuçika’s son knows all about these weapons. He also has the power to create new ones.

And, O descendant of Raghu, there’s nothing in the past, present, or future that this great ascetic doesn’t know. That’s how powerful and famous Viçwāmitra is. So, King, you shouldn’t hesitate to let Rāma go. Viçwāmitra could defeat the Rākshasas himself; he’s only asking for your son because it will be good for Rāma.

After hearing Vasishtha’s speech, Daçarātha—the greatest of the Raghus—was deeply relieved and happy. He started to feel good about Rāma’s journey and began thinking seriously about entrusting his son to Kuçika’s son.
SECTION XXII

After Vasishtha finished speaking, King Dasharatha, smiling warmly, called for Rama and Lakshmana. Once all the necessary rituals had been carried out by Rama’s parents and the priest Vasishtha had chanted the sacred mantras, King Dasharatha, beaming with pride, kissed Rama on the head and handed him over to Vishwamitra (Viçwāmitra). In that moment, a gentle, dust-free breeze began to blow, as if the universe itself was pleased to see lotus-eyed Rama entrusted to Vishwamitra. As they prepared to leave, flowers rained down from above, and the air was filled with the sound of heavenly drums and the loud blasts of conch shells.

Vishwamitra led the way, followed closely by Rama—famous for his side-locks and carrying his bow. Lakshmana, the son of Sumitra, came right behind him. Both brothers had quivers and bows, looking fierce and graceful, almost like three-headed serpents, and they followed Vishwamitra just as the Ashvin twins are said to follow the Creator himself. Rama and Lakshmana, glowing with youthful energy and perfect in form, walked behind the sage, their presence lighting up the path. They looked like Skanda and Visakha accompanying the mysterious god Shiva (Sthānu). Beautiful, strong, and dressed in ornaments, they held their bows and curved swords, their fingers covered in protective animal skin, making Vishwamitra look even more impressive as they accompanied him.

After traveling about half a yojana (about four miles), they reached the right bank of the Sarayu River. There, Vishwamitra turned to Rama and said kindly, “Rama, my boy, take some water now—don’t delay. I’m going to teach you the mantras Bala and Atibala. With these, you’ll never feel tired, sick, or even look weary. Even if you fall asleep or let your guard down, no Rakshasa (demon) will be able to catch you off guard. Your strength will become unmatched—not just in this world, but in all three worlds. No one will equal you. So, Rama, start reciting Bala and Atibala. Once you’ve learned them, no one will be your match—not in luck, talent, wisdom, quick thinking, or debate. Bala and Atibala are the roots of all knowledge. If you chant them as you travel, you won’t feel hungry or thirsty, my dear Raghu. They’ll bring you fame across the earth. These powerful sciences are the daughters of the Creator himself, and I want to give them to you because you have all the right qualities. Don’t doubt yourself. If you treat learning them like practicing meditation, they’ll bring you endless benefits.”

Rama, cheerful and respectful, sipped the water and, after purifying himself, learned the mantras from the calm and wise sage. Armed with this new power, Rama shone even more brilliantly, like the autumn sun blazing with a thousand rays.

Afterward, Rama paid all the proper respects to Vishwamitra as his spiritual teacher. That night, the three of them rested happily by the banks of the Sarayu. Even though Rama and Lakshmana, sons of Dasharatha, slept on a rough bed of grass, Vishwamitra’s kind words made the night pass pleasantly for them.
SECTION XXIII

When night ended, the powerful sage Viśvāmitra spoke to Rāma, who was lying on a bed of leaves. “Rāma, best son of Kausalyā, it’s time for the morning prayers. Get up! You should perform your purification rituals and meditate on the gods.” Hearing the sage’s advice, Rāma and Lakshmana, both brave and disciplined, washed, offered Arghya (a ritual offering of water), and began to chant the Gāyatri mantra. After finishing their daily duties, the two brothers greeted Viśvāmitra, who valued his ascetic life above all else, and stood ready to continue their journey. As they traveled, they arrived at the bright confluence where the Sarayu and the Ganga rivers met, and saw a magnificent river flowing in three branches. Nearby was a sacred hermitage where ascetics had practiced intense meditation and self-control for thousands of years. Seeing this holy place, Rāma and Lakshmana, both descendants of the Raghu line, were overjoyed and asked Viśvāmitra, “Whose hermitage is this? Who lives here? Please tell us, we really want to know.” Smiling, the wise sage replied, “Listen, Rāma, and I’ll tell you about the origins of this hermitage. Once, Kandarpa—better known as Kāma, the god of love—was born on earth. At the same time, the god Sthānu (another name for Shiva) was doing intense meditation here, following strict rules, accompanied by the wind gods, the Maruts. Kāma, acting recklessly, tried to disturb Shiva’s meditation. Enraged, Shiva (also called Rudra) let out a fierce roar and stared at Kāma. Instantly, Kāma’s entire body was burned away by Shiva’s anger. Since then, Kāma has existed without a physical form and is sometimes called Ananga, which means ‘bodiless.’ The land where this happened is called Anga. This hermitage belongs to Shiva, and the ascetics here have been his devoted followers for generations. They are untouched by sin. Rāma, let’s spend the night here among these sacred rivers. We can cross over tomorrow. Come, let’s purify ourselves and enter this holy place. It’s the perfect spot for us to rest—tonight we’ll bathe, chant mantras, and offer fire oblations before settling in, Rāma.”

While they were talking, the ascetics living in the hermitage became aware of their arrival through their deep spiritual insight, and were filled with joy. They welcomed Viśvāmitra (the son of Kuśika) with water for washing his feet and the ritual Arghya, offering him all the traditional signs of hospitality. Then they welcomed Rāma and Lakshmana as well. After enjoying the warm reception, the brothers and their hosts engaged in friendly conversation. As evening came, the ascetics gathered their focus and chanted their prayers. The brothers were shown their sleeping spots, along with other ascetics who kept strict vows. That night, everyone rested comfortably in the welcoming hermitage. Viśvāmitra, wise and kind, entertained the two young princes with stories and conversation, making the evening pleasant and memorable.
SECTION XXIV

The next morning was clear and bright. Rama and Lakshmana, along with Vishwamitra (Viçwāmitra)—who had already finished his morning rituals—walked to the riverbank. The other ascetics, who were also observing their vows, brought a well-made boat and spoke to Vishwamitra: “Please, board the boat with the princes leading the way! May your journey go well—let’s not waste any time!” Vishwamitra replied, “Very well,” and, after paying his respects to the other ascetics, began to cross the river with Rama and Lakshmana. The river that flows from that pool is the sacred Sarayu, and it passes through Ayodhya. Rama, you should show respect to these rivers with a focused mind.” So Rama and Lakshmana bowed to the waters. They landed on the right bank and continued on their journey at a quick pace. But soon, Rama noticed a terrifying, wild forest ahead and asked Vishwamitra,

“This forest is so dense and full of crickets. I hear all kinds of terrifying animals and birds screeching. There are lions, tigers, boars, and elephants here.
