Long ago, there were two prosperous regions here, called Malada and Karusha. Gods themselves had these places built. After Indra killed the demon Vritra, he was left hungry, stained with filth, and guilty of killing a Brahmin. The gods and holy sages washed Indra here, cleaning away all the dirt from his body. The gods left behind the filth and hunger that had clung to Indra, and they were all very relieved. After he was cleansed, Indra regained his brilliance and no longer felt hunger. Grateful, he blessed this land: ‘Because these two places cleansed my body, they will be known as Malada and Karusha, and they will be famous and prosperous.’ The gods approved, and for a long time, Malada and Karusha thrived, rich in crops and wealth. But then, a Yakshini (female demon) was born, powerful enough to change her form and said to have the strength of a thousand elephants. Her name was Taraka, and she was married to Sunda. Their son is the Rakshasa Maricha, who’s as strong as Indra. Taraka has massive arms, a huge head, an enormous mouth, and a monstrous body. Every day, she terrorizes people. Taraka, cruel and destructive, ruins Malada and Karusha daily. Right now, she’s about half a yojana away, blocking our path. Because this forest belongs to Taraka, you must go there and, using your own strength, destroy this evil being. I’m asking you to free this region from its curse, because no one dares to come near while Taraka is around. Now you know the story of this terrible forest. To this day, Taraka hasn’t stopped her attacks in these lands.”
SECTION XXV

After listening to the powerful sage’s impressive explanation, Rāma (sometimes called Rāghava), who was always eager to learn, replied thoughtfully, “Respected sage, I’ve always heard that Yakshas aren’t very powerful. How is it possible that a woman from their race could have the strength of a thousand elephants?” Viśvāmitra, pleased by Rāma’s respectful question, smiled at both Rāma and Lakshmana and began to explain, “Let me tell you how this woman, Tārakā, gained such frightening strength through a boon.

“In ancient times, there was a mighty Yaksha named Suketu. He was known for his strict spiritual discipline and good character, but he didn’t have any children. After years of difficult prayers, the creator god, Brahmā, was pleased with Suketu and granted him a daughter—a remarkable girl named Tārakā. Brahmā gave Tārakā the strength of a thousand elephants, though he did not grant Suketu a son.

“When Tārakā grew up and became both beautiful and strong, her father married her to Sunda, the son of Jambha. Later, Tārakā had a son named Māricha, who was incredibly powerful but ended up becoming a Rākshasa (demon) because of a curse.

“After Sunda died, Tārakā and her son Māricha targeted the great sage Agastya, seeking revenge. Furious, Tārakā attacked Agastya, trying to eat him. But Agastya, seeing her charge, cursed Māricha, saying, ‘Become a Rākshasa!’ He then cursed Tārakā too, saying, ‘Because you have tried to devour a human in this terrifying form, you will lose your original appearance and become truly monstrous!’

“Driven by rage and the curse, Tārakā now terrorizes this peaceful area where Agastya used to meditate. Rāma, for the sake of the Brahmins and the cows, you must defeat this evil Yakshi (female Yaksha), who uses her power only for destruction. No one else in the three worlds but you has the courage or the ability to face and destroy her, especially now that she’s empowered by the curse.

“You might hesitate to kill a woman, but as a prince, it’s your duty to protect the people—even if that means making tough decisions. Sometimes, rulers must do things that seem harsh or even wrong in order to protect their subjects. This has always been the way for those who govern.

“Rāma, great kings of the past have slain wicked women when necessary. For example, Indra (also called Sakra) once killed Mantharā, the daughter of Virochana, when she tried to destroy the world. Vishnu destroyed the mother of Kāvya—Bhrigu’s wife—when she wanted to wipe out Indra and take over the world. Many other princes and heroes have done the same.

“So, Rāma, let go of any hesitation. As your teacher and guide, I command you: destroy Tārakā for the good of all!”
SECTION XXVI

After hearing the bold challenge from the sage Viśvāmitra, Rāma (Rāghava), son of Daśaratha and true to his word, pressed his palms together in respect and replied, “As my father wished, and to honor his promise, I should do exactly as you ask, O son of Kuśika. While we were still in Ayodhyā, my father Daśaratha—wise and noble—asked me to obey you in front of the holy elders. So I cannot ignore your command. That’s why, following the orders of the sage and my father, I will definitely carry out this task and kill Tārakā. For the sake of the Brāhmaṇas, the cows, and the gods, I’m ready to do whatever you ask, no matter how difficult.” With those words, Rāma, determined to fight, clenched his fist and pulled back his bowstring, making a loud sound that echoed in every direction. The sudden noise frightened all the creatures in Tārakā’s forest, and even Tārakā herself was startled and became furious. Blinded by rage, the demoness rushed in the direction of the sound. When Rāma saw her—a terrifying figure with a monstrous face and massive body—he turned to Lakshmana and said, “Look, Lakshmana, at that horrifying Yakshini! Even brave warriors would be scared just seeing her. She’s powerful and skilled in illusions, but I’ll face her and cut off her ears and nose. Still, I won’t kill her just yet, since she’s a woman and protected for that reason. I only mean to stop her and take away her strength.” As Rāma was speaking, Tārakā, crazed with anger, let out a furious roar and charged at him with her arms raised. Right then, the sage Viśvāmitra shouted back at her, scolding her with a mighty voice.

“Victory and blessings to the sons of Raghu!” Viśvāmitra called out. In response, Tārakā kicked up a huge cloud of dust, confusing both Rāma and Lakshmana. Using her magic, she launched a fierce rain of boulders at them. Rāma grew angry and fought back, shooting arrows to break up the falling rocks. Then, with his arrows, he cut off her hands. As she staggered and roared in pain, Lakshmana (Sumitrā’s son) stepped in and sliced off her ears and nose. Wounded but still dangerous, Tārakā began shifting shapes, vanishing and reappearing to confuse her opponents with her illusions. She raged across the battlefield, hurling more rocks at them. Seeing that Rāma and Lakshmana were being overwhelmed, Viśvāmitra (the wise son of Gadhi) called out, “Rāma, don’t hesitate! This wicked demoness is truly evil, and because of her magic, she’ll only grow stronger as night falls. If you wait until evening, she’ll be impossible to defeat—so you must kill her now!” Following Viśvāmitra’s advice, Rāma showed his skill by aiming at sounds, firing arrows that surrounded Tārakā even as she kept up her barrage. Trapped by Rāma’s arrows, Tārakā, using her remaining powers, charged at Rāma and Lakshmana with a deafening roar. But as she came at them, Rāma shot a powerful arrow straight into her chest, and she collapsed to the ground, dead. Seeing the terrifying demoness defeated, Indra—the thousand-eyed king of the gods—and all the other deities cheered and honored Rāma.

“Well done! Well done!” the gods exclaimed. Pleased, Indra (also called Purandara) and the other delighted gods spoke to Viśvāmitra: “O sage, son of Kuśika, you have our gratitude. All the Maruts and Indra himself are pleased with what Rāma has done. Now, please show your favor to Rāma! Grant him the powerful sons of Prajāpati Kṛcchāśva, full of strength and divine energy. Rāma has followed you faithfully, and he deserves to receive these gifts from you. He has a great destiny ahead, one that will help all the gods.” With these words, the gods paid their respects to Viśvāmitra and, joyful, returned to the heavens.

As evening fell, Viśvāmitra, happy with Tārakā’s defeat, gently touched Rāma’s head and said, “Here, Rāma, let’s spend the night. Tomorrow morning, we’ll continue on to my hermitage.” Rāma, pleased with Viśvāmitra’s words, cheerfully spent the night in Tārakā’s forest. From that day on, the forest, freed from fear, became as beautiful as Chaitraratha itself. Having killed the Yaksha’s daughter, Rāma was praised by the gods and sages. That night, he stayed with the sage, and at dawn, Viśvāmitra woke him to begin the next stage of their journey.
SECTION XXVII

After spending the night, the great sage Viṣvāmitra smiled kindly at Rāghava (Rāma) and spoke: “I am very pleased with you. May good fortune follow you, O famous prince! Because you have impressed me so much, I’m going to give you all the divine weapons that can help you defeat even the gods and asuras, along with their allies among the Gandharvas and Uragas. With these, you’ll be unbeatable in battle. I’ll give you every celestial weapon I possess. Rāghava, I will grant you the powerful Dandachakra, Dharmachakra, and Kalachakra. And, greatest of men, I’ll give you the fierce Vishnu Chakra, the Indra Chakra, Indra’s lightning Vajra, Shiva’s Sulavata, the Brahmāciras weapon, and the Aishika, O mighty descendant of Raghu! I’ll also give you the legendary Brahmā weapon, and, Kākutstha (another name for Rāma), two outstanding maces: the blazing Modaki and Cikhari. 

Rāma, I’ll bestow on you the Dharmapāśa and Kālapāśa nooses, and the powerful Vārunapāśa. Descendant of Raghu, I’ll give you the two Ashanis—Sushka and Ardra—the Pināka, the Nārāyana weapon, the fire-powered Agneya called Sikhara, and the wind-powered Vāyavya called Prathama, sinless one! I will grant you the Hayaciras weapon, the Krauncha weapon, and, Kākutstha, a pair of deadly darts. I’ll also give you the Kankāla, the terrifying Mashaia, Kapāla, and Kinkini—each one designed for destroying Rākshasas. Mighty-armed son of the best of men, I’ll grant you the forceful Vidyādhara weapon, the superb scimitar Nandana, the favorite Gandharva weapon Mohana, and also Praswāpana, Pasamana, and Saumya, Rāghava!

And, best of men, you shall receive the Varshana, Soshana, Santāpana, Vilapana, and the irresistible Mādana (beloved of Kandarpa), plus the powerful Gandharva weapon Mānava, and the Pichāsa weapon, O renowned prince. Mighty Rāma, quickly accept the Tāmasa, the extremely powerful Saumana, the unstoppable Samvarta and Maushala, king’s son, as well as the Satya weapon, the supreme Māyamaya, and the Saura. Take Tejaprabha, which can drain an enemy’s energy, and the Soma, Sisira, Tāshtra, and the terrifying Dāruna weapon belonging to Bhaga, plus Sileshu and Madana—all able to change form at will, all extremely powerful, and highly revered.” 

Then, facing east, Viṣvāmitra—the greatest of sages—purified himself and happily began to teach Rāma the mantras for these weapons. The sage gave Rāghava all the weapons—more than even the gods can handle at once. As Viṣvāmitra chanted the sacred mantras, all those precious weapons appeared before the descendant of Raghu. With joined palms, the weapons addressed Rāma: “We are your servants, O generous Rāghava. Whatever you wish, we will do for you—just command us.” Hearing these words from the powerful weapons, Rāma (Kākutstha), delighted, accepted them. He touched each one and said, “Appear before me whenever I remember you!” 

Then, filled with energy and gratitude, Rāma paid his respects to the mighty sage Viṣvāmitra and prepared to continue their journey.
SECTION XXVIII

After accepting the powerful weapons with a clear mind, Kākutstha (Rāma) continued on his journey, his face calm and confident. He spoke to Viśvāmitra, “Respected sage, I’ve received these incredible weapons that even the gods can’t stop. Now, please teach me how to withdraw or control them.” Hearing this, Viśvāmitra—who was known for his discipline, patience, and pure spirit—taught Rāma the mantras needed to restrain the weapons. He said, “Rāma, take Satyavat, Sataykirti, Dhrishta, Rabhasa, Pratiharatara, Parānmukha, Avānmukha, Lakshya, Alakshya, Drihanābha, Sunābha, Dacāksha, Satavaktra, Dacacirsha, Satodara, Padranābha, Mahānābha, Indunābha, Swanābha, Jyotisha, Sakuna, Nairāshya, Vimala, Yaugandhara, Vindra, the two Daityapramathanas, Suchivāhu, Mahāvāhu, Nishkali, Virucha, Archimāli, Dhritimāli, Vrittimān, Ruchira, Pitrya, Saumansa, Vidhuta, Makara, Karavira, Rati, Dhana, Dhānya, Kāmarupa, Kāmaruchi, Moha, Avarana, Jrimbhaka, Sarpanātha, Panthāna, and Varuna. These are the sons of Kricāswa, Rāma—shining, powerful, and able to change their forms at will. You are worthy to receive them, descendant of Raghu. Good luck to you.”

Overwhelmed with happiness, Kākutstha answered, “Thank you! I accept.” Each weapon appeared with a glowing, almost human form—some looked like burning coals, others like smoke, and some shone like the Sun or the Moon. With hands folded, they spoke to Rāma in sweet voices, “Leader of men, we’re here! Tell us what you want us to do.” Rāma replied, “Go wherever you wish for now. But whenever I remember you and need your help, come to my aid.” After bowing to Rāma and circling him in respect, the weapons answered, “As you command,” and disappeared back to where they’d come from.

Now that he had learned everything about these weapons, Rāghava (Rāma) kept walking and spoke kindly to Viśvāmitra. “What’s that forest near the hill over there? It looks like a bank of clouds. I’m really curious—it’s beautiful, full of animals, peaceful, and the air is filled with birds singing sweetly. We just left a wild, terrifying place, but this area feels so pleasant. I can’t help wondering about it. Tell me, sir, whose hermitage is this? And where exactly is the place where those evil demons who disrupt your sacrifices live? Where should I go to protect your rituals and defeat the Rākshasas? Please, I want to know everything, respected sage.”
SECTION XXIX

After hearing Rāma’s question, Viśvāmitra, full of energy, replied, “Rāma, this is the place where Vishnu—respected by all the gods—practiced intense meditation and self-discipline for countless years and ages. This used to be the hermitage of the great sage Vāmana. Because Vāmana achieved spiritual success here, it became known as Siddhāśrama, the Hermitage of Perfection. At the same time, Virochana’s son, King Vāli, defeated the gods—Indra and the Maruts among them—and took control of all three worlds. Vāli, the powerful leader of the Asuras, began a great sacrifice here. As he performed the sacrifice, the gods, led by Agni, came to Vishnu at this very place and said, ‘Vāli, son of Virochana, is performing a sacrifice. Before he finishes, please act. He always gives whatever is asked of him to anyone who visits. Use your power to take a dwarf form and help us, Vishnu.’ 

Meanwhile, the radiant sage Kasyapa, glowing with spiritual energy, completed a hundred-year vow with the help of the goddess Aditi. Together, they began to praise Vishnu, the destroyer of Madhu, asking him to grant a blessing. Kasyapa said, ‘Through my intense penance, I see you as the embodiment of discipline and sacrifice. Within you, I see the whole universe. You have no beginning, and cannot truly be described. I take refuge in you.’

Vishnu, pleased with Kasyapa, replied, ‘Ask for a boon. I believe you deserve it.’ Kasyapa then said, ‘Aditi, the gods, and I all wish for the same thing: we ask you to be born as our son through Aditi. Please become the younger brother of Indra (Śakra) and help the gods, who are suffering. Let this place be called Siddhāśrama because of your grace. Our work here is complete. Now, please leave this place, Lord of the gods.’

So, Vishnu, with all his power, was born as Aditi’s son. He took the form of a dwarf and went before Virochana’s son, Vāli. He asked for just as much land as he could cover with three steps. Then, for the good of everyone, he grew to cover the whole universe in three strides. By doing this, he stopped Vāli and gave the three worlds back to Indra, putting them under his rule.

This is why Vishnu stayed in this peaceful hermitage. Because I respect the Dwarf form (Vāmana), I also live here. But lately, this place has been attacked by Rākshasas who ruin our rituals. Rāma, this is where you must defeat those evil beings.

Today, I will return to this sacred Siddhāśrama. This hermitage belongs to you just as much as to me, Rāma.” 

After saying this, Viśvāmitra, feeling great joy, took Rāma and Lakshmana with him into the hermitage. They looked striking, like the moon shining clearly after mist clears, with the Punarvasu stars. When the ascetics living in Siddhāśrama saw Viśvāmitra, they stood up in happiness, welcomed him warmly, and offered hospitality to the princes.

After resting for a while, Rāma and Lakshmana, the noble sons of Raghu, folded their hands and said to Viśvāmitra, “Please begin the ceremony today, great sage. May this Siddhāśrama finally achieve its purpose, and may your words come true!”

Encouraged, Viśvāmitra—his mind calm and his senses under control—began the ritual. Rāma and Lakshmana, like the twin gods Kumāras, spent a pleasant night. At dawn, after their morning prayers and reciting sacred mantras with self-discipline, they paid their respects to the sacrificial fire and to Viśvāmitra, who was seated and ready to begin.
SECTION XXX

The princes—Rāma and Lakshmana—who were always alert and aware of their surroundings, spoke to Viśvāmitra (let’s call him "Vishwamitra" for ease), making sure to be respectful. “Respected sage, please tell us when exactly we should be ready to fight those night-stalking demons. We don’t want to miss the right moment!” Hearing their eagerness, the ascetics were pleased and started praising the king’s sons. “For the next six nights, you need to protect us. This sage has begun his sacrifice and must remain silent during the ritual.” Hearing this, Rāma and Lakshmana gave up sleep and guarded the hermitage for six days and nights. Dressed in armor and armed with their bows, the two heroic brothers kept watch over the powerful sage and his fellow ascetics.

When the six days had passed and the sixth night arrived, Rāma turned to Lakshmana, son of Sumitrā, and said, “Get ready and stay sharp!” Feeling the tension and ready for battle, Rāma’s words set the stage. Meanwhile, the priests and spiritual guides prepared the altar, lighting it up with Vishwamitra and the family priests. They set up the altar with sacred grass, ladles, firewood, and flowers, getting everything ready for the ritual.

As the priests started chanting mantras and began the ceremony, a deafening and terrifying noise filled the sky. It was as if, during monsoon season, thick clouds were swarming the sky—but these were the Rākshasas (demons), using their magic to create chaos as they charged in. Mārīcha and Suvāhu, leading their monstrous followers and looking terrifying, began to rain blood down on the altar.

Seeing the altar flooded with blood, Rāma rushed forward and spotted the demons in the sky. As they swooped down, Rāma, his eyes like lotuses, looked at Lakshmana and said, “Look, Lakshmana! With the Mānava weapon, I’ll drive away these wicked, flesh-eating demons, just like the wind blows away clouds. I really don’t want to kill them if I don’t have to.” Saying this, Rāma, descendant of Raghu, loaded his bow with the dazzling, powerful Mānava weapon and fired it at Mārīcha’s chest in a burst of anger.

The weapon struck Mārīcha so hard that he was blasted a hundred yojanas (that’s a huge distance) away and landed in the middle of the ocean, knocked out cold. Seeing Mārīcha spinning helplessly and completely overpowered, Rāma said to Lakshmana, “See, Lakshmana, this Mānava weapon—first used by Manu—knocked him out and threw him far away, but it didn’t kill him! But these other shameless, evil, blood-drinking demons who keep ruining sacrifices—I will finish them off.”

Right after saying this, Rāma showed off his skill by pulling out the powerful Agneya (fire) weapon and shooting it straight at Suvāhu’s chest. The arrow hit, and Suvāhu crashed to the ground, dead. Then, Rāma grabbed the Vāyavya (wind) weapon and unleashed it on the rest of the demons, wiping them out completely and bringing relief to the ascetics.

With all the demons defeated and the sacrifice safe, Rāma was praised by the sages, just like Indra was praised in ancient times after defeating the Asuras. When the ritual had ended, the powerful sage Vishwamitra, seeing the area finally free from demons, said to Rāma, “Mighty-armed one, you made my wish come true and did exactly what your teacher asked. You’ve made this place a true Siddhāśrama.” After praising Rāma, Vishwamitra led Rāma and Lakshmana away so they could perform their evening prayers.
SECTION XXXI

That night, Rāma and Lakshmana, happy that their mission was going well, rested peacefully. When dawn broke, they went together to see the sage Viśvāmitra and the other holy men. After bowing respectfully to Viśvāmitra, who seemed as powerful as blazing fire, they spoke to him with gentle words: “We are here, ready to serve you, greatest of sages. Please tell us what you would like us to do next.” Hearing this, the other great sages, led by Viśvāmitra, replied to Rāma, “King Janaka of Mithilā is about to hold a very important sacrifice. We’re all going there, and you should come with us. While you’re there, you’ll get to see an amazing and legendary bow. Long ago, this bow, which is incredibly powerful and dazzling, was given to King Devarāta by the gods during a ceremony. No one—god, Gandharva, demon, or human—has ever been able to string it. Many kings and princes have tried to test their strength on this bow, but none have succeeded. Kākutstha (that’s you, Rāma), you’ll be able to see this bow, which belongs to the wise King of Mithilā, as well as his incredible sacrifice. The bow, which is very hard to handle, was given to King Janaka by the gods as a reward for his devotion, and now it’s treated like a sacred idol in his palace, worshipped with incense and special offerings.” After explaining all this, Viśvāmitra, with Rāma and the other sages, got ready to leave. Before setting out, he spoke to the forest spirits, saying, “Goodbye! Now that my work here is done, I will leave this Siddhāśrama and head north to the Himalayas, past the river Jāhnavi.” With this, the strong-willed sage, Viśvāmitra (son of Kuśika), and the other holy men, all dedicated to their spiritual path, began their journey northward. As they traveled, a group of Brāhmanas who upheld the Vedas came with them, carrying the supplies for the sacrifice on a hundred carts. Birds and animals who lived in Siddhāśrama also followed Viśvāmitra for a while, as if drawn by his spiritual power. Eventually, he sent the birds back. After a long day’s walk, as the sun was setting, the group of sages stopped to rest on the banks of the river Sona. When night came, they bathed and made offerings into the sacred fire. Then, with Viśvāmitra at the head, the sages sat down together. Rāma and Lakshmana, after showing respect to the holy men, sat down near Viśvāmitra. Rāma, curious by nature, asked the sage, “Respected one, what is this country with its thick forests? Could you please tell me about this place?” Smiling, Viśvāmitra, known for his discipline and wisdom, began to tell the story of the land to Rāma and the other sages.
SECTION XXXN

Long ago, there lived a powerful son of Brahmā named Kuça, known for his intense self-discipline and deep understanding of duty. Kuça was always committed to following his vows and honoring good people. He married Vaidarbhi, a woman from a noble family who possessed all the best qualities. Together, they had four sons—Kucāmva, Kuçanābha, Asurtarajas, and Vasu—each strong, impressive, and much like their father. Wanting to increase their family's honor and earn spiritual merit, Kuça told his honest and noble sons, "My sons, rule kingdoms and earn great merit through your leadership." Obeying their father's words, the four brothers went to establish their own cities and rule as kings. Kucāmva built the city of Kaucāmvi; Kuçanābha founded Mahodaya; Asurtarajas created Dharmāranya; and Vasu established Girivraja, which became a shining capital surrounded by five grand mountains. This city was also called Vasumati, and it belonged to Vasu. The Sumāgadhi River flowed through the land of the Magadhas, winding among the five hills like a garland. This river, O Rāma, belonged to Vasu and traveled east, watering fields rich with crops. Now, Rāma, know that Kuçanābha, who was both a great king and a sage, had a hundred beautiful daughters with Ghritāchi. One day, these daughters, youthful and radiant like flashes of lightning during the rainy season, put on their finest jewelry and went to play in their garden. There they sang, danced, and played music, full of life and joy. Their beauty was unmatched—each daughter was flawless, graceful, and glowing with youth, sparkling among the trees like stars among clouds. As they enjoyed themselves in the garden, the wind, who gives life to all, saw them and spoke:

"I desire you all—become my wives. Leave behind your human forms, and you can live forever. Human youth fades quickly, but if you accept me, your youth will never end and you’ll become immortal." Hearing these words from the ever-energetic Wind, the sisters laughed at him and replied, "You stir the hearts of all living beings, O greatest of the gods—we know your power. But why are you disrespecting us like this? We are the daughters of Kuçanābha, O divine one. Even though you’re a god, we could drive you away if we wanted, but we choose not to, because it would cost us our spiritual merit. May the day never come when, ignoring our father’s wishes, we choose our own husbands on a whim. Our father is our lord and our highest guide. We will only marry the men to whom our father gives us." Hearing this, the Wind, deeply insulted, became furious. He rushed into their bodies and twisted their limbs, leaving them physically broken. The sisters, now deformed and overwhelmed with shame and distress, returned to the palace in tears. When their father, the king, saw his beloved daughters so disfigured and miserable, he was shocked. "My daughters, what’s happened? Who would break all rules of decency like this? Who has done this to you? And why do you only weep, instead of answering me?" With a heavy sigh, the king waited anxiously for them to tell him everything.
SECTION XXXIII

When King Kuçanābha heard his daughters' story, the hundred princesses knelt and touched his feet with their heads. They said, “Father, the god of wind, Vāyu (the Air), tried to force himself on us in a dishonorable way. He didn’t care about what’s right or wrong. We told him that we have a father and can’t make choices about marriage on our own—he should ask you first and only if you agree could he marry us. But he ignored everything we said and, as we spoke, he treated us harshly.” Hearing this, King Kuçanābha, who was wise and deeply spiritual, spoke gently to his beautiful daughters: “You’ve shown incredible patience and self-control, setting an example for others to follow. That you all stood together to protect our family’s honor is truly admirable. Patience is a virtue for everyone—men and women alike—and it’s especially hard to show patience when dealing with gods. May everyone in our family have the same strength as you! Patience is like charity, truth, sacrifice, fame, and virtue itself—the whole world rests on it.” After comforting his daughters, the king, known for his wisdom and strength, began discussing with his advisors the best way to arrange marriages for his daughters, considering the right time, place, and suitable families.

At that time, there was a powerful sage named Chuli, famous for his self-control and pure life, who was deep in meditation. While he practiced his austerities, Somadā, the daughter of Urmilā and a Gandharvi (celestial musician), served him faithfully for a long time. Her humility and devotion pleased Chuli deeply. One day, pleased with her service, the sage said, “I am happy with you. Tell me, what can I do for you?” Realizing her chance, Somadā, who was clever and eloquent, replied sweetly, “You’re full of spiritual power, almost like Brahmā himself. I wish for a righteous son with great spiritual qualities, born through your blessing. I have no husband—I serve you alone. Please grant me such a son by your spiritual means.”

Chuli was pleased and granted her wish, creating an extraordinary son through his spiritual power. The son was named Brahmādatta. Brahmādatta grew up to be a great king and founded the prosperous city of Kampilyā, much like Indra (king of the gods) founded the heavens. Eventually, King Kuçanābha decided to give his hundred daughters in marriage to Brahmādatta. He invited Brahmādatta, who was a powerful ruler, and happily gave him all his daughters. Brahmādatta, who seemed almost godlike, married the princesses one by one.

As soon as Brahmādatta touched each of them, the strange deformity caused by Vāyu disappeared. The hundred daughters were instantly healed, free from pain, and their beauty was unmatched. Seeing his daughters restored and freed from the Air god’s curse, Kuçanābha was overjoyed and celebrated again and again. He then bid farewell to Brahmādatta, his new son-in-law, along with the princesses and the priests. Somadā, Brahmādatta’s mother, was thrilled at her son’s marriage. She hugged her new daughters-in-law over and over, praised her son, and expressed her happiness to everyone.
SECTION XXXIV

“So, Rāghava, after Brahmādatta’s marriage, Kuçanābha, still without a son, decided to perform a special sacrifice to have a male heir. Once the ritual began, Kuça—the noble son of Brahmā—spoke to King Kuçanābha. He said, ‘My son, you will have a righteous heir like yourself. You will have Gādhi, and through him, your name will live on.’ After blessing Kuçanābha, Kuça rose into the sky and returned to Brahmā’s eternal realm. In time, Kuçanābha’s prayers were answered—he had a virtuous son named Gādhi. Kākutstha, that same Gādhi is my father. I, called Kauçika, am descended from Kuça’s line. I also had an older sister named Satyavati, who followed a strict spiritual path and married Richika. She was so devoted that when she died, she ascended directly to heaven in her own body. My generous sister, Kauçiki, eventually transformed into a great river. She became a sacred and beautiful river flowing from the Himavat mountains, bringing blessings to all living beings. Because of my love for her, I have always chosen to live near the Himavat, Rāghava. Satyavati—now known as Kauçiki—is a truly pure and pious river, the holiest of streams. Rāma, I only left her side to come to Siddhāçrama and complete my sacrifice. Thanks to your strength, my wishes have been fulfilled. Now you know my family’s story, my own background, and the history of this place, just as you asked, mighty-armed one. But, Kākutstha, notice how the night has slipped away while I was speaking. You should sleep now, so you’ll be rested for the journey ahead. The trees are still, the animals and birds are quiet, and darkness covers everything. Midnight is passing, and the sky is dotted with stars shining like watchful eyes. The gentle, glowing moon is rising, brightening everyone’s hearts. Now, though, night creatures—fierce Yakshas and Rākshasas—roam about.” 

After finishing his story, the powerful sage Viçwāmitra fell silent. The other ascetics praised him, saying, “Wonderful! The Kuçika family has always been noble and righteous. The descendants of Kuça are wise, and you, Viçwāmitra, shine among them. Your sister, Kauçiki, has brought even more honor to your family.” The respected son of Kuçika, happy with their praise, went to sleep—like the sun setting at day’s end. Rāma and Sumitrā’s son (Lakshmana), after admiring and praising the great sage, also settled down to a peaceful sleep.
SECTION XXXV

After spending the rest of the night with the ascetics on the banks of the Sona River, Vishwamitra (Viçwāmitra) spoke as dawn broke. “Rama, the night is over and morning has come. It’s time for our early rituals. Wake up! Get ready to go.” Rama heard him, completed his morning prayers and rituals, and got ready to leave. He said, “This is the Sona River, with its beautiful, deep waters and little islands. Brahmana, which way should we cross?” Vishwamitra answered, “We’ll take the same path that the great sages use.” They traveled for a long time, and by midday, they reached the famous river Jahnavi (the Ganga), respected by ascetics. The river’s sacred waters, filled with swans and cranes, made the ascetics traveling with Rama very happy. They set up camp on the riverbank. After bathing, making water offerings to the gods and their ancestors, performing fire rituals, and eating ghee as delicious as nectar, the wise and blessed group sat down around Vishwamitra. Rama and his brother (descendants of Raghu) also took their seats in places of honor. Feeling cheerful, Rama said to Vishwamitra, “Respected one, I want to hear how the Ganga, which flows in three directions and touches all three worlds, finally joins the lord of rivers.” Moved by Rama’s curiosity, the powerful ascetic Vishwamitra began to tell the story of Ganga’s origin and journey. “Rama, the great mountain Himavat is like a treasure chest of riches. He had two daughters, both incredibly beautiful. Their mother, Menā, the graceful daughter of Meru, was Himavat’s beloved wife. Their first daughter was Ganga, and their second daughter was Uma. One day, the gods, needing to accomplish some divine mission, asked Himavat for Ganga, the river that flows in three directions. Wanting the best for all three worlds, Himavat gave his daughter Ganga, who can flow anywhere and purifies all living things. The gods, happy to have her, took Ganga to help them. The other daughter, Uma, devoted herself to strict spiritual practices and became rich in ascetic power. Himavat gave Uma—who was known for her fierce spiritual energy and was respected by all—to Rudra (Shiva). These, Rama, are the daughters of the king of mountains: Ganga, the greatest of rivers, and the divine Uma. I have now told you how Ganga, whose waters wash away sin and who flows in three different directions, first reached the sky and then rose to the heavens.”
SECTION XXXVI
After the sage finished speaking, Rāma and Lakshmana bowed respectfully to him and said,

“O Brāhmana, your story was truly inspiring and full of wisdom. Now, please tell us about the elder daughter of the mountain king. You know so much about both gods and humans. Why does she, who purifies the worlds, flow in three different directions? Why is Gangā, the greatest of rivers, known for having three courses? And, wise one, what deeds has she done in the three worlds?” Hearing these questions, Viśvāmitra, whose power comes from his spiritual practice, began to tell Kākutstha (Rāma) the story in the presence of the other sages. “Long ago, Rāma, the blue-throated god Mahādeva (Shiva), after marrying the goddess, began to spend time with her. For a divine hundred years, while Mahādeva and the goddess enjoyed their union, no child was born. The gods, led by Brahmā, became very worried. They wondered, ‘Who could possibly handle the child born from these two?’ So the gods went to Mahādeva, bowed to him, and said, ‘O Lord of Lords, you always care for the worlds. Please listen to our plea. The universe cannot bear the power of your union. For the sake of all three worlds, please practice restraint and channel your energy, together with the goddess, through deep meditation. Please protect us—don’t destroy everything.’

Mahādeva agreed and replied, ‘So be it!’ Then he asked, ‘But tell me, gods, who will bear the force of my energy if I release it?’ The gods answered, ‘Let the Earth bear your energy today.’ Assured by this, Mahādeva released his energy, and the Earth—covered with mountains and forests—was flooded with it. The gods then told the Fire god, ‘You and the Wind must enter this powerful energy.’ When the Wind joined with it, the energy became a bright white hill and a forest of shining reeds, glowing like fire or the sun. From the Fire, Kārtikeya—full of incredible power—was born. The gods and sages, overjoyed, worshipped Umā (the goddess) and Shiva. But then, the daughter of the mountain (Umā) glared at the gods in anger and cursed them: ‘Because you interrupted me and Mahādeva as we tried to have a child, you will not be able to have children with your own wives. From now on, your wives will remain childless.’ She also cursed the Earth, saying, ‘O Earth, you will take on many forms, and many will rule over you! Because you denied me a child, you will never feel the happiness of having a child yourself, and you will suffer because of my anger!’ Seeing the gods so troubled, the Lord of the Gods (Indra) left for the direction ruled by Varuna. Mahādeva and the goddess then went to the northern side of the great mountain and began practicing severe austerities on the peak called Himavatprabhava.

Now, Rāma, I’ve told you how the daughter of the mountain (Gangā) became spread out like this. Listen closely with Lakshmana, and I’ll tell you the story of Bhāgirathi’s great power.”
SECTION XXXVII

While the powerful being was deep in meditation, the gods—led by Indra and Agni—came to the Grandfather of all (the Grandsire, Brahmā), hoping to win over the future commander of their armies. Bowing respectfully, the gods said to Brahmā, “O Lord, you once promised us a commander for our armies. Now, that same being is performing intense penance with Umā. Please, with your wisdom, do what’s best for the worlds! We rely on you.” Brahmā listened calmly, comforting the gods with gentle words. “As the Mountain’s daughter (Umā) said, you won’t have sons from your own wives. Her words are absolute—there’s no question. This is the celestial Gangā. Agni will father a son with her—the mighty general of the gods. The elder daughter of the Mountain will treat this son as if Umā herself gave birth to him, and Umā will surely care for him too.” Hearing this, the gods bowed and honored Brahmā. Then, Rama, the gods traveled to Mount Kailāsa, rich in precious metals, and gave Agni a special mission: “Agni, you must help create the son we need. Pour your energy into Gangā, the Mountain’s daughter.” Agni agreed and approached Gangā, saying, “O Goddess, please carry this child—for this is what the gods desire.” Gangā then revealed her divine form, so powerful that Agni felt overwhelmed. Still, Agni released his energy into Gangā from all directions, and her streams filled with that power.

Gangā, looking to Agni, said, “O god, I can’t hold this energy any longer. I’m burning up—it’s too much for me.” Agni, who accepts sacrifices for the gods, replied, “Release the child on the slopes of Himavat (the Himalayas)!” Obeying Agni, Gangā let the blazing embryo flow into her streams. The newborn shone like molten gold, and his fiery power transformed everything nearby and far away: close objects became gold and silver, distant things became copper and iron, and even her waste turned to lead. This is how different metals first spread across the earth. When the child was born, the forests near the mountain shone with golden light. From that day on, gold that gleamed like fire was called Jātarupa. 

As the boy was born, Indra and the Maruts asked the six Krittikā stars to nurse him: “Let him be a son to all of us.” The Krittikās took turns feeding him as soon as he arrived. So, the gods named him Kārtikeya, saying, “This son will become famous in all three worlds.” The Krittikās then bathed the glowing child, born from Gangā, marking him with sacred symbols. Because he was born from Gangā, the gods also called this radiant, strong-armed child Skanda. The Krittikās’ breasts filled with milk, and Kārtikeya, now with six mouths, drank from each of them. Even though he was still a baby, he showed incredible strength: in just one day, he defeated the Danava (demon) armies. Then, led by Agni, the gods gathered and sprinkled him with holy water, officially making him their general. Rama, anyone on earth who honors Kārtikeya is blessed—they gain virtue, long life, children, grandchildren, and when their time comes, they join Skanda in his heavenly realm.
SECTION XXXVIII

After finishing those words to Rama, which sounded almost musical, Kauśika continued speaking to Kākutstha (Rama). “A long time ago, there was a king named Sagara who ruled Ayodhya. Despite really wanting children, he and his wives had no kids for a long time. Sagara’s first wife was Keśini, daughter of Vidarbha. She was known for her honesty and good character. His second wife was Sumati, the daughter of Arishtanemi and the sister of Suparna. With both of these wives, King Sagara went to the Himalayas and started performing serious spiritual practices on Mount Bhriguprasravana, hoping for a blessing. After one hundred years of these hardships, the sage Bhrigu, impressed by Sagara’s devotion, granted him a boon. He said, ‘You, Sagara, will have glorious children, and you’ll become famous among men. One of your wives will have a single son who will carry on your family line, and the other will have sixty thousand sons.’

When Bhrigu said this, both queens were overjoyed. They bowed respectfully and asked him, ‘Please, tell us clearly—who will have the one son, and who will have the sixty thousand? We want your words to come true.’ The wise sage replied, ‘You may each choose—one of you can have a single heir who will continue the family, and the other can have countless sons, all strong and famous. Which do you want?’

Keśini, in front of her husband the king, chose to have just one son who would be the heir. Sumati, Suparna’s sister, chose to have sixty thousand sons, all strong and renowned. After this, the king and his wives respectfully circled the sage, bowed to him, and returned to their capital city.

Eventually, Keśini gave birth to a son named Asamanja. Sumati, on the other hand, gave birth to a large gourd. When the gourd split open, sixty thousand sons came out. Nurses raised these children in jars filled with clarified butter, and over time they grew up into healthy young men. Sagara’s eldest son, Asamanja, would often take the sixty thousand boys to the Sarayu River and, for his own amusement, throw them in to watch them struggle and sink. Because of his cruel and wicked behavior—hurting innocent people and disturbing the citizens—his father, King Sagara, banished Asamanja from the city.

Asamanja had a son named Anshuman, who was strong and well-liked by everyone. He spoke kindly to all and was loved by the people.
“After many years passed, King Sagara decided to perform a great sacrifice. Being skilled in the ancient rituals, he began making preparations for the ceremony with the help of his priests.”
SECTION XXXIX

When Viçwāmitra finished speaking, Rāma, looking genuinely interested, turned to the sage, who seemed to glow like fire, and said, “I really want to know, please tell me the full story of how my ancestor organized the sacrifice.” Viçwāmitra smiled at Rāma’s eagerness and replied, “Listen closely, Rāma, to the story of the great King Sagara’s sacrifice. Himavat, the father-in-law of Shiva, is a famous mountain. The Himavat and Vindhya mountains once faced each other, and the land between them became the site of Sagara’s sacrifice. That land is still known as a perfect place for sacrifices. Now, Kākutstha, Sagara’s powerful grandson Ançumat—who was a skilled warrior—followed the sacrificial horse to protect it, as was the custom. But one day, Indra (also called Vāsava), wanting to disrupt the ceremony, took the form of a demoness (Rākshasi) and stole the horse. When the priests realized the horse was missing, they told King Sagara, ‘Today, the sacred horse has been stolen by force. You must find and punish whoever took it, or the sacrifice will be ruined and we’ll be cursed. Please, act quickly so nothing goes wrong.’ Hearing this, the king called his sixty thousand sons together and said, ‘This great sacrifice is being led by pious Brahmanas, so I don’t see how demons could interfere. Still, sons, you must go and search for the horse. Travel across the whole earth, even beyond the oceans, and search every Yojana. Dig into the ground if you need to, but bring back the horse and the thief. I’ve begun this sacrifice with my grandsons and priests, and it must not fail.’ Fired up by their father’s command, the princes started searching the earth. They dug a Yojana deep and wide using their hands—strong as thunderbolts—and huge ploughs and weapons. As they tore into the earth, it began to wail in pain.

Rāma, as they dug deeper, cries of terror rose from snakes, demons (Asuras), Rākshasas, and other creatures being killed in the chaos. The sons of Sagara kept digging for sixty thousand Yojanas, as if they wanted to reach the very bottom of the world. They tunneled all around the land of Jamvudwipa, which is filled with mountains. Seeing this destruction, the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Asuras, and serpent-people (Pannagas), became afraid and went to Brahmā, the Creator. With worried faces and trembling voices, they pleaded, ‘Lord, the whole earth is being dug up by the sons of Sagara. So many noble beings and water creatures are dying! They say someone disturbed their sacrifice and stole the horse, so now they’re destroying everything in their path.’
SECTION XL

When the gods heard what was happening, they were terrified and shaken by the incredible power of Sagara’s sons, who seemed as unstoppable as Death itself. Seeing their fear, Brahma (the Grand-sire), who possesses all six divine powers, spoke to reassure them: “This entire Earth belongs to the wise Vāsudeva—she is his consort, and he alone is her true lord. Taking the form of Kapila, he supports the world without rest. But the sons of King Sagara will all be destroyed by his anger. The digging of the earth and the destruction of Sagara’s sons were both destined and foreseen by those with great vision.” After hearing Brahma’s words, the thirty-three gods, delighted, returned to their own realms.

As Sagara’s sons continued to tear through the earth, a thunderous noise rose up, as loud as a storm. After they had dug through the whole earth and searched everywhere, they went back to their father and reported, “We’ve searched the entire world. We fought and defeated powerful gods, demons (Dānavas), ogres (Rākshasas), ghosts (Piçāchas), serpent-beings (Uragai), and dragons (Pannagas), but we haven’t found either the horse or the thief. What should we do now? Please advise us.”

When he heard this, King Sagara was furious. He told his sons, “Go back and dig deeper until you find the one who stole the horse. Don’t stop until you do.” Taking their father’s command, all sixty thousand sons of Sagara dove back into the earth to continue their search.

While digging, they came across the elephant of the eastern quarter, named Virupāksha, as massive as a mountain and supporting the earth itself. Virupāksha was holding up the whole world, including its mountains and forests, on his head. Rama, on special days when this mighty elephant grows tired and shakes his head, it causes earthquakes. The sons of Sagara circled around Virupāksha respectfully and continued to dig deeper.

After piercing through the East, they moved to the South, where they found another gigantic elephant, Mahāpadma, who also held up the earth. They were amazed by his strength. After honoring him too, they pressed on toward the West. There, they saw Saumanasa, the western elephant, as huge as a mountain, and greeted him before digging further.

Finally, in the North, they met Bhadra, white as snow, holding up the earth on his broad back. They paid their respects to Bhadra as well and continued downward. Soon, they reached the Northeast, still angry and determined, and began to dig even more fiercely.

In that region, the powerful sons of Sagara finally saw Vāsudeva himself in the form of Kapila. To their delight, they also found their sacrificial horse nearby, grazing peacefully. Realizing Kapila was the one who had stopped the sacrifice, they picked up their spades, plows, trees, and rocks, eyes blazing with fury, and charged at him, shouting, “Stop! You’re the one who stole our horse. You wicked being, you’ve fallen into the hands of Sagara’s sons now!”

Hearing their angry threats, Kapila’s own rage flared up. He let out a deafening roar, and in that instant, the sixty thousand sons of Sagara were burned to ashes by his unstoppable power.
SECTION XLI

When his sons took too long to return, King Sagara (O descendant of Raghu) turned to his grandson. Seeing the young man’s energy and potential, Sagara said, "You’re brave and skilled, just like your uncles. Go find out what happened to them, and also discover where the horse has gone. There are powerful beings living deep within the earth, so be ready to defend yourself—take your bow and your scimitar. Show respect to those who deserve it, but don’t hesitate to fight anyone who tries to stop you. Once you’ve completed your mission, come back and help finish my sacrifice." Inspired by Sagara’s words, Ançumat, swift and determined, armed himself and set out on his quest.

Following his grandfather’s orders, Ançumat searched for the entrance his uncles had made underground. He soon found it and ventured inside. Along the way, he encountered a massive elephant that guarded one of the cardinal points—a creature respected by gods, demons (Danavas), rakshasas, spirits, birds, and serpent-people (Uragas). Ançumat circled the elephant respectfully, greeted him, and asked about his uncles and the missing horse.

The mighty elephant replied, "O son of Asamanja, you’ll succeed in your mission and return soon with the horse." Encouraged, Ançumat continued, asking similar questions of the other elephants guarding the world’s directions. Each of them honored him and gave their blessing, saying, "Go ahead and take the horse!"

With their support, Ançumat pressed on until he reached the place where his uncles, the sons of Sagara, had been destroyed and reduced to a pile of ashes. Seeing the scene, Ançumat was overwhelmed with grief and mourned deeply for their loss.
As he wept, Ançumat noticed the sacrificial horse wandering nearby. He wanted to perform the funeral water rites for his uncles, but he couldn’t find any water close by.

While searching, he spotted Suparna—the lord of birds and the princes’ maternal uncle—soaring above, as swift and powerful as the wind. Suparna (also known as Garuda, son of Vinata) swooped down and spoke to him: "Don’t grieve, noble one. Their end was for the greater good. Kapila, unmatched in power, destroyed them. Because of this, you shouldn’t perform the usual water rites for them. Instead, the sacred river Ganga, Himavat’s eldest daughter, should be used for their final offerings. Let her pure waters cleanse their ashes. When Ganga flows over them, the sixty thousand sons of Sagara will ascend to the heavens. Now, take the horse and finish your grandfather’s sacrifice, O hero."
Encouraged by Suparna’s words, Ançumat, strong in spirit, quickly took the horse and made his way back.

When he reached King Sagara, who was already prepared for the ceremony, Ançumat shared everything that Suparna had told him. Hearing the sad news, the king completed the sacrifice as prescribed by the scriptures.
After the ritual was done, the king returned to his capital. However, he couldn’t figure out how to bring Ganga down to earth as Suparna had advised.
Despite his efforts, the great king never found a way. After a long reign of thirty thousand years, King Sagara eventually passed away and ascended to heaven.
SECTION XLII

After Sagara died, his people chose his righteous grandson Anshumat to be king. Anshumat turned out to be a great ruler, and his son, the famous Dilipa, was also an excellent king. When Anshumat handed the kingdom over to Dilipa, he left to practice intense asceticism on the beautiful peaks of the Himalayas. For 3.2 million years, he lived in the forests performing harsh austerities, and eventually, thanks to his spiritual power, he reached the heavens. Meanwhile, Dilipa was devastated when he learned how his grandfathers had perished, but he couldn’t figure out what to do about it. He constantly pondered how to bring the river Ganga down to earth, how to perform the proper funeral rites with water, and how to redeem his ancestors. While he was deep in these thoughts, a virtuous son was born to him, named Bhagiratha. Dilipa ruled for thirty thousand years and performed many sacrifices, but he died, still unsure of how to free his ancestors. Before his death, he formally made Bhagiratha king and, through his good deeds, ascended to Indra’s realm. Bhagiratha, the royal sage, was deeply righteous. Since he had no children and desperately wanted one, he left the kingdom and its people in the hands of his advisors and dedicated himself to bringing Ganga down to earth. Bhagiratha began a grueling set of austerities at Gokarna: he controlled his senses, ate only once a month, surrounded himself with five fires, and kept his arms raised for long periods. He did this for a thousand years. Eventually, Brahma, the creator and lord of all beings, was pleased by Bhagiratha’s dedication. Appearing with the gods, Brahma said, “Bhagiratha, mighty king, I’m pleased with your intense efforts. Ask for any boon you want.” Bhagiratha, folding his hands, replied, “If you’re truly pleased with me, please grant me this: let Sagara’s sons receive water from my hands, and may their ashes, touched by Ganga, ensure that my ancestors reach heaven. Also, please let my family line never die out—let this be the greatest blessing on the Ikshwaku dynasty.” Brahma answered kindly, “Your request is noble, Bhagiratha. So be it—may good come to you and your family. But to bring down Ganga, the eldest daughter of Himavat (the Himalayas), you’ll need Shiva’s help. Earth alone can’t withstand the force of Ganga’s descent, so only Shiva (Hara, the wielder of the Trident) can handle it.” With these words, Brahma greeted Ganga and returned to heaven with the other gods.

After Brahma left, Bhagiratha pressed his thumb into the ground and spent another year worshipping Shiva. When that year was up, Shiva, the lord of Uma (also called Pashupati), appeared before the king and said, “I’m pleased with you, greatest of men. I’ll do what’s best for you—I’ll catch Ganga on my head.” Then, the river Ganga, Himavat’s eldest daughter, transformed into a powerful, massive form and hurled herself from the sky onto Shiva’s welcoming head. Ganga, knowing she was nearly impossible to control, thought, “I’ll drag Shiva down with me into the underworld with my currents.” Realizing her arrogance, Shiva became angry. He decided to trap her, so when Ganga crashed onto his head—his tangled hair like the Himalayas—she couldn’t reach the earth, no matter how hard she tried. She stayed tangled in Shiva’s hair for many years. Seeing this, Bhagiratha began another round of severe austerities. Eventually, Shiva was satisfied by his devotion and released Ganga towards Lake Bindusaras. As she fell, Ganga split into seven streams: three flowed east, and the Suchakshu, Sita, and Sindhu rivers flowed west. The seventh stream followed Bhagiratha’s chariot. Bhagiratha rode in front on a magnificent chariot, and Ganga followed him, first falling from the sky onto Shiva’s head and then down to earth, her waters thundering. The earth was alive with falling fish, turtles, and river dolphins. Gods, sages, Gandharvas, Yakshas, and Siddhas watched from their divine vehicles, amazed at the sight of Ganga’s descent. The gods in their chariots were stunned, and everyone on earth was in awe. Huge crowds of divine beings came to see the miracle, their glowing ornaments lighting up the sky like a hundred suns. The sky was full of river dolphins, snakes, and fish darting like flashes of lightning, and the air was filled with foamy spray, looking like white autumn clouds crowded with cranes. Ganga’s flow was wild—sometimes fast, sometimes twisting, sometimes wide, sometimes sloping, sometimes climbing hills, then plunging into valleys. The water clashed with itself, sometimes rising, sometimes falling. The clear, pure water, first pouring from Shiva’s hair and then onto the earth, was beautiful to behold. Sages, Gandharvas, and ordinary people all touched the sacred water that had flowed from Shiva’s head. Anyone who had fallen from heaven to earth because of a curse bathed in Ganga, had their sins washed away, and returned to their heavenly homes. The holy waters brought joy to all beings, washing away sins and filling everyone with happiness. Bhagiratha, riding his chariot, led the way, with Ganga following close behind. Gods, sages, demons, Rakshasas, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Kinnaras, giant serpents, and Apsaras—all kinds of divine and magical creatures, along with river animals—followed Bhagiratha’s chariot, joyfully moving along with Ganga. Wherever Bhagiratha went, Ganga—the most sacred of rivers, able to wash away all sins—followed.

But Ganga’s wild waters flooded the sacrificial ground of the great sage Jahnu as he was performing a ritual. Offended by her arrogance, Jahnu got angry and drank up all Ganga’s waters. The gods, Gandharvas, and sages were shocked and began to praise and pray to Jahnu, asking him to release Ganga and adopt her as his daughter. Finally, Jahnu was moved by their pleas and let Ganga flow from his ears. That’s why Ganga is also called Jahnavi, Jahnu’s daughter. After that, Ganga once again followed Bhagiratha’s chariot. When she reached the ocean, she flowed down into the underworld to complete Bhagiratha’s mission. Bhagiratha, overwhelmed, finally found his ancestors reduced to ashes. Ganga’s sacred waters washed over their remains, and, freed from all sin, Sagara’s sons rose up to heaven at last.
SECTION XLIV

When King Bhagiratha finally reached the ocean, following the path of the Ganges, he descended beneath the Earth at the very place where Sagara’s sons had been turned to ashes. As soon as the waters of the Ganges washed over their ashes, Brahma—the creator and lord of all beings—appeared and spoke to the king. “O mighty Bhagiratha, the sixty-three thousand sons of the great Sagara have found deliverance and have risen to heaven, just like the gods. As long as the oceans exist in this world, Sagara’s sons will remain in heaven, shining among the celestials. From now on, Ganga will be your eldest daughter, and she will be famous everywhere, bearing your name. That’s why she’s called Bhagirathi and also Tripathaga—because she flows in three directions. Now, Bhagiratha, offer the water rites here for your ancestors, and fulfill your promise. Remember, your illustrious ancestor Sagara, despite his virtue, couldn’t achieve this goal. Even Anshuman, unmatched in energy, could not bring down Ganga as he wished. And your own father, King Dilipa—a royal sage with great qualities and discipline—tried his best but did not succeed in bringing Ganga down. But now, you have fulfilled the promise that they could not, and for this, you will earn great fame. By bringing Ganga to Earth, you will also reach Brahma’s own realm after this life. Wash yourself in these sacred, untainted waters, purify yourself, and then offer the water rites to your ancestors. Good fortune to you. I will return to my own world now—farewell, King.”

After saying this, Brahma—the Grand-sire of all—returned to the heavens. Bhagiratha, now pure and fulfilled, performed the proper rituals and respectfully offered water to Sagara’s sons. Then he returned to his capital. Blessed with great prosperity, Bhagiratha ruled his kingdom wisely, and his people were happy under his reign. Their sorrows faded, their fortunes improved, and they lived in peace.

So, Rama, this is the story of how Ganga came to Earth. May good fortune be yours! The evening is approaching. Whoever recites this story—which brings prosperity, fame, long life, and even heaven to Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and others—wins the favor of both ancestors and gods. And, O Kakutstha (Rama), anyone who listens to the sacred tale of Ganga’s descent will have a long life, gain their heart’s desires, be freed from sins, and enjoy lasting fame.
SECTION XLV

After hearing Viśvāmitra’s story, Rāma (Rāghava) and Lakshmana were amazed. Rāma turned to Viśvāmitra and said, “Brahmana, the story you just told us about the descent of the Ganga and how she replenished the ocean—it’s incredible. While we were thinking over everything you said, the night passed by so quickly, it felt like only a moment. All night, as I sat with Sumitra’s son Lakshmana, I kept reflecting on your wonderful words.” When dawn broke and the sky was bright, Rāma, always ready to face any challenge, spoke to Viśvāmitra, who had just finished his morning prayers. “The night is over, and I’m eager to hear more of your amazing stories. But first, let’s cross this sacred river—the greatest of all rivers, which flows in three streams. I see some holy men have arrived, bringing a boat with a large carpet, since they heard you were here.” 

Viśvāmitra, hearing Rāma’s words, made his way through the group of gathered ascetics. After they all crossed to the north bank of the Ganga, he paid his respects to the saints there. When they landed on the riverbank, they saw a city called Viśāla. Without delay, Viśvāmitra, along with Rāma, headed toward Viśāla, which was beautiful and shining, almost like a city of the gods. Rāma, ever curious and respectful, folded his hands and asked Viśvāmitra about the city. “Great sage, which royal family lives in that city? I really want to know—please tell me.” 

Viśvāmitra, pleased by Rāma’s interest, began to explain. “Listen, Rāma, to what I once heard from Indra (Sakra) about this place. I’ll tell you everything that happened here. Long ago, during the Krita age, the powerful sons of Diti and Aditi—both incredibly strong and virtuous—started thinking deeply about something. They wondered, ‘How can we become free from old age and sickness, and live forever?’ After some thought, they realized, ‘If we churn the ocean of milk, we can get amrita—the nectar of immortality.’ They decided to do it. Using the great serpent Vāsuki as the rope and Mount Mandara as the churning stick, they began to churn the ocean.

A thousand years went by as they worked. Vāsuki’s serpent heads, acting as the rope, started to spit out deadly poison and bite the rocks with their fangs. The poison was so strong and fiery that the whole universe—gods, demons, and humans—started to suffer. In desperation, they all went to Shiva (Paśupati, Rudra) and prayed, ‘Save us! Save us!’ As they pleaded with Shiva, Vishnu (Hari), holding his conch and discus, appeared and smiled. He said to Shiva, ‘You are the greatest of the gods, so whatever comes out first from the ocean churned by the gods belongs to you. Please, accept this poison as your share.’ After saying this, Vishnu disappeared.

Seeing how upset everyone was, and remembering Vishnu’s words, Shiva drank the deadly poison as if it were nectar. Then, after helping the gods, he quietly left. The gods continued churning, but the mountain they were using as a churning stick sank into the sea. The gods and Gandharvas (heavenly musicians) started to praise Vishnu, saying, ‘You are the path for all beings, especially for the gods. Please help us and recover the mountain.’ Hearing their prayers, Vishnu took the form of a giant tortoise and held the mountain on his back, supporting it in the ocean. Then, standing with the gods, he helped churn the ocean by holding the top of the mountain.

After another thousand years, a man appeared from the ocean—he was Dhanvantari, the father of Ayurveda, carrying a staff and a water jug (kamandalu), and he was known for his wisdom and goodness. Then, from the foamy waters, a group of beautiful women arose—the Apsarās, shining with light. Since they came from the water, they were called Apsarās. Sixty crore (600 million) Apsarās appeared, and their female attendants were countless. Neither the gods nor the demons wanted to claim them, so they became known as women who belong to everyone.

Next, the pious daughter of Varuna, named Vāruni, emerged and looked around, hoping someone would accept her. The sons of Diti (the Asuras) refused her, but the sons of Aditi (the Devas) accepted her. This is why the sons of Diti are called Asuras, while the sons of Aditi are called Suras (gods). The gods were overjoyed to accept Vāruni. After that, Uchchaihśravā, the best of horses, appeared, followed by the precious Kaustubha gem, and then finally the nectar of immortality itself.

At this point, a massive battle broke out over the amrita. The sons of Aditi and Diti fought furiously. The Asuras joined forces with the Rakshasas (demons), and the battle was so fierce that it terrified all three worlds. Many were killed. Vishnu, taking on a dazzling form, stole the amrita. Anyone who tried to stop him was destroyed by Vishnu, who kept changing his appearance. In this terrible war between the two sides, the sons of Aditi finally defeated the sons of Diti. With victory secured and his kingdom restored, Indra (Purandara) began to rule the worlds peacefully, along with the saints and the heavenly Chāranas (bards).
SECTION XLVI

When Diti’s sons were killed, she was overwhelmed with grief. She went to her husband, Kaçyapa (son of Maricha), and pleaded, “My lord, your noble sons have killed my own children. Now I want a son who, after long penance, will be strong enough to defeat Indra (Sakra). I will undergo severe austerities for this, but I need you to grant me the seed for such a son—a son destined to kill Indra. Please promise me this.” Hearing her, Kaçyapa, full of power, replied to Diti, who was deeply saddened, “Alright. May good things come to you—just keep yourself pure, O ascetic. If you remain pure for a full thousand years, you will give birth to a son who will defeat Indra in battle. Through me, you’ll have a son who could even threaten the three worlds.” After saying this, Kaçyapa placed his hand on her and blessed her. He wished her luck and then left to continue his own penance. Feeling joyful, Diti went to Kuçaplava and started her intense austerities.

During this time, Indra (the thousand-eyed god) personally served her. He provided her with everything she needed: fire, grass, firewood, water, fruits, roots, and anything else she wanted. He took care of her constantly, even massaging her and helping her recover from exhaustion. When only ten years remained to complete the thousand-year vow, Diti—very pleased—said to Indra, “Mighty one, I have just ten years left of my austerities. After that, you will see your brother born. I’ll make sure he loves you, even though I originally wanted him to destroy you. That way, your anxiety will be gone and you’ll both rule the three worlds together. Your great father gave me the boon that after a thousand years, I would have a son.”

One day, at noon, Diti accidentally fell asleep with her feet where her head should have been on her bed, making her ritually impure. Indra saw this, and smiled, realizing this was his chance. He entered her womb and, with great control, split the embryo into seven parts. As he struck the embryo with his thunderbolt, the unborn children cried out loudly. This noise woke Diti. “Don’t cry, don’t cry,” Indra urged. But even as the embryos cried, Indra kept dividing them further. “Please stop, don’t kill them!” Diti begged. Out of respect for his mother, Indra finally stopped and left her womb.

With hands folded, Indra addressed Diti, “Mother, you accidentally slept with your feet where your head should be, which made you impure. I took this opportunity to split the child who would have killed me in battle into seven pieces. Please forgive me.”
SECTION XLVII

After the embryo had been split into seven parts, Diti was heartbroken. She turned to Indra (also called the thousand-eyed god), and said humbly, “This is my fault—the embryo was broken into seven because of me. Lord of the gods, you haven’t done anything wrong, O destroyer of Vala. Now that this tragedy has happened, let me at least do something good for you. Let these seven parts become the guardians of the seven Maruts. And, my son, let my children—who will be known as the Marutas and have noble forms—move freely through the regions of the Vātaskandha in the heavens. Let one watch over Brahmā’s realm, another over yours, Indra, and let the third, who will be famous, be known as Divya Vayu and travel around as well. By your command, let the remaining four sons, called by the name you’ve chosen, travel as you see fit during their appointed times.” 

Hearing these words, Indra—destroyer of Vala and king of the gods—bowed his head and replied, “Everything you have asked will be done. There’s no doubt about it. May good fortune come to you. Your sons, gifted with divine forms, will roam as you wish. And it is said that, after figuring all this out in that hermitage, both mother and son, Rama, went to heaven, their wishes fulfilled.”

Rama, this is the very place where mighty Indra once stayed and cared for Diti, who had completed her ascetic vows. Also, the righteous king Ikshwāku had a noble son with Alamvushā, named Viśāla. Here, Viśāla built a palace, which was called Viśālā. Viśāla’s son was the powerful Hemachandra, followed by the famous Suchandra. Suchandra’s son was Dhumrāswa, whose son was Srinjaya. Srinjaya’s son was the mighty Sahadeva, and Sahadeva’s son was the devout Kuśāśwa. Kuśāśwa’s son was the strong Somadatta, and now, Rama, Somadatta’s son—Sumati—rules this city. Sumati is bright, undefeated, and well-known. Because of Ikshwāku’s blessings, all the kings of Viśālā have been long-lived, wise, strong, and pious.

Let’s stay here for the night, and in the morning, Rama, you’ll get to see Janaka. When the famous Viśwāmitra arrived, King Sumati—shining with energy—came forward to greet him. He honored Viśwāmitra with his priests and friends, asking after his well-being with folded hands. Then he said, “We are truly blessed and grateful to have you visit our land, O sage. No one is luckier than I am today.”
SECTION XLVIII

After they greeted each other and made sure all was well, Sumati spoke to the powerful sage. “May good things come your way,” he began. “These young men with the strength of gods, who walk with the power of elephants or lions, who are as brave as tigers or bulls, and whose eyes are wide and bright like lotus petals—they carry swords, bows, and quivers, and move with the grace of the Ashwini twins. They look young and otherworldly, as if they descended from the heavens. Tell me, great sage, who are these boys’ parents, and why have they come here? And why are they traveling on foot? They stand out, as radiant as the Sun or Moon in the sky, and they look so much alike in build, looks, and gestures. They’re armed and seem ready for battle—so how did such impressive young men end up on this difficult path? I really want to know the truth.” After hearing this, Vishwamitra explained everything in detail. The king was amazed and welcomed Rama and Lakshmana, the sons of Dasharatha, as honored guests. He treated them with the respect they deserved. Thanks to Sumati’s warm hospitality, the two descendants of Raghu spent the night there. The next morning, they set out for Mithila. When they finally saw the beautiful city of Janaka, the sages with them exclaimed, “Amazing, amazing!” and couldn’t stop admiring Mithila.

In a grove near Mithila, Rama spotted an old, quiet, and beautiful hermitage. He asked Vishwamitra, “What is this place? It looks like a hermitage, but there are no sages here. Please, respected one, tell me who used to live here.” Hearing these words, the wise and powerful sage Vishwamitra replied, “Listen carefully, and I’ll tell you how this hermitage came to be cursed because of someone’s anger. This was once a sacred place, respected even by the gods, and it belonged to the great sage Gautama. Long ago, Gautama lived here with his wife Ahalya, practicing severe austerities for many years. At one point, Indra, the king of the gods—who is sometimes called the thousand-eyed one—saw an opportunity. He disguised himself as Gautama and approached Ahalya. He said to her, ‘Beautiful one, those who want pleasure don’t wait for the right time. I want to be with you right now.’ Out of curiosity and poor judgment, Ahalya agreed to Indra’s request. After they were together, she said to him, ‘Lord of the gods, I got what I wanted. Now, please leave quickly so no one finds out. For both our sakes, you should go.’ Indra smiled and answered, ‘Lovely Ahalya, I’m satisfied. I’ll go now.’ But as Indra was leaving, he became very nervous because he realized Gautama might return at any moment.

Just then, Gautama, powerful and full of spiritual energy, came back from his ritual bath, carrying firewood and kusa grass. He looked like a blazing fire and was impossible for even gods or demons to stop. When Indra saw Gautama, his face went pale with fear. Gautama instantly recognized the thousand-eyed god, even though he was disguised as an ascetic. Furious, Gautama said, ‘Because you took my form and committed this terrible act, you’ll lose your manhood.’ The moment he said this, Indra’s testicles fell to the ground.

After seeing what happened to Indra, Gautama cursed his wife too. ‘For a thousand years, you’ll live here, surviving only on air, tormented by regret, and invisible to everyone. Only when Rama, the unstoppable son of Dasharatha, comes to this forest, will you be freed from your guilt. When that time comes, welcome him properly, without any selfishness or ignorance, and then, happily and in your own form, you’ll return to my side.’ After giving this curse to Ahalya, the powerful Gautama left the hermitage and went to the beautiful peaks of the Himalayas, where he continued his penance among the Siddhas and Charanas (celestial beings and bards).
SECTION XLIX

After losing his testicles, Sakra (another name for Indra), his eyes wide with fear, turned to the gods—including Agni, as well as the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Charanas—and said, “I did what you asked of me: I made Gautama angry and interrupted his meditation, just like the gods wanted. But in doing so, I lost my testicles, and Ahalyā has also been disgraced. I made Gautama curse me, which took away his spiritual power, so now, gods and sages, I’ve done my part for you. Please give me my testicles back.”

Hearing Sakra’s plea, the gods, along with the Maruts led by Agni, went to see the divine Pitris (the ancestors). Agni spoke to them: “This ram has testicles, while Sakra now does not. Why not take the ram’s testicles and give them to Sakra? Even without them, the ram will still be able to satisfy all your offerings. And to anyone who sacrifices a ram like this for you, you’ll grant endless blessings and merit.”

The Pitris listened to Agni. They took the ram’s testicles and attached them to Indra, the thousand-eyed god. That’s why, Kakutstha (descendant of Raghu), the Pitris accept rams without testicles as sacrifices—they once gave a ram’s testicles to Indra. And ever since, Rāghava, Indra has carried the ram’s testicles, thanks to Gautama’s spiritual power. So now, you should enter the hermitage of that holy man and free the dignified and beautiful Ahalyā.

After hearing Viśvāmitra’s words, Rāma and Lakshmana, with Viśvāmitra leading the way, entered the hermitage. There, they saw Ahalyā, glowing with spiritual energy, her beauty almost impossible to look at—even the gods and demons couldn’t handle it. She seemed like a hidden flame, the full moon covered in mist, or sunlight blocked by clouds. Because of Gautama’s curse, no one in the three worlds could see her until Rāma arrived. Now that the curse was over, she became visible.

The two descendants of Raghu (Rāma and Lakshmana) bowed and touched her feet, but remembering Gautama’s instructions, Ahalyā touched their feet instead. With a calm mind, she washed their feet, gave them water and gifts, and welcomed them according to tradition. Rāma and Lakshmana accepted her hospitality as they were supposed to.

Suddenly, flowers rained down, drums thundered, and the Gandharvas and Apsarās celebrated with joy. The gods cheered, “Wonderful, wonderful!” and honored Ahalyā as she, purified by her long penance, was reunited with Gautama. Gautama, happy to be with Ahalyā again, showed great respect to Rāma and then went back to his meditation.

After receiving Gautama’s warm welcome and honors, Rāma continued his journey toward Mithilā.
SECTION L

Rāma and Lakshmana headed northeast with Viśvāmitra (Vishwamitra) leading the way, eventually reaching the area where King Janaka’s sacrifice was being held. Rāma turned to the powerful sage and said, “Viśvāmitra, this sacrifice by Janaka is truly impressive—the scale and grandeur are amazing. There are thousands of Brāhmanas from all over, experts in the Vedas, and the whole place is packed with ascetics and hundreds of chariots. Can you help us find somewhere quiet to stay?” Hearing this, Viśvāmitra picked out a peaceful, well-watered spot away from the chaos for them to settle in.

When news of Viśvāmitra’s arrival reached King Janaka, the righteous king immediately set out to greet him. He brought his chief priest, Śatānanda, and the family priests with him, carrying the ceremonial arghya (offering). In a show of humility, Janaka offered the arghya to Viśvāmitra just as tradition required. Viśvāmitra accepted the honor, and then asked about the king’s well-being and whether the sacrifice was proceeding smoothly. Janaka and his priests returned the courtesy, greeting the sages warmly and embracing them respectfully. With folded hands, Janaka said, “Please, honored sage, take a seat here with the other great ascetics.” Viśvāmitra sat down, and Janaka, along with his priests and counselors, took their seats in order of rank.

Looking at Viśvāmitra, Janaka said, “Today, thanks to the gods, my sacrifice has truly succeeded. Just seeing you here has made everything worthwhile. I’m so fortunate that you and these revered ascetics have blessed my sacred grounds.
