“Who are these young men with you?” Janaka asked. “They look almost divine—their strength, the way they walk like lions or elephants, heroic like tigers or bulls. Their eyes are large and beautiful, like lotus petals. They carry swords, bows, and quivers, and there’s a certain grace about them, almost like the twin gods, the Ashvins. They seem so youthful, it’s as if they’ve just stepped down from heaven. Who are their parents, sage? Why have they come here, and why are they traveling on foot? They look like brothers, both carrying weapons, and the way they stand out here is like the sun and moon lighting up the sky. Their build, their faces, even their mannerisms match—they wear their hair in side-locks and have a warrior’s air. Please, tell me the truth about them.”

Hearing Janaka’s questions, Viśvāmitra told him everything about Daśaratha’s sons—how they’d stayed at Siddhāśrama, fought and killed the Rākṣasas there, and journeyed on bravely. He described their visit to Viśālā, the encounter with Ahalyā and Gautama, Rāma’s interest in the powerful bow, and how they ended up here to see it. After explaining it all to Janaka, the energetic sage Viśvāmitra paused, waiting for the king’s response.
SECTION LI

After hearing Viśwāmitra’s story, Gautama’s eldest son, the powerful and deeply disciplined Śatānanda, was amazed by Rāma’s presence—his hair even stood on end. Seeing Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa sitting comfortably, he addressed the great sage Viśwāmitra, saying, “O most powerful sage, you introduced my revered mother, who has grown old practicing penance, to the king’s son. Did my famous mother offer Rāma, who deserves the respect of all, food from the forest? And, great sage, did you tell Rāma the old story about how my mother was wronged by that god? And, Kauśika, I hope my mother was reunited with my respected father after meeting Rāma? And, son of Kuśika, did Rāma come here after being honored by my father? And did Rāma properly greet my father, who is calm and wise?” 

Viśwāmitra, skilled in words, replied to Śatānanda, saying, “O best of ascetics, I made sure nothing was left out—everything was done as it should be. Your mother was reunited with your father, just like Renuka was with Bhrigu’s son.” 

Hearing these words, Śatānanda then turned to Rāma and said, “Welcome, chief of men! We are truly fortunate, O descendant of Raghu, that you have come to us with the great sage Viśwāmitra. This powerful Viśwāmitra is a Brahmarṣi of unmatched strength, capable of incredible deeds thanks to his asceticism. You should know him as your greatest guide. Rāma, there is no one on earth luckier than you. Your protector is Kuśika’s descendant, who has performed astonishing acts of discipline. Listen as I describe the spiritual strength of the great Kauśika. 

This righteous man was once a great king. He defeated his enemies, understood justice, was skilled, and always cared for his people. The royal line began with Kuśa, son of Prajāpati. Kuśa’s son was the strong and virtuous Kuśanābha. Kuśanābha’s son was Gādhi. And Gādhi’s son is Viśwāmitra: energetic, mighty, and a great sage who once ruled the earth. He reigned for thousands of years. 

One day, Viśwāmitra set out with his entire army to travel the world. He visited cities, kingdoms, rivers, mountains, and hermitages. Eventually, this great conqueror, Viśwāmitra, reached the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha. It was filled with blossoming trees and plants, home to many animals, and inhabited by sages and holy beings. The place was frequented by gods, demons, gandharvas, and kinnaras. Gentle deer roamed there, and birds filled the air. Many Brahmarṣis and Devarṣis lived there, along with other accomplished ascetics who shone like fire. The hermitage was like another realm of Brahmā—beautiful and surrounded by saints, Vālakhilyas, and Vaikhānasas who lived on water or air, dried leaves, or fruits and roots. They were self-controlled, free from faults, had mastered their senses, and were always busy with chanting and sacred rituals.
SECTION LII

When Viçwāmitra, the legendary sage and heroic leader, arrived, he was welcomed warmly by Vasishtha, who was also a renowned sage and respected for his wisdom and power. Radiant with happiness, Viçwāmitra bowed humbly to Vasishtha. After making sure Viçwāmitra’s journey had been pleasant, Vasishtha, who was known for his kindness, ordered a seat to be brought for him. Once Viçwāmitra was comfortably seated, Vasishtha served him a simple but respectful meal of fruits and roots, as was the custom among ascetics. Viçwāmitra gratefully accepted the hospitality, and then, showing his respect, asked Vasishtha about the well-being of his spiritual practices, his daily fire rituals (Agnihotrās), his students, and even the trees in his ashram. Vasishtha assured Viçwāmitra that everything was going well.

Next, Vasishtha, the son of Brahmā and famous for his intense spiritual discipline, politely asked Viçwāmitra, “My king, is everything well with you? Are you ruling your people kindly and fairly, in line with your royal duties? Are your officers and servants properly paid from the treasury? Do they respect your commands? Have you kept your enemies in check? And how are your army, finances, friends, sons, and grandsons?” Viçwāmitra, still showing humility despite his own power, answered each question and assured Vasishtha that all was well.

The two great men continued talking for a long time, enjoying each other’s company. Their conversation was friendly and made both of them happy. When their talk finally wound down, Vasishtha, smiling, turned to Viçwāmitra and said, “I want to give you and your entire army a proper welcome. Please, let me offer you my hospitality. You are a truly honored guest and deserve every courtesy I can give.”

Viçwāmitra, being both wise and polite, replied, “Just by inviting me and making me feel welcome, you’ve already honored me enough. The fruits and roots you’ve given me, the water to wash my feet and to drink, and even just seeing you—these are all wonderful gifts. You have treated me better than I could have hoped. I bow to you, Vasishtha. Now, I think it’s time for me to leave. Please, let’s part as friends.”

But Vasishtha, ever generous, kept insisting that Viçwāmitra stay and accept more of his hospitality. Finally, Viçwāmitra agreed, saying, “Very well, wise sage. I’ll accept whatever you think is best.”

Delighted, Vasishtha called for his sacred cow, Savalā (sometimes called “Kamadhenu,” the wish-fulfilling cow), whose spiritual purity was legendary. He said, “Savalā, come here and listen. I want to give this royal sage and his whole army a proper feast. Please help me by providing the best food. Grant everyone whatever delicious food they want, with all six flavors. Savalā, please create tasty dishes for chewing, sucking, licking, and drinking, as quickly as possible.”
SECTION LIII

After Vasishtha finished speaking, Savalā (the wish-fulfilling cow), who could give anything people wanted, began to produce whatever anyone asked for. She made sugarcanes, honey, fried rice, excellent Maireya wine, expensive drinks, a variety of delicious foods, piles of steaming hot rice like small mountains, soups, Dadhikulyās (a yogurt-based dish), and thousands of silver plates filled with meats of all kinds. Rama, the entire army of Viswamitra, made up of happy and strong men, was treated to this amazing feast by Vasishtha and felt completely satisfied. Even Viswamitra himself, along with his priests, Brahmanas, and the women of his household, ate until they were full. Enjoying this warm welcome with his courtiers, advisors, and attendants, Viswamitra felt deeply pleased. He turned to Vasishtha and said, "You have received me and treated me wonderfully, Brahmana, and you are truly worthy of honor. Please listen to what I have to say. I would like you to give me Savalā in exchange for one hundred thousand cows. This cow is truly a treasure, and it's a king's duty to collect such jewels. So please, O twice-born one, give Savalā to me — by right, she should belong to me."

When Viswamitra made this request, the wise and respected Vasishtha, the best among ascetics, replied, "O King, I won't give up Savalā for one hundred thousand cows, nor for a hundred crores of cows, nor for piles of silver. This cow should never be separated from me. Just like a powerful person's reputation, Savalā is always connected to me. My offerings to the gods and ancestors, and even my daily needs, all depend on her. My fire sacrifices, my rituals, and my daily worship are possible only because of her. My chants and sacred words, as well as all my learning, rely on her. All of this is absolutely true. She is everything to me, and she brings me happiness. For all these reasons, O King, I simply cannot give you Savalā."

Hearing Vasishtha's refusal, Viswamitra, who was skilled in persuasion, replied eagerly, "Then I will give you fourteen thousand elephants dressed in gold chains, golden necklaces, and golden hooks. I’ll add eight hundred golden chariots, each with bells and drawn by four white horses. I’ll also give you one thousand and ten of the finest horses, and a crore of young, multicolored cows. Please, give me Savalā. And if you want gems or gold, just name your price — I will give you as much as you ask. Please, let me have Savalā."

But Vasishtha, though tempted by Viswamitra’s generous offers, calmly answered, "O King, I will not give Savalā under any circumstances. She is truly my greatest treasure, my wealth, my everything, and my very means of survival. She is the heart of my rituals, my Darsa, my Paurnamasa, my sacrifices, and all the ceremonies I perform. Really, she is the main source of all my sacred duties. There’s no need to say more — I simply cannot give away Savalā, the cow who grants every wish."
SECTION LIV

When the sage Vasishtha refused to give up the magical cow of abundance, Viśvāmitra (Vishwamitra), O Rama, tried to take Savalā by force. Carried away by the powerful king and filled with grief, Savalā was overcome by sorrow and began to weep. She thought to herself, “Has the great Vasishtha abandoned me, since the king’s men are taking me away like this? What have I done to deserve this from such a wise and focused sage? I’ve always served him faithfully—why would he leave me behind when I’ve done nothing wrong?” With these thoughts running through her mind, and sighing over and over, she broke free from the king’s servants and sped like the wind back to the energetic Vasishtha. She pushed past the king’s men and rushed to Vasishtha’s feet.

Standing before Vasishtha and sobbing in a voice like thunder, Savalā cried out in distress, “O son of Brahma, why have you abandoned me and let the king’s servants drag me away from you?” 

Vasishtha, the great sage, answered the sorrowful cow gently, as if speaking to his own sister: “Savalā, I have not abandoned you, and you have done nothing wrong. But this powerful king, proud of his strength, is forcing you away. Honestly, I am not strong enough to stop him. Besides, he is a king—a powerful ruler—and today, as my guest, I cannot harm him. He is a Kshatriya and lord of this land, and he leads a whole army filled with elephants, horses, chariots, and banners.”

Hearing this, Savalā humbly replied to the mighty sage, “The power of the Kshatriyas isn’t everything—Brahmanas are even stronger. Brahmanas have a special, superhuman power that is greater than any Kshatriya’s. Your strength, O sage, is unmatched, and even the great Viśvāmitra cannot compare to you. Your energy is beyond measure. If you command me, I can unleash the power of a Brahmana and crush the pride and armies of that wicked king.”

Encouraged by her words, the famous Vasishtha replied, “Go ahead—use your power to create an army that can destroy his forces.”

At Vasishtha’s command, Savalā created an army. Hundreds of Pahlavas sprang forth at her call and, right in front of Viśvāmitra, began to tear apart his forces. Furious, Viśvāmitra’s eyes burned with rage as he attacked the Pahlavas with all kinds of weapons.

When Viśvāmitra started to slaughter the Pahlavas, Savalā created even more warriors: fierce-looking Sakas mixed with Yavanas appeared on the battlefield. The field was suddenly filled with these brilliant, terrifying warriors, shining like gold, wielding sharp swords and axes, and dressed in yellow clothes. These new fighters burned through Viśvāmitra's army like fire.

Desperate, the powerful Viśvāmitra launched weapon after weapon at them, and with this attack, the Yavanas, Kāmvoyas, and Varvaras suffered heavy losses.
SECTION LV.

Seeing his men being relentlessly attacked and overwhelmed by Vishwamitra’s (Viçwāmitra’s) divine weapons, Vasishtha turned to the cow of plenty, Shabala (Savali), and said, “O cow of plenty, use your mystical powers to create new warriors.” At her mighty roar, fierce warriors called Kambojas appeared, shining as bright as the sun. From her udders came armed Varvaras; from her secret parts emerged Yavanas; from her rear, the Sakas; and from the pores of her skin came more wild tribes—Haritas and Kiratas. Instantly, these new warriors wiped out Vishwamitra’s entire army—infantry, elephants, horses, and chariots alike.

When Vishwamitra’s hundred sons saw their army destroyed by the powerful Vasishtha, they charged forward in a rage, wielding all sorts of weapons. But Vasishtha just let out another mighty roar, and with his spiritual power, incinerated them on the spot. In moments, Vishwamitra’s sons, along with the remaining soldiers, horses, and chariots, were turned to ashes by the great sage.

Seeing everything—his army and sons—wiped out, the famous Vishwamitra was overcome with shame and despair. He felt like an ocean without its waves, a snake with no fangs, or the sun eclipsed by Rahu. With no army and no sons, he seemed like a bird stripped of its wings. Losing everything that had given him confidence, his spirit was crushed.

Handing over his kingdom to one of his surviving sons, Vishwamitra told him, “Rule the land as a true Kshatriya should.” Then, heartbroken, he left for the forest. He journeyed to the slopes of the Himalayas (Himavat), a place filled with mystical creatures like Kinnaras and serpents, and began intense meditation to please Mahadeva (Shiva).

One day, the great god Shiva (called Vrishadwaja here), lord of the gods, appeared before Vishwamitra, ready to grant him a wish. “Why are you performing these penances, O King?” Shiva asked. “Tell me your desire—I am here to grant you a boon.”

Bowing deeply, Vishwamitra answered, “If you are pleased with me, O mighty god, grant me the full knowledge of archery, with all its secrets and mantras, and the power to use weapons from both near and far. And may all the weapons possessed by the gods, demons, great sages, Gandharvas, Yakshas, and Rakshasas be given to me. Please fulfill this wish, O lord of the gods.”

Shiva replied, “So be it,” and then disappeared.

Now armed with Shiva’s divine weapons and knowledge, Vishwamitra—already proud—became arrogant and full of power, like the sea at its highest tide. Convinced he could defeat Vasishtha, he headed straight for the sage’s ashram and unleashed his new weapons, capable of destroying the entire hermitage.

When the other sages saw Vishwamitra’s attack, they panicked and fled in every direction. Vasishtha’s students, along with the animals and birds living there, scattered by the thousands. For a while, Vasishtha’s hermitage was completely empty, as quiet and lifeless as a desert, even though Vasishtha kept calling out, “Don’t be afraid! Today I will destroy Gadhi’s son, just as the sun burns away mist.”

Enraged, Vasishtha then turned to Vishwamitra and shouted, “You fool! Because you have ruined this peaceful hermitage that thrived for so long, your wicked ways will be your end—you won’t live long!” Burning with anger, Vasishtha lifted his staff, which looked as deadly as Yama’s own mace, ready to strike.
SECTION LVI

When Vasishtha finished speaking, Viçwāmitra (Vishwamitra), furious and determined, aimed a blazing magical weapon and shouted, “Stop! Stop!” Vasishtha, just as angry, lifted his Brahmā staff, which looked as deadly as the staff of Death itself, and yelled back, “You wretched Kshatriya! Here I am—show me what you’ve got. Today, son of Gādhi, I’ll crush your arrogance. You disgrace your lineage! Compare your so-called Kshatriya strength to my true Brahmin power. Watch now as I reveal my supernatural Brahmā energy.” And just like water puts out fire, Vasishtha’s Brahmā staff completely neutralized the flaming weapon Viçwāmitra had unleashed.

Enraged, Viçwāmitra unleashed a storm of weapons—Varuna, Raudra, Aindra, Pāsupata, Aishika, and more: Mānava, Mohana, Gāndharba, Swāpana, Jrimbhana, Santāpana, Vilāpana, Soshana, Druna, the unbreakable Vajra, Brahmāpāsha, Kalapāsha, Varunapāsha, Pināka (Siva’s favorite), the two Asanis (wet and dry), Danda, Paiçācha, Krauncha, Dharmachakra, Kālachakra, Vishuchakra, Vāyavya, Mathana, Haraçiras, the twin Saktis, Kankāla, Mushala, the mighty Vidyādhara, the terrifying Kāla, the dreadful Trisula, Kāpāla, and Kankana. He hurled every single one at Vasishtha, who just stood there chanting his mantras. It was an incredible sight. Yet Vasishtha, Brahmā’s son, blocked all these attacks with nothing but his staff.

After all his weapons failed, Viçwāmitra finally threw his deadliest move—a Brahmā weapon. The moment it was released, every god, led by Agni, along with the Devarshis, Gandharvas, and even the mighty serpents, were terrified. The three worlds trembled with fear. But Vasishtha, powered by his Brahmā energy, completely stopped that fearsome weapon too.

When Vasishtha defeated even the Brahmā weapon, his appearance became terrifying, as if he could scare all three worlds. Flames began to burst out from his body, almost like his pores were smoking. The Brahmā staff he held in his raised arm glowed fiercely, blazing like the fire that burns at the end of the world.

All the ascetics who saw this began to praise Vasishtha, saying, “Your strength, O Brahmin, is unbeatable. Please calm your energy for the sake of everyone. Viçwāmitra has been defeated—your power is truly unmatched. Please, let all creatures be at peace again.”

Hearing these words, Vasishtha, exhausted but still powerful, finally calmed down. Viçwāmitra, utterly defeated, sighed deeply and said, “So much for Kshatriya strength! True power comes from Brahmin energy. One Brahmā staff wiped out all my weapons. I see now—I will set out on a path of intense spiritual practice, and earn the status of a true Brahmin.”
SECTION LVII

Still feeling wounded by the humiliation he’d faced, Viśwāmitra (Vishwamitra), whose willpower was legendary, left for the south with his queen. He was burning with anger and determination, and he threw himself into extreme austerities, surviving only on fruits and roots and keeping his senses tightly controlled. Over time, he and his wife had four sons—Havishpanda, Madhushpanda, Drihanetra, and Mahāratha—each of whom was dedicated to truth and duty. After a thousand years of these harsh practices, Brahmā, the creator of all, came to Viśwāmitra and spoke kindly to him: “Son of Kuśika, your intense austerities have earned you a place among the royal sages, the Rājarshis. For this reason, we now recognize you as a Rājarshi.” After saying these words, Brahmā, glowing with energy, left for the heavens with the other gods.

When Viśwāmitra heard this, he hung his head in shame and felt a deep wave of sorrow. He said sadly, “I’ve gone through such severe austerities, but the gods and sages only see me as a Rājarshi. I don’t feel like I’ve achieved the true reward for my efforts.” Determined to go even further, the self-controlled and righteous Viśwāmitra decided to push his penance to even greater heights. Around this time, Trisanku—a famous member of the Ikshwāku line known for his honesty and self-control—made up his mind: “I’ll perform a sacrifice that will let me reach heaven in my own body.” He invited Vasishtha to help, but Vasishtha refused, saying he couldn’t do it. Feeling rejected, Trisanku headed south, hoping to find support elsewhere.

He went to where Vasishtha’s sons were deep in their own penances. There, Trisanku saw all one hundred of Vasishtha’s sons, each glowing with the strength of their spiritual practices. Approaching them with respect, Trisanku bowed his head and folded his hands, then spoke humbly: “I need your help. Vasishtha has turned me away, but I still wish to perform a great sacrifice and reach heaven in my own body. Please, I beg you, guide me. You are powerful sages, dedicated to your path. If you agree to lead this sacrifice for me, I believe I can succeed. Since Vasishtha—our spiritual teacher—has refused, I have nowhere else to turn. For an Ikshwāku king, the family guru is always the most important guide. After him, it’s you, his sons, whom I must honor and rely on.”
SECTION LVIII

Hearing Trisanku speak, the hundred sons of the sage grew furious, Rāma. They said to the king, “You’ve been rejected by our father, who always speaks the truth—so why are you now asking for help elsewhere? The Ikshwāku kings always follow their spiritual guide’s advice. You can’t just ignore what a man like our father says. He said he couldn’t do it—how can we take on the sacrifice when he refused? You’re acting foolishly, King. Turn back now. Besides, our father is powerful enough to perform a sacrifice for all three worlds—how could we possibly disrespect him by doing what he wouldn’t?”

Hearing this, the king, his voice shaking with anger, replied, “Since I’ve been turned away both by your father and by you, his sons, I’ll have to find another way. Farewell, ascetics.” 

The sage’s sons, furious at his answer, cursed him: “You will become a Chandāla (outcaste)!” After saying this, the righteous sons returned to their homes. When morning came, the king had truly become a Chandāla. He wore blue clothes, his skin looked blue and rough, his hair was cropped short, and he wore a garland made from things found in a graveyard. His body was smeared with cemetery ashes, and he wore iron jewelry. 

Rāma, when Trisanku’s followers and advisors saw him transformed into a Chandāla, they were horrified—they abandoned him and ran away together. Still, Trisanku kept his composure. Even though he suffered day and night, he went all alone to see the sage Viśvāmitra.

When Viśvāmitra saw the king in this dreadful shape, he felt sorry for him. Filled with compassion, the great and powerful sage said, “Good fortune to you, brave king of Ayodhyā. You’ve been made a Chandāla by a curse—why have you come to me, mighty prince?”

Trisanku, now an outcaste but still eloquent, folded his hands in respect and answered, “Both my spiritual teacher and his sons rejected me. I not only failed to get what I wanted, but also fell into this disaster. Sage, I wanted to go to heaven in this body. I’ve performed a hundred sacrifices, but still haven’t received the reward. I have never lied before, and I swear by my honor as a Kshatriya that, even now, I never will. I have completed many sacrifices, ruled my people fairly, and always respected my teachers. But now, even though I try to do what’s right and perform a sacrifice, my teachers have abandoned me. So I believe fate is stronger than effort. Destiny rules everything—destiny is the real path. Please, have mercy on me. I am desperate, and fate has defeated me. I have nowhere else to turn. Please, help me face my destiny with your effort.”
SECTION LIX

When the king had finished speaking, Kuçika’s son (Viçwāmitra), feeling compassion, replied kindly to the king who had been forced to live as a Chandāla. “O descendant of Ikshwāku, was your journey safe? I know who you are, and I respect your virtue. I’ll give you my protection—so don’t be afraid, greatest of kings. I’ll call together all the pious Maharshis to help with your sacrifice. Then you’ll be able to achieve your goal easily. And if the curse from your teacher still hasn’t lifted, you’ll even reach heaven in your current form. Since you have come to me and sought my help, I consider heaven already within your reach, O lord of men.” 

After saying this, Viçwāmitra—full of energy—ordered his wise and virtuous sons to gather everything needed for the sacrifice. Then he called his disciples and told them, “Go and invite all the saints, including Vasishtha’s sons, our friends, their students, and the family priests who are experts in the scriptures. If anyone I invite says anything disrespectful or refuses, let me know exactly what they say.” 

The disciples left in different directions, and soon Brahmavādis (learned sages) started arriving from many places. When Viçwāmitra's disciples returned, they told him what the Brahmavādis had said: “After hearing your message, all the holy men from different places are coming—some have already arrived. But Mahodaya and Vasishtha’s hundred sons haven’t come. Listen, great sage, to what they said, their voices shaking with emotion: ‘How can gods and saints accept offerings from someone who is a Chandāla and whose priest is a Kshatriya? And how can noble Brāhmanas, supported by Viçwāmitra, hope for heaven if they eat food from a Chandāla’s house?’ These harsh words—with anger in their eyes—were spoken by Vasishtha’s sons and Mahodaya.”

Hearing this, Viçwāmitra—his eyes now burning with anger—shouted, “Even though I am blameless, these wicked people criticize me for my harsh penances. Because of this, they will be burned to ashes. Today, bound by fate and destroyed by the son of Vivaswata, they will wander these worlds for seven hundred lifetimes, gathering dead men’s clothes, always eating dog meat, called Mushtikas. They’ll lose all sense of disgust and have twisted, frightening bodies and terrible habits. And Mahodaya, who wrongly insulted me, will become a Nishada, despised by all. He will live a cruel life, killing others, and suffer miserably for a long time because of my anger.”

After declaring this in front of the other saints, the powerful and fierce Viçwāmitra fell silent.
SECTION LX

Viśvāmitra, knowing through his yogic powers that Vasishtha’s sons and Mahodaya had been destroyed by his own ascetic energy, spoke to the other sages gathered around him. “This is Trisanku, a well-known descendant of Ikshwāku. He’s a good man, generous, and he’s come to me for help — he wants to reach heaven in his own body. So I ask you all to join me in this sacrifice, so that he can ascend to heaven alive.” The other Maharshis (great sages), hearing Viśvāmitra’s words, quickly agreed. They said, “Viśvāmitra, the descendant of Kuśika, is famous for his temper and his power. We should definitely do what he asks, or else he might curse us. He’s as dangerous as fire if he gets angry. Let’s just take part in the sacrifice, and maybe, through Viśvāmitra’s power, Trisanku really will reach heaven in his own body.” With that, the sages got ready for the ritual. Viśvāmitra himself acted as the chief priest. The other priests, experts in mantras and rituals, did everything by the book, reciting the proper chants and following every rule.

After a long time, when everything was set, Viśvāmitra — known for his intense austerities — called on all the gods to come and accept their share of the offerings. But none of the gods showed up to receive them. Seeing this, Viśvāmitra was furious. He grabbed a ladle and, burning with anger, turned to Trisanku. “Listen, King,” he said, “you’re about to see the real power of my penances. With my own ascetic energy, I’ll send you to heaven in your own body. I still have enough spiritual power left to do this — so get ready to ascend to heaven right now.”

As soon as Viśvāmitra said this, Trisanku, the descendant of Kākutstha, began to rise up towards heaven, right in front of all the other sages. But when Trisanku actually reached the gates of heaven, Indra (the destroyer of Pāka) and the other gods confronted him. “Trisanku,” they said, “go back. You don’t deserve to be here. Because of your guru’s curse, you have no right to live in heaven. Turn back and fall to earth, headfirst.” As soon as Indra said this, Trisanku started to fall from the sky, calling out desperately to Viśvāmitra, “Save me! Please, save me!”

Viśvāmitra heard Trisanku’s cries and was filled with even more rage. “Stop! Stay where you are!” he shouted. Right there among all the sages, Viśvāmitra, like a new creator (another Prajāpati), created seven new rishis on the southern path. Still burning with anger, he created a new set of stars. Dark with fury, Viśvāmitra built an entirely new constellation in the southern sky. Then he declared, “If I have to, I’ll create a new Indra. Or maybe my new world won’t need an Indra at all!” In his rage, he even began creating new gods.

This terrified everyone — the saints, the gods, and even the asuras (demons). They went to Viśvāmitra and pleaded with him: “O great sage, this king has been cursed by his own spiritual teacher. He really doesn’t deserve to enter heaven in his own body.” Viśvāmitra listened to what they said, and replied, “Look, I made a promise to Trisanku that he would ascend to heaven in his body. I can’t break my word. So let Trisanku stay up here in the sky, just as he is, and let the stars I created last as long as the world itself. You gods have to allow this.”

The gods answered Viśvāmitra: “So be it. Let it be as you wish. All these new stars you created will remain in the sky, outside the path of Vaicwanara (the sun). Trisanku will stay there too, shining among them, his head bowed. He’ll be like an immortal. All these new stars will follow Trisanku, the famous king, as if he really had reached heaven.”

Satisfied, Viśvāmitra addressed the sages and the gods: “Thank you, gods. This is good.” After the sacrifice ended, the gods and the sages, pleased with the outcome, returned to their own worlds.
SECTION LXI

When the saints had left, the powerful Viśwāmitra turned to the other forest dwellers and said, “There’s been a huge disturbance coming from the south. Let’s move to another place to continue our spiritual practices. There are vast lands to the west, and in Pushkara we can meditate in peace. That place is truly beautiful.” After saying this, the energetic and strong sage started intense austerities there, living only on fruits and roots.

At this same time, Amvarisha, the mighty king of Ayodhya, was preparing to hold a great sacrifice. But as the ceremony began, Indra stole the sacrificial animal. When the animal disappeared, the priest told the king, “O King, the beast has been stolen, and it’s your responsibility—it’s your fault for not protecting it. A king who fails to protect his subjects brings ruin on himself. There’s only one way to fix this: while the sacrifice is still going on, you must either get the animal back quickly or replace it with a man.”

Hearing the priest’s advice, the wise king set out, searching every land, province, city, forest, and holy place for the missing beast, offering a thousand cows as a reward. Eventually, he arrived at a place called Bhrigutunga. There he saw Richika sitting with his wife and sons.

Amvarisha bowed respectfully to Richika, who glowed with the power of his spiritual practice, and after checking on his well-being, said, “O noble one, son of Bhrigu, I need a substitute for my sacrificial animal. If you’re willing to sell me one of your sons, I can fulfill my duty. I’ve searched everywhere for the animal but had no luck. So, please, would you agree to part with one of your sons for a price?”

Richika replied, “O King, I will never give up my first-born son under any circumstances.”

After hearing this, Richika’s wife spoke to Amvarisha. “My husband has said he can’t part with his eldest son. But please know, my youngest son, Sunaka, is my favorite, so I can’t give him up either. Usually, fathers love their eldest sons most, and mothers, their youngest. That’s why I want to keep my youngest.”

With both parents having spoken, the second son, Sunasepha, spoke up himself. “My father won’t give up my older brother, and my mother won’t give up my younger brother. That leaves me—the second son—as the only option. So, O King, take me.”

When Sunasepha finished speaking, King Amvarisha, delighted, gave huge amounts of cows, piles of jewels, and hundreds and thousands of gold and silver coins in exchange for him. The famous and energetic king placed Sunasepha on his chariot and quickly set off, satisfied with the outcome.
SECTION LXII

As the sun reached its peak, King Ambarisha and his group, bringing Sunasepha with them, stopped to rest at the sacred lake of Pushkara. While the king took a break, Sunasepha, feeling desperate and hopeless, noticed his uncle Vishwamitra (Viçwāmitra) nearby, surrounded by wise sages deep in meditation. Exhausted, thirsty, and with a look of sorrow on his face, Sunasepha rushed over to Vishwamitra, collapsed at his feet, and pleaded, “I have no father, no mother, no family, and no friends left. Please, wise one, save me for the sake of what is right. You’re a protector and a refuge for so many. Can’t you help me? If the king can complete his ritual, and I can survive and someday reach heaven by doing good deeds, that would be true justice. Please, treat me like your own son and save me from this terrible fate.”

Vishwamitra, moved by Sunasepha’s plea, comforted him and then turned to his own sons. He said, “Sons, the reason parents have children is so that they can help each other, especially when it matters most. This young man is begging for my protection, and I want to help him. If one of you volunteers to take his place as the sacrificial victim for King Ambarisha’s ritual, you’ll be doing a great act of virtue. This way, Sunasepha will be spared, the sacrifice will go smoothly, the gods will be pleased, and I’ll be able to keep my promise.”

But Vishwamitra’s sons—Madhuchchhanda and the others—replied with scorn. “Father, how can you even think of sacrificing your own sons to save someone else’s child? That’s as awful as eating your own flesh. We refuse.”

Furious at their disrespect and lack of compassion, Vishwamitra’s eyes blazed with anger. He cursed them, saying, “You have ignored my words and spoken with arrogance and cruelty. For this, you will live as outcasts, eating only dog’s meat, for a thousand years—just as Vasishtha’s sons were once cursed.”

Turning back to Sunasepha, Vishwamitra tried to lift his spirits. He instructed, “Put on a belt made of sacred grass (kusha), wear a garland of red flowers, smear your body with red sandalwood paste, and approach the sacrificial stake. While you do this, recite these special prayers to Agni, the fire god, and also chant these two verses during King Ambarisha’s ritual. If you do this sincerely, you will be saved.”

Sunasepha memorized the prayers and, gathering his courage, returned to King Ambarisha. “Great king,” he said, “let’s not delay. Please begin the ceremony and allow me to start the initiation.”

Hearing this, the king was overjoyed. He quickly led Sunasepha to the sacrificial area, and with his council’s approval, tied Sunasepha to the stake using a kusha grass rope and dressed him in red, as the ritual required.

Bound to the stake, Sunasepha began to sing hymns to Agni, and then prayed to Indra and his brother. Pleased by Sunasepha’s heartfelt prayers, Indra—the thousand-eyed king of the gods—granted him a long life. Thanks to the power of the ritual and the gods’ favor, King Ambarisha successfully completed the sacrifice and received many blessings.

After this, Vishwamitra, with his incredible self-discipline, continued his intense meditation at Pushkara for another thousand years.
SECTION LXIII

After a thousand years of intense meditation and discipline, Viśvāmitra (Visvamitra) finally completed his vow. All the gods came together, wanting to reward him for his dedication. The radiant Brahmā appeared and spoke kindly to him: “You are now a true sage—this honor is yours because of your own hard work.” With that, the king of the gods returned to heaven. But Viśvāmitra, still full of determination, went back to his strict practices. 

Some time passed. Then, the famous Apsarā Menakā was bathing at Pushkara. Viśvāmitra noticed her—she stood out like lightning in storm clouds. Overcome by desire, he called out to her, “Menakā, how has your journey been? Please stay here at my hermitage. Grant me your company; I’ve been completely overwhelmed by love.” Menakā, who was strikingly beautiful, agreed and stayed there. Her presence became a major distraction from Viśvāmitra’s spiritual work. For ten years—five and five—she lived happily in his hermitage, keeping him from his meditation.

When those years had passed, Viśvāmitra was suddenly filled with shame, worry, and regret. He realized that the gods had set this trap for him, and that he had lost years of progress because of his own desires. Those ten years had slipped by so quickly, it felt like only a day and night had passed. Now, this obstacle stood between him and his goal. Sighing deeply, he burned with guilt and self-reproach.

With gentle words, he told the trembling, terrified Menakā—who stood before him with hands pressed in a gesture of pleading—that she should leave. Then Viśvāmitra left for the northern mountains, determined to conquer his desires through even harsher discipline. He practiced a life of complete celibacy, pushing himself harder than ever on the banks of the Kauśikī river.

Viśvāmitra spent another thousand years in severe meditation in the northern mountains. Eventually, the gods and sages met and approached Brahmā. They said, “Let Kuśika’s son earn the title of Maharshi—Great Sage.” Brahmā summoned Viśvāmitra and said kindly, “O mighty sage, has your journey gone well? Your fierce dedication has impressed me, Viśvāmitra. I now acknowledge you as a Maharshi, the highest of sages.”

Viśvāmitra bowed and replied, “The ultimate title—Brahmarshi—is earned by someone who has truly mastered themselves. Since you haven’t addressed me by that name, it must mean I haven’t yet achieved that.” Brahmā answered, “Keep striving until you have complete control over your senses.” With that, Brahmā returned to heaven.

Once the gods had left, Viśvāmitra pushed himself even further. He raised his arms, gave up all physical comforts, and lived on nothing but air. In summer, he surrounded himself with five fires; in the rainy season, he stayed outside with no shelter; in winter, he stood in freezing water day and night. He continued these brutal penances for another thousand years.

Viśvāmitra’s severe efforts deeply worried the gods—especially Indra (Śakra), king of the gods. Indra, along with the wind gods (Maruts), turned to the Apsarā Rambhā. They gave her instructions that would benefit themselves, but spell trouble for Viśvāmitra.
SECTION LXIV

“Rambhā, you have to do something important for the gods,” said Indra, the thousand-eyed leader of the celestials. “You must try to seduce Kauśika (that’s Viśvāmitra) with your beauty and charm.” Hearing this, Rambhā, the Apsara, folded her hands nervously and replied, “Lord of the gods, Viśvāmitra is a terrifying ascetic. I’m certain that if I try to distract him, he’ll get angry and curse me. I’m really afraid, so I beg you, please protect me.” Seeing how scared she was, Indra tried to reassure her. “Don’t worry, Rambhā. Nothing bad will happen to you. Just do what I ask. I’ll disguise myself as a koel bird and stay nearby in this beautiful springtime forest with Kandarpa (the god of love). With your beauty and your skills, try to enchant Viśvāmitra, gentle one.” 

Hearing Indra’s words, Rambhā, her smile radiant, made herself as attractive as possible and tried to arouse desire in Viśvāmitra. He listened to the sweet song of the koel and saw the stunningly beautiful Rambhā, and his heart was filled with pleasure. But as he heard the bird’s singing, her own lovely voice, and looked at Rambhā, Viśvāmitra began to suspect something was wrong. He quickly realized this was a setup by Indra, the thousand-eyed god. Furious, the great ascetic, son of Kuśika, cursed Rambhā: “Rambhā, because you tried to tempt me when I’m struggling to control my anger and desires, you will become a stone for ten thousand years. Only a powerful Brahmin, strong in asceticism, will be able to free you—my anger has stained you.” 

As soon as Viśvāmitra, powerful and intense, pronounced the curse, he was overwhelmed with regret, unable to control his raging anger. Because of his harsh curse, Rambhā instantly turned to stone. When they heard his words, both Kandarpa and Indra left immediately. But Viśvāmitra was still angry, and since he hadn’t fully mastered his emotions, this anger chipped away at his spiritual power. Realizing he was losing his hard-earned ascetic merit, he thought, “I won’t let anger control me anymore. I won’t speak to anyone, or even breathe, for a hundred years. I’ll restrain my senses and dry up my body. Until I reach the highest spiritual state, I’ll hold my breath, eat nothing, and stay in strict meditation. My body will not weaken while I pursue these austerities.” With that, the great sage bound himself to this intense vow of self-control and renunciation.
SECTION LXV

Turning away from the north, the powerful sage Viśvāmitra moved east, Rāma, and began a new round of intense austerities. He took a vow of total silence for a thousand years, pushing himself to incredible limits. After those thousand years passed, Viśvāmitra faced many tests, standing still like a tree, but he refused to give in to anger. Determined to keep his mind pure, he protected his hard-earned spiritual power. When the thousand years ended, he decided he would finally allow himself some boiled rice to eat. But just then, Rāma, Indra disguised himself as a holy man and asked Viśvāmitra for the rice. Without hesitation, Viśvāmitra gave away all his rice to Indra, and so he was left with nothing to eat. Still holding to his vow of silence, he didn’t say a word to the disguised Indra. He then resumed his silent practice, this time holding his breath for a thousand years. As he did this, heat and vapors began to rise from his head. The energy of his meditation became so intense that the entire universe seemed to catch fire, filling everyone with fear. The spirits, gods, Gandharvas, Nāgas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, all shaken and weakened by Viśvāmitra’s energy, gathered and approached Brahmā, the Creator. They pleaded, “Lord, we’ve tried everything to distract the great sage Viśvāmitra with desire and greed, but nothing works—he just becomes more powerful. He shows no signs of anger or lust. If he doesn’t get what he’s seeking, he could destroy all three worlds and everything in them. The directions are in chaos, the oceans are disturbed, mountains are splitting, the earth is shaking, and the wind never stops. We don’t know how to fix this. It’s like everyone is paralyzed. The world is dazed, and even the sun’s light has faded because of his power.”

They continued, “So, Lord, before this mighty sage, intent on destruction, burns everything to ashes like the fire at the end of the world, we have to calm him down. Even if he wants to rule the heavens, give him whatever he wishes.” Then, the gods, led by Brahmā, came to Viśvāmitra and spoke kindly: “Welcome, O Brahmarshi! We’re pleased with your penance. Son of Kuśika, because of your intense austerities, you have become a true Brāhmaṇa. We, along with the wind gods, grant you long life. Blessings to you—go wherever you please!” Hearing Brahmā’s words, Viśvāmitra bowed to the gods and replied joyfully, “If I have truly earned the status of Brāhmaṇa and long life, then let the sacred Omkāra, the Vashatkāra, and the Vedas themselves acknowledge me. And let Vasishtha—Brahmā’s own son, the greatest knower of both the art of kingship and spiritual wisdom—recognize me as a Brāhmaṇa. Once you grant me this, I’ll be satisfied.” The gods agreed, and Vasishtha, the greatest of sages, made peace with Viśvāmitra, saying, “So be it. You are a Brahmarshi—there’s no doubt. Everything you wanted has been achieved.” With that, the gods returned to their realms. Viśvāmitra, now recognized as a Brahmarshi, paid respects to Vasishtha and, having reached his goal, wandered the world in his ascetic life. So, Rāma, that’s how the high-minded Viśvāmitra truly became a Brāhmaṇa. He is the best of sages, the very embodiment of asceticism, always living by duty, and the pillar of spiritual energy.

After telling this story, the wise sage paused. Hearing Satānanda’s tale in front of Rāma and Lakshmana, King Janaka pressed his palms together and spoke to Viśvāmitra: “I am truly blessed that you, O Kauśika, have come to my sacrifice with Rāma. Just seeing you, great sage, makes me feel purified and inspired. We’ve listened in detail to the story of your incredible austerities, and everyone here—myself, Rāma, and the courtiers—has heard about your immense power and virtues. Your strength and qualities are beyond measure, son of Kuśika. I could never get tired of hearing such an amazing story. Now, great sage, it’s time for our daily devotions—the sun is setting. Tomorrow morning, I hope you’ll see me again. You are always welcome, master of wisdom—please show me your favor.” With these words, the king, full of respect, circled Viśvāmitra along with his priests and friends, then left. Viśvāmitra, along with Rāma and Lakshmana, honored by everyone, also settled in for the night.
SECTION LXVI

The next morning was bright and clear. After finishing his daily prayers, King Janaka welcomed Viśvāmitra and the two princes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. Following the proper rituals, Janaka honored both the sage and the two sons of Daśaratha. With respect, he asked, “Greetings, respected sir! What can I do for you, O sinless one? Please tell me your wish. I am ready to serve you.” 

Viśvāmitra, who was wise and full of virtue, replied, “These sons of Daśaratha—both Kṣatriyas, famous among men—are eager to see the legendary bow you have in your possession. Please show it to them, and may all go well for you. Once they have seen the bow, their wishes will be fulfilled, and they can choose to return as they like.”

Janaka answered the great sage, saying, “Listen to the story of why the bow is here. Long ago, there was a king named Devarāta, the elder brother of Nimi. This powerful bow was entrusted to him. In the past, Lord Śiva, intending to destroy Daksha’s sacrifice, drew this bow in anger and threatened the gods, saying, ‘Since you deny me my share of the sacrifice, I will use my bow to cut off your heads.’ The gods, terrified, pleaded with Śiva, and he was eventually pleased with them. He then gave this bow to those noble ancestors of mine. This very bow, a treasure from the great god himself, was finally entrusted to our family.

As for my daughter, Sītā, she appeared from the earth as I was ploughing a sacred field. Because I found her during this holy act, she is called Sītā. She grew up as my daughter, though she was not born in the usual way. I decided that whoever could string this bow would win her hand in marriage.

Many kings have come here, hoping to marry my daughter Sītā. But since the condition was that her suitor must show his strength by stringing the bow, I refused to give her away to any king who could not do it. As a result, many rulers gathered in Mithilā, wanting to test their strength with the bow. I showed it to them, but none could even lift or handle it. Seeing that these powerful kings were not strong enough, I dismissed them.

But then, angry and frustrated, these kings laid siege to Mithilā, doubting their own strength and blaming me. They attacked my city furiously, and after a year, my defenses were exhausted. I was deeply troubled by this. I prayed to the gods, and they answered me by granting me a mighty four-division army. With this help, the wicked kings were defeated, and they fled in all directions, their strength and confidence broken.

Now, O great sage, I will show this radiant bow to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. If Rāma can string the bow, I will give my daughter Sītā—who was not born from a woman—to the son of Daśaratha.”
SECTION LXVII

After hearing what Janaka had said, the powerful sage Viśvāmitra turned to the king and said, “Show the bow to Rāma.” Janaka then ordered his ministers, “Bring the legendary bow here, the one covered in oils and decorated with garlands.” Following his command, the ministers entered the city and, putting the massive bow at the front, began to bring it out. It was stored in an iron case mounted on a cart with eight wheels, and even then, it took five thousand strong men to pull it out, straining with all their might.

When the ministers finally arrived, they spoke to Janaka, who seemed almost godlike, and said, “O King, here is the greatest of all bows, honored by every ruler. O lord of Mithila, if you think it’s appropriate, show it.” Hearing this, Janaka joined his hands respectfully and spoke to the great Viśvāmitra, as well as to Rāma and Lakshmana. “This bow,” he said, “has always been worshipped by the kings of my family, as well as by powerful rulers who couldn’t even lift or string it. Not even the gods, demons, rakshasas, gandharvas, yakshas, kinnaras, or giant serpents have been able to string it, stretch it, or even fit an arrow to it. If these beings can’t use it, how could any human succeed? Still, here it is, O great sage. Please show it to these sons of the king.”

Viśvāmitra answered Janaka and said to Rāma, “Rāma, my dear, take a look at this bow.” At the sage’s words, Rāma opened the iron case, looked at the bow, and said, “I want to touch this divine bow. Should I also try to lift and string it?” Both Janaka and Viśvāmitra answered, “Go ahead.” In front of thousands of onlookers, Rāma, with calm confidence, grasped the bow in the center, strung it easily, and pulled it back. As he did, the bow snapped in two right in the middle.

The sound of the breaking bow was like a giant thunderclap. The ground shook violently, as if a mountain had split apart nearby. The shockwave was so intense that everyone except Viśvāmitra, Janaka, and the two brothers, Rāma and Lakshmana, were knocked off their feet.

Once the crowd had recovered, Janaka, relieved and with his hands joined, spoke to Viśvāmitra. “O revered one, I have witnessed the incredible strength of Daśaratha’s son. This is truly amazing and hard to believe—I never thought it possible. Now that my daughter Sītā will be joined with her husband, Rāma, son of Daśaratha, our family will be honored. My promise—that I would give Sītā’s hand to whoever could string the bow—has been fulfilled, O son of Kuśika. Sītā, who is dearer to me than life itself, will now be given to Rāma. With your permission, O Brāhmana, let my counselors quickly travel to Ayodhyā in chariots. Let them respectfully invite King Daśaratha to my city, tell him about Sītā being given to Rāma for stringing the bow, and reassure him of the safety of his sons under your care. Let them bring the delighted king here as soon as possible.”

Viśvāmitra, the son of Kuśika, replied, “So be it.” Then Janaka called his counselors and sent them to Ayodhyā with a letter, telling them to inform King Daśaratha of everything and invite him to Mithila at once.
SECTION LXVIII

Following Janaka’s orders, the messengers spent three days traveling before finally reaching the city of Ayodhya. Their carts and horses were worn out from the journey. Once inside the city, they went straight to the royal palace, just as Janaka had instructed. They soon met the elderly King Dasharatha, who looked almost otherworldly in his dignity. Feeling at ease, the envoys bowed respectfully and spoke in gentle, polite voices: “Great King, Janaka of Mithila, together with his priests, sends his warmest greetings. He hopes that you, your priests, and your servants are all well. After making sure you are well, King Janaka—by the blessing of Sage Kaushika—asks us to tell you this: ‘You know the promise I once made—to give my daughter in marriage to whoever could string the great bow. Many kings tried and failed, losing their pride and even blaming me for their defeat. But now, your son, who came here with Sage Vishwamitra, has succeeded. Rama broke the sacred, jeweled bow right in front of everyone. He has won my daughter Sita, whose hand was to be given only as a reward for such strength. I wish to fulfill my vow by marrying Sita to Rama, if you give your blessing. Please, honored King, come quickly to Mithila with your priests. Witness the union of your sons and see me freed from my vow. May you share in the happiness of their wedding.’ These are the words of King Janaka, passed on with the approval of Vishwamitra and Satānanda.” Hearing this message, King Dasharatha was overjoyed. He turned to Vasishtha, Vāmadeva, and his advisors and said,

“Thanks to Sage Vishwamitra’s protection, Rama—the pride of Kausalya—is safe in Mithila with his brother Lakshmana. King Janaka has seen what Rama can do and wants to make him his son-in-law. If all of you agree, let’s not waste any time. We should leave for Mithila as soon as possible.” The advisors and the Maharshis quickly agreed, exclaiming, “Excellent!” Dasharatha, beaming with happiness, told his staff, “We set out tomorrow morning.” That night, Janaka’s envoys, who had been treated with every courtesy by Dasharatha and his people, rested happily and comfortably in Ayodhya.
SECTION LXIX

At dawn, after a restful night, King Dasharatha gathered his priests and followers. He was in high spirits as he spoke to Sumantra: “Today, have the treasury officers take plenty of fine wealth and precious gems and send them ahead with a proper escort. The army should move out quickly. Make sure the horses, chariots, and all the fancy vehicles leave at my order. Vasishtha, Vamadeva, Javali, Kashyapa, Markandeya, and the sage Katyayana—all these revered sages—should go ahead too. And you, Sumantra, get my chariot ready. We can’t waste any time; the messengers are urging us to hurry.” Following the king’s instructions, the army and the sages all traveled behind him. After journeying for four days, they reached the kingdom of Videha.
When King Janaka heard that Dasharatha had arrived, he was thrilled. He welcomed the elder king with honor and respect, treating him as a distinguished guest.

Janaka said warmly, “Did you have a good journey, greatest of men? I’m lucky to have you here, descendant of Raghu. Enjoy the happiness your sons have brought you. I’m also fortunate to welcome the powerful and respected sage Vasishtha, along with these eminent sages—just as the gods honor Indra, who performed a hundred sacrifices. By good fortune, every obstacle has been overcome, and my family is now tied to the mighty Raghus, gaining new honor. Tomorrow morning, after the sacrifice is complete, let’s hold the weddings, with all the great sages present.” 

Hearing this, Dasharatha replied in front of everyone, “A gift should be accepted—so I’ve learned. And we will do as you say, since it’s the right thing.”

Janaka was impressed by Dasharatha’s honest and honorable words. The sages, filled with joy, spent the night enjoying each other’s company. Dasharatha, delighted to see his sons—the Raghus—passed the night in great happiness, treated splendidly by Janaka. Meanwhile, Janaka, wise and knowledgeable, completed the sacrificial rituals and all the preparations for his daughters’ weddings, then rested for the night.
SECTION LXX

The next morning, after completing his daily rituals with the great sages, King Janaka—who was skilled with words—spoke to his priest, Satānanda. He said, “My powerful and righteous brother, Kusādhwaja, lives in the blessed city of Sānkāçyā. Its walls are lined with sharp weapons, it sits on the banks of the Ikshumati River, and it looks almost heavenly, like the flying chariot Pushpaka. I want to see him—he’s in charge of my sacrifice, and I want him to share in our happiness today.” After telling this to Satānanda, Janaka called for some capable messengers and ordered them to travel to Sānkāçyā. Taking his orders, they mounted fast horses and sped off—ready to bring Kusādhwaja back, just as Vishnu comes when Indra calls. When they reached Sānkāçyā, the messengers met Kusādhwaja and faithfully shared Janaka’s message. Hearing this, Kusādhwaja immediately set out for Videha, obeying his brother’s summons. When he arrived, he greeted both Janaka and Satānanda with respect, then took a seat fit for a king. Once seated, both Janaka and Kusādhwaja, glowing with energy, turned to their chief counselor, Sudāmana. They said, “Go quickly, Sudāmana, and bring the great Ikshwāku king along with his sons and ministers.” Sudāmana hurried to the camp and found King Daçarātha, the pride of the Raghu dynasty. Bowing deeply, he said, “O mighty king of Ayodhyā, Janaka, ruler of Mithilā, wishes to see you and your priests.” Hearing this, Daçarātha gathered his sages, priests, and advisors, and went to meet Janaka. Surrounded by his court, Daçarātha spoke to Janaka, “O noble king, you know that the wise sage Vasishtha has always been our family’s spiritual guide. He’s the one who speaks for us in every ceremony. With the approval of Viçwāmitra and all the other sages, Vasishtha will now tell you about my ancestry.” Daçarātha fell silent, and the revered sage Vasishtha, master of words, began to speak to Janaka and his priests: “The eternal Brahmā was born from the Unmanifest. From Brahmā came Maricha, and Maricha’s son was Kaçyapa. Kaçyapa’s son was Vivaswat, and Vivaswat’s son was Manu. Manu—also called Prajipati—was the father of Ikshwāku. Ikshwāku, as you know, was the first king of Ayodhyā. His son was the noble Kukshi, whose son was Vikukshi. Vikukshi’s son was the mighty Vāna, and Vāna’s son was the powerful Anaranya. Anaranya’s son was Prithu, whose son was Trisanku. Trisanku’s son was the famous Dhundumāra; his son was the great charioteer Yuvanaçya. Yuvanaçya’s son was Māndhātā, ruler of the earth. Māndhātā’s son was the noble Susandhi, and Susandhi had two sons: Dhruvasandhi and Prasenajit. Dhruvasandhi’s son was Bharata, and Bharata’s son was Asita. Asita faced powerful enemies—the Haihayas, Tālajanghas, and Sasavindas. Outnumbered, Asita fled to the Himalayas with his two wives, and died there. Legend says both wives were pregnant; one, jealous, secretly gave the other poison to destroy her baby. At that time, the sage Chyavana, son of Bhrigu, was living in the Himalayas. One of the widowed queens, Kālindi, approached Chyavana and asked for his blessing for a son. Chyavana told her, ‘You will soon give birth to a powerful, energetic, and noble son, even though he has been poisoned. Don’t worry.’ With Chyavana’s blessing, Kālindi—widowed and grieving—gave birth to a son. And because her rival tried to poison her unborn child, that son was named Sagara, meaning ‘with poison.’

Sagara’s son was Asamanja, and Asamanja’s son was Ançumāt. Ançumāt’s son was Dilipa, and Dilipa’s son was Bhagiratha. From Bhagiratha came Kākutstha, then Raghu. Raghu’s son was the fierce Pravridha, who once ate human flesh and became known as Kalmāshapāda. His son was Sankhana; Sankhana’s son was Sudarçana. Sudarçana’s son was Agnivarna; Agnivarna’s was Sighraga; Sighraga’s son was Maru. Maru’s son was Praçucruka, and his son was Amvarisha. Amvarisha’s son was Nahusha, ruler of the earth. Nahusha’s son was Yayāti, and Yayāti’s son was Nābhāga. Nābhāga’s son was Aja, and Aja’s son was Daçarātha. And from Daçarātha came the brothers Rāma and Lakshmana. It is for Rāma and Lakshmana—heroes from the noble, honest, and pure Ikshwāku dynasty—that we now ask for your daughters’ hands in marriage. O great king, it is fitting to unite worthy brides with worthy grooms.”
SECTION LXXI

After Vasishtha finished speaking, Janaka folded his hands respectfully and replied, “Please allow me to tell you about my family line, as is proper when giving away daughters in marriage. It’s important for someone with a noble lineage to describe their ancestry themselves. So, listen closely, great sage. There was a king named Nimi, famous throughout the three worlds for his deeds—he was deeply religious and strong. His son was Mithi, and Mithi’s son was Janaka. Because of this King Janaka, all of us in our line have been called by that name. From Janaka came Udāvasu, whose son was the righteous Nandivardhana. Nandivardhana’s son was the brave Suketu, and Suketu’s son was the mighty and just Devarāta. Devarāta’s son was Vrihadratha, and Vrihadratha’s son was the powerful Mahāvira. Mahāvira’s son was Sudhriti, who was both patient and truthful. Sudhriti’s son was the virtuous and just Dhritaketu, and Dhritaketu’s son was Haryyaçya. Haryyaçya’s son was Maru, and Maru’s son was Pratindhaka. Pratindhaka’s son was the righteous Kirtiratha. Kirtiratha’s son was Devamirha; Devamirha’s son was Vibudha; Vibudha’s son was Mahidhraka. Mahidhraka’s son was another Kirtiratha, known for his strength. This Kirtiratha’s son was Mohāromā, and Mohāromā’s son was Sarnaromā, who was virtuous. Sarnaromā’s son was Hraswaromā, a wise king who understood right and wrong. Hraswaromā had two sons: I am the elder, and my younger brother is the brave Kuçadhwaja. After making me king and putting Kuçadhwaja under my care, our father left for the forest. When he passed away, I ruled the kingdom fairly and looked after my brother Kuçadhwaja with love, as if he were a god.

One day, a powerful king named Sudhanwā from the city of Sankaçya came to Mithilā and threatened to attack. He sent me a message demanding the great bow of Siva and the hand of my daughter, the lotus-eyed Sitā. Because I refused him both, Sudhanwā started a war against me. I defeated and killed him in battle. After that, I made my brother Kuçadhwaja the king of Sankaçya. So, noble sage, Kuçadhwaja is my younger brother, and I am the elder. I am happy to offer my daughters to you as daughters-in-law: Sitā to Rāma, and Urmilā to Lakshmana. I swear three times that I genuinely and gladly give you my second daughter Urmilā, as well as Sitā, who is as radiant as a goddess and has bravery as her dowry. Now, please arrange the Godāna ceremony for Rāma and Lakshmana’s weddings, perform the ancestral rituals, and then finish the marriage ceremony. Today, the star Maghā is ascendant. On the third day, when Phālguna moves north, please perform the marriage ceremony, O king. In the meantime, you should give gifts to bless Rāma and Lakshmana.”
SECTION LXXII

After Sita (Vaideha) finished speaking, the powerful sage Vishvamitra, along with Vasishtha, turned to the king and said, “O mighty king, the families of the Ikshwakus and the Vaidehas are truly remarkable—no other lineages can compare to them. And now, the young couples—Rama and Lakshmana with Sita and Urmila—are perfectly matched in every way. Their union is full of grace and dignity. Now, please listen to what I have to say. Your brother, King Kushadhwaja, is a man of great virtue and morality. He also has two daughters, who are said to be the most beautiful women on earth. We would like to ask for their hands in marriage—for them to become the wives of Prince Bharata and the wise Shatrughna—just as we have asked for your own daughters for Rama and Lakshmana. The sons of Dasharatha are young, handsome, and strong, almost god-like in their appearance and abilities. So, great king, by joining their families through both brothers, you would unite the Ikshwaku line even more closely. Don’t hesitate about this decision!”

Hearing these words from Vishvamitra, supported by Vasishtha, King Janaka folded his hands in respect and replied, "I feel blessed that such powerful sages wish for this alliance. Whatever you desire, I will make it happen—may good fortune come to us all. Let Kushadhwaja’s daughters marry Shatrughna and Bharata. On the same day, let all four princes wed the four princesses. According to tradition, the most auspicious time for a wedding is the day after the Phalgunis are in ascendance, with Bhaga as the presiding deity.”

After saying these kind words, King Janaka rose and respectfully addressed the two sages again: “I have gained great spiritual merit from these marriages, and I am also your devoted student. Please, both of you, take seats on these thrones of honor. Just as this kingdom belongs to Dasharatha, so does Ayodhya belong to me. Don’t have any doubts about your authority here; do whatever you think is best.”

As Janaka spoke, King Dasharatha, son of Raghu, replied with a smile, “You and your brother, lords of Mithila, have so many virtues. You always honor both saints and kings—may you always have good fortune. I will now go back to my quarters to perform the Sraddha ceremonies as tradition requires.”

With that, Dasharatha greeted Janaka and, leading the sages, left for his chambers. Once he arrived, Dasharatha performed the Sraddha ritual as required, and the next morning he completed the Godana ceremony at the proper time. He gave away hundreds and thousands of cows to the Brahmins, wishing for the well-being of his sons. In total, he donated four hundred thousand cows, each with golden-tipped horns and a calf, along with bronze vessels for milking. Dasharatha, devoted to his sons, also gifted the Brahmins many other valuable items. Surrounded by his sons, the powerful king looked like Prajapati himself, encircled by the guardians of the world.
SECTION LXXII

On the same day that King Daçarātha gave out generous gifts of cows, a heroic man named Yudhājit—son of the king of the Kekayas and Bharata’s maternal uncle—arrived to see Daçarātha. After greeting the king and checking on his health, Yudhājit said, “My father, the lord of the Kekayas, sends his love and wishes you well. He adds that everyone you care about is doing fine. And, O great king, eager to see my nephew Bharata, my father traveled to Ayodhyā. But when he found out in Ayodhyā that you and your sons had all gone to Mithilā for marriage, I hurried here to see my sister’s son.”

Daçarātha welcomed his beloved guest with all the respect he deserved. After spending the night with his wise sons, Daçarātha woke up early, finished his morning rituals, and, along with the holy sages, went to the entrance of the sacrificial grounds. At the auspicious moment called Vijaya, Rāma, with Vasishtha and the other great sages leading, came forward with his brothers. They were all wearing wedding ornaments, having completed the rituals for their marriages.

Vasishtha respectfully approached King Janaka (also called Vaideha) and said, “King Daçarātha, the greatest of rulers, has brought his sons—who have finished all the wedding rituals—and now waits for you, the giver of the brides. The meeting of giver and receiver is essential for such a ceremony. Please honor tradition by completing this sacred wedding.”

Janaka, generous and wise, replied, “Who stands at my gate and stops my guests? Who would question someone entering his own house? This kingdom is as much yours as mine. My daughters, radiant as fire, are ready for their weddings and waiting at the foot of the dais. I’ve been looking out for you every moment. Let’s proceed—there’s no reason to delay.”

After Janaka spoke, Daçarātha and his sons, along with the sages, entered the ritual grounds. Vasishtha then said to Janaka, “O wise king, please, together with the holy men, begin the wedding ceremony for Rāma, who is loved by all.”

Janaka agreed. Vasishtha, with Viçwāmitra and the saintly Satānanda in front, set up the wedding platform. They decorated it with fragrant flowers, golden ladles, colorful water-pots, trays with barley, incense burners, conch shells, sacrificial spoons, vessels with offerings, fried rice, and blessed grains. Vasishtha then spread a sacred grass canopy over the dais, reciting the proper mantras. Lighting the ritual fire, he began the offerings.

Janaka brought forward Sītā, adorned with beautiful jewelry, and placed her in front of Rāma. He said to him, “Here is my daughter Sītā. Take her hand as your partner in all duties. May she be virtuous and devoted, following you as faithfully as your own shadow.” Saying this, Janaka poured consecrated water on Rāma’s hand while the gods and sages cheered, “Wonderful! Wonderful!” Heavenly drums sounded and flower petals rained down from above.

Overjoyed after giving Sītā to Rāma, Janaka said, “Come, Lakshmana. Take Urmilā, who is ready to wed you. Take her hand, and don’t delay.” Then he turned to Bharata: “O descendant of Raghu, take Mandavyā’s hand as your wife.” Finally, he addressed Satrughna: “O mighty one, take Srutakirti’s hand. May you all be blessed and live excellent lives with your wives. Don’t wait any longer.”

Hearing Janaka’s words, the four sons of Raghu, guided by Vasishtha, took the hands of their brides and circled the sacred fire, the dais, the king, and the holy sages. With their wives, they performed the marriage rituals exactly as tradition required. From the sky came a dazzling rain of flowers, and the air filled with the music of divine drums, singing, and instruments. The Apsarās danced and the Gandharvas sang to celebrate the marriage of the princes. It was a spectacular sight.

With trumpets blaring, the newly married couples circled the fire three times and then left for their camp. King Daçarātha, satisfied that all the sacred rituals were complete, followed them, along with the sages and his followers.
SECTION LXXIV

When dawn broke, the powerful sage Viśvāmitra greeted King Daśaratha and then set out toward the northern mountains. After Viśvāmitra left, King Daśaratha paid his respects to King Janaka (Mithilā’s lord, sometimes called Vaideha) and began getting ready to return to his own capital. To honor the occasion, King Janaka gave a generous dowry filled with all sorts of gifts. He presented many hundreds of thousands of cows, fine woolen blankets, countless ordinary cloths, elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers, as well as a hundred beautifully adorned young women to serve as maids. Delighted, King Janaka also gave gold, silver, pearls, and coral as part of this noble dowry.
