Rāma greeted them all with kind words, then climbed into a magnificent chariot—glittering with silver, lined with tiger skin, and shining like fire. The chariot rumbled like thunder, decorated with jewels and gold so bright it almost hurt to look at, just like the golden peaks of Mount Sumeru. Two powerful horses, as strong as young elephants, were harnessed to the chariot, pulling it swiftly like Indra’s own ride. As Rāma—the radiant Rāghava—set out, the sound filled the air like distant thunder. He left his home like the moon emerging from behind a thick cloud. Lakshmana stood behind him on the chariot, holding a shining fan to guard his brother. The crowd outside erupted in excitement as Rāma appeared. Hundreds, then thousands, of beautifully decorated horses and elephants joined the procession, looking like moving mountains. Ahead of him marched rows of warriors, their bodies scented with sandalwood and aguru, carrying swords and weapons, while priests and singers chanted blessings. On the way, Rāma heard music, cheering, and loud praise from the crowd. Beautifully dressed women leaned out from windows, showering him with flowers, and praised him from rooftops and streets: “Son of Kauśalyā, today your mother must be so proud to see you headed for your coronation!” The women admired Sītā too, whispering that she must have been blessed in a past life to become Rāma’s wife—just as Rohini is to the Moon. Rāma heard all these kind words as he passed. The citizens, coming from every direction, chatted excitedly: “Rāma will soon receive great fortune from the king. When he becomes our ruler, all our wishes will come true. It’s such a blessing for us that he will lead the entire kingdom. With him in charge, we’ll never have to fear misfortune.” Rāma, like Vaisravana himself, moved forward, led by the thunder of his horses and elephants, his name sung by poets and bards praising his noble lineage. He saw the palace courtyards filled with elephants, horses, and chariots, and the streets crowded with people, pearls, and merchants selling their wares.
SECTION XVII

Rama, with his friends thrilled around him, climbed into his chariot and looked out over the city. The streets were decorated with flags and banners, and the air was thick with the scent of incense and aguru wood. The highway was packed with people and the houses lining it were as white as pale clouds. Everywhere between the buildings, the air was filled with the fragrance of incense and sandalwood. The road itself was wide and beautiful, covered with sandalwood, aguru, and other luxurious scents. There were silks and red fabrics draped around, strings of pearls and crystals, and colorful flowers scattered everywhere. Food of every kind was piled high. The atmosphere felt almost heavenly—Rama saw the highway and the courtyard, both covered with curd, clarified butter, puffed rice, incense, aguru, sandalwood, garlands, and other fragrances.

As he made his way forward, he heard people offering blessings, saying things like, “Now that you’re being crowned, follow the path of your father and grandfathers—protect us and take care of the kingdom. With you as king, we’ll be even happier than we were under your ancestors. We don’t care about riches or the afterlife—if we can just see Rama crowned, nothing could make us happier. There’s nothing better than seeing the powerful Rama on the throne.” Rama listened to all these good wishes and, though they praised him, he stayed calm and kept walking. As he passed, no one could take their eyes off him—he was truly admired by everyone. If someone didn’t see Rama, or Rama didn’t notice them, that person was looked down on and even felt ashamed. Rama was kind to everyone, young and old, of all backgrounds, so naturally everyone respected and obeyed him.

He walked on, leaving the crossroads, temple paths, sacred fig trees, and altars to his left, and finally arrived at the royal family’s residence. The palace was magnificent, with towers reaching up into the sky, shining white like clouds, as tall as Mount Kailasa, and dotted with pleasure houses decorated with pearls. Rama, the king’s handsome son, entered his father’s palace—the greatest palace on earth, worthy of Indra himself.

He rode through three heavily guarded chambers, each watched over by armed warriors, and then passed two more, guarded by men on foot. After making his way through all these, he told his followers to wait outside and went into the private quarters alone. As Rama entered to meet his father, everyone inside was filled with happiness and had been eagerly awaiting his arrival, just as the ocean longs for the moon to rise.
SECTION XVIII

When Rāma entered, he saw his father, King Daśaratha, sitting on a beautiful couch next to Kaikeyi. The king looked miserable, weak, and drained, with sadness written all over his face. Rāma bowed respectfully at his father's feet, then greeted Kaikeyi with proper respect. The king could only say “Rāma,” and his eyes filled with tears. He couldn’t look at his son or find the words to speak. Seeing his father in such an unexpected and terrible state—like a snake crushed underfoot—Rāma was shaken with fear. He grew anxious, his heart aching with worry and regret. He sighed heavily, feeling like his heart was tossed around by waves, confused and dark like the sun during an eclipse, or like a monk caught in a lie. The king’s unexpected grief made Rāma feel like the ocean in turmoil under a full moon. Always caring for his father’s well-being, Rāma wondered, “Why isn’t the king happy to see me today? Even when he was upset, he’d smile when I walked in. Why is he still sad, even now?” Worried and pale, Rāma turned to Kaikeyi and asked her, “Did I accidentally offend my father somehow? Please, help me make it right. Why is he so upset and looking so sick when he always greeted me with love? Is he unwell in body or mind? I hope nothing bad has happened to Bharata or to Satrughna. Are my mothers all right? I couldn’t bear to disappoint the king or go against his wishes, not even for a moment. How could anyone ignore their own father, who’s like a god and the source of their life? Mother, did you say something harsh to my father in anger or pride that made him so unhappy? Please, tell me the truth—I need to know why this unexpected sorrow has taken hold of the king.”

After Rāma (also called Rāghava) spoke, Kaikeyi—showing no shame—gave him a blunt answer, only thinking of herself. “Rāma, the king isn’t angry, and he’s not in danger. There’s something he wants to say but he’s afraid to tell you. You’re his favorite son, so he can’t bring himself to say anything that might hurt you. But you need to fulfill a promise he made to me. Long ago, he gave me two boons because he valued me so highly, and now he regrets it, just like anyone might after making a promise they can’t keep. He said, ‘I grant you these boons,’ but now it’s too late to take it back. You know that telling the truth is the foundation of all virtue—he can’t break his word, not even for you. If you agree to do whatever the king asks, whether it’s good or bad, I’ll tell you everything. If you promise that you’ll follow through with what I say (with the king’s approval), then I’ll explain. Otherwise, the king won’t say anything.”

Hearing Kaikeyi’s words, Rāma felt a stab of pain in his heart. In front of his father, he replied, “Please, don’t talk to me like that. I’m not afraid to do anything the king commands—even if he told me to jump into fire, drink poison, or walk into the ocean, I’d do it. He’s my father and my king. Just tell me what he wants, and I’ll obey—Rāma keeps his word.” Then Kaikeyi revealed her cruel demands. “Long ago, during a war between gods and demons, your father was wounded and I helped him recover. In return, he promised me two boons. Now I’m asking for them: First, I want Bharata to be crowned king. Second, I want you, Rāma, to leave for the Dandaka forest today. If you truly want to honor your father’s promises and your own, listen to me. Your father is bound by his word, so you must go into the forest for fourteen years. Bharata will be crowned using all the royal items the king prepared for your coronation. Give up your claim and head to Dandaka forest for fourteen years, wearing only bark and growing out your hair. Let Bharata rule Kosala, surrounded by jewels, elephants, horses, and chariots. The king is overwhelmed with sorrow and can’t even look at you. So, Rāma, do what your father promised, and save him from breaking his word.” Hearing all this, Rāma stayed calm, unaffected by Kaikeyi’s harsh words, but the king was crushed by the pain of losing his son.
SECTION XIX

When Rāma (Ram) heard these harsh, almost deadly words, he didn’t flinch. Calmly, he replied to Kaikeyi, “If that’s your wish, I’ll honor the king’s promise and go to the forest, wearing bark clothes and letting my hair grow wild. But there’s just one thing I want to know: why is my father, the great king who always welcomed me warmly, now avoiding me? Please don’t be upset—I’m speaking honestly. I’ll leave for the forest dressed as an ascetic, just as you ask. Is there anything I wouldn’t do, if ordered by my father—my king, my mentor, the person I trust most? Still, it hurts that he didn’t tell me himself about Bharata’s (Bharat’s) coronation. But if that’s what he wants, I’ll gladly hand over my crown, Sītā (Sita), all my wealth, and even my life to Bharata, just to fulfill your wish and keep my word. Please, try to comfort the king. Why is he just sitting there, staring at the floor and crying? Send messengers with fast horses to bring Bharata back from his uncle’s house, as the king wishes. I won’t question my father’s orders. I’ll leave for the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, immediately.” Hearing Rāma’s words, Kaikeyi was satisfied, knowing for sure he would go, and urged him on. “Yes, messengers will fetch Bharata. But if you’re so eager, Rāma, I don’t think you should delay. You need to leave for the forest right away. The king is too ashamed to speak to you himself—there’s nothing more to it. Please, end his misery. As long as you stay, your father won’t eat or bathe.” Crying out in pain, the king, overwhelmed with grief, fainted and collapsed on his golden couch. Rāma helped his father up, and, following Kaikeyi’s orders, got ready to leave for the forest—like a horse being spurred on. Even after hearing these cruel demands from Kaikeyi, Rāma stayed calm and answered her.

“Mother,” Rāma said, “I don’t care about riches or comfort—I live for what’s right, like the sages do. If there’s any way I can please my father, even if it costs me my life, I’ll do it. There’s no greater virtue than obeying your father. Even if he hadn’t told me, I’d still go to the forest for fourteen years, just because you asked. Maybe you don’t really know how much I value duty—otherwise you wouldn’t have needed to ask the king for this favor. Please, let me say goodbye to my mother and comfort Sītā. I’ll leave for the Dandaka forest today. You should make sure Bharata rules well and takes care of our father—that’s the right thing to do.” Hearing this, Rāma’s father was so heartbroken he couldn’t speak—he just cried. Rāma bowed respectfully to his unconscious father and to Kaikeyi, then left. He circled his father and Kaikeyi with respect and stepped out of the women’s quarters, where he saw his friends and relatives waiting. Lakshmana (Lakshman), Sumitrā’s son, followed him—furious, eyes full of tears. Rāma walked around the hall prepared for his coronation, taking one last, longing look before moving on. Losing his kingdom didn’t dim his beauty or the people’s love for him, just like the moon doesn’t lose its glow when it wanes. He showed no sign of regret, even as he prepared to leave everything behind and live in exile—like someone who’s already free inside. He left behind the royal umbrella, the decorated fans, his family, his chariot, and his people. Calm on the outside, but feeling the pain inside, Rāma went to tell his mother the terrible news. Everyone in her chambers was dressed up for the coronation—they had no idea anything was wrong. Rāma’s face showed none of his inner turmoil. Like the bright full moon, Rāma stayed calm and cheerful, keeping his composure. With gentle words and deep respect, Rāma—famous for his goodness—entered his mother’s room. Lakshmana, just as strong and noble as his brother, followed, carrying his own sorrow. Rāma saw that his mother’s quarters were filled with music and laughter. Even though Rāma himself wasn’t upset about losing his wealth, he worried that his loved ones might not survive this blow.
SECTION XX

As Rāma left, hands folded, a wave of grief swept through the women’s quarters. “Rāma, who always helped us without even needing his father’s permission, who protected and looked out for us—he’s going to the forest. From the day he was born, Rāghava cared for us as much as he did for his own mother, Kauśalyā. Even when he was treated unfairly, he never got angry; instead, he calmed those who were upset and always avoided saying or doing anything that would hurt others. And now, today, he’s leaving for the forest. Our king must have lost his mind to turn his back on Rāghava, our greatest support—he’s hurting all his people by doing this.” So the queens of Daśaratha cried out, blaming him loudly, like cows mourning the loss of their calves. Hearing this terrible wailing from the women’s quarters, King Daśaratha, broken by his grief for his son, hid his face in his seat, head hanging down.

Rāma, though struggling with sorrow for his family, kept his composure and, like an elephant held in chains, entered his mother’s chambers with his brother. At the entrance, he saw a respected old man and several others. When they saw Rāma, they all offered blessings to him, the greatest of heroes, saying, “Victory to you!” Passing through the first room, Rāma came to the second, where he saw many elderly Brahmins, wise in the Vedas and honored by the king. Bowing to them, he moved on to the third room, where women, children, and old men were all gathered at the gate, watching. The female guards greeted Rāma with joy and, hurrying into his mother’s room, quickly told Kauśalyā the happy news.

Kauśalyā, always concerned for her son’s well-being, had stayed up all night, deep in meditation, and was now performing her morning worship to Vishnu. Dressed in silk, calm and radiant, she was carrying out her daily rituals, making offerings into the sacred fire. As Rāma entered his mother’s blessed home, he saw her in the middle of the fire sacrifice. Around her were all the things needed to serve the gods—curd, grains, ghee, sweets for offering, fried rice, white garlands, rice cooked with milk and sugar, sesame and pea mixtures, sacrificial wood, and jars of water. He saw his virtuous mother in white silk, worn down by her strict religious practices, offering water to the gods.

When Kauśalyā saw her son approaching—the very one who always brought her happiness—she was overjoyed and hurried forward, like a mare running to her foal. Rāghava bowed deeply as his mother embraced him and kissed his head. Filled with love, Kauśalyā spoke kind and hopeful words to her unstoppable son, Rāghava: “May you have a long life and great fame, like the noble kings of old. See, Rāghava, how truthful your father, the king, is! Today, that virtuous man will make you the heir to the throne.”

Rāghava, always humble, was invited by his mother to sit and eat. Bowing with his hands together and head lowered in respect, he only touched the seat, then began to explain why he had come. “Mother, you don’t know the disaster that’s about to happen. I’m leaving for the Dandaka forest because of the suffering that’s about to fall on you, Lakshmana, and Sītā (Vaidehi). There’s no point in me sitting down now. It’s time for me to sit on kusa grass instead. For fourteen years, I’ll live in the forest like an ascetic, eating only roots and fruits, never animal flesh. The king is giving the throne to Bharata and sending me away as a hermit. I’ll spend those fourteen years—eight and six—alone in the woods, living on roots and fruit and fulfilling the duties of a hermit.”

Hearing these devastating words, Kauśalyā collapsed suddenly, like the trunk of a tree cut down, or a goddess who’s fallen from heaven. Seeing his mother, who never deserved such pain, faint and fall like a banana plant toppled to the ground, Rāma quickly lifted her up. She was covered in dust, like a mare after rolling on the ground from exhaustion; gently, Rāma brushed the dust from her body.

Still overwhelmed by the destruction of her happiness, Kauśalyā—who deserved only joy—spoke to Rāghava, the best of men, with Lakshmana watching. “Oh my son, Rāghava, if you hadn’t been born only to bring me pain, it would have been better to have no children at all than to suffer like this. A woman with no son has only one sorrow—she has no child. But I, my son, have never known the happiness that women feel when their husbands truly love them. I’ve stayed alive only in hopes of seeing the happiness that comes from having a son. Now, as the eldest queen, I’ll have to hear cruel and heartbreaking words from my younger co-wives. There’s no greater misery for a woman than this endless grief and crying. While you were here, they already made my life miserable—who knows what they’ll do when you’re gone? I’m certain I’ll die, my dearest. Ignored by my husband, I’m less than even Kaikeyi’s maids. Those who once served me won’t even talk to me when Kaikeyi’s son is crowned. Kaikeyi is always irritable—how can I, already suffering, bear to see her face and hear her harsh words?

“O Rāghava, for seventeen years since your second birth, I’ve waited and hoped my sorrow would end. But even though I’m worn out now, I don’t know how I’ll survive your endless exile and the contempt of my co-wives. How can I bear to spend my days in grief, never seeing your face, so bright like the full moon? All my fasting, meditation, and hard spiritual practices—raising you with so much effort—seem wasted now. My heart must be made of stone, since it doesn’t break like a riverbank eroding in the rain. Death refuses to take me—there must be no empty place in Yama’s realm, or else I’d be gone like a lion snatching a crying deer. My heart is truly iron, since it won’t shatter from this pain, and my body, heavy with sorrow and collapsed on the ground, won’t break apart. It seems I’m doomed to live until my time is up.

“What hurts most is that all my prayers, charity, self-control, and harsh discipline to have a son have turned out to be useless, like seeds scattered on barren ground. If anyone could die simply from heartbreak, I’d already be gone, like a cow separated from her calf. Oh, my moon-faced son, my life is worthless without you—I’ll follow you to the forest, drawn by love, like a weak cow following her calf. Kauśalyā, feeling like a divine musician (Kinnari) unable to handle such disaster, fearing even worse to come and seeing Rāma trapped by his duty, began to mourn in many ways.
SECTION XXI

At this moment, Lakshmana, deeply troubled, spoke to Kauśalyā, Rāma’s mother, while she wept. “Mother, I can’t accept that Rāma should leave all this royal splendor and go to the forest. The king is old, obsessed with his wife, and his judgment is clouded by desire for pleasure and power. Under Kaikeyi’s influence, who knows what he might say? I can’t see any crime or fault in Rāma that would justify banishing him. Even our worst enemies couldn’t accuse Rāma of any wrongdoing, even if he weren’t here to defend himself. By what standard of justice does the king exile such a son, who is like a god—humble, disciplined, and even respected by his rivals? What kind of son would take seriously the words of a father who’s behaving like a child? Before people hear about this exile, let’s secure the throne for you and Rāma, with my help. Who could stop your coronation, Rāma, if I’m here to protect you with my bow, as deadly as Death itself? If anyone opposes us, I’ll wipe out the whole city of Ayodhyā with my arrows. I’ll destroy anyone who supports Bharata or sides with him—sometimes being too gentle only leads to defeat. If our father, swayed by Kaikeyi, turns against us, I won’t hesitate to kill him. Even a spiritual leader deserves punishment if he’s arrogant, can’t tell right from wrong, and loses his way. Tell me, Rāma, by what law or reason does the king want to give the kingdom to Kaikeyi, when it rightfully belongs to you? Who dares grant Bharata the throne against us? Mother, I swear to you on my honor, my bow, and everything I love—if Rāma goes to the forest, I’ll throw myself into fire before that happens. I’ll use my strength to drive away your sorrow, just like the sun drives away darkness—let Rāma and you be my witnesses. I’ll kill my father if he clings to Kaikeyi and acts so shamefully in his old age.” Hearing Lakshmana’s passionate words, Kauśalyā, still weeping and crushed by grief, turned to Rāma and said, “You’ve heard what Lakshmana said, my son. If you agree, do what you think is right. But you shouldn’t leave me, tormented with sorrow, just because of your stepmother’s cruel words. If you want to do what’s right, stay here and serve me; that’s the highest virtue. Listen, my son—once, the great sage Kasyapa stayed at home and served his mother faithfully, and because of that, he reached heaven. I am as worthy of your respect as your father. I don’t give you permission to go to the forest. Without you, I have no desire for life or happiness; I’d rather survive on grass with you than be left behind. If you leave for the forest and abandon me in my grief, I’ll fast until I die. Then you’ll face the punishment of hell, just as the ocean, lord of rivers, suffered for a similar crime.” Hearing his mother’s desperate words, Rāma, righteous and steady, replied to her, “I can’t disobey my father’s command. I bow to you, but I must go to the forest. The wise sage Kandu lived in the forest and, though he knew it was wrong, killed a cow just to keep his father’s word. The sons of Sāgara, our ancestors, were destroyed while digging the earth, all because they followed their father’s orders. Rāma, son of Jamadagni, beheaded his own mother in the forest because his father told him to. These great people, Mother, all obeyed their fathers, and so will I. I’m not unique in this—others before me have done the same. I’m not inventing some new kind of virtue that hurts you; I’m just walking the path of those who came before. I’ll do what’s right in this world—obeying my father’s word is not shameful.”

After speaking to his mother, that master of words and archery turned to Lakshmana. “Lakshmana, I know how much you love me, and I know your power and courage. My mother is so overwhelmed with grief because she doesn’t understand how firmly I believe in truth and peace. Doing what’s right is the most important thing in the world, and truth is part of that. My father’s command is in line with righteousness, and those who truly follow dharma can’t ignore the orders of their father, mother, or a Brahmin. Since Kaikeyi has spoken for my father, I can’t disobey these orders. So drop this idea of rebellion—even if it fits the warrior’s code, it’s not right. Stay on the side of justice, not violence, and let’s stick to my decision.” Out of brotherly love, Rāma then spoke again to Kauśalyā, bowing respectfully with his hands joined. “Mother, I beg you—let me go into the forest. Please give me your blessing. Just like King Yayati, who once fell from heaven but returned after fulfilling his duties, I’ll come back home after keeping my promise. Please, don’t grieve. I’ll return from the forest after honoring my father’s word. I, Lakshmana, Sītā (Vaidehi), Sumitrā, and you will all follow my father’s wishes—this is eternal virtue. Give up the idea of my coronation and calm your heart, Mother. Please accept my choice to go to the forest.” Hearing Rāma’s calm, reasonable words, his mother slowly came back to her senses and looked at him. She said, “My son, I deserve your respect just like your father does. I raised and loved you as much as he did. I can’t let you go to the forest, and you shouldn’t leave me here in such grief. Without you, what good are my life, my family, rituals for our ancestors, prayers to the gods, or even knowledge itself? Just a moment with you is worth more than all the world to me.” Hearing his mother’s pain, Rāma was filled with anger, like an elephant lashed with a burning stick in the darkness. But he held onto his sense of what’s right and spoke firmly to both his mother, who could barely speak for sorrow, and to Lakshmana, still grieving. “Lakshmana, I know your deep respect for me and your strength. But please, don’t add to my pain or my mother’s, now that you know my intentions. In this world, people value virtue, wealth, and pleasure, but when it’s time to enjoy the results of good deeds from past lives, all three come together in righteousness—like a loyal, loving wife with a son. We shouldn’t chase goals where these don’t combine—righteousness is the standard we should follow. Someone who chases wealth alone is often despised, and those who pursue pleasure without virtue are never admired. How could any of us, who aren’t evil, disobey our father’s command, knowing it is righteous? He’s our king, our teacher, and our father—no matter if his orders come from desire, anger, or happiness. That’s why I can’t break my father’s vow—he’s our father and has authority over both of us, and he’s also my mother’s husband, her support, and righteousness itself. The righteous king still lives and is keeping his promise, even if it means losing me—so how can you, Mother, follow me like some widow whose husband is dead? Please, let me go to the forest and give me your blessing so I may return, like King Yayati regaining heaven by his truthfulness. I can’t sacrifice my reputation just for the sake of power. Life is short, Mother, and I don’t want to win the earth by unrighteous means.” After calming and convincing his mother, and fully explaining the path of righteousness to Lakshmana, Rāma, the greatest of men, respectfully circled his mother and resolved to leave for the Dandaka forest.
SECTION XXII

After calming himself and regaining his composure, Rama turned to his brother Lakshmana (the son of Sumitra), who was deeply upset, furious, and weighed down by the unfairness of Rama’s situation. Lakshmana’s eyes were blazing with anger, like a wild elephant. Rama said, “Lakshmana, control your anger and sadness. Be patient, accept what’s happened, and try to keep your spirits up. Let’s stop thinking about my coronation and instead focus on preparing for my journey into the forest. Please, put as much effort now into halting the preparations for my installation as you did before when you helped arrange everything. I honestly don’t remember ever doing anything, whether on purpose or by accident, that would hurt my father or any of my mothers. My father is a man of his word and he’s terrified of breaking his vows—let’s help him keep them, so he doesn’t have to fear for his soul. If we don’t stop the coronation, he’ll be heartbroken, thinking he’s failed to keep his promises, and that would hurt me too. Once I’m gone, Kaikeyi will get what she wants—Bharata will be crowned king without any problems. When I leave for the forest, wearing tree bark, animal skin, and with my hair in matted locks, Kaikeyi will finally be happy. Whoever inspired Kaikeyi to act like this and made her so determined, I can’t be angry with them. I’ll leave right away. Lakshmana, see this whole situation as the work of fate—Destiny is the only reason the kingdom has been taken from me and I’ve been banished. If Destiny hadn’t made Kaikeyi act this way, she wouldn’t have been so relentless in making me suffer. You know, Lakshmana, I’ve never treated my mothers differently, and Kaikeyi never used to treat me any differently from her own son. So it must be Destiny that’s making her say these harsh, cruel things to stop my coronation and send me into exile—otherwise, why would she, a princess with a good heart and great qualities, suddenly talk to me this way in front of her husband, like some ordinary woman? Destiny is mysterious and impossible to fully understand, and no one can avoid its effects. It’s because of Destiny that Kaikeyi has changed and I’ve lost my right to the throne. Who can stand against this unseen force, Lakshmana? Destiny is behind everything—joy and pain, fear and anger, gain and loss, birth and death. Even the greatest sages, despite their discipline, sometimes fall prey to anger and desire because of Destiny. Whenever something you plan falls apart and something unexpected takes its place, that’s Destiny at work. If you accept this truth, there’s no reason to be sad about my coronation being canceled. So calm down, come with me, and quickly stop the coronation preparations. We can use the water that was brought for my coronation for the ritual bath I need to take before becoming an ascetic. Or really, I don’t need any of these coronation items—water I draw from a well myself will be enough to begin my exile. Don’t be sad, Lakshmana, about losing the kingdom. Between ruling and exile, going to the forest can be just as honorable. Now you see how powerful Destiny is. So don’t blame my younger mother or my father—they’re both just caught up in Destiny’s plan.”
SECTION XXIII

After Rama spoke, Lakshmana, the fierce warrior, hung his head in frustration. He thought for a while, torn between anger and sorrow, his brows furrowed deeply as he struggled to contain his emotions. He was like an enraged snake cornered in a strange cave—his face was so fierce that no one dared look at him. His hands moved restlessly, like the trunk of an agitated elephant, and he kept shifting his head. Finally, with a sideways glance, Lakshmana spoke to his brother. “You want to go into exile to avoid breaking your father’s word and setting a bad example for others. But you’re wrong to be so eager about this. If you weren’t confused, how could a hero like you, a true Kshatriya, talk like someone powerless? Why do you praise fate, as if it’s all-powerful? Why don’t you see the wrongdoing in what Dasaratha and Kaikeyi have done? Don’t you realize that some people fake goodness just to trick others? They’re pretending to be righteous, but it’s all for their own gain—they want to get rid of you by deceit. If they hadn’t planned this, things wouldn’t have turned out like this, Rama. If the story of these old promises is really true, why wasn’t it mentioned before? The king has done something shameful—he’s making the younger brother king and ignoring you, the rightful heir. Forgive me, Rama, but I can’t take this. I hate even that so-called virtue that has taken hold of you and made your mind swing between extremes. Why should you, who are so capable, follow these evil and unfair commands from your father, who’s just being controlled by Kaikeyi? What really gets me is that you won’t admit this whole mess about your coronation happened because of these supposed boons; your idea of virtue deserves criticism. People will mock you for giving up the kingdom just to keep your father’s promise. Who else but you would even think of giving in to the wishes of the king and Kaikeyi—who act like our enemies, always plotting against us, even though they’re supposed to be our parents? Even if you think their interference is just fate, just ignore it—I can’t accept it. Only weak and helpless people blame fate; real heroes—respected for their strength—don’t accept it. Someone who can change his own fate with courage doesn’t just give up, even if things look bad. Today, people will see whether fate or courage is stronger. Those who saw fate stop your coronation will see it beaten today by my strength. I’ll crush this so-called fate, like a wild elephant breaking free from its chains and rampaging. Forget your father—even all the gods and everyone in the three worlds couldn’t stop your coronation if I stand in their way. Anyone who supported your exile will be the ones banished for fourteen years, not you. I’ll destroy my father’s and Kaikeyi’s hope of putting Bharata on the throne instead of you. Destiny won’t bring them happiness—but my power will bring them misery. You can rule for a thousand years, and after you, your sons can take over. That’s how the great kings of old did it—only going to the forest after passing the throne to their sons. Are you afraid the king will just give the kingdom to someone else if you stay? Is that why you don’t want to rule, Rama? I promise you, I’ll protect your kingdom like a shoreline protects the sea, or else I’m not worthy to be called a hero. Get ready for your coronation—gather everything you need for the ceremony. I can defeat any king who stands against you with my own strength. My hands aren’t just for show, this bow isn’t just decoration, this sword isn’t for chopping wood, and these arrows aren’t for carrying bundles. All of them are for destroying our enemies. I have no problem cutting down anyone who stands against us, even if they’re as powerful as Indra himself. I’ll make the battlefield impassable—cutting down elephants, horses, and soldiers alike. My enemies will fall, their heads and limbs taken by my sword, their blood covering the ground like storm clouds lit by lightning. Who could possibly stand against me when I show up ready for war, bow in hand and armor on? Sometimes I’ll kill one enemy with many arrows, sometimes many with a single shot—I’ll strike down men, horses, and elephants alike. Today, I’ll prove my skill by ending the king’s rule and putting you on the throne. These hands, which should be covered in sandalwood paste and bracelets, giving gifts and making friends, will finally do what they were meant to do—wipe out those trying to stop your coronation. Tell me, Rama, who do you want me to destroy—who should I take from their wealth, their lives, and their families? I’m yours to command; just give the order and I’ll bring the whole world under your control.” 

Rama, descendant of Raghu, wiped away Lakshmana’s tears and gently comforted him again and again. Then he said, “My dear brother, I truly believe the best thing is for me to obey our father’s word.”
SECTION XXIV
When Rāma made it clear he was determined to follow his father’s orders, Kauśalyā (Rāma’s mother), her voice trembling with tears, spoke to him in a gentle but heartbroken tone.

“How will my son Rāma, who has always been loved by everyone and never known hardship, survive on scraps he finds in the forest? How will he, born to Daśaratha and used to being served fine meals by his attendants, live on just fruits and roots? Who could believe—or, if they do, not be terrified—that Rāma, so accomplished and so beloved by the king, is being sent into exile? Fate must be the strongest force in the world—it gives happiness and suffering as it pleases. How else could you, my dear Rāma, be forced to flee into the woods? The sorrow in my heart feels like a fire—fed by my grief, fanned by your absence, and burning more fiercely with every sob and every tear. Just as fire consumes dry grass in the summer, this pain will eat away at me while you are gone. Like a cow follows her calf, I want to follow you wherever you go, my son.” Hearing his mother’s words, Rāma, always calm and wise, answered her gently, seeing how much pain she was in. “Mother, the king was deceived by Kaikeyi. If you also abandon him after I leave, he might not survive the grief. For a woman, nothing is more cruel than leaving her husband—it would be wrong for you to even consider it. Please stay by my father’s side, serving him as long as he lives. This is the right path—the eternal virtue.”

Rāma’s words comforted Kauśalyā, and she replied gratefully to her son, who always eased her worries. “You’re right.” Rāma, ever devoted to duty, continued, “It’s the duty of both of us to obey father’s command. He is your husband, my teacher, and the lord of all. I promise, after I spend these fourteen years in the forest, I’ll happily return to you and follow your wishes.” Despite his words, Kauśalyā, deeply attached to her son and crying, answered, “Rāma, I can’t bear to live among my co-wives if you leave for the forest to fulfill your father’s promise. Please take me with you, like a wild deer follows its mate.” Rāma, hiding his own pain, replied to her, “A husband is a wife’s god and master as long as he lives. The king can command both you and me. As long as he lives, we aren’t free to do as we wish. Bharata is kind and well-loved; he will care for you while I’m gone. Please make sure father isn’t overwhelmed by grief after I leave—don’t let this sorrow destroy him. Always look after him. Even if a woman performs all sorts of religious duties and fasts, it’s meaningless if she doesn’t serve her husband. Only by serving her husband can a woman reach the highest place, even above worshipping the gods. This is what the Vedas and Smritis teach. While I’m away, spend your time waiting for me by worshipping the gods with flowers and fire offerings, and by caring for the Brahmins. Be disciplined, fast, and stay devoted to your husband—then, when I return, you’ll have everything you wish for, if father is still alive.” Hearing Rāma’s words, Kauśalyā, devastated by the thought of losing her son, spoke to him through her tears:

“My son, I can’t change your mind or stop you from going to the forest. I can’t escape this pain of being separated from you. So go, my dear, with all my blessings—my only comfort will be your safe return. I will be truly happy only when you come back, having fulfilled your promises and your duty to your father. Destiny is a strange thing, my son—it’s pushing you into exile despite my pleas. Go now, brave Rāma, and return safe. When you come back, comfort me with your gentle words. Will that day ever come, when I see you return from the forest, dressed in bark and with matted hair?” With these words, full of hope and sadness, Kauśalyā watched Rāma, determined to bless him before he left and to perform the rituals for his protection.
SECTION XXV

Kausalya fought to control her sorrow and, after touching holy water, began performing blessings and rituals for Rama. She spoke to him, saying, “Rama, my dearest son and the pride of the Raghu family, I see that nothing I say can change your mind, so please go now—but promise me you’ll come back soon. Follow the path of the great ones who came before you. Let the virtue you’ve always followed with such joy and discipline protect you. May the gods you worship every day at the temple, along with the great Maharshis, watch over you in the forest. May those weapons that Visvamitra gave you always keep you safe. Let your devotion and service to your father and mothers be your shield, protecting you always. May all sacred things—holy fires, ritual grass, altars, places blessed by Brahmins, mountains, every kind of tree, lakes, birds, snakes, and lions—guard you. May the Sidhyas, Vishvadevas, Maruts, great sages, and gods like Pusa, Bhaga, Aryama, the Lokapalas led by Indra, the six seasons, all the months, days, nights, and even moments, along with the Srutis, Smritis, and the spirit of virtue, protect you, my son, from all directions. May Skanda, Soma, Brihaspati, the Saptarishis, Narada, the moon, and other sages keep you safe. May all the regions and their guardians, pleased by my prayers, defend you in the forest. As you enter the woods, may the mountains, oceans, Varuna, the heavens, sky, earth, air, all things moving and unmoving, planets and stars with their gods, day, night, and dusk all protect you. May the changing seasons, months, years, and every part of time bring you comfort as you wander the forest dressed as an ascetic. May the gods and demons work for your happiness, and may you never fear the cruel Rakshasas, Pishachas, or wild beasts who feed on flesh. May monkeys, scorpions, gnats, snakes, and insects not harm you. May elephants, tigers, fierce bears, boars, buffalo, and horned animals not injure you. Even from afar, may my prayers keep you safe from every kind of dangerous creature. May your journey be blessed and your efforts succeed. Go, my son, into the forest, and may you find plenty of fruits, roots, and all that you need. May all creatures of the sky and earth—and even the gods who might wish you harm—help you instead. May Sukra, Soma, the Sun, the god of wealth, and Death himself protect you as you go to the Dandaka forest. May fire, air, smoke, and the mantras of the Rishis guard you whenever you bathe. May Brahma, the Rishis, and all the other gods defend you while you live in the forest.

Kausalya, famous and gentle-eyed, honored the gods with garlands, sweet scents, and prayers. She offered sacrifices for Rama’s safety, working with respected Brahmins and using ghee, white flowers, sacred fig branches, and white mustard seeds. The family priest performed the ceremonies, offering gifts to the gods of the four directions, and then shared curd, ghee, and honey with the Brahmins, who blessed Rama with prayers for his journey to the forest. After giving the Brahmins generous gifts, Kausalya turned to Rama and spoke again: “May you receive the same blessing that Indra, king of the gods, received when he defeated the mighty asura Vritra. May you be blessed as Vinata once blessed Garuda, the king of birds, when she prayed for the nectar of immortality for him. May you find the fortune that Aditi prayed for when she helped Indra defeat the giants during the search for the nectar of immortality. May you have the prosperity that was given to Vishnu when he crossed the universe as a dwarf in three steps. May the Rishis, oceans, islands, the three worlds, the Vedas, and all the realms support your well-being.” Saying this, Kausalya placed grains on Rama’s head, sprinkled him with fragrant water, and tied protective twigs (visalyakarani) to his wrists, chanting mantras for his safety. Overcome with emotion, she hugged Rama and kissed his head. Though her voice was choked with tears, she spoke as if she were joyful, blessing him with prayers: “My son, Rama, may you achieve all you wish. Go where you must, but I will look forward with joy to seeing you return to Ayodhya, healthy and triumphant, ready to rule your kingdom. I will be freed from sorrow and my face will shine with happiness when I see you come back from the forest, as beautiful as the full moon rising. I will watch you sit on your throne, fulfilling your father’s wishes, and returning from exile. When you come home, dressed in royal clothes and jewels, may you make your wife’s dreams come true. I have worshipped Shiva and all the gods, great sages, spirits, and snakes; may they—and the spirits of the four directions—protect you, Rama, as you leave for such a long time.” Tears filled Kausalya’s eyes as she finished the rituals, walking around Rama with care, sighing deeply as she looked at him again and again. After his mother had circled him in blessing, Rama—famous and radiant—bowed at her feet several times, then left to go to Sita’s rooms.
SECTION XXVI

Rama, preparing to leave for the forest and determined to follow the path of righteousness, respectfully took leave of Kausalya. As he walked along the royal road, crowded with people, his grace and noble qualities won everyone’s admiration. Meanwhile, Sita (also called Vaidehi), devoted to sacred rituals, was unaware of the recent events; her heart was filled only with excitement about Rama’s upcoming coronation. After finishing her prayers to the gods, following all the proper royal customs, she waited eagerly for Rama, feeling grateful and happy. When Rama entered the beautiful palace, which was splendidly decorated and full of joyful people, he kept his head bowed in embarrassment. Sita, seeing her husband looking distressed and anxious, immediately stood up from her seat, trembling. Seeing her, the noble Rama couldn’t hide his sorrow any longer; his pain was visible on his face. Sita, noticing Rama’s pale and sweaty face and realizing how deeply troubled he was, spoke to him with deep concern:

“My lord, why do you look so different today? The Pushya star is aligned with the moon, and Jupiter is watching over this moment—it’s supposed to be the most fortunate day, according to the wise Brahmins. So why are you so sad? Why hasn’t your handsome face been shaded by a royal white umbrella, sparkling like foam on water? Why aren’t the servants fanning you with moon-white fans, their eyes as beautiful as lotus petals? I don’t hear the court singers and bards praising you with songs, as they should on such an occasion. Why haven’t the Brahmins performed the ritual of pouring honey and curd on your head, after washing it, as part of your coronation? Why aren’t the townspeople and nobles dressed up and ready to follow you in celebration? Why isn’t your grand chariot, drawn by four swift horses with golden decorations, leading the way? Why isn’t the royal elephant—huge and dark like a thundercloud—marching before you? Why aren’t the servants carrying the golden-embroidered royal seat ahead of you? Why does your face look so pale and joyless, when everything for your coronation has been prepared?” 

Rama, seeing Sita in tears, answered her: “Sita, daughter of a noble family, wise in religion and devoted to sacred duties, my father has banished me to the forest. Listen, daughter of Janaka, to how this disaster has come upon me. Long ago, my mother Kaikeyi was granted two promises by my father, King Dasaratha. Now, when everything was ready for my coronation, Kaikeyi demanded her boons and persuaded my father to keep his word. So, I must live in the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, and my brother Bharata will be crowned as heir to the throne. I have come here to see you before I leave for exile. Please, don’t praise me in front of Bharata—people who suddenly gain power are sensitive about hearing others praised. Even with your friends, don’t talk about my virtues; it will help you get along better with Bharata, who is now the king. The throne is his now, so please treat him with special respect. Today I must go to the forest to keep my father’s promise. Stay here, Sita, and keep your mind calm. Spend your time in worship and fasting, while I live among the sages in the forest. Each morning, after you wake, pray to the gods, then bow to my father Dasaratha. My mother Kausalya is old and heartbroken—show her all the love and respect you can, as it’s the right thing to do. Bow to my other mothers as well, with the same affection. Treat Bharata and Shatrughna as if they were your own brothers or sons—they are dearer to me than life itself. Please, Sita, don’t do anything to upset Bharata, since he rules both the family and the kingdom now.

Kings are pleased when treated with respect and a good attitude, but they turn away from those who act otherwise. Sometimes, they even reject their own children if they feel betrayed, and accept outsiders who are loyal to them. So, Sita, you must obey Bharata and keep up your religious duties and honesty. I am leaving for the forest now, my dear. Please, do as I ask, just as you always have before.”
SECTION XXVII

After hearing Rama’s words, Vaidehi (Sita), who was loving and gentle, spoke to her husband with a mix of affection and hurt. “Do you really think so little of me, that you speak to me this way? Honestly, I find your words almost funny, but also a little insulting. For someone as noble and skilled as you, these thoughts just don’t suit you, Rama. They’re not fit to even be spoken, let alone by a great prince. Look, everyone in this world—father, mother, son, brother, daughter-in-law—follows their own destiny. But a wife’s fate is always tied to her husband’s. That’s why, from the moment you were ordered to go to the forest, I knew I would go too. A woman doesn’t rely on her parents, her children, her friends, or even herself—not in this life or the next. Her husband is her only true support. If you must go into that wild forest, then I’ll go ahead of you, clearing the thorns and tough grass so you don’t have to. Please, trust me and take me with you, Rama. Let go of your doubts and anger, like water poured away after drinking. I haven’t done anything to deserve being left behind. For a wife, the comfort of being at her husband’s side—even in hardship—is better than living in a palace or riding in a flying chariot. My parents raised me to always stand by my husband, through anything. I’m just doing what I’ve always been taught; I won’t listen to any advice that tells me otherwise.

I’ll gladly walk into that wild forest with you, even though it’s full of deer, tigers, and other dangerous creatures. I’ll find happiness there, just as I did in my childhood home, not caring about riches or the wonders of the world, but only about caring for you. We’ll enjoy the beauty of the forest together, and I’ll look after you, control my desires, and live simply. You have the strength to support thousands in the forest—so surely you can take care of me. I’m going with you, Rama, and nothing will change my mind. There’s no way you can stop me. I’ll live on roots and fruit, and being with you is all I want. I’ll always walk ahead of you on the path and eat only after you’ve eaten. I want to see the forests, the mountains, the streams, and the lakes. With you to protect me, I’m not afraid of anything. I’ll see ponds full of wild geese and ducks, covered in blooming lotuses, and I’ll bathe there with you every day, sharing this life with you. I’ll be happy with you in that forest, Rama, for a hundred or even a thousand years. I don’t care for luxury or heaven itself if I have to be there without you—it means nothing to me. I want to live in that wild forest filled with deer, monkeys, and elephants, and cling to you as my happiness. Please accept my plea—I belong to you completely, I couldn’t love anyone else, and if you leave me behind, I’d rather die. I promise I won’t be a burden to you.”

Hearing Sita speak so passionately, Rama—who loved her deeply but was determined to follow his duty—tried again to explain just how difficult and dangerous life in the forest would be, hoping to convince her not to come.
SECTION XXVIII

Rāma, always guided by what’s right, couldn’t stop thinking about how hard life in the forest would be. He decided he shouldn’t take Sitā with him, even though she was wise in spiritual matters and had already spoken her mind. Gently comforting Sitā, whose eyes were brimming with tears, Rāma—determined to protect her—tried to talk her out of coming along. “Sitā, you come from a noble family and are always devoted to doing what’s right. Please, stay here and keep following the path of virtue; it would bring me peace of mind to know you’re safe. Sitā, listen to me: there are too many dangers in the forest, and I want you to know about them before you decide. Give up your plan to join me in exile—the forest is known for being wild and full of dangers. I say this for your own good; there’s no real happiness there, only endless hardship.

The roars of lions echoing from mountain caves, mixed with the crash of waterfalls, make the forest a frightening place. Wild animals, often aggressive and unpredictable, roam alone and sometimes attack people; the forest is full of danger. The rivers are crowded with crocodiles, sharks, and other scary creatures; the water is muddy, often impossible to cross, and sometimes raging elephants block the way. The forest paths are tangled with vines and thorns; there’s hardly any clean water to drink, and loud calls from wild birds fill the air—life in the forest is harsh. After exhausting days, people have no choice but to sleep on beds of fallen leaves right on the ground. You have to be satisfied with whatever fruit drops from the trees, morning and evening—this is what forest life is like, Sitā.

You’d need to fast when food is scarce, wear rough clothes made of bark and tangled hair, worship the gods and honor your ancestors with proper rituals, welcome any guests, and stick to strict routines—like bathing three times a day. Forest life means living simply and making flower offerings you gather yourself, following the ancient ways of ascetics. There’s never much food, so you have to eat whatever you can find, Sitā. Violent winds, darkness, hunger, and constant fear are always present in the forest.

Snakes and all kinds of reptiles slither across the paths, acting as if they own the place. Venomous river snakes wait for travelers, blocking their way. Birds, scorpions, insects, mosquitoes, and gnats are always around to bother you. There are thorny trees with swaying branches and sharp grasses whipping back and forth—the whole place is uncomfortable. Living in the forest brings all sorts of physical pains, fears, and difficulties. You have to give up anger and desire, commit yourself to self-discipline, and get used to letting go of fear, even when things get scary. The forest is just full of misery.

That’s why I don’t want you to come—it won’t be good for you. I’ve thought it through, and the forest is filled with too many dangers.” But even as Rāma tried to persuade Sitā not to go with him, she couldn’t accept his words. Deeply upset, she answered him firmly.
SECTION XXIX
When Sita heard Rama’s words, she was deeply upset. Tears filled her eyes as she spoke softly to him.

“All those dangers you described about living in the forest, Rama, don’t scare me. Because of my love for you, I see them as challenges worth facing. The deer, lions, elephants, tigers, saravas, chamaras, srimaras, and all those wild animals you mentioned—they won't come near you, Raghava, because they’ll be afraid of you. I want to come with you, but I’ll ask permission from our elders first; without you, Rama, I’d rather die. If I’m with you, Raghava, not even Indra (Sakra), king of the gods, could harm me. You once told me that a woman cannot live without her husband, and I believe that completely. Also, I remember, back at my father’s house, the Brahmanas told me I was destined to live in the forest someday. I heard this from palm readers and holy men, and ever since, I’ve been curious and eager to go to the forest. So please, let me come with you—nothing will change my mind. I know the dangers of the forest, but those bad things usually happen only to people who can’t control themselves. When I was a girl, an ascetic woman visited my mother and told her I would one day live in the forest. I’ve asked you before, many times, to let me join you in the forest for adventure, and you agreed. So now, for your sake and with your permission, I want to serve you, Raghava, even in the hardships of forest life.

Rama, if I follow you out of love and loyalty, I’ll be pure and blameless—because my husband is like a god to me. I’ve heard from famous Brahmanas that being with you will bring me blessings, even in the next life. They say that when a woman is given in marriage, with all the proper rituals, she belongs to her husband forever—even after death. So why won’t you let me come with you, when I’m faithful and devoted? Please, Kakutstha, take me with you—I’m loyal, I share in your happiness and pain, and I only want to serve you. If you don’t let me come, I’ll end my life—by poison, by fire, or by drowning. Sita pleaded with Rama in every way she could think of, but the mighty hero still refused to take her into the dangerous forest. Hearing his answer, Maithili (Sita) fell silent, lost in thought, tears streaming down her face. Rama, always in control of himself, saw how upset and anxious she was, and tried to comfort her with gentle words.
SECTION XXX

After listening to Rāma’s comforting words, Maithili (Sitā), daughter of Janaka, tried to fight back her sadness. Half-teasing and half-serious, she laughed at Rāma, her broad-chested husband, and spoke to him because she was determined to go with him into exile. “Rāma, what did my father, the king of Mithilā, see in you when he chose you as his son-in-law? Did he think you were a man only in looks but weak inside, like a woman? If people ever say the sun isn’t as bright as you, they are wrong. Why are you so downcast and scared that you’d leave behind your own wife, who has no one but you? I am completely devoted to you, just like Sāvitri was to her husband Satvavān, son of Dumat Sen. I have never, not even once, thought of anyone but you, and I will follow you to the forest. Do you really want to hand me over to someone else, like some casual actor, even though I’ve always been faithful and loved only you? If you want me to serve some other man instead, then you should become his servant too, since you’d be the one telling me to do it and giving up your own rights. It’s just not right for you to go into exile without taking me. Whether it’s a life of harshness, the forest itself, or even heaven, I want to be wherever you are. No matter how tough the journey gets, it will feel like luxury to me if I’m by your side. The sharp grasses and thorns—Kusa, Kāsa, Sara, Ishika—and all the brambles on the way will feel as soft as linen or deer-skin if I’m with you. Even the dust that covers me from the wind, Rāma, will seem like fine sandalwood powder. When I sleep on green grass in the forest, it’ll feel better than any fancy bed. Any fruits, roots, or leaves you bring for me, no matter how little, will taste like nectar. I won’t miss my father, mother, or home. I’ll enjoy the wild fruits and flowers that grow in different seasons. You won’t see me upset, you won’t have to worry about me, and I won’t be a burden. Please take me with you, Rāma. Your presence is like heaven, your absence like hell. If you leave me behind in a world I now think of as full of suffering, I’ll rather drink poison than fall into the hands of our enemies. If I can’t survive this pain of separation, it’s better for me to die right away than be left alone. I can’t bear even a moment of this sorrow. How could I possibly live without you for fourteen years?”

As she spoke, Sitā was overcome by grief. She hugged her husband and started crying loudly. Like a female elephant wounded by sharp arrows, she wept, letting out tears she had long held back, as if they were sparks from dry wood. Her tears, clear as crystal, streamed down her face and fell like drops from a lotus petal. Her beautiful face, with its wide, moon-bright eyes, looked faded and dry with sorrow, like a lotus plucked from water. Seeing Sitā almost faint from sadness, Rāma put his arms around her, reviving her with gentle words: “My beloved, I don’t even want the heavens if it means hurting you. I am not afraid, just as Brahmā himself has no fear. Before, I didn’t fully understand how much you wanted to go. That’s why I hesitated to take you with me, even though I could have. Now that you’re so determined, Maithili, I can’t leave you behind—just as a wise person can’t abandon generosity. Your loyalty reminds me of Suvarchalā, who followed the Sun. I must go to the forest, Janaka’s daughter, because I have to keep my father’s promise. Obeying your parents is a son’s greatest duty. I couldn’t live if I disobeyed my father’s order. Why should we worship distant Fate and ignore our parents, who are right in front of us? Serving our parents achieves the goals of religion and duty and is better than worshiping anything else. That’s why I’m following this path.”

“Truth, charity, honor, and grand sacrifices aren’t as powerful for the soul as serving one’s parents. With that, you get everything—heaven, wealth, food, knowledge, children, happiness. Great people who serve their parents gain the blessings of the gods, the Gandharvas, and even reach the realms of Brahmā and Vishnu. That’s why I want to obey my father and stay loyal to the truth. I was set on not taking you, Sitā, to the Dandaka forest, but now you’ve changed my mind by your determination to share this life with me. Since you’re ready, beautiful one, I allow you to come. Follow me, my gentle wife and partner in virtue. Your decision to join me is perfect—it matches our family’s values and my own heart. Get ready for the journey, because even heaven wouldn’t make me happy without you now. Please, give away your jewelry to the Brāhmanas and food to the beggars who need it. Don’t delay. Give the Brāhmanas your best ornaments, clothes, toys, beds, vehicles, and other fine things. Whatever’s left, share with the servants.” Realizing her husband wanted her to come with him, Sitā happily and quickly began giving away her possessions.
SECTION XXXI

Hearing this conversation, Lakshmana (sometimes called Laksh), who had arrived earlier, couldn't hold back his tears. He was overwhelmed by this huge sorrow. Kneeling at his brother’s feet, he spoke to both Sita and Rama, who were both respected and loved by all. “If you’re really set on going to the forest, full of wild deer and elephants, then I’ll go with you.
