When you demanded your promise, you weren’t thinking about Sītā.” Even after hearing all this from the great sage, Sītā—wanting nothing more than to be with Rāma—did not refuse the ascetic dress that Kaikeyi had given her.
SECTION XXXVIII

While Sitā, who technically had a husband but felt completely alone, was putting on the clothes of an ascetic, the people around became furious. They shouted, “Oh Daśaratha, shame on you!” Overwhelmed by the angry outcry, the king gave up caring about his own life, his morals, or his reputation. Sighing heavily, the descendant of Ikshwāku turned to his wife and said, “Kaikeyi, Sitā shouldn’t have to wear these rough clothes. She’s young, gentle, and deserves happiness—she could never survive in the forest. My spiritual guide was right. What did she ever do wrong? She’s the daughter of a great king, and now she’s being forced to dress like a beggar in front of everyone, having nothing. Let Janaka’s daughter take off these harsh clothes. This isn’t what I promised you before. If the princess is going to the forest, she should at least go with comfort and jewels. My time is nearly up—I made this cruel promise and swore an oath. But this idea of sending Sitā away was yours, made out of ignorance! Don’t let it come back to haunt you, like a bamboo plant dying from its own flower. If, Kaikeyi, Rāma did something to offend you, what did Vaidehi (Sitā) ever do to deserve this? She has eyes like a gentle deer, a kind nature, and is truly good—what harm did Janaka’s daughter ever cause you? Isn’t it enough for you that Rāma is already exiled? Why are you determined to commit even more terrible deeds? Kaikeyi, when you asked for Rāma’s banishment—the same Rāma I once planned to make king—I agreed to that. But now, seeing Mithilā’s daughter dressed like a beggar, you’re going beyond what I promised. Surely you’re sending yourself straight to hell.” 

Assigned to go to the forest, Rāma sat silently and finally spoke, “Father, my mother (Kausalya) is old, respected, and has a noble heart. Please don’t let her be mistreated. You should honor her even more when I’m gone, because she’ll be drowning in grief and suffering more than ever. Please, great king, take good care of her while I’m away, so that, devastated by my absence, she doesn’t lose the will to live and end up in the realm of Yama (the god of death).”
SECTION XXXIX

When Rāma finished speaking and the king saw him dressed like a wandering monk, Daçarātha sat among his wives, completely stunned. Grief overwhelmed him so much that he couldn’t even look at Rāma, let alone speak to him. He sat in silence for a while, lost in sorrow, then finally started to lament, thinking about Rāma’s fate. “This must be karma for the wrongs I’ve done in my past—I must have separated many cows from their calves or taken the lives of innocent creatures. That’s why this disaster has come upon me now. Life really doesn’t leave the body until its time, because even after all that Kaikeyi has done to me, I’m still alive. And now I see my own son, who used to wear royal clothes, standing before me in the clothes of an ascetic, looking like fire. All of this is happening because of Kaikeyi’s scheming and her selfishness.” After saying this, Daçarātha, completely overwhelmed by sorrow, cried out, “Rāma!” but couldn’t say anything more. Eventually, he regained his senses. Tears in his eyes, he turned to Sumantra and said, “Go get a chariot with the best horses, and bring it here. Take Rāma to the southern border of the kingdom. Even though Rāma is virtuous and brave, his own father and mother are banishing him. I guess this is what comes from being too good.” Sumantra, always quick and efficient, followed the king’s orders, hitched up a beautiful chariot, and brought it over. With hands folded in respect, he told Rāma that the golden chariot with its fine horses was ready. Then, Daçarātha, who was wise and self-controlled, quickly called his treasurer and gave him a firm order.

“Immediately bring Vaidehi (Sitā) fine clothes and expensive jewelry—enough for the entire fourteen years,” he said. The treasurer did exactly as ordered, collected everything from the treasury, and quickly brought the gifts to Sitā. Sita, pure as ever, put on the beautiful ornaments and clothes she’d been given, even as she prepared to head to the forest. Dressed up this way, she seemed to light up the whole room, glowing like the sun in the sky. Then, Kauśalyā—her mother-in-law—embraced her warmly, held her close, and kissed the top of her head. She said to Sita, “Some women, even when their husbands have always cared for them, ignore them in hard times—and people call such women unfaithful. It’s just how women are, they say: after enjoying happiness with their husbands, they turn against them or even abandon them when trouble comes. Women who are dishonest, thoughtless, unkind, or selfish are unfaithful. No matter how much you do for some women—give them a good family, gifts, education, or forgive their mistakes—their hearts can still be fickle. But truly good women, who are honest and follow their elders’ teachings, stay loyal to their husbands and see them as their best chance at spiritual growth. So even though my son is being sent to the forest, you must never ignore him. Whether he’s rich or poor, you should treat him as a god.” Sita listened closely and replied with hands folded, “I will do everything you say, Mother. I know how a wife should treat her husband—I learned it from my parents. Please don’t compare me to women who act wrongly. Just as the moon never loses its brightness, I can never turn away from virtue. A lute without strings is silent, a chariot without wheels doesn’t move—so even if a woman has a hundred sons, she can’t find happiness without her husband. Fathers and sons give only so much, but a husband gives endlessly—who wouldn’t honor that? I’ve learned all my duties, big and small, from my elders—so how could I disregard my husband? To a wife, her husband is like a god.” Hearing Sita’s heartfelt words, Kauśalyā—pure in spirit—couldn’t help but cry, feeling both joy and sorrow. Then Rāma, hands folded, addressed his mother, who sat among all his other mothers, and said, “Mother, don’t be sad. Please take care of Father, and remember, my time in the forest will be over before you know it. Fourteen years will pass as quickly as a dream. When I return, you’ll see me again, surrounded by friends and family.” After comforting his mother, Rāma looked at his three hundred and fifty other mothers and spoke to them with respect.

“If I’ve ever said anything harsh out of familiarity, or made any mistakes without realizing it, please forgive me. I bow to you all.” As Rāma spoke these gentle, respectful words, the women—overwhelmed with grief—listened in silence. But then, as soon as he finished, a loud wailing broke out from Daçarātha’s wives, sounding as mournful as the cries of wild birds. The palace, which used to echo with music, was now filled with cries of sadness and heartbreak.
SECTION XL

Overwhelmed with grief, Rāma, Sitā, and Lakshmana bowed before King Daçarātha and walked around him in respect. With the king’s permission, Rāma—still stunned by sorrow—went with Sitā to pay respects to his mother. Lakshmana, following his brother’s example, bowed to Kauçalyā and then touched the feet of his own mother, Sumitrā. As Lakshmana honored her, Sumitrā lovingly kissed the top of his head and spoke warmly to her strong-armed son: “Even though you care for your friends here, I give you permission to go to the forest. Once Rāma leaves for the woods, don’t ever neglect him, my son. Whether things are good or bad, your duty stays the same. It is right for a younger brother to follow his elder; this is a righteous path. Our family has always kept certain duties—like charity, sacrifice, and bravery in battle. Treat Rāma like your father Daçarātha, and treat Janaka’s daughter, Sitā, as you would treat me. See Ayodhyā as nothing more than a wilderness—go, my son, and follow your heart.” After saying this to her beloved son, who had already decided to go, Sumitrā encouraged him again and again—

“Go! Go!” Then Sumantra, the humble and wise charioteer, bowed with folded hands and said respectfully to Rāma (also called Kākutstha), “Great prince, may all go well—please climb onto the chariot. I’ll take you wherever you wish. You must spend fourteen years in the forest, starting today—your stepmother has ordered it.” Sitā, after getting dressed and adorning herself, gladly climbed onto the shining chariot. Counting out the years they’d be away, her father-in-law Daçarātha gave Sitā clothes and jewelry for her journey with Rāma. He also placed weapons, armor, a leather-bound basket, and a hoe at the front of the chariot. Finally, Rāma and Lakshmana quickly climbed aboard the beautiful, gold-trimmed chariot. With Sitā joining them, Sumantra drove off with horses as swift as the wind. As Rāma left for his long exile in the forest, everyone in the city—people and animals alike—felt devastated. The city erupted in chaos as people rushed about, elephants grew wild, and horses neighed loudly. Old and young, the entire city—overcome with sorrow—rushed after Rāma, like people desperate for water in scorching heat.

All along the sides and behind the chariot, people leaned forward, faces streaked with tears and sighing deeply. They called out to the charioteer, “Please, slow down—let the horses go gently. We want to see Rāma’s face one last time, since we may never see him again. Rāma’s mother must have a heart of iron, since it doesn’t break watching her son, so much like the god Skanda, leave for the forest. Sitā, having made her choice, follows her husband like a shadow—she’s so loyal, she’ll never leave his side, just as the sun never leaves Mount Meru. Lakshmana, you’re lucky—you get to serve your god-like brother, who always speaks kindly. What you’re doing is amazing; it’s your great good fortune, and it will lead you to heaven, because you’re following him.” As they spoke, their fear and sadness only grew, and the people kept following Rāma, the beloved prince from the Ikshwāku line. Meanwhile, the king, overcome with grief and surrounded by his distraught wives, left his house, saying, “I need to see my dear son.” Ahead of him, he heard a loud wailing from the women, like the cries of wild elephants when one is captured. At that moment, Rāma’s father, the noble Kākutstha, seemed to lose all his radiance—like a full moon covered during an eclipse. Then Daçarātha’s son, Rāma, whose spirit was impossible to grasp, ordered Sumantra, “Go faster!” While Rāma urged the charioteer to hurry, the people—

—cried out, “Stay!” With Rāma saying, “Go!” and the crowd begging, “Wait!” the charioteer couldn’t please both at once. As the chariot rolled on, the dust kicked up from its wheels was quickly dampened by the tears pouring from the citizens. Because of Rāma’s departure, the whole city was thrown into despair, and the people, barely aware of themselves, cried out with shouts of

“Oh!” and “Alas!” Everyone was deeply stricken. The tears of the women, flowing from their grief, looked like raindrops falling from lotuses shaken by swimming fish. Seeing the entire city united in sorrow, the king collapsed in grief, like a tree that’s been cut at its roots. When the crowd saw their king unconscious and overwhelmed by pain, they broke out in loud cries behind Rāma’s chariot. Hearing the king and his wives wailing—some calling,

“Oh Rāma!” and others, “Oh, Rāma’s mother!”—the people began to weep even more. Turning around, Rāma saw his heartbroken, confused father and mother following him on foot. Like a young horse stuck in a snare unable to reach its mother, Rāma, trapped by his sense of duty, couldn’t openly look at his mother. Seeing his parents—who deserved comfort and a carriage—walking on foot behind him, Rāma said to Sumantra, “Drive faster.” He just couldn’t bear the sight of his father and mother, much like an elephant, hurt by the hook, can’t look at what’s on its back.

Rāma’s mother ran after him like a cow desperate to see her calf that’s been tied up. Rāma watched as Kauçalyā chased the chariot, crying out, “Rāma, Rāma! Oh Sitā! Lakshmana!” She was weeping for all three of them, moving in a way that seemed almost frantic. The king called, “Wait!” but Rāma insisted, “Go on!” Sumantra felt torn, as if he was caught between two armies eager to fight. Rāma told him, “When the king asks you later, just say, ‘I didn’t hear you.’ But if you delay now, it will only make things harder for me.” Obeying Rāma, Sumantra urged the people to stop and made the horses go even faster. The king’s servants paused after going around Rāma’s chariot, but their hearts didn’t want to turn back. The rest of the crowd couldn’t go back—either in body or in spirit. Some courtiers told King Daçarātha, “You shouldn’t follow someone who’s expected to return too far.” Hearing this, the king—sweating, pale, and completely distraught—finally stopped and stood with his wife, watching his son leave.
SECTION XLI

As Rama (Rāma), the best among men, left the city with his hands pressed together in farewell, a wave of cries rose from the women in the palace’s inner chambers. “Where is he going—the one who was our support and shelter when we were alone, weak, or helpless? He never let anger get the best of him, even when he was falsely accused. He calmed everyone down by letting go of things that might stir up more anger. He cared for each of us equally. Where is he going now? Where is that strong and generous man, who treated us just like his own mother, Kausalya (Kauçalyā)? Hurt by Kaikeyi and ordered by the king to go to the forest, where is the one who saved us all—who saved the whole world—going now? How can the king be so foolish, sending the protector of everyone—the just and honest Rama—into exile in the woods?” The queens, crushed by grief, cried out like cows mourning their lost calves. Their wailing echoed loudly through the palace.

Hearing the heartbreaking sounds coming from the women’s quarters, King Dasaratha (the lord of earth), already burning with sorrow for his son, felt even more pain. Ritual offerings to the fire were left undone, the sun went down, elephants stopped eating, and cows wouldn’t nurse their calves. In the sky, Trisanku, Lohitanga, Brihaspati, Budha, and the other planets gathered around the moon, looking fierce and ominous. The stars lost their brightness, the planets seemed dull, and the constellation Visakha (Viçakhā) was hidden by haze. Winds pushed the clouds across the sky, making them look like ocean waves in the heavens. The whole city trembled with fear and sorrow as Rama left for the forest.

The directions themselves seemed upset, wrapped in darkness. No stars or planets could be seen. Suddenly, poverty struck the city, and no one cared about eating or drinking. The people of Ayodhya, consumed by grief and sighing constantly, grew angry with the king. Tears streaming down their faces, the travelers in the city showed no happiness—everyone was weighed down by sadness. The cool breeze had stopped, the gentle moon was gone, and the sun no longer warmed the world—the entire earth seemed lost in grief.

Children no longer depended on their parents, husbands ignored their wives, and brothers forgot each other. Everyone, abandoning their loved ones, thought only of Rama. Overwhelmed by their sorrow, Rama’s friends couldn’t rest. Like the earth stripped of its mountains if Indra (Purandara) left, Ayodhya shook in fear and sadness, now that Rama was gone. The citizens, along with their elephants and soldiers, cried out in distress.
SECTION XLII

As long as he could see the dust rising from Rama’s (Ram’s) chariot as it headed toward the forest, King Dasharatha couldn’t look away. He strained his eyes and stood on tiptoe, desperate to catch a final glimpse of his most virtuous and beloved son. Only when even the cloud of dust had faded did the king, overcome by grief and a heavy heart, collapse to the ground. Kausalya quickly lifted him up and supported him on his right arm, while Kaikeyi stayed at his left side. With pain and justice in his voice, the king glared at Kaikeyi and spoke: “Kaikeyi, you’ve chosen the path of wrongdoing. Don’t touch me—I don’t want to see you. You’re no wife of mine—not even a servant of a friend. I have nothing to do with those who depend on your favor, and they mean nothing to me. I reject you, since you only care for yourself and have turned your back on what’s right. I give up all the happiness I could have had in this life or the next by marrying you and walking with you around the sacred fire. If Bharata is happy ruling the whole kingdom, I hope he spends nothing from my funeral on me.” Then, as Kausalya brushed the dust from Dasharatha and stopped with him, her heart full of grief, the king was lost in regret, feeling as if he’d committed a terrible crime or burned himself in fire. While he paused again and again, staring at the track left by Rama’s chariot, his face looked as dim as the moon covered by an eclipse. Stricken with sorrow, he kept remembering his beloved son, thinking Rama must have reached the city gates by now, and cried out, “I see only the footprints of the horses and men carrying my son away—he himself is gone. My good son, who used to rest his head on soft pillows, scented with sandalwood, and be fanned by beautiful women in jeweled clothes—tonight he’ll have to sleep under a tree, his head on bare wood or stone. Covered in dust, he’ll wake up from the cold ground with a heavy sigh, like a mother elephant rising from the side of a mountain. The forest animals will see Rama, with his long arms and kingly presence, getting up from the ground like someone lost and alone. Sita, who Janaka loved and always kept comfortable, is now heading to the forest, tired and scratched by thorns. She doesn’t know the wilds, and must be terrified by the roars of fierce animals that could make anyone’s hair stand on end. Kaikeyi, you’ve gotten what you wanted—rule this kingdom as a widow, because I can’t live without the best of men.” 

Crying like this, the king entered the city, surrounded by a grieving crowd. It was as if he were a ghost after his own funeral—the city’s streets were empty, shops were closed, and everyone looked weak and sorrowful. Still thinking only of Rama, Dasharatha saw the whole city as dark and empty, like the sun hidden in heavy clouds. It felt like a sea where all the snakes had been driven away, with no sign of Rama, Lakshmana, or Sita. Tears filled the king’s eyes as he mumbled broken, barely understandable words: “Take me quickly to Kausalya’s room. Nowhere else can my heart find rest.” When he said this, the attendants led him to Kausalya’s chamber, where he lay down, worn out and defeated. Lying on Kausalya’s bed, Dasharatha was overwhelmed by emotion. He looked around the mansion, now missing both his sons and his daughter-in-law, and it felt as empty as the night sky without the moon. Lifting his arm, the king cried out, “Rama, you’ve left us! How lucky are those people who, after this long wait, will see Rama return and get to embrace him.” 

When night fell, dark and ominous like the night of his own death, Dasharatha turned to Kausalya at midnight and said, “Kausalya, I can’t see you. Please touch me with your hand. My eyes are still searching for Rama—they can’t come back.” Seeing the king completely lost in thoughts of Rama, Kausalya sat beside him. Her grief was even deeper than his, and she began to sob, letting out heavy sighs.
SECTION XLIII

Seeing the king lying there, overwhelmed by grief, Kausalya, heartbroken for her son, spoke to her husband, the ruler of the land. “O greatest of men, Kaikeyi (Kay) has poured out all her poison onto Rama (Raghava), and now she’ll slither around like a snake that’s shed its old skin—dangerous, but satisfied for now. Having gotten what she wanted, she’ll only become more terrifying to me, like a venomous snake loose in the house. If Rama had just stayed here in the city, even if he had to beg for food, or if I’d made him Kaikeyi’s servant, that would have been better than sending him to the forest. Just like the sacrificial offerings thrown to demons during festivals, Rama—the mighty archer, who moves with the grace of a royal elephant—has been cast away by Kaikeyi and forced to seek shelter in the wild with Sita and Lakshmana.

You sent them to the forest at Kaikeyi’s command, but how will they survive, when they’re not used to the harshness of forest life? Stripped of their fine clothes, how will these young people—exiled during what should be the best years of their lives—endure the hardship of living off roots and fruit? Will there ever come a day when my sorrow is gone and my wish fulfilled, and I see Rama again with his wife and brother by his side? When will Ayodhya, decorated with flags and garlands, become famous and full of joy at the news of their return? When will the city overflow with happiness, like the ocean during a festival, as these heroes come back from the forest?

When will Rama, the strong-armed hero, ride into Ayodhya with Sita in the chariot before him, like a bull proudly leading his mate? When will crowds of people throw popped rice over my sons as they enter the city, celebrating their return as conquerors? When will I see those two, their earrings shining, carrying their weapons and swords in front of them, looking like two great mountains with their peaks? When will they circle the palace, accepting flowers from young women and fruit from Brahmins, their faces lit up with joy? When will Rama, wise beyond his years and almost godlike, finally return, bringing happiness to everyone like a rain after a long drought?

I must have done something terrible in a past life. Maybe, I once cruelly cut off the udders of cows and kept their calves from their mothers’ milk. Maybe it’s for that sin that I’m now being punished, losing my beloved Rama to Kaikeyi—like a cow losing her calf to a lion. Rama is my only son, perfect in every way and learned in everything. I can’t bear to live without him. If I don’t see my precious Rama and the brave Lakshmana, I don’t think I can survive. Just as the summer sun scorches the earth with its fierce heat, this burning grief for my son is consuming me.”
SECTION XLIV

While Kauçalyā was deep in grief, Sumitrā—always wise and virtuous—spoke gently to comfort her. “Respected lady, your son has every good quality and is the best among men. So why are you mourning and crying so bitterly? Think about it: your powerful son has given up the throne to fulfill the promise of his noble and truthful father. Rāma is doing what is right, following the path of virtue that always brings good results, both in this world and beyond. There’s no reason to grieve for him. And Lakshmana, who is kind to everyone, will serve Rāma with all his heart. This will only help Rāma, who is so full of strength and goodness. Even though life in the forest will be hard, Sītā (also called Vaidehi), who deserves happiness, is willingly going with your righteous son. What does your son lack? He controls his desires, speaks the truth, keeps his promises, and his reputation is known everywhere. Rāma’s purity and greatness are so clear that even the Sun would not dare to harm him with its rays. The pleasant forest air, warm and cool at different times, will refresh him. When he lies down at night, the Moon will shine softly on him, embracing him like a father and bringing him comfort.

Rāma is a mighty hero, blessed with divine weapons by Brahmā himself. Remember how he defeated the great demon, the son of Timidhwaja, in battle? Like a tiger, he relies on his own strength and will live in the forest without fear, as if it were his own home. Why shouldn’t the world be ruled by someone whose enemies fall within his reach? With his grace, bravery, and good fortune, it’s certain that Rāma will return from the forest and soon reclaim his kingdom. He is the brightest among the bright, the most fortunate of the fortunate, the most patient of the patient, and the greatest among the great—truly the best of all beings. Whether he is in the city or in the forest, what fault could anyone find in him?

Soon enough, Rāma—the best of men—will rule again, with the Earth, Sītā, and the goddess of victory by his side. The people of Ayodhyā are heartbroken to see him go to the forest in simple clothes made of grass and bark, but with fortune (Lakshmī) on his side, there’s nothing he can’t achieve. And with Lakshmana—the greatest archer—carrying weapons before him, there’s nothing he can’t overcome. You will see your son again when he returns from the forest. Please, let go of your grief and sadness—I say this sincerely. Soon, you will see your son, like a new moon, bowing at your feet in respect. When you see him return, blessed with good fortune, you will be filled with joy and happiness.

So, noble lady, don’t be sad or cry. No harm can come to Rāma. Soon, you will see your son again, along with Sītā and Lakshmana. You are pure and blameless, so it’s up to you to comfort the people around you. Why let your heart be overcome by grief? Especially when Rāma is your son! No one in this world is more honest or virtuous than him. Soon, surrounded by friends and bowing to you, your son will make you cry tears of joy. When he returns, bringing gifts, he will gently press your feet with his soft, strong hands. Just as clouds speak to the mountains, you will speak to your heroic son as he stands before you with his friends, bowing at your feet.”

After saying these hopeful words, Sumitrā—wise, kind, and gentle—fell silent. Hearing Lakshmana’s mother speak, Kauçalyā felt her sorrow lift, like a raincloud in autumn that quickly disappears.
SECTION XLV

The people of Ayodhyā, who deeply loved Rāma for his honesty and strength of character, followed him as he made his way to the forest. Even after King Daçarātha had managed, with great difficulty, to control his own grief for the sake of his son, the citizens kept following Rāma’s chariot and wouldn’t give up. Rāma, perfect in every way, was like the full moon to the people of Ayodhyā—someone they adored. But even as the people begged him to stay, Rāma, true to his promise to his father, kept heading toward the forest. He is Kaikeyi’s joy, a good man, and he will do everything to make you happy. He may be young, but he’s wise, gentle, and brave—he will protect you all and be a worthy king. For my sake, do what you can to make sure the king doesn’t suffer after I’m gone.” But even as Rāma tried to convince them to honor the royal order, the people only wanted Rāma to rule over them. Rāma, with Lakshmana by his side, moved the crowd so much that many stood there with tears streaming down their faces. Among them were the elders of the priestly class—the Brāhmanas—distinguished by age, wisdom, or spiritual discipline, their heads trembling with age. From a distance, they cried out, “You noble horses pulling Rāma’s chariot, stop! Don’t go! Do what is truly best for your master. And you, horses—if you really understand us—please listen and stop. Your master, so pure, brave, and true to his word, deserves to be carried back to the city, not taken into the forest.” 

Suddenly, seeing these old Brāhmanas so heartbroken, Rāma quickly got down from his chariot. Along with Lakshmana and Sītā, he began walking beside them on foot, still headed for the forest. Rāma, always kind and loyal to good people, couldn’t bear to ride while the Brāhmanas struggled to follow him on foot. Seeing Rāma walking, the Brāhmanas—hearts pounding and full of sorrow—spoke to him: “All of us Brāhmanas are following you, wishing you only good. Even the sacred fires, carried on our shoulders, come along behind you. Look at these umbrellas we earned from the Vājapeya sacrifice—they’re like autumn clouds following you, ready to shade you now that you don’t have your royal white umbrella to protect you from the sun. Our minds, usually focused on Vedic mantras, are now fixed on following you into the forest for your sake. The Vedas, our greatest treasure, live within our hearts, and our wives—protected by their faithfulness—are safe at home. We’re already set on following you, so there’s no point trying to change our minds. But if you, who always stand for what’s right, ignore what’s good and just, then what will become of righteousness itself? We beg you, with our white hair bowed to the ground, please don’t go. Many of us Brāhmanas are in the middle of important sacrifices, and they can only be completed if you return. Every living thing, animals and plants alike, respects you. All of them beg you to show some compassion for those who care about you. Even the tall trees, rooted to the earth and unable to follow, seem to be trying to stop you by rustling in the wind. Birds perched on the branches, not flying away or looking for food, seem to be pleading with you to have mercy on all creatures.” 

As the Brāhmanas loudly begged Rāma to come back, night began to fall, almost as if the darkness itself wanted to stop him. Sumantra then unharnessed the tired horses from the chariot, and the horses immediately rolled in the dust to rest. After washing them and letting them drink, as dusk settled in, he prepared their evening feed.

Rāma (also called Rāghava) paused on the banks of the Tamasā River, looked at Sitā, and spoke to Lakshmana (Sumitrā’s son): “Lakshmana, this is our first night exiled in the forest. From today, you shouldn’t let yourself get lost in memories of happier times—don’t let your mind dwell on the past. Right now, the people of Ayodhyā—my father’s city—are probably grieving because we’ve left for the woods. The people love you, our father the king, Bharata, Satrughna, and me, because of our good character. I feel sorry for our father and my noble mother—I’m worried that if they keep crying, they might even go blind from sorrow. But I trust that Bharata, who is so good and sincere, will comfort our parents with wise, caring words. When I think about how genuine Bharata is, I worry less about our parents. Lakshmana, it was your duty to come with me; if you hadn’t, I would have had to look elsewhere to keep Sitā (Vaidehi) safe. Tonight, I’ll stay here and only drink water, even though the forest is full of fruits. That feels right to me.” After saying this, Rāma turned to Sumantra and said, “Please, take care of the horses.” As the sun set, Sumantra tied up the horses and fed them lots of grass, then returned. Seeing that night had fallen, Sumantra performed the evening prayers and, together with Lakshmana, set up a bed for Rāma. Looking at their makeshift bed under the trees by the river, Rāma, Sitā, and Lakshmana lay down to sleep. Once Rāma and Sitā had fallen asleep, Lakshmana stayed awake and started talking to Sumantra about all of Rāma’s good qualities. As Lakshmana kept watch through the night, describing Rāma’s virtues to the charioteer, the sun finally began to rise.
SECTION XLVI

Rāma spent that night with the people, a bit away from the riverbank, where cattle grazed. When he woke up, full of energy, he saw that the people who had followed him were still asleep. He spoke to Lakshmana, who had lucky marks on his body: “Lakshmana, these people have left their own homes for our sake and are sleeping under the trees. They’re hoping to convince me to turn back to the city—they’d rather die than give up on that. Let’s leave quickly, while they’re still asleep, and head out in our chariot so they can’t try to stop us. If we go now, the people of Ayodhyā won’t keep sleeping outdoors because of me. A good ruler should save his people from trouble, not drag them into hardships he brought on himself.” Lakshmana replied, “Rāma, I agree completely. Let’s go—get in the chariot.” Rāma then told Sumantra, “Please get the chariot ready right away. I’m going into the forest. Let’s leave quickly.” Sumantra hurried off, harnessed the horses to the chariot, and respectfully said to Rāma—

“Rāma, the chariot is ready for you, Lakshmana, and Sitā. Please get in.” Rāma got into the chariot, armed and prepared, and they crossed the fast-flowing Tamasā River, swirling with currents. On the other side, Rāma, strong and blessed, found a safe and open road that would give even nervous travelers confidence. Wanting to throw off anyone who might try to follow, Rāma told Sumantra, “Drive the chariot north for a while, then double back and turn. Do it carefully, so the people don’t realize which way we’ve gone.” Sumantra understood and did exactly as Rāma asked, then came back and told Rāma to get in the chariot again.

Once Rāma, Lakshmana, and Sitā were seated in the chariot, Sumantra drove the horses down the road that led to the hermitage. He first pointed the chariot north for good luck, then, with Daçarātha’s sons safely on board, he set off into the forest.
SECTION XLVII

When night ended and the sun rose, the people of Ayodhyā realized that Rāma (Rāghava) was gone. Grief hit them hard—they felt lost and confused, wandering around with tears streaming down their faces. They searched everywhere, desperate, but they couldn’t even find any trace of the dust from Rāma’s chariot. Heartbroken and disoriented, these thoughtful citizens, their faces showing how much they were suffering, began to speak in sorrowful voices.

“How terrible that we slept through this! Because we were unconscious, we won’t see Rāma today—Rāma with his broad chest and powerful arms. How could someone like Rāma, so strong, just leave us and go into exile as a hermit, abandoning the people who love him so much? Why would Rāma, the best of the Raghus, who has always cared for us like a father cares for his own children, leave us and head into the forest? If things are like this, we might as well die here or head north to meet our end. What’s the point of living if Rāma is gone? There are plenty of big, dry logs around. If we light a funeral pyre, we could all walk into the flames together. What would we even say to people? How could we explain, ‘We let Rāma, who was strong, kind, and forgiving, leave us’? When people see us without Rāghava, the city—its women, children, and adults—will be plunged into misery. We followed that noble hero out of the city, but now that he’s gone, how can we face returning home?” With these words, they raised their arms in despair, grieving like cows who’ve lost their calves. They tried to follow the tracks of Rāma’s chariot for a while, but when the trail disappeared, they were overcome with sadness. Eventually, they retraced their steps back to Ayodhyā, feeling lost and defeated. “What’s happening to us? What can we do now? It’s like some supernatural force is working against us.” So, they returned home through the same streets they had come, their hearts heavy and their eyes filled with tears as they looked at their city.

“Ayodhyā without Rāma doesn’t even look beautiful anymore,” they said. “It’s like a lake after Garuda has taken away its serpent, or a sky without the moon, or the sea with all its water dried up.” Their minds were troubled as they saw the whole city drowning in sorrow. When they entered their own grand houses, their hearts so dark with grief, they couldn’t even recognize their own homes. No matter how carefully they looked, everything seemed unfamiliar and joyless.
SECTION XLVIII

The people of Ayodhyā, crushed by grief and with tears streaming down their faces, left Rāma and returned to the city. It felt as if their very lives were about to leave them. When they reached their homes, their families gathered around them, but everyone was lost in sorrow, washing their faces with tears. No one felt any joy; the marketplace was empty, no stalls were set up, household fires stayed cold, and no one celebrated even if they found lost possessions or gained unexpected wealth. Mothers didn’t smile at their firstborns. In every house, women, overwhelmed with sadness, scolded their husbands as soon as they arrived—pushing them with words as cruelly as elephant drivers use hooks: “What’s the point of homes, wives, wealth, sons, or comforts if we can’t see Rāghava (Rāma) among us? There’s only one truly good man left—Lakshmana—who, along with Sitā, is following Rāma into exile. The rivers, lotus-filled ponds, and pools Rāma will bathe in are lucky to have him. Beautiful forests, huge lakes, and wide mountain plateaus are blessed because Rāma will travel there. Wherever Rāma goes, the forests and hills will honor him like a guest. Trees bursting with colorful flowers and fresh shoots, alive with bees, will bloom just for Rāma. The hills will offer him their best flowers and fruits, even out of season, and give him clear springs of water. Trees on mountaintops will create beautiful fountains to delight Rāma. Where Rāma is, there’s no fear or defeat—he’s a true hero, the mighty son of Daçarātha. While he’s still near, let’s follow him. Even the dust from our master’s feet would make us happy. He’s our lord, our refuge, the reason for our virtues. Let’s serve Sitā and Rāghava together.” In their grief, the women begged their husbands like this. “Rāghava will create new opportunities and protect what you have, even in the forest. Sitā will do the same for us women. Who could find joy in a house where the heart feels dead, where there’s no happiness, where everyone is always worried, and everything feels wrong? If Kaikeyi rules this kingdom, it will lose all goodness and be like a kingdom with no king. What’s the point of living, let alone having sons or wealth? Kaikeyi has already betrayed her own husband and son for power—who will she betray next? We swear by our children, as long as Kaikeyi lives, we won’t stay in her kingdom, even if she tries to provide for us. How could we ever be happy with someone so cruel and shameless, who drove the son of the greatest king into exile? The kingdom will fall apart—rituals will stop, chaos will spread, and without a real ruler, everything will be destroyed because of Kaikeyi. Once Rāma leaves for the forest, King Daçarātha won’t survive, and when he dies, everything will fall apart. So, if you’ve lost your virtue and are crushed by grief, swallow poison, follow Rāghava, or go far away—anywhere Kaikeyi’s name can’t reach you. Rāma, Sitā, and Lakshmana have been sent away through trickery, and we’re trapped under Bharata like a sacrificial animal waiting for slaughter. Surely, that mighty prince—broad-shouldered, with a face like the full moon, dark-skinned, fearless, arms down to his knees, lotus-like eyes—Rāma, Lakshmana’s older brother—always polite, honest, powerful, loved by everyone, as attractive as the moon, and as strong as a raging elephant, will bring glory to the forests he travels through.” As the women mourned throughout the city, their sorrow made Ayodhyā feel as panicked and desperate as a city struck by plague.

While the women wept for Rāghava in their homes, the sun set and night fell over Ayodhyā. The city was swallowed by darkness; the ritual fires went out, and the usual sounds of Vedic study and wise conversation faded away. The shops were shut, the joy of festivals disappeared, and everyone felt defenseless. The city seemed as empty and lost as a sky with no stars. The women, crying for Rāma as if he were their own son or brother, mourned so deeply that Rāma meant more to them than their own children. The music, dancing, and laughter died down, and with the shops closed, Ayodhyā felt like a great ocean that had been drained of all its water.
SECTION XLIX

Rāma, determined to follow his father’s orders, traveled quickly and covered a lot of ground before the night was over. As dawn broke, he performed his morning prayers to Sandhyā, the goddess of twilight, and then entered a new region. Along the way, he passed villages surrounded by plowed fields and blooming forests. With his excellent horses, he moved so fast that it barely looked like he was moving at all. As Rāma continued his journey, he overheard the villagers talking among themselves: “Shame on King Daçarātha—he’s lost in his own desires! And Kaikeyi, so cruel and sinful, has thrown away her honor and is doing something truly horrible—sending the king’s wise and kind son into exile. How can King Daçarātha have no love for his own child, wanting to send away Rāma, who’s innocent and beloved by everyone?” Hearing their words, Rāma, the prince of Koçala, left his homeland behind. He then crossed the sacred river Vedaçruti, heading south toward the land where the sage Agastya lived.

After traveling for some time, Rāma crossed the cool, flowing river Gomati, whose banks were crowded with cattle and flooded at the edges. Once past the Gomati, Rāma—with his swift horses—crossed the river Sandika, where the air rang with the cries of cranes and peacocks. Rāma pointed out to Sītā (also called Vaidehi) these prosperous lands that King Manu had once given to Ikshwāku, and which were now full of people. Then, often turning to the charioteer and calling him “Suta,” Rāma, who had a gentle voice as smooth as a swan’s song, said, “When will I return to hunt in the blossoming woods along the Sarayu river with my father and mother? Honestly, I don’t care that much for hunting in the Sarayu’s forests, but the pastime is considered special and respected by the royal sages. Hunting was created for the enjoyment of the Rāghavas, but it’s never really been my passion, even though it’s a favorite sport for Manu’s descendants and for archers everywhere.” As he spoke about this, Rāma, the descendant of Ikshwāku, continued his journey, chatting kindly with the charioteer.
SECTION L

After leaving behind the vast and beautiful land of Kosala, Rama, the wise older brother of Lakshmana, faced toward Ayodhya. With his hands pressed together, he prayed, “O greatest of cities, ruled by the house of Kakutstha, I speak to you and to all your guardian spirits. When my time in exile is over and my duty to my father is done, I will return to see you again, together with my father and mother.” Then, eyes shining with tears and sadness, Rama raised his right hand and spoke to the people of the provinces: “You have shown me kindness and sorrow at my leaving. But it’s not right to mourn forever. Please, go home and take care of your lives.” The people, overwhelmed with grief, circled Rama, bowing and crying, unable to walk away. They lingered, staring at him, unable to get enough of his face, as Rama moved out of their sight—like the sun setting at dusk.

Rama climbed onto his chariot and left behind Kosala—a land rich in cattle, filled with generous people, peaceful, beautiful, and free from fear. The region was scattered with altars and stakes for sacrifices, gardens and mango groves, ponds full of happy people, and the sounds of Vedic chanting. Traveling at a steady pace, Rama passed through lands that were cheerful and prosperous, lined with elegant houses—places any king would envy. 

Soon, Rama saw the sacred Ganga river, flowing in three streams with cool, clear water. The river was beautiful, visited by sages, and lined with lovely hermitages. It was home to heavenly beings: Apsaras played in the water, celestials, Danavas (demons), Gandharvas (celestial musicians), and Kinnaras (celestial beings) all gathered there. The riverbanks were filled with the wives of Nagas (serpent beings) and Gandharvas, and hills nearby served as playgrounds for the gods. The Ganga was famous in heaven, covered with celestial lotuses, her waters laughing as they crashed over rocks. Sometimes her current moved in braids, sometimes swirling in eddies, sometimes calm and deep, other times wild and roaring. Gods bathed in her waters, and her banks were decorated with lotus flowers, sandy stretches, and the cries of cranes and water birds. There were trees along the banks, heavy with garlands of flowers, and masses of lilies and buds. The air was thick with pollen. The Ganga was like a proud, beautiful woman; she washed away sin and was as clear as crystal. Elephants—wild and tamed, some carrying gods—roamed the nearby woods, trumpeting. The river was decorated like a queen, overflowing with flowers, fruits, and birds, sacred because she flowed from the feet of Vishnu. She was divine, pure, able to wash away sin, and full of dolphins, crocodiles, and snakes. She had sprung from Shiva’s hair thanks to the power of Sagara’s descendant. The Ganga, queen of rivers, echoed with the calls of cranes and kraunchas (herons).

Rama, strong-armed and mighty, arrived at the Ganga near the town of Sringaverapura. Seeing the river’s swirling currents, Rama said to his charioteer, Sumantra, “Let’s rest here today. There’s a huge ingudi tree close by, full of flowers and fresh leaves. We’ll stay here. I see before me the greatest of rivers, honored by gods, humans, Gandharvas, animals, snakes, and birds.” Sumantra and Lakshmana answered, “Very well,” and led the horses to the ingudi tree. When they arrived, Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita got down from the chariot. Sumantra took care of the horses and stood respectfully before Rama, who sat at the base of the tree.

At that place lived a king named Guha, a close friend of Rama and the ruler of the Nishadas—a strong and respected leader. When Guha heard that Rama had arrived, he came at once with his elders and family. Seeing Guha in the distance, Rama walked toward him with Lakshmana. Guha was deeply moved and hugged Rama, saying, “Rama, my kingdom is yours, just like Ayodhya. What can I do for you? Who else gets to greet such an honored guest?” Guha quickly brought all kinds of delicious rice and offerings, asking, “Mighty Rama, was your journey safe? This land is yours. We serve you; you are our lord. Please accept these foods, drinks, treats, comfortable beds, and fodder.”

Rama replied, “You’ve already welcomed us so well, Guha. Just your affection means everything. I’m grateful to see you well with your family. Is your kingdom peaceful? Is the forest calm? I appreciate your gifts of food, but I must live simply in the woods now, wearing grass and bark, surviving on fruits and roots. All I need is food for the horses. These horses belonged to my father, Dasharatha. If you care for them, I’ll feel completely honored as your guest.”

Guha gave orders right away: “See that the horses have plenty to eat and drink.” Then Rama wrapped himself in his cloth and performed his evening prayers. When he finished, he drank water that Lakshmana brought for him. Rama and Sita lay down on the ground to sleep, while Lakshmana washed their feet and then stood guard under the tree.

Lakshmana, his bow in hand and mind alert, stayed awake with Guha and Sumantra, talking quietly and watching over Rama. In this way, the whole night passed with Rama—the noble, wise son of Dasharatha—who had never known such hardship and truly deserved happiness.
SECTION LI

Lakshmana kept careful watch over his brother Rama, driven by deep love and a sense of duty. Guha, overwhelmed by sorrow, spoke to Lakshmana—“Look, my friend, we’ve set up a comfortable bed for you. Please, prince, rest here if you want. These forest people are used to rough living, but you deserve comfort. We’ll stay up all night to guard Rama. There’s no one on earth I care about more than him, and I swear that’s the truth. Through his friendship, I hope to gain honor, religious merit, and happiness in this life. My family and I will keep watch, weapons in hand, while my dear friend sleeps beside Sita. I know these woods better than anyone, and nothing here can surprise me. Even if a huge army attacked us, I’d fight them off.” Hearing this, Lakshmana replied—

“Guha, you’re a good man, and with you watching over us, we have nothing to fear here. But how could I sleep when Rama, son of Dasaratha, is lying on the cold ground beside Sita? What joy could I possibly find in rest or happiness while he suffers? Look at him—sleeping on grass next to Sita, he’s the same Rama that even gods and demons couldn’t defeat in battle. Remember, Dasaratha gained Rama as his son through incredible effort, prayers, and rituals, and Rama’s virtues truly reflect those sacrifices. Now that Rama’s been banished, I doubt the king will live long; soon the whole kingdom will be left without his guidance. I bet the women in the palace have cried themselves hoarse by now, and the royal home must be quiet and empty. I can’t believe that Kausalya, the king, or even my own mother are still alive. If they are, it’s only for tonight. Even if my mother lives on for Satrughna’s sake, I know Kausalya—Rama’s mother—will die of grief. The palace, once filled with laughter and light, will fall into ruin after this tragedy. How can the king survive, now that he can’t see his beloved eldest son? After he dies, Kausalya will follow him, and then my mother will pass away too. My father wanted nothing more than to make Rama king, but now—robbed of that hope—he’ll probably die, crying ‘All is lost.’ The lucky ones will be those who are there to perform his funeral rites when that time comes. They’ll still get to live in our beautiful city—Ayodhya—with its grand terraces, wide roads, palaces, beautiful women, busy markets, elephants, horses, music and festivities, and happy, prosperous people. If Dasaratha somehow survives, maybe we’ll return from the forest and see him again, still true to his vows. If everything goes well, maybe we’ll all come back together, with Rama, to Ayodhya.” As Lakshmana poured out his grief, sitting awake through the night, dawn finally broke. The devoted son’s words, spoken from the heart, touched Guha deeply. Out of love for Rama, Guha began to cry, overcome with sorrow, as if struck by a great pain.
SECTION LII

As dawn broke, Rama—the renowned prince with a broad chest—turned to Lakshmana, Sumitra’s son, who was marked by good fortune. “The sun is rising, and the night is over,” Rama said. “Listen—the black-plumed koel is singing, and I can hear peacocks calling in the forest. Let’s cross the fast-flowing Jahnavi (Ganga) now.” Lakshmana, always eager to help, passed Rama’s words on to Guha and the charioteer, then stood ready by his brother’s side. Guha, chief of the Nishadas, heard their plan and quickly called his advisors. “Bring a sturdy, well-made boat here,” he ordered, “with a rudder and a skilled helmsman—one that can carry us all safely.” Guha’s men soon returned with the boat and told him it was ready. Bowing respectfully, Guha said to Rama, “The boat is here, noble one. What more can I do for you? Please, climb aboard and cross the river that flows to the ocean.” Rama replied, “Thanks to you, Guha, our needs are met. Please load our baggage on the boat.” Then, putting on their armor and taking their bows, quivers, and swords, Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita walked down to the riverbank.

The charioteer approached Rama respectfully and asked, “What should I do now?” Rama took Sumantra’s right hand and said kindly, “Sumantra, you must return to the king now. Keep your mind clear.” He continued, “Your duty was to bring me this far, as the king commanded. From here, I’ll travel on foot into the forest.” Hearing this, Sumantra’s heart broke. He said to Rama, “How cruel fate is, making you live like an outcast in the forest with your brother and wife. What’s the use of self-control, study, or even kindness, if someone as virtuous as you suffers like this? Still, by living in the forest with Sita and Lakshmana, you achieve greatness—as if conquering the three worlds. It is we, left behind, who are ruined, because we’ll be left with the misery Kaikeyi has brought.” Sumantra wept for a long time, unable to bear the thought of Rama leaving. When he had finally calmed himself, touching Ganga’s water for strength, Rama spoke gently, “No one is a better friend to the sons of Ikshwaku than you. Please, do everything you can to keep King Dasaratha from grieving too much. He’s old and weakened by sorrow, so it’s important that you help him. Whatever the king asks to please Kaikeyi, do it quickly. That’s what kings are for: to carry out their will. Make sure the king faces nothing unpleasant, and help him through this pain. When you see him, bow for me and tell him this: ‘Neither Rama nor Lakshmana are sad about leaving Ayodhya or living in the forest. After fourteen years, all three of us—Lakshmana, Sita, and I—will return to you.’ Tell my mother Kausalya and Kaikeyi and the other queens that we are well, and give my respects, as well as Sita’s and Lakshmana’s, to Kausalya’s feet. Also tell the king, ‘Call Bharata home soon and make him king. Once you have embraced him and crowned him, don’t grieve for us anymore.’ And tell Bharata, ‘Treat all your mothers equally, just as you treat the king. See Sumitra and Kausalya as you do Kaikeyi. Rule as prince for our father’s happiness, and you’ll find joy in this life and the next.’” Rama finished, and Sumantra, overwhelmed with emotion, replied, “Please forgive me for speaking so plainly, but I can’t help it. How can I return to Ayodhya without you? The city already feels empty, as if it’s mourning for a lost child. When people see my chariot without you, their hearts will break—as if a hero has died in battle, leaving only the charioteer. The people will starve themselves, hoping you’ll return. You saw how much they suffered as you left for the woods. When they see me coming back alone, their grief will be even worse than before. How can I lie to the king and say, ‘I’ve taken your son to his uncle’s house—don’t worry’? But telling the truth is too painful. And these horses, who always carried you and your friends, how can they pull the chariot without you? I can’t go back without you. Please, let me follow you into the forest. If you leave me behind, I’ll set myself on fire along with the chariot. With the chariot, I can help you face any challenges in the woods. You gave me the honor of driving you—I only ask now to live with you in the forest. Please, let me stay by your side. Even the horses would be honored to serve you there. I’d gladly serve you with all my heart, and I’d give up Ayodhya—or even heaven—before leaving you. Just as a wrongdoer can’t enter Indra’s city, I can’t return to Ayodhya without you. My one hope is that when the exile is over, I can drive you back home in this chariot. Fourteen years with you will pass in a blink, but without you, they’ll feel like a hundred years. Please, don’t abandon your loyal servant, who has always followed you faithfully.” Rama, moved by Sumantra’s loyalty, replied,

“I know you care deeply for me, Sumantra, and I’m grateful. But listen to why I need you to go back to Ayodhya. When my youngest mother, Kaikeyi, sees you return without me, she’ll be sure I’ve left for the forest. She’ll have no doubts about the king’s honesty, and she’ll be satisfied that her wish was granted. That’s my first concern: that Kaikeyi gets her son’s kingdom, well protected by Bharata. Please go to the palace and do what’s best for both the king and me. Tell everyone what I’ve said.” After comforting Sumantra, Rama turned to Guha and said, “Guha, I shouldn’t stay in a forest where people live. I need to live like an ascetic, as my father wishes. Sita and Lakshmana agree. I’ll take on the look of a hermit, with matted hair. Please bring me some banyan-tree starch.” Guha quickly brought it, and helped prepare matted locks for Rama, Lakshmana, and himself. Now, dressed like hermits with tangled hair, Rama and Lakshmana looked like true saints.

Taking on the vows of a forest-dweller, Rama said to his loyal friend Guha, “Watch over the army, the treasury, the city, and all the provinces. A kingdom needs its king’s constant attention.” Then, after saying goodbye to Guha, Rama steeled himself and set out with Sita and Lakshmana. When they reached the riverbank, Rama said, “Let’s get on the boat, but first help Sita in gently.” Lakshmana, always careful, helped Sita onto the boat, and then boarded himself. Rama followed, and Guha encouraged his own people to row. Once they were all on board, Rama, skilled and powerful, recited protective mantras suitable for warriors and priests. Lakshmana, following tradition, sipped water from the river and bowed to it with Sita, feeling hopeful. Then Rama, standing in the boat, told Sumantra, Guha, and the soldiers goodbye, and ordered the boatmen to start. The helmsman and the rowers, using their strong oars, pushed the boat quickly into the water. As they reached the middle of the Ganga, Sita, pure-hearted, folded her hands and prayed to the river:

“O Ganga, may you keep Rama, son of the wise and mighty Dasaratha, safe, so he can fulfill his father’s promise. After fourteen years, he’ll return with Lakshmana and me. Then, O sacred river, I’ll worship you when we’re safely back and Rama has reclaimed his kingdom. You flow in three streams and are known as the spouse of the Ocean King. When we return in good fortune, I’ll offer you hundreds and thousands of cows, clothes, delicious rice, wine, and feasts for the priests. I’ll honor all the gods along your banks and every holy spot, as soon as Rama comes home from exile with Lakshmana and me.” After this prayer, Sita, ever devoted to her husband, quickly reached the southern bank. Once they landed, Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita stood together on the far side of the river. Rama said to Lakshmana, “Whether we’re alone or among people, your job is to protect Sita. We must watch over her, especially in lonely places. You go first, Sumitra’s son. Sita will follow you, and I’ll come behind, protecting you both. From now on, we need to look after each other—our hardest challenges are ahead. Today Sita will feel the true pain of forest life, leaving behind all comfort and entering a wild, uneven, and empty land.” Hearing Rama’s words, Lakshmana led the way, with Sita following and Rama behind them.

Once Rama had crossed the Ganga, Sumantra stood gazing after him until he could no longer see him. Tears ran down his face as grief overwhelmed him. Meanwhile, Rama, noble and strong as a guardian spirit, wasted no time after crossing the river. He and his companions entered the beautiful and fertile land of the Vatsas. That evening, the two brothers hunted and killed wild boars, deer, antelope, and great rurus, gathering their meat. Hungry after the day’s journey, they rested for the night beneath a massive tree.
SECTION LIII

After taking shelter under a tree and finishing his evening prayers, Rāma, who had a natural charm about him, spoke to Lakshmana. “Tonight is our first night outside the city, away from people, and without Sumantra with us,” he said. “Don’t let that bother you. From now on, we’ll have to be extra careful and protect Sītā at all times. It’s up to us to keep her safe and provide whatever she needs. Let’s just do our best to get through the night. We’ll gather some leaves and make a bed on the ground for ourselves.” With that, Rāma, who was used to luxury but now lay on the bare earth, continued speaking to Lakshmana. “Lakshmana, I’m sure the king is having a restless night, and Kaikeyi must be pleased now that she’s gotten her way. Do you think that Kaikeyi, once Bharata arrives and she sees her plan succeed, would go so far as to take the king’s life just to make Bharata king? Our father is old, alone, and now separated from me—who knows what he’ll do, especially since Kaikeyi controls him. Seeing all this—what’s happened to us and how the king has lost control—I feel like desire is stronger than either morals or common sense. Lakshmana, what kind of person, even if he’s ignorant, abandons his own son just because of a woman, like our father did to me? Honestly, Kaikeyi’s son Bharata is the lucky one—he and his wife will enjoy ruling Kosala alone, now that our father is old and I’m living in exile. He’ll have all the happiness of being king. When someone gives up what’s right for their own desires, they end up in trouble, just like King Daśaratha. I really think Kaikeyi was born just to destroy Daśaratha, send me away, and give the throne to Bharata. Right now, Kaikeyi, drunk with her success, will make life miserable for Kauśalyā and Sumitrā just to hurt me. Your mother, Sumitrā, will suffer because of us. SECTION LXI

As Rāma, the most charming and righteous of men, set out for the forest, Kauśalyā (Rāma's mother) wept in sorrow and turned to her husband, Daśaratha. “Your fame is known across the three worlds, and Rāma, your son, is kind, generous, and always speaks with honesty. So why have you abandoned such a remarkable man, along with Sītā? They were raised in comfort, but now they’re forced into hardship—how can they possibly endure it? And how will Sītā, the young and delicate daughter of Mithilā, who deserves happiness, survive the harsh heat and cold? She used to eat delicious meals with all the best dishes—how will she manage on wild forest grains? She once listened to beautiful music—how will she cope with the terrifying roars of wild animals? Where will Rāma sleep now, the mighty warrior whose arm is as strong as a mace, who once rested so comfortably? When will I see Rāma’s face again, beautiful as a lotus, his hair curling softly, his breath sweet as the flower, and his eyes as gentle as lotus petals? My heart must be made of stone, since it hasn’t shattered from the pain of not seeing him.

All this suffering is because of your actions. My own family, who should have lived happily, are wandering in misery through the forest. Even if fifteen years pass and Rāma returns, do you really think Bharata will give up the throne and the treasury? It’s like when people, during the Śrāddha ritual, feed their friends first and only then think of inviting the respected Brāhmaṇas. But true and wise Brāhmaṇas—those who deserve the highest respect—won’t accept even the best food if they’re served last, just like proud bulls would never quietly let their horns be cut. I can’t bring myself to follow him into the forest, so you’ve completely destroyed me. You’ve ruined your own kingdom, your advisors, your son, your wife, and even your citizens—only your son and your new queen are happy.” 

Hearing these heartbreaking words, Daśaratha was overwhelmed with grief and lost consciousness. In his suffering, he remembered again the wrong he had done.
SECTION LXII

After being harshly spoken to by Rāma’s angry mother, Kauśalyā, King Daśaratha sat in silence, overwhelmed by sadness. He spent a long time lost in thought, barely aware of his surroundings because of his grief. Eventually, he snapped out of it, sighing deeply as he glanced at Kauśalyā sitting next to him. But as soon as he started thinking again, he remembered a terrible thing he had done in the past—a mistake he had made when he shot an arrow guided only by sound, not sight. The memory of that old sin, combined with his pain over Rāma’s exile, tormented him. Caught between these two sorrows, the king trembled and, with his hands folded and his head hung low, turned to Kauśalyā to try and calm her.

“Please don’t be angry with me, Kauśalyā,” he said, folding his hands in supplication. “You’re always kind, even to people who don’t deserve it. Tears streaming down, she gently took the king’s folded hands and placed them on her head, then quickly spoke with deep love, “Please forgive me. I beg you, with my head bowed. I fall at your feet. If you ask for my forgiveness, I am truly lost. A good woman should never let her own husband—who deserves praise in this world and the next—have to beg her like this. I know what’s right, and I know you speak the truth. I only spoke that way because I was overwhelmed by grief for my son. Sorrow destroys patience, ruins wisdom, and shatters everything—it’s the worst enemy anyone can have. You can survive a beating from an enemy, but even a little sorrow can destroy you. By my count, this is the fifth night since Rāma was exiled, but for me, suffering in his absence, it feels like five years. And the more I think about it, the more my pain grows—like the ocean swelling from so many rushing rivers.” As Kauśalyā spoke these heartfelt words, the sunlight faded and night arrived. Comforted by her kindness, the grief-stricken king finally managed to fall asleep.
SECTION LXIII

King Daçarātha woke suddenly from sleep, nearly losing consciousness from overwhelming grief. The exile of Rāma and Lakshmana weighed heavily on him, and his sorrow was as deep as darkness covering the sun. After Rāma had left with Sītā, Daçarātha—the ruler of the Koçalas—couldn’t stop remembering a mistake from his past. He felt an urgent need to confess to his wife, Kauçalyā, whose eyes were dark at the corners, especially now that she was mourning her son. Six nights had gone by since Rāma had gone into the forest, and on this midnight, Daçarātha was haunted by memories of a terrible, unjust act he’d committed. Anyone who jumps into something—whether it’s about this life or the next—without thinking about the possible consequences is just being childish. It’s like someone who cuts down a mango grove and then waters a bunch of Palāsa trees. When he sees the flowers bloom, he hopes for fruit, but when harvest comes, there’s nothing but regret. If someone acts without understanding cause and effect, they’ll only grieve when the results arrive—just like the fool who tends kinsuka trees after destroying his mango orchard. I’m that fool, Kauçalyā. I destroyed my own ‘mango grove’ and cared for the wrong things, and now, after turning my back on Rāma at the very time I should have cherished him, I’m left mourning.
