I brought this pain on myself, like a child who eats poison without knowing better. I acted without foreseeing the consequences of firing at a sound in the dark, just like someone distracted by the beauty of Palāsa trees. Back then, you and I weren’t yet married—I was a young man, and the rainy season only made my restlessness worse. The sun drew the moisture from the earth, then retreated, bringing on cooler days. Clouds gathered, frogs croaked, deer and peacocks celebrated the rain. Wet and shivering birds sought shelter in trees shaking under wind and rain. The hills, covered by showers and filled with excited deer, looked like flowing rivers. The water, though clear, turned black and red as it mixed with mountain minerals and ash, running in twisting streams. On one of those lovely evenings, I took my bow and arrows, got into my chariot, and set out for the Sarayu River to hunt—hoping to find a buffalo, elephant, or any wild animal that might come to the water at night. It was so dark I couldn’t see a thing, but I heard the sound of someone filling a pitcher in the river. It sounded almost like an elephant’s roar. Thinking it was an animal, I aimed my flaming arrow, sharp as a venomous snake, and shot toward the sound. But then, from the place where my arrow struck in the darkness, I heard human cries—someone shouting in pain and falling into the water. The voice belonged to a forest-dweller, wounded deeply by my arrow. I heard him cry out, ‘Why did this weapon strike me? I only came here alone to fetch water. Who has wounded me with this arrow? What have I done to deserve this? How can killing someone like me—a hermit with matted hair, dressed in bark and deer-skin, living only on forest food and harming no one—be justified by any scripture? Who could possibly benefit from my death? What harm did I ever do? Such a pointless act can only end in disaster. This is as wrong as violating a teacher’s wife. I’m not as sad for myself as I am for my parents. What will happen to my old mother and father, who depend on me? They are elderly and I am their only child. Now, with my death, they are as good as dead too. What kind of reckless boy has killed us all?’”

“Hearing his heartbreaking words, I, who always tried to do the right thing, was crushed by guilt. My bow slipped from my hand and fell to the ground with the arrow still nocked. The saint’s grieving voice in the night filled me with fear and deep sorrow; I felt paralyzed. Still, I forced myself to follow the sound, my mind frantic and shaken. On the banks of the Sarayu, I found the wounded ascetic—his matted hair scattered, his water jug by his side, his body streaked with blood and dust, suffering terribly from my arrow. He looked at me—shaken and distressed—and spoke harshly, his anger almost burning: ‘What harm did I ever do to you, O king, that you wounded me while I was just gathering water for my parents? With your arrow, you’ve not just wounded me—you’ve effectively killed my old, blind father and mother too. Right now, they’re waiting for me, dying of thirst and hope, not knowing I’ll never return. What good is all their religious practice or learning, if my father can’t even sense what’s happened to me? And even if he did, he’s too weak to help—like one tree unable to save another from being blown down. You, descendant of Raghu, must go to my father and tell him what happened. But beware—if he gets angry, he could destroy you like a raging fire burns a forest. This narrow path will lead you to his hut. Go to him, calm him down, so he doesn’t curse you. But first, O king, please pull out the arrow. Your sharp shaft is tormenting my body, like a river’s current wearing away a sandbank.’ I hesitated, unsure if pulling out the arrow would kill him faster or leave him in more pain. My heart was heavy with dread and regret. The dying ascetic sensed my struggle. Weak and barely moving, his eyes rolling back, he managed to say, ‘I’m restraining my sorrow and trying to remain calm. Don’t let your heart be torn up by guilt for killing a Brāhmana—I am not of that caste. My father was a Vaicya, my mother a Sudra.’ As he lay there, broken and trembling, his body curling in pain, I finally drew out the arrow. He looked at me one last time—then, terrified, he died on the spot. Seeing him there, drenched and mortally wounded, struggling for breath after crying out in agony, I was filled with grief as I mourned his death by the Sarayu’s edge, my heart heavy with guilt and sorrow, O gentle lady.”
SECTION LXIV

Remembering the strange and tragic death of the sage’s son, King Dasharatha, son of Raghu, continued his story to Kausalya, still grieving for his own son. “After I had accidentally committed that terrible sin, I was overwhelmed with guilt and wondered how I could make things right. I picked up the water jug and followed the path the dying boy had told me about, until I reached the hermitage. There, I found his elderly, frail parents, alone and helpless—like birds with broken wings. They were talking to each other about their son, clinging to a hope that I had just destroyed. I was nearly paralyzed with grief and fear, and my heart sank as I approached their home.

Hearing my footsteps, the sage called out, ‘Why are you taking so long, my son? Bring the water quickly. Your mother was worried because you stayed so long at the river. Please come inside. Don’t let anything we’ve said or done upset you. You are all we have—you are our eyes in our blindness, our hope in our old age. Our lives depend on you. Why won’t you answer us?’ His voice shook with emotion, his words barely clear. Even as I was falling apart inside, I tried to sound steady and told him the truth about what had happened: ‘I am Dasharatha, a Kshatriya king, not your son. By a terrible accident, I’ve brought disaster on you. I was hunting by the Sarayu river and heard the sound of water being drawn. I thought it was an animal and shot my arrow. But when I went to check, I found your son, a young ascetic, on the ground, dying from my arrow. Following his last words, I pulled out the arrow, and as soon as I did, he died, crying out for you, his parents. I never meant to hurt anyone. Please, tell me what I should do now.’

Hearing my words, the sage was so grief-stricken he could have destroyed me with a curse. Tears ran down his face as he said, ‘If you hadn’t come and confessed this to us yourself, your head would have shattered into a thousand pieces. I have the power to bring down even Indra, king of the gods, if he were to kill an ascetic knowingly. If you had shot your arrow on purpose at someone like my son, your head would have split into seven pieces. But because you did this by accident, you live. Otherwise, your whole family would have been wiped out.’

He continued, ‘Take us to our son. Today we will see him one last time, lying lifeless and covered in blood, his deer-skin robe slipping off his body, as he leaves this world for the next.’

I led the heartbroken couple to the spot where their son lay. They touched his body and fell across him in grief. The father spoke to his dead son, ‘You don’t greet me today, or speak to me. Why are you lying on the ground, my child? Are you angry with us? If not for me, please look at your mother. Why won’t you embrace me or say a kind word? Who will now read the scriptures to me in the morning? Who will perform the rituals and bring me food, now that I am old and helpless? And how will I care for your blind mother, who counted on you and now suffers in misery? Please stay for our sake, my son. Tomorrow, you, your mother, and I will all go together to Yama’s realm. I will ask the god of death to forgive me and let you stay to care for us. You died innocent, killed by my mistake. Because of this truth, may you reach the world of heroes—go the way of warriors who die bravely in battle, the path of Sagara, Saivya, Dilipa, Janamejaya, Nahusha, Dhundhumara, and all who have left this world—ascetics, donors, sacrificers, loyal husbands, dutiful sons, and those who gave up their lives through fasting. No one born in your line will ever meet a bad end. But as for the one who killed you—may he suffer for what he’s done.’”

“After all these tears, the sage and his wife began the funeral rituals for their son. Suddenly, their son appeared in a shining, heavenly form, joined by Indra (Sakra), and comforted his parents: ‘Because I served you faithfully, I have reached a high place. Come join me soon.’ With that, he rose to heaven in a splendid chariot. When the rituals were done, the sage turned to me and said, ‘King, kill me now. I have no reason to live—you have left me childless with your arrow. Because I suffer this grief for my son through your actions, I curse you: you too will die of heartbreak over your son. Since you, a Kshatriya, killed a Brahmin’s son by mistake, you won’t be cursed with the full sin of killing a Brahmin. But soon, you will be destroyed by this terrible sorrow, just as a donor is parted from what he gives away.’

After cursing me and crying for a long time, the couple climbed onto the funeral pyre and followed their son to heaven. Kausalya, that crime from my youth—striking by sound alone—has haunted me ever since. Now, just as eating spoiled food brings sickness, this disaster is coming back to me. The words of that wise sage are coming true.” King Dasharatha finished his story, weeping. He told his wife, “I’m dying of grief for my son. I won’t see you again, Kausalya. Touch me, because those who go to Yama’s realm never see their loved ones again. If Rama could only see me or inherit the throne, maybe I would survive. What I did to Rama was out of character for me, but his response was pure and noble. What kind of father sends his son away, even if he’s done wrong? And what kind of son, exiled, doesn’t hate his father? But now I can’t see you, and my mind is going. The messengers of Yama are calling for me. My greatest regret is that I can’t see Rama’s face one last time. Not seeing my incomparable son dries up my spirit like the sun dries a drop of water. Only the gods will be lucky enough to see Rama’s face again in fifteen years, adorned with his beautiful earrings. Blessed are those who will see his face again, with eyes like lotus petals, perfect teeth, and a noble nose—like the moon itself. Even more blessed are those who will see him return to Ayodhya, bright as the planet Venus at its brightest.

Kausalya, my heart is heavy with grief. I can’t hear, feel, or taste anything anymore. My senses are fading, like a dying lamp. My own actions have destroyed me, like a river eroding its own banks. My son, my strength, my joy, you’re gone. Kausalya, I can’t see. Poor Sumitra! And you, Kaikeyi—you’ve ruined everything!” With these words, King Dasharatha grieved in front of Kausalya and Sumitra—and then he died.
And so the heartbroken king, suffering from the loss of his beloved son, died in the middle of the night, overcome by grief.
SECTION LXV

As dawn broke the next day, the palace filled with life. Praisers, skilled bards, genealogists who could recite royal histories, and talented singers all took their places before the king’s chambers, each performing in turn. Their loud blessings and songs echoed through the halls, praising the monarch. As the bards sang, musicians clapped rhythms celebrating the deeds of the Raghu dynasty. The noise woke up the birds, both those perched on branches and those kept in royal cages, who began to sing in response. The sacred words, sweet notes from the vina, and the singers’ farewell songs blended together, filling the palace with sound. As on other important mornings, servants who specialized in ritual cleanliness, accompanied by women and eunuchs, entered to prepare for the day. Attendants familiar with the ceremonial bath arrived at the proper time, bringing water scented with precious sandalwood in golden vessels. Noblewomen, along with many young girls, brought cows and other ritual items to be touched for luck, Ganges water for sipping, mirrors, fine clothes, ornaments, and other gifts. Everything brought for the king was ritually blessed, marked with good omens, and chosen for its excellence and auspiciousness. The whole group waited for the king to appear, watching the horizon as the sun still hadn’t risen. But as time passed, anxiety grew. Something felt wrong.

Inside the royal chambers, the king’s wives gathered around his bed, gently trying to comfort him. They spoke to him in soft, soothing voices and, knowing the ways of sleep, checked for signs of life—but they could not feel his ever-steady pulse. Fear for the king’s life made them tremble, like grass shaking in a rushing stream. Seeing the king so still, the women’s doubts grew into certainty: what they had feared had happened. Sumitra and Kausalya, overwhelmed by grief for their sons, were still asleep, looking almost lifeless themselves. Kausalya, robbed of her glow and pale with sorrow, lay curled up, resembling a star hidden by clouds. First Kausalya, then the king, and after him Sumitra; all three looked diminished, with Sumitra’s face faded from sadness. The other women, seeing Kausalya and Sumitra asleep and the king unmoving, appeared as if their own spirits had left them. Suddenly, grief exploded among them; they wailed like female elephants mourning the loss of their leader. The sound of their cries startled Kausalya and Sumitra awake. Realizing what had happened, they touched the king, then collapsed to the floor, crying out, “Oh, my lord!” Kausalya, daughter of the king of Kosala, rolled on the ground, covered in dust, her beauty hidden, like a fallen star. When the king’s death was clear, the women saw Kausalya collapsed, like an elephant mourning her mate. All of the king’s wives, led by Kaikeyi, were overcome with grief and tears, nearly fainting. Their cries joined the earlier wailing, swelling into a heart-wrenching chorus that filled the hall. The palace quickly filled with alarmed, frightened people desperate to know what had happened. All joy vanished, replaced by sorrow and chaos. The king’s wives gathered around his body, sobbing loudly and clutching his hands, their hearts broken and their cries echoing through the hall.
SECTION LXVI

When King Daśaratha died, Kauśalyā was completely shattered. She looked like a fire that had gone out, an ocean drained of water, or the sun stripped of its light. With tears streaming down her face, she took the king’s head in her lap and spoke, “Congratulations, Kaikeyī. You finally got what you wanted—enjoy your kingdom now that you’ve eliminated your competition. You’re heartless and selfish, turning your back on the king just to get your son on the throne. Rāma is gone, abandoning me, and now my husband has died. I can’t go on like this, completely alone, as if I’ve been left behind in a deserted wilderness. What kind of woman, besides Kaikeyī—someone who’s lost all sense of right and wrong—would want to keep living in a kingdom that isn’t hers, after losing both her god and her husband? It’s like someone so greedy they drink poison out of spite, not even caring about the consequences; that’s you, Kaikeyī, pushed to this by Mantharā’s scheming. Because of that hunchbacked woman’s plotting, you’ve destroyed the whole Rāghava dynasty. When King Janaka hears how you manipulated Daśaratha into doing something so wrong—banishing Rāma and Sītā—he’ll be just as devastated as I am. He doesn’t even know yet that I’m now helpless and widowed. Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals, has been taken from me while still alive. Sītā, Janaka’s gentle daughter, never deserved any of this suffering, yet she’s out in the wilds dressed like an ascetic, living in fear and hardship. Janaka, already old and with only one daughter, will be so heartbroken thinking of Sītā that he might just give up on life altogether. Then, they placed the king’s body in a large oil-filled vat and began the mourning rituals for him. Finally, when everyone realized for certain that the king was truly gone, the palace women broke down in tears. Raising their arms and sobbing uncontrollably, they grieved deeply, their faces stained with tears.

“O King, why are you leaving us now, after we’ve already lost Rāma—the one who always spoke kindly and kept his promises?” they wailed. “With Rāma gone, how can we, now widowed, live under the same roof as the cruel Kaikeyī, who shares our husband? Rāma, who was truly free in spirit, was our lord just as he was yours. He gave up his royal life to go into exile. Now that we’ve lost both you and our hero Rāma, and suffering so much misfortune, how can we survive, especially with Kaikeyī always looking down on us? She’s already abandoned the king, Rāma, Lakshmana, and Sītā—what’s left for her to betray?” In tears, the wives of Daśaratha, descendants of Raghu, cried out in agony, showing all the signs of deep sorrow. Ayodhyā felt empty, like a night without stars or a beautiful woman left by her husband. The city didn’t have its usual charm; everywhere, people were crying, women were wailing, and the royal terraces and courtyards were deserted. With the great king dead from grief and his wives left behind, the sun set and night took over. The idea of cremating the king without his son present didn’t sit right with his followers. So, they left Daśaratha’s dignified body resting in the oil vat. The city’s balconies and terraces overflowed with mourners’ tears, making Ayodhyā feel like the sky without the sun’s radiance, or a night with all its stars hidden. With the king’s death, crowds of men and women in the city blamed Bharata’s mother, Kaikeyī, and were overwhelmed with sorrow and unrest.
SECTION LXVII

Finally, the long, miserable night in Ayodhyā came to an end. The city was filled with people whose voices were hoarse from crying, and there was little comfort anywhere. When the sun rose, the royal priests and advisors—Mārkandeya, Maudgalya, Vāmadeva, Kāçyapa, Kātyāyana, Gautama, and the well-known Jāvāli—gathered together. They spoke about many things, but soon turned to the urgent crisis facing the kingdom. Looking to the chief priest, the wise Vasistha, they said, "That night felt as long as a hundred years, but somehow we survived it. The king, heartbroken over his son, has died and passed on to the next world. Rāma has gone into exile in the forest, and Lakshmana went with him. Bharata and Satrughna, both strong and capable, are in Kekaya, staying in Rajagriha with their grandfather. We need to choose someone from the Ikshwāku family to be king today. A kingdom without a king quickly falls apart. Just like clouds can't bring rain without thunder and lightning, the land can't thrive without a ruler.

In a kingdom without a king, no one plants crops. Sons ignore their fathers, and wives don’t listen to their husbands. Wealth disappears, and families fall apart. Fear and chaos rule where there’s no one in charge. Morality breaks down. People don’t form communities or build beautiful gardens and temples. The priests stop performing rituals, and generous Brāhmanas no longer give gifts at sacrifices. There are no celebrations or festivals with music and drama. Arguments can’t be settled, and those who love hearing stories and teachings are left disappointed.

Girls dressed in gold jewelry don’t go out to the gardens to play. The rich aren’t safe, and farmers and shepherds can’t sleep peacefully with their doors open. People don’t go out for fun in the woods with their friends and partners. Majestic elephants with long tusks and jingling bells don’t walk down the main roads. You don’t hear the sound of archers practicing anymore. Merchants from far away are afraid to travel with their goods. Wandering holy men, who rely on their own discipline, can’t move about freely and pray as they like.

No one can protect what they have or get what they need. The army can’t defend against enemies. People don’t ride fine horses or decorated chariots. Scholars can’t meet in the forest to debate and share ideas. Devotees don’t bring offerings or gifts to the gods. Princes, covered in sandalwood and fine perfumes, no longer look as grand as flowering trees in spring. A kingdom without a king is like a river with no water, a forest with no grass, or cattle with no herder.

A chariot is known by its flag, fire by its smoke, and our kingdom was known by its king—but now he’s gone. In a country with no ruler, it’s hard for anyone to survive. People turn on each other like fish in a drying pond. Even criminals who once feared punishment now do whatever they want, with no one to stop them.

Just as eyes look after the body, the king looks after the people, keeping truth and justice alive. The king is the symbol of truth, morality, and family honor. He is like a father and mother to his people. By his noble character, a king even surpasses mighty gods like Yama, Vaiśravana, Indra, and Varuna. If there were no king to tell right from wrong, the world would be plunged into darkness, and no one would know what to do.

Like the ocean stays within its shores, we followed your guidance when the king was alive. But now, with our efforts wasted and the kingdom falling into chaos without a ruler, we ask you, O best of Brāhmanas, to choose a descendant of Ikshwāku—or anyone worthy—to become king and save our land."

After hearing everyone, Vasishtha turned to the Brahmanas, the king’s loyal followers, and the royal advisors. They traveled west past Aparatala, crossed the Malini River in the middle, then headed north past Pralamva. They crossed the Ganga at Hastinapura, then made their way to Panchala, continuing west through Kurujangala. They raced past the Saradanda River, which was overflowing with sparkling water and surrounded by birds of every kind. As the king’s wives walked slowly by the Mandakini River, they noticed the spot on the riverbank where Rama and Lakshmana usually came ashore. Kauśalya, her eyes full of tears and her face pale with sorrow, turned to the grieving Sumitra and the other royal wives. She said, “Like a first wife’s sacred place, this landing spot in the forest belongs to those unlucky sons who, though full of energy, lost their kingdom. From here, Sumitra, your son Saumitri (that’s Lakshmana), always alert, fetches water for my son. Even though your son does this humble task, it’s not shameful—only if he did something useless for his brother would there be anything to blame. But today, let your son rest from these tiring chores that really should be for someone of lower status.” As Kauśalya spoke, she noticed on the ground the Ingudi fruit cake that Rama had placed for his father on sacred darbha grass, with the tips pointing south as tradition required.

Seeing the simple offering that Rama had laid down for his late father, Kauśalya called out to the other wives of Dasaratha, “Look at what Rama has offered to the great king, the descendant of Raghu, lord of the Ikshvaku dynasty. I can’t believe this is all that noble king—who lived like a god and had every luxury—has to eat now. After ruling this vast earth surrounded by oceans, how can the mighty ruler, who was like Indra himself, survive on just this Ingudi cake? I don’t think there’s anything sadder in the world than seeing Rama give this meager offering to his father. How does my heart not shatter into a thousand pieces at the sight? There’s an old saying: ‘Whatever a person eats, his ancestors eat too.’ Now I know it’s true.” The other wives gathered around Kauśalya, trying to comfort her in her pain. Then, entering the hermitage, they saw Rama—looking almost like a god fallen from heaven.

When the mothers saw Rama, stripped of all comfort and honor, they were overwhelmed by grief and couldn’t help but cry and mourn. Rama, true to his respectful nature, helped his mothers to their feet and humbly touched their feet in greeting. The women, with their gentle, soft hands, lovingly brushed the dust from Rama’s back. Once Rama had greeted them, Lakshmana (Sumitra’s son) also, holding back tears, bowed gently to all his mothers, showing his love and respect. The women treated Lakshmana with the same kindness and affection they had shown Rama, honoring him as a son of Dasaratha. Sita, with tears in her eyes, also approached and touched the feet of her mothers-in-law, standing before them in obvious distress.

Kauśalya embraced Sita, who was suffering in exile, just as a mother would hold her own daughter. Grieving deeply, she said, “You are the daughter of King Videha, the daughter-in-law of Dasaratha, and Rama’s wife—why should someone like you have to suffer in this lonely forest? Vaidehi (another name for Sita), seeing your face—once as lovely as a lotus now wilted by the sun, or gold dulled by dust, or the moon hidden by clouds—my heart burns with pain from all this disaster, like a house consumed by fire.”

As his heartbroken mother spoke, Rama walked over to Vasishtha and respectfully touched the sage’s feet. Vasishtha, glowing with spiritual power, seemed almost like a living flame. Rama, just as Indra would honor his teacher Brihaspati, then sat down beside Vasishtha.

Bharata, along with his advisors, city leaders, generals, and holy men, sat behind Rama and Vasishtha in the gathering. He took his place respectfully in front of his elder brother. Seeing Rama dressed like a hermit, glowing with dignity, Bharata—strong and self-controlled—sat with his hands pressed together in respect, just as Indra would sit before the creator Prajapati.

Everyone present was full of curiosity: “What will Bharata say to Rama after bowing and paying his respects?” They all waited, eager to hear. Rama, full of truth and patience; Lakshmana, great-hearted; and Bharata, righteous—surrounded by their friends—looked like the three sacred fires in a Vedic ritual, each shining in their own way.
SECTION CV

As the brothers and their friends sat together, filled with sorrow, the night slowly passed. When morning finally arrived, bright and clear, Bharata and his friends performed the sacred Homa and recited prayers by the Mandakini River. Afterward, they returned to Rama. The group sat quietly—nobody spoke a word. Finally, Bharata broke the silence, addressing Rama in front of everyone. "My mother was satisfied by being granted the kingdom," he said. "Now the kingdom is mine—but I want to give it to you, Rama. Please take your rightful place and rule the kingdom, free from all troubles. Protecting this great kingdom is like trying to hold back a flood during the rainy season—it’s almost impossible for anyone but you. I can no more fill your shoes than a mule can run like a horse, or a regular bird can soar like the mighty Garuda. I just don’t have your strength, Rama. It’s always better to be the one others depend on, rather than to depend on someone else. Imagine planting a tree, caring for it until it grows tall and strong, but if it never bears fruit, it’s disappointing for the person who planted it. That’s how I feel: you are the tree, Rama, and we all depend on you. You are our true leader, but you’re leaving us without guidance. Let everyone—our advisors, our allies—see you on the throne, as bright and powerful as the sun itself. Let the royal elephants trumpet in celebration as you lead, and may the women of the palace rejoice with all their hearts." As Bharata pleaded with Rama, many of the citizens listening cheered and shouted, "Well said!"

Seeing his brother so upset and desperate, Rama, always calm and thoughtful, tried to comfort Bharata. He began, "No one can really control what happens in life. We aren’t independent; fate has power over us all, both now and in the future. Everything that grows will eventually decay. What goes up will come down. People who come together will eventually part ways, and all who are born will one day die. Just like a ripe fruit has no other fate but to fall, every person who is born must one day die. As a strong building eventually weakens with age, so do people as they grow old and near death. A night that passes never returns, just like a river that flows into the sea never comes back. Day and night keep passing, quietly taking pieces of our lives, just like the summer sun dries up water. So why mourn for others? If anything, mourn for yourself, since everyone’s life is getting shorter, whether they’re moving or sitting still. Death is always with us—walking with us, sitting with us, and no matter how far we travel, it’s always close. Our skin wrinkles, our hair turns gray, our bodies grow weak with age—and nothing we do can stop this. People are happy when the sun rises and when night falls, but don’t realize each day shortens their lives. We celebrate the start of each new season, not noticing that time is quietly slipping away. Like two logs drifting together in the ocean before eventually parting, people meet and then separate—spouses, children, family, and wealth all eventually leave us. No one can change their fate. Mourning someone who has died won’t stop our own death. It’s like someone watching another walk down a road, saying, ‘I’ll follow you soon’—we’re all headed in the same direction as our ancestors. So why mourn, when we’re all destined for the same end? Knowing that life only moves forward, like a river that never flows backward, we should focus on living well and finding happiness, because that’s what life is for.

My dear brother, our father lived a righteous life, performed many great sacrifices, and was respected by all. He’s now gone to heaven, honored by the good, and doesn’t deserve our grief. He left behind his tired, old body and has reached the world of the gods, where Brahma dwells. Wise people like you and me, who know these truths, shouldn’t mourn for him. Intelligent people should give up excessive grief and mourning, no matter the situation. Let go of this sorrow, Bharata—don’t let it overwhelm you. Go back to our city and live there, just as our father, with his strong will, instructed you. I have to honor our father’s wishes, too. I can’t ignore his commands, and you shouldn’t either. He was our father and our friend. As the descendant of Raghu, I will honor his order by living in the forest, as he asked. The next world is open to those who live honestly and virtuously, always respecting their elders. Bharata, remember that our father Dasharatha has achieved a great destiny. So work toward your own goodness, using all your strengths and noble qualities."

Rama finished speaking, hoping his words would convince Bharata to follow their father’s last wishes.
SECTION CVI

After Rāma finished speaking his wise and thoughtful words, Bharata—who was known for his virtue—spoke to him on the banks of the Mandākini River. He said, “Rāma, you’re truly unique. Pain doesn’t seem to bother you, and pleasure doesn’t make you lose control. Even though you set the example for elders, you still turn to them for advice when things are uncertain. If someone has learned to live detached—like being alive but unaffected, almost like the living dead—what could possibly make that person upset? You, Rāghava, know the soul and the world so well that you shouldn’t fall into despair, no matter what happens. You’re as strong as the gods, generous, always keep your word, and you understand everything with sharp intelligence. Even the worst disaster shouldn’t break someone like you, who understands life and death so well.

The terrible thing my selfish mother did while I was away disgusts me. Please, show me kindness. I’m bound by my sense of duty—that’s the only reason I haven’t punished my mother, even though she really deserves it. How could I, the son of Daśaratha—a good and blameless king—commit such a terrible act, especially since I know right from wrong? Daśaratha was our father and king, a noble man, and now he’s gone. That’s why I don’t blame him, even though what happened was wrong. He’s still like a god to us. Rāma, what kind of person who understands what is right would do something so terrible just to please his wife? There’s an old saying: when people’s end is near, they lose their judgment. Daśaratha’s actions have just proved that true.

Please, do what’s right and fix the harm our father caused, even if it came from his anger, ignorance, or recklessness. In this world, the real son is the one who puts right his father’s mistakes, even if that means going against him—not the one who just follows along. You should be that true son. Don’t support what our father did—it was wrong. Save everyone—Kaikeyi, me, our father, our friends, all the citizens, and the people in the regions. Think about it: what does living in the forest have to do with being a Kshatriya ruler? What’s the point of wearing matted hair when you should be leading the kingdom? This isn’t the right path for you. The main duty of a Kshatriya is to be installed as king so he can govern well. What kind of cowardly Kshatriya ignores the clear path of duty and instead chooses a path meant for old men or hermits?

But if you’re really set on living this strict life in the forest, then at least rule the kingdom properly first, and then you can retire. People who know about duty say that out of all ways of life, being a householder is the best—so why are you running from it? I’m not as smart, high-born, or experienced as you are. How can I rule the land while you’re still here? I’m just a kid compared to you, and I don’t have your strengths or qualities. I couldn’t possibly live without you.

So please, Rāma, rule this kingdom with your friends, following the right path, and keep our ancestral land peaceful and safe. Let the people, the priests, and Vasishtha (who knows all the rituals) install you as king right here. Once you’re crowned, return to Ayodhyā and rule the city, defeating your enemies with our help, just like Indra does with the Maruts. Pay off all your debts—to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors—and rule wisely, protecting your friends and defeating your foes. Let your friends celebrate your coronation today. Let those who wish you harm flee in fear. Restore my mother’s honor and free our father from his guilt. I beg you—show mercy to me, to our friends, and to everyone. But if you ignore my pleas and insist on heading into the forest, then I’ll go with you.”

Even though Bharata begged Rāma with his head bowed, Rāma—true to his father’s word and strong in his resolve—refused to change his mind. The people who saw Rāma’s amazing determination felt both happy and sad. They were upset that he wouldn’t return to Ayodhyā, but they admired how firm he was in his decision. Then the priests, the citizens and their leaders, and the mothers (crying and out of their senses) all praised Bharata for his speech, and together they bowed to Rāma and pleaded with him.
SECTION CVII

As Bharata continued to plead with him, Rama—his older brother, dignified as always—responded in front of all their relatives. “Bharata, you are truly your mother Kaikeyi’s son and King Dasharatha’s child—your words reflect that. When our father married your mother, he promised her that her son would be king one day. Later, during the war between the gods and the Asuras, he was so pleased with her that he offered her a boon. Your mother, being wise, asked for two things: that you be crowned king, and that I be sent into exile. Our father granted her these wishes. Because of that promise, I was ordered to live in the forest for fourteen years, and now I’m here in exile with Lakshmana and Sita, keeping my father’s word.

You, Bharata, should also help our father keep his promise—get yourself crowned king, just as he wanted. For my sake, set him free from the debt of his word. Make our father’s soul at peace and bring joy to your mother. There’s an old Vedic hymn from the time of Gaya’s sacrifice that says: ‘A son saves his father from the hell called Put, and so he’s called putra. He protects his ancestors in every way. People should wish for many worthy sons, so at least one will travel to Gaya to perform the rites.’ The great kings of the past have agreed on this. So, Bharata, it’s your duty to save our father from that fate.

Go back to Ayodhya with Satrughna, make the people happy, and take the priests and elders with you. As for me, I need to head deeper into the Dandaka forest with Lakshmana and Sita. You’ll be king of men, and I’ll be king of the deer. Go to our great city with a joyful heart, and I’ll go to Dandaka just as gladly. Let the royal umbrella shade your head from the sun, while I find comfort in the shade of these forest trees. Satrughna is smart and will help you; and Lakshmana, son of Sumitra, is my closest friend. The four of us—sons of the great King Dasharatha—will all keep his word true. Bharata, don’t let yourself lose hope.”
SECTION CVIII

As Rāma, who understood right and wrong, was comforting Bharata, Javali—the most learned among the Brāhmanas—spoke up. His words were blunt and completely ignored traditional morality. “Rāghava,” he said, “you’re wise and live like an ascetic, but don’t let your mind get stuck on pointless ideas like a fool would. Who really is anyone’s friend? What is anyone owed, and by what right? Who even am I to you, or you to me? We’re all born alone and die alone. So, anyone who loves their parents deeply is just acting crazy. No one truly belongs to anyone else in this world. Think about it: when someone’s about to travel, they stay in a place for a night and then leave it behind without a second thought. That’s how it is with parents, homes, and wealth—they’re just temporary stops.

O Kākutshta, wise people don’t get attached to things that are just temporary shelters. So, why are you giving up your ancestral kingdom and choosing to stay in this dangerous, miserable forest? You should go back to Ayodhyā and rule. The city is waiting for you, hoping you’ll return as king. Enjoy all the luxuries of royalty in Ayodhyā, just like Indra (Sakra) enjoys the heavens. Daçarātha wasn’t really your father, and you’re not truly his son—you have no real connection. He was just someone who helped create you. You should do what I’m suggesting.

A father is nothing more than the biological cause of a child. When his seed mixes with a mother’s blood at the right time, a new person is born. The king has died, which is simply the way of the world. So why deny yourself the power and strength that comes with being king? I actually pity those who ignore their own interests for the sake of virtue, not those who seek happiness—because in the end, the self-sacrificing ones just wind up with nothing.

People perform rituals like Ashtaka for their ancestors and the gods, but look at all the food that gets wasted. Do the dead really eat any of it? If eating something could magically feed someone else, then you could just send food to someone traveling far away, and it would keep them full for the journey. The texts that command us to worship, give to others, perform rituals, and renounce things—they were written by clever people to encourage charity and good behavior.

Honestly, generous one, there is no afterlife. Focus on what’s real and right in front of you instead of chasing after things nobody knows about. Use your mind and do what everyone agrees is wise. Bharata wants you to be king, so accept the throne, and let him be happy.”
SECTION CIX

After listening to Javali’s words, Rama—who was known for his dedication to truth—replied with a sharp, clear mind. He said, “Javali, even though you’re trying to help me, what you’ve suggested might look good on the surface, but it would actually lead to misery. When someone acts wrongly or tells others to do things that go against our scriptures, they never earn respect from good people. Your advice would let people with bad character pretend to be noble, or make the impure seem pure. Someone unlucky might look blessed, and even the dishonest could appear honest. If I take this path you’ve suggested—one that would break down our traditions and encourage acts not approved by our scriptures—I’d be giving up good for evil. Why would anyone respect me if I became known for doing wrong and deserved only blame? Whose path would I be following, and how would I reach heaven if I broke my promise now? If I put my own desires above everything else, others would follow my example—people always take after their leaders. True kingship is based on kindness and truth; this is an eternal rule. Our whole world stands on truth. Saints and gods value only truth. In this world, a truthful person reaches Brahma’s realm, while liars are as dangerous as snakes. Virtue itself is rooted in truth. Truth is the source of everything—there’s nothing higher. Even the Vedas, which teach us about giving, sacrifice, and self-discipline, are based on truth. Some protect their people, some their families; some end up in hell, others are honored in heaven. So why shouldn’t I obey my father’s command? My father always kept his promises and lived righteously; he made me take this vow so he could keep his word. Having sworn to my elders, I’ll never break my promise for money, forgetfulness, or pride. We’ve heard that the gods and ancestors won’t accept offerings from someone who is dishonest or unreliable. Keeping truth is the highest duty—worthy people have always carried this burden, and that’s why I respect it so much. I reject that version of Kshatriya morality that pretends to be right but is really just selfishness, followed by the wicked and greedy. Sin can be committed by body, mind, or words—lying is a triple sin. The earth, fame, good fortune, and blessings all follow those who are truthful. Good people always stick to the truth, so everyone should seek it. So, even though your suggestion seems reasonable and well thought out, I can’t accept it as noble. How could I break my promise to my elders just to make Bharata happy? Because I kept my word, Kaikeyi was pleased. So I’ll live in the forest, stay pure, eat simply, and make offerings to the gods and ancestors with whatever I can find. I’ll honor the five duties, keep my life simple, and stay true to what’s right and wrong as I finish my exile. In this world, everyone must do what’s right in their situation—even Agni, Vayu, and Soma face the results of their own actions. Indra earned his place in heaven through his deeds; the great sages reached the heavens by their hard work and discipline.”

After hearing Javali’s earlier speech, which was so full of disbelief that Rama couldn’t help but criticize it, the prince spoke again, his energy fierce. He said, “Truth, righteousness, courage, kindness to all beings, honesty, and respect for priests, gods, and guests—these are the paths to heaven, according to the wise. After learning this and thinking it through, good priests (Brahmanas) always try to follow these rules carefully, so they can reach the highest good. I blame my father for one thing: choosing a priest who thinks this way—someone who’s lost his way, who’s basically an atheist, and has left the path of righteousness. A thief and a heretic are the same, and an atheist is just like them. People who hurt society should be punished like thieves—and no Brahmana should even speak to an atheist. There are other priests better than you, who have served both this world and the next through their good deeds. Those Brahmanas who have saved lives, practiced honesty, given to charity, performed penance, and helped others—they perform sacrifices according to the Vedas. The best ascetics, surrounded by good people, full of energy, generous, free from envy and any kind of stain—these are the ones truly honored in this world.”

After Rama, in all his strength, had spoken so angrily, Javali—humbled—spoke again, now with words of morality and spiritual wisdom. “I’m not actually an atheist,” he said. “I don’t deny religion, nor do I believe that nothing exists after death. When it comes to rituals for the next world, I speak like a believer; when it’s about this world, I speak like a skeptic. Rama, the time had come for me to try to make you turn back by using skeptical arguments. But now, to calm you, I speak as a believer once more.”
SECTION CX

Seeing that Rāma (sometimes called Ram) was angry, Vasishtha spoke up: “Jāvāli understands what happens after death and rebirth. He was just trying to convince you to turn back. Now, Rāma, let me explain how living beings first came into existence. In the beginning, there was only water everywhere. The earth took shape within it. Then the self-created Brahmā appeared along with all the gods. Brahmā became a boar and lifted the earth, and with his sons, who had mastered themselves, he created everything else. This eternal Brahmā—who exists in all times and never fades—came from the sky. Marichi was born from him, and Marichi’s son was Kaçyapa. Vivaswat was born from Kaçyapa, and Manu from Vivaswat. Manu was once known as Prajāpati. Ikshwāku was Manu’s son, and Manu gave this world to Ikshwāku. Remember, Ikshwāku was the first king of Ayodhyā. His son was the noble Kukshi. Kukshi’s son was Vikukshi. Vikukshi’s son was the powerful Vāna, who was full of energy. Vāna’s son was the mighty-armed Anaranya, who practiced great self-discipline. During Anaranya’s reign, there were no droughts or famines in Ayodhyā, and there were no thieves either. From Anaranya came King Prithu. Trisanku, known for his great strength, was Prithu’s son. Because of his honesty, Trisanku went to heaven in his own body. Trisanku’s son was the famous Dhundumāra. Dhundumāra’s son was Juvanāsya. Juvanāsya had a handsome son named Māndhata, and Māndhata’s son was Susandhi. Susandhi had two sons: Dhruvasandhi and Prasenajit. Dhruvasandhi’s son was the famous Bharata, a destroyer of enemies. Asita was born from Bharata, but Asita faced many enemy kings—Harhayas, Tālajanghas, and Sasavindus—all strong warriors.

Asita fought them in battle and became deeply troubled. He retreated to the sacred mountain, Himavat, to meditate. At that time, both of his wives were pregnant. One of the noble ladies, whose eyes looked like lotus petals, greeted Bhrigu’s son, a sage who shone like a god, hoping for a blessing so she could have a great son. But the other wife secretly gave her poison to destroy her pregnancy. The sage Chyavana, son of Bhrigu, was staying on Himavat then. Kalindi, the first wife, came before him and greeted him respectfully, hoping for a blessing. The sage replied, “You will have a son with a powerful soul, known among men, righteous and strong, who will carry on his family’s name and defeat enemies.” After this, Kalindi circled the sage in respect and returned home. There she gave birth to a son with lotus-like eyes and a glow like the inside of a lotus. Because her co-wife poisoned her, and the unborn child survived the poison, he was named Sagara—which means “poisoned one.” 

King Sāgara became famous for performing a sacrifice that led to the digging of the ocean—his actions were so intense they terrified people. Sāgara’s son was Asamanja, who was so wicked that his father exiled him while he was still alive. Asamanja’s son was the strong Ançumat. Ançumat’s son was Dilipa, and Dilipa’s son was Bhagiratha. Bhagiratha’s son was Kākustha, from whom the Kākustha line is known. Kākutstha’s son was Raghu, after whom the Rāghava family is named. Raghu’s son was the energetic Pravirda, who, it is said, even ate human flesh. He was known by names like Kalmāshapāda and Saudāsa. Kalmāshapāda’s son was Sankhana, who was strong but was destroyed in battle along with his army. Sankhana’s son was the handsome and brave Sudarçana. Sudarçana’s son was Agnivarna, whose son was Sighraga. Sighraga’s son was Maru, and Maru’s son was Praçuçruva. Praçuçruva’s son was the generous Amvarisha. Amvarisha’s son was Nahusha, famous for his honesty. Nahusha’s son was Nābhāga, who was extremely virtuous. Nābhāga had two sons: Aja and Suvrata. Aja’s son was the noble king Daçarātha, and you, Rāma, are his eldest son, known far and wide by your name. 

So, you should reclaim your kingdom and take care of your people. In the Ikshwāku tradition, the eldest son always becomes king. If the eldest son is alive, a younger son cannot take the throne. That’s why you must not break the long-standing tradition of the Raghu family. Rule this world, which is full of treasures and glory. Govern it wisely, like a father caring for his children, and watch over the many kingdoms within it.”
SECTION CXI

After speaking to Rāma, the royal priest Vasishtha spoke again, his words full of wisdom and righteousness. “Rāma (Kākutstha), every person has three main superiors: their teacher, their father, and their mother. The father gives life, the teacher gives knowledge—which is why both deserve respect. I have been the teacher for both you and your father, Rāma. If you follow my advice, you’ll stay on the right path. These courtiers, your relatives, and the other kings—if you protect and guide them with virtue, you won’t stray from what’s right. You should not dismiss the words of your wise and elderly mother. By listening to her, you will not lose your righteousness. And if you do as Bharata asks—since he’s appealing to your sense of truth—you will remain a truly moral person.” Hearing Vasishtha speak kindly and directly to him, Rāma replied, “A son can never fully repay what his parents do for him—the care, the food, the comfort, their kind words, and their love. Because of this, I must honor what my father, King Daçarātha, commanded me. I cannot go back on his word.”

After Rāma said this, Bharata, feeling completely downcast, turned to the charioteer nearby and said, “Charioteer, please spread some Kuça grass on the ground here. I’ll stay right here by Rāma until he changes his mind. Like a priest who’s lost everything and sleeps outside the door of someone unjust, giving up food and lying in the dark, I’ll stay here in front of this cottage until Rāma returns to Ayodhyā.” With no hope left and seeing Sumantra looking at Rāma, Bharata spread out the Kuça grass himself and lay down on it. Then Rāma, the wise prince, spoke to him, “Bharata, my dear brother, what have I done for you to lie down like this beside me? Only a Brahmin can try to stop someone by lying down like this; there’s no tradition for a warrior to do that. Please get up, brother. Give up this hard vow and go back to Ayodhyā, our great city.”

Still sitting, Bharata looked at the citizens and people from the provinces and asked, “Why aren’t any of you asking Rāma to come back?” The people of the city and the provinces answered him:

“We see that Rāma is saying and doing what’s right. He’s keeping his father’s word and acting with great virtue. Because of that, we can’t just demand something else from him.”

Hearing this, Rāma said, “Listen to these friends who care about what’s right. Hear what they say about both of us, and make your decision, Bharata. Now get up. Touch me, then perform the water ritual.” Bharata got up, touched Rāma and then water, and said, “Courtiers and ministers, listen to me! I never wanted to take my father’s kingdom, and I didn’t push my mother to make it happen. I didn’t even know that Rāma was going to be sent to the forest. But if Rāma is forced to stay here because of our father’s promise, then I’ll stay in the forest for fourteen years as well.”

Amazed by Bharata’s resolve, Rāma looked at the citizens and the people from the regions and said, “Neither Bharata nor I can undo any decisions—like deals or promises—made by our father while he was alive. So I can’t accept anyone else living in the forest in my place, since that would bring criticism onto me. Kaikeyi spoke her mind, and my father acted as he saw fit. I know Bharata is forgiving and always respects his elders. Everything about him shows his goodness and love for the truth. When I return from the forest, I’ll rule this land with Bharata at my side, as it should be. My father agreed to Kaikeyi’s request, and I have obeyed. Now, Bharata, the best thing you can do is act in a way that will free our father from the burden of his promise.”
SECTION CXII

When the two brothers, Rāma and Bharata, met, their energy was so intense that it amazed everyone watching. Even the great sages, mystics, and holy men gathered, though they stayed hidden, to witness the powerful bond between the Kākutstha brothers. They admired Rāma and Bharata, whispering, “How lucky is the father whose sons are so devoted to virtue and truth. Just hearing their conversation fills us with happiness.” The sages, all hoping for the downfall of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, came together and spoke directly to Bharata, the respected king: “You come from a noble family, you’re wise, honorable, and famous. If you care about your father’s happiness, you should listen to Rāma. We want Rāma to keep honoring his father’s wishes. Rāma replied, “So be it,” and hugged Bharata lovingly, then embraced Satrughna as well. He said, “Take good care of your mother Kaikeyi. Don’t be angry at her. After hearing these hopeful words from Bharata, the sage Bharadwaja responded:

But as Bharata looked at Ayodhya, missing both his father and mother, he was overwhelmed with sorrow. He said to his charioteer, “Look at Ayodhya—without its usual brightness and decorations, and sunk in sadness, it doesn’t look beautiful at all.”

Sita replied, “Of course—listen as I tell you the story. My father, King Janaka of Mithilā, is a just and heroic ruler, always doing his duty as a Kshatriya. One day, as he was plowing a field for a sacrifice, I appeared from the earth itself—so in that sense, I’m his daughter. Covered in dust, I was picked up by Janaka, who was spreading dust to level the ground. Childless, he took me onto his lap and, moved by affection, said, ‘This is my daughter.’ At that moment, a voice from the sky announced, ‘King, in all righteousness, this is your daughter.’ Delighted, my righteous father accepted me and considered himself very fortunate. He gave me to his chief queen, who wanted a child, and she raised me lovingly, as if I were her own.

Later, when I was old enough to be married, my father became anxious—like a poor man who has lost his last bit of wealth. No matter how great a man is, even like Indra himself, if he can’t marry off his daughter, he faces criticism from others. Seeing this scorn looming, my father grew deeply worried, as if lost at sea without a raft. Because I wasn’t born of a woman, my father struggled to find a suitable husband for me. Then he decided: ‘I’ll hold a swayamvara for my daughters.’

Long ago, at Daksha’s great sacrifice, Varuna had given a magnificent bow, along with two endless quivers, to Devarāta. The bow was so heavy that no king could even hope to string it. My honest father took this bow and told the gathered kings, ‘Whoever can lift and string this bow will marry my daughter.’ The kings tried, but after greeting the bow, they left, unable to move it even a little.
