He rushed forward, grabbed Sita, and slung her around his waist. Then, stepping back a little, he shouted at the brothers: "Hey, you guys with your bark clothes and wild hair! You look pretty weak, wandering through Dandaka forest with your bows, arrows, and swords. If you're really ascetics, why are you traveling with one woman? You’re a disgrace to ascetics everywhere! I’m Viradha, a rakshasa, and this forest is my domain. I roam here, armed, and I eat ascetics for food. This beautiful woman will become my wife, and I’ll drink your blood in battle!"

Sita, terrified by Viradha’s bragging and evil words, started trembling in fear like a sapling blown by the wind. Seeing Sita trapped at Viradha’s waist, Rama turned pale and said to Lakshmana, "Look, Lakshmana—Sita, the daughter of King Janaka, my pure and noble wife, raised in luxury—now in the grip of this monster. What Kaikeyi wished for us is happening right now. The cruel favor she asked for has come true. My stepmother, who wasn’t satisfied just getting the kingdom for her son, and who banished me to the forest even though I was dearer to her than anyone, has finally gotten everything she wanted. Nothing hurts me more than seeing another man lay hands on Sita—not even losing my father or my kingdom compares to this pain."

As Rama spoke, tears welled up in his eyes. Lakshmana, furious, answered like a chained, raging elephant: "Why are you grieving like this, Rama? You’re the master of all beings, as powerful as Indra himself, and you have me by your side. There’s no reason to despair. This demon, Viradha, will die today—my arrows will bring him down, and his blood will soak the earth. All the anger I felt toward Bharata for taking the throne—I’ll unleash it now on Viradha, just like Indra throws his thunderbolt at a mountain. Let my arrow, fired with all my strength, smash into Viradha’s chest, rip out his life, and send him crashing to the ground!"
SECTION III

Virādha spoke again, his voice echoing through the forest, “Tell me—who are you, and where are you going?” Rāma, full of energy and anger, replied to the Rākshasa, introducing himself as a prince of the Ikshwāku dynasty. “Know that we are Kshatriyas of good standing, traveling through this forest. But I also want to know—who are you, wandering around Dandaka?” Virādha answered Rāma, who was known for his truthfulness, “I’ll tell you, king. Listen. I am the son of Java and my mother is Satarhadā. All the Rākshasas on earth call me Virādha. By pleasing Brahmā with my penance, I got a boon—no one can kill me by wounding my body with weapons. So, give up on this woman and any hope of defeating me. Go back the way you came—or I’ll kill you both.” Hearing this, Rāma, his eyes burning with anger, shouted back at the misshapen Rākshasa, “How dare you, you disgrace! You’re asking for your own death, and you’ll get it. You won’t escape alive.” Rāma quickly strung his bow, aimed, and shot seven sharp arrows, their golden feathers flashing as they flew like birds of prey or the wind. The arrows, glowing like fire and tipped with peacock feathers, struck Virādha and fell to the ground, stained with his blood. Hurt, Virādha dropped Sītā (Vaidehi), grabbed a massive spear, and charged at Rāma and Lakshmana with a roar, looking like a demon out of a nightmare. The brothers rained blazing arrows down on him, but the Rākshasa, unmoved, just laughed horribly, yawned, and the arrows dropped harmlessly from his body, thanks to Brahmā’s boon. Drawing on his supernatural power, Virādha raised a huge pike and lunged at Rāma and Lakshmana. But Rāma, skilled in weapons, cut the spear in two with his arrows, sending it crashing to the ground like a shattered boulder. Not stopping, both brothers drew their swords, dark as snakes, and attacked Virādha up close. The terrifying Rākshasa then grabbed both of them in his arms, trying to crush them, but Rāma and Lakshmana stayed calm. Sensing what Virādha was doing, Rāma said to Lakshmana, “Let him carry us, Lakshmana. There’s no use fighting him right now. Let’s see where he takes us—maybe it will help us.” With his monstrous strength, Virādha heaved both brothers onto his shoulders as if they were children. Then, roaring, he marched deeper into the forest, which was as dark as thunderclouds, thick with trees, alive with birds, and full of wild animals, jackals, and snakes.
SECTION IV

When Sitā saw Rāma and Lakshmana—the bravest of the Raghus—being dragged away, she screamed desperately, raising her arms. “Rāma, son of Daçaratha, strong, honest, pure—you and Lakshmana are being carried off by this terrifying Rākshasa! Wild animals will devour me—bears, tigers, panthers. If you’re abandoning the Kākutsthas, then take me with you instead!” she pleaded to the demon. “I bow to you, greatest of Rākshasas.” Hearing Sitā’s cries, Rāma and Lakshmana snapped out of their shock, determined to kill the monster. Lakshmana (Sumitra’s son) broke the demon’s left arm, while Rāma smashed his right. With both arms broken, the Rākshasa—who looked like a storm cloud—collapsed to the ground, stunned, like a mountain shattered by lightning. The brothers attacked him with their fists and feet, lifting him up and slamming him down, stomping on him over and over. Even though the Rākshasa was already covered in wounds from arrows and swords, and was being crushed into the dirt by every possible means, he still wouldn’t die. Seeing that their weapons couldn’t kill him, and that he looked as immovable as a mountain, Rāma—the very symbol of hope in danger—said,

“Lakshmana, weapons won’t work on him. His powers from penance make him immune. We have to bury him instead. Dig a big pit here in the forest—big enough for this huge, terrifying demon.” While Rāma pinned Virādha’s throat underfoot, Lakshmana started digging. Hearing this, the Rākshasa spoke in a softer tone, “You have defeated me, mighty Rāma. I didn’t realize who you were before—now I do. You are Rāma, son of Kauçalyā, and with you are the noble Vaidehi (Sitā) and the famous Lakshmana. I was once a Gandharva, cursed by Vaiçravana to become this monster because I fell in love with Rambhā. He said, ‘When Rāma kills you, you’ll be freed and return to your true form in the heavens.’ He cursed me out of anger when I wasn’t even there to defend myself. But now, thanks to you, I’m finally free from this nightmare. Thank you, Rāma. Not far from here—about half a Yojana away—lives the wise sage Sarabhanga, who shines like the sun. Go see him quickly; he will help you. Please, just bury me here and continue your journey. It’s the rule among Rākshasas: those who die in the forest gain peace in the next world.” After saying this, Virādha—wounded all over—was placed in the pit by Rāma and Lakshmana, finally gaining release and ascending to heaven. After hearing Virādha’s final words, Rāma instructed Lakshmana again, “Dig a big hole for this huge and fearsome Rākshasa.” Rāma kept his foot firmly on Virādha’s throat as Lakshmana dug deep beside the demon’s massive body. Once Lakshmana freed his throat, they shoved Virādha—whose ears were sharp like spears and whose screams echoed—into the pit. Victorious, Rāma and Lakshmana, full of energy and skill, lifted the howling demon and threw him into the hole. Knowing that weapons were useless, they used their wits to finally defeat Virādha. Virādha himself had wished for Rāma to end his cursed life, and had warned him that weapons would not work. Rāma understood, and decided to bury him instead. As the powerful Rākshasa was thrown into the pit, his screams filled the forest. With the threat gone, Rāma and Lakshmana felt safe again, their faces bright with relief, and they roamed the forest with the confidence and brilliance of the sun and moon in the sky.
SECTION V

After killing the powerful demon Virādha in the forest, Rāma, still full of courage, hugged and comforted Sītā. Then he spoke to his energetic brother Lakshmana, saying, “This thick forest is a tough place to live in, and we don’t really know our way around. Let’s quickly go visit the sage Sarabhanga.” So, Rāma started toward Sarabhanga’s hermitage. As they approached, he saw something incredible near the sage, who had earned great spiritual power through his deep meditation. Rāma saw Indra, the king of the gods, glowing like the sun, sitting in a brilliant chariot floating in the sky—never touching the ground—dressed in shining clothes and surrounded by other celestial beings in similar attire. From afar, Rāma could see the chariot in the sky, pulled by green horses that looked as bright as the rising sun. Above the chariot was a spotless white umbrella that glowed like a full moon, decorated with colorful garlands. Indra’s head was being cooled by two fancy fans with golden handles, held by two stunning maidens. All around him, countless Gandharvas, Siddhas, and great sages were singing his praises as he stood there in the sky. Rāma noticed Sarabhanga talking to Indra, and pointed this out to Lakshmana. “Look, Lakshmana, that chariot up there in the sky is amazing—so bright, so beautiful, it’s like the sun has fallen to earth. Those horses must be the ones we’ve heard about, belonging to Indra, the lord of many sacrifices. And check out those young men surrounding him—hundreds of them, wearing earrings and carrying swords, with broad chests and strong arms, dressed in red like fierce tigers. All of them wear blazing chains across their chests, and they look about twenty-five years old—which I guess is the eternal age of gods. Lakshmana, stay here with Sītā while I go find out who’s in that glowing chariot.” After telling Sumitrā’s son to stay put, Rāma headed toward Sarabhanga’s hermitage. When Indra saw Rāma coming, he asked Sarabhanga for permission to leave and told the other gods, “Rāma is coming this way. Let’s go before he talks to me. It’s not time for him to see me yet. When he has defeated his enemy and achieved victory, I’ll appear to him. He still has a task ahead that no one else could accomplish.” Indra then paid his respects to Sarabhanga and, after a short conversation, left for heaven in his chariot pulled by the green horses. Once Indra had gone, Rāma, Sītā, and Lakshmana entered Sarabhanga’s sacred fire chamber. They touched the sage’s feet, and with his blessing, sat down as Sarabhanga welcomed them and gave them a place to stay. Rāma then asked about Indra’s visit, and Sarabhanga explained everything: “Rāma, Indra came here to take me to Brahmā’s realm—heavenly places that are impossible to reach without years of strict discipline. I earned them through my tough austerities. But knowing you were near, I wanted to wait and see you, my dear guest, before leaving for those supreme worlds. I have already earned the best realms of Brahmā and Nākaprishtha. I offer them to you, as my heir.” Rāma, skilled in all knowledge, replied, “Great sage, I’ll earn those realms myself. But right now, please just tell me where I should live in this forest.” Sarabhanga, wise and calm, answered, “Rāma, in this forest lives another holy man, Sutikshna, full of spiritual power. He will help you. Just follow the Mandākini River here—it flows differently than usual, but if you track it among the flowers, you’ll find him. This is your path. But first, my child, stay and watch me as I leave my body, like a snake sheds its old skin.” Sarabhanga then built a fire, recited sacred mantras, and offered sacrifices into the flames. With great energy, he walked into the fire. The fire consumed all his old flesh, hair, and blood, and then Sarabhanga emerged from the flames as a youthful, radiant being. He rose up past the worlds of the great sages and gods, ascending to Brahmā’s realm. There, this pure soul—the best of the twice-born—stood before Brahmā, surrounded by his followers. Brahmā, seeing Sarabhanga, was filled with joy and said—
“Welcome!”

After Sarabhanga went to heaven, a gathering of ascetics appeared before Rāma. They were from all kinds of spiritual orders—Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, Sanprakhālas, Marichipas, Açmwakuttas, Patrāhāras, Dantolukhalas, Unmajjakas, Gātracayyas, Açayyās, Anavakāçikas, Salilāhāras, Vāyubhaksbas, Akāçanilayas, Sthandilaçāyis, Urddhavāsis, Ardrapattavāsas, and others—each practicing different forms of meditation, physical discipline, and self-control. All of them glowed with the power of their spiritual practices and deep concentration. Coming together before Rāma at Sarabhanga’s hermitage, these wise and moral sages spoke to Rāma, who was famous for his virtue: “You are a mighty warrior, the greatest of the Ikshwāku family, and respected throughout the world—like Indra among the gods. Your reputation for truth, virtue, and obedience to your father is legendary. Please, Rāma, don’t be offended if we come to you with a request. A king who takes a share of his people’s earnings but doesn’t protect them is guilty of a great sin. But a king who truly cares for his people, guarding them as if they were his own life or beloved son, earns lasting glory and, in the end, ascends to Brahmā’s heaven. A just king also receives a share of the spiritual merit that holy ascetics win through their penance. Rāma, we are a large group of Brahmanas and forest hermits, but lately we are suffering—attacked by Rākshasas, as if we had no protector at all. Come and see for yourself the bodies of countless pure-hearted ascetics who have been slain in horrible ways by these demons in the forest. The people living near the rivers Pampi and Mandākini, and those at Chitrakuta, are all being tormented. The suffering of the holy men here is unbearable because of the cruel deeds of these Rākshasas. That’s why we’ve come to you for help—because you are the only one we can turn to. Please, Rāma, save us from these demons of the night. You are our only hope on earth. Rescue us, son of the king, from the Rākshasas.” Hearing the sages’ plea, Rāma, always righteous, answered, “You shouldn’t have to beg me for help. I should be taking orders from sages like you. I came to this forest because my father ordered it, but also because I wanted to put an end to the suffering you face from these Rākshasas. I chose to come here for your sake, and if I can help you, my time in the woods will be truly worthwhile. I want to defeat the enemies of the ascetics in battle. Let all the sages witness the strength of both me and my brother.” With the blessings of the ascetics, Rāma took on this noble mission and, together with Lakshmana and the sages, set off toward the hermitage of Sutikshna.
SECTION VII

Rama, along with his brother Lakshmana and Sita, traveled to the hermitage of Sutikshna, accompanied by several Brahmins. After journeying a long way and crossing many wide rivers, Rama spotted a sacred mountain rising high into the sky, as massive as Mount Meru itself. The noble descendants of the Ikshwaku family—Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita—entered a lush forest filled with all kinds of trees. As they moved deeper into the dense woods, abundant with flowers, fruits, and towering trees, Rama noticed a secluded hermitage shining with bark robes and garlands. There, Rama respectfully greeted an ascetic sitting cross-legged in meditation—Sutikshna himself—and said, “O wise one, please speak with me, Maharshi, you who live by truth and righteousness.” 

Sutikshna looked closely at Rama. Calm and self-controlled, this great sage—famous for his devotion—embraced Rama and said warmly, “Welcome, Rama, greatest of the Raghus and the most righteous among men. Your arrival has brought true purpose to this hermitage. Heroic one, I have been waiting for you and haven’t left this world for heaven, even though I could have. I had already heard that you, after losing your kingdom, had come to stay at Chitrakuta. The king of the gods himself, Indra—lord of a hundred sacrifices—once visited me here. He told me that my penance had won me all the heavenly realms. He said, ‘By my blessing, you, your wife, and Lakshmana can live happily here, in these lands filled with divine sages, which your penance has earned.’”

Rama, composed and humble, replied to the radiant and truthful Brahmin, much like Indra would speak to Brahma. He said, “Great sage, I want to earn those realms myself through my own actions. What I seek now is a place to stay in this forest. I’ve heard from the wise Sarabhanga of the Gautama clan that you have the power to help and care for all beings.” 

Hearing Rama’s words, the sage—famous in all worlds—smiled and spoke kindly, “Virtuous Rama, this hermitage is for you. Stay here and enjoy its peace. Many saints live here, and there is always plenty of fruit and roots. Herds of deer roam these woods, gentle and beautiful, never harming anyone. The only trouble they cause is by enchanting people with their beauty; there’s no other danger here.” 

After listening to the sage, Rama, the calm older brother of Lakshmana, picked up his bow with an arrow ready and said, “Respected one, if I were to kill these deer with my sharp arrows, I’d only bring you pain—and what could be worse than that? So I can’t stay long in this hermitage.” 

With that, Rama fell silent and began his evening prayers. When he had finished, he settled in Sutikshna’s hermitage for the night with Sita and Lakshmana. After sunset, once night had arrived, Sutikshna paid his respects to the noble brothers and offered them a fine meal suitable for ascetics.
SECTION VIII

After being warmly welcomed by Sutikshna, Rama and Lakshmana (Sumitra’s son) spent the night there. When morning came, Rama woke up with Lakshmana and Sita. The three of them bathed in the cool, lotus-scented waters. At the right time, they performed their daily worship of Fire and the gods. Now cleansed of their sins in this forest full of ascetics’ homes, Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita saw the sun rise and went to speak with Sutikshna. Rama said gently, “Revered sir, our stay here has been wonderful, thanks to your kindness. We thank you and must take our leave now. The other ascetics have urged us to hurry. We want to visit the many hermitages of the great sages living in the Dandaka forest. Please give us your blessing, and ask these other holy men—so devoted and pure, like smokeless flames—to bless us too. We’d like to leave before the sun gets too hot and unbearable.” After saying this, Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana bowed at Sutikshna’s feet. As they did, Sutikshna helped Rama and Lakshmana up, hugged them warmly, and said, “Rama, travel safely with Lakshmana and Sita, who is always by your side. Go and see the beautiful hermitages of the pure-hearted sages living in the Dandaka forest. You’ll come across blooming woods full of fruit and roots, gentle deer, friendly birds, ponds with blooming lotuses, clear water, and plenty of waterfowl. There are lovely mountain springs and forests filled with peacocks. Go now, my child, and you too, Lakshmana. And please come back to visit me after your journey.” With these words, Rama (also called Kakutstha) and Lakshmana circled Sutikshna as a sign of respect and got ready to leave. Sita, with her wide eyes, handed both brothers their best quivers, bows, and shining swords. Rama and Lakshmana strapped on their quivers and picked up their bows, then left the hermitage. With Sutikshna’s permission, the two brothers, graceful and armed with bows and swords, set off quickly with Sita.
SECTION IX

After Rama (the son of Raghu) had received Sutikshna’s blessing to leave, Sita spoke to him gently but seriously. “Even though you’re a great person who always tries to do what’s right, you’re about to step into something that isn’t right. You could avoid this mistake by not acting on a desire that leads to evil. This kind of desire causes three main problems: the first is lying, the second is getting involved with someone else’s wife, and the third—maybe the worst—is holding a grudge against someone who hasn’t wronged you. Lying has never been your way, Rama, and I know it never will be. And as for chasing after other men’s wives, even in your imagination—that could destroy all your goodness, but you’d never do that. You always focus on me, your own wife. You’re honest, you follow your father’s wishes, and you stick to the truth and to virtue. You have strong self-control, and because of that, you can handle anything. You’re kind, and you control your desires. But now, the third kind of evil I mentioned—harming someone without a real reason—is starting to come up. You promised to protect the sages living in the Dandaka forest by fighting and killing the Rakshasas. That’s why you and your brother are heading there, armed with bows and arrows. Seeing you leave like this, I can’t help but worry about you—about whether you’ll keep your truthfulness and find happiness, both here and in the next life. Honestly, I don’t feel good about this trip to Dandaka, and I want to tell you why. Please listen. You’re going into the forest with weapons, and if you see fierce creatures there, you might end up using them. Just like how dry wood near a fire catches flame, having a weapon in your hand can make the urge to use it even stronger for a warrior. There’s an old story about this: Long ago, in a holy forest full of animals and birds, there was an honest ascetic who lived a pure life. Indra, the king of the gods, wanted to disturb his meditation, so he disguised himself as a warrior and brought a sword to the hermitage, asking the ascetic to keep it safe. The ascetic agreed, and from then on, he never went anywhere—even just to gather fruit or roots—without that sword. Over time, always carrying the weapon made him think less about his spiritual life and more about violence. Eventually, this changed him so much that he lost his peace and fell from the path of righteousness, ending up in hell. This old story shows that, just like fire changes wood, always carrying weapons changes a person’s mind. I’m only telling you this because I care about you so much—I’m not trying to lecture you. Since you’re carrying weapons, please don’t attack the Rakshasas in Dandaka unless they actually threaten you. No one should be killed without cause. As a Kshatriya, your duty is to protect the innocent—people who are helpless or suffering—not to seek out enemies without reason. Weapons don’t really fit with forest life, and being a warrior isn’t the same as being an ascetic—they don’t go together. We should honor the code of conduct that fits our situation now. Using weapons can cloud your judgment. When you go back to Ayodhya, you can take up the duties of a warrior again. For now, if you give up the kingdom and live as a hermit, your parents will truly be proud. Real happiness and success come from righteousness—it’s the only thing that lasts. Wise people gain virtue by disciplining themselves, but if you just chase pleasure, you’ll never find true happiness. Please, Rama, keep your heart pure and focus on what’s right while we’re in this forest. You know everything—nothing in the three worlds is hidden from you. I’m only saying this because, as a woman, I worry sometimes. Who am I to teach you about what’s right? Think it over, and you and your brother do what you decide is best.”
SECTION X

When Rāma heard Vaidehi (Sitā)'s thoughtful words, he felt a deep respect for her. He replied to Janaka's daughter, “Sitā, your words are gentle, wise, and meaningful. You really understand the duties of Kshatriyas. Honestly, what more can I say? By speaking this way, you’ve already answered your own question. Kshatriyas carry bows so that people don’t have to suffer. Sitā, the holy ascetics in Dandaka forest, who face constant danger, have come to me for help. They live in the forest, surviving on fruits and roots, but because of the cruel Rākshasas, they find no peace. These monsters, who eat human flesh, hunt down the ascetics. The anchorites living in Dandaka—some of the best among the twice-born—came to us and pleaded, ‘Please help us.’ When I heard their words, I decided to do what they asked, and I replied, ‘Don’t worry, I will help you.’ Honestly, I feel ashamed that such noble Brahmins, who should be protected, have to turn to me for help. What else could I do? I told them this in person. Then all of them said, ‘Rāma, we are being tormented by Rākshasas in Dandaka forest, monsters who can change their shapes at will. Please save us. These unstoppable Rākshasas attack us, especially during our sacred rituals and important holy days. You are the best protector we have. We could destroy these demons with our spiritual power, but we don’t want to waste the ascetic energy we’ve built up over the years. Rāghava, our meditations are constantly interrupted, and it’s getting hard to keep up our practices. That’s why, even though we are suffering and sometimes even killed by these Rākshasas, we don’t curse them. You and your brother are our protectors here.’ After hearing all this, I promised the saints in Dandaka forest that I would protect them, Janaka’s daughter. I can’t break that promise as long as I live—truth means everything to me. I would rather give up my life, or even you, Sitā, or Lakshmana, than ever break my word—especially to Brahmins. Sitā, protecting these saints is my duty, even if they hadn’t asked me—but now that I’ve promised, I have no choice. You told me all this because you care about me. I appreciate it, Sitā. You wouldn’t give advice like this unless you loved me. What you said shows how much you love me and how noble your family is.” After saying this to Sitā, princess of Mithilā, Rāma—noble and determined—took up his bow, and with Lakshmana, headed deeper into the forest, towards the places where the ascetics lived.
SECTION XI

Rama walked ahead, Sita walked in the middle, and Lakshmana followed behind, holding his bow. As they traveled with Sita, they saw many mountain peaks, forests, beautiful streams, flocks of chakravaka birds on islands, ponds full of lotuses and water birds, herds of deer, wild buffaloes in rut, boars, and elephants—strong enough to knock down trees. After traveling for a long time, when the sun was slanting in the sky, they all spotted a lovely pond about a yojana wide. It was filled with red and pale lotuses, surrounded by groups of elephants, and full of cranes, swans, and kadanivas birds. The water was clear and inviting, but what really caught their attention was the sound of singing and musical instruments coming from the pond—yet they couldn’t see anyone. Curious, Rama and Lakshmana asked a nearby ascetic named Dharmabhrit, “We’re hearing this incredible music and it’s making us really curious. Can you tell us what’s going on here?” Dharmabhrit smiled and began to explain the mystery of the pond.

“This pond is called Panchapsara, and it never dries up,” the ascetic said. “It was created by the sage Mandakarni through his intense meditation. Long ago, Mandakarni lived on nothing but air and performed extreme austerities here for ten thousand years. The gods, led by Agni, grew worried—‘He’s so powerful, he might want to take one of our places!’ So, to distract him, they sent five main Apsaras—heavenly dancers—each as dazzling as lightning. The Apsaras lured Mandakarni into falling in love, and eventually, he married all five. They built their hidden home in this very pond. The singing and music you hear come from those Apsaras, who still please the sage with their songs and instruments.” Rama and Lakshmana were amazed by the story. They continued on, soon coming to a cluster of hermitages covered in kusa grass and tree bark, filled with a sense of spiritual power. With Sita and Lakshmana, Rama entered and was warmly welcomed by the ascetics. They stayed in these peaceful ashrams for a while, honored by the sages, and moved from one hermitage to another, visiting those Rama knew from before. Sometimes they stayed ten months, sometimes a year, sometimes just a few months. In this way, nearly ten years passed as Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana lived among the hermits and enjoyed their kindness. After visiting all the hermitages, Rama returned to Sutikshna’s ashram. Once, while sitting there, Rama respectfully asked Sutikshna, “I’ve always heard people talk about the great sage Agastya living in this forest. The forest is so vast, I don’t know where his hermitage is. Can you tell me where to find this famous sage? I’d like to visit him with Sita and Lakshmana, and serve him myself.” Sutikshna, pleased by the request, replied, “I was about to suggest the same thing! You should go see Agastya with Sita and Lakshmana. I’ll tell you how to find him. Head south from here for four miles and you’ll reach the hermitage of Agastya’s brother, in a beautiful forest full of pippali trees, fruits, and flowers, and alive with birdsong. There are ponds filled with swans and karandavas, and flocks of chakravakas. Spend the night there, and in the morning, head further south. After another yojana, you’ll reach Agastya’s own ashram, in a lovely woodland full of trees. Sita and Lakshmana will be happy there. If you want to meet Agastya, you should set out today.” Rama thanked Sutikshna and, with his brother and Sita, set out on the path described. As they walked, they enjoyed the beautiful forests, cloud-like hills, lakes, and streams. Rama said to Lakshmana, “I think we’ve reached the ashram of Agastya’s brother. There are thousands of fruit- and flower-laden trees, just as Sutikshna described. The air smells strongly of ripe pippali fruit. I can see piles of firewood, and darva grass shining like gemstones. There’s smoke rising from the fire in the ashram, like a dark mountain peak. I see sages performing their rituals, offering flowers they’ve gathered themselves. This must be the place. Agastya is the one who, through his power, killed a demon as deadly as Death itself, making this region safe. Long ago, two powerful asura brothers, Vatapi and Ilwala, lived here and killed brahmins for sport. Ilwala would disguise himself as a brahmin and invite sages to a ritual meal. He’d cook his brother Vatapi—who had turned into a ram—and serve him as food. After the sages had eaten, Ilwala would call, ‘Vatapi, come out!’ and Vatapi would burst out of their bodies, killing them. This trick killed thousands of sages. But one day, Agastya was invited and ate Vatapi. When Ilwala called for his brother, Agastya laughed and said, ‘Your brother can’t come out—he’s gone to the land of the dead.’ Furious, Ilwala attacked, but Agastya’s fiery gaze destroyed him. This ashram, with its pools and groves, belongs to Agastya’s brother, whose sibling performed that act to save the sages.” As Rama finished the story, the sun set and evening came. After performing their evening prayers, Rama and his companions entered the hermitage and greeted the ascetic. They were warmly received and spent the night eating fruits and roots. In the morning, Rama respectfully greeted Agastya’s brother and said, “Thank you for your hospitality. I will now go visit my teacher, your elder brother.” The ascetic told him to go, and Rama set out on the path. On the way, he saw forests filled with many kinds of trees—niharas, panasas, salas, vanjulas, tinisas, chirivilwas, madhukas, vilvas, tindukas—all blooming and covered in vines, with trees battered by elephants, monkeys everywhere, and the air loud with the calls of birds. Rama turned to Lakshmana and said, “The leaves here are shiny, and the animals are gentle, just as we were told. Agastya’s ashram must be close. I can see smoke from the ashram and decorations of bark and garlands. There are gentle deer and the calls of birds everywhere. This is the ashram of Agastya, who destroyed the demon and made the South safe for everyone. Thanks to him, the rakshasas are too afraid to come here. Since Agastya made this place his home, the demons have stopped attacking and become peaceful. This southern region, made safe by Agastya, is famous throughout the three worlds. This peaceful ashram belongs to Agastya, the legendary sage, whose command even the great Vindhya mountain obeys—it no longer blocks the sun’s path. Agastya, honored by all, always works for the good of the righteous, and I’m sure he’ll help us too. I plan to pay my respects to Agastya and spend the rest of our exile here. Gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and saints worship Agastya here, following strict diets. No liar, cheater, or wicked person can survive here. Only the pure-hearted and righteous live in this place, along with gods, yakshas, nagas, and birds, all living simply. Saints and Siddhas who die here are taken to heaven in shining chariots, and the gods reward them with positions among yakshas, gods, and kings. Lakshmana, go inside and tell the sages that Sita and I have arrived.”

Ilwala would call out, “Vatapi, come out!” and Vatapi, still in the form of a ram, would tear out of the brahmins’ bodies, killing them. This cruel trick killed thousands of sages. But everything changed when Agastya was invited to one of their feasts. He ate Vatapi as the meal, and when Ilwala called for his brother, Agastya calmly said, “Your brother can’t come out—he’s gone to the world of the dead.” Furious, Ilwala tried to attack, but Agastya’s fiery power destroyed him instantly. That’s how Agastya saved this region and made it safe for sages once again. As Rama finished telling this story to Lakshmana, the sun set. Rama and his companions performed their evening prayers, entered the hermitage, and greeted the resident sage, who welcomed them warmly. They spent the night eating fruits and roots. In the morning, Rama thanked Agastya’s brother, saying, “Thank you for your kindness. Now I’ll go see your elder brother, my teacher.” With the sage’s blessing, Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana continued on, passing through forests filled with flowering trees and lively animals. Rama soon spotted Agastya’s ashram, smoke curling above it, garlanded with bark and flowers, and peaceful animals all around. He said to Lakshmana, “This must be the ashram of Agastya, the great sage who tamed this wild region. Because of him, the demons no longer threaten the South. His power is so great that even the mighty Vindhya mountains obey his commands. Agastya is known everywhere for helping the righteous. We’ll be safe here and spend the rest of our exile in peace. This place is so pure that only the honest and good can live here. Even the gods and saints come here to worship. Lakshmana, go ahead and let the sages know that Sita and I have arrived.”
SECTION XII

After entering the hermitage, Lakshmana—Rama’s younger brother—approached one of Agastya’s students and spoke to him: “There was a king named Dasharatha. His eldest son, the strong Rama, has come here to this hermitage with his wife, Sita, to meet the sage. My name is Lakshmana—I’m his younger brother, loyal and devoted to him. Maybe you’ve heard about us. We’ve come into this wild forest because our father ordered us to, and now we wish to see your revered teacher. Please tell him we’re here.” Hearing Lakshmana’s words, the student replied, “Of course!” and went straight into the inner sanctum, where the sacred fire was kept, to inform Agastya. When he got inside, Agastya’s favorite disciple, with hands pressed together in respect, told the legendary sage exactly what Lakshmana had said: “Dasharatha’s sons, Rama and Lakshmana—both known for defeating their enemies—have arrived with Sita to see you and serve you. Please tell us what you wish us to do.” When Agastya heard from his student that Rama had come with Lakshmana and the virtuous Sita (also called Vaidehi), he said, “What luck! After such a long time, Rama has finally come to visit me. I’ve been hoping he would. Go and welcome him properly—bring him in to see me. Why didn’t you bring him right away?” The disciple, bowing respectfully, replied, “Yes, teacher.” Then he went outside and said to Lakshmana, “Where is Rama? He should come in now.” So Lakshmana, together with the disciple, led Rama and Sita to the hermitage. The disciple cheerfully repeated Agastya’s invitation to Rama and welcomed him with the honor he deserved. As Rama entered the hermitage with Lakshmana and Sita, he noticed the place was full of gentle deer, giving it a peaceful atmosphere. Inside, Rama saw shrines dedicated to many gods: Brahma, Agni, Vishnu, Indra, Vivaswat, Soma, Bhaga, Dhata and Vidhata, Vayu, Varuna (who holds a noose), Gayatri, the Vasus, the king of the Nagas, Garuda, Kartikeya, and the god Dharma. 

Soon, Agastya himself arrived, surrounded by his students. Rama saw the radiant sage leading the group of hermits and said to Lakshmana, “Look, Lakshmana—the great sage Agastya is coming. I can recognize his powerful presence.” After saying this about Agastya, who shone like the sun, Rama stepped forward and bowed down, touching the sage’s feet. Then, with Sita (daughter of King Janaka) and Lakshmana beside him, Rama stood respectfully, hands pressed together. Agastya embraced Rama, welcomed him with water and a seat, and asked kindly about his well-being, saying, “Welcome!” He offered the visitors fire oblations, presented arghya (a ceremonial welcome), and honored them with food, as was proper for a forest-dwelling sage. After sitting down himself, Agastya, the respected sage, addressed Rama, who stood with hands joined: “Rama, if a sage neglects a guest, he’ll suffer for it in the afterlife—like a false witness, he’ll be forced to eat his own flesh. You, ruler of the world, hero, and man of honor, are my honored guest today.” With that, Agastya offered Rama fruits, roots, and flowers, and continued, “Rama, here is a great divine bow that once belonged to Vishnu, made by the master craftsman Vishvakarma. Here is also the best arrow, called Brahmadatta—unerring and bright as the sun—and a pair of never-empty quivers filled with sharp arrows, blazing like fire. Indra himself gave these to me. And here is a golden scabbard and a sword decorated with gold. In the past, Vishnu used this very bow to defeat the powerful asuras (demons) in battle and win the gods their fortune. Take this bow, these quivers, this arrow, and this sword, Rama—just as Indra would take up his thunderbolt—to ensure your victory.” After saying this, the powerful sage Agastya entrusted all these weapons to Rama.
SECTION XIII

“Rāma, I’m truly pleased with you—may good things come your way! And Lakshmana, you’ve made me just as happy. I can see you’re both exhausted from your long journey, and Janaka’s daughter, the noble Maithili (Sitā), clearly needs some rest too. She’s still young and has never faced real hardship before, but here she is in this challenging forest, all because of her deep love for you. Rāma, you need to make sure Sitā is as comfortable as possible during your exile. It’s not easy for her to leave everything behind and follow you out here. Generally, women are known to support those who are successful and abandon those who fall on hard times. They can be as unpredictable as lightning, as sharp as weapons, and as quick as Garuda or the wind. But your wife is nothing like that—she’s loyal and devoted, just like the legendary Arundhati among the gods. Hearing these words from the sage, Rāma folded his hands respectfully and replied, “I’m truly fortunate and honored to have earned your approval, both for myself, my brother, and my wife. Please, can you direct me to a well-watered area full of trees, where I can build a home and live happily?” The great sage thought for a moment and then said, “Two Yojanas from here is a beautiful place called Panchavati. It’s full of fruits and roots, teeming with deer, and it’s a wonderful spot to live. Go there with Lakshmana and fulfill your father’s wishes. I know everything about your situation and about Daçaratha, thanks to my spiritual insight. Even though you promised to stay with me in this grove, I can tell what you truly want. So I advise you to go to Panchavati. It’s a lovely forest near the Godāvari River where Sitā will be happy. The area is rich in fruit, roots, and birds, peaceful and beautiful—a perfect retreat. You, Rāma, who are pure of heart and skilled at protecting sages, will keep everyone safe there. Look, over there is the great Madhuka forest. Head north past the Madhuka woods, and you’ll come to a place near a hill—that’s the famous Panchavati, covered in blossoming trees.”

After Agastya finished speaking, Rāma and Lakshmana respectfully greeted the wise, truth-telling sage. They bowed at his feet, asked for his blessing, and then set out with Sitā toward Panchavati. Carrying their bows and quivers, the two princes—always ready for action—followed the path the great sage had described, making their way to their new home in Panchavati.
SECTION XIV

As he continued on his way to Panchavati, Rama (Raghu’s son) spotted a massive vulture with an intimidating presence. Rama and Lakshmana, who were talking as they walked through the forest, immediately sensed that this bird was actually a Rakshasa in disguise. They stopped and asked it directly, “Who are you?” The vulture answered in a gentle, friendly tone: “My child, I am a friend of your father.” Once Rama realized this bird was indeed a friend of King Dasharatha, he showed his respect and asked for the vulture’s name and background. The vulture responded by telling the story of his own family, beginning with the origin of all beings: “Listen, Rama. Long ago, the first Prajapatis—creators—were Kardama, Vikrita, Sesha, Sancraya, the powerful Vahuputra, Sthanu, Marichi, Atri, the mighty Kratu, Pulastya, Angira, Pracheta, Pulaha, Daksha, Vivaswat, Arishtanemi, and the energetic Kasyapa. Daksha, as we've heard, had sixty well-known daughters. Kasyapa married eight of them—Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kalika, Tamra, Krodhavasā, Manu, and Anala. Kalika had two sons, Naraka and Kalaka.

Kraunchi’s children were the owls; Bhasi’s were the bhasas; Syeni’s were hawks and vultures; Dhritarashtri’s were swans, different kinds of kalahansas, and chakravakas; Suki’s daughter was Nata. Nata’s daughter was Vinata. Krodhavasā had ten daughters: Mrigi, Mrigamanda, Hari, Bhadramada, Matangi, Sarduli, Sweta, Surabhi, Surasa, and Kadruka.

Mrigi’s children were deer; Mrigamanda’s were bears, Srimaras, and Chamaras. Bhadramada had a daughter, Iravati, whose son is the mighty elephant who rules all elephants. Hari’s children are lions and agile monkeys. Sarduli’s sons are Golangulas and tigers. Matangi’s children are mad elephants. Sweta gave birth to the elephants that guard the four directions. Surabhi had two daughters, Rohini and Gandharbi; Rohini’s children are cows, while Gandharbi’s are horses.

Surasa gave birth to nagas (serpents), and Kadru gave birth to pannagas (another serpent race). Manu, another wife of Kasyapa, gave birth to humanity—Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras, who came from the mouth, chest, thighs, and feet respectively. Anala gave birth to all fruit-bearing trees. Vinata was Suki’s granddaughter, and Kadru was Surasa’s aunt. Kadru gave birth to a thousand nagas, including the one who supports the world. Vinata’s two sons were Garuda and Aruna.

From Aruna came me and my elder brother Sampati. So, Rama, know that I am Jatayu, son of Syeni. If you wish, I can help you while you live in the forest. Rama then entrusted the powerful bird with the safety of Sita. With Lakshmana by his side, Rama continued on to Panchavati, determined to defeat his enemies and protect the world.
SECTION XV

When they reached Panchavati—a place full of all kinds of animals and wild creatures—Rāma turned to his energetic brother and said, “We’ve arrived at the spot the sage told us about. Rāma took Lakshmana’s hand and led him to the beautiful place, saying, “This area is flat, lovely, and surrounded by flowering trees. Build our shelter here. There’s a beautiful pond nearby, covered in lotuses, shining like the sun, and filled with a sweet scent. Lakshmana made a large hut for Rāma using bamboo, leaves, and clay. It had sturdy pillars, was decorated with samī branches, tied tightly with strong cords, and its floor was flat and tidy. The hut was draped with kuça grass, reeds, and leaves. It looked beautiful and inviting—a perfect home. After finishing the hut, Lakshmana went to the Godavari river, bathed, and collected lotuses and fruit, then returned to the shelter. He offered flowers and performed rituals to bless their new home. Then Lakshmana proudly showed the hut to Rāma.

Rāma was overjoyed when he saw the beautiful shelter, especially with Sitā beside him. He hugged Lakshmana and said warmly, “I’m really pleased with you. You’ve done something great, and my embrace is your reward. While you, my father’s thoughtful, loyal, and wise son are alive, it feels like my father isn’t really gone.” After saying this, Rāma, feeling happy and content, settled into his new life there, enjoying the abundant fruits of the forest. With Sitā and Lakshmana caring for him, Rāma lived like a god among the heavens.
SECTION XVI

While Rāma (also called Rāghava), noble son of the Raghu dynasty, was living peacefully in the forest, winter quietly arrived after autumn's end. One morning, after sunrise, Rāma went to the beautiful river Godāvari to bathe. Lakshmana (Rāma’s loyal brother and the son of Sumitrā) followed behind, carrying a water pot, with Sitā walking just behind them. Lakshmana spoke up, saying, “Rāma, the season you love has finally come. It’s the time that seems to make the whole year shine. People’s skin gets rough from the dew, the fields are full of crops, water is cold and hard to use, and everyone enjoys the warmth of fire. After the Agrayana festival, when people offer the first rice to the gods and their ancestors, they feel cleansed of their sins. The land is overflowing with food, milk, and all sorts of dairy treats, and kings go out to inspect their territories. Now that the sun has moved toward the north, a direction ruled by the Destroyer (Shiva), the north seems bare, like a woman without her forehead mark. The Himalayas (Himavān), always snowy and now even colder with the sun far away, truly live up to their name. Midday is the best time—pleasant sun, great for walking, but shade and water feel too cold. The days are chilly, covered in dew, the woods are quiet, and the lotuses have withered from the frost. At night, nobody wants to sleep outside, and the constellation Pushyā marks the season. Nights are long and bitterly cold, with the air looking brown from the mist. The moon’s luck seems to have passed to the sun; the moon appears dull and reddish, covered in haze, like glass fogged by breath. Its light is pale, not beautiful—kind of like Sitā, who looks pale from being out in the sun too much. Even the western wind, already cold, blows even colder now. The forests are shrouded in mist, the fields full of wheat and barley shine at sunrise, and the air is filled with the cries of cranes and kraunchas (waterbirds). The golden rice plants bend under their own weight, looking elegant, like clusters of date blossoms heavy with grain. The sun, even when high in the sky, seems weak and pale, its light dulled by fog. Early in the day, the sunlight is faint and cool; it only becomes pleasant at noon, but even then it’s soft and hazy. In the woods, the grass sparkles with dew in the morning sun, looking especially fresh and green. Wild elephants, thirsty, hesitate before touching the cold, clear water with their trunks. The waterbirds just sit by the riverbank and refuse to enter, like cowards avoiding a fight. Trees, stripped of flowers, look as if they’re fast asleep, covered by dew at night and mist in the morning. The rivers are cloaked in fog, echoing with the cries of cranes, their banks wet with fresh dew. With the snow, the gentle sun, and the cold, even water from a mountaintop tastes sweet now. Lotuses, battered by the cold, have lost their petals and wilted; they’re no longer beautiful. And Rāma, I’m sure that right now, Bharata—because of his love for you—is suffering and practicing self-control back in the city. He’s given up his throne, his comforts, and all his pleasures, lying on the bare ground this winter, living like an ascetic and eating very little. Every day, probably at this very hour, he goes with his people to the river Sarayu to bathe, despite having grown up in luxury. How can someone as gentle as him stand bathing in the freezing river at night’s end? Bharata—with eyes like lotus petals, calm and strong, deep-naveled and mighty—really understands what’s right. He always tells the truth, controls his desires, is respectful of other men’s wives, and is gentle and sweet in his speech. He’s long-armed, a true warrior, and has given up every pleasure to honor you. Your noble brother is as good as in heaven, living as an ascetic and following your example in the forest. People often say that sons follow their mothers, not their fathers—but Bharata proves that wrong. How could Kaikeyi, wife of Daçaratha and mother of the righteous Bharata, act so selfishly?” As Lakshmana spoke with such affection, Rāma—unwilling to hear his mother Kaikeyi criticized—responded,

“Brother, please don’t blame our second mother. Let’s talk about Bharata, the true hero of the Ikshwāku family. Even though I’ve made up my mind to stay in the forest, my heart can’t help but waver because I miss Bharata so much. I remember his kind and loving words—they’re like nectar, bringing joy to my soul. When will I see Bharata again, along with the brave Satrughna and you, Lakshmana?” After speaking this way, Rāma, along with Lakshmana and Sitā, reached the Godāvari and bathed together. Then they made water offerings and prayers to the gods and their ancestors, singing hymns to the rising sun and other deities. With Sitā on one side and Lakshmana on the other, Rāma looked magnificent, like the god Rudra flanked by Nandi and the daughter of the mountain king.
SECTION XVII

After bathing in the river Godāvari, Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana (Sumitra’s son) returned to their forest hut. Once they arrived, Rama and Lakshmana performed their morning prayers before entering the cottage. Rama, respected by the great sages, lived happily in that cottage. Sitting with Sita, the strong-armed Rama looked as radiant as the Moon beside the star Chitra. He spent his time talking about all sorts of things with Lakshmana. While Rama was deep in conversation, a Rakshasi (female demon) showed up in the area, moving wherever she pleased. This was Surpanakha, the sister of the ten-headed demon Ravana. She saw Rama and was immediately struck by his almost divine appearance—his lion-like chest, powerful arms, broad eyes like lotus petals, graceful walk like an elephant, matted hair, and glowing face marked by regality. Surpanakha was overwhelmed by desire as she gazed at Rama, whose dark blue skin was like a lotus, whose charm rivaled that of the love god Kamadeva, and who seemed as powerful as Indra. But while Rama was handsome and graceful, Surpanakha was the opposite: her face was ugly, her stomach huge, her eyes frightening, her hair coppery and wild. Rama’s presence was pleasant; hers was off-putting. Rama’s voice was deep and pleasant, hers was harsh and shrill. He was young; she was old. He spoke gently; she spoke roughly. He lived by justice; she lived without rules. He was beautiful; she was hideous. Burning with lust, Surpanakha spoke to Rama:

“You, with your matted hair and weapons—why have you and your wife come to this place, which is full of Rakshasas? Tell me what you’re doing here.” Hearing this, Rama—ever honest and fair—answered her directly: “There was a king named Dasaratha, as powerful as a god. I am his oldest son—my name is Rama. This is my younger brother Lakshmana, who is devoted to me. And this is my wife, Sita. My parents sent me here, and I am living in this forest to follow their wishes and to practice righteousness. But I’d like to know about you. Who are you? What’s your name, and where do you come from? You have a striking appearance—you look like a Rakshasi to me. Be honest: why have you come here?” Surpanakha, driven by desire, replied, “Listen, Rama. I’ll tell you the truth. I am a Rakshasi, able to change my shape as I please. My name is Surpanakha. I roam these forests alone, and everyone fears me. My brother is Ravana—you may have heard of him. There’s also my brother Kumbhakarna, who is always sleeping; Vibhishana, who is righteous and doesn’t follow the other Rakshasas; and Khara and Dushana, both famous warriors. But Rama, I am stronger than all of them. The moment I saw you, I wanted you as my husband. I have power, and I can go wherever I want. Be my husband forever. Why do you want Sita? She’s ugly and doesn’t deserve you. I am perfect for you. Take me as your wife. I’ll eat this ugly, skinny, unfaithful human—your wife Sita—and your brother too. Then, free to do as you wish, you and I can roam the Dandaka forest together, exploring all the mountains and woods.” Hearing all this, Rama—whose eyes were kind and whose words were always clever—smiled and began to reply.
SECTION XVIII

Smiling, Rāma teased Surpanakha, who was completely infatuated with him. He spoke gently, “Listen, beautiful one, I’m already married—this is my beloved wife. Sharing a husband with another woman is miserable for someone like you. But my younger brother here is single. He’s good-looking, has a great character, and he’s never been married. His name is Lakshmana. He’s young and attractive, and I think you two would make a perfect match. Just as sunlight seeks out Mount Meru, you should choose him as your husband. That way, you won’t have to worry about sharing your husband with another woman.” 

Surpanakha, swept up by her desire, immediately turned away from Rāma and went to Lakshmana. She said, “I’m the perfect wife for you. With my beauty and your charm, we could explore these Dandaka forests together and be happy.”

Lakshmana, son of Sumitra and skilled with words, smiled and replied, “Why would you want to be with me? I’m just a servant to my noble brother. Honestly, you’d be much better off marrying him than settling for me. Just imagine—if he left this old, thin, unpleasant wife, he could devote himself to someone as beautiful as you. Really, what man in his right mind would choose a human woman over someone as graceful as you?” 

But Surpanakha didn’t realize Lakshmana was joking. She took his words seriously. 

A short while later, as Rāma was sitting in the cottage with Sītā, Surpanakha, burning with lust and rage, stormed in. She shouted at Rāma, “Why do you ignore me for this ugly, old, pathetic woman? Today, right in front of you, I’ll eat this human girl. Then I’ll finally have you to myself, with no rival.”

With wild eyes full of fury, Surpanakha lunged at Sītā, ready to attack, as violently as a meteor crashing into the moon. Seeing this, Rāma jumped up, blocking Surpanakha like someone snatching away a deadly noose. Angry, he said to Lakshmana, “Saumitri, there’s no point in joking with someone this twisted and evil. Look—Vaidehi (another name for Sītā) is terrified. It’s time you teach this horrible, lust-crazed demoness a lesson—disfigure her so she won’t bother us again.”

Obeying his brother, the furious and powerful Lakshmana drew his sword. Right in front of Rāma, he sliced off Surpanakha’s nose and ears. Screaming in pain, blood pouring from her wounds, the hideous Surpanakha ran back into the forest, howling like thunderclouds in a storm. Deformed and covered in blood, she raised her arms and let out more terrifying cries as she disappeared into the trees.

Wounded and enraged, Surpanakha finally reached her brother Khara, who was in Janasthāna surrounded by other Rākshasas. She collapsed to the ground like a thunderbolt crashing down from the sky. Bleeding and terrified, she told Khara everything: how Rāma had come to the forest with Lakshmana and his wife, and how she had been horribly disfigured.
SECTION XIX

When Khara, the Rākshasa, saw his sister Surpanakhā lying on the ground, badly injured and covered in blood, he was furious. He demanded, “Get up! Stop being afraid and shocked. Tell me clearly—who did this to you? Who dared to harm a deadly black snake just for fun, not realizing the danger? Whoever attacked you has unknowingly wrapped a fatal noose around his own neck. With my strength and skills, able to change forms and roam as I please—like death itself—tell me who left you in this state? Who among the gods, Gandharvas, other creatures, or even the great sages, has the power to harm you like this? In this world, I don’t think anyone would dare mess with me. Just as a thirsty crane picks only the milk from water, leaving the rest, I will single out and destroy this enemy—even if it’s mighty Indra himself. Whose blood, foaming as I pierce his bones, does the earth crave to drink? Whose flesh, torn from his corpse in battle, will the birds feast on? Hearing her brother’s furious words, Surpanakhā, with tears streaming down her face, answered, “There are two men—young, handsome, powerful, with large, lotus-like eyes. They wear simple clothes made from bark and dark deer-skins, living on fruits and roots. They have incredible self-control, living as ascetics and following brahmacharya. They are the sons of Daśaratha: Rāma and Lakshmana, brothers who look like the kings of the Gandharvas and seem born for greatness. I can’t even tell if they’re gods or humans. As Surpanakhā finished, Khara, burning with anger, said, “So, two armed humans wearing bark and deer-skins, along with a woman, have entered this deep Dandaka forest. SECTION XX

Surpanakha, furious and humiliated, returned to Rāma’s forest hut, bringing a group of Rākshasas (demons) with her. When Khara saw Surpanakha (let’s call her “Surpa” for short) lying on the ground again, he grew furious. After Surpanakhā mocked him, Khara turned to the other Rākshasas and spoke harshly. “Your insults have made me angrier than ever,” he said. “I can't stand this, just like pouring salt water on an open wound. When Rama ordered this, Lakshmana grabbed his bow and arrows and led Sita to a secret cave, hidden and hard to get to. Then, seeing Rama alone but full of energy, everyone felt a wave of fear. Rama’s presence was as intense as Rudra (an enraged form of Shiva) ready to destroy. While the gods, Gandharvas, and Charanas talked, the Rakshasa army began its war cries. Their forces were loud, armored, carrying weapons and banners, talking bravely, roaring, stretching their bows, yawning out of battle-hunger, shouting, and blowing their trumpets. Khara’s army, as huge and noisy as the ocean, charged at Rama at top speed with all kinds of weapons. Rama, a master of warfare, looked around and saw Khara’s forces ready for battle. He drew his terrifying bow and grabbed his arrows, burning with anger and determined to destroy the Rakshasas. He looked as fierce as a raging fire at the end of the world, impossible to gaze at directly. The forest spirits themselves felt afraid seeing him so charged with energy.

Rama’s wrathful appearance was like Shiva (the holder of the bow Pinaka) when he was about to destroy Daksha’s sacrifice. Khara’s army, covered in fiery armor and decked with bows, ornaments, chariots, and weapons, looked like storm clouds glowing red in the morning sun.
SECTION XXV

As Khara arrived at the ashram, leading his troops, he spotted Rāma standing alone, bow in hand, ready for battle. SECTION XXVIII
