And he’s the one who, for no reason, mutilated my sister in the forest—he cut off her nose and ears. I’ve decided: I’m going to kidnap his wife, Sitā, who looks like a goddess, from Janasthāna. I need your help. With you at my side, and if my brothers join too, I don’t even worry about the gods themselves. So come with me, because you’re the only one who can pull this off. In battle, you’re unmatched—no one is as tough or as skilled in magic as you are. That’s why I’ve come to you, Māricha. Here’s what I need you to do: transform yourself into a golden deer with silver spots and wander near Rāma’s forest hut, where Sitā can see you. She’ll be so fascinated that she’ll beg Rāma and Lakshmana to catch you. When they leave to chase you, I’ll swoop in and kidnap Sitā from their empty hut, just like Rāhu swallowing the Moon. Then, when Rāma is devastated at losing his wife, I’ll escape with Sitā and finally have what I want.”

When Māricha heard Rāvaṇa’s plan, his face went pale and he was filled with dread. He nervously licked his dry lips and stared at Rāvaṇa, eyes wide and unblinking, looking almost lifeless from shock. Terrified of Rāvaṇa, but remembering all too well Rāma’s power in the forest, Māricha pressed his palms together in fear and began to speak, hoping his words would help both himself and Rāvaṇa.
SECTION XXXVII

After hearing the words of Ravana, king of the Rakshasas, the powerful and wise Maricha replied skillfully, “O king, it’s easy to say nice things, but it’s rare to speak or listen to harsh truths that are actually for your own good. You’re reckless, and since you don’t use spies, you really don’t understand just how strong Rama is—he’s as powerful and righteous as Indra or Varuna. Honestly, I’ll be lucky if Rama, in his anger, doesn’t destroy all the Rakshasas; or if Sita, King Janaka’s daughter, hasn’t come into your life just to bring about your ruin; or if Lanka, along with you and the other Rakshasas, doesn’t get wiped out because of her. A ruler who is cruel, unpredictable, and evil like you only brings disaster upon himself, his kingdom, and even his family. Rama, who brings joy to Kausalya, wasn’t abandoned by his father, nor is he lacking in virtue or good behavior. He’s not greedy or evil, nor is he out to destroy the Kshatriya race. He doesn’t lack integrity or achievements, and he isn’t cruel or intent on causing suffering. When his honest father was manipulated by Kaikeyi, Rama chose to go to the forest. He did this for the sake of his father Dasaratha and for Kaikeyi; that’s why he entered the Dandaka forest. Rama, my friend, isn’t harsh or foolish; he has total self-control. He never lies—not even by accident. So it’s wrong for you to insult him like this. He’s the embodiment of virtue, devoted to truth, and a leader among men just as Basava leads the gods. How can you even think of taking away his wife, Vaidehi (Sita), who’s protected by her own chastity and goodness, like trying to steal the rays of the sun? It’s madness for you to throw yourself into Rama’s fire, where his arrows are like burning rays and his bow and sword are the fuel. You should not go up against Rama, giving up your kingdom, your happiness, and even your life—he’s as deadly as death itself when armed with his bow and arrows, and no one can stand against him. His power is unmatched; Janaka’s daughter is his wife, living in the forest with total faith in his strength. You won’t be able to take her. She’s the beloved wife of the greatest of men, whose chest is like a lion’s—he loves Sita more than his own life and is always devoted to her. Young Sita, who is so dear to mighty Rama and shines like fire, can never be taken by you. What’s the point of this foolish plan, chief of the Rakshasas? The moment Rama sees you in battle, you’ll be finished. Life, happiness, and a kingdom are hard to keep—so you should act wisely. Talk to your ministers, especially Vibhishana, and consider Rama’s strengths and weaknesses, as well as your own, before making your move. I’m telling you, this fight with the son of the King of Kosala will only bring disaster to you. So listen to me again, prince of night, and hear these words that are full of sense and meant for your own good.”
SECTION XXXVIII

There was a time when I traveled all over the world. My body was gigantic, like a massive mountain, and I had the strength of a thousand Nāgas (serpents). I carried a heavy iron club in my hands, wore a crown on my head, and golden earrings. My skin was dark blue, like a thundercloud. People were terrified of me as I wandered through the Dandaka forest, living off the flesh of Rishis (sages). The holy sage Viswamitra became so afraid of me that he went to King Dasaratha himself and said, “When I am deep in meditation during the festival, let Rama protect me, O King. I am truly afraid of this Maricha.” Answering him, the noble King Dasaratha said, “Raghava (Rama) is still under twelve years old and not yet trained in the ways of war. But I have plenty of soldiers; if you allow it, great sage, I will send my army to defeat your enemies, these night-dwelling demons.” Viswamitra replied, “It is true that you fought for the gods in the great war and your reputation is known everywhere, but only Rama can stand against the Rakshasas. Even though Rama is still a boy, he is strong enough to defeat them. So, let your soldiers stay here and let me take Rama with me. May the gods bless you.” With these words, Viswamitra, pleased, left for his hermitage with Rama.

After this, once the preparations for the sacrifice in the Dandaka forest were complete, Rama, having unstrung his mighty bow, approached the sage to guard the ritual. He wore a gold chain around his neck, a crest on his head, and held a bow in his hand. His eyes were striking, and he wore just one simple piece of clothing. His face was greenish and incredibly handsome, and he didn’t yet have a mustache or any signs of adulthood. Rama’s presence lit up the entire Dandaka forest, making him look like the newly risen moon. 

Then, filled with confidence from boons granted by Brahma, I—looking like a dark cloud with golden earrings—entered the hermitage, proud of my power. As soon as Rama saw me, he calmly picked up his spear and strung his bow with expert care. Foolishly, I ignored him, thinking he was just a child, and rushed toward Viswamitra’s sacrificial altar. But Rama struck me with a sharp arrow designed to destroy his enemies, and the force of it hurled me a hundred yojanas away into the ocean. He could have killed me but chose to spare my life. I was knocked out by the blast of his arrows and sank deep into the ocean, unconscious. 

After a long time, I finally regained consciousness and returned to the city of Lanka. Though I survived, all my followers were killed by Rama—who, even as a mere boy and beginner in warfare, was tireless and unstoppable. That’s why I’m warning you: if you fight Rama, you will suffer disaster and destruction. You will only bring misery to the joyful, fun-loving Rakshasas who celebrate so many festivals. And you will bring about the ruin of Lanka, which is filled with treasures and golden buildings, all for the sake of Sita.

Good people who associate with someone evil are destroyed by his actions, even if they do nothing wrong themselves—like fish in a pond full of snakes, who get eaten by Garuda. Because of your recklessness, you’ll see the Rakshasas—dressed in celestial ornaments and scented with sandalwood—killed and lying on the ground. The survivors will scatter everywhere, some escaping with their wives, others alone because their wives have been taken by the enemy. You’ll see all the buildings of Lanka covered in arrows and flames, burned down to ashes.

There is no greater sin than stealing another man’s wife. You already have a thousand women in your palace, O King. Cherish your own wives and protect your family, your people, your life, your kingdom, your riches, and your honor. If you want to be happy with your wives and friends, don’t provoke Rama. I am your friend, and I’m begging you again—stop this, let go of your evil plan. If you go after Sita, Rama’s arrows will destroy you and your family, and you will all end up in Yama’s realm.
SECTION XXXIX

Somehow, Rāma saved me during that battle. Let me tell you what happened next. Even after nearly dying, I wasn’t humbled. I went back into the Dandaka forest, this time with two other Rākshasas who disguised themselves as deer. I took on a terrifying form — my tongue was like fire, my teeth were huge, my horns were razor-sharp, and I survived by eating the flesh of ascetics. Looking so monstrous, I rampaged through the forest, especially targeting holy places like the Tirtha, the Agnihotri, and other places of worship. I killed ascetics, ate their flesh, drank their blood, and disrupted every religious ritual I could find. My appearance was hideous, and the blood drove me insane, terrifying all the animals in the forest. While I was causing chaos and blocking religious ceremonies in Dandaka, I spotted the righteous Rāma, who lived simply, along with the respected Sitā and the powerful Lakshmana. They all practiced strict asceticism, ate little, and were devoted to the welfare of all beings. Remembering my past grudge and hungry for power, I became furious. Still in my deer form, with my deadly horns, I charged at Rāma, thinking he was just another forest hermit, not realizing who he truly was. But Rāma strung his massive bow and shot three sharp arrows at me. These arrows were terrifying — twisted like thunderbolts, designed to kill, and moved as swiftly as Garuda or the wind. They seemed to merge together as they flew at us. I already knew how dangerous Rāma was — I’d been scared of him before — so I barely managed to escape with my life, but the other two Rākshasas weren’t so lucky. Rāma’s arrows killed them both. Rāvana, I was lucky to survive Rāma’s attack. After that, I gave up my old ways, became an ascetic, and have been practicing Yoga here ever since.

From that day on, I keep seeing Rāma everywhere — wearing tree bark and deer skin, sometimes even appearing in the trees themselves, like Death waiting with a noose. I’m so terrified that I see thousands of Rāmas all around me, as if the whole forest is filled only with him. Even when I look into empty spaces, I imagine I see Rāma. He haunts my dreams, and when I wake up, I look around in fear. Rāvana, I can’t even say words that start with “Ra,” like “Ratna” (jewel) or “Ratha” (chariot), without panicking. That’s how afraid I am of Rāma. I know exactly how powerful that descendant of Raghu is. You shouldn’t pick a fight with him — he’s strong enough to defeat Vāli and Namuchi. Rāvana, whether you fight Rāma or not, please don’t even mention his name in front of me if you want me around. Many good and devoted ascetics have been destroyed because of someone else’s crimes, and I fear I’ll end up the same way because of your actions. Do whatever you want, king of the Rākshasas, but I won’t be part of it. Rāma is truly as deadly to us as death itself. Sure, Khara of Janasthāna was killed by Rāma because of Surpanakhā’s actions, but how can you blame him for that? Be honest. You’re my friend, so I’m telling you this for your own good. If you ignore my warning, you and all your family will be killed by Rāma in battle.
SECTION XL

Just like someone who refuses medicine when they actually want to die, Rāvana, the king of the night-dwelling Rākshasas, ignored the wise and well-meaning words of Māricha, who was known for his skill with words and good advice. Instead, Rāvana snapped at him harshly. “Māricha,” he said, “everything you just told me is pointless—like planting seeds in a desert. Your warnings aren’t going to scare me away from fighting that fool Rāma—a mere human who acts recklessly. Right in front of you, I’m going to take away Rāma’s beloved wife—the same Rāma who killed Khara and who wandered into these forests, giving up his parents, his kingdom, and his friends just because of her. I’ve made up my mind, Māricha, and not even Indra, with all the gods and demons combined, could change it. Maybe your words would have made sense if I’d actually asked for your advice—if I wanted to know whether what I was doing was right or wrong, or what the risks were. But a smart advisor, if he cares about his own future, should only speak his mind when his king asks for it. There’s a right way to talk to royalty: only say what helps your king, and always follow proper manners. Even if a king hears good advice delivered rudely, he won’t like it. Kings, especially those with real power, are almost like the five main gods: Agni, Indra, the Moon, Yama, and Varuna. Kings can be proud, powerful, calm, or content, and they have to punish those who break the rules. That’s why kings deserve respect and honor at all times. But you don’t understand how kings work—you’re caught up in your own illusions, and that’s why you’ve spoken to me, your guest, in such an insulting way. I’m not asking you, Māricha, whether what I’m doing is right or whether it will turn out well. I’m just telling you what I want you to do for me. Listen closely: I need you to take the form of a deer with a golden hide, covered in silver spots, and go to Rāma’s forest hut. Run around where Sītā can see you, and once she’s entranced by the sight of you, lead her wherever you want. Sītā will be amazed by the magical golden deer, and she’ll beg Rāma to catch you for her. Once Rāma leaves the hut to chase you, you should run far away and then cry out, ‘O Sītā! O Lakshmana!’ imitating Rāma’s voice. When Lakshmana hears those cries, Sītā will send him after Rāma too. Once both Rāma and Lakshmana are out of the way, I’ll finally have the chance to take Sītā, just like Indra once stole Sachi. After that, you can go wherever you want. If you do this for me, Māricha, I’ll give you half my kingdom. So come with me to the Dandaka forest and help me pull this off—I’ll be right behind you in my chariot. With Sītā in my grasp, and without having to fight Rāma at all, we’ll both head back to Lankā as victors. But if you refuse, Māricha, I’ll kill you myself. I’m ordering you to do this. Nobody gets ahead in life by disobeying their king. Yes, approaching Rāma might cost you your life, but if you defy me, your death is certain. Think it over and decide what you’re going to do.”
SECTION XLI

After being ordered by Rāvana, who acted every bit like a king, to go against his own wishes, Māricha (Maricha) stood his ground and spoke boldly to the lord of the Rākshasas. He said, “Whoever gave you this terrible advice, Rāvana, clearly wants you and your entire kingdom—your advisors, your children—wiped out. Who could be so evil-hearted that they feel no happiness at your success? Who has shown you a path that will only lead to your own death, but disguised as a clever plan? Rāvana, it looks like your enemies are hoping you’ll destroy yourself by starting a fight with someone far stronger than you. Which petty, malicious person has given you this counsel? Honestly, it’s as if they want you to ruin yourself by your own actions. And yet, you don’t punish your advisors, even though they deserve it for not stopping you from going down this dangerous road. Good advisors always hold a king back when he’s acting out of impulse or passion, but in your case, they just don’t care, even though you should absolutely be stopped. 

Listen, Rāvana, the best kings owe their success—virtue, wealth, desires, and fame—to their ministers’ loyalty and advice. But if the king doesn’t trust or respect his advisors, none of those things are possible. In fact, when a king loses his good qualities, his people are put in danger too. The king is the foundation of virtue and honor for his subjects, and so they should always work to protect him. But arrogant kings who rule cruelly and ignore their people always fail. And ministers who give cruel advice end up destroyed, just like a chariot crashes when the driver doesn’t know what he’s doing. Many good people—always busy with rituals and religious deeds—have been destroyed along with their families, not because of their own mistakes, but because of someone else’s stupidity.

Rāvana, your people can never thrive under a hot-headed ruler who acts against them, just like deer can never feel safe under the protection of a jackal. All the Rākshasas you rule over will die because you’re reckless, cruel, and ruled by your passions. Honestly, I won’t be upset if I’m killed suddenly—but what really bothers me is that you’ll be destroyed too, along with your entire army. By killing me, Rāma will wipe you out in no time—and I’ll actually feel lucky to die in battle against such an enemy. You know as well as I do that if I face Rāma, I’ll be killed right away. But if you kidnap Sitā with my help, not one of us will survive—not me, not you, not the city of Lankā, not the Rākshasas. You ignore what I’m saying, even though I’m warning you because I care about your well-being. But people who are already close to death, whose time is almost up, never listen to good advice from friends.”
SECTION XLII

After hearing Rāvana’s harsh threats, Māricha (also Maricha) replied, his voice trembling with fear, “Fine, I’ll go with you. But if I face Rāma again—Rāma with his sword and bow—I know he’ll kill me. And if you confront his strength, you won’t survive either. He’s like the noose of Death for you, even if you think you’ve escaped it before. You’re set on this evil path—what else can I do but go along? Good luck, O lord of the night. I’ll go.” Rāvana, pleased with Māricha’s answer, hugged him tightly and said, “Now that’s true heroism, following my wishes despite your fears. You were just another Rākshasa before, but now you’re truly Māricha. Come, let’s get on my flying chariot—adorned with jewels and pulled by donkeys with demon faces. When you enchant Vaidehi (Sītā), I’ll seize the daughter of Mithilā’s king while neither Rāma nor Lakshmana are around.” Tāraka’s son, Māricha, agreed. The two of them climbed into the chariot, shining like something out of heaven, and set off toward the hermitage. As they traveled, towns, forests, mountains, rivers, kingdoms, and cities sped by beneath them until they finally reached the Dandaka forest and Rāma’s hut. Climbing down from the golden chariot together, Rāvana took Māricha’s hand and pointed. “There’s Rāma’s hut, surrounded by palm trees. Now do what we came here for.” Taking Rāvana’s words to heart, Māricha transformed himself into a stunning golden deer and started roaming in front of Rāma’s home. Its horns shone like priceless gems, its face a mix of white and black, with a red-lotus glow. Its ears were blue like lotuses, its neck arched gracefully, its belly gleamed like sapphire, its sides were as pale as Madhuka flowers, and its whole body glowed like the golden threads of a lotus. Its hooves were dark like the Baidurja gem, its legs slender but strong, and its joints firm. Its tail, rainbow-colored, waved high, sparkling with jewels, and its coat seemed to shimmer with a cool, magical light.

In just moments, Māricha had completely taken the form of a breathtaking deer. Intent on luring Vaidehi (Sītā), he made himself look even more magical, his body gleaming with metallic colors, lighting up the forest and the area near Rāma’s hut. He wandered freely over the green grass, nibbling at plants and blending in with the forest life. His coat was speckled with hundreds of silvery spots as he moved among the trees. Sometimes he strolled into the plantain grove, sometimes around the Karnikā forest, always staying just within Sītā’s sight. With his back painted gold, he wandered slowly around the hermitage, always close enough to be noticed. Sometimes he’d walk, then suddenly stop, darting away and then pausing again—a mesmerizing show. He played around, lay down in the grass, or followed groups of real deer right up to the edge of the hermitage, sometimes leading them, sometimes being followed, but always circling back to make sure Sītā could see him. He roamed through the beautiful forest, covering a wide area. When other deer came close and sniffed him, they sensed something off and quickly scattered in all directions. Even though Māricha was an expert hunter, he didn’t harm or eat any of the deer—he wanted to keep his true identity hidden. Meanwhile, Sītā—whose eyes sparkled and whose beauty was like wine—was busy picking flowers, moving between the Karnika and mango groves. Used to living in the forest and always graceful, she wandered along, her arms full of flowers, when she suddenly spotted the jeweled deer. Its body was covered in what looked like pearls and diamonds, its teeth and lips perfect, its soft fur shining silver. Sītā stared at the magical animal, her eyes wide with amazement and affection. The illusory deer, catching her gaze, began circling the area, its beauty lighting up the forest like fire. Sītā had never seen anything like it before; amazed, she couldn’t take her eyes off the dazzling, bejeweled deer.
SECTION XLIII

While picking flowers, Sitā spotted a deer with sides that shimmered gold and silver. She was so delighted by its beauty—her own skin shining like pure gold, her features flawless—that she called out excitedly for her husband Rāma and his brother Lakshmana, both carrying their curved swords. “Come quickly! Come quickly, son of my noble father-in-law, bring your brother too!” she called again and again, her eyes never leaving the deer. Hearing the princess of Videha, Rāma and Lakshmana looked around and saw the animal. But as soon as Lakshmana saw it, fear struck him, and he said,

“I’m pretty sure that deer is actually the Rākshasa Māricha in disguise. Māricha is dangerous, Rāma—he often turns into a deer to lure kings hunting in the forest, then kills them for his own amusement. He’s a master of illusions, and that’s how he looks like this. His appearance is almost unreal, as beautiful as the legendary homes of the Gandharvas, as radiant as the sun—there just aren’t jeweled deer like this in the real world. Rāma, Lord of the earth, this has to be a trick.” 

But Sitā, enchanted by the deer’s magic, just smiled and gently disagreed with Lakshmana. Still captivated, she said, “Son of my noble father-in-law, I can’t take my eyes off this deer. Please, strong one, could you catch it for me? It would be wonderful to have as a pet. We’ve seen so many beautiful deer near our hermitage—Chamara, Srimara, Rik, Prishata, Bānara, and Kinnara. They’re all impressive, but I’ve never seen anything like this one. No other deer matches its energy, strength, and beauty. Its body is covered in every color, it’s a real living jewel. Watching it move, it lights up the forest like the moon. Just look at that shine, those colors, even its gentle voice—this magical creature has totally won me over! If you could catch it alive, that would be amazing! When our exile ends and we return to our kingdom, this deer would make our palace even more beautiful. Imagine how surprised Bharata, you, me, and my mothers-in-law would be! But even if you can’t catch it alive, the skin alone would be gorgeous to have. I’d love to pray on kusa grass with the deerskin spread out. I know it seems bold and maybe even wrong for a wife to ask her husband like this, but I just can’t help myself—I’m so taken with it.”

Rāma was just as surprised by the deer—its fur shone like gold, its antlers sparkled like diamonds, its color glowed like a sunrise, and its brilliance was almost otherworldly. Fascinated by its beauty and encouraged by Sitā’s request, Rāma turned to Lakshmana and said, “Look, Lakshmana, Sitā really wants this deer. With beauty like that, it’s doomed—it won’t survive today. There’s nothing like it anywhere—not even in the gods’ gardens or the legendary Chaitraratha forest. Its fur patterns are amazing, marked with little golden spots. And when it opens its mouth, its tongue flashes out like fire, almost like lightning in a storm. Its face is as blue and clear as the finest sapphire, its belly looks like pearl and conch—its whole shape is mysterious. Who wouldn’t be mesmerized by it? Its beauty is like golden rays, mixed with every color of precious gems. Who could see such a magical creature and not be stunned, Lakshmana?

“Princes like us hunt deer in the deep woods, either for food or for sport. While exploring, we also find rare jewels and metals like gold and silver. Honestly, these natural treasures are better than any regular wealth—like how the gods enjoy their pleasures in heaven. Whatever people chase after without thinking, just to gain wealth, is what the political experts call the real definition of wealth. Vaidehi, with her slim waist, wants to sit beside me on this golden deerskin. I doubt there’s any other deerskin as soft—not from Kādali, Priaki, Prabeni, or Abiki. Really, only two deer are this beautiful—the one in the sky (Mrigashirā constellation) and this one on earth.

“And if you’re right, Lakshmana, and it’s actually a Rākshasa’s illusion, then I have to kill it. This cruel, evil Māricha has murdered many holy sages in these woods, and in this kind of disguise, he’s killed plenty of kings as well. That’s why I need to deal with him. Remember the story of Bātapi? He used to sneak into the bodies of holy men, then tear them apart from the inside, just like a mule’s unborn foal destroys its mother. But once, Bātapi tried the same trick on the great sage Agastya, who simply digested him after a ritual meal. When the ritual was done and Bātapi tried to return to his demon form, Agastya just smiled and said, ‘Blinded by your own strength, you’ve destroyed many holy men, and now I’ll digest you.’ So any Rākshasa who thinks he can outsmart someone like me—someone who’s trained, disciplined, and devoted—will meet the same fate as Bātapi. That’s why Māricha, if he comes near me, will be destroyed, just like Bātapi was by Agastya.

“So Lakshmana, while I’m gone, guard Vaidehi carefully—put on your armor and stay alert. Protect Jānaki at all costs; that’s our top priority. I’ll either kill the deer or catch it alive. Look, Lakshmana, Sitā really wants its skin, so I’m going after it now. This deerskin is definitely the finest I’ve ever seen, and the deer won’t make it through today. Until I return, stay here with Sitā and keep a close watch over her. I’ll be back soon—one arrow will be enough to bring it down and get its skin. Stay alert here with Jānaki, and let Yatāyu, wise and pious, watch over her with you.”
SECTION XLIV

After giving Lakshmana his instructions, Rama, the determined son of Raghu, armed himself with his gold-hilted sword and slung his bow, which curved elegantly and looked almost like a piece of jewelry. He also strapped on two full quivers of arrows. Ready for action, Rama set out with fierce energy. As he approached, the magical deer—actually Maricha in disguise—vanished out of fear, only to reappear again. With his bow and sword at his side, Rama chased after the deer, watching as its glowing beauty lit up the forest around it. Sometimes the deer seemed just out of arrow range, taunting Rama, while at other times it appeared close enough to lure him further. The deer, driven by fear and confusion, seemed to almost leap through the air, now visible in the trees, now gone in a flash—like the moon peeking out from behind broken clouds. Maricha, still in his magical deer form, kept leading Rama farther and farther from the hermitage, playing a game of hide-and-seek. Frustrated and exhausted by the chase, Rama finally stopped for a moment, taking shelter in the shade and resting on the grass. But Maricha, still disguised, kept drawing Rama on, appearing again in the distance, surrounded by other deer. Seeing the magical deer yet again, Rama’s determination returned and he rushed off at full speed. Each time Rama got close, the deer would vanish, only to show up again behind a tree, just out of reach. Now furious and determined to end it, Rama, with all his strength, pulled out a blazing arrow that shone like the sun. He drew his bow tight, took careful aim, and shot the powerful, glowing arrow forged by Brahma—a weapon that looked like a streak of lightning. The arrow struck Maricha, still in his deer disguise, right in the chest. With a final leap as high as a palm tree, Maricha, knowing the end had come, let out a terrifying cry and collapsed to the ground. As he lay dying, Maricha dropped his magical disguise and became his true Rakshasa (demon) self again. Remembering Ravana’s instructions, Maricha began to think.

"How can I get Sita to send Lakshmana away, so Ravana can kidnap her while she’s alone?" Wounded horribly by Rama’s arrow, Maricha let go of his deer form and turned back into his massive Rakshasa body. Seizing his last chance to help Ravana, Maricha used his dying breath to scream in Rama’s exact voice, “Ah, Sita! Ah, Lakshmana!” His cry echoed through the forest. Rama, seeing the grim-faced Rakshasa lying on the ground, covered in blood and thrashing in pain, turned back toward the hermitage, worrying about Sita and remembering Lakshmana’s earlier warnings.

"Lakshmana told me before that this was Maricha’s trick!” Rama thought. “He was right. Now I’ve killed Maricha, but he died shouting, ‘Ah, Sita! Ah, Lakshmana!’ What will Sita do when she hears that? And what will strong-armed Lakshmana do?” As these thoughts raced through his mind, Rama felt a chill run down his spine, his hair standing on end. The fear and sadness from killing the demon and hearing his awful scream weighed heavily on him. Gathering himself, Rama killed a real deer for food and hurried back toward Janasthana, anxious about what might be happening back at the hermitage.
SECTION XLV

Hearing her cries, Ravana—the king of the rakshasas—rushed at Sita. She looked lost and heartbroken, clutching a big tree as if it could help her, her flower garland wilting on her head. As she wept for Rama in the wilderness, she kept calling his name.

Still shouting “Rama!” Sita was grabbed by Ravana, who looked as menacing as death itself, determined to carry out his plan even if it meant his own doom. As Ravana yanked Sita by the hair, the whole world seemed to darken. Everything—moving and unmoving—felt changed. A thick shadow covered everything; the wind stopped blowing, and the sun went dim. Far away, the god Brahma (the Great-father) saw with his divine vision that Sita had been captured and said, “It’s done—our goal is set in motion.” The great sages living in the Dandaka forest saw this too. They realized that Ravana’s destruction was now inevitable, but felt both joy and sadness at the same time. Meanwhile, Sita kept crying “Rama! Lakshmana!” as Ravana, lord of the rakshasas, flew off into the sky with her.

Sita, the king’s daughter, glowed like molten gold in her yellow silk dress. Even in her terror, she looked striking—like a flash of lightning. Her yellow sari billowed in the wind, making Ravana look almost regal, like a dark mountain set on fire. As Ravana carried her, flower petals from Sita’s hair—fragrant and coppery—fell and scattered all around him. Her golden scarf fluttered in the sky, looking like clouds colored by the setting sun. But Sita’s beautiful face, resting on Ravana’s lap as they flew, looked pale and sad without Rama—like a lotus without its stem, or a moon rising through dark clouds.

In the sky, her face—framed by her soft hair and perfect forehead, glowing like a lotus, with shining teeth and lovely eyes—should have looked enchanting, but tears and fear had dulled her beauty. Without Rama, even her golden radiance seemed faded—like the moon shining during the day, out of place and pale. Sita, Mithila’s golden daughter, beside Ravana’s dark form, looked like a bright sash around a black elephant. Dressed in shining ornaments, Sita in Ravana’s arms was like lightning wrapped in storm clouds. Her jewelry made soft sounds in the wind, making Ravana seem like a rumbling thundercloud.

As Ravana carried her away, flowers fell from Sita’s hair and rained down to earth, but the wind swept them back up to swirl around Ravana. The shower of petals around him looked like stars circling a towering mountain. As Sita struggled, her gem-studded anklets slipped off and fell, flashing like bolts of lightning. Her skin, glowing like new leaves, made Ravana’s darkness stand out even more—like gold draped over an elephant. Ravana, younger brother of Kubera (Vaisravana), sped away with Sita, who shone in the sky like a blazing meteor.

Her fiery jewelry began falling to earth with a jingling sound, like stars losing their light and dropping from the sky. The moon-shaped necklace slipped from her chest and fell, glittering like the Ganga river pouring down from the heavens. Trees swayed in the strong winds stirred by Ravana’s flight, their branches waving as if to reassure Sita, “Don’t be afraid.” The ponds below, their lotuses wilted and fish disturbed, seemed to mourn for Sita as if she were their friend. Wild animals—lions, tigers, and birds—chased her shadow angrily as she passed overhead. The mountains, their waterfalls like tears and their peaks like raised arms, seemed to be crying for her too.

Even the sun looked dim and sad as he watched Sita being carried away, his rays dulled and his face shadowed. All living things mourned: “What happened to justice and truth? Where is kindness, if Ravana can just take Rama’s Sita like this?” The young deer wept, their faces full of sorrow. Forest spirits trembled, their eyes wide with fear. Carrying Sita away for his own ruin, Ravana fled through the sky while Sita, sobbing and afraid, called out again and again for Lakshmana and Rama, glancing down at the ground with her hair loose and her tilak smeared away. Overwhelmed by terror and heartbreak, Sita, once so radiant, now looked pale and lost—cut off from her husband and friends, her face drained of color.
SECTION LIII

As she saw him lift into the sky, Janaka’s daughter, Maithili (Sitā), was overtaken by fear and panic. Her eyes burned with anger, mixed with tears and terror, as Sitā, weeping helplessly while being carried away, spoke to the grim-eyed king of the Rākshasas: “Don’t you feel any shame, Rāvana, for what you’re doing? You waited until I was alone and now you’re running away with me like a coward. You used tricks and illusions—like that magical deer—to lure my husband away, just so you could kidnap me. And you killed the old king of vultures, Jatāyu, who tried to save me—he was a dear friend to my father-in-law. That’s your idea of strength? You only managed to take me because you announced your name, not because you faced me or my husband in a real fight. Don’t you feel disgusted with yourself, stealing another man’s wife when her husband isn’t there to protect her? Everyone will talk about how low you’ve sunk, how wrong and shameful this act is. So much for your supposed honor and truth—you’ve stained your own family’s name with this crime.

“But what can I do while you’re speeding away with me? If you’d just stop for a second, you wouldn’t survive—my husband and his brother would destroy you. Even if you had an entire army with you, you wouldn’t last a moment if Rāma and Lakshmana saw you. You’re like a bird flying into a raging forest fire—you can’t withstand their arrows. If you care at all about your own life, Rāvana, let me go now. If you don’t, my husband and his brother will hunt you down. You think you can enjoy yourself by kidnapping me, but this plan of yours is doomed to fail. I can’t bear to live long, trapped by my enemy and separated from Rāma, who is like a god to me.

“You can’t even see what’s good for you, just like a dying person who can’t taste what would help them. I see you already caught by Death’s noose. You’re not even afraid, even though you should be terrified. Soon, you’ll find yourself facing horrors: the golden trees of the underworld, the dreadful Vaitarani river flowing with blood, the terrible forest with sword-shaped leaves, and the sharp Silk Cotton tree with golden flowers and iron thorns. You, shameless as someone who’s drunk poison, won’t escape the consequences of what you’ve done to Rāma. Death has you in its grip, and there’s nowhere you can run for safety after this.

“Do you really think Rāma—the strong, heroic master of every weapon, who once killed fourteen thousand Rākshasas by himself—will let you get away with stealing his wife?” So, as Rāvana flew with her in his arms, Sitā, the daughter of Videha, poured out her grief and fear in desperate, angry words. And Rāvana, trembling with anxiety, carried her away—while Sitā, deeply distressed, kept struggling and crying for help, trying everything she could to free herself.
SECTION LIV

As Rāvana carried Sītā (also called Vaidehi) away, she realized no one was coming to save her. Desperate, she spotted five important monkeys standing on top of a hill. Hoping they might tell Rāma what happened, she threw her gold-colored silk scarf and her beautiful jewelry down toward them. But Rāvana, in his rush, didn’t notice her tossing away the scarf and ornaments. The monkeys, with their intense, tawny eyes, watched Sītā—her large eyes full of tears—as she was overcome by grief. Meanwhile, the lord of the Rākshasas (demons), having crossed the river Pampā, headed straight for the city of Lankā, carrying Sītā with him while she cried out in sorrow. Rāvana, thrilled by his success, held Sītā on his lap like a venomous serpent clutching its prey. He moved through the sky as fast as an arrow shot from a bow, leaving behind forests, rivers, mountains, and lakes. When he reached the ocean—the endless home of Varuna, filled with whales and alligators—he crossed over it. Because of Sītā’s abduction, even the ocean seemed to freeze in shock, its waves stilled and its creatures unmoving. In the sky, the heavenly beings called Chāranas cried out, "O Ten-headed one, this will be your end!" The Siddhas echoed this warning.

Still holding Sītā, who desperately tried to escape, Rāvana entered Lankā. The city was huge, its streets neatly arranged and its gates crowded with people. He went straight to his private chambers and placed Sītā—her eyes dark at the corners and her face marked by sorrow—there, as if the demon Maya had placed his own illusion in the palace. Then Rāvana spoke to some of his terrifying female attendants. "No man or woman is to see Sītā without my permission. If she asks for pearls, rubies, gold, clothes, or ornaments, make sure she gets them. Anyone who says anything unkind to her, whether on purpose or by accident, will pay with her life." After giving these strict orders to the demonesses, Rāvana, the powerful lord of the Rākshasas, left the inner chambers, thinking about what to do next.

He soon found eight fierce, flesh-eating Rākshasas known for their strength. Seeing them, Rāvana—drunk on his magical powers—praised their might and bravery, and then commanded, "Arm yourselves with every weapon you can. Go immediately to Janasthāna, that bloody battlefield where Khara once lived. Even though all the Rākshasas there were killed by Rāma, you must stay there without fear. Many powerful troops, along with Dushana and Khara, were wiped out by Rāma’s arrows. That’s why my anger against Rāma is so great now—I can barely control myself. I want revenge on my powerful enemy. I can’t sleep until I destroy him in battle. Once I kill the one who killed Khara and Dushana—Rāma—I’ll feel the joy of a poor man who suddenly becomes rich. Stay in Janasthāna and keep close watch on Rāma. Find out what he’s up to. Do whatever it takes to kill Rāma, you night-stalkers. I know your strength from many battles, and that’s why I’m sending you to Janasthāna." Hearing Rāvana’s orders, the Rākshasas bowed to him and left Lankā, traveling invisibly as a group toward Janasthāna.

Now that he had Sītā in his house, Rāvana felt triumphant. Even though he’d made a powerful enemy of Rāma, Rāvana—blinded by arrogance—rejoiced at what he’d done.
SECTION LV

After sending off those eight fierce and powerful Rākshasas, Rāvana—blinded by his own arrogance—believed he had already succeeded. Tormented by his obsession with Vaidehi (another name for Sītā), and overwhelmed with desire, he hurried into his lavish palace, determined to see her. Entering the room, Rāvana, the king of the Rākshasas (demons), saw Sītā sitting there in misery, surrounded by demon women. Her face was streaked with tears and heavy with grief, like a boat battered by a storm and about to sink, or a young deer separated from its herd and trapped by hounds. Sītā sat there hopeless, head bowed low in sorrow. Rāvana, the lord of the night, tried to impress her by showing off his palace, which looked almost divine—filled with grand buildings, crowded with hundreds of women, alive with birds of all kinds, and decorated with gems. The halls were supported by pillars of ivory, gold, crystal, and silver, all sparkling with diamonds and lapis lazuli. With Sītā, Rāvana climbed up the beautiful golden staircase, which echoed with the sound of drums and was covered in golden decorations. The tall buildings had windows made of ivory and silver, covered by golden grilles. The floors glittered with gems and even drops of ambrosia. Rāvana showed Sītā massive pools and gardens full of flowers, all within his palace. He showed her everything, even though she was still lost in grief.

After showing Sītā this magnificent mansion, Rāvana—clearly trying to tempt her—began his pitch: “Sītā, except for old men and children, I rule thirty-two crores of terrifying night-dwelling Rākshasas. Whenever I need anything, a thousand of them will come running to serve me. With all this power, my entire life is tied up in you. You’re more precious to me than my own life. Be the queen among all these extraordinary women—be my wife, Sītā. It’s the best choice for you, so why fight it? Listen to me, please. Open your heart to me. I’m burning for you. This city of Lanka is a hundred yojanas wide, surrounded by ocean—untouchable even by the gods and Indra himself. No god, Yaksha, Gandharva, or serpent can match my strength. What do you see in Rāma? He’s just a mortal, short-lived, poor, weak, wandering around like a beggar. Sītā, choose me—I’m the right husband for you. Life is short, and youth fades quickly—enjoy it with me now. Don’t waste your beauty waiting for Rāma. Honestly, what could he possibly do? He can’t even dream of getting here. No one can catch the wind or hold fire in their hands—just like no one could take you away from me while I’m guarding you. Rule this great kingdom of Lanka with me. Every being—gods, mortals, and everything in between—will serve you. Cleanse yourself, and let’s be together. Whatever wrong you did by living in the forest, you’ve already paid for. Now, enjoy your good fortune. Here are garlands with divine perfumes, and gorgeous jewelry. Enjoy them with me, Sītā. The Pushpaka chariot, which shines like the sun and once belonged to my brother Vaiśravaṇa, is mine now—I won it in battle. It’s vast, beautiful, and moves as fast as thought. Come, ride on it with me whenever you want. Your beautiful face, as lovely as a lotus, is dulled by all this sadness. Don’t waste your beauty on grief.”

When Rāvana finished, Sītā pulled her sari up to hide her moon-bright face and began to cry softly. Seeing her so heartbroken and lost in thought, Rāvana tried again: “Sītā, don’t let shyness stop you from doing what’s right. My longing for you is natural—it’s what the wise say is proper. I’d press your delicate feet to my ten heads if you’d let me. Please, say yes. I’ll be your servant—always loyal to you. Don’t ignore my words, spoken out of love. I’ve never bowed to any woman before.” After saying all this, Rāvana—completely under the sway of fate—looked at Sītā, Janaka’s daughter, and told himself, “She’s mine.”
SECTION LVI

Despite her deep grief, Sita (Vaidehi) wasn’t afraid when she answered Ravana. She placed a single blade of grass on the ground between them—a silent gesture of contempt—and replied, “There was once a king named Dasharatha, a true pillar of righteousness, whose name was respected everywhere. His son is Rama (Raghava), my husband—known for his virtue throughout the three worlds. He’s strong, broad-shouldered like a lion, with striking eyes, almost godlike in his looks. Rama was born in the Ikshwaku dynasty, and his light shines bright. He and his brother, Lakshmana, will be your end. If you had tried to kidnap me in front of him, you’d already be dead—just like Khara was in Janasthana.”  

“All the powerful Rakshasas you brag about would lose their strength before Rama, just like snakes lose their poison in front of Garuda. The golden-tipped arrows Rama fires will tear through their bodies like the Ganga’s waves batter its banks. Ravana, even if gods or demons can’t kill you, once you make Rama your enemy, you won’t escape with your life. Rama will end your days, the way an animal can’t escape once it’s tied to the sacrificial post. If Rama ever looks at you in anger, you’ll be destroyed—just as Manmatha was by Rudra. The only person who could stop Rama from rescuing me would be someone who could pull down the moon or drink the ocean dry. Your time is running out. Good fortune has left you. You’re weak now, and your mind is clouded. Because of you, Lanka will soon mourn for its lost men. Kidnapping me from my husband was a terrible crime, and it will never bring you happiness.  

“My radiant husband and his younger brother are both alive and determined—they’re living bravely in the empty Dandaka forest, gathering their strength. In battle, Rama’s arrows will strip you of your power and pride, and wipe away your evil. When fate decides it’s time for someone to be destroyed, they start acting recklessly, as if controlled by the Destroyer himself. By kidnapping me, you’ve set your own end in motion, as well as the end of all the Rakshasas and everyone close to you.  

“A criminal can’t stand on the altar at a sacred ritual blessed by priests—and just like that, I, a faithful wife devoted to virtue and my vows, can never be touched by the likes of you, Ravana, the vilest Rakshasa. How could a woman who’s always been loyal to her husband, who’s played among lotuses, even look at a wild beast hiding among reeds? You can imprison or even kill this body if you want. I don’t care about protecting it or even my life—because I won’t do anything that would bring shame on myself in this world.”  

After delivering these harsh words in anger, Sita (Janaki, daughter of Videha) fell silent and refused to speak to Ravana again.  

Ravana, stung by Sita’s fierce and chilling words, replied in a voice that would terrify anyone: “Listen to me, Maithili. If, by the time I set, you haven’t agreed to be mine, my cooks will cut you into pieces for my breakfast.”  

After his threat, Ravana—furious and losing control—turned to the demonesses (Rakshasis) and ordered, “You terrifying Rakshasis, who feed on flesh and blood, break her spirit right now!”  

Immediately, the hideous Rakshasis gathered around Sita with their hands pressed together in obedience.  

Then Ravana, with a look that seemed to shake the earth, strode a few steps and commanded, “Take Sita to the Ashoka grove. Keep her surrounded and guard her in secret. Try to break her will—sometimes by threatening her, sometimes by speaking softly. Do whatever you must to make her obey, like taming a wild elephant.”  

Following Ravana’s command, the Rakshasis led Sita to the Ashoka grove—a magical place filled with wish-granting trees, flowers, fruits, and birds all year round. Like a helpless deer surrounded by tigresses, Sita (Maithili, daughter of Janaka) was overcome by grief and powerless before the Rakshasis.  

Trapped like a frightened fawn in a snare, Sita was devastated by sorrow and found no peace. The Rakshasis glared at her with fierce, angry eyes, and Sita, overwhelmed by grief and fear, could only think of Rama and Lakshmana—until she finally fainted from despair.
SECTION LVI

After killing the demon Māricha—who could change his form at will and had been disguised as a deer—Rāma quickly made his way back along the path. Meanwhile, as Sitā entered Lankā, the great creator (Brahmā) spoke to Devendra (Indra), the king of the gods who had performed a hundred sacrifices. “For the good of all three worlds, and to bring disaster upon the Rākshasas, Sitā has been taken to Lankā by the evil Rāvana. Sitā, devoted to her husband and raised in comfort, is now surrounded by Rākshasi women and longing desperately to see Rāma. Lankā is located on the shore of the great ocean. How can Rāma ever learn where Sitā is, while she remains hidden there? She’s suffering after all she’s been through, and there’s a real risk she might give up hope. I’m deeply worried that Sitā might choose to end her life. You must go there yourself, find Sitā, and offer her this pure ghee as a blessing.” 

Indra, addressed like this by the wise Brahmā, set out for Lankā, taking the goddess of sleep (Nidra) with him. He told Sleep, “Go and put all the Rākshasas into a deep slumber.” Happy to help the gods, Nidra gladly cast a spell of sleep over the Rākshasas, making them all fall unconscious. While this was happening, Indra, the thousand-eyed king of the gods, found Sitā in the woods where she was kept prisoner, and spoke to her: “I am Indra, lord of the gods. Good fortune to you, Sitā of the shining smile! I’m here to help Rāma succeed in his quest. Don’t grieve, daughter of Janaka. By my grace, Rāma and his allies will cross the ocean and reach you. I’ve used my divine power to put the Rākshasis to sleep. That’s why I’ve come here with Sleep herself, bringing you this rice cooked in ghee. If you eat this food from my hand, you won’t feel hunger or thirst for years, no matter what happens.”

Hearing this, Sitā was scared and said, “How do I know you’re really Indra, king of the gods and husband of Sachi, and not some trick? When I was with Rāma and Lakshmana, I saw the signs that set the gods apart. If you truly are Indra, show me those signs right now.”

Indra understood, and revealed his divine traits: he floated above the ground without touching it, his eyes never blinked, he glowed with youthful energy, and the flowers he wore never wilted. Seeing this, Sitā realized he was truly Indra and felt relief. In tears, she spoke of Rāma: “I’m so lucky to hear news of my strong husband and his brother. Just like my father-in-law, the king, and the ruler of Mithilā, you are also a protector to me today. Thanks to you, my husband is not alone. By your command, Indra, I will eat this sweet rice cooked with milk, which you offer, and may it bring prosperity to our family line.”

Sitā took the sweet rice from Indra’s hands. In her heart, she offered it first to her husband Rāma and to Lakshmana: “If my powerful husband and his brother are alive, then let this food, offered with my love and respect, be for them too.” She then ate the sweet rice herself. After eating, her hunger and sorrow faded away; she also received courage and hope from Indra’s blessing, and grew more hopeful about Rāma and his family (the Kakutsthas). Indra, pleased to help Rāma’s mission succeed, returned to the realm of the gods, bidding Sitā farewell again and again. With Sleep beside him, he went back to his own heavenly home.
SECTION LVII

After killing the Rākshasa, Māricha, who could change his form at will, took the shape of a deer and ran off, while Rāma hurried back toward his home. As Rāma rushed, eager to see Sītā (Maithili), he suddenly heard jackals howling ominously behind him. Their cries were harsh and chilling, making him uneasy and fearful. “This can’t be good,” Rāma thought. “Jackals howling like this is a bad sign. I hope Vaidehi is safe and hasn’t fallen prey to the Rākshasas.” He worried that Lakshmana might have heard the fake cries that Māricha—using Rāma’s own voice—had made while pretending to be a deer. “If Saumitri (Lakshmana) heard that, he probably left Sītā on her own, since she would have insisted he help me. That would leave Sītā an easy target for the Rākshasas, who must all want to harm her. Māricha tricked me by becoming a golden deer, lured me far away, and then showed his true form as a Rākshasa when I shot him. He even cried out, ‘Lakshmana, I’ve been killed!’ using my voice. Now, with both of us gone, who knows what’s happening to Sītā? My actions in Janasthāna have made many Rākshasas my enemies, and all these bad omens around me only make things worse.” Thinking this as he listened to the jackals, Rāma hurried back to the hermitage, deeply worried after being lured away by the Rākshasa in the deer's form.

As Rāma made his way back to Janasthāna, animals and birds approached him, and their strange, alarming cries only deepened his sense of dread. Some of them gathered on his left side and shrieked, which, according to tradition, was another bad omen. While Rāma was still noticing all these frightening signs, he finally saw Lakshmana approaching, looking pale and troubled. Lakshmana came up to Rāma, and seeing his brother’s sad face only made Rāma’s own anxiety worse. Realizing that Lakshmana had left Sītā alone in the dangerous forest, Rāma began to scold him.

Grabbing Lakshmana’s left hand, Rāma—overwhelmed with worry—spoke to him in a gentle but urgent tone: “Lakshmana, you shouldn’t have done this. You left Sītā alone and came here. Is she alright? I fear the worst, that the Rākshasas in the forest might have killed or carried her off. With all these terrible omens, I’m scared we might never see her alive again. The howling of these animals and jackals from the south is especially terrifying, and I don’t know if Sītā is safe. The Rākshasa who tricked me by pretending to be a deer is dead, but it took everything I had to kill him, and he turned back into a monster just before dying. Still, I can’t shake this awful feeling—my heart is heavy and even my left eye keeps twitching, which is another bad sign. Lakshmana, I’m afraid Sītā is gone—maybe taken, maybe dead, or maybe lost and wandering somewhere in the forest.”
SECTION LVIII

When Lakshmana came back looking upset and without Sita, Rama immediately asked him, “Lakshmana, where is Sita? She followed me all the way to the Dandaka forest, and now you return without her. Where is she, the one who’s always stood by me through every hardship, especially now that I’ve lost my kingdom and spend my days wandering the Dandakas? I can’t survive a moment without her—where is Sita, my lifeline, who is as radiant as a celestial’s daughter? Lakshmana, without Janaka’s daughter, who shines like molten gold, I don’t care about ruling the gods or the earth. Is Sita still alive—she means more to me than my own life. Has this exile all been for nothing if she’s gone? Tell me, son of Sumitra: if I die searching for Sita and you return to the city, will Kaikeyi finally get everything she wanted, celebrating her victory? Will my mother Kausalya, grieving my death, be reduced to begging from Kaikeyi after she’s secured the throne for her own son? If Sita is still alive, I’ll return to our hermitage; but if that noble woman is dead, I’ll give up my own life too. If I reach the hermitage and Sita, always smiling before she speaks, doesn’t greet me, I don’t want to go on living. Lakshmana, just tell me: is Sita alive, or through some mistake on your part, has she been left behind and attacked by Rakshasas? She’s so delicate, just a young woman, and she’s never known real pain—she must be heartbroken and crying because I’m not there. When that terrible Rakshasa screamed your name, ‘Lakshmana,’ were you scared? I’m afraid Sita heard that voice, which probably sounded like mine, and sent you to me in fear. You acted recklessly leaving Sita alone in the forest. By doing that, you gave the cruel Rakshasas the perfect chance to take revenge on me. The Rakshasas, who live off of flesh, are furious over Khara’s death; now, for sure, those monsters have killed Sita. I’m completely lost, Lakshmana—what am I supposed to do now? I feel like this was my fate all along.” Thinking of Sita, the best among women, Rama hurried toward Janasthana with Lakshmana. Angry at his younger brother, who looked miserable, Rama, weak with hunger and thirst and pale with worry, let out heavy sighs as they entered the hermitage—only to find it empty. Going inside, Rama searched Sita’s favorite places, remembering the spots where she used to play. Standing there, grief overwhelmed him and his hair stood on end.
SECTION LIX

As Rāma (sometimes called Raghu’s descendant) walked out of the hermitage, he was silent for a while, weighed down by grief. Then, turning to Lakshmana (the son of Sumitrā), he said, “Lakshmana, I trusted you to look after Sītā (Maithili) when I left her with you in the forest. So why did you leave her alone? When I saw you coming toward me, without Sītā, I felt something was terribly wrong. My left eye and arm started twitching, and my heart has been pounding ever since I saw you coming without her.” Hearing these words, Lakshmana—who was known for his good fortune—felt deep sorrow and replied to the distressed Rāma, “I didn’t leave Sītā on my own. She practically forced me to come to you, and she was really harsh about it. She heard someone shouting, ‘Lakshmana, help me!’—it sounded like you, calling for help. Because of her love for you, she panicked, started crying, and begged me to go help you. She kept insisting, ‘Go! Go!’”

“I tried to reassure her,” Lakshmana continued. “‘I don’t see any demon (Rākshasa) who could scare your husband. Calm down. Those cries aren’t from Rāma, they must be from someone else. There’s no way Rāma, who could save even the gods themselves, would shout something so desperate and shameful as “Save me!” Some demon must be imitating his voice for some reason, calling out, “Lakshmana, help me!” Don’t worry, Sītā. No one in the three worlds—nothing living or yet to be born—could ever defeat Rāma in battle. Not even the gods led by Indra could beat him.’ But Sītā was completely overwhelmed. She started crying and said these harsh words to me: ‘You must be hoping that if Rāma dies, you’ll get me—but that will never happen. You’re not going to help him even though he’s calling for you, so maybe you’re following Rāma just like Bharata suggested. Maybe you’re a hidden enemy, watching Rāma for weaknesses, and that’s why you won’t go help him?’ Hearing this, I got so angry—my eyes turned red and my lip started to swell. I stormed out of the hermitage.”

When Lakshmana (also called Saumitri) finished, Rāma, overwhelmed by grief, said, “Lakshmana, you made a big mistake by leaving Sītā alone. You knew I could handle any demon, but you still left the hermitage just because Sītā spoke harshly to you. I’m not happy with you for letting her words, said in anger, drive you away from your duty. You didn’t follow my instructions just because Sītā pressured you and made you mad. As Rāma walked on, his legs started to give out, his left eye twitched, and his whole body began to shake. Sensing these bad omens, he kept asking Lakshmana, "Is Sitā okay?"
