Just look, Lakshmana, at the trees dropping flowers like rain—flowers scattered all over the rocks by the wind.”

“The breeze plays with these fallen petals, and bees, humming, chase after the wind as it moves through the flowering branches. As the wind rushes from the mountains, it seems to make the trees dance and the cuckoos sing even more. When the wind blows, the tree-tops knock together as if they’re strung on an invisible thread. The cool, fragrant breeze eases exhaustion and is everywhere, carrying the scent of flowers. The buzzing of bees makes the forest feel alive. There are hills covered with bright, flowering trees, and the trees themselves sway and seem to dance, surrounded by bees.”

“Everywhere you look, Karnikara trees are covered in gold flowers, almost like people dressed up in yellow clothes and golden jewelry. This season, with the birds singing, is just making my loneliness worse. Cupid’s arrows hurt even more now, and the happy cuckoos just remind me of what I’ve lost. The Dātyuha birds at the springs are singing so joyfully, but their songs only increase my pain. Sita used to love listening to the birds when we lived in the forest—she’d always tell me to enjoy the sound with her.”

“See, Saumitri, birds of all colors are landing on the trees and vines, singing from every direction. The birds and bees, so happy with their partners, hang out by the lake, joined by flocks of vultures. The trees are alive with the seductive calls of Datyuhas and Punskokilas, which only stirs my longing more. It’s like spring itself is a fire: the Ashoka tree flowers are its burning coals, buzzing bees its crackling sound, and the red tips on branches its flames. Saumitri, what’s the point of living if I can’t see Sita, with her soft voice, long eyelashes, and curly hair?”

“Oh, Lakshmana, this season—when the woods are beautiful and the air is filled with cuckoo songs—was always Sita’s favorite. Now, because she’s gone, my pain feels like it’s going to consume me. My desire grows more intense every moment I don’t see her, especially with all these beautiful trees around. Her absence and this spring breeze, which used to dry my sweat, just make my longing worse. Sita, with her gentle eyes, and this merciless spring wind are both tormenting me.”

“Peacocks and peahens are dancing everywhere, their feathers shining like crystal. The male peacocks, surrounded by their mates, make my heart ache with longing. Look, Lakshmana, that peahen is dancing with her partner on the mountainside, lost in passion. The peacock fans his feathers and follows his mate, almost mocking me with his cry. The demon (Rakshasa) who stole Sita didn’t bring her here—so the birds are free to dance with their loved ones. I can’t bear to live without Sita, especially during this season of flowers. Even animals feel love—the peahen goes to her mate just as Sita would have come to me, if only she hadn’t been abducted.”

“Now, the flowers of spring mean nothing to me—they fall to the ground with the bees, useless. The birds sing to each other, excited and happy, while I can only imagine Sita, wherever she is, feeling the same pain if spring has reached her too. Even if it hasn’t, how could Sita, with eyes like blooming lotuses, survive being apart from me? If spring is there, what can it do to her—she’s already a prisoner of a powerful enemy. I’m afraid my delicate, loyal wife will give up her life when spring arrives. I know for sure that Sita can’t survive this separation—her love for me is as deep as mine for her. This cool, fragrant breeze, which used to make me happy, now feels like a burning brand because I can only think of her. What once brought me pleasure is now just pain.”

“That bird cried out in the sky when Sita was taken, and now it’s singing happily in the tree. The same bird that saw her kidnapped might lead me to her. Listen, Lakshmana, to the wild cries of the birds on the flowering trees, their songs driving me mad. Bees are drawn to the tilaka trees, tossed by the wind like drunken girls. The Ashoka tree, its flowers swaying, seems to taunt me, stirring up my desire even more. See those mango trees, Lakshmana? They look like people painted with sandalwood paste, lost in passion.”

“Look, Saumitri, even the kinnaras (mythical beings) are wandering the forest by the banks of Pampa. The red lotuses shine like the rising sun, and the lake is full of blue lotuses, swans, and Karandhaba birds. The red lotuses are as bright as sunlight, their filaments crushed by the bees. The woods around the lake are beautiful, filled with chakrabaka birds and herds of elephants and deer coming to drink. Look at the lotuses swaying on the water, pushed by the wind. None of this matters to me if I can’t see Sita, her eyes wide as lotus petals and her love for lotuses unending.”

“How cruel is love, Lakshmana—it tortures me by constantly showing me visions of Sita, who now feels impossibly far away. If it weren’t for the overwhelming beauty of spring, I might be able to handle my pain. Everything that used to be beautiful when Sita was with me now seems empty. My eyes search for lotus petals because they remind me of her eyes. The gentle breeze, brushing the flowers, feels like Sita’s breath. Look at the golden karnikara flowers on the mountaintop, Lakshmana! The mountain shines with colored dust, and the slopes burn with the bright, leafless kinsuka trees.”

“All these fragrant flowers—malati, mallika, karavi, lotuses, ketaki, sindhubara, basanti, matulinga, purna, kunda, chiribili, maduka, banjula, vakula, champaka, tilaka, naga, padmyaka, blue ashoka, ankola, kuranta, churnaka, paribhadra, and yellow lodhra—cover the hills like a lion’s mane. The hills are also bright with chuta, patala, kobidara, muchukunda, arjuna, ketaka, uddalaka, sirisa, singsapa, dhaba, salmali, kingsuka, rakta, kurava, tinisa, naktamala, sandalwood, syandana, hintala, tilaka, and naga trees, all blooming. Look at the creepers, Lakshmana, winding around the trees, their flowery tips tossed by the breeze—like drunken women embracing their lovers. The wind, full of different scents, moves from tree to tree and mountain to mountain. Some trees are covered in flowers, some in buds, and the bees jump from one to another, loving every blossom.”

“This whole forest is strewn with flowers, like a soft sheet spread on the ground. The flower-filled hills look like beds, and everywhere you look, new blossoms are opening as winter ends. The trees seem to compete, blooming even brighter in this season. The bees hum around the branches, and the trees greet each other with flowers. Even the swans in Pampa’s clear water swim together with their mates, making my longing worse. This lake is as beautiful as Mandakini itself—famous across the world. Lakshmana, I don’t care about ruling Ayodhya or having the power of Indra if only I could find Sita here and live with her in this beautiful forest. I’d give up every other desire just to be with her.”

“But now, these trees, dressed in blossoms, only remind me of what I’ve lost. Look at Pampa, Saumitri—its cool water is surrounded by lotuses and filled with birds and deer. The birds singing only remind me of Sita’s sweet face and eyes, so much like lotus petals. On the mountain, deer run and play, but I’m left behind, abandoned by Vaidehi (another name for Sita), whose eyes are like an antelope’s. Watching the deer wander only makes my heart ache more. I’ll only be at peace if I can see Sita on these beautiful hills, full of birds and deer. I’ll only breathe easy again if I can sit with her, feeling the gentle, lotus-scented breeze of Pampa that chases away all sorrow.”

“Lakshmana, how is my beautiful wife, the perfect daughter of Janaka, living under someone else’s control, away from me? What will I say to King Janaka when he asks about Sita? Where is she now, the one who followed me into the forest when I lost my kingdom? How can I survive without her, having lost everything? My heart is breaking without her sweet, spotless face, her eyes like lotuses, her gentle scent.”

“When will I hear Sita’s voice again, Lakshmana—her sweet, elegant words always brightened by her smile? Even when we suffered in the forest, she’d welcome me with love, trying to cheer us both up. What will I tell Kausalya in Ayodhya if she asks about her amazing daughter-in-law? Please, Lakshmana, go to Bharata—he’s a good brother. I can’t go on without Sita.”

At that, Lakshmana answered Rama, who was drowning in grief, with calm and wise words: “Don’t give in to your sorrow, Rama. You’re a great man—don’t let despair take over. Even the best people can lose their way when they’re heartbroken, but you must let go of your attachment. Remember, when a lamp has too much oil, even the wick burns out. No matter where he hides—even in the underworld—Ravana won’t escape me. We’ll find out where that evil Rakshasa is. Either he’ll give Sita back or he’ll be destroyed. I’ll kill him, even if he hides her inside the earth itself. Please, control yourself and don’t lose hope. Nothing is achieved without real effort, and energy is the greatest force in the world. With enough determination, nothing is impossible. People with true spirit never give up, and that’s how we’ll get Sita back. Don’t forget, you’re wise and strong. Let go of your grief and focus on what we have to do.”

Hearing Lakshmana’s words, Rama slowly regained his composure, letting go of his worst sorrow. Together, they walked along the beautiful banks of Pampa, the trees around them shaken by the breeze.

So Rama, still mourning, walked on, looking at the forests, waterfalls, and caves, thinking over what Lakshmana had said. Lakshmana, steady and focused on Rama’s well-being, tried to cheer him up with wise and encouraging advice, moving through the woods like a determined elephant. 

Meanwhile, near Mount Rishyamuka, the chief of the monkeys, Sugriva, caught sight of Rama and Lakshmana. Their unusual appearance made Sugriva freeze in fear; he stopped moving, terrified. Other monkeys, seeing the powerful Rama and Lakshmana, were also scared and rushed into their safe, holy retreat—a place they always used for shelter—deep inside the woods.
SECTION II

Seeing the two brothers, Rāma and Lakshmana, both strong and carrying huge scimitars, Sugriva felt a wave of fear wash over him. The great monkey king couldn't calm himself. He looked around nervously, unable to stand still anywhere. Just the sight of Rāma and Lakshmana, with their obvious strength, made his heart sink. Sugriva, always thoughtful, became deeply anxious, not just for himself but for his whole band of monkeys. He turned to his counselors and said, “I’m sure these two warriors, dressed in disguise and wearing tree bark, have been sent here by Vāli. They must have crossed the whole forest to find us.” Sugriva’s counselors, seeing the two powerful archers, quickly left that mountain area and moved to another, safer hill. Soon, the leaders of all the monkey groups rushed to surround Sugriva, their king, and their main chiefs. The monkeys, sharing their leader’s worry, jumped from one hill to another, moving so fast they shook the mountain tops. In their rush, they broke branches and flowers from the trees covering their hiding place. These monkeys, the best among their kind, leapt all over the hills, scaring away deer, wildcats, and tigers as they went. When they finally stopped on the best hilltop, Sugriva’s ministers gathered in front of him, clapping their hands to get his attention. Then Hanumān, who was wise and a great speaker, spoke up to Sugriva, who was clearly shaken and worried about Vāli’s tricks. “Everyone should stop being afraid of Vāli,” Hanumān said. “Here on Mount Malaya, we’re safe from him. I don’t see Vāli, that wicked one with the scary face, anywhere nearby—he’s the one you keep running from, but there’s no sign of him here. Honestly, you’re letting your monkey instincts get the best of you. You need to calm down and think things through. As a king, you should act with intelligence, not panic. If a king loses his head, he can’t lead his people.” After listening to Hanumān’s smart advice, Sugriva replied, his voice a little steadier, “Who wouldn’t be scared seeing those two heroes? They have strong arms, huge bows, and deadly blades, and their eyes are sharp and watchful—like sons of the gods. I really think Vāli sent them. Kings have a lot of friends, and I can’t trust strangers so easily. Enemies can pretend to be friends, wear disguises, and trick you when you least expect it. Vāli is a master at these kinds of schemes. Rulers know all sorts of ways to destroy their rivals, so it’s smart to check them out with spies in disguise. Hanumān, I want you to approach them undercover. Watch their faces, listen to what they say, and figure out what they really want. If they seem friendly, try to win their trust for me—praise me a little and explain my side. If you think they’re good people, ask them directly why they’ve come into this forest. Pay close attention to how they act and what they say, to decide if their intentions are good or bad.” Hanumān, the son of the wind-god Maruta, agreed to Sugriva’s orders. “Alright,” he said, and set off to meet Rāma and Lakshmana, ready to do whatever was needed.
SECTION III

After hearing the words of Sugriva, Hanumān (sometimes called Hanuman), full of energy, leapt from Mount Rishyamuka and headed toward the two descendants of Raghu. To avoid raising suspicion, the son of the wind god (Maruta) gave up his monkey form and changed his appearance to that of a wandering holy man. Approaching them respectfully, Hanumān bowed and praised them sincerely with gentle, flattering words. Following Sugriva’s instructions, he greeted the two heroes—who were famous for their truthfulness—and spoke to them in a friendly, inviting tone. “You both look like powerful ascetics, similar to royal sages, gods, or the best of celibate students. Why have you come here, frightening the deer and wild animals in this forest? As you walk among the trees near Lake Pampā, you make this beautiful lakeside even more stunning. Who are you two young men with strong arms, wearing bark clothes, looking patient and yet troubled, startling the animals? You’re heroic, with lion-like looks and great physical strength. You carry bows as impressive as Indra’s. Graceful and pleasant-faced, you seem as mighty as wild bulls, your arms thick like elephant trunks. You light up this mountain just by being here. You look like you belong on a throne—or even among the gods. Why are you here? With lotus-shaped eyes, matted hair, and matching features, have you come from the heavens? It’s as if the Sun and the Moon themselves have come down to earth. Broad-chested, heroic, with shoulders like lions, full of energy, built like prize bulls, you look like gods even though you’re human. Why aren’t your long, round arms decorated with jewelry, as they should be? I get the feeling you two could easily protect the whole earth, with its forests, oceans, and great mountains like Vindhya and Meru. Your painted, smooth bows look like Indra’s thunderbolts, decorated with gold. Your quivers are filled to the top with sharp, deadly arrows that look like blazing fire or fierce snakes. Your two large daggers, gleaming with gold, are as intimidating as unleashed serpents. Why don’t you answer me when I ask? There’s a brave and noble monkey chief named Sugriva, who’s been wandering these lands, heartbroken because his brother drove him away. I’ve come here, sent by that great Sugriva—my name is Hanumān, the foremost among monkeys. Sugriva wants to be friends with you. I’m his advisor—a monkey, son of the wind god Pavana. I can travel anywhere I wish, and I’ve come here disguised as a holy man from Mount Rishyamuka, on Sugriva’s behalf.” 

After saying all this to Rāma and Lakshmana, Hanumān—who was an expert speaker—fell silent. Hearing his words, the radiant Rāma, with a happy smile, turned to his younger brother, Lakshmana, who sat beside him. “This is the advisor of Sugriva, the noble king of the monkeys. He’s come to ask for our friendship on Sugriva’s behalf. Welcome him warmly, Saumitri (another name for Lakshmana)—he’s Sugriva’s minister, skilled with words, loyal, and a friend to us. Nobody could speak like this unless they’ve truly mastered the Rigveda, learned the Yajurveda, and deeply studied the Samaveda. He must have studied all the grammars, too, because he hasn’t used a single awkward word, even though he’s spoken at length. There was no awkwardness in his face, eyes, forehead, eyebrows, or any part of him. His words were few, clear, pleasing, and gentle—they flowed easily from his chest and throat. His speech was wonderful, quick-witted, polished, uplifting, and captivating. Who could hear such amazing words—from someone’s heart, throat, and mind—and not be moved? Even an enemy about to strike would hesitate. How can any king succeed without a messenger like this? If someone has such talented messengers, they can accomplish anything with just their words.” 

After Rāma said this, Lakshmana—who was also skilled in speech—welcomed Hanumān, the wise advisor of Sugriva and son of the wind god. “O learned one! We already know of Sugriva’s many abilities. We’ll seek out the king of the monkey tribes. Hanumān, best of monkeys, we’ll do whatever you say, following Sugriva’s instructions.” 

Hearing these gracious words, Hanumān—the wind god’s son—was thrilled. He started thinking about how best to create a strong friendship between Rāma and Sugriva, planning the next steps for Sugriva’s success.
SECTION IV

When Hanumān heard Rāma’s words and realized that Rāma was friendly toward Sugriva and willing to help him, he was overjoyed. Hanumān immediately thought of Sugriva. “Now that things are looking up and we have this chance, Sugriva, that noble soul, will probably become king,” he thought. Filled with happiness, Hanumān—the best among monkeys—turned to Rāma and asked, “Why have you come to this deep and wild forest, full of dangerous beasts, with your younger brother?” In response, Lakshmana, following Rāma’s signal, began to tell Hanumān everything about Rāma, the son of Daçaratha. “There was once a king named Daçaratha. He was wise, radiant, and always did what was right, ruling all four classes of people justly. He never hated anyone, nor did anyone hate him. He cared for everyone like a father. He performed many sacrifices and gave generously to the Brahmins. Rāma, his eldest son, is famous among men. He is the protector of everyone and always obeyed his father’s wishes. Among Daçaratha’s sons, he is the most virtuous. Rāma has every sign of royalty and once enjoyed all the wealth of a kingdom. But now, deprived of his throne, he has come here with me to live in the forest. And, noble one, his wife Sitā follows him faithfully, just as the radiant Sun is followed by his consort, Splendour, at sunset. I am his younger brother, Lakshmana, devoted to him out of gratitude and love. Because of his noble qualities, I have dedicated my life to serving him. Though he deserves happiness and respect, he now lives in the forest, without wealth, and his wife has been kidnapped by a Rākshasa—a demon who can change form at will. We don’t yet know who this Rākshasa is. A son of Diti called Danu, who was cursed to become a Rākshasa, told us about the mighty Sugriva.—

“Danu said that Sugriva would be able to discover who took your wife.” After saying this, Danu, glowing with a divine light, went to heaven. So I have told you everything as it happened. Both Rāma and I have come to seek Sugriva’s help. Rāma, who once ruled the world and gave away great riches, now wishes to serve Sugriva. This virtuous man, who once protected everyone, has now come to Sugriva for protection. Rāghava (another name for Rāma), who used to be the one everyone turned to for help, now turns to Sugriva for shelter. The happiness of Rāma used to mean happiness for all his people, and now he seeks Sugriva’s favor. Rāma is known throughout the three worlds as the eldest son of the king who honored all other kings. Now, he seeks the help of Sugriva, lord of the monkeys. Since Rāma is suffering, overcome with grief, and has come to Sugriva for help, it is only right that Sugriva and his monkey chiefs help him.” When Lakshmana, son of Sumitra, finished speaking, tears in his eyes, Hanumān—who was skilled with words—replied, “People like you, wise and self-controlled, are a blessing to meet, and only the lucky get such an opportunity. Sugriva himself has been driven from his kingdom and made an enemy of Vāli. He’s lost his wife and lives in fear, tormented by his brother. But Sugriva, son of the Sun, along with us, will help you find Sitā.” After saying these kind and eager words, Hanumān told Rāma, “I will take you to Sugriva now.” After Hanumān finished, Lakshmana respectfully greeted him and said to Rāma, “From the happy way Hanumān, son of the wind god, is talking, it’s clear that he wants to help you. Coming here, you have found success. He speaks openly, with a bright and cheerful face; I don’t think Hanumān would ever lie.” Then Hanumān, wise son of the wind god, left, bringing Rāma and Lakshmana with him to meet the monkey king. Dropping his disguise as a beggar and becoming a monkey again, Hanumān—the best among monkeys—carried the two heroes on his back. With a pure heart and great excitement, feeling that everything was going right, Hanumān, the famous son of the wind god, reached that mountain with Rāma and Lakshmana.
SECTION V

After leaving Rishyamuka, Hanumān and the others reached the Malaya hill. There, Hanumān told the monkey king, Sugriva, about the arrival of the princes from the Raghu dynasty. "O wise king, the man who has come here is Rāma, whose strength is his truth. This is Rāma, and with him is his brother, Lakshmana. Rāma, son of Daçaratha, belongs to the Ikshwāku family. He's always obeyed his father's wishes, and that's why he's been sent here—to keep his father's word. Rāma’s father ruled the world with honesty and performed great sacrifices, giving away thousands of cows and gifts. Now, because of a woman, Rāma himself has come to the forest. While he was living here, his wife was kidnapped by Rāvana. That’s why he seeks your help. Please, grant Rāma and Lakshmana an audience—they both deserve your respect and are eager to be your friends. Welcome them as honored guests." Listening to Hanumān, Sugriva, the monkey king, made himself visible and happily spoke to Rāma.

"Sir, you know what is right, and you care about everyone," Sugriva said. "Hanumān (the wind-god’s son) has told me all about your virtues. That you, a great man, want to be friends with me, a monkey, is a huge honor for me. If you really want this friendship, take my outstretched hand and join yours with mine—let’s seal our bond with a promise." Hearing these kind words, Rāma was overjoyed and took Sugriva’s hand. Their friendship sealed, Rāma hugged Sugriva with real warmth. Then Hanumān, dropping his disguise as a beggar, returned to his true form and made a fire by rubbing two sticks together. He worshipped the fire with flowers, pleased, and placed it between Rāma and Sugriva as a witness. Sugriva and Rāma walked around the fire together, officially binding their friendship. Overjoyed, the monkey king and Rāma kept looking at each other, unable to get enough.

"You are my true friend. From now on, our joys and sorrows are one," Sugriva said to Rāma, beaming. Sugriva then picked a beautiful, flowering Sāla branch and made a leafy awning, sitting down with Rāma beneath it. Hanumān, full of happiness, handed Lakshmana a blooming sandalwood branch. With his eyes shining with excitement, Sugriva turned to Rāma and spoke gently, "I have been suffering, Rāma. I live in constant fear. My wife was taken from me, and I have fled to hide in this thick forest, always anxious. My brother Vāli wronged me and turned against me, Rāma. Please, Rāghava, rid me of this fear that Vāli causes. I beg you, Kākutstha, to help make sure I never have to live in fear again." Hearing this, Rāma—the powerful Kākutstha, who always stands for what’s right—smiled and replied, "Mighty Sugriva, I know that true friendship means helping each other. I will kill your enemy, Vāli, who stole your wife. My arrows never miss—they’re as bright as the sun, feathered with eagle plumes, sharp as lightning, and deadly as angry serpents. When I unleash them, they’ll strike down the wicked Vāli. Today, you’ll see Vāli defeated by my arrows, lying on the ground like a mountain torn apart." Hearing these words, Sugriva was filled with joy and replied, thrilled,

"Hero! Lion among men! With your help, I’ll get back both my wife and my kingdom. God among men, please make sure my brother, my enemy, never wrongs me again." At that moment, Sitā’s left eye, Sugriva’s left eye, and the left eye of a great rakshasa (night ranger) all twitched—each resembling a lotus, gold, or fire—as a sign of the powerful new friendship between Rāma and Sugriva.
SECTION VI

Sugriva, looking pleased, spoke to Rāghava (Rāma), son of Raghu: “Rāma, my top advisor Hanumān told me why you’ve come to this lonely forest. Your wife, Maithili (another name for Sītā), daughter of King Janaka, was taken from you and your wise brother Lakshmana by a demon (Rāksha) while she wept. That Rāksha, always looking for a chance to do harm, killed Jatāyu and has left you suffering from being separated from your wife. But your pain won’t last much longer. I promise you, I’ll bring her back to you—just like the gods once recovered Devaçruti. No matter where she is—even if she’s in the underworld or high above the sky—I’ll find her and return her to you. Believe me, Rāghava, I’m telling the truth. Even the gods and demons, with Indra leading them, couldn’t handle your wife; she’s like poison to them. So, don’t be sad, mighty Rāma—I will bring Sītā back. From what I remember, I’m sure it was Mithilā’s daughter I saw while she was being carried off by that terrifying Rāksha. She was crying, ‘Rāma, Rāma, Lakshmana, Lakshmana,’ and in Rāvana’s lap she looked as helpless as the wife of the serpent king. When she spotted me and my four advisors on the hill, she dropped her scarf and her jewelry. I picked them up and have kept them safe. I’ll bring them to you now—you should see if you recognize them.” 

Rāma turned to Sugriva and said, “Bring them here, my friend. Why wait?” Sugriva didn’t hesitate. He hurried into a deep cave in the mountain to do what Rāma needed. Then he grabbed the scarf and the jewelry.

“Look at these,” said Sugriva, holding out the items to Rāma. As Rāma took Sītā’s scarf and ornaments, his eyes filled with tears, like a moon blurred by dew. Overcome with love for Sītā, Rāma’s tears kept flowing, and he lost all composure, sinking to the ground. He hugged the beautiful ornaments to his chest and sighed over and over, like an angry snake coiled in its hole. Seeing Sumitra’s son, Lakshmana, nearby, Rāma, still crying, began to mourn out loud: “Lakshmana, look at this scarf and these ornaments. Vaidehi (another name for Sītā), while being carried away, must have dropped these to the ground. I bet she let them fall on the grass as she was being taken, because they’re just as they were.” Hearing this, Lakshmana replied,

“I don’t recognize her bracelets or her earrings. But I definitely know her anklets, since I always bow at her feet.” Then Rāghava (Rāma) turned to Sugriva and asked, “Sugriva, tell me—where did you see Sītā, the one as precious to me as life itself, when that fierce Rākshasa was taking her away? And where does that demon live—the one who caused all this trouble, the one I swear I’ll destroy along with all the Rākshasas? Whoever stole Mithilā’s daughter and made me this angry has basically signed his own death sentence. Tell me everything about that night-stalking demon who tricked us and took my beloved from the forest. Today, lord of the monkeys, I’ll send that enemy straight to Yama’s door.”
SECTION VII

Hearing Rāma’s pain-filled words, Sugriva the monkey (let’s call him “Sugriva” throughout), with his voice choked up and tears in his eyes, folded his hands respectfully and spoke. “Rāma, I don’t know where that evil Rākshasa is hiding. I don’t know his strength, courage, or even his background—he comes from a cruel family. But please, stop blaming yourself and grieving. I promise you, truly, I’ll do everything I can to help you get Sītā (Maithili) back. I’ll fight Rāvana and his entire army for you, and I’ll do whatever it takes to make you happy. Don’t let your sadness control you—remember your courage. Someone as strong as you shouldn’t let yourself fall apart. I’ve also suffered deeply from being separated from my wife, but you don’t see me losing control or giving up hope. I’m just a simple monkey, and yet I don’t let grief destroy me—so someone as great, patient, and noble as you definitely shouldn’t. Hold back your tears and be patient. Don’t give up your self-control; staying calm in tough times is what makes someone truly good. People with strong minds use their reason, and even when they lose loved ones, money, or face danger from thieves or wild animals—or even death—they don’t lose themselves to panic. If someone lets their sorrow take over, they end up drowning in it, just like a boat overloaded with cargo sinks in water. I say this as your friend, because I care about you. Be strong—don’t let sadness win. People who give in to grief never find happiness, and it drains away their inner strength. So it’s important not to give in. Don’t let your anger control you—fighting Rāma, the son of the King of Koçala and powerful as the god Indra, won’t end well for you.” Tārā finished speaking, giving Vāli wise and caring advice. But Vāli, blinded by fate and the approach of his own destruction, refused to listen.
SECTION XVI

After Tārā, whose face was as lovely as the moon, spoke, Vāli replied, trying to reassure her. “Listen, beautiful Tārā, my brother—who is now also my enemy—is out there making a big show of himself, acting both smug and loud. How can I just stand by and let him insult me? Brave warriors like me, who have never lost or run from battle, would rather die than accept such humiliation. I can’t tolerate Sugriva’s arrogant shouting, especially when he’s got that injury on his neck and is clearly looking for a fight with me. You’re worried about danger from Rāghava (Rāma), but you don’t need to be. Why would Rāma, who’s known for his virtue and gratitude, do anything wrong? Tārā, graceful and gentle, hugged Vāli tightly and circled him with tears streaming down her face. She performed the Sastayana, a traditional blessing ritual, using her knowledge of sacred chants, and wished him victory, though her heart was full of sorrow. Then, overwhelmed with grief, she returned to her private quarters, accompanied by the other women.

Once Tārā had gone back inside with her companions, Vāli came out of the city, breathing heavily like an angry serpent. Moving quickly, full of rage, he looked all around, searching for his enemy. Soon, Vāli spotted Sugriva, who had a golden-brown complexion, was dressed tightly for combat, and stood his ground, shining like a block of burning gold. Seeing Sugriva waiting for him, Vāli, his muscles tense and arms powerful, tightened his clothes even more. Ready for battle, he clenched his fists and advanced toward Sugriva, prepared to fight. Sugriva did the same—clenching his fists, furious, and wearing his golden garland, he stepped up to face Vāli.

As Sugriva, skilled in combat and his eyes burning with anger, rushed forward, Vāli called out, “Look, I’ve made this fist—my fingers tight and ready. Just one punch from me and you’re done for.” Sugriva, just as angry, shot back, “My fist is going to smash your head and take your life!”

The fight exploded. Vāli struck Sugriva hard, and Sugriva, furious and charging in, started coughing up blood, like a mountain gushing with red springs. Sugriva fought back fiercely, grabbing a Sāla tree and hitting Vāli with it, as if the tree was a thunderbolt crashing on a mountain. The blow from the Sāla tree shook Vāli, leaving him struggling like a boat overloaded and tossed in stormy seas.

Both brothers, huge and powerful like the mythical bird Suparna, fought each other with everything they had, like the Sun and Moon clashing in the sky. They were locked in a bitter rivalry, each trying to find the other’s weakness. Vāli, stronger and more skilled, started to get the upper hand, and Sugriva—the mighty son of the Sun—was being beaten back. Humiliated and weakened by Vāli, Sugriva angrily signaled to Rāma to help.

The battle intensified, with the brothers using anything they could get their hands on—trees with branches, rocks, their nails as sharp as knives, fists, knees, feet, and arms. The two of them, wild monkeys of the forest, fought brutally, their bodies soaked in blood, their roars echoing like thunderclouds.

Rāghava (Rāma) watched closely, noticing that Sugriva was getting weaker and more desperate with every moment. Seeing Sugriva in serious trouble, Rāma, powerful and brave, looked to his bow, knowing what had to be done—Vāli’s defeat. He set a snake-like arrow on his bow and drew it back, the string creaking like the sound of doom itself. The twang of the bowstring was so frightening that birds and animals scattered in every direction, as if the world was ending.

Rāma loosed a mighty arrow, glowing like fire and as deadly as a thunderbolt. It shot straight to Vāli’s chest. The wounded Vāli, the powerful monkey king, fell hard to the ground. Like the banner of Indra (Sakra) crashing down in the middle of a festival, Vāli, choking and gasping, lost his senses and collapsed, dying on the spot.

Just as Lord Shiva once breathed out fire and smoke, Rāma—like Death himself—had fired a blazing, golden, unerring arrow that brought down his foe. Bathed in blood, the son of Vāsava (another name for Indra), Vāli fell unconscious to the earth, his body sprawled out like an asoka tree in full bloom on a hillside, or a festival flag of Indra toppled to the ground.
SECTION XVII

Vāli, who was highly skilled in battle, was struck by Rāma’s arrow and crashed to the ground like a fallen tree. His body, still decorated with shining gold ornaments, lay stretched out on the earth, resembling a royal flag that’s been torn from its place and tossed aside. With Vāli defeated, his entire kingdom seemed as empty as the night sky without the Moon. Despite being knocked down, Vāli’s strength, energy, and brilliance didn’t leave him. The golden, jeweled garland that Indra (Sakra) had given him kept his vitality and spirit intact, even now. Wearing this garland, Vāli looked almost like a glowing evening cloud. Even lying flat on the ground, his beauty seemed split into three parts: the garland around his neck, his powerful body, and the arrow piercing his chest. Rāma’s arrow, which had pierced his heart, seemed to show him the path to the heavens — a worthy end for a great hero. Seeing Vāli lying there — broad-chested, strong-armed, the son of Indra, with his golden garland, fierce face, and intense yellow eyes — Rāma and his brother Lakshmana approached. Vāli looked like a fire that had lost its flame, or like Yayati, cast down from the heavens for losing his virtue, or a massive tree toppled at the end of the world, as mighty and hard to defeat as Indra himself. With respect, the two brothers stood near him, taking in the sight of this fallen hero, still powerful even in defeat. As Rāma and Lakshmana drew closer, Vāli, now weakened and lying still, turned to them and spoke.

He addressed Rāma directly, his voice bold but also full of sorrow and meaning: “What have you gained by killing me when I wasn’t even fighting you? I was caught up in anger and fighting someone else, and you destroyed me for that. People praise you, Rāma — they say you come from a noble family, that you’re brave and strong, that you always look out for your people, that you’re kind, full of energy, determined, and wise. They talk about the virtues of a king: justice, self-control, forgiveness, righteousness, firmness, truth, strength, and punishing the wicked. Knowing all this about you, and knowing your royal background, I went after Sugriva even though Tārā warned me not to. Before I met you, I thought, ‘Surely Rāma would never attack me while I’m fighting someone else — he wouldn’t fight unfairly.’ But now I see you’ve acted against your true self, pretending to be righteous while actually doing wrong, just like a well covered in grass hides its danger, or a fire that’s hidden. I never harmed you or your kingdom, never crossed your path. So why did you kill me — a monkey who lives in the forest, eats only fruit and roots, and came here to fight someone else? You’re from the famous Raghus, known everywhere for being good and righteous. So why, with that reputation, have you done something so wrong?

But you’re a human, a king. Land, gold, and silver are what usually cause conflict, but who would be greedy enough to want our forest and our simple food? People who betray their friends, kill priests or cows, steal, destroy life, reject faith, or act selfishly all end up in hell. The same goes for those who do evil, are greedy, kill their loved ones, or run off with their teacher’s wife — there’s no doubt about it. My skin isn’t fit for your touch, my bones and hair should be avoided by the virtuous, and my flesh shouldn’t be eaten by someone like you, who claims to be pious. Only five animals with five toes — the hedgehog, porcupine, iguana, hare, and tortoise — are fit to be eaten by warriors and priests, Rāma. Wise people wouldn’t touch my skin or bones, and my flesh isn’t meant for you — and yet, you’ve killed me, a monkey with five toes. 

If only I’d listened to Tārā’s wise and honest advice, maybe I wouldn’t have ended up here, at the mercy of Death. Rāma, it’s like the Earth has married you, but you’ve turned away from your own principles. How could someone so wicked, narrow-minded, dishonest, and eager to cause pain be born from the noble Daçaratha? I’ve been killed by you, like a wild elephant, ignoring the path of virtue and breaking every moral principle. By doing this disgraceful thing, what are you going to say to the good and righteous people when you return to them? The power you showed against me, you never use against real wrongdoers. If you’d fought me openly, face-to-face, you’d be the one seeing the land of the dead — I would have killed you. If you’d just told me what you wanted, I could have brought your Sītā back in a single day and dragged Rāvana, that wicked demon, to you — without needing to kill anyone in battle. With these words, the great monkey chief’s son — wounded, his face pale from pain, and his eyes locked onto Rāma, bright like the sun — fell silent.

As Vāli, wounded and weak, spoke to Rāma, his words were humble, honest, and sincere. Hearing Vāli’s reproach, Rāma addressed the great monkey king—once so bright and powerful, now like the sun dimmed, a rainless cloud, or a fire snuffed out. “Why do you blame me like a child, Vāli? This land, full of hills and forests, belongs to the Ikshwaku dynasty. Along with it, they received the right to rule over animals, birds, and humans—to reward or punish as needed. Bharata, our righteous king, understands virtue, knowledge, and desire, and always strives to reward the good and punish the wicked. He rules this kingdom with discipline, humility, truth, and strength. All of us—myself and other kings—follow his orders, traveling the world to promote virtue. Who would dare commit a crime when Bharata, lover of virtue, rules the earth? Guided by his commands and our own sense of duty, we must punish those who stray from the path. But you, Vāli, have broken the rules. You’ve let your desires control you and ignored your royal responsibilities. An elder brother, a father, or a teacher should be treated like a father if they follow virtue—while a younger brother, son, or loyal follower should be loved as sons. Virtue is the foundation of all these relationships. O monkey, true religion is subtle and deep—only the soul can truly judge right from wrong. How can you, impulsive as you are, understand what’s proper when you only consult other monkeys who are just as careless, like the blind leading the blind? I didn’t kill you out of anger alone. These are Bharata’s orders, and I am following them. You have disregarded virtue. A wise person who lives by virtue cannot ignore wrongdoing. Bharata commands us to punish the lustful, and so I have been right to destroy you for your crimes. Like Lakshmana, I became friends with Sugriva. For all these serious reasons, supported by virtue, I was justified in punishing you. Accept it—your defeat is in line with morality, and helping a friend is a sacred duty. Listen to what Manu said—these verses guide character and are honored by the wise and by me: Those who commit crimes and accept punishment from their king are purified and reach the heavens, just like the virtuous. After saying this, Vāli’s eyes widened, his mouth fell open, and his face took on a frightening look. Hurt deeply by arrows, he drew his last breath and died. The monkeys, who were famous for leaping through the forests, mourned loudly for their lost leader. With the death of their king, Kishkindhā became empty and lonely; the gardens, hills, and forests seemed deserted. Vāli had once fought a fierce battle with the mighty Gandharva named Golava, fighting day and night for fifteen years straight. In the sixteenth year, Vāli finally killed Golava, saving the monkeys from fear and destroying the wicked Gandharva. Now, the monkeys were shocked—how could someone so powerful be killed like this? They felt lost, like cows terrified in a forest full of lions after losing their leader. None of them could find peace after their king’s death. Meanwhile, Tārā, overwhelmed by grief, stared at Vāli’s lifeless face. She collapsed to the ground, wrapping herself around his body, like a vine clinging to a great but fallen tree.
SECTION XXIII

Tārā knelt beside her husband, the fallen king of the monkeys, and gently touched his face. Through her tears, she spoke to him again, her words full of grief: “My love, you ignored my warnings and now you’re lying here on this rough, stony ground. The earth must mean more to you than I do, since you’re holding her close instead of greeting me. My brave king, it’s strange that fate—taking the form of Rāma—has put you at Sugriva’s mercy. Now Sugriva will be called a true hero. Why won’t you wake up, even when you hear the cries of the bears and monkeys who once served you, and the voices of Angada and me? Now you lie on the same battlefield where you once defeated your enemies, and they lay defeated at your feet. You were born into a noble family and loved to fight—where have you gone, leaving me alone? Maybe wise people shouldn’t let their daughters marry warriors. Look at me: a hero’s wife, a widow in a moment. My pride is crushed, my happiness destroyed, and I’m drowning in sorrow. My heart must be made of stone not to shatter, seeing you dead like this! You were my friend, my husband, a great hero—and now you’re gone, killed by another’s hand. No matter how rich or how many sons she has, a woman without her husband is always called a widow. You’re lying in a pool of your own blood, as if it’s a red blanket on your bed. Your whole body is covered in blood and dust, and I can’t even hold you in my arms, my beloved king. Sugriva finally got what he wanted—Rāma’s arrow gave him the courage to do this. Now that you’re dead, I can only look at you, unable to touch you because of the arrow still in your heart.”

At that moment, Neela stepped forward and gently pulled the arrow from Vāli’s chest. It looked like a burning snake pulled from a cave. The arrow, shining like a sunbeam on a mountain at sunset, glowed as blood poured from Vāli’s wounds, like streams of molten metal. Tārā washed his battered body with her tears, wiping away the blood and dust. Seeing her husband like this, she turned to Angada, her son with the copper-colored eyes, and said, “Look at what’s become of your father. This is the end that all his fighting brought him. Bow before your father, the great king who honored so many, now gone to the land of the dead, shining like the rising sun.”

Angada stepped forward, his arms strong, and knelt to embrace his father’s feet, saying, “I touch my father’s feet.” Tārā, watching him, cried out, “Why don’t you bless Angada like you used to, telling him to live a long life, now that he’s bowing to you? My son and I are here by your side, like a cow and her calf mourning the bull killed by a lion. Why did you go to your final battle—the sacrifice of your life—without me? Why do I not see your favorite golden garland, the one the lord of the gods gave you when you fought so bravely? Even in death, you haven’t lost your royal dignity—just like the sun’s rays lingering on a mountain after sunset. You didn’t listen to me, and I couldn’t stop you. Now, my son and I are lost with you on this battlefield. Truly, even the goddess of fortune has left me.”
SECTION XXIV

Seeing Tārā completely broken by grief, Sugriva (Vāli’s younger brother) was overwhelmed by guilt over his brother’s death. Her face streaked with tears, Tārā’s pain only deepened Sugriva’s regret. He slowly approached Rāma, carrying his bow and arrows—each arrow as deadly as a serpent—surrounded by his followers. When he reached Rāma, who was sitting calmly, Sugriva spoke: “Lord Rāma, you kept your promise, but as for me, I can’t enjoy anything today. How can I care about ruling when Tārā is crying like this, and everyone is mourning the king? The kingdom means nothing to me now that my brother is dead. Yes, I wanted Vāli dead because I was angry and hurt by how he treated me, but now that he’s really gone, I feel crushed by guilt. I’d honestly rather go live on Mount Rishyamuka and get by however I can, than have a kingdom won by killing my own brother. Vāli was wise and noble—he told me, ‘Go wherever you want; I don’t want to hurt you.’ That was the right thing to say, Rāma. But my actions were the opposite—I acted out of anger, greed, and stupidity. How could I, as a brother, ever think the happiness of being king would be worth the pain of killing Vāli? He never wanted to kill me because he cared about his reputation, but I let my jealousy and bitterness destroy my family. Sometimes when I fled from him and he hit me with tree branches, he just told me, ‘Don’t do it again,’ and tried to comfort me—even then, he stayed loyal, honest, and kind, while I just gave in to anger and my monkey instincts. Rāma, I feel like Indra when he killed Biswarupa and was cursed for it—except my sin is even worse, and no one else can help bear it. Indra’s guilt was shared by the earth, water, trees, and women, but who would want to share the blame for what I’ve done? I’ve done something so wrong, so shameful, it’s ruined my family—I don’t deserve respect or the right to rule, let alone the throne. I’m guilty of a terrible crime; everyone will blame me for it. My grief is like a river that only flows downward, dragging me with it. My guilt feels like a massive, raging elephant—its body is the death of my brother, and its trunk, head, and tusks are regret, crushing me. This unbearable guilt is burning away any goodness in me, like gold losing its shine in the fire. Rāma, even the monkeys and Angada are half-dead with sorrow. Good sons are rare—who could compare to Angada? But I know I’ll never see my brother again. Angada might not survive this, and if he does, maybe his mother will try to raise him, but she probably won’t live long without her son. That’s why I want to step into this fire, to join my brother and nephew in death. Let all the other monkeys search for Sītā and follow your orders, even if I’m not here. Please, Rāma, tell me to end my life—I don’t deserve to go on after destroying my own family.” 

When Sugriva finished, Rāma, the great warrior and descendant of Raghu, was silent for a moment, tears in his eyes. As Rāma composed himself, he looked again and again at Tārā, who was lost in her grief. Meanwhile, the royal advisers gently lifted Tārā from the ground, where she lay clutching Vāli’s body with trembling arms. As she was pulled away, she looked at Rāma—armed with his bow and arrows, glowing with his own energy like the sun. Seeing him, with his noble features and bright eyes, she thought, “This must be Kākutstha (another name for Rāma).” 

Overcome by sorrow, Tārā, her heart shattered by tragedy, approached Rāma. He seemed almost godlike, and just being near him was intimidating. When she reached Rāma, who stood victorious in battle, Tārā, voice shaking with grief, said to him: “You’re beyond measure, wise, powerful, and self-controlled. You forgive like the earth itself, and your eyes burn red with intensity. With your bow and arrows, you look more like a god than a man. Please, kill me with the same arrow you used on my husband. That way, I can join Vāli—he never wanted any other woman but me. If I’m not with him, even in the heavens, he won’t care about being surrounded by the Apsarās or their golden crowns. Even among the gods, he’ll be miserable without me—just like you were when you were separated from Sītā, the daughter of King Videha. You know how painful it is for a man to lose his wife; so, kill me and save Vāli from that suffering. You might worry that killing a woman is a sin—but if you see me as part of Vāli’s soul, not just as a woman, then you won’t be guilty. The sacred texts say that a wife and her husband are inseparable. Giving a wife as a gift is the highest offering. If you send me to him, you won’t be sinning. Don’t leave me like this, alone and destroyed. Rāma, I can’t live without my husband, the wise and powerful king who moved like an elephant and wore his golden garland.” 

Hearing this, Rāma gently comforted Tārā. “Don’t lose yourself in grief, brave queen,” he said. “Everything happens according to fate, to the will of God—happiness and sorrow both. No one, not even the gods, can escape what’s meant to be. Your son will become the next king, and you’ll find happiness in that. This is destiny. The wives of heroes are strong—they never give in to despair.” 

Consoled by Rāma’s kind words, Tārā, still wearing her beautiful clothes and the dignity of a true queen, finally stopped weeping.
SECTION XXV

Then Rāma (also called Kākutstha), along with Lakshmana—both grieving just as much—tried to comfort Sugriva, Tārā, and Angada. He said, “Mourning and endless grief don’t help the one who’s passed away. It’s time to perform the last rites. You’ve honored your love for Vāli with your tears, but now you must do what’s necessary. We can’t put off the duties that tradition demands. Time controls everything in this world—it’s what causes all things to happen, good or bad. People act according to their fate and their past actions, and Time simply pushes them along. No one really controls anyone else; not even the gods can resist Time. Time is unstoppable—no one is its friend, and it has no favorites. The wise can see how Time shapes everything: religion, wealth, and even our deepest desires. Vāli, king of the monkeys, has now reached his true reward—he’s gained the results of his actions, thanks in part to his generosity and courage as a ruler. He’s now gone to the world of the gods, which he earned through his good deeds. This is the natural path of Time, and Vāli has followed it. So there’s no point in more grief. You need to carry out the proper rituals for him.” After Rāma finished, Lakshmana, always reliable in battle, turned to Sugriva—who was almost senseless with sorrow—and spoke clearly: “Sugriva, you should lead the funeral rites for Vāli, together with Tārā and Angada. Gather plenty of dry wood for the pyre, and bring sandalwood if you can. Try to comfort Angada, who is completely lost in grief. Remember, you’re king now—don’t let your sadness stop you from doing what’s needed. Angada, bring funeral clothes, garlands, perfumes, ghee, oil, and anything else we need. Tārā, please go and get a carriage quickly—it’s really important to act fast right now. The monkeys who are strong enough should help carry the body. Only the strongest and bravest should lift Vāli.” After giving these instructions, Lakshmana, the pride of his mother Sumitra, stood by Rāma. Hearing Lakshmana’s words, one of the counselors respectfully entered the cave to fetch the carriage. He soon came out with a grand carriage, fit for heroes and carried by monkeys. It had a throne and looked almost like a war chariot, decorated with paintings of trees, birds, and soldiers, with intricately carved wooden panels and latticed windows. It was beautifully built, covered in bright garlands and rich fabrics, sprinkled with red sandalwood, and shone like the rising sun. Seeing this impressive carriage, Rāma said to Lakshmana, “Let’s start Vāli’s funeral right away.” Then Sugriva and Angada gently lifted Vāli’s body onto the carriage, and the weeping began.

Once Vāli’s lifeless body was placed on the carriage, they covered him with ornaments, garlands, and silken cloths. Sugriva, now king of the monkeys, ordered the start of the funeral rites. “Let the monkeys go ahead, scattering precious jewels, and the carriage will follow. We should honor Vāli with a send-off worthy of a great king.” The counselors and other monkeys, devastated by their loss, hugged Angada and moved forward, crying. All the other monkeys joined in. The female monkeys, led by Tārā, wept loudly, crying out, “O hero, O hero!” Their sorrowful cries echoed through the hills and forests, as if nature itself was mourning. The monkeys built funeral pyres along the riverbanks and in quiet, hidden spots. When they reached the spot, the strongest monkeys set down the carriage and stepped aside, overcome with grief. Tārā, seeing her husband’s body, put Vāli’s head in her lap and broke down, sobbing. “O king of monkeys, my beloved! You loved comfort and had such strong arms. Why won’t you look at me? Why don’t you see these monkeys, broken by sorrow? Even now, your face looks peaceful, like you’re just sleeping, your skin glowing orange like the sunset. O Vāli, Death himself, in Rāma’s form, has taken you from us with a single arrow, leaving us all widows. Your wives, with faces like the moon, have always cared for you—can’t you see how far they’ve come on foot to be with you? Why won’t you look at them, or at Sugriva? Your counselors, your wives led by Tārā, and all your people are mourning around you. O warrior, send your counselors back to the city and let us stay here in the forest, lost in our love and grief.” Other she-monkeys, also grieving, gently lifted Tārā from her husband’s body. Then Angada and Sugriva, hearts heavy with sorrow, placed Vāli’s body on the funeral pyre and lit the fire, walking around it in respect for his final journey. After Vāli’s body was cremated, the monkeys went to a sacred river to perform the water ritual for the dead. Along with Sugriva, Tārā, and Angada, they sprinkled water in his honor. Rāma, just as sad as Sugriva, also took part in Vāli’s funeral rites. When the ceremonies were finished, Sugriva—now king, but deeply grieving for his powerful brother—came before Rāma and Lakshmana.
SECTION XXVI

The leading monkeys waited together, surrounding Sugriva, who was still grieving and in wet clothes. They all approached Rama—who was strong and tireless—and stood before him with folded hands, like wise sages gathering around the Creator. Hanuman, son of the wind god, stood out among them, looking as impressive as a golden mountain and as radiant as the rising sun. With his hands respectfully joined, Hanuman spoke: “With your help, O Kakutstha (Rama), Sugriva has gained this great kingdom of the powerful monkeys—something even the greatest heroes couldn’t win. On your command, he and his friends will now enter the city and take up royal duties. After his coronation bath, he’ll honor you with garlands, jewels, perfumes, and sacred herbs. Please, enter this beautiful mountain cave and let Sugriva’s coronation bring joy to all these monkeys.” After Hanuman finished, Rama—wise, eloquent, and a slayer of enemies—replied:

“Dear Hanuman, I must follow my father’s command, so I can’t enter any town or city for these fourteen years. Sugriva, the greatest among monkeys, should go into this amazing cave and you should all crown him king right away.” Then Rama spoke directly to Sugriva: “Since you know the customs, make Angada—brave, generous, and honorable—the heir to your throne. As the eldest son of your older brother, Angada truly deserves it. Now, the month of Sravana has begun, marking the start of the rainy season, so this isn’t the right time to look for Sita. Go into your blessed city, and I’ll stay here on the mountain with Lakshmana. This mountain cave is comfortable, spacious, and has fresh air, water, and lots of lotuses. Once the month of Kartika arrives, you can start planning Ravana’s defeat. For now, this isn’t the right time—please, go to your city. As king, bring happiness to your friends.” Following Rama’s instructions, Sugriva—the monkey lord—entered the pleasant city of Kishkindha, which had been built by Vali. Thousands of monkeys surrounded him as he went in. The people of the city bowed low, touching their heads to the ground in respect. Sugriva greeted them warmly, lifting them up, and then entered the grand inner rooms of his brother’s palace. Once inside, his friends crowned the mighty Sugriva king, just as the gods crown Indra, lord of heaven. The monkeys brought him a coppery-gold umbrella, white fans, an exquisite golden staff, many jewels, all kinds of seeds and medicinal plants, roots and flowers from fig trees, fine white clothes, white sandalwood paste, beautiful garlands, flowers from water and land, divine perfumes, roasted grain, gold, Priyangu honey, clarified butter, curd, tiger skin, a pair of excellent sandals, gorochana (yellow pigment), and red arsenic. Sixteen joyful maids carried all these gifts. The monkeys honored the priests with jewels, clothes, and food to make the coronation perfect. The priests, skilled in sacred rituals, poured clarified butter into the fire, chanting mantras. They seated Sugriva on a splendid throne facing east in a golden hall at the top of the palace, decorated with elegant blankets and flowers. They gathered pure water from many rivers, holy places, and oceans, storing it in golden jars. Gaya, Gavaksha, Gavaya, Sarava, Gandhamadana, Mainda, Dvivida, Hanuman, and Jambavan performed the coronation, using sacred bull horns and the golden jars, following all the ancient rules, just as the gods crown Indra with pure, scented water. After Sugriva’s coronation, the monkeys—by the hundreds and thousands—cheered and celebrated. Following Rama’s advice, Sugriva hugged Angada and made him crown prince. With Angada as heir, the monkeys were overjoyed and praised Sugriva, honoring him again and again. With both Angada and Sugriva established in their new roles, everyone celebrated Rama and Lakshmana, singing their praises. Kishkindha, filled with strong, proud people and decorated with banners and flags, looked beautiful nestled in the mountains. Sugriva, now king and reunited with his wife Ruma, sent word to Rama about his coronation and ruled his kingdom like Indra, king of the gods.
SECTION XXVII

After Sugriva was crowned king and the monkeys returned to their cave, Rāma and his younger brother Lakshmana made their way to Prasrabana Hill. The hill was alive with the sounds of tigers and deer, home to fierce lions, and covered in all kinds of trees, vines, and shady spots. Bears, monkeys, Gopuchyas, and wildcats lived there too. The whole hill looked like a gathering of dark clouds and always seemed to bring good luck. Rāma and Lakshmana found a large cave at the top of the hill and decided to stay there. After making his deal with Sugriva, Rāma, always calm and thoughtful, spoke to Lakshmana (also called Saumitri), who was loyal and wise. He said, “Saumitri, brave brother, let’s spend the rainy season in this comfortable, airy cave. This hilltop is stunning, with stones in shades of white, black, and copper, rich with minerals and river frogs, covered in lush trees and vines. Birds sing all around us, peacocks call, and the trees are in full bloom—Malati, Kunda, Sindubara, Sirisa, Kadamba, Arjuna, and Sarja. There’s a pond full of blooming lotuses right by the cave. Our cave is perfect, with a lower northeast side and a higher western side. At the entrance is a smooth, flat black stone, shiny as eyeliner. Look to the north, brother—the hilltop is dark like a storm cloud. To the south, there’s a bright white hill, shining with metals, almost like Mount Kailasa. In front of our cave flows a clean, eastern-running stream, like the sacred Janhavi river winding through the Trikuta mountains. The banks are lined with trees—sandalwood, tilaka, sala, tamala, atimukta, padmaka, sarala, asoka, banira, timida, vakula, ketaka, hintala, tinica, neepa, vetasha, and kritamalaka. The river is full of birds of every kind, pairs of chakravaka ducks, geese, and sarasa cranes. Its banks are beautiful, dotted with gems, and the water sparkles as if it’s laughing. Some parts are covered in violet lotuses, some in red, and some in divine white water-lilies. Birds and saints both love this peaceful stream. See the rows of sandalwood trees and the kukuva trees, which seem to grow as if they’re alive with emotion. This place really is beautiful, brother, and we’ll be happy here. Not far from us is Sugriva’s city, Kishkindhā, hidden in the forest. Listen—the city is alive with music and the sounds of monkeys, mixed with the beat of mridanga drums. Sugriva must be celebrating: he’s got his wife and his throne back, and now he’s king again.” After saying all this, Rāma and Lakshmana settled into life on Prasravana Hill, making their home among the caves and greenery. But even in such a lovely place, Rāma couldn’t find true happiness. He kept thinking about Sītā, who meant more to him than his own life. Every night, when the sun went down, he would lie down to rest but couldn’t sleep. Lakshmana, suffering just as much, tried to comfort his brother. Nearly overwhelmed by grief for Sītā, Lakshmana said, “Don’t give in to sorrow like this. You know that if you stay lost in grief, you’ll only wear yourself out. You’ve always followed the path of goodness and honored the gods. You are strong, and you believe in doing what’s right. But if you let yourself lose hope, you’ll never defeat your enemy—the cunning and terrifying Rakshasa. Let go of your grief and focus your energy. Only then will you be able to destroy that demon and his whole family. Forget just defeating Rāvana—you could lift up the earth itself if you wished. Now that the rains are here, wait for autumn. Then you can destroy Rāvana, his kingdom, and all his kin. In the meantime, I’ll help keep your spirit strong, like stoking embers into flame.” Rāma listened to Lakshmana’s wise and caring words and replied with affection:

“Lakshmana, what you say is exactly right. You’re loving, loyal, honest, and always looking out for me. If I let sadness stop me, I’ll never get anything done. I need to be strong and ready to act. I’ll stay here, waiting for autumn, following your advice, and respecting Sugriva’s promise. Good people always return favors; those who don’t are sure to lose their friends.” Lakshmana agreed with Rāma’s words, bowing his head and showing his respect. He said, “You’re absolutely right. Sugriva will soon help us. Let’s wait out the rains here, and when autumn comes, we can go after your enemy. Stay calm and patient, and let’s spend these next four months here among the deer and hills. When the time is right, you’ll defeat your enemy.”
SECTION XXVIII

After defeating Vāli and putting Sugriva (let’s call him “Sugri”) on the throne, Rama and Lakshmana settled on top of the Mālyabana hill. Rama turned to Lakshmana and said, “Look, this is the start of the rainy season. The sky is full of thick, cloud-mountains. After soaking up the ocean’s water for nine months, the sky is now pouring down rain. If you could climb the clouds, you could hang garlands of Kutaja and Arjuna flowers on the sun itself. The sky looks like a wound covered by a torn cloth—dark clouds tinged copper by the setting sun on one side and yellow on the other. Breezes drift by, cool and scented, with yellow clouds glowing in the evening light—it’s almost as if the sky is lovesick. 

The earth, sweaty and full of fresh water, sends up steam, just like Sita’s sorrow rising from her heart. The Ketaka-scented wind can be caught in cupped hands and drunk like chilled water mixed with camphor. Our hill, brushed by Arjuna and Ketaka trees and cleansed of enemies like Sugriva was, has been washed clean by rain. The smaller hills, with dark clouds for deerskin cloaks, heavy rain for sacred threads, and caves filled with swirling air, look like young Brahmins who’ve finished their studies. Thunder shakes the sky like golden whips, making it sound like the sky itself is groaning in pain. The lightning flashing among the purple clouds reminds me of poor Vaidehi—Sita—trapped in Ravana’s arms.

The moon and stars are hidden behind the clouds, making the night perfect for lovers. Look, Lakshmana, at the hilltops where Kutaja flowers bloom, shrouded in mist from the wet earth, celebrating the rainy season even as my own heart aches for Sita. Now the dust has settled, the air is thick with dew, the heat of summer is gone, kings pause their campaigns, and travelers return home. The Chakrabaka birds, always with their mates, head for Lake Manasa, and because of all the rain, wagons and chariots can’t travel the muddy roads.

In some places the sky is clear, in others hidden by clouds, so it looks like a vast ocean ringed with hills. Mountain streams rush by, echoing with peacock cries, carrying Sarja and Kadamba flowers and picking up coppery minerals from the rocks. People feast on sweet rose-apples, and the wind shakes ripe, multicolored mangoes from the trees. The clouds pile up like mountain peaks, lightning flashing like banners, cranes flying like garlands, and their deep rumbling sounds like angry elephants in battle.

The forests are flooded, the grasslands underwater, peacocks dance joyfully, and the rain pours nonstop—making the evenings beautiful. Clouds, heavy with water and trailed by cranes, drift across the sky, sometimes resting on mountain peaks and always rumbling. Lines of cranes, soaring through the air and whipped by the wind, look like necklaces of white lotuses strung across the sky. The earth, covered in green grass and crawling with new insects, looks like a girl in a white blanket dotted with red lac.

At this time of year, even the great god Narayana grows sleepy, the rivers rush to the sea, the cranes fly up to the clouds, and lovers hurry to reunite. Peacocks dance at the forest’s edge, Kadamba trees burst into bloom, bulls chase after cows, and the fields and woods are full and green. Rivers flow fast, clouds pour down, elephants trumpet fiercely, forests look even more beautiful, men separated from their wives grow lonelier, peacocks dance, and the monkeys are happy now that Sugriva is king.

By the forest springs, elephants, crazy with the scent of Ketaka flowers and the crashing waterfalls, roar along with the peacocks. Black bees, huddling on the dripping Kadamba trees, seem to ooze honey from the flowers they’ve collected. The branches of rose-apple trees, heavy with fruit as dark as charcoal, look like black bees drinking their juice. Thick clouds, split by lightning and booming thunder, look like battle-mad elephants. The king elephant, wandering the hills and hearing the thunder, mistakes it for a rival’s roar and charges back, ready to fight.

Everywhere, bees hum, peacocks dance, and elephants wander—the whole forest comes alive in countless ways. It’s like a drinking party, with Kadamba, Sarja, Arjuna, and land lotuses everywhere, water as sweet as honey, and wild peacocks dancing and shrieking. Birds with rain-soaked wings, happy and thirsty, drink the clean water drops that fall from the leaves, flung down from the sky by Indra himself.

The deep humming of bees, joined by croaking frogs and the rumbling of thunder like giant drums, makes the forest sound like an orchestra tuning up. The peacocks, sometimes dancing, sometimes calling out, sometimes perching high in the trees, have started their own concert in the woods. The frogs, woken by the thunder, come out in all shapes and colors, croaking madly as the fresh rain pours down. Rivers, carrying Chakrabaka birds on their surface and leaving their old banks behind, race excitedly to the ocean, bringing all sorts of new gifts.

Clouds, heavy with new rain, mix with purple ones, and sometimes, when they touch hills scorched by wildfire, look like dark, ancient mountains. Elephants wander these beautiful woods, carrying the scent of Neepa and Arjuna, pastures full of red Indragopa bugs, with peacocks dancing everywhere. Happy black bees drink flower honey, clinging to the drenched petals of lotuses and Kadamba blooms. In this season, elephants go wild, bulls are excited, lions are stronger, hills are more beautiful, kings take a break from ruling, and Indra himself plays with the clouds.

The clouds thunder and pour down, rivers and ponds flood the land, and rain falls in endless sheets. The wind howls, rivers burst their banks, and roads vanish under water. The mountains, washed by the rain pouring from cloud-jars sent by Indra and blown in by the wind, look as if they’ve been ritually bathed like a crowned king. The sky is so thick with clouds that you can’t see the sun or stars; the earth is soaked, and darkness makes it hard to see in any direction.

The mountain peaks, washed by waterfalls stretching down like strings of pearls, shine in the distance. The roaring mountain streams, loosening rocks and echoing with peacock cries, look like necklaces of pearls dropped onto the caves below. Water pours everywhere like strings of pearls from the jewelry of heavenly women. When the sun sets, birds fly to their nests, lotuses close, and Malati flowers open. All royal campaigns are on hold; soldiers wait out the rain, and both war and travel are shut down by floodwater.

This is the month of Bhadra, the time when Brahmins who chant the Sama Veda do their studies. Bharata, king of Kosala, has roofed his houses and stocked up food and is now performing the Ashara sacrifices. The river Sarayu is full to the brim, and the city of Ayodhya seems to celebrate at my return. Every sign of the rainy season is clear. Sugriva, finally free of enemies, has his kingdom and his wives back—he’s as happy as can be.

But I, Lakshmana, feel myself fading away more and more each day, like a riverbank being washed down, separated from Sita and cut off from my kingdom. My sadness is huge, this rainy season is like a prison, and Ravana, my enemy, is stronger than ever. I can’t attack now—the roads are impossible—and I can’t ask Sugriva for help, even though he’s promised to obey me. He’s just gotten his wives back after so much suffering, and my request would be a heavy burden; I don’t want to bother him right now. But when he’s rested and the time is right, I’m sure Sugriva will remember what he owes me and will help.

So, Lakshmana, I’ll wait here for Sugriva’s signal and for the rivers to clear up in autumn. True heroes always pay back their debts. Only the ungrateful lose the good wishes of great people.” 

Hearing this, Lakshmana bowed respectfully and answered Rama, “Sugriva will definitely do everything you ask. So let’s stay here for the rainy season and wait for autumn to come.”
SECTION XXIX
