Check Murachipattana, the lovely Jatapura, Avanti, Angalapa, the forest called Alakshita, and all the great kingdoms and trade cities. There’s a huge mountain at the mouth of the Sindhu River where it empties into the sea, called Somagiri. It has a hundred peaks and tall trees. In its high meadows live birds called Sinhas, who can carry off whales and elephants to their nests. The elephants, once carried up and fed, wander around the wide, water-filled mountain top, their roars echoing like thunder. The monkeys, who can change their shape at will, should search the golden summit of Somagiri, which rises up toward the sky and is filled with beautiful trees.

Farther on, the monkeys will see Pariyatra’s golden summit rising from the sea, stretching over a hundred yojanas. Around it live twenty-four crore (240 million) ascetic Gandharvas, who look like fire and have a frightening, wild appearance. They’re powerful and not to be messed with. Don’t approach them or take any fruit from their land. They’re tough to deal with, but they’re honest and strong. They guard their fruits and roots carefully. You should still search for Sita there, but don’t worry—they won’t bother you as long as you act like regular monkeys.

There’s also a massive blue (lapis-colored) mountain called Vajra, with a base as hard as diamond, beautiful and famous, a hundred yojanas wide and tall. The monkeys need to carefully check the caves there. On the fourth side of the ocean is a mountain named Chakravan. This is where Vishwakarma forged the famous discus, Sahasrara. Here, after killing Panchajana and the demon Hayagriva, the best of the gods gained both the discus and the conch shell. Thoroughly search all the plateaus and huge caves there for Ravana and Sita.

Deep beneath the sea is another great mountain, Varaha, with golden peaks and stretching sixty-four yojanas. There’s a golden city there called Pragjyotisha. The evil demon Naraka lives there. Search everywhere in those beautiful caves and plateaus for Ravana and Sita. Beyond this golden mountain, whose very appearance hints at the gold hidden within, you’ll find Sarvasauvarna, a mountain with springs and waterfalls. There you’ll hear elephants, boars, lions, and tigers roaring nonstop, their calls echoing off the cliffs. This is the Megha mountain, where the green-horsed god Mahendra, conqueror of Paka, was made king by the gods.

After passing that mountain guarded by Mahendra, you’ll reach sixty thousand golden hills, glowing like the rising sun and covered with blooming golden trees. In their midst stands Meru, the king of mountains. Long ago, the Sun was pleased and gave Meru a blessing: he said, ‘By my grace, all the mountains under your care will be golden day and night, and the gods, Gandharvas, and demons living here will respect me and shine with golden light.’ At Meru, the Vishwadevas, Vasus, Maruts, and other gods gather to worship the Sun at sunset. After being worshipped, the Sun disappears and goes to the Setting Hill. In half a muhurta (about 24 minutes), the Sun quickly crosses this mountain, which is ten thousand yojanas across. On its peak is a palace built by Vishwakarma, shining like the Sun itself, with beautiful trees full of birds—the home of the great Varuna, the god who holds a noose.

Between Meru and the Setting Hill stands a tall, ten-headed palm tree, golden and beautiful, on a colorful platform. In all these tough-to-reach places, rivers, and ponds, you must search carefully for Ravana and Sita. There you’ll also find Merusavarni, a righteous and famous sage, holy and almost as powerful as Brahma himself. Bow down with your heads to the ground and ask the sage Merusavarni, who shines like the Sun, about Sita, daughter of Mithila. When night ends, the Sun lights up the world only as far as this, before it disappears behind the Setting Hill. Monkeys, you can only go this far; beyond this, in the dark and endless lands, I know nothing.

When you find Sita and Ravana’s home, or reach the Setting Hill, return within a month. Don’t stay longer than a month, or I’ll have you punished by death. My father-in-law, the hero Sushena, will go with you. Listen to all his orders and follow his lead. He’s not just strong, he’s my spiritual teacher as well. All of you are brave and clever—you’ll know what’s wise or foolish. Use Sushena as your guide and explore the western region. Once we’ve returned the favor to Rama, our mission will be complete. Decide what else you can do for Rama, as fits the place, time, and situation.”

With this, the monkey chiefs, led by Sushena, listened to Sugriva’s skillful directions and set off toward the western lands, the direction protected by Varuna.
SECTION XLIII

After sending his father-in-law to search in the West, Sugriva—the wise monkey king and leader of the vanaras—turned to the brave monkey Satavala. He gave him careful instructions: “Satavala, gather hundreds and thousands of forest-dwelling warriors like yourself. Bring along Yama’s offspring and all the counselors as well. Head north, to the lands where the Himalaya mountains stand, and search every corner for Rama’s famous wife.

If you complete this mission and help us find Sita, we’ll finally repay our debt to Rama, son of Dasharatha, who has done so much for us. If we can help him now, our lives will have real meaning. Even helping someone who never helped you before is a great deed—so just imagine the value of helping someone who has already helped us! That’s why everyone working for our cause should focus on finding Janaki. Rama—the conqueror of enemy cities—deserves honor from all. He trusts us and has shown us kindness. Use your intelligence and strength to explore every hard-to-reach place, river, and mountain.

Search for Sita and Ravana in places like the lands of the Mlechchhas, Pulindas, Surasenas, Prasthalas, Bharatas, Kurus, Madrakas, and Varadas. Don’t forget the cities of the Kambojas, Yavanas, and Sakas, and be sure to search the Himalayas. Look in the regions of Lodhras and Padmakas, and in the Devadaru forests. Leave no stone unturned.

Next, reach the Soma hermitage, a sacred place visited by gods and gandharvas. From there, head to Mount Kala, which has wide plateaus. Search all the caves and peaks of these mighty mountains for Sita, Rama’s blameless wife.

After crossing the golden-bellied mountain, continue to Sudarshana mountain. Then you’ll come to Devasakha, home to many kinds of birds and decorated with beautiful trees. Search every golden stretch, cave, and spring there for Ravana and Sita.

Beyond that lies a vast empty land—a hundred yojanas wide—with no mountains, rivers, trees, or living creatures. Cross this eerie desert as quickly as you can. On the other side, you’ll reach the pale Kailasa mountain, and your spirits will lift.

There you’ll see the stunning palace of Kubera, shining like pale clouds and made of pure gold by Vishwakarma. Nearby is a huge pond overflowing with lotuses and lilies, full of swans and karandavas, and often visited by groups of apsaras. King Vaishravana (Kubera), lord of the yakshas and giver of wealth, enjoys himself there along with the guhyakas.

Search the moon-bright peaks and deep caves of Kailasa for Ravana and Vaidehi (another name for Sita). Then move on to the challenging Krauncha mountain. Its main cave is famous for being almost impossible to enter, so be careful.
Inside live great rishis—sages glowing like the sun—who look almost divine and are respected even by the gods. Search all the caves, plateaus, peaks, passes, and slopes of Krauncha thoroughly.

After Krauncha comes the treeless Manasa mountain, home to birds and the site of Kama’s (the god of love’s) penance. There’s no path for normal beings, gods, or rakshasas, but you must search it anyway, covering every plain and plateau.
Beyond Krauncha, you’ll find Mainaka mountain. The danava (demon) Maya built his own home there. Check every part of Mainaka—plains, plateaus, and forests.

Around there, you’ll encounter strange homes full of women whose faces look like horses. After that, you’ll come to the hermitage of the Siddhas, where powerful ascetics like the Valakhilyas, Siddhas, and Vaikhanasas live.
Pay your respects to these holy Siddhas, purified by their severe penance, and humbly ask them if they know anything about Sita.

Nearby is the Vaikhanasa pond, filled with golden lotuses and visited by elegant cranes with feathers like the rising sun. Kubera’s elephant, Sarvabhauma, often roams this area with his herd of female elephants.
Past this pond, you’ll reach a sky that’s completely black—no stars, no sun, and no moon. The only light comes from the self-luminous, godlike beings resting there after their intense penances.
Move on from that region and you’ll reach the Sailoda River, whose banks are lined with Kichaka bamboos. These bamboos can carry the Siddhas across the river and bring them back again.

Here you’ll find the northern Kurus, a land for those who have earned religious merit. The area is filled with ponds covered in golden lotuses, and thousands of rivers flow, their waters decorated with blue lapis leaves.
The pools shine like the morning sun, dotted with golden-red lotuses. The whole place is full of jewels and precious stones, blue lotus groves with golden filaments, pearls, and gems everywhere.

The rivers are lined with golden islands and beautiful golden hills sparkling with all kinds of precious stones. The trees, filled with birds, bloom and fruit every day. Their delicious flavors and sweet scents grant any wish.
Some trees even grow magical clothes and jeweled ornaments, decorated with pearls and lapis, desired by both men and women.
Other trees bear fruit that’s always in season, while others provide precious beds covered in colorful fabrics and jewels.

Some trees give out beautiful garlands, fancy drinks, and a variety of food. Women with every talent and beauty, along with gandharvas, kinnaras, siddhas, nagas, and vidyadharas—all glowing with brilliance—play and enjoy themselves there.
Everyone is happy—there’s no sadness or unmet desire. Joyful music, singing, and laughter fill the air every day, making the place truly magical.

Beyond this paradise is the northern ocean. In its depths lies the huge golden mountain Somagiri. Even though there’s no sun, the Soma mountain glows so brightly it lights up the land as if it were day.

There, Lord Shambhu (Shiva), the soul of the universe and embodiment of the eleven Rudras, lives with Brahma and the brahmarshis. You can’t go farther north than the land of the Kurus—no one else can, either. The Soma mountain is off-limits, even to the gods. Once you see it, turn back right away.

You monkeys are strong and swift like the wind or fire, but you should only go as far as I’ve described—beyond that, I don’t know what’s out there. Search all these places, and anywhere else I might have missed. By finding Sita, you’ll do something incredibly important for Rama and for me. Once you succeed, you and your friends will be honored by me, and, with your enemies defeated, you’ll be able to live happily with your families, supporting all living beings.”
SECTION XLIV

Sugriva had already made it clear that he placed his trust especially in Hanumān. Convinced that Hanumān was the best one for the job, Sugriva—the king of all the forest-dwellers—happily spoke to Hanumān, the son of the wind-god (Vāyu), saying, “Hanumān, you’re the greatest of all monkeys. There’s nowhere—on earth, in the sky, in space, or even in the water—that can stop you. You know every world: the Asuras, Gandharvas, Nāgas, humans, gods, oceans, the earth itself, and everything below it—nothing is hidden from you. Your speed, strength, and energy are just like your father’s, the powerful wind-god. Honestly, no one on earth matches your power. That’s why I want you to think about how we can find and rescue Sitā. You have everything we need: strength, brains, courage, strategy, and you know how to act at the right time and place.” 

Hearing this, and realizing that their hopes rested with Hanumān, Rāma (also called Rāghava) thought to himself, “Sugriva has total faith in Hanumān, and Hanumān himself seems even more confident that he can do this. Someone who’s already proven himself and has been chosen for this mission by his leader—success is almost guaranteed.” Seeing Hanumān, who was clearly the best choice for the job, Rāma felt a wave of excitement and hope, as if their mission was already as good as done. Filled with happiness, Rāma gave Hanumān a ring inscribed with his own name—a personal token for Sitā. “With this ring, Hanumān, Janaka’s daughter (Sitā) will know you’ve come from me, and she won’t be afraid. Your determination, your real strength, and what Sugriva says about you all make me feel sure we’ll succeed.” 

Hanumān accepted the ring, respectfully raised his joined palms to his head, bowed at Rāma’s feet, and left. Leading the vast army of monkeys, Hanumān—the wind-god’s son—looked like the bright full moon surrounded by stars after the clouds have cleared. “Hanumān, your strength is incredible. I’m counting on you,” Rāma said. “You have the power of a lion. Please, son of the wind, do everything you can—use all your strength—so we can bring back Janaka’s daughter.”
SECTION XLV

Sugriva, the king of the monkeys and their greatest leader, called all the monkeys together to talk about Rāma’s mission. “Every monkey chief must search their assigned region,” he said, making it clear he expected everyone to do their part. With his orders given, the massive monkey army set out, spreading across the land like a swarm of locusts.

Rāma stayed near the waterfall with Lakshmana during that month, waiting anxiously for any news about Sitā. The brave monkey Satavali headed north, toward the snowy mountains. Vinatā, another chief, took his team east. Hanumān, the legendary monkey leader, went south with Tāra, Angada, and other warriors, traveling into the lands ruled by the sage Agastya. Sushena, another fierce leader, marched west to the region watched over by Varuna, the lord of the seas.

After sending his monkey troops in all four directions, Sugriva, satisfied with his plan, allowed himself to relax a bit. The monkey captains set off quickly towards their destinations. Their troops, full of energy and confidence, filled the air with loud cries, howls, and roars, making their presence known as they charged ahead.

As they rushed out, the monkey leaders shouted their promises: “We’ll find Sitā and defeat Rāvana!” One boasted, “I’ll fight Rāvana myself and bring Sitā back today, even if she’s exhausted and scared!” Another declared, “I’ll rescue Jānaki from anywhere, even the underworld. I can pull up trees, split mountains, tear open the earth, and stir up the ocean if I have to!”

Some bragged about their abilities: “I can jump a whole Yojana in one leap!” said one. Another replied, “I can cross a hundred Yojanas!” A third insisted, “I can go even farther—there’s nothing, not land, sea, mountain, or forest, that can block my way!” The monkeys, proud of their strength, all boasted in front of Sugriva, eager to prove themselves.
SECTION XLVI

After the monkey-chiefs had left, Rāma turned to Sugriva and asked, “How do you know so much about every part of the world?” Sugriva, calm and respectful, bowed and replied, “Let me explain. I’ll tell you everything. When Vāli was chasing the demon Dunduvi—who had taken the form of a buffalo—toward the Malaya mountain, Dunduvi ran into a cave on that mountain. Vāli also went in, determined to kill the demon. He told me to stand guard at the entrance, so I waited there, not daring to leave. But Vāli didn’t come out, even after a whole year had passed. 

Then, blood suddenly started pouring out of the cave, flooding the entrance. I was shocked and heartbroken, thinking my brother must have been killed. Overwhelmed with grief and confusion, I assumed Vāli was dead. So I rolled a huge boulder—almost as big as a hill—over the cave’s mouth to trap the demon inside, thinking that if Mahisha (Dunduvi) couldn’t escape, he’d die too. Believing Vāli was gone for good, I returned to Kishkindhā. There, I took over the kingdom, along with Tārā and Uma, and tried to rule peacefully with Vāli’s advisors.

But then Vāli came back, having killed Dunduvi. Terrified of him and respecting his power, I handed the kingdom back to him. Still, Vāli was furious and wanted me dead. He chased me, along with his followers, and I had to run for my life. While fleeing from Vāli, I crossed countless rivers, forests, and cities. I explored the earth as thoroughly as someone studying a cow’s hoof print, a reflection in a mirror, or a spinning torch.

First, I escaped to the East, seeing different trees, mountains, beautiful caves, and many lakes. I saw the golden Ascending mountain—the daily home of the Apsarās—and the sea of milk. But Vāli kept chasing me, so I had to dodge and change direction suddenly. Next, I headed South, through the forests of the Vindhya mountains, filled with sandalwood trees. Even there, I spotted Vāli among the trees on the mountainside. So I switched again and ran West, passing through new lands until I reached the great Asta mountain. Then I turned North, crossing the Himavat and Meru mountains, and even reached the Northern sea. But no matter where I went, Vāli was always on my heels, and I couldn’t find any safe place.

That’s when Hanumān, who’s always wise, remembered something. He said, ‘O king, I recall that Vāli was cursed by Matanga right here in this hermitage. If Vāli ever enters this place, his head will split into a hundred pieces. We can stay here safely, without any fear.’ So, prince, we went to the Rhisyamuka mountain, and Vāli was too afraid of Matanga’s curse to follow us there. That’s how I really did see the whole world, and it’s from there that I eventually came to this cave.”
SECTION XLVII

The main monkey leaders, after getting their instructions from the monkey-king Sugriva, quickly set out in every direction to find Vaidehi (Sita). They searched everywhere—rivers, streams, meadows, open fields, cities, and even places made dangerous by floods. The monkey chiefs explored all the lands Sugriva had described, including mountains, woods, and forests. During the day, they searched for Sita, and at night, they found places to sleep. Wherever they went, they’d find trees full of fruit and make their beds beneath them at night, enjoying whatever each season brought. Counting that first day, the monkey leaders searched for a whole month. When it ended and they’d lost hope, they gathered at the Fountain and met again with Sugriva.

After searching the Eastern regions as ordered, Vinata, who was incredibly strong, failed to find Sita and returned with his advisors. Then the mighty Satavali, feeling defeated, came back with his troops after searching the North. Sushena, who had been searching the West with his group, also came back to Sugriva when the month was over. They all approached Sugriva, who was sitting with Rama behind the Fountain, and greeted him respectfully. Sushena spoke to Sugriva: “We’ve searched every mountain, deep forest, stream, island in the ocean, and all the provinces you described. We looked through every cave you mentioned, every grove tangled with vines, every thicket, and all the rough, hard-to-reach places. We even had to fight and kill huge wild animals along the way. We went over every difficult place more than once. Lord of the monkeys, you are strong and noble, but it’s Hanuman who will actually be able to find Mithila’s daughter. Hanuman, son of the Wind, has followed the same path that Sita took.”
SECTION XLVIII

Hanumān, along with Tāra and Angada, quickly set out for the area assigned to them by Sugriva. With the other top monkeys, they traveled a long way, searching the caves and forests of the Vindhya mountains—places that were hard to reach because of streams and rough terrain. They looked through ponds, woods full of wild trees, and all kinds of mountain areas. But even after searching everywhere, they couldn’t find Maithili, Janaka’s daughter, Sitā. Living off whatever fruits and roots they could find, the monkeys grew tired after searching terrifying forests—some dry and lifeless, others just as harsh. They searched every kind of land, including huge forests filled with caves, and even braved places where trees had no fruit, flowers, or leaves; where streams had dried up and even roots were scarce. There were no buffalo, deer, elephants, tigers, birds, or any forest animals at all. There weren’t even bushes, vines, herbs, or pleasant pools with cool leaves and blooming lotuses—the black bees had abandoned the place. In this lonely forest lived a great sage named Kandu, known for his deep piety, truthfulness, and fierce temper—made even stronger by his strict self-control. Years ago, his ten-year-old son died there, and Kandu’s grief turned to anger. Because of his powerful curse, the whole forest became lifeless and empty, impossible for any animal to survive in. The monkeys, careful and thorough, searched the woods’ edges, the caves in the mountains, and the sources of streams. But, loyal to Sugriva, they found neither Janaka’s daughter nor her kidnapper, Rāvana. Then, as they entered yet another part of the forest, they suddenly spotted a terrifying Asura, hiding among the bushes and plants—he was infamous for his evil deeds and wasn’t even afraid of the gods. Seeing this monster, who sat there like a living mountain, the monkeys tightened their belts, ready for a fight. The Asura glared at them and shouted, "You’re finished!" He raised his fist and charged at them in a fury. As he rushed forward, Angada, the son of Vāli, realized,

"This must be Rāvana," and landed a powerful slap on him. Struck by Angada, the Asura spat blood from his mouth and crashed to the ground like a toppled mountain. Once he was dead, the monkeys, proud of their victory, thoroughly searched the mountain cave he had come from. After making sure they hadn’t missed anything, the monkeys moved on and entered another scary mountain cave. But after searching it too, they came out exhausted. With heavy hearts, they sat down at a distance, resting in the shade of a tree.
SECTION XLIX

Angada, who was known for his wisdom, spoke to the exhausted monkeys, trying to encourage them. “We’ve searched every forest, mountain, river, wild area, valley, and cave we could find,” he said. “But we still haven’t found Jānaki (another name for Sita), or that evil Rākshasa who kidnapped her. We’ve already used up most of the time Sugriva gave us, and he has a reputation for being strict. So let’s shake off our tiredness, sadness, and sleepiness, and search again together. We need to look for Sita in a way that will make sure we actually find her. Success comes from energy, skill, and taking action—so that’s why I’m telling you this. All of you who live in the forest, today let’s search this dense jungle again. Don’t give in to sadness; if you keep acting, you’ll see results, but if you just sit around feeling sorry for yourselves, you’ll lose your strength. Remember, monkeys, King Sugriva has a temper and punishes harshly. We should all be careful of him—and of the great Rama, too. I’m telling you this for your own good. Do what you think is best, and let me know if you have any other ideas.” After hearing Angada, Gandhamādana, weak from thirst and exhaustion, replied honestly, “Everything Angada said makes sense and is good advice. Let’s follow what he suggested. We should search the hills, caves, rocks, empty forests, and mountain streams again, just like Sugriva told us. Let’s all search together—through the woods and caves.” 

So, the powerful monkeys got up and started searching the southern forests near the Vindhya mountains once more. They climbed the Silver Mountain, which looked as bright as the autumn sky, beautiful with its peaks and valleys. Eager to find Sita, these brave monkeys searched the Lodhra woods and the Saptaparna forests. They climbed to the top of the mountain, but even though they were strong, they were getting tired, and still couldn’t find Vaidehi (another name for Sita), Rama’s beloved wife. They carefully checked every cave and spot on the mountain that they could see, then looked around one last time before climbing back down. 

Once they were on the ground again, the monkeys, confused and starting to lose hope, rested for a while under a tree. After a short break, they felt a bit better and got ready to search the entire southern region again. Led by Hanuman, the monkey leaders set out to explore the whole Vindhya area.
SECTION L

Hanumān, along with Tāra and Angada, searched through the caves and forests of the Vindhya mountains. These caves were full of wild animals like lions and tigers, and huge, hidden waterfalls made the search even harder. The group made their way to the southwestern peak of the mountain. Although their deadline hadn’t run out yet, the area was so full of caves, grottos, and thick woods that exploring it was a real challenge. Hanumān, the son of the wind-god, led the search across the mountain. Each member of the group—Gaya, Gavākha, Gavaya, Sarava, Gandhamādana, Maindi, Dwivida, Hanumān himself, Jambavān, the young prince Angada, and Tāra—searched close to one another but spread out enough to cover ground. After searching the southern lands, filled with mountain ranges, they spotted a mysterious cave called Vrikshavila. The cave was hard to get into, not fenced in, and guarded by a Dānava (a type of demon). Hungry, thirsty, and exhausted, the group looked for water and found the cave surrounded by trees and plants. Birds like kraunchas, swans, cranes, and chakravākas, dripping with lotus dust, were coming out of the cave. Curious and amazed by this strange, sweet-smelling and nearly unreachable place, the monkeys wanted to go inside but felt uncertain. Still, these brave monkeys, full of doubt but eager to continue, approached the cave, which was packed with all kinds of animals and looked like something out of a demon lord’s palace—shining, scary, and impossible to get through. Hanumān, shining like a mountain peak and an expert in forests, turned to the other serious-faced monkeys and spoke.

Hanumān said, "We’ve searched the southern lands and all of these mountain chains. We’re exhausted, but we still haven’t found Sītā, the daughter of Mithilā. But look—birds like swans, cranes, kraunchas, and chakravākas keep coming out of that cave, all wet. There must be a water source inside. Plus, there are cool, shady trees right at the entrance." After Hanumān said this, all the monkeys went into the dark cave. There was no sunlight or moonlight at all, and the darkness made your skin crawl. Despite the terrifying lions, birds, and beasts wandering around, the monkeys marched bravely into the shadows. Even in the pitch-black, their senses, strength, and courage didn’t fail them. They moved as fast as the wind, and their eyesight stayed sharp. The monkeys charged into the cave and soon found themselves surrounded by an incredible, beautiful scene. Huddling together in the spooky cave full of strange trees, they traveled for what seemed like a hundred yojanas (a huge distance). Lost, thirsty, confused, and desperate for water, they carefully made their way down into the darkness. Weak, with faces full of despair, the monkeys were almost ready to give up when they finally saw light. Coming out of the darkness, they found themselves in a dazzling place filled with golden trees that glowed like fire. There were sāla and palm trees, tamālas, punnāgas, vanjulas, dhavas, champakas, nāga trees, and karnikāras in bloom—all with golden leaves and branches, shining like a young sun, growing on platforms made of lapis lazuli. Some trees sparkled gold and purple, and the monkeys saw lotus ponds swarming with birds, big golden trees everywhere, and tanks full of giant golden fish and blooming lotuses in crystal-clear water. They also saw gold and silver vehicles and elegant houses with pearl nets hanging over them, golden balconies, floors paved with gold and silver, and decorations of lapis lazuli. All around were trees with coral-like fruit and flowers, golden bees buzzing, honey everywhere, and comfy golden beds and seats set with jewels. While searching the cave, the heroic monkeys found piles of gold, silver, and bronze vessels, heaps of precious aguru and sandalwood, fresh fruits and roots, fancy vehicles, all kinds of delicious honey, stacks of fine clothes, colorful woolens, and deer skins. Then, they saw a woman up close. She wore a black deer-skin and looked like an ascetic (a religious hermit) with a strict lifestyle, glowing with spiritual energy. The monkeys stopped, amazed, and sat together. Hanumān stepped forward and asked her, "Who are you? And who owns this cave?" Hanumān, looking as solid as a mountain, bowed to the old woman, joined his hands in respect, and asked again, "Please tell us who you are, and who owns this place and all these treasures."
SECTION LI

After speaking to the woman dressed in a black deer-skin, Hanumān turned to the deeply religious ascetic who was busy with her rituals and asked, “We rushed into this dark cave without thinking, and now we’re starving and thirsty—we’re exhausted. Since we entered this huge underground cave, our thirst has only grown. All these strange sights have left us shaken and confused—we’re totally lost. Who owns these golden trees that look like the sun rising, these perfect fruits and roots, and these houses and vehicles made of gold and silver, all covered in jeweled nets and golden windows? And whose power causes these golden trees to bloom, with flowers and fruits, filling the air with their sweet smell? There are even golden lotuses in clear water, and I see golden fish and turtles swimming in it. Did you make all of this, or is it the work of some other ascetic’s spiritual power? Please, tell us—we don’t know anything about what’s going on here.” When Hanumān finished, the ascetic woman, who was devoted to doing good for all beings, answered him:

“O Hanumān, leader among monkeys, there was once someone named Maya—the master of illusions. He built this entire golden grove using his incredible skills. Maya, who created this beautiful golden grove and this amazing mansion, was once the main architect—the Viśwakarmā—for the greatest of the Dānavas. After spending a thousand years doing intense meditation in this huge forest, he received a blessing from the Great-father (Brahma), which gave him unmatched skill and total control over all the materials he needed. After finishing his creations, Maya enjoyed every possible pleasure here, living happily in this vast forest for a while. But when he fell in love with an Apsarā named Hemā, Indra (also called Purandara), wielding his thunderbolt, killed him. Afterwards, Brahma gave Hemā this beautiful forest and golden mansion, along with the right to enjoy every pleasure here forever. My name is Sayamprabhā, daughter of Merusāvarni, and I watch over Hemā’s home, Hanumān. Hemā, who is an expert in dance and song, is my close friend. With her permission, I protect this great forest. But what brings you here? Why have you come to these lonely woods? And how did you even find your way into this hidden place? Please—eat and drink from these fruits and roots meant for guests, and then tell me everything.”
SECTION LII

After the monkey-chiefs had rested, the female ascetic, who lived a life of virtue, eagerly spoke to them: “Monkeys, now that you’ve eaten the fruit and your pain has eased, if it’s something I’m allowed to hear, I’d like to know your story.” Hearing her request, Hanuman, son of the wind-god, started to tell her everything honestly.

After leaping over the vast, impossible ocean, Hanumān (Hanuman), strong and tireless, landed on the plateau of Chitrakuta. He took a moment to catch his breath, then gazed toward the city of Lankā. Fighting them would be nearly impossible. Only four monkeys—Vāli’s son, Nila, our smart king, and me—could even make it here. First, I have to find out if Sitā is still alive. Sitting on the mountain, Hanumān paused, thinking about how Rāma could ever succeed. “There’s no way I can sneak into the Rākshasa city like this,” he thought. “It’s crawling with clever, powerful guards. How do I make sure Rāma’s plan doesn’t fall apart? I need to see Sitā alone, in secret. If I mess up now, everything could be lost—just like darkness disappears at sunrise, one wrong move could ruin everything. Even the smartest king with the best advice can fail if his messenger is careless. I have to make sure I don’t mess this up. If the Rākshasas spot me, Rāma’s whole mission to destroy Rāvana could be ruined. Even if I disguise myself as a Rākshasa, I won’t fool these guys. Having seen Sitā in this sad condition, Hanumān thought of Rāma and, in his heart, praised his master.
SECTION XVI

After praising Sita, who truly deserved all honor, and also remembering Rama for his many virtues, Hanuman (the greatest of the monkeys) sat quietly and began to think deeply again. Hanuman looked at Sita—her golden skin glowing, bringing happiness to everyone like the goddess Lakshmi herself. In his mind, Hanuman thought about Rama, remembering, “For Sita’s sake, the mighty Vali and Kavanda, who was as strong as Ravana himself, both died. For her, the terrifying demon Viradha was killed by Rama, just as Indra defeated Shambara. Fourteen thousand demons with horrifying deeds were destroyed at Janasthana by Rama, his arrows blazing like fire. Khara was killed in combat, Trishira was defeated, and the powerful Dushana too—all by Rama, who knows his own strength. Honestly, it would have made sense if Rama had conquered the whole world for her. If you compare ruling all three worlds to having Sita, even a hundredth of her worth is greater than the universe. Sita, daughter of the noble King Janaka of Mithila, was born from the earth itself, raised from a furrow in the ground. She’s the eldest daughter-in-law of King Dasharatha, famous for her good character and strength. She’s the loving wife of the noble, grateful Rama, and now she’s trapped by these demon women.

She gave up all luxuries, didn’t care about pain, and followed her husband out of love into the lonely forest. But now, this golden-skinned woman—who never knew suffering and was always joyful—endures pain beyond belief. Rama longs to see her, desperate like a thirsty man searching for water, because Sita, so noble and now tormented by Ravana, is lost to him. When a king loses his kingdom and then gets it back, he’s overjoyed—Rama will feel the same when he finds Sita again. Sita, too, keeps herself going only by hoping to see Rama again, even though she’s cut off from friends, comfort, and everything she loved.

She doesn’t even notice the demon women around her, or the beautiful trees heavy with fruit and flowers; her whole heart is focused on thoughts of Rama. A woman’s husband makes her shine more than any dress or jewels—so even though Sita is beautiful, her beauty is dimmed in Rama’s absence. It must be so hard for Rama, too—he’s managed to keep living without her, even though his heart must be breaking. My own heart aches for Sita, with her deep blue eyes like lotus petals, who deserves happiness but is suffering so much.

Patient as the earth, Sita—whose eyes look like lotuses—was once protected by Rama and Lakshmana, but now she’s guarded by terrifying demon women under the trees. Endless suffering has drained all her beauty, like a water-lily crushed by frost, and she’s as lost as a doe separated from her mate. Even the Ashoka tree branches, heavy with flowers, seem to deepen her sadness, and the bright full moon at winter’s end only adds to her loneliness.” 

Thinking all this, and now sure that this was indeed Sita, that powerful leader of the monkeys, Hanuman, stayed quietly in the tree, hidden and watchful.
SECTION XVII

The moon, as white and clear as a water lily, moved slowly across the sky like a swan gliding through blue water. Its gentle light bathed Hanuman, the son of the Wind God (Maruta), in cool, comforting rays. As Hanuman watched Sita, he noticed a group of terrifying Rakshasi women nearby. Some had only one ear, some only one eye; some had enormous ears, while others had none at all. A few had ears so huge they seemed monstrous, and some had noses that stuck up awkwardly.

There were Rakshasis with unusually long or thick upper bodies, some with stretched, thin necks, others with wild, tangled hair, and some whose bodies were so hairy they looked wrapped in fur. Some had long ears, big foreheads, huge bellies, or sagging breasts. Others had lips that stretched down, or lips and chins that seemed fused together. Some had long faces, others long knees. There were short ones, tall ones, deformed ones, some so dark they looked almost black, some with twisted, frightening faces and copper-red eyes. Some were just plain terrifying, with wild tempers, always arguing, and holding iron clubs, hammers, or mallets.

A few had faces like wild boars, deer, tigers, buffaloes, goats, or jackals. Some had legs like camels, elephants, or horses, and some even had their heads set low on their chests. A few only had one arm or one leg. Their ears came in all shapes: like horses, cows, donkeys, elephants, or lions. Some had giant noses, some crooked, some had none. Others had elephant-like trunks or noses growing on their foreheads. Some had huge legs like elephants, some had cow-like legs, and some had legs so hairy they looked like pillars. A few had massive heads or chests, others had huge bellies. Some had faces and eyes bigger than normal, with long tongues or stretched features. Faces could be like goats, elephants, cows, boars, horses, or donkeys.

Most of these Rakshasis looked fierce or angry, always ready to fight, holding weapons like maces and darts. Some had faces twisted beyond recognition, with smoke-colored hair. They drank wine constantly, loved meat, and their bodies were often smeared with blood from eating flesh. Hanuman saw all these fearsome Rakshasis sitting around a huge, branchy tree.

At the base of that tree, Hanuman finally saw the noble Sita, daughter of King Janaka. Imprisoned by the lord of the Rakshasas and separated from her friends, she was like a female elephant torn from her herd and captured by a lion, or like the moon’s rays hidden behind clouds at the end of the rainy season. Surrounded by these terrifying women and sunk in misery, Sita looked out of place in the Ashoka grove, like the star Rohini eclipsed by the shadowy Rahu. Hanuman saw her like a vine stripped of flowers, her dress torn and dirty, her beauty hidden like a lotus covered in mud. Even though her face had lost its brightness, her spirit stayed strong, fueled by her trust in Rama’s strength. Sita’s character protected her, her eyes dark and deep like a young deer’s. Her body was graceful and proportional, even without jewels, and Hanuman was filled with joy seeing her at last.

Tears of relief and happiness filled Hanuman’s eyes as he gazed at Sita, her eyes hazy and tired. He bowed respectfully toward Rama and Lakshmana, overwhelmed with gratitude and happiness to have finally found Sita. Hanuman stayed hidden among the branches, quietly watching over her.

SECTION XIX

When Rāvana—the king of the Rākshasas, still young, handsome, and dressed in fine clothes—approached, Sītā (Vaidehi), the flawless daughter of a king, shivered like a banana tree shaken by the wind. The ten-headed Rāvana saw Sītā surrounded by demon women, looking miserable and crushed by sorrow, like a boat sinking in a stormy sea. In her mind, she longed for Rāma, her only hope, and clung to thoughts of him like a chariot racing forward on the horses of determination. Like the daughter-in-law of an elephant king, captured, separated from her family, and tied up, she was crushed by grief, sighing over and over. And when Rāvana saw flawless Sītā—her eyes wide and beautiful, her love for Rāma obvious, and tears streaming down her face—he tried to win her over, not knowing he was sealing his own fate.
SECTION XX
Ravana, using soft words and charming gestures, tried to persuade Sita, who was miserable, joyless, surrounded by Rakshasi demonesses, and living a life like an ascetic.

“Sita, your thighs are as graceful as elephant trunks. I see how you cover your chest and stomach when you look at me—maybe you’re afraid to reveal yourself. SECTION XXI

When Sita heard the words of that terrifying Rakshasa, she was overwhelmed by grief. Her voice was weak as she answered him slowly. “I can’t live with you because I’m someone else’s wife, and I’m faithful. You should keep your eyes on what’s right and follow the path of goodness. Just as sacred knowledge is reserved for the Brahmins, I am only for my husband, who married me in truth and ritual. May good fortune find you, Ravana. Take me back to Rama, who is suffering for me, just as an anxious female elephant longs to return to her mate. If you want to save your kingdom and yourself, make peace with Rama, the best of men. Everyone knows Rama respects what’s right and is kind to those who ask for his help. If you want to keep living, you should seek his friendship. Please, show him respect—take me back to him. If you do, things might go well for you. But if you don’t, disaster will come. Even a thunderbolt might miss you, even Death might pass you by, but you won’t escape if Rama gets angry. Janasthana is already destroyed, your Rakshasas are dead, and you’re weakened. You’ve committed a terrible crime. When Rama and Lakshmana left to chase the magical deer, you kidnapped me from our empty hut, you coward.
