It doesn’t matter if you run to Kuvera’s city or hide with Varuna, the god of the sea—no matter where you go, you’ll be destroyed by Dasharatha’s son, just like a giant tree struck down by a thunderbolt.
SECTION XXII

Hearing those harsh words, Rāvana, the lord of the Rākshasas, replied to Sitā, who was graceful and beautiful, with even crueler threats. “It’s common in this world that when a woman is pursued by a man, she eventually gives in to him. But with you, the kinder I am, the more you push me away. Honestly, my love for you is the only thing holding back my anger, like a skilled charioteer controlling wild horses. Love is powerful for men—when it takes over, even someone who deserves anger is treated with affection. That’s why, even though you insult me and act like a fake ascetic, I haven’t killed or dishonored you, though you deserve it for every harsh word you’ve said to me.” After saying this to Vaidehi (Sitā), Rāvana managed to calm his anger and spoke again: “I’ll wait two months, just as I promised. After that, you’ll have to share my bed. If you still refuse to accept me as your husband, my cooks will chop up your body and serve you for my breakfast.” Seeing Rāvana torment Janaka’s daughter this way, the daughters of the gods and Gandharvas watching felt deep sorrow. Some comforted Sitā with their words, some with their eyes, and some with gentle gestures, trying to encourage her as she suffered under Rāvana’s threats.

Encouraged by their support, and confident in her virtue and her husband’s strength, Sitā answered Rāvana, the lord of the Rākshasas: “Clearly, no one in this city cares about your well-being, or they’d stop you from committing such a terrible act. Who in all the worlds would even think of desiring me, the devoted wife of righteous Rāma, just as no one would dare covet Indra’s wife, Sachi? You, the lowest of Rākshasas, how do you think you’ll escape Rāma’s vengeance for speaking such vile words to his wife? You’re like a wild elephant picking a fight with a rabbit—except you’re the rabbit, and Rāma is the elephant. You insult the great lord of the Ikshwāku dynasty, but only because he hasn’t seen you yet. Why don’t your fierce, blood-red eyes, glaring at me so wickedly, just fall from your head? I am the wife of virtuous Rāma and daughter-in-law to Daçaratha; for saying such evil things to me, why doesn’t your tongue fall out? O Ten-necked one, I could burn you to ashes right now if it weren’t for Rāma’s command and my vows. You never could have kidnapped me if Rāma had been present. Clearly, the gods have let this happen only to bring about your destruction. You call yourself a hero, brother of Kuvera, and a mighty warrior—so why did you have to sneak around and take me by trickery, after sending Rāma away from the hermitage?”

When Sitā finished, Rāvana, lord of the Rākshasas, glared at her, his terrifying eyes swirling with rage. He looked like a dark thundercloud, with long, thick arms and necks. His walk was heavy and powerful, like an elephant’s, and his sharp tongue and burning eyes made him even more intimidating. His jeweled crown trembled as he moved, garlands hung around his neck, and his body was smeared with scented paste. He wore red garlands and clothes, his arms covered in shining ornaments, and a sword-belt circled his waist. He looked like the mighty Mandara mountain wrapped with a serpent during the churning of the ocean. His two strong arms were like the twin peaks of a mountain, and with his sun-bright earrings, he resembled a hill covered in blooming red Ashoka trees. He was as magnificent as the wish-granting Kalpa tree and as vibrant as spring—yet, even with all his ornaments, he appeared as terrifying as a funeral monument in a cremation ground. With his eyes blazing red with anger, Rāvana sighed again and again like a hissing snake, staring hard at Sitā.

Once more, Rāvana spoke to her: “You pretend to be an ascetic, but your vows are meaningless and outside all morality. I’ll destroy you today, just like the sun burns away the darkness.” After threatening Maithilee (Sitā) again, the furious king Rāvana turned to the monstrous Rākshasīs that guarded her.

Among these Rākshasīs, some had enormous ears, some had cow-like ears, and some had ears as long as their arms, while others had none. Some had legs like elephants, some like cows, and some legs were thickly covered in hair. There were those with only one eye or one leg, some with massive legs, and some with none at all. A few had gigantic heads and necks, or oversized chests and bellies, and others had faces and eyes far too large for a human. Some had huge tongues and claws, while some were missing noses altogether. There were Rākshasīs with lion faces, some with cow faces, and others with the snouts of boars.

Rāvana looked over these fearsome women and commanded, “You Rākshasīs, do all you can to bring Sitā, daughter of Janaka, under my control. Whether by kindness or cruelty, persuasion or gifts, threats or sweet talk—do whatever it takes to make Vaidehi (another name for Sitā) give in to me.” He ordered this again and again, his voice filled with both desire and rage, then turned back to Sitā and roared fiercely.

At that moment, one Rākshasī named Dhānyamalini rushed to Rāvana and hugged him. She said, “Come enjoy yourself with me, great king. Why bother with her? She’s just a human—pale and thin. Surely, the gods didn’t mean for her to enjoy all the treasures you’ve gained. Besides, anyone who pursues an unwilling woman only causes himself pain, while winning over a willing one brings true happiness.” After saying this, Dhānyamalini pulled Rāvana away by force.

The Rākshasa, looking like a storm cloud, laughed and turned away. The Ten-necked Rāvana strode off as if shaking the whole earth, and entered his palace, which shone like the sun. Around him, the daughters of the gods, Gandharvas, and Nāgas followed into a splendid hall. After leaving behind Sitā—steadfast and virtuous but trembling—Rāvana, burning with desire, entered his own palace.
SECTION XXIII

After Ravana (the king of the Rakshasas) gave his orders to the group of demon women and spoke to Sita (also called Maithilee and Vaidehi), he left. As soon as Ravana had gone back into his private chambers, the terrifying Rakshasi women surrounded Sita. Furious and almost shaking with anger, they began to threaten her. “You don’t seem to realize, Sita, how lucky you are that the great Ravana—the ten-headed son of Pulastya—wants you as his chosen wife,” one of them sneered. Then another Rakshasi named Ekjata, her eyes red with rage, spoke to Sita, who sat trembling: “Pulastya, the fourth of the six Prajapatis, was a mind-born son of Brahma and is famous everywhere. From Pulastya came the wise sage Vishrava, and from Vishrava was born Ravana, who’s feared by all his enemies. Sita, you should be honored to marry Ravana, the lord of the Rakshasas. Don’t ignore what I’m saying to you, beautiful girl.” Next, Harijata, a Rakshasi with cat-like eyes, glared at Sita and said, “You should want to be the wife of Ravana, who defeated the thirty-three gods and their king in battle. Don’t you want to be with someone so heroic, so powerful, who never loses a fight? Even though he already has a beloved wife and a palace filled with thousands of women and treasures, mighty Ravana wants you. He would worship you above all others.” Then Bikatā, another Rakshasi, added, “Ravana has conquered the Gandharvas and the Nagas in battle—he’s standing right here for you. Why wouldn’t you want to be with someone as rich and powerful as Ravana?” Right after her, another Rakshasi named Durmukhi spoke up.

“Why won’t you go to him, Sita, when even the sun seems afraid to shine and the wind to blow in his presence? Don’t you see that Ravana is so powerful that trees blossom and the clouds pour rain just because he commands them? Why won’t you accept him as your husband? We’re telling you this for your own good. Do what we say, or you will definitely die.”
SECTION XXIV

The Rakshasi women, their faces twisted with rage, kept harassing Sita with harsh, cruel taunts. “Why won’t you accept life here, Sita?” one sneered. “You could live in Ravana’s palace, surrounded by luxury, beautiful beds, and all the comforts you could want. Why are you so obsessed with being loyal to your human husband? Turn away from Rama—he’ll never be able to give you what you want. Be happy and accept our lord Ravana, king of the Rakshasas. He commands the wealth of all three worlds. You’re a beautiful woman, Sita, but you waste your youth pining for Rama—a man who’s lost his kingdom, who is suffering and powerless.”  

Sita, her eyes brimming with tears, replied, “What you say is against everything I believe in. I could never even think of such things. A human woman cannot be the wife of a Rakshasa. If you want to eat me, go ahead—I will never listen to your words. My husband, whether rich or poor, is my guide and my world. I will always be devoted to him, just like Subarchala was to the Sun. Like Sachi with Indra, Arundhati with Vashishta, Rohini with the Moon, Lopamudra with Agastya, Sukanya with Chyavana, Savitri with Satyavan, Sreemati with Kapila, Madayanti with Sandasa, Keshini with Sagara, and Damayanti with King Nala—I will always stay loyal to my husband Rama, the greatest of the Ikshvaku line.”  

Hearing Sita’s words, the Rakshasis sent by Ravana were furious. They attacked her with an even harsher barrage of insults. All this time, Hanuman stayed completely silent and hidden up in the branches of the Shingshapa tree, listening as the Rakshasis tried to bully Sita. Their anger boiling over, the Rakshasis crowded around Sita, who was shaking with fear. They licked their lips hungrily, baring their sharp teeth. Grabbing their spears, they threatened her, shouting, “She doesn’t deserve Ravana, the king of the Rakshasas!”  

Surrounded and tormented by these terrifying women, Sita, tears streaming down her face, edged closer to the Singshapa tree. She stood there, surrounded by the Rakshasis, overwhelmed by grief. The demon women circled her, hurling insults from every direction. Sita looked pale and worn out, her clothes dirty and torn.  

Then, a fierce-looking Rakshasi named Vinata, with huge belly and hideous teeth, spoke up. “Sita, your loyalty to your husband is admirable, but too much of anything is bad. You’ve done your duty as a wife. Now listen to me for your own good. Accept Ravana, king of the Rakshasas, as your husband. He’s strong and generous, like Indra among the gods—kind, charitable, and charming. Forget Rama, who’s lost everything. If you choose Ravana, you’ll be covered in precious perfumes and jewels, and become queen of the world, just like Sachi is to Indra or Svaha is to the fire god. Why waste your life on Rama, who has nothing and may not live long? If you refuse, we’ll eat you right here and now.”  

Next, a Rakshasi named Vikata, whose breasts hung down to her waist, clenched her fists and roared, “You foolish girl from Mithila, we’ve tolerated your nonsense only because you’re weak and pitiful. But if you don’t listen, it’ll be the end of you. You’re trapped here, across the ocean, in Ravana’s terrifying home, locked up and guarded by us. Even Indra couldn’t rescue you now. Listen to me: stop crying and let go of your useless sorrow. Be happy! Enjoy yourself with Ravana, lord of the Rakshasas. Youth doesn’t last forever, and while you still have it, you could live in pleasure, wandering through gardens and forests with him. Take Ravana as your husband and you’ll have thousands of maids at your service. If you don’t do as I say, I’ll rip out your heart and eat it.”  

Another Rakshasi, Chandodara, waving her dreadful spear, said, “Sita has the eyes of a frightened deer and her body is trembling. I’m pregnant, and all I can think about is devouring her—her eyes, liver, spleen, soft arms, heart, limbs, and head.”  

Then Praghasa, another demon woman, snarled, “I’ll crush her throat myself. What are you all waiting for? Once she’s dead, we’ll tell the king, and he’ll say, ‘Go ahead and eat her.’”  

Ajāmukhi, another Rakshasi, spoke up:

“I don’t want to fight about this. Let’s divide her up equally among us. Bring our favorite drinks and flower garlands!”  

Then Surpanakha added, “I completely agree with Ajāmukhi. Bring out the wine—it makes everything better. After feasting on human flesh, I’ll dance for Queen Nikumbhila!”  

Faced with all these terrifying threats from the hideous Rakshasis, Sita—who looked as beautiful and delicate as a daughter of the gods—couldn’t hold back her tears any longer. She broke down and wept.
SECTION XXV

The terrifying Rākshasees (demonesses) kept hurling harsh insults at her, making Sita, the daughter of King Janaka, break down in tears. Terrified by their words, Vaidehi (Sita), her voice trembling and choked with emotion, replied, “A woman can never be the wife of a Rākshasa. Go ahead and eat me if you want, but I will never listen to you.” Surrounded by the demonesses and threatened by Rāvana, Sita—who seemed almost otherworldly in her beauty—was overwhelmed with sadness and couldn’t calm herself. She trembled, shrinking away from them like a lost fawn surrounded by wolves. She clung to a flowering branch of an Ashoka tree, sinking deeper into her grief as she thought of her husband. Tears soaked her chest, and she was so weighed down by sorrow that she felt she would never escape her pain. Her body shook like a banana tree in the wind, and she collapsed to the ground, trembling. Her cheeks lost their usual color from fear of the Rākshasees, and even her long, beautiful hair shook, twisting like a restless snake. Overcome with grief and anger, the princess of Mithilā cried out in misery, “Mother Kausalyā! Queen Sumitra! The wise are right—death never comes before its time to anyone, man or woman. Otherwise, I would have died the moment I was separated from Rāma and attacked by these demons. My virtue must be weak, since I’m doomed to die alone and abandoned, like a boat tossed in the middle of a stormy sea. Kept from seeing my husband and tormented by these monsters, I’ll be destroyed by sorrow, just like riverbanks washed away by floods. Blessed are those who get to see my kind and gentle lord—Rāma, with his graceful walk and eyes like lotus petals! Separated from Rāma, it’s as hard for me to breathe as it would be for someone who’s swallowed deadly poison. What terrible sin did I commit in a past life to deserve this disaster? I want to end my suffering, but I’m trapped by the Rākshasees and can’t reach Rāma. Oh, how cursed is this human life, that we can’t even choose to end it when we want!”
SECTION XXVI

As she spoke, Sītā, the daughter of King Janaka, broke down in tears. Hanging her head, she wept openly, overcome by grief. She collapsed onto the ground, rolling and thrashing like a wild foal, as if she had lost her mind or was possessed. “I am Rāma’s wife,” she cried, “but after being lured away by that Rākshasa Māricha, who could change his shape, I was kidnapped and carried off by Rāvana. Now I’m a prisoner among the Rākshasas, tormented by their threats and jeers, trapped in sadness and fear. I don’t even want to go on living. What use are riches, jewelry, or even life itself, when I’m trapped here among these demons, cut off from Rāma, my mighty husband? My heart must be made of stone, unbreakable and cursed to endure, since it hasn’t shattered from this suffering. Shame on me! I must be unworthy and shameful if I can still breathe while separated from my lord. I could never even touch that night-dweller Rāvana—not even with my foot, let alone give in to his advances. He doesn’t understand himself, his own kind, or how much I despise him. There’s nothing more to say—I will never give in to Rāvana, even if he tears me apart or burns me alive. Rāghava (Rāma) is loyal, true, wise, and compassionate. It must be my bad luck that he hasn’t come for me yet. Did he not defeat thousands of Rākshasas at Janasthāna? I was taken by Rāvana, who isn’t even the strongest of his kind. My husband could easily kill him in battle. Didn’t Rāma defeat Virādha in Dandaka Forest? If anyone can reach Lankā—even though it’s surrounded by ocean—it’s Rāghava, with his fierce arrows. Why hasn’t he come for me yet? Maybe he doesn’t know I’m here—otherwise, as powerful as he is, he wouldn’t have let this outrage stand. The only one who could have told him—Jatāyu, the king of vultures—was killed by Rāvana. The old bird did everything he could for me, fighting to bring Rāvana down. If Rāghava knew I was here, he’d unleash his fury and wipe the Rākshasas off the face of the earth. He’d burn Lankā to the ground, dry up the sea, and erase Rāvana’s name forever. The cries of Rākshasa widows would echo from every ruined house, just like my own. With Lakshmana at his side, Rāma would destroy Lankā and leave no enemy standing. Soon, Lankā would look like a cemetery, its roads filled with smoke from funeral pyres and swarming with vultures. My wish will come true soon. My words may sound impossible now, but they spell out your doom. The bad omens I see around me show that Lankā’s days of glory are ending. When the evil Rāvana, lord of the Rākshasas, is dead, Lankā will be stripped of its riches and look like a widow. The city, once full of rituals and ceremonies, will become empty and lifeless after the Rākshasas and their leader are gone. I’ll hear the wailing of Rākshasa women mourning their husbands in every home. If Rāma, with his deep blue eyes, finds out I’m trapped in the Rākshasa’s lair, he’ll burn Lankā with his arrows. The city will fall into darkness and the Rākshasas will be destroyed. The deadline Rāvana set for me is here. That wicked monster has decided to destroy me now. There’s no crime the Rākshasas wouldn’t commit. But this crime will bring their ruin—these flesh-eating demons don’t even know what’s right or wrong. One of them might even eat me for breakfast. What am I supposed to do without my handsome husband? Separated from Rāma, drowning in sorrow, unable to see his blue eyes, I feel like death is close. Rāma, Bharata’s older brother, must not know I’m alive. Otherwise, he and Lakshmana would have searched the world to rescue me. Or maybe, overwhelmed by grief for me, Rāma has given up his life and gone to heaven. The gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and great sages are lucky—they get to see my heroic, lotus-eyed Rāma. Or maybe Rāma, wise and seeking righteousness, has left behind worldly troubles and no longer needs a wife like me. Or maybe people only care for what’s right in front of them, and forget about it once it’s gone. The ungrateful can abandon love, but not Rāma. Or maybe there’s some flaw in me—or maybe I’m just unlucky, and that’s why I’ve been separated from such a great man. I’d rather die than go on living apart from Rāma, that noble, heroic, and blameless man who destroys his enemies. Maybe the two brothers have put down their weapons and are just surviving on fruit and roots, wandering the forest. Or perhaps, by some trick, Rāma and Lakshmana have been killed by Rāvana, the evil lord of the Rākshasas. In this moment of despair, I long for death with all my heart—but even death won’t come to me. The truly blessed are the great sages who live by truth, control their senses, and have no attachments or hatred. They aren’t tormented by sorrow for loved ones or for those they dislike. They’re free from all that, and I bow to such souls. Abandoned by my beloved Rāma, powerless and at Rāvana’s mercy, I will end my life.”
SECTION XXVII

After Sita spoke to them in anger, some of the Rakshasi women, furious, went straight to Ravana to tell him what had happened. The other terrifying demons surrounded Sita again and started threatening her with harsh, cruel words. “You worthless Sita, you sinner, today we Rakshasis will tear you apart and eat your flesh until we’re satisfied!” As these horrible demons threatened Sita, an old and wise Rakshasi matron named Trijata stepped in. She shouted, “You vile creatures, if you’re so hungry, eat yourselves! Don’t touch Sita, daughter of Janaka and respected daughter-in-law of King Dasaratha. Last night, I had a terrifying dream that gave me chills. In that dream, I saw the fall of the Rakshasa race and the victory of her husband.” Hearing Trijata’s words, the other Rakshasis, both angry and scared, demanded, “Tell us about this dream you had last night!” Trijata began to describe her dream, which had come to her in the last part of the night: “I saw Rama, dressed in white and wearing garlands, riding in a divine chariot with Lakshmana. The chariot, made of ivory and pulled by a hundred horses, soared through the sky. In my dream, Sita appeared on a bright white hill by the ocean, dressed in pure white, finally reunited with Rama—like sunlight joining the sun itself. Then I saw Rama and Lakshmana glowing with their own light, sitting together on a massive elephant with four tusks, looking as strong as bulls. Those two brothers, shining like the sun, wearing white clothes and garlands, stood near Janaka’s daughter. Sita, with her lotus eyes, first fell into her husband’s lap, then climbed onto the elephant’s back, guided by Rama himself. I saw Sita, with both hands, reaching out to touch the Sun and the Moon. Then that great elephant, with the two princes and wide-eyed Sita riding on it, stood high above Lanka. Again, I saw Rama, in white and decked with flowers, riding beside Lakshmana in a chariot pulled by eight white bullocks. Once more, I saw Rama—the greatest of men, whose strength is his truth—along with Lakshmana and Sita, flying north in a heavenly, flower-covered chariot shining like the sun. 

Then I saw Ravana, his head shaved, oiled up, wearing red clothes and a garland of oleander flowers, fall from a flowered chariot to the ground. A woman, also shaved, dressed in red and covered with red powder, dragged Ravana as he rode in a chariot pulled by donkeys. Ravana drank oil, laughed wildly, and danced, totally out of his mind, speeding south on that chariot. Then I saw Ravana, lord of the Rakshasas, terrified, fall to the ground without a head. He suddenly got up and started shouting nonsense like a madman, overwhelmed with fear and confusion, only to fall again into a filthy, stinking pit that looked like hell itself. He then went further south and entered a lake with no water or mud. A dark woman, dressed in red and covered in mud, wound herself around his neck and dragged him down. After that, I saw the mighty Kumbhakarna and all Ravana’s sons, also shaved and oiled up, following him south—Ravana on a boar, Indrajit on a dolphin, and Kumbhakarna on a camel. I only saw Vibhishana, carrying a white umbrella and accompanied by four attendants, floating in the sky. Music and stringed instruments played in a large gathering. All the Rakshasas, dressed in red and wearing garlands, were drinking oil. The beautiful city of Lanka, with its horses, chariots, and elephants, was drowned in the ocean, its gates and decorated arches broken. The city was covered in dust, and Rakshasi women, laughing and making terrible noises, were drinking oil. I saw all the leading Rakshasas—Kumbhakarna and the others—dark-skinned, dressed in red, sinking into a pit of cow dung.

So I warn you: stay away from Sita, or you’ll all be destroyed when Raghava (Rama) comes to reclaim her. He won’t stand for his beloved wife being insulted and threatened by you demons. Stop using harsh words. Apologize to her and beg for forgiveness. That’s my advice. I truly believe Sita will soon be free from her troubles and reunited with her loving husband, just as I dreamed. You Rakshasis have threatened her—now beg for her forgiveness instead of taunting her. Disaster for the Rakshasas will come from Raghava. If Maithili, daughter of King Janaka, is pleased by your apology, maybe you’ll be spared. I see no sign of bad luck on this wide-eyed lady. She only looks pale because of her suffering. In my dream, I saw this noble woman, who doesn’t deserve such pain, standing in the sky. I’m certain Vaidehi’s (Sita’s) fate will be fulfilled, Ravana will be destroyed, and Raghava will win. Look! Sita’s left eye, wide as a lotus petal, is twitching with joy at hearing this good omen. Her left arm and her beautiful left thigh—strong as an elephant’s trunk—are all trembling with happiness, as if she’ll soon be reunited with Raghava. Birds are flying happily back to their nests again and again, singing loudly as if announcing a coming celebration.” Hearing all this, Sita was filled with hope for her husband’s victory and said,
“If your dream comes true, I promise I’ll save you all.”
SECTION XXVIII

When Sita heard Ravana’s harsh threats, she was overwhelmed with fear and sorrow for Rama. Surrounded by Rakshasi demonesses, she felt like a terrified young elephant cornered by a lion in the wild. Threatened and alone, Sita broke down, crying out like a girl lost and abandoned in a lonely forest. “It’s true what the wise say—death never comes before its time. Otherwise, how could I still be alive after all this, scared and threatened like this? My mind is full of misery, empty of happiness, yet somehow it hasn’t shattered—like a mountain top struck by lightning but still standing. Maybe I really am to blame, if I deserve to be killed by this ugly demon. But just as a Brahmin cannot teach the Vedas to those of other castes, I will never give my heart to Ravana.

If Rama doesn’t come to save me within the deadline, then this wretched demon king will hack me to pieces with his arrows, like a surgeon cutting apart an unborn child. Two months will pass in a blur, and then I’ll face a painful death, drowning in sorrow, just like a criminal locked in chains, waiting for the king’s order to be executed at dawn. Rama! Lakshmana! Sumitra! Rama’s mother! My mothers! I am lost in a sea of grief, tossed around like a boat in a stormy ocean.

I’m sure those two strong, lion-like sons of the king—Rama and Lakshmana—must have been killed by this demon, who first appeared in the form of a shining deer. I let myself get tricked by that magical deer, which was really death disguised, and that’s how I lost Rama and Lakshmana, the sons of my honored father-in-law. Oh Rama, man of your word, with long arms and a face like the full moon! My love, you’re always busy helping others, but do you even know I’m about to die at the hands of these Rakshasas? 

All my devotion as a wife, my patience, my sleeping on the bare ground, my religious vows—none of it matters now, just like kindness wasted on someone who’s ungrateful. My prayers and loyalty are pointless, since I can’t see you, and I’m pale and weak in your absence, with no hope of ever seeing you again. After fulfilling your father’s command and surviving the forest, you’ll return safely and enjoy the company of beautiful women with big eyes. But as for me, I ruined myself by loving you with all my heart and soul. My faithfulness and virtue have turned out to be worthless. Shame on me! I want to end my suffering quickly—with poison or a sharp weapon—but there’s no one here in this city of demons who would give me either.”

Crying out in despair, longing for Rama with all her heart, Sita’s face grew pale and she trembled. She walked over to the largest flowering tree. Gripped by grief, she grabbed her braid of hair, thinking, “I’ll hang myself with my hair and join the dead.” She moved toward the tree, held onto a branch, and thought of Rama, Lakshmana, and the honor of her family. Yet, on Sita’s body there were many auspicious signs—marks known for bringing hope and patience, and hinting that good fortune was still to come.
SECTION XXIX

As Sita sat there, still weighed down by sorrow and stripped of happiness, all sorts of good omens began to surround her, as if she were someone important with loyal attendants. Her large left eye, framed by thick lashes and dark pupils, started to twitch and dance—almost like a lotus flower quivering in a pond when a fish swims by. Her soft, round left hand—which once had been pampered with expensive sandalwood and aguru oil, and had often served as Rama’s pillow—began to twitch, too, moving again and again after a long time of stillness. Even her strong, shapely left thigh, which looked like an elephant’s trunk, started trembling, as if it was announcing that she would soon see Rama again. The golden cloth she wore, now dusty and faded, slipped slightly out of place on her body, revealing her teeth, white as pomegranate seeds. All these little signs, and others like them, gave Sita a sudden burst of hope, like a seed that had almost dried up in the sun and wind but springs back to life when the rains come. Her face, with lips as red as bimba fruit, lovely eyes, long eyebrows reaching toward her ears, curling lashes, and shining white teeth, became bright and beautiful again—like the moon reappearing after being hidden during an eclipse. Her sadness faded, her tiredness lifted, and she felt real happiness well up inside her. With her glowing face, Sita looked as radiant as a night lit by moonbeams.
SECTION XXX

Hanumān, strong and clever, listened closely as Sitā cried out her grief, heard about Trijata’s dream, and the threats from the Rākshasīs. Looking at Sitā—who seemed almost like a goddess trapped in the Ashoka grove—Hanumān felt a surge of worry and doubt. “After all this searching, finally my eyes have found her—the one countless monkeys have been looking for everywhere. Today I’ve seen her, while spying to figure out the enemy’s strength, sneaking around in secret. I’ve carefully observed the city of the Rākshasas and learned about Rāvana’s power. Now, my job is to comfort Rāma’s wife—a woman of remarkable strength and kindness—who is desperate for her husband. I have to console her, this woman with a face as bright as the full moon, who’s never known this much pain before and who might not come out of it anytime soon. If I leave without comforting her, when she’s nearly unconscious with grief, I’ll be failing my duty. And if I just go, the princess Jānaki (Sitā), seeing no hope, might actually decide to end her life. She deserves comfort, just like Rāma deserves to see Sitā again. But I can’t speak in front of the Rākshasas—so what should I do? I’m really stuck here. If I don’t say something before the night ends, she might give up on life. How can I face Rāma if I return without comforting Sitā, especially if he asks, “What news of my Sitā?” If I just rush back without any word from her, Kākutstha (another name for Rāma) might burn me up with his angry glare. And if I try to get Vibhīṣaṇa (the king on our side) to attack with his army, all his effort will be wasted. I have to wait for a moment when she’s alone, free from her demon guards, so I can comfort her in her darkest hour. But if I, a little monkey, speak in Sanskrit—the fancy language used by scholars—Sitā might think I’m Rāvana in disguise. So I should speak in everyday language, or else I won’t be able to calm her down. But even then, seeing a monkey talking like a human might scare her even more, since she’s already been terrorized by the Rākshasas. She might just think I’m Rāvana, who can change his shape, and start screaming for help. If she makes a sudden noise, those terrifying Rākshasīs—who look like death itself and are armed with all kinds of weapons—will rush over. If they spot me, they’ll try to capture or kill me. If they see me jumping from branch to branch, they’ll panic and shout for the other demon guards. Soon, the whole place will be swarming with Rākshasas, all armed and ready to attack. If I’m surrounded and forced to fight, even if I defeat some, I might be too tired to escape across the ocean. If they capture me, my whole mission fails, and Sitā will never know why I came. Or worse, the cruel Rākshasas might kill Sitā—and then Rāma and Sugrīva’s whole plan will fall apart. This place is hidden, surrounded by the ocean and guarded on all sides by demons—it’s almost impossible to reach. If I die or get caught, who else will help Rāma? No other monkey can leap a hundred leagues over the sea like I did. Sure, I can take on thousands of Rākshasas, but then I’d never make it back across the ocean. Battles can go either way—win or lose—so why risk everything on a fight I might not survive? Who would risk a sure thing for something so uncertain? Honestly, it’s risky even to talk to Sitā, but if I don’t, she might die. When a nearly finished mission gets handed to someone careless, it usually gets ruined—like night vanishing when the sun comes up. Important jobs, no matter how well-planned, often get wrecked by messengers who think they know everything. What can I do to make sure my mission succeeds, I don’t look foolish, and my journey here isn’t wasted? How can I talk to Sitā so she believes me, without terrifying her?” After thinking hard about all this, Hanumān finally made up his mind.

“I shouldn’t just blurt out Rāma’s name all of a sudden—he’s so dear to her, and she’s so devoted, it might shock her. Instead, I’ll gently mention Rāma—the greatest of the Ikshwāku line—and praise his goodness and fame in a way she’ll trust.” With these thoughts, Hanumān, still perched on the tree branch, began to speak to Sitā in a soft and reassuring voice.
SECTION XXXI

As he thought carefully about his next steps, the clever monkey spoke in a gentle, clear voice that Vaidehi (Sita) could hear. “There once was a noble and righteous king named Dasharatha, famous among the Ikshwaku dynasty. He was the master of chariots, horses, and elephants. He had no jealousy in his heart, was generous, honest, and kind, the greatest of the Ikshwakus. He was wealthy, made others prosperous, and carried the marks of a true king. He was handsome, respected by other rulers, and known throughout the world, bringing happiness to his people and enjoying happiness himself. 

His oldest and most beloved son was Rama—wise, as radiant as the moon, and the best at the art of archery. Rama always protected his own morals, his family, the world, and all that was good. He defeated his enemies and followed his father’s word, even when it meant being banished to the forest. With him went his wife, Sita, and his loyal brother Lakshmana. While living in the woods, Rama defeated many powerful Rakshasas—demons who could change their forms at will. 

After hearing about the destruction of the Rakshasas at Janasthana, and the deaths of Khara and Dushana, the tricky Ravana, who could also change his form, used deception to kidnap Rama’s wife, Janaka’s daughter. Rama searched everywhere for the innocent and worshipped Sita, and in his search, he became close friends with Sugriva. After helping Sugriva defeat Vali, Rama crowned him king of the monkeys. By Sugriva’s order, thousands of monkeys with the power to change their shape have been searching for Sita in all directions. 

On Sampati’s advice, and for the sake of Sita, I crossed the ocean in one leap—a hundred leagues. Now, I have found her. And she matches the description of her looks, grace, and signs that Rama gave me.” 

Having finished his story, Hanuman (the monkey) fell silent. Sita listened in amazement to his words. The shy woman with beautiful curly hair slowly lifted her face, brushing her hair aside, and looked up into the branches of the Singshapa tree. She listened to the monkey’s message and looked all around, her heart filling with joy as she thought of Rama. Looking up and around, she finally saw, like the rising sun, Hanuman—the son of the Wind God, with a mind beyond imagination, and the trusted advisor of the monkey king.
SECTION XXXII

When Sita saw the golden-brown monkey, wearing a white cloth and hidden up in the tree, her mind was thrown into turmoil. The monkey looked humble and spoke in a gentle voice, and his appearance was striking—like a cluster of fully-bloomed Ashoka flowers, with eyes shining like molten gold. As Sita watched this impressive monkey quietly sitting there, she became even more amazed, thinking, "This monkey must be the fiercest of his kind—so strong and dangerous that he’s hard to approach or even look at." This thought filled her with fear again. Overcome by sorrow, she cried out softly, "Oh Rama! Oh Lakshmana!" and then wept quietly to herself. 

But as she watched the monkey come towards her in a respectful way, the princess of Mithila wondered, "Am I dreaming right now?" She looked again at the son of the Wind God—Hanuman—the smartest and bravest of the monkeys, with his unusual, slightly odd face, and the same simple clothes as before. Seeing him, Sita was so frightened she could hardly breathe. But after a moment, she managed to calm herself a little, and thought, "I must be having a bad dream—sages say that seeing a monkey in a dream is a bad sign. I hope Rama, Lakshmana, and my father, King Janaka, will be safe." 

Then she realized, "But this can’t be a dream—I haven’t slept at all, my mind is too troubled and sad. Since Rama left, I haven’t found even a moment of happiness. I’m always thinking about him, and everything I see or hear somehow reminds me of him. That’s why his image keeps appearing in my mind, making my pain even worse, because I’m trapped in thoughts of him. I keep seeing him in front of me and hearing his voice. Maybe this monkey is just a trick of my imagination. But even as I tell myself that, I still see him so clearly. An illusion shouldn’t have such a real form. Yet here is this monkey, speaking to me directly." 

She closed her eyes for a moment and prayed, "May the gods—Vachaspati, Indra, self-born Brahma, and Agni—grant that this being who stands before me is truly real, and not just a figment of my imagination."
SECTION XXXIII

Hanumān, the radiant son of the Wind God, climbed down from the tree. His face glowed a deep red, and he wore simple, humble clothes. With respect, he approached Sitā, joined his hands in greeting, and spoke to her in a gentle voice: “Who are you, you with eyes like lotus petals and a worn silk dress, sitting here clinging to a branch? Why are you crying, your tears falling like drops from a lotus? Are you a goddess, or one of the Asuras, Nāgas, Gandharvas, Rākshasas, Yakshas, or Kinnaras? Were you born from the Rudras, the storm-riding gods, or maybe the Vasus? You look like someone from the heavens. Are you Rohini, the brightest star, who has been cast down from the sky, separated from the Moon? Or are you the pure Arundhati, angry or hurt and gone from your husband Vashishtha’s side? Tell me, whose loss are you mourning—a son, father, brother, or husband who has died? But from your tears, your sighs, the ground you walk on, and how you call out a king’s name, I think you’re not a goddess. Still, from your features, you must be the wife or daughter of a king. Are you Sitā—the one Rāvana kidnapped and carried away from Janasthāna? I hope you are safe. From your desperate state, your beauty, and your simple clothes, I am sure you must be Rāma’s queen.” 

Hearing Hanumān’s words, and thrilled to hear Rāma’s name, Sitā replied, “I am the daughter-in-law of Daçaratha, who truly knows himself, the greatest of kings, and a destroyer of his enemies. I am also the daughter of Janaka, the wise king of Videha. My name is Sitā, and I am the wife of Rāma, who is known for his intelligence. I lived for twelve years in Rāma’s home, enjoying every comfort and happiness. At the start of the thirteenth year, the king, following his priest’s advice, began to arrange for Rāma, the Ikswaku prince, to be crowned. But as the preparations were happening, Queen Kaikeyi told her husband, ‘I won’t eat or drink for days, and I will die if Rāma is crowned. If you care about the promise you made to me, please send Rāma to the forest instead.’ The king, always true to his word, was devastated by Kaikeyi’s harsh demand. Still, remembering his vow, the old king, in tears, begged his oldest son to give up the throne. 

Rāma respected his father’s wishes even more than the idea of being king. He promised to obey and never broke his word. Rāma is honest to the core—he never goes back on his promises, never lies, and always tells the truth. He gave up his royal clothes, left the kingdom behind, and handed me over to his mother. But I dressed in simple clothes like an ascetic and quickly joined him. I couldn’t bear to be separated from him, not even in heaven. Lakshmana (the son of Sumitrā), who always supports his friends, also dressed simply and followed his older brother. So, following our father’s orders, the three of us took vows and entered a wild, unfamiliar forest. While Rāma, shining with virtue, lived in the Dandaka forest, I was kidnapped by the evil Rākshasa, Rāvana. He’s given me two months to live—after that, he says he will kill me.
SECTION XXXIV
Hearing Sitā’s grief-filled words, Hanumān—the bravest and cleverest of the monkeys—answered her gently, trying to calm her down.

“Lady,” Hanumān said, “I’m here as a messenger from Rāma, sent by his command. He’s safe, Vaidehi (Sitā), and he sends his love and asks how you’re doing. Rāma, son of Daçaratha, master of the Vedas and greatest among those who know the Vedas, wants to know that you’re well. Lakshmana, your brother-in-law and Rāma’s loyal companion, is also thinking of you; he’s worn out with worry and sends you his deep respect.” Hearing that both Rāma and Lakshmana were safe, Sitā felt a rush of joy, as if she were reunited with them in person. They started talking more openly. As Hanumān moved closer to Sitā, trying to reassure her, her suspicion grew—she worried he might actually be Rāvana in disguise. “Oh no, why did I talk to him? This must be Rāvana, using another trick to fool me!” Sitā, overwhelmed by fear and sadness, let go of the Asoka branch she was clinging to and sat on the ground. Hanumān respectfully bowed to her, but she was so scared that she couldn’t bring herself to look at him again. Watching Hanumān bow, Sitā, her face as pale as the moon, let out a weary sigh and spoke softly: “If you’re Rāvana again, using magic to change your shape and torment me, it’s cruel and beneath you. I remember seeing you as a fake beggar at Janasthāna—always changing your form. It’s wrong of you to keep torturing me, especially when I’m so weak and hungry. But then again, you can’t be the one I suspect, because seeing you has brought me hope. If you really are Rāma’s messenger, may good fortune find you. Please, tell me something about Rāma that will lift my spirits. Tell me about my beloved Rāma’s greatness. You’re stirring up my emotions, Hanumān, like a river overflowing its banks. Just seeing you, after being apart from my husband for so long, fills me with happiness—as if I’m dreaming. I wish I could see Rāma and Lakshmana in a dream, but even my dreams seem determined to keep me miserable. But this doesn’t feel like a dream. Seeing a monkey in a dream is supposed to be unlucky, but meeting you has given me hope. Maybe I’m just losing my mind? Or possessed by a demon? Or maybe I’m just seeing a mirage, like sunlight on hot sand? No, I’m not mad—if I were, I’d be confused, but my mind is clear. I know I’m here, and you’re here.” As she thought about all this, Sitā tried to figure out whether Hanumān was truly a friend or an enemy in disguise. After thinking it over, she decided Hanumān might be Rāvana tricking her again, so she stopped talking to him. Hanumān realized what Sitā was thinking, so he tried to win her trust back with words that were gentle and full of hope: “Rāma is as bright as the sun, as beloved as the moon, and as generous as Kubera, the god of wealth. He’s as strong as the famous god Vishnu, always honest and speaks kindly, like the great teacher Vāchaspati. He’s handsome, graceful, and beautiful like the celestial musician Kandarva. He only gets angry at the right times—he’s truly the best of men and a mighty warrior. The whole world feels safe under his protection. You’ll soon see what happens to the one who, disguised as a deer, led Rāma away and kidnapped you. Rāma will destroy Rāvana in battle with his blazing arrows. Rāma sent me to you as his messenger. In your absence, he’s been miserable and continually asks how you’re doing. Lakshmana, who brings joy to his mother Sumitrā, also bows to you in respect. The king of the monkeys, Sugriva—Rāma’s friend—also asks about your well-being. Rāma, Sugriva, and Lakshmana are always thinking of you, Sitā. We’re grateful you’re still alive, even after all you’ve suffered among these demons. Soon, you’ll see Rāma, Lakshmana, and Sugriva, along with the whole army of monkeys. I am Hanumān, Sugriva’s minister. I crossed the ocean to get to this city of Lanka, and with my own power I’ve come here, stepping over Rāvana’s pride, just to see you. I’m not the one you fear, Lady. Please, let go of your doubts and trust me.”
SECTION XXXV

After hearing Hanumān, the best among monkeys, tell Rāma’s story, Sītā (also called Vaidehi) spoke to him in a gentle, soft voice: “Where did you meet Rāma? How did you get to know Lakshmana? How did the monkeys and humans become allies? Please, monkey, tell me again about the royal marks and qualities of Rāma and Lakshmana. Describe Rāma’s looks for me—the shape of his thighs and arms, and Lakshmana’s too—so I can let go of my sorrow.” Hearing this, Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, began to describe Rāma in detail. “Since you, with your lotus-like eyes, want to hear about your husband through me, his messenger, I will tell you everything about Rāma and Lakshmana. Listen, great-eyed lady, as I describe the royal features I noticed on both of them. Rāma’s eyes are shaped like lotus petals, and his face glows like the full moon. He is incredibly handsome and good-hearted. He shines like the sun, is as patient as the earth, as wise as Brihaspati (the guru of the gods), and as famous as Indra (Vāsava). He protects the world and his own people. He always does what’s right, never strays from his royal duties, and defeats his enemies.

Rāma honors people of all four castes, gives them respect, and keeps them safe. He is worshipped by everyone like the sun. He follows strict vows, understands when to honor holy men, and knows the right way to do things. He is well-versed in royal responsibilities and listens to the advice of Brahmins. He is wise, has great character, is humble, and is a powerful warrior. He is a master of the Yajur Veda and respected by Vedic scholars. He is skilled in archery, the Vedas, and their branches. Rāma has broad shoulders, long arms, a neck shaped like a conch, and a beautiful face. His throat is strong and his eyes are red. He is famous everywhere as Rāma.

His voice is loud and clear, his complexion is cool and green, and he is extremely strong. His body is perfectly proportioned. Three parts of him—his thigh, fist, and wrist—are hard. Three others—his brow, arms, and scrotum—are long. The hair on his head, his scrotum, and his knee joints are all equal in size, and three parts—his navel, abdomen, and chest—are prominent. His eye corners, nails, and palms are coppery; three parts are cool to the touch; and his voice, navel, and walk are deep. His belly and throat have three folds of skin. The soles of his feet, the lines on them, and his nipples are evenly curved. His neck, eyes, and back are short. He has three locks of hair on his head. Four lines on his thumb show his mastery of the four Vedas. He’s four handspans tall; his arms, thighs, and cheeks are full and strong. Everything—his eyebrows, nostril hollows, eyes, ears, lips, nipples, wrists, knees, scrotum, hips, hands, and feet—are perfectly balanced. Four teeth on each side of each row have auspicious marks from the scriptures. He walks like a lion, tiger, elephant, or bull. His lips and jaws are thick and stand out; his nose is long; his words, face, nails, hair, and skin are all cool. Both his arms, pinky fingers, thighs, and legs are long. His face, eyes, mouth, tongue, lips, palate, nipples, nails, and feet are all like lotuses. His chest, forehead, neck, arms, navel, feet, back, and ears are broad. Rāma is graceful, famous, and radiant. His family, on both his mother’s and father’s sides, is noble. His armpits, belly, chest, nose, shoulders, and forehead are prominent. His fingers, hair, skin, beard, eyesight, and mind are sharp and keen.

Rāma divides his time wisely between religious duties, earning wealth, seeking liberation, and fulfilling desires. He is truthful, graceful, and uses his wealth to protect his people. He understands time and place, and everyone loves him. His brother Lakshmana (also called Saumitri) is incredibly strong and matches him in loyalty, looks, and abilities. Lakshmana’s skin is golden, while Rāma is famously green. Both of them, these two “lions among men,” wanted nothing but to find you. Searching the world for you, they met us in the forest.

While searching, they found Sugriva, a handsome monkey king hiding at the foot of the tree-covered Mount Rishyamuka, after being exiled by his older brother Vāli. We were helping Sugriva, who had lost his kingdom to his brother. When Sugriva saw Rāma and Lakshmana—dressed in bark and carrying bows—he got scared and jumped to the top of the hill. Then he sent me to talk to them. On Sugriva’s orders, I approached Rāma and Lakshmana with my hands joined in respect. They were pleased when I explained everything. I carried both of them on my back up the hill and introduced them to Sugriva. The two pairs—Rāma and Lakshmana, Sugriva and me—talked and became friends, sharing their troubles and comforting each other.

Rāma consoled Sugriva, who had been driven away by his powerful brother Vāli over a fight about his wife. Then Lakshmana told Sugriva about Rāma’s pain because you had been taken by Rāvana. When Sugriva heard Lakshmana, he turned pale, like the sun covered by a dark shadow. The monkey leaders collected all the jewelry you dropped while you were being carried away, and they brought it to Rāma, hoping it would help find you. I gathered those ornaments myself when they fell to the ground and gave them to Rāma, who was overwhelmed with grief. He put them in his lap and broke down, crying out in pain. His sorrow only grew worse. He collapsed to the ground, unable to bear it. I comforted him with gentle words and helped him get up again. Rāma and Lakshmana looked over your jewelry many times, then Rāma handed them to Sugriva.

Rāma is burning with sadness without you, like a volcano with an endless fire inside. Your absence causes him sleepless nights, grief, and worry—like three separate fires burning him down. He is shaken by your loss, like a huge mountain hit by an earthquake. He wanders through beautiful forests, rivers, and springs, but nothing brings him joy. But soon, O daughter of King Janaka, Rāma will destroy Rāvana and his family, and win you back.

That’s how Rāma and Sugriva formed their alliance—to defeat Vāli and to help search for you. After returning to Kishkindhā with Rāma and Lakshmana, Sugriva killed Vāli in battle. With Vāli gone, Rāma made Sugriva king over all monkeys and bears. This is how Rāma and Sugriva became allies. And I am Hanumān, their messenger, sent to you. Once Sugriva regained his kingdom, he gathered all the powerful monkeys and sent them in every direction to search for you. These great monkeys, as big as mountains, set out to all corners of the earth. Fearing Sugriva’s orders, they have been searching everywhere for you—and I am one of them.

Angada, Vāli’s strong and noble son, led three armies in the search. We spent many days and nights lost in grief on the slopes of Mount Vindhya, running out of time and hope. Afraid of failing Sugriva, we even considered ending our own lives. We searched mountains, rivers, and springs, but couldn’t find you, so we prepared to give up. On top of the hill, we began fasting, ready to die. Seeing us in despair, Angada cried for you, for Vāli’s death, for our suffering, and for the death of Jatāyu. As we waited for death, having lost all hope, suddenly a mighty vulture appeared—Sampāti, the brother of Jatāyu.

When Sampāti heard that his brother had died, he became angry and asked, “Who killed my younger brother, and where? Tell me, you monkeys.” Angada told him all about Jatāyu’s death at Janasthāna, killed by the demon who took you. Hearing about Jatāyu’s death, Sampāti, son of Aruṇa, was filled with sorrow, but he told us, beautiful lady, that you were being kept in Rāvana’s home. Sampāti’s words lifted our spirits, and we all, led by Angada, left that place. We jumped from the top of Mount Vindhya and reached the edge of the ocean. Eager to find you, those strong monkeys arrived at the shore, but when they saw the ocean, their courage failed. I reassured them, then leaped a hundred leagues over the sea and entered Lankā at night, a city full of demons. I have seen Rāvana, and I have seen you, suffering and sad. I have told you everything, step by step. Please speak to me, noble lady—I am Rāma’s messenger. Know that I am the son of the Wind-god, a counselor to Sugriva, and I have come here for you.

Rāma, the greatest warrior, and Lakshmana—who is marked with all good signs, always honors his elders, and cares deeply for Rāma—are both safe and well. Sugriva sent me alone to find you. I can travel alone and change my form at will, which is how I reached this southern land to search for you. By good fortune, I’ll be able to bring your news to the monkeys who are worried about you. I’m lucky that my leap over the sea was not in vain. I’ll be celebrated for finding you, and soon Rāma will destroy Rāvana and his followers and win you back.

There is a mountain called Mālyavān, the best of all hills. My father, the great monkey Kesari, lives there. At the request of holy sages, he once traveled to Mount Gokarna and at the sacred river destroyed the demon Samvasādana. That’s where I was born, O Vaidehi. I am known across the world as Hanumān because of my deeds. I’ve told you about Rāma’s greatness to earn your trust. And I promise, soon Rāma will take you back.”

Hearing all this and seeing the proof, Sītā realized Hanumān truly was Rāma’s messenger. Overcome with happiness, she began to cry tears of joy. Her beautiful, wide-eyed face shone like the moon freed from an eclipse. She now believed Hanumān was indeed a real monkey and no one else. Then Hanumān, who had a noble appearance, spoke again: “I have told you everything, Maithilee. Please try to be comforted. Now tell me—what do you want me to do next? I’ll leave soon. When my father, the great monkey, killed the demon Samvasādana for the sages, I was born from the Wind-god, Maithilee. I might look like a monkey, but I have power to match him.”
SECTION XXXVI

Hanumān, the bright and powerful son of the Wind-god, wanted to reassure Sitā, so he spoke to her again: “O great lady, I am a monkey—Rāma’s messenger. Look at this ring with Rāma’s name engraved on it. Your noble husband gave it to me to bring to you, so you’d know you can trust me. Take heart—good things are coming, and your suffering will end soon.” When Jānaki (Sitā) saw the ring, the same one that used to be on Rāma’s finger, it was as if she had her husband right there with her. Her beautiful face, with its large eyes, lit up with joy, just like the moon emerging from behind an eclipse. Overjoyed to finally have news of her husband, Sitā warmly welcomed Hanumān and praised him: “O best of monkeys, you are brave, strong, and wise. You’ve managed to invade the home of the Rākshasas all on your own. With your amazing strength, you leaped a hundred leagues across the ocean, ignoring the sea monsters below as if the ocean was just a puddle. I don’t think you’re just an ordinary monkey—no one else would dare to face Rāvana without fear. You deserve my respect, because Rāma, who truly knows people, has sent you. Rāma—so hard to reach—wouldn’t have chosen you for this task if you hadn’t already proven your strength. 

By my good fortune, is everything alright with Rāma, who is virtuous and truthful, and with Lakshmana, who brings joy to Sumitrā? If Kākuthstha (Rāma) is safe, then why hasn’t he burned this whole earth in his anger, like the fire that destroys the world? I know he could defeat even the gods in battle, but maybe my bad luck means my troubles aren’t over yet. Is Rāma in great pain? Does he grieve for me? Is he preparing to rescue me? Or has fear and despair made him forget his mission? Is he still acting bravely? Is he, who defeats his enemies and rewards his friends, still doing all he can—making alliances, sowing discord among his enemies, and using every strategy? Are more friends joining him? Is he honoring his friends and are they honoring him? Is he praying for the blessings of the gods? Has he found inner strength and help from the gods? Has Rāghava stopped caring about me because we’re apart? Will he save me from this disaster? Rāma has always known happiness and not much suffering—has this disaster broken him? Does he keep track of how Kausalya, Sumitrā, and Bharata are doing? Is Rāghava so overwhelmed by grief at my absence that he can’t think straight? Will Rāma come to save me? Will Bharata, who loves his brother, send an army of fierce soldiers to rescue me? Will the noble Sugriva, king of the monkeys, come with his monkey army to help me? Will Lakshmana, who’s a master of weapons and brings joy to Sumitrā, burn down the Rākshasas with his arrows? Will I soon see Rāvana and his kin destroyed in battle by Rāma’s terrifying weapons? Is Rāma’s golden, lotus-scented face dried out and sad because I’m gone, like a lotus wilting in shallow water under the sun? Does he still have patience—the man who gave up his kingdom for what’s right, and walked with me into the forest without fear or sadness? His love for his mother or father isn’t even equal to his love for me. O messenger, I will keep living as long as I hear news of my beloved.” After saying these heartfelt and tender words to Hanumān, Sitā fell silent, hoping to hear more about Rāma from him.

Hearing Sitā’s words, the mighty Hanumān (also called Māruti) put his hands together and bowed his head. He said, “Rāma doesn’t know you’re here—that’s the only reason he hasn’t rescued you yet, just like Purandara (Indra) once rescued his wife Sachi. But once he hears from me, Rāghava (Rāma) will come here right away, bringing a massive army of monkeys and bears. He’ll hold back the ocean itself—building a bridge with his arrows—and storm into Lanka, wiping out all the Rākshasas. Rāma will destroy them, even if the gods or Death himself tries to stop him. O noble lady, Rāma is suffering in your absence. He’s as restless as an elephant wounded by a lion. I swear to you, by the mountains Mandāra, Malaya, Vindhya, Sumeru, and Dardura, and by all fruits and roots, that you’ll soon see Rāma’s face again—handsome, with eyes like lotuses, lips like ripe fruit, and beautiful earrings—just like seeing the full moon rise. Soon, Vaidehi, you’ll see Rāma atop Mount Prasravana, shining like the king of the gods on his elephant Airavata.
