Climbing up the huge building, Hanumān, the leader of the monkey army, seemed to shine like a second sun rising in the sky. Then, with unstoppable strength, he smashed the magnificent building. His energy was blazing, making him look as grand as the legendary Pariyātra mountain. Growing even larger through his power, Hanumān fearlessly pounded his chest with his fists, filling all of Lanka with the booming sound.

The noise from Hanumān’s chest-beating was so loud it could almost deafen anyone nearby. Birds dropped from the sky, and even the guards of the temple collapsed, overwhelmed by the shock. Hanumān shouted, “Victory to Rama, master of weapons! And to Lakshmana, who has incredible strength! And victory to King Sugriva, protected by Rama! I, Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, destroyer of enemy armies, am Rama’s devoted servant. Not even a thousand Ravanas could fight me if I start throwing stones and trees by the thousands. I will destroy Lanka, pay my respects to Sita, and, having accomplished my mission, leave in full view of all the Rakshasas.”

After saying this, Hanumān, massive and intimidating, sat on the Chaitya and let out a thunderous roar that sent terror through the hearts of the Rakshasas. His cry was so fierce that a hundred temple guards rushed out, armed with all sorts of weapons—spears, curved swords, and axes. They surrounded Hanumān, who kept growing in size. They attacked him with maces, axes, golden armlets, and arrows that shone like the sun. The swarm of Rakshasas attacking Hanumān looked like a huge and wild whirlpool in the Ganga river.

Enraged, Hanumān—the mighty son of the Wind-god—ripped a massive gold-plated pillar with a hundred designs from the temple and began to swing it through the air. The fire that broke out from this act quickly set the entire building ablaze. When Hanumān saw the temple burning, he killed the hundred Rakshasas, just as Indra once destroyed the Asuras with his thunderbolt. Hovering in the sky, Hanumān declared, “Thousands of powerful, skilled, and heroic monkeys just like me have been created and serve under Sugriva. We—along with countless others—are spread all over the world. Some monkeys have the strength of ten elephants, some a hundred, some a thousand, and some even more. Some are as fast and strong as the wind, and some have strength beyond measure. With such monkeys—armed with just their claws and teeth, numbering in the hundreds, thousands, millions (kotis), and tens of millions (ayutas)—Sugriva, the destroyer of enemies, will come. Neither Lanka, nor you, nor even Ravana, will survive if you make an enemy of that great hero from the Ikshvaku dynasty.”
SECTION XLIV

Following the orders of Ravana, the lord of the Rakshasas, Prahasta’s son Jamvumali stepped out to fight. Jamvumali was huge and intimidating, with large teeth, swirling eyes, and an unstoppable presence. He wore a bright red outfit with a matching wreath, a garland around his neck, and stylish earrings. Jamvumali’s bow looked as impressive as Indra’s own weapon, and when he pulled it back, it thundered through the air like a storm. The sound of his bowstring echoed everywhere, filling the sky and all directions with deafening noise.

Hanuman, full of energy and confidence, saw Jamvumali approaching in a chariot pulled by donkeys. Excited, Hanuman let out a loud shout. Jamvumali, full of power, immediately fired sharp arrows at Hanuman, who was sitting on a crooked wooden plank at the gate, which pigeons used as a perch. Jamvumali’s arrows struck Hanuman’s face with crescent-shaped tips, wounded his head with a hook-tipped arrow, and hit his arms with ten more arrows. Despite being hit, Hanuman’s copper-red face looked striking, almost like a red lotus in autumn sunlight. The blood only made his naturally red features more vivid, glowing like a red ashoka flower touched by honey.

Stung by the arrows, Hanuman’s anger flared. He quickly spotted a massive rock nearby, tore it from the ground, and hurled it at Jamvumali with all his strength. But Jamvumali countered by shooting ten arrows at the flying rock, shattering it. Hanuman, seeing his attack fail, grabbed a huge sala tree, ripped it up, and swung it around in the air. Jamvumali, not backing down, fired several arrows. He cut the sala tree apart with four arrows, struck Hanuman’s arm with five more, hit his chest with one, and shot ten arrows into his torso.

Now covered in arrows and burning with rage, Hanuman grabbed the same heavy wooden plank and spun it furiously. With incredible force, he hurled it straight at Jamvumali’s chest. The blow was so powerful that, in an instant, Jamvumali’s head, arms, thighs, bow, chariot, horses, and arrows simply vanished from the scene. Jamvumali, the mighty warrior, was killed instantly and crashed to the ground like a tree with its trunk smashed.

Hearing that Jamvumali and his strongest fighters had been slaughtered, Ravana was consumed with fury. His eyes turned blood-red with anger. With the powerful son of Prahasta dead, the lord of the rakshasas, his eyes wild with rage, quickly ordered the sons of his counselors—warriors with enormous energy and power—to go out and take on Hanuman in battle.
SECTION XLV

Following the orders of the lord of the Rākshasas (Rāvaṇa), seven sons of his top advisors—each one as impressive as fire—marched out of his palace. They were surrounded by a massive army, armed with bows and skilled in battle. All were eager for victory. They rode in huge chariots pulled by horses, with gold decorations, flags, and banners, and the rumbling of their wheels sounded like thunder. These warriors, with their gold-adorned bows drawn, looked like storm clouds full of lightning as they charged into battle. When the mothers, friends, and families of the servants who had been killed heard the news, they were overwhelmed with grief.

The seven warriors, each trying to outdo the others, all glittering in polished gold jewelry, came face-to-face with Hanumān, who was standing by the gate. Their chariots roared as they poured arrows at Hanumān, moving across the battlefield like dark rain clouds during a storm. The showers of arrows hid Hanumān from sight, just as heavy rain hides a mountain.

But Hanumān, fast and agile, jumped through the clear sky, dodging both the arrows and the charging chariots. He seemed to be toying with the warriors, like the playful wind messing with rain clouds. Suddenly, Hanumān let out a terrifying shout that echoed across the battlefield, striking fear into the hearts of the entire army. Then, bursting with energy, he attacked the Rākshasa army.

Hanumān defeated some of the Rākshasas with powerful slaps, tore others apart with his nails, crushed some with his fists, and smashed others with the force of his chest. Some even fell dead on the spot just from the sound of his yell. As more and more of them were killed or collapsed to the ground, the rest of the army panicked and ran in every direction.

The elephants wailed in terror, and horses collapsed to the ground. The battlefield was littered with shattered chests, broken flagpoles, umbrellas, and even the smashed remains of the chariots. Rivers of blood flowed across the land, and cries of fear echoed throughout Lankā.
After destroying these gigantic Rākshasas, Hanumān—now even more determined and eager for another fight—returned to the same entrance, ready to face whatever Rākshasas might come next.
SECTION XLVI

When Rāvaṇa—the Ten-necked king—heard that the sons of his counselors had been killed by the powerful monkey, he forced himself to stay calm, pushing down his fear and regaining control of his mind. He then called for five of his top generals: the brave Virupāksha, Yupāksha, the demon Durdharsha, Praghasa, and Māsakarna. These leaders were known for their sharp minds, lightning speed in battle, and readiness for any situation. Rāvaṇa ordered them to capture Hanumān alive. “You commanders, take a massive army with horses, elephants, and chariots. Punish that monkey. When you reach him—he lives in the forest—stay alert and plan carefully, adapting to the situation. Based on what he’s done, I doubt he’s just a regular monkey. He must be some great being with incredible power. Honestly, I can’t believe he’s just a monkey. Maybe Indra created him by magic just to hurt us. With your help, I’ve defeated gods, Nāgas, Yakshas, Gandharvas, Asuras, and great sages before. This feels like one of their tricks. So don’t hesitate—capture him by force. And remember: take a huge army with horses, elephants, and chariots. Don’t underestimate this monkey; he’s not ordinary. I’ve seen powerful monkeys before—Vāli, Sugrīva, the mighty Jāmbavān, Nila the general, and others led by Dwivida. None of them had speed, power, intellect, or shape-shifting skills like this one. So treat him as something more than a monkey. Do whatever it takes to defeat him. Even the combined forces of gods, mortals, and demons couldn’t stand against you for long in battle. Still, a wise leader should protect himself because victory in war can be unpredictable.” Fired up by their king’s words, the five generals charged out, leading an army packed with chariots, wild elephants, fast horses, sharp weapons, and every kind of troop.

They soon spotted Hanumān, the radiant and mighty monkey, sitting at the gate. He shone with his natural power, like the sun at sunrise—strong, fast, and noble-minded. As soon as they saw him, his appearance terrified them, and they attacked with their deadliest weapons. Durdharsha fired five white iron arrows with golden tips, each shining like a lotus leaf, aiming straight at Hanumān’s head. The arrows struck him, but Hanumān only roared in pain and leapt high into the sky, his voice echoing in every direction.

Then Durdhara, a fierce and skilled fighter, rode forward in a chariot, his bow ready, unleashing hundreds of arrows at Hanumān. But just as the wind scatters storm clouds at the end of the rainy season, Hanumān, still in the sky, dodged and blocked Durdhara’s attacks. Pressed hard by Durdhara, Hanumān let out another mighty roar and grew even larger in size. Shooting far up into the sky, Hanumān suddenly plunged down onto Durdhara’s chariot with the force of a lightning bolt crashing into a mountain. The crash smashed the chariot’s wheels and pole, killing all eight horses. Durdhara was thrown from the wreckage and hit the ground, dead.

Seeing Durdhara fall, Virupāksha and Yupāksha—fierce warriors who never backed down—became enraged and jumped into the fight. They lunged at Hanumān, swinging heavy maces at his chest as he hovered in the clear sky. Hanumān, facing their wild assault, dropped to the ground as fast as the legendary Garuda bird swooping down. Once on the ground, Hanumān grabbed a giant sāla tree, ripped it from the earth, and used it to smash both Virupāksha and Yupāksha, killing them instantly.

When Praghasa heard that three of his fellow generals had been killed by Hanumān, he charged forward, laughing mockingly. Bhāsakarna, also furious, grabbed a deadly dart and rushed at Hanumān. As they closed in, Praghasa slashed at Hanumān with a sharp axe, while Bhāsakarna stabbed at him with his spear. Blood ran down Hanumān’s wounds, staining his fur, but instead of slowing down, he only became more furious. With a roar, Hanumān ripped a massive mountain peak from the ground—complete with wild animals, snakes, and trees—and hurled it at the two demons. The mountain crushed Praghasa and Bhāsakarna, smashing them to dust.

With all five generals dead, Hanumān turned on the rest of the army. Like Indra destroying the demons, Hanumān went on a rampage—crushing horses with horses, elephants with elephants, warriors with warriors, and chariots with chariots. The battlefield was soon blocked by dead horses and elephants, shattered chariots, and the bodies of Rākshasas. After wiping out the generals and their entire force, Hanumān calmly returned to his spot at the gate, looking like Death itself taking a break after destroying all life.
SECTION XLVII

When Rāvana heard that five of his top generals had been killed by Hanumān alone—along with their chariots, elephants, and troops—he looked at his son, Prince Aksha, who was ready and eager for battle. With just a glance from his father, Aksha jumped up, his energy flaring like a fire fed with ghee in a sacred ritual. Aksha, a powerful warrior among the rākshasas, climbed into a dazzling chariot that shone like a newborn sun. The chariot was covered in gold, decorated with pennants and gemstones, and pulled by eight incredible horses—so fast they seemed to move at the speed of thought, able to travel over any terrain, and impossible for gods or demons to stop. The whole chariot sparkled like lightning, complete with quivers of arrows, swords strapped to the banners in all directions, and every weapon perfectly arranged. Gold threads glimmered everywhere, making the chariot glow like the sun and moon.

As Aksha and his forces moved out, the sounds of their horses, elephants, and chariots thundered across the sky and land, even shaking the mountains. They confronted Hanumān, who was waiting at the city gate. Aksha, with eyes sharp as a lion’s, stared at Hanumān—who looked as fierce as the fire that destroys the world at the end of an age. Aksha sized up Hanumān’s wild energy and strength, comparing it to his own, and felt himself grow stronger, like the sun rising at the dawn of a new era.

Then, burning with anger but staying calm and focused, Aksha challenged Hanumān by shooting three sharp arrows at him. Seeing that Hanumān was proud, relentless, and clearly a formidable opponent, Aksha readied his bow and arrows. Wearing golden armor, bracelets, and earrings, glowing with fiery strength, Aksha closed in. Their confrontation was unlike anything ever seen—impressive enough to make even gods and demons stop and stare. As Aksha and Hanumān clashed, the earth cried out, the sun dimmed, the wind stilled, the mountains trembled, the sky boomed, and the ocean roared.

Aksha, a master archer, fired three golden arrows tipped with feathers at Hanumān’s head, each like a venomous snake. Blood ran down Hanumān’s face, but his eyes blazed, and he looked almost like a sun rising with arrows for rays. Seeing Aksha ready with his weapons, Hanumān, the wisest of Sugrīva’s advisers, felt his fighting spirit surge and prepared to meet the challenge. Now truly angry, Hanumān’s glare burned like the sun’s rays from the peak of Mount Mandara, scorching Aksha and his army.

Aksha rained arrows on Hanumān like storm clouds dumping rain on a mountain, his bow forming a thunderous arc. Hanumān, whose roars sounded like thunder, saw Aksha’s vicious attack and strength, and let out a triumphant shout. Aksha, overconfident and acting like a reckless youth, charged at Hanumān with eyes burning red with rage. As Aksha kept firing arrows, Hanumān’s powerful arms and legs whipped around, and with a roar like rolling thunder, he leaped into the sky, his energy exploding.

Aksha, a top chariot warrior, chased after Hanumān, firing arrows like hail as if he were a storm attacking a mountain. But Hanumān, fast as the wind, twisted through the air, dodging every arrow and flying freely. As Aksha kept shooting, filling the sky with arrows, Hanumān paused, carefully watching and thinking about his next move. Wounded by Aksha’s arrows, Hanumān recognized the prince’s skill in battle and began to assess Aksha’s true strength.

Hanumān thought, “This guy is insanely strong, shining like a young sun. He’s pulling off feats that you wouldn’t expect from someone his age, and honestly, I don’t want to kill someone this brave. He’s got spirit, focus, and can handle real pain in battle. I bet even the Nāgas, Yakshas, and sages would respect him. He’s coming straight at me, full of confidence and skill—his talent would make even gods and demons nervous. But if I let my guard down, he could beat me: his power is growing fast. So, I have to finish this now—there’s no sense letting a fire get out of control.”

Having made up his mind, Hanumān gathered his strength and focused on defeating Aksha. Flying in the air, Hanumān slapped down all eight of Aksha’s incredible horses, killing them instantly. Aksha’s chariot crashed to the ground, its seat shattered and its pole broken. With his chariot destroyed, Aksha leapt into the sky armed with his bow and sword, looking like a fierce ascetic rising to the heavens.

But Hanumān, powered by the wind, caught up to Aksha as he flew through the sky—just as Garuda, the king of birds, grabs a massive snake. Hanumān grabbed Aksha by the legs, swung him around, and hurled him violently to the ground. Aksha’s body was smashed—his arms, legs, chest, and eyes broken, his bones shattered, and his blood staining the earth. Hanumān’s attack terrified Rāvana and shocked all the sages, spirits, and beings who had gathered to watch, including the Yakshas and serpent-people.

As Aksha lay dead, Hanumān was stared at in awe by the gods and Indra himself, who were amazed. Having killed Prince Aksha—who had seemed almost like a son of the gods—Hanumān returned to the city gate and waited there, as grim and unstoppable as Death itself.
SECTION XLVIII

After Hanumān killed Prince Aksha, Rāvana—the powerful king of the Rākshasas—was furious. Still, he held back his anger and called for Indrajit (also known as Meghanada), who was as impressive as any god, to take on Hanumān. “You’re the best warrior among us,” Rāvana said. “You’ve fought and defeated gods and Asuras in battle. Even the gods with Indra saw your skill, and you’ve earned a divine weapon from Brahmā himself. Not even all the gods together, led by Indra and the Maruts, could stand against your strength. In all three worlds, only you don’t get tired in battle. Your power and your spiritual strength protect you, and you’re the most intelligent when it comes to understanding time and place. There’s nothing you can’t do on the battlefield or figure out through wisdom and debate. Everyone knows your strength and skill. Your spiritual energy is like mine, and in battle, your power is unmatched. With you fighting, I’m sure of victory and don’t feel any doubt. My other warriors—Jamvumāli, the five generals, the sons of my best advisors, and even Aksha and Mahodara—are dead, along with countless soldiers, horses, elephants, and chariots. But I never had the confidence in them that I have in you. Now, after seeing our army destroyed, Hanumān’s power, and considering your own strength, I ask you to use all your energy against him. When you reach the battlefield, judge your strength against the enemy’s and fight so that Hanumān, who’s now resting after his rampage, will be worn down. The army is useless here; our soldiers run from Hanumān or are simply wiped out. Even powerful weapons, like thunderbolts, aren’t enough. Nothing can stop the son of the Wind-god—he’s like fire and can’t be killed by weapons. Think about what I’ve said and, if you want to succeed, focus your mind on the divine power of your bow. Go to battle and do your best to defeat the enemy by countering his attacks. Honestly, sending you might not be the best choice, but this is what Kshatriya warriors and kings are expected to do. You must be skilled in both wisdom and warfare. Anyone who wants to win must master many kinds of knowledge.”

Hearing his father’s words, Indrajit—gifted with supernatural power—was ready to fight. He walked in a circle around his father to show respect, then, energized and eager for battle, set out, cheered on by the other Rākshasas. Indrajit, radiant and graceful, had eyes as wide and red as lotus petals. He looked like the ocean rising during a full moon. His strength was almost too much to face—he was like a god himself—as he climbed into a chariot pulled by four fierce, fast horses that looked as swift as Garuda. Indrajit was a master of chariots and a top archer, skilled with every weapon, and a great swordsman. He raced his chariot toward Hanumān. As Hanumān heard the sound of the chariot and the bowstring, he felt a surge of excitement. Indrajit, with his bow and sharp arrows, followed every rule of war as he charged toward Hanumān. As he entered the battlefield, delighted and armed with arrows, the sky turned dark, and jackals began to howl terribly. Spirits like Nāgas, Yakshas, great sages, planets, Siddhas, and birds filled the sky, making noise as if celebrating. Hanumān saw the chariot approaching fast, with a banner like Indra’s, and he let out fierce roars, growing larger in size. Indrajit, sitting in his magical chariot with his beautifully decorated bow, pulled the string, making a sound like thunder. The battle began between these two powerful fighters—quick and fearless—like gods and demons clashing. Hanumān dodged the arrows from Indrajit, who was a master archer and warrior, and grew even bigger as he leapt into the sky. Indrajit, determined to win, launched a nonstop rain of huge, sharp, gold-tipped arrows as fast as lightning. Hanumān heard the chariot, the war drums, and the bowstrings again and leapt into the air to dodge. No matter how carefully Indrajit aimed, Hanumān managed to avoid the arrows, keeping his distance. Then, stretching out his arms, Hanumān jumped up again to face the arrows. Both heroes, quick and skilled, fought a duel everyone admired. Neither could find a weakness in the other—Hanumān couldn’t spot a flaw in Indrajit, and Indrajit couldn’t find a weak point in Hanumān. Their battle became so intense that they could hardly stand each other. Indrajit, seeing that his perfect arrows couldn’t hurt Hanumān, calmed himself and entered deep meditation, trying to discover Hanumān’s true nature. Realizing Hanumān couldn’t be killed, Indrajit decided to try and bind him instead. He used a powerful weapon given to him by Brahmā, the creator god, and, using his mastery of weapons, shot it at Hanumān, binding the Wind-god’s son with its magical power. Hanumān was suddenly bound tight and fell to the ground, unable to move. But because of a blessing from Brahmā, he felt no pain. Hanumān remembered the boons Brahmā had given him and realized that, because this was a Brahmā weapon, he couldn’t free himself on his own. He thought, “This is Brahmā’s will. I’ll just endure this for now.” He considered the weapon’s power, Brahmā’s blessing, and his own strength but decided to obey Brahmā’s wishes—“I’m not afraid while I’m bound, since Brahmā, Indra, and the Wind-god are protecting me. If the Rākshasas take me to their king, it might actually help my mission. So I’ll let them take me.” With this plan, Hanumān stayed still, pretending to be helpless. The Rākshasas tied him up roughly, scolding him, and Hanumān let out pitiful groans. Seeing that Hanumān wasn’t moving, the Rākshasas tied him up with cotton and strips of bark. Hanumān gladly allowed himself to be tied and insulted, thinking he might get a chance to speak with Rāvana if the king wanted to meet him. Once he was tied with bark, the magic of the Brahmā weapon faded, because its spell is broken if anything else is used to bind its victim. Indrajit saw Hanumān tied with bark and realized the Brahmā weapon’s power had been canceled. He thought, “They’ve ruined my great victory—they don’t understand how these divine weapons work. If the Brahmā weapon fails, no other weapon will work either. Now we’re in trouble.” Even though Hanumān was freed from the weapon, he didn’t let anyone notice. He stayed limp as the Rākshasas dragged him along, even though the bonds hurt. They pulled Hanumān, who could crush enemies in a second, toward Rāvana. Indrajit presented the mighty Hanumān—now tied with bark, but no longer bound by the Brahmā weapon—to the king and his followers. The Rākshasas told their king everything about Hanumān, describing him as an extraordinary, wild monkey who had been captured. “Who is he? Whose son is he? Where did he come from? What’s his mission? Who sent him?” the warriors wondered aloud. Others shouted, “Kill him!” “Burn him!” “Eat him!”—all growing angrier by the second. As they marched Hanumān along, he saw Rāvana’s old advisors sitting at the king’s feet, and he noticed a palace sparkling with countless jewels. Rāvana, full of energy and radiance, caught sight of Hanumān being dragged by fierce-looking Rākshasas. Hanumān, too, spotted Rāvana, who looked as powerful and bright as the sun. With his eyes glowing red, the ten-headed king stared at Hanumān and told his top advisors—men known for their high birth and wisdom—to question their prisoner. Each counselor, in turn, asked the monkey about his mission and what brought him to Lanka. Hanumān, standing tall, answered:
“I am a messenger from Sugriva.”
SECTION XLIX

Hanumān—fierce and powerful, his eyes burning with anger—locked his gaze on the lord of the Rakshasas, Rāvaṇa. Rāvaṇa looked striking, with a golden crown set with pearls, dazzling jewelry sparkling with diamonds and rare gems, and luxurious clothes. His skin was smeared with red sandalwood paste and decorated with intricate designs in many colors. His eyes were both captivating and terrifying, his teeth long and sharp, his lips hanging down. Hanumān took in every detail: Rāvaṇa’s ten radiant heads, which made him look like the mountain Mandara crowned with serpents, his dark blue complexion like a thick cloud, his chest draped with a gleaming chain, and a face shining like the moon—almost like a storm cloud next to the rising sun. Rāvaṇa’s massive arms were covered in jeweled armlets and sandalwood, looking as dangerous as five-headed snakes. He sat on a magnificent throne draped with a lavish, crystal-studded cloth, surrounded by beautiful women waving fans. Four of his closest Rakshasa advisors—Durdhara, Prahasta, Mahāpārçwa, and Nikumbha—stood nearby, wise and formidable, like the four oceans encircling the world. Even more counselors, handsome and clever, offered advice, making Rāvaṇa seem like the king of the gods among his court. Hanumān saw the mighty lord of the Rakshasas at the center of this grand scene, as impressive as a rain-filled cloud atop Mount Meru. Though Hanumān was suffering from the harsh treatment of Rāvaṇa’s fierce guards, he couldn’t help but stare in shock and awe at the Rakshasa king’s overwhelming presence.

In his mind, Hanumān thought, “What a form! What patience! What strength! What brilliance! How completely Rāvaṇa embodies everything a king should be! If only he weren’t so wicked, he could easily protect the heavens alongside Indra himself. But because of his ruthless, evil deeds—hated by all—everyone, gods and demons alike, fears him. If he got angry enough, he could probably flood the whole world. Seeing the incredible power of the Rakshasa king, Hanumān’s mind spun with thoughts and questions, amazed by what he witnessed.
SECTION L

When Ravana, the mighty-armed terror of the worlds, saw the tawny-eyed figure standing before him, he was overwhelmed with intense anger. He stared at the powerful monkey, feeling a mix of rage and anxiety, and wondered to himself, “Is this Nandi himself, the one who cursed me in Kailasa when I mocked him? Or is this just a monkey in disguise—maybe Vali’s son, Vana?” With his eyes burning red with fury, Ravana turned to his chief counselor, Prahasta, and spoke carefully, “Find out who this troublemaker is. Where does he come from? Why did he destroy the grove and attack the Rakshasas? What business does he have entering my city—which should be impossible for outsiders—and why did he fight my soldiers? Ask him all these questions.”

Hearing Ravana’s order, Prahasta said to Hanuman, “Don’t be afraid. Good fortune to you. There’s no need to panic, monkey. If Indra sent you to Ravana’s palace, just tell us the truth. You have nothing to fear—we’ll let you go. If you belong to Kubera, Yama, or Varuna, and have snuck into our city in disguise—or if Vishnu sent you here for victory—be honest about it. Your strength is definitely not ordinary for a monkey; you just look like one. Tell us the truth and you’ll be set free. But if you lie, you’ll pay with your life. So tell us—why are you really in Ravana’s palace?”

Then the monkey, Hanuman, spoke to the king of the Rakshasas, “I’m not sent by Indra, or Yama, or Varuna. I have no connection to Kubera, and Vishnu didn’t send me either. I’m simply a monkey, and I came here to see the Rakshasa king. That’s why I destroyed the beautiful grove—to get your attention. When your powerful Rakshasas attacked me, I fought back to protect myself. Weapons can’t harm me—not even those of the gods or asuras. The Great Creator gave me this power. I allowed myself to be captured because I wanted to meet the king. Even though your Rakshasas brought me here, I’m not really held back by any weapon. I came to you on behalf of Rama. Know that I am Rama’s messenger, with powers beyond measure. Listen to what I have to say—it’s in your best interest.”
SECTION LI

When Hanuman, that powerful and intelligent monkey, came face to face with Ravana—the ten-headed king—he spoke calmly, choosing his words carefully. “I’ve come here on behalf of Sugriva, King of the Monkeys, who sends you his greetings, O Lord of Rakshasas. Sugriva, your brother, wishes you well. Please listen to what he asks—his words are fair and just, meant for your good now and in the future. King Dasaratha, known for his chariots, elephants, and horses, was a friend to everyone, almost like a father, shining with the glory of the gods. His oldest son, Rama, strong and respected, followed his father’s command and entered the Dandaka forest with his brother Lakshmana and his wife Sita. Rama is famous for his energy and his commitment to doing what’s right. His wife, Sita, daughter of King Janaka of Videha, either died or was kidnapped in Janasthana. As Rama searched for Sita with Lakshmana, they met Sugriva at Rishyamuka. Sugriva promised to help Rama find Sita, and in return, Rama promised to make Sugriva king of the monkeys. Rama then killed Vali in battle and crowned Sugriva as their king. You knew Vali well—Rama defeated him with a single arrow. True to his word, Sugriva sent out his monkey army in every direction to search for Sita. Thousands upon thousands of monkeys are searching everywhere—on land and in the sky. Some are as fast as Garuda, and some as swift as the wind—nothing can stop them. I am Hanuman, son of the Wind-god. Driven by my wish to find Sita, I leapt over the ocean, a hundred yojanas across, to get here. While searching, I found Janaka’s daughter in your palace.

You understand right and wrong, and you’ve gained power through your spiritual practices. That’s why, as a wise ruler, you should not imprison another man’s wife. Keeping someone else’s wife is against what’s right. It brings endless trouble and leads to ruin, especially for someone like you. No god or demon can stand against the arrows of Lakshmana and Rama when they’re angry. There is no one in all three worlds who can harm Rama and remain safe. Do what’s right and in your best interest—listen to me, for your own good—and give Janaki back to Rama. Finding Sita here was a difficult task, but I have done it. The rest, Rama will handle himself.

I found Sita in deep sorrow—she’s trapped in your palace like a coiled serpent, and yet you don’t see the danger. Just as food mixed with deadly poison can’t be digested, Sita can’t be truly possessed, not even by gods or demons. Don’t throw away all the spiritual merit and years of life you’ve gained through your harsh penances. You think your powers make you invincible to gods and demons, and maybe your spiritual strength does protect you from them. But Sugriva is not a god, yaksha, or rakshasa—he’s the king of monkeys, and Rama is a mortal. How will you defend yourself against them? If you rely only on your power and do evil, your past good deeds won’t save you—your crimes will catch up with you. Goodness destroys evil, but evil like yours ruins all goodness. You’ve already enjoyed the benefits of your good deeds, but you’ll soon pay for your crimes.

Remember what happened in Janasthana, the killing of Vali, and the alliance between Rama and Sugriva—think about what’s best for you. I alone could destroy Lanka, its horses, elephants, and chariots if I chose, but the one I serve—Rama—has not given the order. Rama has promised, in front of the golden-eyed monkeys, to destroy the enemy who has hurt Sita. Even Indra, king of the gods, couldn’t escape if he wronged Rama—so what chance do you have? The Sita you hold captive is really the goddess of destruction for Lanka—she’s the doom that will destroy you all. Beware—by keeping Sita, you’re putting the noose around your own neck! Think carefully about your future. Soon you’ll see this city, with all its towers and markets, burning in flames fed by Rama’s anger and Sita’s power. Don’t doom your friends, ministers, family, sons, and all you care for—your pleasures, your wives, and the whole of Lanka.

O King of Rakshasas, please listen to me—a monkey, but also Rama’s messenger and servant. Rama could wipe out all the worlds, with every living and nonliving thing, and create them again if he wished. There is no being—god, demon, yaksha, rakshasa, serpent, vidyadhara, naga, gandharva, beast, siddha, kinnara, or bird—no one anywhere or at any time who can stand up to Rama, who’s as powerful as Vishnu himself. After what you’ve done to the greatest of all beings—Rama, that lion among kings—your life is in serious danger. Not the gods, not the demons, not the strongest rakshasas, gandharvas, or vidyadharas, not nagas or yakshas—no one can stand against Rama, ruler of these three worlds. Not even Brahma with his four faces, or Shiva the three-eyed destroyer, or mighty Indra could stand against Rama in battle.”

After Hanuman finished his fearless, honest speech, Ravana—his eyes wild with anger—ordered his guards to kill the mighty monkey.
SECTION LII

When Rāvana heard the words of Hanumān, the brave monkey, his rage took over and clouded his judgment. Furious, Rāvana ordered that Hanumān should be put to death. But Vibhishana, his younger brother, refused to go along with this decision—especially since Hanumān had come openly as an envoy. Vibhishana knew Rāvana was blinded by anger and realized things were getting out of control. Wanting to do what was right, Vibhishana thought carefully about what to do next. Finally, he decided to speak up. Showing respect to his older brother, he began, “O Lord of the Rākshasas, please forgive me and let go of your anger. Hear me out. Kings who are wise and fair never kill messengers. Taking Hanumān’s life would go against all moral codes and traditions—it’s not worthy of you. You know what’s right and wrong, you’re grateful, and you understand the laws of rulers. If even someone as wise as you lets passion take over, then what’s the point of all the effort spent learning the scriptures? Please, calm down. Think carefully about what’s right before you punish this envoy.”

Hearing Vibhishana’s words, Rāvana, still furious, replied, “You say I shouldn’t kill him, but destroying evil-doers doesn’t create sin. So I will kill this monkey who has done so much wrong.”

Vibhishana, shocked by this response and realizing how unjust it was, spoke up again, “O Lord of Lankā, please listen. I’m only speaking for your good, and for the good of the kingdom. It is well known everywhere that envoys should not be executed for carrying out their duties. Yes, Hanumān is an enemy and has caused us great harm. But even the best people say messengers are not to be killed, no matter what. There are other punishments for envoys—like marking them, beating them, or shaving their heads—but I’ve never heard of death being used. Why are you, who are so wise and skilled at judging right from wrong, letting anger rule over you? True strength means not giving in to rage. Whether it’s religion, society, or understanding the scriptures, no one is better than you, my brother. You’re the greatest among gods and demons. You have defeated the strongest warriors among gods and kings in battle. Even those who have secretly hated you, O enemy of gods and asuras, you haven’t killed them just for that. So what good would killing this monkey do for us? If you want revenge, target those who sent him here. Hanumān is just a messenger, acting for someone else, and it’s not right to kill an envoy. If you kill him, no other messenger will ever dare come to us again. Instead, focus your anger on the gods led by Indra. If Hanumān dies, there’s no one else who could provoke the sons of kings to fight you. And, as a leader, it’s not right for you to let down your loyal warriors, the Nairitas, who are eager to do battle for you. They are brave, loyal to you, raised in noble families, and have always supported you. So, let a part of your army go today under your orders and capture those foolish princes. That way, you can truly show your power to your enemies.”

Hearing this, Rāvana—lord of the night-dwelling Rākshasas, mighty enemy of the gods, and king among his kind—thought over his brother’s words. In the end, he accepted Vibhishana’s wise advice.
SECTION LIII

After listening to his brother, the powerful ten-headed Rāvaṇa (Ravana) said, “You’re right—it’s wrong to kill a messenger. But he does deserve a punishment, just not death. A monkey’s tail is his pride, so set it on fire right away. Once it’s burned, let him go. Then all his friends, family, and everyone he knows will see him humiliated, his body disfigured.” Rāvaṇa ordered, “Take him all over the city of Lanka with his tail on fire.” Hearing this, the Rakshasas, angry and cruel, wrapped Hanumān's tail in old pieces of cotton cloth. As they did this, Hanumān’s body grew larger, like a fire spreading quickly when it finds dry wood. After soaking the cloth in oil, they set it on fire. Furious, Hanumān’s face glowed like the sun as he swung his burning tail at them. The Rakshasas—men, women, young and old—dragged Hanumān through the city, cheering at his humiliation. Even as they tied him up, Hanumān kept his mind focused. He thought, “Even tied up, these demons can’t handle me. If I break free, I could kill them all. But I’ll endure this so I don’t mess up Rāma’s victory. I’ll use this chance to see more of Lanka—last night, I couldn’t fully inspect the city’s defenses. Let them bind me again. The pain from the burning tail doesn’t break my spirit.” The Rakshasas, thrilled with themselves, marched Hanumān—strong as an elephant—around the streets, blowing conch shells and trumpets, and making a spectacle for all to see. While being led through the massive city, Hanumān took in the sights: colorful chariots, enclosed courtyards, rooftops, crowded streets, intersections, alleyways, and inside people’s homes. Everywhere, Rakshasas announced, “This is a spy!” When Hanumān’s tail was set ablaze, the demon women ran to tell Sītā (Sita) about what had happened to the monkey she’d spoken with.

“Sita, the red-faced monkey who talked with you is being paraded through the city with his tail on fire,” they said. Hearing these cruel words—like a death sentence—Sītā was filled with anguish and turned to Agni, the god of fire, for help. Desperate to protect Hanumān, she prayed with all her heart: “If I have ever served my husband faithfully, if I am pure in character, if I have gained spiritual merit, if I have only ever belonged to one man, then, Agni, keep Hanumān safe and cool.” In response, the flames burned brighter, as if signaling Sītā that Hanumān would be unharmed. Even with fire blazing on his tail, Hanumān felt only a cool sensation, as if a cold wind was blowing—thanks to the blessings of Sītā, the power of Rāma, and the friendship between his father, the Wind-god, and Agni. Hanumān wondered, “Why isn’t this fire burning me? It shines brightly, but it doesn’t hurt. At the end of my tail, it actually feels cold. Maybe this is another miracle from Rāma’s power, like when the ocean and the mountain Maināka helped me during my leap. If the ocean could help Rāma, why wouldn’t fire?” Convinced that Sītā’s goodness, Rāma’s strength, and his father’s friendship with Agni protected him, Hanumān decided not to stay tied up any longer. “Why should I let these evil Rakshasas keep me captive? It’s time to fight back.” With a burst of strength, Hanumān snapped his bonds and leapt into the sky, roaring fiercely. He landed at Lanka’s city gate, now empty of guards. Growing as big as a mountain, then shrinking back to free himself, Hanumān picked up a massive iron bolt and attacked the guards, defeating them all. Wreathed in light from his flaming tail, looking as brilliant as the sun, Hanumān scanned Lanka once more, ready for what came next.
SECTION LIV

Hanumān (Hanuman), his mission nearly complete and his confidence soaring, looked out over the city of Lankā. He wondered what final act he could accomplish to truly shake the Rākshasas (Rakshasas) and make his efforts count. “What else can I do here to finish the job and make the enemy suffer even more?” he thought. “I’ve already destroyed the gardens, killed many of the top Rākshasa warriors, and crushed part of their army. The only thing left is to take down their fortifications. Once I do that, I’ll have truly completed my task. If I push just a bit further, all my pain and effort will finally pay off. And since my tail is on fire—like the flames that feed on offerings during a sacrifice—it’s only right that I devote this fire to destroying these grand buildings.” With that, Hanumān—his tail burning like a lightning-streaked cloud—ran through the streets of Lankā, moving from house to house, his mind calm and focused.

Hanumān went from one mansion to the next, through gardens and around towering palaces, his burning tail leaving a trail of destruction. With explosive energy and the strength of the wind itself, he leaped up and set fire to Prahasta’s house. Then, using his power, Hanumān jumped up and torched Mahāparçwa’s mansion, the flames raging like the fire that ends the world. He didn’t stop there—he set fire to Vajradanshtra’s house, then Suka’s, and Sārana’s—the clever Rākshasa. The leader of the monkey army kept going, burning down the home of Indrajit, then Sumāli’s, Jamvumāli’s, Raçmiketu’s, Suryyacatru’s, Hraswakarna’s, and even the Rākshasa Romaça’s. He also set fire to the houses of Yuddhonmattn, Matta, Dwajagriva, Vidyujjibhwa, and Hastimukha. The destruction continued with the mansions of Karāla, Viçāla, Sonitāksha, Kumbhakarna, Nikumbha, Yajnaçatru, and Brahmaçatru. Hanumān spared only the house of Vibhishana, moving on to burn almost all the others. As he passed through these luxurious homes, Hanumān—the most famous of monkeys—destroyed all the wealth owned by these rich Rākshasas.

After burning nearly every house in Lankā, Hanumān approached the palace of Rāvana, the king of the Rākshasas. This mansion was covered in jewels and gems, as dazzling as the mythical mountains Meru and Mandara, decorated with all sorts of beautiful things. Hanumān set his flaming tail to the palace, setting it ablaze. As he did, Hanumān let out a roar like thunder at the end of the world. The wind fanned the flames, making the fire burn hotter and brighter, and soon the blaze spread everywhere. The golden mansions, sparkling with pearls and gems, lost all their splendor as the fire devoured them. Buildings cracked and collapsed, falling to the ground like the palaces of heavenly beings cast down for losing their virtue.

The Rākshasas cried out in panic and despair as they saw their homes being destroyed, realizing they had no hope left. “It must be Fire himself who has come here in the form of a monkey!” they shouted, running in every direction. Women holding babies to their chests rushed desperately into the flames. Some women, their hair loose and wild, surrounded by fire as they fell from the rooftops, looked almost beautiful—like flashes of lightning in the night sky. Hanumān saw streams of precious metals mixed with diamonds, coral, lapis lazuli, pearls, and silver, flowing from the burning mansions.

And just as a fire can never get enough wood, Hanumān never grew tired of destroying the Rākshasas. The earth itself could barely hold the bodies of all the Rākshasas he had slain. Like the god Rudra burning down the three cities, Hanumān—filled with unstoppable energy—set all of Lankā on fire. Climbing to the top of Lankā’s mountain, Hanumān’s fire blazed out with incredible force, its flames reaching everywhere.

With the wind’s help, the smokeless fire burned fiercely through all the buildings, feeding on the Rākshasas as if they were offerings in a ritual. The fire grew bigger and bigger, stretching across the horizon, like the flames that end the universe. The fire’s energy was as intense as a million suns, surrounding all of Lankā and splitting the world open with thunderous noise. The flames, as red as blooming Kinçuka flowers, shot up into the sky. Smoke clouds from the burning houses rose up, blue as lotuses, making the scene strangely beautiful.

The Rākshasas, watching their city being destroyed along with its people, homes, and trees, gathered together and whispered in fear: “Is this Indra, king of the gods, in disguise? Or Yama, the god of death? Or Varuna? Or the Wind-god? Or maybe it’s the fire born from Rudra’s third eye, or the Sun, or Kubera, or Soma? This can’t be just a monkey—this must be Time itself, come to end us. Or maybe it’s the world-destroying fire of Brahmā, the creator, taking monkey form. Or could it even be Vishnu’s own energy, impossible to understand or describe, now appearing here as a monkey?” As Lankā burned, Rākshasas of rank and power talked like this, stunned by the devastation.

Meanwhile, Lankā was filled with chaos and grief. The city was burning along with its people, horses, chariots, snakes, flocks of birds, animals, and forests. Cries of loss filled the air: “Father! Son! My love! My friend! My lord! All our good deeds are gone!” The Rākshasas wailed in terror and heartbreak, their city echoing with haunting laments. Surrounded by flames, with its champions dead and its warriors wiped out, Lankā looked cursed, destroyed by the sheer rage of Hanumān.

Hanumān saw the Rākshasas terrified, shocked, and hopeless, and he looked at Lankā blazing with fire and light—much like the creator god Brahmā might look at the world after destroying it in anger. Hanumān, having wrecked the forest, killed so many Rākshasas, and burned the entire city filled with beautiful houses, stopped for a moment and stood there, thinking of Rāma.

At that moment, all the gods in the heavens praised Hanumān—the mighty son of the Wind-god and the bravest of all the monkeys. Even the greatest sages, Gandharvas (celestial musicians), Vidhyādharas (magical beings), Pannagas (serpent spirits), and other legendary heroes were amazed and delighted by what Hanumān had done.

After destroying the forest, killing the Rākshasas in battle, and burning down the grand city of Lankā, Hanumān stood tall. He climbed to the top of a brightly colored, high mansion. With his tail still blazing, Hanumān looked like a many-rayed sun shining over the ruins.

Once the city was in ashes, Hanumān cooled his burning tail in the ocean. Seeing Lankā reduced to rubble, the gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas (perfected beings), and great sages watched in awe and wonder at what Hanumān had accomplished.
SECTION LV

Watching the city of Lankā burning, destroyed, and its demon inhabitants terrified, Hanumān (Hanuman) stood still, deep in thought. Waves of fear and guilt crashed over him. He thought, “What a terrible thing I’ve done, setting Lankā on fire all by myself! Those who can control their anger, like putting out a fire with water, are truly wise. When you’re angry, there’s nothing you won’t do—you can even harm the good and insult the innocent without a second thought. Anger makes you forget what’s right or wrong to say or do. There’s no limit to the mistakes an angry person can make. The real strength is in someone who can let go of their anger, like a snake sheds its old skin. Shame on me for being reckless and letting my anger take over. I didn’t think about Sitā (Sita)—what if I killed her in the fire? Janaki, the noble one, must have been burned, since the whole city is in ashes. If she’s gone, then all my efforts have been for nothing. I set out to find and protect Sitā, but instead I might have destroyed her. Burning Lankā was easy, but in my rage, I lost sight of my true mission. I can’t see a single place in Lankā untouched by fire, so surely Janaki is gone. After making such a horrible mistake, maybe I deserve to die here. I could leap into the flames, or drown myself, or let the sea creatures take me. I can’t face Sugriva or the other monkeys after failing so badly, and how could I ever show my face to Rāma (Rama) and Lakshmana? Because of my reckless anger, I’ve lived up to the stereotype that monkeys are wild and impulsive. Passion and rashness lead to disaster—even though I had the power, I failed to protect Sitā. If Sitā dies, both Rāma and Lakshmana will die of grief. Then Sugriva and his friends will lose hope and perish too. When Bharata and Satrughna hear the news, how will they go on? If the royal family is wiped out, the whole kingdom will be plunged into sorrow. Because of my cursed temper, I’ve destroyed all that was good and caused the ruin of so many lives.” 

As Hanumān was lost in these thoughts, he remembered the good omens he’d seen earlier. “Or maybe,” he thought, “someone as pure and strong as Sitā survived by her own power. Fire can’t burn fire, after all. The wife of someone as virtuous and powerful as Rāma—protected by her own goodness—should be safe from harm. Maybe the fire didn’t touch her, just like it didn’t burn me, thanks to Rāma’s energy and Sitā’s virtue. Why should a woman so dear to all three brothers—Bharata, Lakshmana, and Rāma—someone who has captivated Rāma’s heart, be destroyed? The fire spirit didn’t burn my tail, so why would it harm the noble Sitā?” Then Hanumān remembered, amazed, the vision of the golden mountain beneath the sea. “With her devotion, truthfulness, and loyalty to her husband, Sitā could easily overcome fire; fire can’t harm her.”

While Hanumān was thinking about Sitā’s immense spiritual strength, he overheard the conversation of some wise Chāranas (celestial bards) nearby. “Wow! Hanumān has pulled off an incredible feat,” they said. “He set off a terrifying blaze in the home of the Rakshasas. The demon women, with their children and elders, are fleeing in panic, and the whole city is echoing with their cries. All of Lankā—its towers, walls, and gates—has been burnt, but we’re amazed that Jānaki (Sitā) isn’t harmed.” 

Hearing these words was like nectar to Hanumān. Joy filled his heart. With all the good omens and the Chāranas’ words, Hanumān was overjoyed, certain that Sitā was safe. Now that he knew the king’s daughter was unharmed, he decided to go back to see her one last time before returning.
SECTION LVI

Seeing Sita (Jānaki) sitting under the Sinsapa tree, Hanuman greeted her with a respectful bow and said, “I’m so lucky to find you safe and unharmed.” As Hanuman prepared to leave, Sita kept glancing at him, her voice full of longing for her husband. “If you don’t mind, dear child, please stay a little longer,” she said gently. “Find a quiet place and rest here tonight. Tomorrow, after you’ve recovered, you can go. Just having you here, even for a short time, eases a bit of my endless sorrow. Once you leave, I’m not sure I’ll survive long enough to see you again, before you return. Not seeing you will be almost unbearable for me, since I’ve gone from one tragedy to an even worse one, and grief is tearing my mind apart. And I keep wondering, how can Rama—so strong—or all those monkeys, or even Rama’s two sons, cross the ocean that can’t be crossed, even with all their power? Only three beings are known to leap across the sea: Garuda (Vinatā’s son), you, and your father, the Wind-god. So, with this massive challenge ahead, what plan do you, who are so clever, have to actually make it work? Honestly, you’re the only one who can pull this off, and your reputation will skyrocket because of your courage. But if Rama, that warrior who crushes his enemies, comes here with his army and takes me away after defeating Lanka, that would truly suit his greatness. So please, do whatever you can to make sure that Rama, with all his power and honor, comes here and acts in a way worthy of himself.” Hearing Sita’s sincere, loving, and thoughtful words, Hanuman replied, “Noble lady, Sugriva—the king and greatest of monkeys—is completely committed to helping you. Sugriva, surrounded by thousands, even millions of monkeys, will soon arrive here to help. And the best of men, Rama and Lakshmana, will come together and strike Lanka with their arrows. Rama, son of Raghu, will defeat Ravana and his followers, and soon you’ll return to Rama’s palace. Please, gentle Sita, try to stay strong and keep hope. Soon, you’ll see Rama slay Ravana in battle. When the demon king is killed along with his sons, advisors, and friends, you’ll reunite with Rama, just like the star Rohini joins the Moon. Rama will come with the best of monkeys, conquer Ravana in battle, and end your suffering.” After comforting Sita, Hanuman, son of the Wind-god, prepared to leave, bowing once more to her.

Having calmed Sita and shown his incredible strength—making the city uneasy and outsmarting Ravana—Hanuman was ready to head back across the ocean. Eager to see Rama again, he climbed Mount Aristha, the tallest mountain around. The mountain looked like it was covered in a blue blanket of padmaka trees, with clouds floating between its peaks, gleaming in the sunlight. The scattered minerals on its slopes looked like eyes, the sound of its waters was like chanting, and its many springs sang clear songs. The devadaru trees reached upward like raised arms, and waterfalls echoed all around, as if the mountain was crying out in distress. The autumn woods waved, making the mountain seem to tremble, while the wind through the kichaka trees made music. Poisonous snakes hissed as if in anger, and caves covered with snow gave the mountain a thoughtful, mysterious look. Its hills looked like legs made of clouds, and its highest peaks reached up as if the mountain were yawning into the sky. The mountain was dotted with caves, surrounded by sal, palm, tamala, karna, and bamboo trees, and covered in flowering plants and undergrowth. Wild animals roamed everywhere, and streams of minerals ran through it. There were countless boulders, and the place was home to Maharshis, Yakshas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and serpents. It was hard to cross because of all the thick plants and trees, and its caves sheltered lions, tigers, and other fierce animals. The trees were loaded with delicious fruits and roots.

Hanuman, the Wind-god’s son and leader of the monkeys, climbed the mountain. As he stepped onto its level top, his excitement to see Rama was so intense that the rocks beneath his feet cracked and scattered. Once at the summit, Hanuman grew to his full, massive size, getting ready to leap from the southern shore to the northern side of the ocean. Looking out from the peak, he studied the vast, dangerous sea below, home to terrifying snakes. In his mind, Hanuman crossed from the southern shore to the northern, almost as if he was flying through the air.

But the mountain itself, under Hanuman’s weight and power, began to shake and moan. All kinds of creatures on it scrambled to escape as the peaks wobbled and trees toppled over. The pressure from Hanuman’s thighs crushed flowering trees, smashing them to the ground as if struck by lightning. The roars of lions, wounded and frightened in their caves, echoed loudly, almost shattering the sky. Vidyadharis—celestial women—with their clothes and jewelry in disarray, shot up from the mountain into the sky. Huge, poisonous snakes with burning tongues writhed on the ground, their hoods and necks injured. Kinnaras, serpents, Gandharvas, Yakshas, and Vidyadharas fled their mountain home in terror, seeking safety in the sky. Even the mountain itself, tormented by Hanuman’s power, sank into the earth with its trees and peaks. Where it once stood ten yojanas wide and thirty high, it was now flattened to the ground. Ready to leap over the ocean, whose waves crashed against its shores, Hanuman launched himself into the sky.
SECTION LVII

Hanumān (sometimes called Hanuman), full of energy and unstoppable, leapt up like a mountain with wings and began to soar through the sky. The sky below him was like a vast sea, with blown-open lotuses and lilies, snakes, Yakshas, and Gandharvas scattered across it. The Moon looked like a beautiful white water lily, and the Sun looked like a bright Kārandava bird. Star constellations like Tishya and Srāvana seemed like swans gliding across the sky, while clouds looked like patches of moss and grass. The constellation Punarvasu was a giant fish, Mars was a massive sea creature, Airāvata the elephant looked like a distant island, Swāti was a playful swan, breezes were the waves, and moonlight was like the cool water of this sky-ocean. As Hanumān sped forward, it seemed like he was swallowing up the sky, reaching for the stars, blocking out the sun and the twinkling lights, and parting the clouds. Tireless, he kept crossing the vast expanse above the ocean.

All around him, huge clouds—black, red, blue, dark purple, and greenish-red—looked incredibly beautiful. Sometimes Hanumān disappeared into the clouds; sometimes he burst out of them, briefly visible before vanishing again. He looked a lot like the Moon when it’s hidden and then revealed among clouds. Dressed in white, Hanumān kept flashing in and out of sight as he moved through the sky. He scattered clouds as he flew, sometimes dipping down and then soaring up again. His powerful voice, deep and thunderous like a storm cloud, echoed as he went—this was the same Hanumān who had killed the chief Rākshasas, made himself famous, filled Lanka with cries of grief, struck fear into Rāvana, challenged the might of his enemies, and paid his respects to Sītā (also called Vaidehi). Now, he was racing back across the ocean.

Hanumān touched down briefly on Maināka, the greatest of mountains, then shot off again like an iron dart released from a bowstring. As he neared the massive, cloud-like mountain Mahendra, Hanumān let out a loud roar. His voice, as deep as thunder, filled the sky in every direction. When he landed, eager to see his friends again, he roared even louder and waved his tail energetically. His cries echoed through the paths where eagles fly, and it seemed like the sun itself was being split apart by his shouts.

Meanwhile, the other powerful monkeys who had been waiting on the northern shore of the ocean heard the deep, thunder-like sounds coming from Hanumān as he sped toward them. These monkeys, who had been feeling hopeless and worn out, recognized the roars of Hanumān, their strongest warrior, sounding like storm clouds ready to burst. Hearing these cries, the monkeys gathered around, suddenly anxious and excited to see their friend return.

Jāmbavān, the wise and respected bear-leader, spoke up with joy to the rest of the monkeys: “Hanumān has succeeded—there’s no doubt. If he had failed, he wouldn’t be roaring like this.” As the monkeys listened to the crashing sounds of Hanumān’s arms and his triumphant shouts, they were filled with happiness and began leaping around in excitement.

Eager to see Hanumān, the monkeys jumped from mountain to mountain and from peak to peak, all of them in high spirits. Their joy was obvious as they clung to tree branches at the tops of trees, waving their clean garments in celebration. Hanumān himself, the powerful son of the Wind-god, roared through the air like a storm wind howling in a cave.

When the monkeys saw Hanumān—a massive figure like a thundercloud—landing among them, they pressed their hands together in greeting. The mighty Hanumān, looking like a living mountain, landed on the top of another forest-covered peak.

Overflowing with happiness, Hanumān dropped down near a sparkling spring, looking almost like a mountain whose wings had been clipped. All the leading monkeys quickly gathered around him, their hearts filled with joy.

We, the guards, tried to stop them from wrecking the place, but the monkeys didn’t care at all. Some of them acted really badly, others just ate whatever they wanted, and all of them glared at us. When my attendants got insulted and angry, they tried to fight back, but those powerful, furious monkeys drove us out of the garden. There were thousands of them, all worked up and with eyes burning red. Some of my guards had their arms broken, others had their knees smashed, and a few were even thrown up into the air. All this happened while you’re still the king! The heroes are beating up the guards, and the whole Madhuvana orchard is being taken over by them.”

Lakshmana, who was standing nearby, listened to all this and turned to Sugriva, asking, “Sugriva, why has this forest guard come to you like this? What’s upsetting him so much?” Sugriva, who was good at reading people and picking the right words, replied, “Lakshmana, Dadhimukha is saying that the monkeys, led by Angada, have been drinking the honey in Madhuvana. They wouldn’t have done something so out-of-line unless they had good news. This probably means they’ve succeeded in their mission. That’s why they fought the guards who tried to stop them, and why they even ignored Dadhimukha, who’s a pretty powerful monkey himself. I personally put Dadhi in charge of the orchard. Honestly, only Hanuman could have found Sita—no one else. Hanuman is extremely smart, knows how to get things done, is brave, strong, and knows all the strategies. And with leaders like Jambavan and Angada working with Hanuman, there’s no way they’d fail. So, I’m sure Angada and the others have trashed the orchard after completing their mission. They searched the southern direction, found what they were looking for, and came back to Madhuvana to celebrate. The whole orchard was explored and enjoyed, and the guards were beaten up. Dadhimukha came here to tell me all this—he’s known for his strength and gentle way of speaking. Lakshmana, son of Sumitra, they must have seen Sita, because they wouldn’t have started feasting and partying otherwise. These monkeys are famous for their sense of duty; they wouldn’t have dared to destroy an orchard given to us by the gods unless they had huge news.”

Sugriva’s words, which were optimistic and reassuring, made Lakshmana and Rama (Raghava) really happy. After listening to Dadhimukha’s report, Sugriva, now satisfied, turned to him and said, “I’m really pleased that they succeeded and explored the forest. Let’s forgive them for celebrating a little too hard. Go back there and protect the orchard now, and send Angada, Hanuman, and the rest of the monkeys here. Rama, Lakshmana, and I are eager to hear from Hanuman and the others about what they found out about Sita and how we can get her back.” Seeing how happy Rama and Lakshmana looked—smiling with their eyes lit up—Sugriva realized that their mission was about to succeed. The monkey king felt a wave of joy and hope, certain that the great task was close to being accomplished.
SECTION LXIV

After hearing Sugriva’s words, the monkey Dadhimukha (Dadhi), happy and relieved, bowed respectfully to Sugriva, Rama (Rāghava), and Lakshmana. Showing his respect to Sugriva and the powerful descendants of Raghu, Dadhimukha, along with his brave monkey companions, leapt into the air. He sped away just as quickly as he had arrived, and, landing back on the ground, entered the orchard. Inside the forest, he saw all the monkey leaders relaxing and celebrating. They had just urinated, a side effect of drinking so much honey. Dadhimukha approached them, hands folded and cheerful, and spoke to Angada:

“O gentle Angada, please don’t be offended. The monkeys guarding the garden only tried to stop you out of anger—they didn’t realize it was you. You’ve come a long way and must be exhausted. Please, enjoy the honey—you’re our prince and the true master of this orchard. Forgive us for our ignorance and anger. Just as your father did before you, you and Sugriva are the real leaders of the monkeys—no one else. My prince, I’ve told your uncle everything that happened—how you and the others arrived and how the garden was destroyed. He wasn’t angry at all; instead, he was delighted. Overjoyed, your uncle Sugriva, king of the monkeys and the land, said, ‘Send them all to me at once.’”

When Dadhimukha finished, Angada, skilled and confident, spoke to the other monkeys: “Leaders of the monkey army, I think Rama knows everything now. Dadhimukha was so cheerful when he told us, which makes me sure of it. Our mission is complete, and it’s time for us to leave. You’ve all had your fill of honey, and there’s nothing left to do here. We should go to King Sugriva now. I’ll go along with whatever all of you decide together. Even though I’m the prince, I don’t have the right to command you—I follow your lead. You’re all skilled and experienced; I can’t force you to do anything.”

The monkeys, happy with Angada’s words, replied, “King, best among monkeys, who else but you would speak like this when in charge? Anyone else would be proud and arrogant. Only you could say something so humble, which proves you’ll be a great leader one day. We all want to go to Sugriva, our king. Honestly, we wouldn’t take a single step without your permission.”

After hearing this, Angada said, “Alright, let’s all go.” Then he leapt into the sky, and all the monkeys followed, filling the air like a storm of flying stones. With Angada and Hanuman leading them, the monkeys soared into the sky, roaring like thunderclouds pushed by the wind.

As they neared Sugriva, Angada spoke to Rama, who was still grieving, “Good news for you, Rama. Take heart. We’ve found the lady you’re looking for—there’s no doubt. Otherwise, we wouldn’t have returned now that the deadline has passed. I can tell from Angada’s excitement, too. If Angada hadn’t succeeded, he wouldn’t have come back to me at all. If the monkeys had done something this reckless without completing their mission, Angada would look miserable and be lost in grief. And if they hadn’t actually seen Janaka’s daughter, they would never have dared to destroy Madhuvana, the orchard my ancestors preserved.”

“Don’t be sad, Rama, whose mother Kaushalya is so proud of him. I’m sure Hanuman is the one who saw the lady—no one else could have done it. Hanuman is smart, determined, brave, and knows the scriptures. He’s the perfect one for this task. With Jambavan, Angada, and Hanuman working together, there’s no way the mission could have failed. Don’t worry, Rama. The monkeys are returning, proud and joyful from their success. They wouldn’t be celebrating like this if they had failed. The way they broke into the orchard and drank all the honey tells me they succeeded.”

Just then, Sugriva heard the monkeys’ joyful shouts echoing in the sky as they flew toward Kishkindha, celebrating Hanuman’s achievement. Sugriva, thrilled, lifted his tail high. With Angada and Hanuman in front, the monkeys hurried towards Rama.

Excited and a little tipsy, the heroes led by Angada landed before Rama and Sugriva. Hanuman, respectful and humble, bowed his head and told Rama all about Sita’s wellbeing, both physical and spiritual. As Hanuman described seeing Sita, Rama and Lakshmana were overwhelmed with happiness. Lakshmana, now certain, looked gratefully at Sugriva. Rama, too, full of joy, looked at Hanuman with great respect.
SECTION LXV

After arriving at Mount Prasravana, which was surrounded by a colorful and dense forest, the monkey army bowed respectfully to Rāma and Lakshmana. Please, tell me every detail.” The monkeys, seeing how much Rāma was hurting, turned to Hanumān—since he was the one who had actually met Sitā—and asked him to explain everything.

Hanumān, son of the Wind-god and gifted speaker, lowered his head in honor of Sitā and in the direction of the south (where she was being kept). He began to tell the story of how he managed to find her. Lankā is located on the southern shore of the southern sea. There, in Rāvana’s inner chambers, I found Sitā. She was thinking only of you, Rāma. I saw her being harassed again and again by the demon women. She’s being guarded in a garden by fierce-looking rākshasīs. This noble lady, who was once happy, is now suffering because you’re not with her. Locked away in Rāvana’s palace, watched closely by demon women, she was dressed simply, with just one braid, and looked miserable. She spends all her time thinking of you.

Sitā was lying on the ground, stripped of her beauty—like a lotus withered by winter. She has absolutely no interest in Rāvana and is ready to end her own life. O Kākutstha (another name for Rāma), O innocent prince, after asking around for a while, I found this noble lady, still completely devoted to you. I earned her trust by telling her about the glory of the Ikshvāku family, and then I explained everything to her. When Sitā heard about your friendship with Sugriva, she was overjoyed. Her love and respect for you never wavered, and everything she does is for you. Rāma, I saw Janaka’s daughter in this heartbreaking state—fasting, suffering, but always faithful to you.

O wise Rāghava (Rāma), Sitā gave me this jewel as proof, asking me to remind you of the time with the crow at Mount Chitrakuta. Jānaki (Sitā) told me, ‘Son of the Wind-god, please tell Rāma everything you have seen here. And when you see Sugriva, give him this jewel, which I have kept safe with great care. Remind Rāma of the mark he made on my forehead with red powder. Dear monkey, I am so happy to see this bright jewel that Rāma has sent through you. I can survive for only one more month—after that, if the demons keep tormenting me, I won’t last.’ That’s what Sitā said to me—she’s become thin, follows strict vows, locked away in Rāvana’s palace, her eyes wide and scared like a deer’s. I’ve told you everything, Rāghava. Now, please make plans to cross the ocean.”

After comforting the two princes, Hanumān handed the jewel to Rāghava as a token from Sitā and explained the whole story from beginning to end.
SECTION LXVI

After Hanumān spoke, Rāma (also called Rāghava), the son of Daçaratha, held the jewel to his chest and began to cry, with Lakshmana by his side. Seeing the beautiful jewel, Rāma, overwhelmed with sorrow and his eyes filled with tears, turned to Sugriva and said, “Looking at this jewel makes my heart ache, just like a cow’s milk flows at the sight of her calf. My father-in-law gave this jewel to Sitā at our wedding, and she wore it on her head to make herself look even more beautiful. The jewel was originally found in the ocean and given to Janaka by the wise god Indra, as a reward for his devotion during a sacrifice. “Please, tell me again and again what Vaidehi (Sitā) said,” Rāma continued, turning to Hanumān. “Hearing her words is like cool water reviving me when I feel faint. Saumitri (Lakshmana), is there any pain greater than this? I have the precious jewel that came from the ocean, but not Vaidehi herself. She must be incredibly strong to have survived for a month in that place, but I don’t think I could last even a moment without her, my beloved with the deep blue eyes. Take me to where you saw her, because now that I know she’s alive, I can’t bear to be apart from her any longer. How is she still alive, so frightened, surrounded by the terrifying and cruel Rakshasis? Her face must have lost its glow, like a full autumn moon hidden by clouds, even though the darkness is gone. Hanumān, please tell me exactly what Sitā said to you. Her words are like medicine keeping me alive. What did my sweet, beautiful wife say, separated from me for so long? How is she surviving all these hardships?”
SECTION LXVII

After listening to Rama, Hanuman began to tell him everything Sita had said. "Rama," Hanuman said, "the respected Janaki asked me to remind you of everything that happened at Mount Chitrakuta, from start to finish. She remembered how, one morning while sleeping happily by your side, she woke up early, and during that time, a crow attacked her chest with its beak. You were asleep on Sita’s lap when the crow came again and hurt her. It wounded her once more, and her chest started bleeding. In pain, she woke you up. When you saw her injured, you got furious—your eyes burning with anger. You asked her, ‘Who did this to you? Who dared to scratch your chest—who would mess with an angry five-headed serpent?’

You looked around and saw the crow, claws bloody, facing Sita. That crow, the king of birds, was actually the son of Indra (Sakra). It quickly tried to escape, almost vanishing into the earth with the speed of the wind. But you were determined to punish it. You took a blade of kusa grass from your seat, turned it into a weapon charged with Brahma’s power. It blazed with fire like the end of the world. You hurled it at the crow, and it chased the bird everywhere. Even the gods were terrified and abandoned the crow. The bird couldn’t find safety anywhere in the three worlds. Finally, it came back to you, desperate, and threw itself at your feet, begging for mercy.

Even though the crow deserved to die, you spared its life, Rama. But because you couldn’t waste the power of the Brahma weapon, you destroyed its right eye instead. The crow bowed to you and to King Dasaratha, then flew off to its home. Sita said, ‘Rama, you’re the greatest warrior, skilled with every weapon, strong and noble—so why don’t you use your weapons against the Rakshasas? Not even the gods, Gandharvas, Asuras, or Maruts are your equals in battle. If you care for me at all, then please, destroy Ravana with your arrows and save me. And why hasn’t Lakshmana, your brave brother and my protector, come to help me? You two shine like Wind and Fire—no one can stand against you, not even the gods. Yet here I am, ignored by you both. Maybe I’ve done something terribly wrong, since you two, who could easily save me, haven’t come.’

When I heard these sad and gentle words from Vaidehi (Sita), I told her, ‘I swear to you, Rama is crushed by grief because you’re gone. Lakshmana also suffers when he sees Rama so full of pain. But now that I’ve found you, you don’t need to despair anymore. Very soon, your suffering will end. Once Rama and Lakshmana know I’ve met you, they’ll be filled with energy and burn Lanka to ashes. Rama will defeat the terrible Ravana and his family in battle, and will take you back to his city, I promise. Please, give me something—some sign—that I can show Rama to prove I’ve met you and to bring him some happiness.’

She looked around, then took a beautiful jewel from her clothing—the kind you wear in your hair—and gave it to me. I took the gem for you, Rama, bowed to her, and got ready to leave quickly. As I was about to grow in size and leap into the sky, Sita, the daughter of King Janaka, stood there in tears, her voice choked with sadness. She said, ‘You are truly blessed, Hanuman, because you will see Rama, whose arms are strong and whose eyes are like lotuses, and Lakshmana, his famous younger brother.’

I answered her, ‘Climb onto my back, noble lady! I’ll carry you out of here right now and show you your husband, Rama, along with Sugriva and Lakshmana.’ But she replied, ‘That’s not the right thing to do, Hanuman. Even though I was touched by Ravana before, I had no choice. I can’t willingly climb onto your back. Please, you should go back to those two princes yourself.’

Then she said, ‘Hanuman, tell Rama and Lakshmana, those lion-hearted heroes, that I am alive. Tell Sugriva and his followers, too. Describe my suffering so that Rama will come and save me from this sea of sorrow. Tell him about the pain I’ve endured from the she-demons here. May your journey be safe, Hanuman, greatest of monkeys.’

That’s what Sita said to me, pouring out her grief. So Rama, you can be sure that she is alive and well, and this is her message to you."
SECTION LXVIII

Then, O greatest of men, out of her deep love for you and respect for our friendship, that noble lady spoke to me again. She said, “Please tell everything to Rama, son of Dasharatha, so that he will come soon to rescue me by defeating Ravana in battle. O hero, O destroyer of enemies, if you wish, you can rest from your exhausting journey by hiding somewhere safe and then continue tomorrow. O monkey, when I’m with you, I almost forget the heavy weight of my sorrow, even though I’m so unfortunate. But when you leave, I’ll be waiting for your return, though honestly, I’m not sure I’ll survive until then. O master of words, what is your plan to accomplish this difficult task? It’s true that only you can do this, O slayer of enemy heroes—but if you do it alone, it will only add to your own fame. But if Rama wins and takes me back to his city, that will be his true glory. The brave Raghava shouldn’t rescue me in secret, like Ravana did when he kidnapped me from the forest in disguise. They never tire, are incredibly brave, and possess strength beyond measure. These powerful monkeys have traveled around the earth many times, flying through the air. Sugriva has many monkeys who are as strong as I am, and even some who are stronger—none are weaker. If I could cross the ocean, imagine what these heroes can do! The greatest warriors are never sent on missions—only the lesser ones are. So please, noble lady, stop grieving. Let go of your sorrow. With a single leap, these monkey leaders will reach Lanka. O great princess, the two princes will ride on my back and come to you, shining like the Sun and Moon. Soon you will see Raghava, the lion-like slayer of foes, and Lakshmana with his bow, standing at Lanka’s gates. You’ll soon see groups of heroic monkeys, as strong as lions and tigers, with claws and teeth as their weapons. You’ll hear the roars of the leading monkeys on Mount Malaya, sounding like thunderclouds. And soon you’ll see Raghava, the destroyer of enemies, returning from the forest and sitting beside you on the throne of Ayodhya.” Hearing my encouraging words, which promised the fulfillment of her wish, the daughter of the king of Mithila, though weighed down by sorrow in your absence, found great comfort and hope.
SECTION I

By the rakshasas.

Sataghni: An ancient weapon, sometimes a rocket or a mace covered in sharp iron spikes, about two yards long.
