My eyelid is twitching—it’s a good omen.” Honored by both the monkey-king and Lakshmana, Rāma continued, “Surrounded by thousands of our fastest monkeys, let Nila lead the way and scout ahead. Nila, as the general, make sure the army follows a route with plenty of fruit, roots, cool streams, and honey. The evil Rākshasas might try to poison the food and water along the way, so you must stay alert and protect our supplies. Have our scouts check every hollow, mountain hideout, and forest for enemy troops. Anyone who isn’t up to the task should stay behind—this is dangerous work, and we need the best. So, let the strongest monkeys lead the best troops, in groups of hundreds and thousands. Gaja—huge as a mountain—along with the mighty Gavaya and Gavaksha (the leader of the leapers, like a bull among cattle), should take the front. Rishava will guard the right flank, Gandha—unstoppable as a wild elephant—and the fierce Gandhamādana will guard the left. I’ll ride Hanumān into battle, like a god on his elephant Airāvata, cheering on our army. Lakshmana, like the god of destruction, will ride Angada, just as the god of wealth rides Sārvabhauma. In the rear, king Jāmbavān the bear, Sushena, and Vegadarçi the monkey will keep watch.” Hearing Rāma’s plan, Sugriva quickly gave orders to his troops. Instantly, powerful monkeys poured out from caves and mountaintops, leaping in every direction. Then, with Lakshmana and the monkey-king honoring him, Rāma set off south with his army. He was surrounded by countless monkeys—hundreds, thousands, even millions—each as strong as elephants. As they marched, the monkeys cheered and showed their excitement. Some guarded the sides, others leapt ahead to clear the way, all roaring like lions and making loud cries as they moved south. Some monkeys enjoyed honey and fruit, some carried whole trees, and others wrestled each other for fun. Some fell and sprang up, some knocked each other down, but all shouted together, “We’ll kill Rāvana and all his demon followers!” Ahead, Rhrishabha, Nila, and Kumuda led squads of monkeys, clearing the path. In the center marched Sugriva, Rāma, and Lakshmana, surrounded by a massive, powerful force. The heroic monkey Satavali, with ten million troops, guarded the whole army. Kesari, Panasa, Gaja, and Arka, each leading another hundred million, protected the flanks. Behind, Sushena and Jāmbavān watched over the rear with a swarm of bears. Nila, ever alert, patrolled up and down the ranks. Vālimukha, Prajangha, Jambha, and Rabhasa kept spirits high and urged the monkeys on. As the army moved, the monkeys—full of pride and strength—spotted the great Sahya mountain, covered in trees and bright with flowers, its lakes sparkling. Following Rāma’s orders, the massive, fearsome army moved forward, leaving cities, villages, and provinces behind, rumbling like thunder. Close by Rāma, the bravest monkeys bounded ahead like racehorses. With Rāma and Lakshmana riding on the monkeys, they looked as bright as the sun and moon, with Hanumān and Angada like cosmic shadows. Rāma, righteous as ever, led his forces south. Then Lakshmana, wise and quick-thinking, riding Angada, spoke to Rāma in a voice full of meaning.

“Soon you’ll rescue Vaidehi and defeat Rāvana, and then you’ll return to Ayodhyā, bringing happiness to everyone. Rāghava, I see all the best omens—both on earth and in the sky—promising you victory. The wind behind us is gentle and sweet, bringing comfort to the troops. Birds and animals call out loudly, and every direction looks calm and bright. The sun shines without a cloud. Even Bhrigu’s son, Uçanas, and Dhruva the Pole Star, shine favorably for you. The sages, glowing with purity, circle around Dhruva. Ahead of us I see the ancestor of the Ikshwāku dynasty, the pure Rājarshi Triçanku with his priest. The constellation Visākhā is clear and undisturbed—this is the family star of the Ikshwākus. But Nairita, the star of the Rakshasas, is in trouble, struck by the comet Dhumketu. All these signs mean doom for the Rākshasas. When someone is about to die, their stars are always afflicted. The water tastes sweet, the forests are full of fruit, the breeze is gentle, and the trees are blooming. Our monkey army looks as majestic as the gods’ army when they fought Tāraka. With all this, you should be filled with hope.” Encouraged by his brother’s words, Lakshmana felt energized, and the monkey army marched on covering the land. The bears, monkeys, and even tigers raised so much dust with their claws and teeth that the world seemed covered, and the sun’s light was blocked. Like clouds blanketing the sky, the monkey horde filled the southern quarter, hiding the mountains, forests, and sky. As they crossed many miles, the rivers looked like they were flowing backward, churned by the monkeys’ rush. The monkeys rested by clear pools, on tree-covered mountains, open plains, and fruit-filled forests. Some rushed ahead, some zigzagged, some stuck to the ground, but together they spread out, covering everything. Their faces were bright with joy, and they moved as fast as the wind, putting all their strength into Rāma’s mission. They showed off to each other, shouting in excitement, leaping, waving tails, stomping the ground, breaking hills and trees, climbing peaks, making wild noises, and tearing vines with their powerful legs. Some played with rocks and trees, and the earth was soon blanketed by millions of energetic monkeys. Day and night, the army pressed on, eager for battle and desperate to save Sitā. They barely stopped to rest. Soon they reached Mount Sahya, covered in all kinds of trees and woods. The monkeys climbed its slopes while Rāma admired the colorful forests, rivers, and waterfalls of both Sahya and Malaya. The monkeys broke down trees—Champakas, Tilakās, mangos, Prasekas, Sindubarakas, Tiniças, Karaviras, Ashokas, Karanjas, Plakshas, Nyagrodhas, Jambukas, and Amalakas. Sitting on scenic rocks, they were showered with flowers blown by the wind from the trees. The forests smelled of honey, and a cool, pleasant breeze hummed with bees. The mountain glittered with different metals, and dust from them, stirred up by the wind, spread over the monkey army. In the valleys, Ketakas, Sindubaras, Vasantees, Mādhabis, Gandhapurnas, Kandas, Chiravilyas, Mahikas, Vanjulas, Vakulas, Ranjakas, Tilakās, Nagas, Chutas, Patalikas, Kobidaras, Muchlindas, Arjunas, Singsapas, Kutajas, Pintalas, Tiniças, Churnkas, Neepakas, Neela-Sokas, Saralas, Ankolas, and lotuses bloomed. The monkeys, thrilled by the view, couldn’t resist shaking the trees. The mountain had beautiful lakes and ponds, full of ducks, cranes, and other birds. Wild boars, deer, huge bears, lions, tigers, and other fierce animals roamed everywhere. The water was covered in lotuses and lilies. Birds sang on the mountain peaks. The monkeys bathed, drank, played, and leapt everywhere. Drunk on the fruits and honey, they smashed the sweet-smelling fruits, roots, and flowers. The monkeys, golden as honey, feasted on giant mangoes. Leaping from tree to tree, breaking branches, and shouting, they made Sahya mountain echo with their excitement. Whether climbing trees or splashing in the water, the whole land looked golden, like ripe fields of rice. Then, reaching Mount Mahendra, Rāma—strong-armed and lotus-eyed—climbed to the top, which was covered in diverse trees. From the summit, he saw the vast sea below, teeming with turtles and fish. Passing Sahya and Malaya, and keeping the army together, they gradually reached the roaring ocean. Climbing down, Rāma, along with Lakshmana and Sugriva, entered the forest by the seashore. They reached broad, rocky beaches, constantly washed by waves. Rāma said, “Sugriva, we’ve arrived at Varuna’s domain. Now I’m faced with a challenge I hadn’t considered—the ocean is so wide, I don’t see how we can cross it without a plan. Let’s camp the army here and think of a way to reach the other side.” Saddened for Sitā, Rāma ordered, “Sugriva, set up camp near the water’s edge. It’s time to think and plan how to cross the sea. The Rākshasas are tricky, so let each leader stick with their own troops and not wander off.” Following Rāma’s orders, Sugriva and Lakshmana camped the army at the forested shore. Their blue-grey color made the monkeys look like a second sea beside the real one. Then the monkey leaders began to discuss how to cross the huge ocean. The noise from the camp was louder than the waves. The massive army, under Sugriva’s command and split into three divisions, focused on carrying out Rāma’s mission. From the shore, the monkeys gazed at the restless sea, its far side rumored to be home to demons and filled with strange sea creatures. At sunset, the ocean foamed and roared, as if it was laughing or dancing. As the moon rose, its reflection glimmered across the water. The sea—Varuna’s kingdom—was full of giant sharks, whales, and monstrous Timingalas. The wind whipped up the waves, which teemed with fiery snakes, strange animals, and rocks, making it seem bottomless. There were rocky outcrops along the shore, and the far side seemed unreachable. Makaras and sea-serpents, disturbed by the wind, churned the water. The sea, sparkling with light from the serpents below, looked like it was sprinkled with fire. The demons’ underwater world stretched all the way to the land of the Nagas. The ocean and the sky looked the same—both vast, both glittering, one with stars, one with gems. With storm clouds above and surging waves below, the sky and sea blended together. The crashing waves sounded like a trumpet echoing in the clouds. The sea sparkled with gems, but the air above was poisoned. It was filled with all kinds of creatures, heaving with anger. The monkeys watched in awe as the sea tossed and rolled, surprised by the endless, restless water before them.
Ebam ājnāpaya: Rāmānuja explains this passage. If you want the main monkeys to go first, call them; if you want the whole army to march, call everyone and leave at the right moment.—T.
The time is called abhijit.—T.

Hasta, which comes after Punarvasu, is a star of doom, signaling Rāvana’s death. The Northern Phālguni is Sitā’s birth star. Beginning the campaign under this star is a good sign for rescuing Vaidehi.—T.
Poison, among other things.—T.
[11] Refers to monkeys.—T.
The verb is singular instead of dual, as is the adjective Pārçamadishthita. But the meaning is clear.—T.
This Gaja is different from the first-mentioned Gaja.—T.

Kataka says: “Just as the moon seems to move when clouds pass in front of it, as the monkey army marched, the rivers looked like they were flowing backward.” Rāmānuja explains that the rushing monkeys actually pushed the water the other way. The latter makes more sense.—T.
The “monkey leaders.”—T.
A huge imaginary fish.—T.
A sea monster, often confused with a shark or crocodile.—T.
SECTION V

The army camped on the northern shore of the ocean, with Nila organizing the troops. Mainda and Divida, two of the most important monkeys, kept watch all around to protect the monkey army. As the soldiers settled on the coastline, Rama stood with Lakshmana at his side and spoke, “I know that grief is supposed to fade over time, but my sadness from being separated from Sita only grows stronger each day. I’m not just upset that the demon took her away in secret — what really hurts is knowing that her life might be in danger. O Wind, please go to where my beloved Sita is, and after touching her, come touch me too. Maybe then I’ll feel closer to her, especially if I look at the Moon and you’ve just touched us both. When she was taken, she cried out ‘O lord, O lord’ — those words still echo in my mind and burn me like poison. Day and night, I feel consumed by longing for her; my separation is the fire, and my thoughts of her are the flames. Lakshmana, son of Sumitra, maybe if I left you and jumped into the ocean, this fire inside me would finally be put out. The only thing that keeps me going is knowing that Sita and I are still alive on the same earth. Like dry ground soaking up water from a nearby spring, I survive just by hearing that Janaki still lives. When will I finally defeat my enemies and see Sita again — her slender waist, her lotus-like eyes — as a hero claims his prize? Like a sick man desperate for medicine, I long for the day when I can gently lift her face, with its beautiful lips and teeth, and kiss her. When will she laugh and hug me, her chest rising like a palm fruit? It hurts to think that this pure woman, with her bright eyes, is surrounded by demons and wishing for someone to save her, even though I am her husband. How is she surviving among the demon women, my beloved Sita, daughter of King Janaka and daughter-in-law of King Dasaratha? When I finally destroy those fierce Rakshasas, she’ll shine like moonbeams breaking free from dark clouds. Sita is naturally slender, and I’m sure she’s become even thinner from all her grief, hunger, and suffering. When will I finally shoot my arrows into Ravana’s chest and be free from this pain? And when will my devoted Sita, like a goddess herself, rush into my arms and cry tears of happiness? When will I finally be able to let go of this sorrow, like someone throwing away dirty clothes?” Rama, deep in thought and sorrow for Sita’s absence, spent the day like this. As the sun slowly set, Lakshmana tried to comfort him. Still lost in thoughts of Sita, with her lotus-petal eyes, Rama turned to the evening rituals and prayers.
SECTION VI

Watching from within Lankā, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākshasas, saw the terrifying destruction caused by Hanumān—a feat that reminded him of the powerful god Indra. Embarrassed and angry, Rāvaṇa addressed his assembled followers: "That monkey alone has managed to break into Lankā, a city that’s supposed to be impossible to reach. He found Sitā, King Janaka’s daughter. He smashed the palace and the sacrificial altar, killed some of our top Rākshasas, and basically threw the whole city into chaos. So, what do we do now? What should you all suggest? I want advice that’s truly worthy of me and will help keep my reputation. The wise always say, ‘Victory comes from good counsel.’ So, let’s talk seriously about what our next steps should be regarding Rāma. 

There are three kinds of people in the world: superior, average, and inferior. You can’t always tell the difference right away, so let me explain what sets them apart. The superior kind are those who seek advice from trusted friends—people who know what they’re doing or share the same goals—and sometimes even from outsiders, and who trust in fate. The average kind only rely on themselves and fate, acting on their own without much input. The inferior kind act without thinking things through, ignore fate, and just say, ‘I’ll do this,’ but end up doing nothing in the end.

Advice can also fall into three categories, just like people. The best advice comes when everyone giving it is wise, understands the rules of politics, and agrees completely. The middle kind is when people argue but eventually come to an agreement. The worst is when the advisers keep disagreeing and only barely settle on something, usually with no good result. You’re all intelligent—so I need you to work together and figure out what’s best for me and our future.

Rāma is coming toward Lankā, surrounded by thousands of determined monkeys, aiming to capture our city. He might even cross the ocean with his younger brother and that huge army of his. Rāma has the strength to dry up the sea or build a bridge over it if he wants. Since he’s coming with hostile intentions and an army of monkeys, you must come up with a plan to defend our city and our troops."
Manaswina, according to Rāmānuya, means hero.—T.
[19] That is, build a bridge across the ocean.—T.
SECTION VII

Hearing these words from their king, the powerful Rakshasas—who weren’t exactly known for their wisdom—bowed with folded hands and spoke up. "My lord, you already have enough soldiers and weapons. Why are you so worried? Remember, you defeated the serpent-people in battle after praying to the goddess Bhagavati. Even the God of Death, who lives on Mount Kailasa and is always surrounded by Yakshas, fell to you in a massive fight. You even beat that mighty human king, who was proud of being friends with Shiva, when he challenged you. After crushing the Yaksha army, you brought back this beautiful chariot from Mount Kailasa. Out of fear and wanting your friendship, Maya, the king of the Danavas, even offered you his daughter (Mandodari) to marry. With your incredible strength, you also defeated the unstoppable Danava (Madhu) for Kumbhinasi’s (your sister’s) happiness. You went underground and conquered the powerful serpent kings—Vasuki, Takshaka, Sankha, and Jati—bringing them all under your control. Remember the Kalakeyas, those fierce Danavas who were nearly invincible because of their magical boons? You fought them for a whole year and finally defeated them, learning all sorts of magical tricks from them. You even beat the heroic sons of Varuna, who had a huge army behind them. Facing Death’s own terrifying kingdom—where his staff is like giant sea creatures, agonies like trees, his noose like crashing waves, his helpers as snakes, and his fever as the deep’s darkness—you dove in and defeated Death himself, coming out victorious. Everyone celebrated your win. Back then, the earth was full of powerful warriors, each as strong as Indra, like the world is filled with all kinds of trees today. Even Rama (Raghava) can’t compare to their might. Yet you crushed all those unbeatable heroes, my king. So, please, just wait here and don’t worry yourself. Indrajit alone can destroy all these monkeys. After all, he performed the Maheshwara sacrifice and got a rare and powerful boon. He once fought the entire army of gods—the ocean of gods, with weapons as fish, arms as moss, elephants as turtles, horses as frogs, Rudra and Aditya as the wild beasts, Maruts and Vasus as the great serpents, chariots, horses, and elephants as the water, infantry as the shore. Indrajit even captured the king of the gods and brought him here to Lanka. Later, following Brahma’s orders, he let the king of the gods go, who then returned to heaven. So, my king, let Indrajit handle this—he’ll destroy the monkey army and Rama. And don’t dismiss this threat just because it comes from someone you think is unworthy. You will defeat Rama.”
This refers to Mandodari, Ravana’s favorite queen.—T.
This refers to Madhu.—T.
Ravana’s sister, who was married to Madhu.—T.
Refers to Maheshwara—the Great Lord, another name for Shiva.—T.
SECTION VIII

The powerful Rakshasa general Prahasta, who looked as dark and imposing as a storm cloud, stepped forward with his hands folded in respect. “I’m strong enough to defeat gods, demons, spirits, even magical birds and serpents—so what are two mere humans to me?” he declared confidently. “We let our guard down and got fooled by Hanuman. But as long as I’m alive, that forest-dweller won’t escape again. I’ll wipe out every monkey on earth, from the mountains to the seas. Just give me the order. I promise, Lord of the Night, I’ll save our people from the monkeys, and you won’t have to suffer any consequences from your actions.” 

At that, another Rakshasa named Durmukha, burning with anger, spoke up. “We can’t just forgive what’s happened to us—the humiliation of having our capital and even your private chambers invaded by that monkey! I’ll go right now, alone, and wipe out all the monkeys, even if they hide in the ocean, the sky, or underground.”

Then Vajradanshtra, a fierce Rakshasa wielding a massive, bloodstained club, said furiously, “Why bother with the weak Hanuman when Rama, the unstoppable, is still out there with Sugriva and Lakshmana? Today, I’ll kill Rama, Sugriva, and Lakshmana myself with this club, and after crushing the monkey army, I’ll return. But, my king, listen to my idea! Success comes to those who are clever and prepared. Let’s send thousands of terrifying Rakshasas, shape-shifters chosen by you, to find Rama. They should appear before him in human form and calmly say, ‘We’ve been sent by your younger brother.’ When Rama hears this, he’ll quickly gather his forces and come here. Then, armed with weapons—spears, axes, bows, swords—we’ll attack from the sky in groups, raining rocks and weapons down on the monkeys and destroy them. This way, we’ll trick Rama and Lakshmana, and if our plan works, they won’t survive.”

Next, Nikumbha, the mighty son of Kumbhakarna, stepped forward, filled with rage. He said to Ravana, the destroyer of worlds, “You all stay here with our great king. I’ll go alone and kill Rama, Lakshmana, Sugriva, Hanuman, and all the monkeys.”

Then Vajrahanu, a Rakshasa as big as a mountain, licked the corners of his mouth hungrily and said, “Relax—do whatever you want without worry. I’ll devour the entire monkey army myself. You can just sit back and drink Varuna wine. I’ll take care of Sugriva, Lakshmana, Hanuman, Angada, and every last monkey, all by myself.”
[24] Meaning Ravana’s abduction of Sita. —T.
“Twarita”—meaning “with speed”—is unnecessary here. —T.
Varuna wine, also called Varuni, is made from hogweed mixed with date or palm juice, then distilled. —T.
SECTION IX

The Rākshasas—Rabhasa, the formidable Suryyaçatru, Saptaghna, Yajnakopa, Mahāpārçwa, Mahodara, Agniketu (who was unstoppable), Raçmiketu, Indraçatru (Rāvana’s own son), Prahasta, Virupāksha, the powerful Vajradanshtra, Dhumrāksha, Nikumbha, and Durmukha—were furious. They grabbed their weapons—clubs, spears, axes, bows, arrows, swords shining like clear water, and more. Fired up, they turned to Rāvana and declared, “Today we’ll kill Rāma, Sugriva, Lakshmana, and the defenseless Hanumān, who dared to attack Lankā.”  

But before they could act, Vibhishana stepped in and made them sit down. With his hands pressed together, he spoke earnestly: “The wise say you should only fight when all other options have failed. Direct confrontation only works if you plan carefully and catch your enemies off guard, distracted, or already weakened. Why are you so eager to fight Rāma? He’s alert, determined to win, blessed by the gods, self-controlled, and nearly impossible to defeat. Who ever imagined Hanumān could cross the terrifying ocean, the ruler of all rivers, to get here? Friends, Rāma’s strength is beyond measure, so don’t underestimate him. And ask yourselves: What did Rāma ever do to Rāvana to deserve having his wife stolen from Janasthāna? If Khara was killed by Rāma because he invaded where he shouldn’t have, well, anyone would defend themselves if attacked.

This huge fear we feel is all because of Sitā’s capture—if she’s returned, the danger ends. Why cause more trouble? Rāma is powerful, but he’s also just; he wouldn’t attack for no reason. So, give him back his wife, Maithili (another name for Sitā). Before Rāma destroys Lankā with his arrows, and before the unstoppable monkey army closes in, return Sitā. If you don’t, Lankā will fall, and all the brave Rākshasas will die. I’m only trying to help because we’re family—please listen. What I’m saying is true and for your own good: return Maithili to Rāma. Before Rāma’s arrows, sharp as the autumn sun’s rays, rain down to destroy you, do the right thing and give her back. Let go of your anger—it only brings ruin. Follow what’s right, and we can all survive with our families. Return Maithili to Daçaratha’s son.”

Hearing Vibhishana’s words, Rāvana, lord of the Rākshasas, left everyone behind and went into his private chambers.
The other three options are negotiation, giving gifts, and creating division among enemies.
Meaning, when the enemies are in the hands of others—captive, distracted, or weakened.
The fear is rooted in revenge for Khara’s death and others killed by Rāma.
SECTION X

At dawn, Vibhishana (Vibhi), loyal to virtue and skilled in politics, brave and dignified, prepared to risk everything. Like the rising sun entering storm clouds, he stepped into the grand palace of his older brother, Ravana. The palace was huge, its towers rising like mountain peaks, and inside it was organized into large, beautiful rooms. Powerful and respected people loyal to Ravana gathered there. Fierce Rakshasa guards stood watch, while the air buzzed with the breath of restless elephants. Conch shells blared and trumpets echoed through the halls. The palace was full of beautiful women, and the corridors overflowed with conversation. Doors were plated with shining gold, and the whole place sparkled with decorations and gems, looking almost supernatural—like the homes of the Gandharvas or Maruts, or even the legendary serpent palaces. As Vibhishana entered, he heard the chanting of Brahmanas, learned in the Vedas, singing of Ravana’s victories. He saw priests being honored with offerings of yogurt, clarified butter, flowers, and roasted rice. Vibhishana, strong and wise, bowed to Ravana, who was sitting there, and after being politely acknowledged, took a gold-covered seat indicated to him. When they were alone, or only with trusted advisors present, Vibhishana spoke up. He addressed Ravana with careful but honest words, hoping to help him. After greeting his brother with respect, Vibhishana began, “Ever since you brought Vaidehi (Sita) here, I’ve noticed bad omens everywhere. When the sacred fire is lit, it’s choked with smoke and sparks, the flames dim and weak, even when offerings are made with the proper chants. Snakes appear in kitchens, in the rooms for sacrifice, and where the Vedas are recited. Ants are found in the ghee. The cows aren’t giving milk, and the best elephants no longer drip their usual must. Even though the horses are well-fed, they neigh anxiously. Donkeys, camels, and mules, their fur bristling, cry and shed tears, and even with treatment, they don’t improve. Everywhere, crows gather on rooftops, cawing harshly. Vultures sit in misery on house-tops. At dawn and dusk, jackals appear and howl ominously. Wolves and other wild beasts, even deer, gather at the palace gates, roaring like thunder. I believe only one thing can end these evil signs: give Vaidehi back to Rama. If I’ve spoken out of ignorance or selfishness, forgive me, great king. But everyone in the palace—Rakshasas, Rakshasis, servants, and family—will suffer if this continues. None of your advisors have dared to say this to you, but I must speak the truth as I see it. You should act wisely, for everyone’s sake.” Thus, Vibhishana, in front of Ravana and his counselors, spoke honestly, hoping to save his brother and their people. Ravana listened to his brother’s careful, wise advice—clear, logical, and meant for his good both now and in the future—but the king, obsessed with Sita, exploded with anger. “I have no fear, none at all! Rama will never get Mithila’s daughter. Even if Rama comes with Lakshmana and all the gods led by Indra, how could he ever defeat me in battle?” With that, the ten-headed Ravana, who had crushed the gods themselves, dismissed Vibhishana, ignoring his honest warning.
Vibhishana knew that trying to convince Ravana to make peace was dangerous, given Ravana’s fierce nature.
Kuvera—Ravana was Kuvera’s younger brother.
The comment explains: “Even after eating their fill, the horses still act hungry.”
Meaning, “as I advised.”
SECTION XI

The corrupt king Rāvana, overwhelmed by his obsession with Sita, was weakened both by his own wrongdoing and by the shame he felt after losing the respect of his friends. With no other reason left to hold back, and his mind constantly fixated on Vaidehi (Sita), Rāvana and his advisers decided that the time for war had finally come. He set out, climbing into a massive chariot with golden mesh, decorated with pearls and coral, and pulled by expertly trained horses. As he rode in this impressive vehicle—its sound like rolling thunder—the ten-headed lord of the Rakshasas made his way to the royal court. Ahead of him walked fierce Rakshasas armed with swords, shields, and all kinds of weapons. Some wore terrifying costumes and glittered with different ornaments, forming a protective ring around his sides and rear. Elite warriors rode in their own chariots, alongside huge elephants and spirited horses, all carrying maces, clubs, spears, and heavy weapons. As Rāvana approached the court, the air filled with the deafening blare of a thousand trumpets and the wild blasts of conch shells. His powerful chariot raced forward, echoing off the buildings and making the city streets come alive with excitement. Above him, a spotless white umbrella was held aloft, shining like a full moon. On either side, two white whisks with golden threads waved gracefully. All the Rakshasas on the ground folded their hands in respect and bowed their heads as their king passed by in his chariot. As the Rakshasas sang and cheered for his victory, the energetic and terrifying Rāvana arrived at the grand court—built by Vishwakarma himself. Rāvana entered the hall, its floor paved with silver and gold, the center sparkling with crystal, and covered in fine silk embroidered with gold. The place was magnificently built by Vishwakarma and guarded by six hundred spirits. Rāvana sat down on a luxurious high seat made of lapis lazuli, with a pillow and a soft deerskin cover. Sitting proudly, he ordered his fast-moving messengers:

“Go quickly and summon all the Rakshasas. We need to make a major effort against our enemies.” As soon as he spoke, the messengers hurried through Lanka, going to every house and boldly gathering the Rakshasas from their games, bedrooms, and gardens. Some sped off in chariots, others rode proud horses, and some went on foot. The city became crowded with people arriving in chariots, on elephants, and on horses—like the sky filled with flocks of birds. Leaving their vehicles at the entrance, they entered the court on foot, like lions stepping into mountain caves. They bowed and touched the king’s feet, and he honored them in return. They sat down—some on raised seats, some on kusa grass cushions, and some on the floor—each according to their status, obeying the king’s command. Scholars and wise men, skilled at making sound judgments, also arrived and took their seats in order of rank. Courtiers with high character and broad knowledge, along with hundreds of heroic warriors, gathered in the court to discuss the best course of action. Then Vibhishana, Rāvana’s noble and well-known younger brother, rode up in a large, splendid chariot decorated in gold and pulled by horses. Announcing himself, he bowed at Rāvana’s feet. Suka and Prahasta helped everyone find seats appropriate to their rank. The entire court became filled with the scent of fine agarwood, sandal, and garlands from the Rakshasas, who were dressed in gold, gems, and expensive clothes. No one spoke out of turn, lied, or raised their voice. Having achieved what they wanted, these fierce warriors stared intently at their king. Amid this gathering of clever, strong, and armed Rakshasas, Rāvana looked as majestic as Indra, king of the gods, among his own celestial warriors.
SECTION XII

Ravana, surveying the whole assembly, turned to Prahasta—the general of his army—and said, “General, you need to organize the four divisions of our forces so they can protect the city effectively.” Prahasta, carefully following Ravana’s orders, positioned troops both inside and outside the city. Once the defenses were set up, Prahasta sat before Ravana and reported, “I’ve placed your strong forces everywhere, both within and outside the city. So don’t let yourself be anxious—go ahead and do whatever you have in mind.” Hearing Prahasta’s reassuring words, Ravana, eager for pleasure, addressed his followers: “In times of crisis—whether it’s about virtue, happiness, or our interests—you must know how to act, whether it’s pleasant or not, profitable or not, good or bad. None of my plans have ever failed when you all have taken counsel with me. Just as Indra is surrounded by the moon, stars, planets, and the Maruts, I am surrounded by you—and that’s what’s brought me such success. I will definitely need your help now. Because I was asleep, I couldn’t inform him about this matter earlier. After sleeping for six months, that mighty warrior—one of the greatest—is finally awake. Janaka’s daughter, Sita—Rama’s beloved wife—has been brought here from the Dandaka forest, the territory of the Rakshasas (demons). Yet, this beautiful woman refuses to share my bed. There’s no one in the three worlds who compares to Sita. She’s slim-waisted, has perfect hips, and her face is like the autumn moon, shining like gold. She’s gentle and looks like a masterpiece crafted by the magical Maya, with endless charms. When I see her delicate feet, their pink soles, and coppery nails, my desire burns inside me. Her beauty is like the flame of a sacred fire or the brilliance of the sun; her lovely face, elegant nose, and striking eyes make me lose control. My passion for her isn’t mixed with anger or happiness, but it’s making me pale and constantly tormented. Sita, with her wide, beautiful eyes, asked for a year’s time, hoping Rama would save her, and I promised her this. But my desire is wearing me out, like a horse exhausted from too much running. How could forest dwellers or Dasharatha’s sons possibly cross the wild sea, teeming with strange creatures and fish? Yet even a single month has brought us serious trouble. It’s clear that destiny is unpredictable. Each of you should act as you think best. Even though mortals shouldn’t be a threat to us, you must still discuss what we should do. In the past, I’ve won victories with your help; stand by me now as you did then. Rama’s sons, having learned that Sita is across the ocean, have come with Sugriva and his monkey army to the seashore. Give me your advice—how can I keep Sita here and destroy Dasharatha’s sons? But be sure your advice is solid. No one else in this world could cross the sea with an army of monkeys—so victory should be certain for me.” 

Hearing Ravana’s sorrowful words, full of longing, Kumbhakarna was furious and replied, “When you first saw Sita with Rama and Lakshmana, and then kidnapped her by force, it was clear your mind had been completely taken over by her—like a river in full flood. Ravana, what you did wasn’t worthy of a great king. If you had asked our advice from the start, we would have guided you properly. A wise king—one who makes decisions after careful thought and acts justly—never has to regret his actions. But actions taken without thinking, like pouring pure butter into a dirty fire, only cause harm. Someone who does things out of order—putting the cart before the horse—doesn’t know what is right. Others notice the mistakes of those who act rashly, even if they seem powerful—like swans finding the hole in Mount Krauncha made by Kumara’s dart. Honestly, it’s only luck that Rama hasn’t killed you already for this reckless act, which is as dangerous as poisoned food. Still, since you’ve set things in motion, even if it’s wrong, I will help you by destroying your enemies. I swear, I’ll wipe out your foes—even if Indra, the sun god, Agni, the war god Kartikeya, Kubera, and Varuna all fight me. Purandara himself (another name for Indra) will tremble when I, towering like a mountain and wielding my massive club, roar and take them on. Before Rama can shoot a second arrow at me, I’ll drain his life. Take comfort—I’ll make sure Dasharatha’s son is killed and victory is yours. After killing Rama and Lakshmana, I’ll devour the most important monkeys. So relax—drink Varuni (the liquor of the gods) and take care of your affairs with a calm mind. Once Rama is sent to the land of the dead, Sita will belong to you forever.”
This passage really brings Cleopatra to mind. The Bengali translators, apparently unsure how to handle "Mayava Mayanirmita," just kept the phrase as it was in their versions.—T.
I don’t really get what “no other person” (anyasya) means here, and the commentator isn’t any help.—T.
This part is very confusing, and the commentator’s notes don’t clarify anything.—T.
[37] In other words, we would have stopped you.—T.
This refers to the hole made in Mount Krauncha by Kumara’s dart.—T.
SECTION XIII

Seeing that Rāvana was furious, the powerful Mahāpārcwa paused for a moment to think, then spoke with his hands pressed together in respect: “Anyone who goes into the forest, full of deer and wild beasts, and doesn’t taste the honey there is just being foolish. O conqueror of enemies, who could possibly rule over you, when you yourself are the ruler? Enjoy Sītā (Vaidehi), having taken your enemy’s wife. You have incredible strength—live your life boldly, like a rooster strutting in its territory. Keep visiting Sītā as often as you want, enjoy her, and take pleasure from it. Once you’ve achieved your goal, what do you have to be afraid of? Whether you’re on guard or relaxed, you’ll be able to handle any threat. With Kumbhakarna fighting alongside us, and the mighty Indrajit as well, we’re strong enough to defeat even the thunder-wielding god Indra. I don’t care for peaceful solutions like gifts, negotiation, or sowing dissent, even though the wise say these are ways to win. I prefer victory through force. We will, without a doubt, defeat all your enemies with our own strength.” When Mahāpārcwa finished speaking, King Rāvana, pleased with his words, replied, “Mahāpārcwa, you’ve spoken boldly, so I’ll share something secret about myself—something that happened after I saw Panjikasthalā, glowing in the sky as she flew to the Great-father’s mansion. She slowed down when she noticed me. I seized her and stripped her clothes away. She went to the Great-father looking wilted, like a crushed lotus. The Great-father learned everything I had done, and in his anger, he told me, ‘If from this day you ever force yourself on a woman, your head will be shattered into a hundred pieces.’ That’s why, even though I want to, I have not forced Sītā, the daughter of Videha, to sleep with me. I’m terrified of that curse. My might is like the ocean’s surge, and I move as fast as the wind. Daçaratha’s son (Rāma) doesn’t realize this—that’s why he thinks he can cross the ocean. Who would dare disturb a sleeping lion in its cave, especially when it’s as deadly as Death itself? Rāma has never seen the arrows I shoot, which are like venomous snakes—if he had, he wouldn’t approach me. Like a fire burning down an elephant, I will destroy Rāma with hundreds of arrows as powerful as thunderbolts. When the Sun rises, it makes the stars disappear; in the same way, surrounded by my massive army, I’ll crush Rāma’s strength. Not even Indra, the thousand-eyed god, or Varuna, the god of the ocean, can take me on. With the power of this army, I once conquered this very city, which used to be ruled by Vaiçravana.”
SECTION XIV

After hearing the words of the king of the Rākshasas (Rāvana) and the loud roar of Kumbhakarna, Vibhishana spoke up for Rāvana’s own good. He said, "You’re trapped, brother, like a giant snake has wrapped itself around your neck. That snake is Sita—her body is the snake’s coils, her anxiety is its venom, her smile is its fangs, and her five fingers are its hood. Before the monkey army—who are like living mountains, with teeth like fists and claws like weapons—overruns Lanka, give Sita back to Dasharatha’s son (Rāma). And before Rāma’s arrows, which strike as hard as thunderbolts and fly as fast as the wind, start cutting off the heads of our best warriors, return Mithila’s daughter to him. Not even Kumbhakarna, Indrajit, Mahāpārcwa, Mahodara, Nikumbha, Kumbha, or Atikaya, O King, can stand against Rāma in battle. No matter where you run—behind the Sun, into the wind, into Indra’s own lap, or even if you escape to the sky or the underworld—you won’t be able to escape death." After hearing Vibhishana’s warning, Prahasta replied, "We don’t fear gods, demons, spirits, or even giant snakes. We’re not afraid of fighting birds or serpents either. So why should we be scared of Rāma, just a king’s son?" Vibhishana, still hoping to save the king and thinking carefully about what was best, answered with real seriousness: "Prahasta, what you, Mahodara, the king, and Kumbhakarna are saying about Rāma is as pointless as a sinner hoping to reach heaven. Without a raft, no one can cross the ocean—how can you, I, or even all the Rākshasas together, ever hope to defeat Rāma, who understands everything? Even the gods can be stunned by the ruler of the Ikshwāku line—Rāma, who stands for justice, is a hero in battle, and is highly capable. You speak so confidently only because Rāma’s deadly arrows, tipped with eagle feathers, haven’t yet struck you. You talk this way because you haven’t felt what it’s like when his sharp, thunderbolt-like arrows hit. Not even Rāvana, nor the incredibly strong Triçirsha, nor Kumbhakarna’s son Nikumbha, nor Indrajit can stand up to Dasharatha’s son in battle—he’s like Indra himself. And neither Devāntaka nor Narantaka, neither Atikāya nor the mighty Atiratha, nor the equally strong Akampana, can stop Rāma in a fight. The king—who is naturally hot-tempered and sometimes careless—is being led to ruin by people who pretend to be his friends but are actually his enemies. You need to save him, because he’s now trapped by a terrifying, giant, thousand-headed serpent—Rāma’s strength. Just as friends would pull someone possessed by a powerful ghost back to safety, you should work together to rescue the king. He’s drowning in the ocean that is Rāma. Join forces and save him fast. He’s fallen into the depths created by the Kākutstha clan. I’m telling you this for the good of our city, the Rākshasas, the king, and all his followers. Give Maithili (Sita) back to the son of the king. A true advisor is someone who gives his master honest advice after properly judging the strengths and weaknesses of both friends and enemies.
That is, destroyer of the gods.
That is, destroyer of men.
That is, huge-bodied.
SECTION XV

After listening carefully to Bibhisana’s advice, Indrajit—the leader of the demons and known for his sharp mind—replied, “Uncle, why are you talking like this, as if you’re scared? Even someone who wasn’t born into our family wouldn’t say such useless things. In our whole family, only you, Uncle Bibhisana, lack energy, strength, courage, patience, and heroism. Why are you so afraid of them? Any one of these Rakshasas could kill those two princes—they’re just humans. I’ve already beaten the king of the gods himself and brought him down to earth. All the other gods ran away in fear. I dragged down the mighty Airavata, the celestial elephant, and tore out its tusks. The gods were terrified. If I can do all that—scare the gods and defeat the strongest demons—don’t you think I can handle two ordinary human princes?” 

Bibhisana, who was a master of weapons and known for his wisdom, replied to Indrajit, whose energy seemed unstoppable and who was almost like a god himself: “My son, you’re still young and your mind isn’t mature. That’s why you can’t tell right from wrong, and you’re talking like someone who’s lost his mind—leading yourself to disaster. People call you Ravana’s son, Indrajit, but in truth, you’re acting like his enemy, since you know Raghava will destroy him and yet you do nothing to stop it. You’re brave but naive, driven by foolish ideas. You’ll die along with the one who brought you into this council. Indrajit, you’re reckless, lack judgment, aren’t humble, get angry too easily, and don’t think things through. You’re speaking like a child. Who could survive in battle against Raghava’s arrows, which are like the staff of Death or the burning rod of Brahma himself? Give Sita back to Rama, along with riches, jewels, fine clothes, and gems—then we can all live here in peace, without sorrow.”
SECTION XVI

After Bibhishana (let's call him "Bibi" for short) finished speaking, offering wise and thoughtful advice, Ravana, driven by his own doom, shot back with harsh words. “It’s better to live among obvious enemies or angry snakes than with people who pretend to be friends but are really plotting against you. I know how relatives are in every world, Bibhishana—one always takes pleasure in the other’s problems. Relatives, especially among Rakshasas, rarely respect their own king, even if he’s protecting the kingdom, educated, and religious. If he’s a true hero, they just want to see him fall. These so-called family members are the real enemies—hypocrites who secretly enjoy each other’s misfortunes. Listen, I’ll tell you what elephants once said when they saw people coming at them with ropes: ‘We don’t fear fire, weapons, or even deadly traps—we only fear our own kind, blinded by their selfishness. They alone reveal the ways we can be destroyed—no doubt about it. Fear of family is the worst fear.’ Cows give milk; relatives give you fear. Women are unpredictable; Brahmanas are devoted to discipline. I guess you’re not happy that I’m respected in all three worlds, wealthy, and have crushed my enemies. Friendship with unworthy people is as short-lived as water on a lotus leaf. It’s like a raincloud in autumn—threatening, but never delivering. It’s like a bee that leaves after taking the honey, or one that finds no nectar in the Kasa flower—totally pointless. Or like an elephant who, right after bathing, just covers itself in dust again. That’s what it’s like to trust people who aren’t worthy. Shame on you, monkey! You disgrace our family. If anyone else had said this to me, they’d be dead by now.” 

After being insulted like this, Bibhishana, sticking to the truth, stood up with four other Rakshasas, each holding a mace. Then, rising up into the sky, graceful and furious, Bibhishana addressed Ravana: “You’re wrong, brother. Say whatever you want—you’re my older brother, someone I respect like a father. But you’re no longer following the path of virtue. I can’t just accept your cruel words. I spoke up for your own good, Ravana, but you ignored me, blinded by death itself. So many people say nice things, but it’s rare to find someone who’ll tell the hard truths, or who’ll listen to them. How can I ignore your downfall, which is coming for you like a burning house, now that Death has got you in its grip? I don’t want to see you killed by Rama’s sharp, gold-tipped arrows, blazing like fire. Even the strongest warriors, masters of weapons, are worn down in battle when Death calls. I still respect you—please forgive me for saying what I did, because I meant it for your good. Protect yourself, and protect this city full of Rakshasas. I wish you well, but I have to go. I hope you can be happy without me. What I said was meant to help you, but you didn’t want to hear it. When someone’s time is almost up, they never listen to good advice from their friends.”
Because he was born first—T.
They later abandon the friends they once had.—T.
SECTION XVII

After speaking harshly to Rāvana, his younger brother Bibhishana wasted no time and flew straight to where Rāma and Lakshmana were. The monkey leaders on the ground saw him in the sky, as massive as the peak of Mount Meru and shining with a lightning-bright glow. He was followed by four fierce attendants, all decked out in fine ornaments and protected by armor, each wielding a heavy mace. Bibhishana himself looked like a storm cloud, mighty as thunder, holding his own impressive mace and covered in shining jewelry. When Sugriva, the clever king of the monkeys, spotted Bibhishana with his four companions, he paused to think. After a moment, he turned to the monkeys gathered around Hanumān and said, “Look, there’s a Rākshasa (demon) coming, armed with weapons and followed by four others. I’m certain they mean to kill us.” The monkeys, hearing Sugriva’s warning, grabbed huge trees and boulders and said, “Just say the word, King, and we’ll destroy these evil demons. Their time is almost up anyway.” While they discussed this, Bibhishana landed on the northern shore. Seeing Sugriva and his group nearby, the wise Bibhishana called out in a loud voice, “Is Rāvana, the demon king, still alive—the same one responsible for so many terrible deeds? I am his younger brother, Bibhishana. Rāvana killed the vulture Jatāyu and kidnapped Sītā from Janasthāna. Now Sītā is locked away, watched closely by demon women. I tried to convince Rāvana, using every argument, that he should return Sītā to Rāma. But Rāvana, blinded by fate, ignored me, like a dying man refusing medicine. After he insulted me and treated me like a servant, I decided to leave everything—my home, my family—and come seek Rāma’s protection. Please let the great Rāma know that I, Bibhishana, have come to him.” 

Hearing this, Sugriva, quick-tempered and suspicious, turned to Rāma and said, “An enemy has sneaked in among us. He’ll kill us if he gets the chance, like an owl preying on crows. You need to be extra careful now—watch our counsel, our battle plans, our friends and spies, and especially the enemy’s spies. These Rākshasas are dangerous; they can change shape, ambush us, and plot secretly. We can’t trust them. This must be one of Rāvana’s agents, sent to stir up trouble in our camp or to attack us when we let our guard down. We should gather our allies and servants and keep them close. This man is a demon, Rāvana’s own brother—so he’s our enemy. How can we trust him? Bibhishana, Rāvana’s brother, has come here with four demons, asking for your protection. But I think he was sent by Rāvana and should be killed. If we trust him, he’ll use his tricks to kill you when you least expect it.” When Sugriva finished, he fell silent.

Rāma listened to Sugriva and then addressed the monkeys—including Hanumān—near him. “You all heard Sugriva’s reasonable words about Rāvana’s brother. When someone wants to protect their fortune and is wise, they should give good advice to their friends in tough times.” At Rāma’s invitation, the monkeys began sharing their own opinions, all focused on Rāma’s safety. 

They said, “Rāghava, nothing in the three worlds is hidden from you. You ask our advice out of respect, not because you need it. You are honest, brave, pious, strong, wise, and loyal to your friends. Let your most trusted advisors give their honest opinions.” After this, Angada, one of the smartest monkeys, spoke up to judge Bibhishana’s intentions: “We should be suspicious—he’s come from the enemy’s side. We can’t just trust him right away. Evil people hide their true selves, waiting to take advantage and cause disaster. We always need to weigh right and wrong. If you find he’s up to no good, reject him. If he’s truly good, accept him.”

Next, Sarava spoke up, “Rāma, you should send messengers to test Bibhishana. Use skilled spies to check if he’s really a friend, and if he is, win him over.” Then Jāmbavān, wise and learned, added, “Bibhishana comes from our enemy Rāvana, who hates us. He’s shown up at a bad place and a bad time. We should be cautious.” Mainda, another thoughtful monkey, offered, “He’s Rāvana’s brother, Bibhishana. The best thing to do is speak to him kindly and find out why he’s here—whether for good or evil—then decide what to do.”

Finally, Hanumān, the smartest advisor and master of the scriptures, spoke up in a calm, sincere voice. “No one, not even Vrihaspati (the god of wisdom), is a better speaker or thinker than you, Rāma. I’m not giving this advice out of pride or just to show off my skills—only for your sake. I think the idea of testing Bibhishana, as some have suggested, won’t work. We can’t just order him to reveal his motives; that would be wrong. And sending spies probably won’t help either. Jāmbavān said Bibhishana came at a bad time and place, but I think it’s the opposite—it’s a good time and a good place. Bibhishana realized that Rāvana is cruel and you are just. Rāvana is full of vices while you have many virtues. Rāvana is a tyrant and you are strong. Considering your preparations for war, Rāvana’s arrogance, the defeat of Vāli, and Sugriva’s rise, Bibhishana has made a smart choice coming here—maybe he’s even hoping for a kingdom. Judging by his words and his expression, I didn’t see any sign of deceit. He didn’t seem sneaky or fearful. People can’t easily hide their true nature—it always shows. So I think Bibhishana’s actions make sense. If we accept him, it could benefit both him and us. I believe he’s sincere, and that’s my honest opinion. Now, Rāma, it’s up to you to decide what you think is right.”
Able to understand the truth in all the scriptures.—T.
To ask him directly why he’s come.—T.
SECTION XVIII

After hearing what Hanuman (the son of the Wind-god) had to say, Rama—who knew all the ancient texts and was never shaken—shared his own thoughts. “I’ve been considering what to do about Vibhishana too,” he began. “I want you all, who care about my safety, to listen. Vibhishana has come here as a friend, so I can’t just turn him away. Even if he does have bad intentions, it’s not wrong for good people to offer him shelter.” The monkey king Sugriva listened and then answered in a more hopeful tone, “No matter if this rakshasa (demon) is honest or evil, we shouldn’t trust him—he’s abandoned his own brother when things got tough. Why should we think he won’t do the same to us if we end up in trouble?”

Rama looked at his companions and, with a slight smile, spoke to Lakshmana, who was known for his goodness. “Sugriva, you’re speaking wisely—words like these usually come from someone who’s studied the scriptures or spent time with elders. Still, I see two deeper reasons why brothers sometimes turn against each other, especially among kings. One is obvious, and the other is more about human nature. There are two kinds of enemies: those from your own family and those who are outsiders. Both can bring disaster when given the chance. That’s why Vibhishana is here. Relatives who don’t plot against each other usually want the best for one another, but even well-meaning family members can make a king nervous. Let me explain what the scriptures say about taking in someone who was once an enemy: We aren’t Vibhishana’s family, and he’s come here because he wants the throne. Even rakshasas are smart enough to know what’s best for them—so we should accept Vibhishana. Brothers who trust each other stay together, but when trust is broken, it leads to fear and eventually, war. Clearly, there’s trouble between Ravana and Vibhishana, which is why Vibhishana left him. Not every brother is like Bharata, not every son is like me to his father, and not every friend is as loyal as you, Sugriva.”

After Rama finished, Sugriva—the wise monkey king—stood up with Lakshmana, bowed his head, and said, “Rama, you are the most forgiving person I know, but I believe Vibhishana has been sent by Ravana. It would be safer to kill him. Driven by his own twisted mind, this rakshasa is here to destroy us, and he’ll attack when we think we’re safe. That’s why I think we should kill Vibhishana—the younger brother of the ruthless Ravana—along with his advisors.” Sugriva, skilled in debate, fell silent after saying this.

Rama listened carefully to Sugriva’s words, thought them over, and then replied to the monkey king with even more reasonable arguments. “Whether Vibhishana is good or bad, he can’t really harm me. I could destroy all the Pisachas, Danavas, Yakshas, or every rakshasa on earth with just my fingertips if I wanted, Sugriva. I once heard a story about a pigeon who welcomed its enemy—the killer of its mate—and even offered its own flesh as food. If even a pigeon can treat an enemy who seeks shelter so kindly, how could I do otherwise? Let me tell you a story I heard from the great sage Kandu, the son of Kanya. He said that even if an enemy is cruel, if he comes to you with folded hands and a humble heart, begging for your protection, you should not kill him. If someone, out of pride or fear, asks for shelter, a great person should protect him—even if it means risking their own life. Ignoring someone who seeks your help—whether out of fear, ignorance, or choice—is a serious sin and brings shame to everyone. If you let someone be killed after they’ve put their trust in you, you lose all your virtue. The sin of refusing shelter to someone in need is so great that it can block your path to heaven, ruin your reputation, and sap your strength. So I will follow Kandu’s wise advice—it brings goodness, fame, and even a place with the gods. I always promise safety to anyone who comes to me and says, ‘I am yours’ and wants my protection. That’s my vow. Sugriva, go bring Vibhishana here—whether he’s Ravana or Vibhishana—and I will promise him safety.”

Hearing this, Sugriva—overflowing with loyalty—spoke to Rama, “I’m not surprised you would say such noble things. You’re the best of kings, wise, strong, and always on the right path. Honestly, I don’t think Vibhishana has any evil intentions. I’ve watched his body language and signs. Rama, let’s treat Vibhishana as an equal and welcome him as a friend.” When Sugriva finished, Rama—the king of men—instantly made friends with Vibhishana, just like a conqueror making an alliance with the king of birds.

(More reasonable words.—T.)
