SECTION XIX

After Rāma (also called Raghava) reassured him, Bibhisana—Rāvana’s younger brother—lowered his head and looked at the ground. Along with his loyal followers, Bibhisana, who was known for his virtue and wisdom, descended from the sky, happy and respectful, and bowed before Rāma. He touched Rāma’s feet with four other Rakshasas and spoke to Rāma with humble and sincere words. “I am Rāvana’s younger brother. He has treated me badly, so I have left Lankā behind, given up my friends and riches, and come to seek your protection—the protector of all. My kingdom, my life, and my happiness are all yours to command.” Rāma listened and comforted him, both with his words and his welcoming attitude. “Tell me honestly about the strengths and weaknesses of our enemies,” Rāma said. Asked this by Rāma, who never tired of action, Bibhisana began to describe Rāvana’s forces.

“Prince,” Bibhisana began, “thanks to a blessing from the Creator, the Ten-headed Rāvana can’t be killed by any creature—neither spirits, snakes, nor birds. My older brother, Kumbhakarna, is a great warrior and shines with power—he’s as strong as Indra in battle. You may have heard of Prahasta, Rāvana’s commander, who once defeated Manibhadra on Mount Kailāsa. Rāvana’s son, Indrajit, wears unbeatable armor and uses a bow and finger-guard made from iguana skin. He can make himself invisible in battle. He worships Fire, disappears from sight, and then strikes down his enemies—even when their armies are huge and well-organized. Other commanders—Mahodara, Mahāpārcwa, and the Rakshasa Akampana—are just as powerful as the guardians of the world.” (see note [130]) “Rāvana’s army has a hundred billion Rakshasas who can change their form whenever they want; they live in Lankā and feast on flesh and blood. Even the guardians of the world and the gods lost to Rāvana and his army.” After hearing all this, Rāma thought it over and replied, “Bibhisana, you’ve given me a clear picture of Rāvana’s power. Now listen: I swear I’ll defeat the Ten-headed Rāvana, Prahasta, and his sons, and I’ll make you king. Even if Rāvana hides in the lowest hell” (see note [132]) “or under the earth, or tries to get the gods’ grandfather to protect him, he won’t escape me. I swear on my three brothers that I’ll return to Ayodhyā only after killing Rāvana, his sons, family, and friends in battle.” Hearing this, Bibhisana bowed low and said, “I’ll help you destroy the Rakshasas and the city of Lankā. I’ll even fight in the middle of Rāvana’s army.” Rāma hugged Bibhisana and, pleased, said to Lakshmana, “Brother, bring water from the ocean. I want to anoint Bibhisana right now and make him king of the Rakshasas, because I’m truly happy with him.” Lakshmana, following Rāma’s order, brought the water and made Bibhisana king of the Rakshasas in front of all the monkeys. Seeing how kindly Rāma treated Bibhisana, the monkeys cheered and shouted praise.

“Excellent! Excellent!” they cried. Then Hanumān and Sugriva turned to Bibhisana and asked, “Can you tell us how we can cross the ocean—the home of Varuna—with our army of powerful monkeys? What’s the best way for all of us to get across this vast river lord?” Bibhisana answered, “Rāma should ask the Ocean for help. This endless sea was dug out by King Sagara.” (see note [134]) “Since Rāma is from Sagara’s line, the Ocean will surely help him.” After Bibhisana gave this advice, Sugriva went to Rāma and Lakshmana and explained Bibhisana’s suggestion, urging Rāma to ask the Ocean for help. Rāma, who was naturally good-hearted, liked this idea. Smiling, he told Lakshmana and Sugriva to gather what was needed for the ritual. “Lakshmana, I think Bibhisana’s advice is wise. Sugriva is smart, and you’re also skilled at giving counsel. Talk it over together and tell me what you think.” Lakshmana and Sugriva answered respectfully, “Of course, Rāghava. Why wouldn’t we listen to Bibhisana’s good advice? Without a bridge over the sea—the dangerous home of Varuna—not even the gods or Indra could reach Lankā. So let’s follow Bibhisana’s plan, ask the Ocean for help, and get moving with our army toward Rāvana’s city.” After hearing this, Rāma went to the seashore, which was covered in sacred grass, like a flame arriving at an altar.
The “guardians of the world” are gods who protect different regions, like the Sun, Moon, Fire, Wind, Indra, Yama, Varuna, and Kuvera.
Rasātala is one of the seven hells under the earth—the home of Nagas, Asuras, and Daityas. It’s the deepest part of the underworld.
Sagara was a king of Ayodhyā, and an ancestor of Rāma.
SECTION XX

The powerful rakshasa named Sārdula spotted Sugriva’s army gathered along the ocean’s shore. Seeing all the monkeys and bears preparing for battle, Sārdula, who was a messenger for the evil-hearted Rāvana, hurried back into the city of Lankā. He went straight to his master and reported, “Sugriva’s army of monkeys and bears is right outside Lankā. They’re as vast as the ocean. And Rāma and Lakshmana, the two sons of King Daçaratha—both strikingly handsome—have come to rescue Sitā and are now camped on the shore. Rāma’s army stretches across the sky for ten yojanas. I’ve come to tell you the whole truth. You need to decide, O King, whether to give Sitā back, try to make peace, or create divisions among the enemy.” 

Hearing Sārdula’s report, Rāvana—the rakshasa king—anxiously considered his options. He turned to Suka, his wisest advisor, and said, “Go to Sugriva and deliver my message politely and clearly: ‘You come from a noble family and are the mighty son of the king of bears. I have no quarrel with you—I actually see you as a brother, O King of the Monkeys. Even though I took the wife of Rāma, what does that have to do with you? Go back to Kishkindhā. There’s no way your monkeys can attack Lankā—if even the gods and Gandharvas couldn’t do it, what chance do men and monkeys have?’” Given this order, Suka transformed himself into a bird, soared quickly into the sky, and traveled over the ocean. From above, he relayed Rāvana’s words to Sugriva.

As soon as Suka finished, the monkeys jumped up, determined to tear off his wings or kill him with their fists. They grabbed him from the sky and threw him down to the ground, beating him fiercely. Suka cried out, “O Kākutstha (Rāma), you shouldn’t kill a messenger. Please stop the monkeys! Anyone who adds their own opinion instead of delivering their master’s message isn’t loyal and deserves punishment, but I’m just relaying Rāvana’s words.” Hearing Suka’s desperate plea, Rāma told the monkeys, “Don’t kill him.” 

Freed, Suka returned to the sky and called down, “Sugriva, you’re powerful and energetic—what should I tell Rāvana, who is feared by all?” 

Sugriva, the mighty monkey king, answered, “Rāvana, you aren’t my friend, nor do I pity you. You’re not my benefactor, and I don’t like you. You’re Rāma’s enemy, and you deserve to be destroyed by him, just as Vāli was. I’ll destroy you, Rāvana—along with your sons, friends, and family—and burn down all of Lankā with my army. You won’t escape Rāghava (Rāma), even if you’re protected by the gods. Rāma will kill you and your brother, whether you run into the sky, hide underground, or take shelter with Mahadeva (Shiva). No one in all three worlds—whether they’re spirits, rakshasas, gandharvas, or asuras—can protect you. You killed the king of vultures, who was already old and weak. You kidnapped Sitā from right beside Rāma and Lakshmana, but you have no idea what kind of strength you’re up against. Rāma, the greatest of the Raghus, incredibly strong and unstoppable even by the gods, will end you.”

Then Angada, Vāli’s son and one of the bravest monkeys, said, “This guy isn’t just a messenger—he’s obviously a spy. He’s here to check out our whole army. Grab him! Don’t let him go back to Lankā—that’s what I say.” On Sugriva’s command, the monkeys pounced on Suka, tied him up, and he wailed like he’d lost all hope. Beaten and restrained by the relentless monkeys, Suka cried out to Rāma, “They’re ripping off my wings and stabbing at my eyes! If I die, may all my sins fall on you!” Hearing this heartbreaking cry, Rāma ordered the monkeys to stop, saying, “Let this messenger go—he came here on someone else’s orders.”
The commentator has an odd note about the phrase “decrepit through age.” Someone who’s old might avoid frailty using some drug, and someone young might become weak because of a curse.
SECTION XXI

On the shore of the sea, Rāma (also called Rāghava) spread kusa grass and lay down facing east, palms pressed together in prayer to the vast ocean. He used his own arm as a pillow—an arm strong and shining like a serpent, always adorned with golden ornaments, often caressed by beautiful maidens (or perhaps by caring attendants), decorated with gem-studded armbands and pearl jewelry, and scented with sandalwood and aguru. That same arm had once cradled Sita’s head; it was as powerful as Takshaka, the serpent king beneath the Ganges, and shaped like a yoke. In battle, it brought fear to his enemies and joy to his friends. His left arm, scarred from the bowstring, was like a protector of the world; his right, as solid as a club, had given away thousands of cows in charity. Using this mighty arm as a pillow, Rāma made a vow: “Today, either I will die, or the Ocean will.” With this grim determination, Rāma stayed silent and focused, lying there according to sacred rules. For three nights, he slept on the kusa grass, never breaking his vow. During these nights, Rāma—wise in statecraft and devoted to righteousness—prayed to the lord of rivers, the Ocean. But despite Rāma’s devotion and focused prayers, the stubborn Ocean did not appear to him. This made Rāma furious; his eyes turned red with anger. He turned to Lakshmana (Sumitra’s son) and said, “Look at how arrogant the Ocean is, refusing to come before me. Calmness, patience, honesty, and gentle words—good qualities like these are seen by the arrogant as weakness. People who are boastful, wicked, and aggressive brag about themselves and punish others wherever they go—and they’re the ones who get respect in the world. Restraint doesn’t bring fame or victory, Lakshmana; not in this world, not in the heat of battle. Watch as I fill the Ocean with my arrows, blocking its waters with the bodies of crocodiles I slay. You’ll see the bodies of snakes, giant fish, and even elephant carcasses torn apart by my arrows. Today, in a terrible battle, I will dry up the Ocean, leaving only shells, oysters, fish, and sea-monsters behind. The Ocean thinks I am weak because I’m patient—enough of that! My patience has only made him ignore me. Lakshmana, bring me my bow and my snake-like arrows. I’ll dry up the Ocean so the monkeys can cross on foot. Even if it’s supposed to be untouchable, today I’ll shake the sea itself. With my arrows, I’ll make Varuna’s domain, roaring with a thousand waves, overflow its shores. I’ll stir up the deep, home to many powerful demons.” After saying this, Rāma took up his bow. His eyes blazed with anger, and he was unstoppable—like fire at the end of the world. He drew his terrible bow, making the earth tremble, and shot fierce arrows, just like Indra (the god of a hundred sacrifices) throwing his thunderbolt. Rāma’s blazing arrows, charged with immense power, plunged into the sea, terrifying the serpents within. Instantly, the ocean became violent, churning with fish, crocodiles, and roaring winds. The waves rose up, smoke covered the water, and massive billows appeared everywhere. The serpents panicked, their faces glowing with fear, and the powerful demons and beings from the underworld were shaken. Huge waves like the Vindhya or Mandara mountains rose up, full of crocodiles and sea-monsters by the thousands. Varuna’s home was in chaos: waves spun wildly, serpents and demons were terrified, ferocious sea creatures were tossed about, and the ocean echoed with terrible sounds. Then Lakshmana sprang up and spoke to Rāma, who was still tense and drawing his bow. “This isn’t right,” Lakshmana said, taking the bow from Rāma’s hands. “You can achieve your goal without destroying the Ocean. Heroes like you shouldn’t be ruled by anger. Think carefully, and look for another way.” At that moment, invisible in the sky, celestial sages and saints cried out, “Stop! Don’t do it!” Their voices rang out in warning.
The commentator says that since Rāma had only one wife, these “damsels” must actually be his nurses or attendants.—T.
The word here is “naram,” meaning “man.”—T.
[53] That is, punishing people indiscriminately.—T.
“Rana murddhani”—meaning “on the dangerous edge of battle when it raged.” (See Paradise Lost Book I.)
Celestial saints.
SECTION XXII

Rāma, the greatest of the Raghus, spoke to the Ocean in a harsh tone: “Today, I will dry you up completely, Ocean—along with everything below your surface. When my arrows burn your waters and all your creatures are destroyed, a huge cloud of dust will rise from your dry bed. Then, with your waters gone, my army of monkeys will simply walk across to the other side. You’ve grown arrogant because of your vastness, but you don’t know my strength. But know this: you, home to the Dānavas, will soon regret provoking me.” With that, Rāma fixed a powerful arrow, charged with the Brahma Mantra, onto his best bow and drew it back with great force. As he pulled the bowstring, it felt as if the sky and earth were splitting apart, and the mountains shook. Darkness fell everywhere, hiding the directions. Rivers and oceans churned violently. The stars appeared alongside the sun and moon. The sky was both brightly lit by the sun and yet shrouded in darkness, streaked with a hundred burning meteors. Thunderbolts crashed louder than anything else, falling from the sky. Fierce winds tore through, breaking trees, scattering clouds, and smashing mountain peaks. The thunder, wild and fast, roared together and filled the air with lightning. Visible creatures shrieked like thunder, while hidden ones made terrifying noises. Overwhelmed by fear, all living things froze in terror, some collapsing in fright. The ocean itself, full of animals, waves, serpents, and Rākshasas, suddenly thrashed about with wild energy. Even though it wasn’t the end of the world, the ocean surged past its shores for a hundred yojanas. But even seeing the Ocean, lord of all rivers, overflow its boundaries in alarm, Rāma—the enemy-destroyer—did not back down.

Then, from the middle of the sea, the Ocean himself rose up—just like the sun rises from the golden mountain Meru. He was surrounded by brilliant Pannagas (fiery-faced serpents), and looked as cool as blue stone, adorned with gold jewelry, wearing a gem-studded robe, and a garland made of all sorts of flowers. His eyes were like lotus petals, and he wore shining ornaments of gold and jewels, just as the mountain Himavān gleams with its own metals. Waves swirled around him, winds blew through the clouds, and he was surrounded by the great rivers—Ganga, Sindhu, and others. Approaching Rāma, who was ready to unleash his arrows, Ocean greeted him respectfully, hands pressed together, and spoke: “Rāghava, earth, air, sky, water, and fire—these five elements always follow their own nature. My nature is to be deep and uncrossable; to be shallow would go against what I am. So let me explain how you can cross. It’s not out of desire, greed, fear, or anger that I keep my waters moving with so many alligators; it’s simply my nature. I will show you a way to cross, and I will help you. No dangerous sea creatures will attack while your army is crossing. I will make the crossing as steady as land for your monkeys.”

Rāma replied, “Ocean, I hear you. But this arrow of mine must still fulfill its purpose. Where should I send it?” Ocean looked at Rāma’s deadly arrow and answered, “There’s a place in my northern part that is especially pure—it’s called Drumakulya, as famous as you are. There, many violent robbers, led by herdsmen, drink my water and pollute me with their evil acts. I can’t tolerate their sins any longer. Rāma, let your arrow fall there and achieve its purpose.” Hearing this, Rāma immediately shot the flaming arrow. Where it landed—a place as bright and deadly as a thunderbolt—became known as Marukāntāra. The earth itself groaned at the strike, and water started to gush out from the wound deep below. This place became known as Vrana, because the ocean’s water could be seen bubbling up from underground. The impact made a terrifying sound, and because of the arrow and the thunderous noise, the water in the local tanks dried up.

After drying up Marukāntāra, which was famous across the three worlds, and emptying the water tanks, Rāma—wise and powerful, son of Daçaratha—blessed the desert with a boon: “Here, food for animals will always be plentiful. Sickness will be rare. Fruits and roots will be tasty, there will be plenty of oil and milk, and the land will be rich in fragrant herbs.” Thanks to Rāma’s blessing, the desert became lush and pleasant.

Once the land was scorched, the Ocean, lord of rivers, spoke to Rāma, who was expert in all knowledge: “Rāghava, this is Nala, son of Viçwakarmā. His father once granted him a special gift. Nala is eager to help you—let him build a bridge over me. I will support it. He is just like his father.” Saying this, the Ocean disappeared.

Then Nala, the best of monkeys, stood up and said to Rāma, “Thanks to my father’s skills, I can build a bridge across this vast ocean. The Ocean has spoken wisely. Even when dealing with those who don’t help, sometimes punishment is needed. Forget patience or generosity—this mighty sea only agreed to help after seeing you were ready to force the issue. Long ago, Viçwakarmā, my father, blessed my mother: ‘Your son will be like me.’ I am his son, and I share his talents. I hadn’t mentioned this before because you didn’t ask, but I can definitely build a bridge over the ocean. Let’s get started today. The best monkeys should help.”

Following Rāma’s orders, the top monkeys hurried into the great forest in their hundreds and thousands. Each as big as a mountain, they began chopping down trees and dragging them toward the sea. The monkeys filled the ocean with sālas, açwakarnas, dhavas, bamboos, kutajas, arjunas, palms, tilakas, tiniças, billakas, aparnas, blossoming karnikāras, mangoes, and other trees. The strongest monkeys carried the trees—some with roots, some without—lifting them like banners of Indra. With their immense strength, they also brought palms, pomegranates, coconuts, itakas, kariras, vakulas, nimbas, and even rocks the size of elephants. They ripped crags from the earth and tossed them into the water using machines. When the rocks dropped into the sea, the waves surged high into the sky before settling again. The falling trees and rocks stirred up the ocean everywhere. Some monkeys made lines to keep the bridge straight. In the middle of the sea, Nala began building a massive bridge a hundred yojanas long, with help from powerful monkeys. Some took measurements, others carried timber. Hundreds of monkeys, their colors like forests or mountains, worked under Rāma’s command, building the bridge from grass and wood. Blossoming trees formed the top layer. Monkeys—some as mighty as Dānavas—rushed around carrying rocks as big as hills and mountain peaks. The noise from all the crags and rocks hitting the sea was deafening.

On the first day, the huge, powerful monkeys finished fifteen yojanas of the bridge. On the second day, they built twenty more. On the third day, they managed twenty-one yojanas. On the fourth day, the energetic monkeys added another twenty-two yojanas. On the fifth and final day, the fast-working monkeys completed the remaining twenty-three yojanas, reaching the far shore. Nala, talented and graceful like his father Viçwakarmā, had successfully built the bridge across the sea. The bridge looked stunning—like a shining path across the ocean, much like the Milky Way in the night sky.

Gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and great sages gathered in the sky to witness this marvel. They saw Nala’s bridge—an incredible construction, ten yojanas wide and a hundred long—something almost impossible to imagine. The monkeys, leaping, roaring, and bounding, along with all the world’s creatures, watched the bridge’s creation in awe.

With the bridge complete, the thousands upon thousands of strong monkeys crossed over to the other side of the vast ocean. The bridge, wide, well-built, and beautiful, looked like a part in the hair on the Ocean’s head. On the far shore, Bibhishana stood ready with his mace and a few advisors, preparing to defend against any enemies. Sugriva turned to Rāma—who always kept his word—and said, “Rāma, climb onto Hanumān. Lakshmana should ride on Angada. This ocean is huge, but our monkey warriors can carry you both.” So Rāma and Lakshmana, armed and ready, set out at the head of the army with Sugriva. Some monkeys traveled through the middle, others swam, some went by land, and others bounded through the air like birds. The noise of their crossing drowned out even the roar of the sea.

Once the army crossed using Nala’s bridge, the king led them to the shore, which was rich in fruits, roots, and fresh water. Seeing Rāma accomplish something so incredible, the gods, Siddhas, Charanas, and great sages appeared before him. They sprinkled him with holy water, blessing him, and said, “May you be victorious, O Rāma—human and divine! May you rule the Earth forever!” In many auspicious ways, they honored Rāma, the one revered by Brahmins.
The commentator notes that this strange event—sun, moon, and stars appearing together—happened because the heavenly bodies’ paths were disturbed.
Nātichakrāma can also mean Rāma didn’t shoot any more arrows.
Pannagas are semi-divine serpents.
Sāgaradarçanāt can also mean “following Ocean’s advice.”
[60] That is, the sound.
SECTION XXIII

After noticing a series of ominous signs, Rama (Lakshmana’s older brother, and well-versed in interpreting such things) hugged Sumitra’s son, Lakshmana, and spoke seriously: “Lakshmana, let’s stay here for now, in this area with cool streams and fruit-filled forests. We should split up our forces and organize them. I have a strong feeling of danger approaching—a threat of destruction for our people, and the deaths of many of the bravest among the bears, monkeys, and Rakshasas. The wind is blowing strangely dark, and the ground is shaking. Mountain peaks are trembling, and trees are falling over. The clouds are gray and wild, thundering loudly, and, as they gather, they seem to rain down drops of blood. The twilight is terrifying, glowing red like sandalwood paste. A ring of fire is dropping from the burning sun. All around us, birds and animals are crying out in distress, their faces twisted with fear, shrieking at the sun and making everything feel even more dangerous. The moon, even though it’s not supposed to be out, burns in the sky with dark red rays, as if it wants to wipe out everyone. The sun looks smaller, harsher, and threatening. Lakshmana, look—a blue mark appears on the clear face of the sun. The stars are fading, lost in a huge cloud of dust. Lakshmana, look at this scene—it’s as if the whole world is ending. Crows, hawks, and lesser vultures are circling everywhere. Jackals are howling in an unsettling way, making everything scarier. Soon, the ground will be littered with darts, javelins, and swords—thrown by monkeys and Rakshasas—and the earth will be soaked with blood and flesh. With all these monkeys together, we need to act fast—we’ll push ahead today and enter Lanka, Ravana’s city, which is nearly impossible to conquer. After saying this, Rama (the warrior, also known as the enchanter of men) grabbed his bow and led the way toward Lanka. All the major monkeys—Sugriva and Vibhishana included—followed, letting out fierce battle cries, determined to destroy their enemies. Seeing the courage and energy of these powerful monkeys, Rama was pleased, knowing they were ready to fight for what mattered most to him.
The moon seems to appear, but doesn’t shine clearly.—T.
Praçasta—I don’t think this word fits here. It could be a mistake.—T.
The word ‘Rama’ appears twice, once as the name from the solar dynasty, and the other meaning ‘enchanter of men’.—T.
SECTION XXIV

With the king present, the gathering of warriors looked even more impressive, like a night in autumn made beautiful by the full moon among shining stars. The ground shook under the sheer energy of the army, which was as vast and restless as the ocean. Suddenly, the monkeys heard shouts and the loud blare of trumpets and drums coming from Lankā—sounds so powerful they made your hair stand on end. Excited by the noise, the monkey leaders let out roars even louder than the Rākshasas’ instruments. The Rākshasas, in turn, heard the monkeys’ booming cries, which sounded like thunderclouds battling in the sky.

Rāma, son of Daçaratha, looked up at Lankā, which was decorated with colorful banners and streamers. His heart was heavy as he thought of Sitā, who was being held captive there by Rāvana. “There she is,” he thought, “with eyes like a young deer, trapped by Rāvana like Rohini caught by Mars.” Rāma let out a long, deep sigh and glanced at his brother Lakshmana. He spoke quietly but firmly: “Look, Lakshmana, at Lankā—so tall it seems to pierce the sky. Viçwakarmā built it on the mountaintop, and it looks like something out of a dream. Its buildings are packed close together, making the city look like the sky covered by pale clouds. Lankā’s gardens remind me of Chitraratha—beautiful, filled with the songs of birds, and bursting with fruit and flowers. See the drunk birds and the buzzing black bees mixing with the blossoms. The breeze moves the trees, and you can hear the coels singing.”

Following the ancient rules of war, Rāma divided his army and gave orders to Lakshmana. He said, “Let the powerful and unbeatable Angada (Angad), along with Nila, take their troops and hold the center of the army. Rishabha, surrounded by his band of monkeys, should guard the right flank. The unstoppable Gandhamādana, as strong as a wild elephant, will guard the left. You and I, Lakshmana, will lead from the front. Jāmbavān, Sushena, and Vagadarçi—the three great bears—will protect the middle. And just as the sun watches over the far side of the world, the monkey king should defend the rear.” With the army neatly organized and protected by mighty warriors, it looked like a sky full of storm clouds.

Then, grabbing huge mountain peaks and massive trees, the monkeys charged toward Lankā, eager to smash it in battle. “We’ll destroy Lankā by throwing these mountain peaks—or with our bare hands if we have to,” they thought, fired up for the fight.

Next, Rāma turned to Sugriva and said, “Our army is ready. Let’s release Suka now.” Sugriva, strong and confident, obeyed and freed Suka, the messenger, just as Rāma had ordered. Beaten and terrified by the monkeys, Suka rushed back to Rāvana, the king of the Rākshasas.

Rāvana laughed when he saw Suka and teased him, “Have your wings been tied up? You look like they’ve been cut off! Did those wild monkeys catch you?” Shaking with fear, Suka answered Rāvana with respect: “I went to the north shore of the sea and politely gave your message to Sugriva. But as soon as the monkeys saw me, they got angry, grabbed me, tried to tear off my wings, and almost beat me to death. You can’t reason with them. It’s clear, lord of the Rākshasas, that monkeys are naturally fierce and quick-tempered. Now, Rāma—the same one who killed Virādha, Kavandha, and Khara—is here with Sugriva, searching for Sitā. He built a bridge across the sea, crossed over with his bow ready, and now stands here, ignoring the Rākshasas. Their army of thousands of monkeys and bears covers the land like mountains and clouds. There’s no chance for peace between your Rākshasas and the monkey king’s forces—just like the gods and the demons never get along. They’re right outside your walls. You have to choose: hand over Sitā without delay, or get ready to fight.”

Rāvana’s eyes burned with anger as he listened to Suka. He said coldly, “Even if the gods, Gandharvas, and demons all joined against me, I would never give Sitā back out of fear—never. I can’t wait for my arrows to chase Rāma like crazed bees rushing to a flowering tree in spring. Soon, my flaming arrows will burn Rāma, covering him in blood, just like a meteor strikes down an elephant. When I’m surrounded by my army, I’ll break his ranks like the rising sun makes the stars disappear. Rāma doesn’t know how fierce I am—my fury is like the ocean, my strength like the wind. That’s the only reason he dares to fight me. He hasn’t seen my arrows, waiting in my quiver like poisonous snakes, or heard my bow, which sounds like a deadly instrument, echoing with the screams of terrified people and the clash of weapons. On the battlefield, I’ll play that music for him. Not even Indra, the thousand-eyed king of the gods, or Varuna, or Yama, or even Kubera could defeat me when I’m fighting with my fiery arrows.”
Rāma.—T.
[65] i.e. mentally.—T.
Angāraka.—T.
The epithet 'bears' coming after 'monkeys' may look incongruous; but, I fancy, 'monkeys' is used in the general sense of being connected with the monkey-host.—T.
SECTION XXV

After Rāma, son of Daçaratha, crossed the ocean with his army, the commanding and impressive Rāvana called his two advisors, Suka and Sārana, to him. “Rāma’s monkey army just crossed the entire ocean—a feat no one thought possible. On top of that, they built a bridge over the sea! No one’s ever done something like this before. I can hardly believe it myself. Still, we need to know exactly how many monkeys there are. I want you to sneak into their army without being noticed and figure out the size of their forces, their strength, who their top fighters are, who Rāma’s and Sugriva’s main advisors are, who leads them, which monkeys are the bravest, how they built the bridge, where the strongest monkeys are stationed, and what Rāma and Lakshmana’s plans and skills are—plus what weapons they use. Also, find out who commands the monkey army. Once you know all this, come back to me as quickly as you can.” Given these orders, the two Rākshasas, Suka and Sārana, disguised themselves as monkeys and slipped into the army. But once inside, they realized it was impossible to count the monkey forces—the army was so huge, it was terrifying just to look at, and it stretched everywhere: on mountaintops, near springs, and inside caves. Suka and Sārana saw monkeys who had already crossed the ocean, others still crossing, and some getting ready to move. There were also those resting or sitting down, the whole army filling the air with deafening roars. It was a sea of warriors, impossible to disturb or measure.

As they stayed undercover, Vibhishana spotted them. He quickly captured them and brought them to Rāma. “These two are Rāvana’s advisors—Suka and Sārana. They’ve come as spies from Lanka,” he explained. Seeing Rāma, the two Rākshasas were terrified, convinced they were about to die. Scared for their lives, they put their hands together in a gesture of surrender and said, “We’re here on Rāvana’s orders, Rāma. We only came to gather information about your army, son of Raghu.” Rāma, always looking out for others’ welfare, just laughed and said, “If you’ve already seen everything you need to see, or finished your mission, you can go back safely. If you missed anything, feel free to look again—Vibhishana can even show you around. Don’t worry, you won’t be killed for being caught, even though you’re spies. Even if you were armed, I wouldn’t have you executed. And even though you came in disguise to try and mess with us, Vibhishana, let them go.” Then Rāma turned to Suka and Sārana and added, “When you get back to Lanka, tell your king—Rāvana, brother of the god of wealth—exactly what I say: ‘Whatever strength you relied on to kidnap my Sītā, use it however you want, with all your friends and forces. But tomorrow morning, you’ll see Lanka’s walls and gates, and the Rākshasa army, destroyed by my arrows. Just as Indra strikes the demons with his thunderbolt, I’ll unleash my fury on you and your army tomorrow.’”

Following Rāma’s instructions, Suka and Sārana bowed respectfully, wishing him victory, and hurried back to Lanka. They went straight to Rāvana and reported, “Lord of Rākshasas, Vibhishana caught us and was about to have us killed, but we were brought before the righteous Rāma, who let us go. These four—Rāma, his heroic brother Lakshmana, Vibhishana, and the mighty Sugriva, who’s like Indra himself—together are strong enough to tear Lanka down and rebuild it from scratch, even without help from the rest of the monkeys. Rāma alone could destroy Lanka with his power—he doesn’t even need the others. And with Rāma, Lakshmana, and Sugriva leading them, the monkey army will be nearly impossible to defeat, even for the gods or the Asuras. The forest warriors are fired up and ready to fight. There’s no point in arguing anymore—your best move is to make peace. Return Sītā to Rāma, son of Daçaratha.”
SECTION XXXI

After listening to Sārana’s honest and heartfelt words, King Rāvana replied, “Even if the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas all attacked me, I would never give up Sitā out of fear of anyone. Sārana, you’ve been beaten up by the monkeys and are clearly shaken, so you think we should just hand Sitā back right now. But tell me—what enemy of mine could possibly defeat me in battle?” With those harsh words, Rāvana, the elegant yet fearsome lord of the Rākshasas, decided to get a better look at the monkey army. He climbed a tall, snow-white building—towering as if several palm trees were stacked—burning with anger. Standing with his spies, Rāvana looked out over the sea, the mountains, and the forests. What he saw was astonishing: the land was completely covered with monkeys—an immense, unstoppable force. After taking it all in, Rāvana asked Sārana, “Among these monkeys, who are the main leaders and the bravest warriors? Who are the strongest? Who are the ones leading at the front lines, and whom does Sugriva listen to? Who leads the leaders? Tell me everything about their strengths.” Sārana, who knew all the chiefs of the monkey army, answered him, explaining who headed the woodland troops.

“That monkey out front of Lankā, roaring loudly and surrounded by hundreds and thousands of other monkey leaders—the one whose thunderous shouts make Lankā’s walls, gates, hills, and forests shake—that’s Nila, a heroic commander and the leader of Sugriva’s main forces. Next, the powerful one who’s walking back and forth with his arms folded, constantly yawning in anger as he stares at Lankā, looking like a mountain peak or the filaments of a lotus, and who whips his tail so hard the sound echoes in all directions—that is Angada, Sugriva’s chosen heir and the son of Vāli. He’s challenging you directly to battle. Angada is always loyal to Sugriva and shows his strength like Varuna does for Indra. In fact, it was Angada’s advice that led Hanumān, Rāma’s devoted ally, to find Sitā. Now Angada is marching here with countless troops, determined to defeat you with his army. Behind Angada, you’ll see Nala, the hero who built the bridge, surrounded by a mighty force.

Those monkeys lying still but letting out wild roars and cries are warriors from the Chandana region. Sweta, the silver-colored monkey with fearsome strength, thinks he can conquer Lankā with his own army. He’s rallying his troops, and once he’s met with Sugriva, he’ll head back fast. Then there’s Kumuda, another leader, who rules his kingdom on Ramya Mountain (also called Sanrochana) beside the Gomati River—a place thick with trees. Chanda, the energetic monkey with a long tail of copper, yellow, black, and white hair, is gathering hundreds and thousands of monkeys and is eager for battle; he hopes to take Lankā with his own forces.

That lion-like monkey over there with the tawny fur and long mane, standing apart and staring at Lankā as if he could burn it down just by looking—is Rambha, a band leader who lives in the Vindhya, Krisha, Sahya, and Sudarçana mountains. He’s followed by three hundred million fierce and powerful monkeys, all determined to destroy Lankā with raw strength. Another is Sarabha, who keeps flapping his ears and yawning, showing no fear of death, trembling with rage and glaring sideways—look at that furious tail lashing!—letting out huge, fearless roars. Sarabha lives on Mount Sālweya and commands forty thousand powerful monkey chiefs.

Among the crowd, the one who stands out like a thundercloud in the middle of the monkey hosts, just as Indra stands among the gods, is Panaça. He lives on the beautiful Parijatra hill and is always unstoppable in battle. Fifty hundred thousand (five million) monkey leaders surround him in carefully organized ranks. On the ocean’s edge, in the midst of the loud and busy army, you’ll find Vitata, who looks as vast as the ocean itself. He drinks from the Venā River, and leads sixty hundred thousand (six million) monkeys. Krathana is another monkey who’s openly challenging you; he leads strong, well-organized generals and troops.

Then there’s Gavaya, whose fur is the color of red chalk. He’s so confident in his own power that he ignores all the other monkeys. He’s coming at you in a fury, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of his own. He plans to bring down Lankā with their help. These are the main heroes—too many to count—who lead the monkey army. I’ve named the chiefs and described their formations on the battlefield.”
The mention of Sweta in the next verse refers to this same monkey.—T.
“Chandana” may mean sandalwood forests, but the commentator doesn’t explain further.—T.
Durdara is the name of a famous monkey leader.—T.
SECTION XXVII

Watch closely, and I’ll point out the leaders who are ready to fight for Rāghava (Rama), willing even to die for him. See that fierce monkey with a long, colorful tail? The hair on his tail shines copper, yellow, black, and white, looking like streaks of sunlight as it drags along the ground. That’s Hara, and hundreds, even thousands, of monkeys follow him. They’re all raising up trees as weapons, determined to climb the walls of Lankā. These are the commanders and warriors of the monkey-king’s army. Now, take a look at those dark, massive shapes—they look like thunderclouds, or thick black eyeliner, strong and impossible to count. These terrifying beings come from mountains, forests, and rivers all over. In their midst is their king, with gray eyes and a fierce look, like Parjanya (the rain god) surrounded by storm clouds. He lives on the mighty mountain Rikkhavān and drinks from the Narmadā river.

Look over there at the one who’s as big as a hill—that’s the younger brother of Dhumra, the lord of the bears. He’s just as handsome as his brother, but even stronger. His name is Jāmbavān. He’s gentle and obedient to his elders, but fierce in battle. Jāmbavān once helped Indra (Sakra) during the war between the gods and the Asuras, and he received many blessings for his bravery. These warriors climb mountain peaks and hurl down gigantic boulders, as huge as storm clouds. They never fear death. With their fur-covered bodies, they look like demons or ghosts as they fight.

Now, see the one bursting with energy, surrounded by countless troops? He’s leaping and pausing, never still. This is another monkey chief, who lives close to Indra, the thousand-eyed god. His name is Rambha, and he’s strong and leads many bands. Next, there’s the one who brushes against a mountain a full Yojana (about eight miles) away just by walking, and then leaps the same distance. He’s more beautiful than any other four-legged creature and is called Sannādana, the grandfather of the monkeys. He once fought Indra and was never defeated. He commands the whole army.

Then there’s a leader whose power matches Indra’s. He was born from Fire and a Gandharva’s daughter, created to help the gods in their ancient war. This strong and graceful monkey lives on a mountain filled with magical creatures, where King Vaiçravana eats rose apples. This mountain, dear king, is a place your brother enjoys visiting. Another leader, who never brags about himself in battle, is Krathana. He commands a million troops and believes he can conquer Lankā with just his own soldiers.

See that leader who roams near the Ganges River, scaring elephant herds? There’s a long-standing rivalry between monkeys and elephants, and he never forgets it. He fights wild elephants in mountain caves, crushes trees, and is the greatest among the monkey warriors. He’s like Indra in the heavens, and he lives near Uçiravija on Mount Mandara, by the golden river. A hundred million monkeys, full of energy and strength, follow him, making a thunderous noise and swinging their long arms. He is their chief.

Now, look at that one over there who looks like a storm cloud whipped up by the wind. That’s Pramāthi, another leader. His troops move quickly, kicking up clouds of red dust all around. Then there are the fierce Golāngulas—hundreds of thousands of them. When they saw the bridge being built, they surrounded their chief, Gavāksha, another Golāngula, roaring and ready to tear down Lankā with their strength.

In the golden mountains, where every tree is always in fruit and bees swarm, where the sun’s light makes the birds and animals shine, and where the great sages never leave the high plateaus, you’ll find another leader. The trees there grant every wish, and the honey is the best in the world. This beautiful place is home to Kaçari, the leader of another band of monkeys. There are sixty thousand golden hills, and in the center stands the greatest one—just as you, King Rāvaṇa, are the greatest among the Rākshasas.

Inside this mountain live monkeys with tawny fur, white coats, copper faces, and honey-colored hair. They have sharp teeth and claws, four fangs like lions, and the power of tigers. They’re as strong as fire itself and look like venomous snakes aflame. With long tails, they’re like wild elephants, as massive as hills, and roar like thunderclouds. Their eyes are yellow and round, and their appearance is terrifying. They glare at Lankā, as if they’re about to tear it apart. In their midst stands their chief, Satavali, who always shines like the sun. He’s powerful and confident, certain he can destroy Lankā with just his own forces. For Rāma’s sake, he doesn’t care about risking his life.

Then there are Gaya, Gavāksha, Nala, and Nila—each surrounded by a hundred million warriors. Besides these, there are many more special monkeys living in the Vindhya mountains, but there are so many, it’s impossible to list them all. Every single one of them is incredibly powerful, with bodies as huge as mountains. Any of them could move mountains in a second, or scatter the earth with their strength.
Indra.
The word "in battle" was left out as it was unnecessary.
Gangā—the Ganges River.
Mentioned earlier.
Sāvarni Meru—the great golden mountain.
SECTION XXVIII

After listening to Sārana describe the monkey army, Suka turned to Rāvana, king of the Rākshasas, and said, “O King, look at those warriors over there—like wild elephants, huge and unstoppable, as tall as banyan trees from the banks of the Ganga, or as mighty as the peaks of the Himalayas. They’re not just strong—they can also change their shapes whenever they want. They fight with the power of gods and demons. There are thousands upon thousands of them—nine, five, and seven thousand kotis, plus thousands of sankus and a hundred vrindas. These are Sugriva’s top ministers, living in Kishkindhā—monkeys born from gods and Gandharvas, all able to transform at will. And see those two, equal in size and almost god-like? They are Mainda and Dwivida—no one can match them in battle. Brahmā himself blessed them to taste ambrosia, and now they’re determined to bring Lankā to its knees.

And that monkey over there, standing out like a furious elephant—the one with the power to stir up the ocean when he’s angry, the one who came searching for Sita and stood before you once already—see, he’s here again! He’s the eldest son of Kaçari, born from the Wind-god, known as Hanumān. He’s famous for leaping over the ocean. Hanumān can change his shape at will, and he’s both graceful and incredibly strong—unstoppable, just like the wind itself. When he was just a boy and saw the sun rise, he decided, ‘I’ll travel three thousand yojanas and bring back the sun for my breakfast,’ and he actually tried to do it. But he couldn’t reach the sun, who can’t be beaten by gods, sages, or demons, and eventually fell down on a mountain called the Ascending-hill. That fall cracked his jaw a little, which is why he’s called Hanumān (which means ‘broken-jawed’). I know this monkey and his whole story. I can’t even put into words how strong, handsome, or powerful he is. He alone thinks he can destroy Lankā. And have you forgotten how he burned Lankā with fire before? 

Next to him is a dark-skinned hero with lotus-like eyes, a mighty warrior from the Ikshwāku dynasty, who’s famous for his strength and virtue—he never wavers from what’s right. He knows the sacred Brāhma Mantra and the Vedas better than anyone, can shoot arrows that pierce the sky and even split the earth, and when he’s angry, he’s as deadly as death itself and as powerful as Indra. This is Rāma, whose wife Sita you kidnapped from Janasthāna, and now he’s coming for you. 

At Rāma’s right side stands a warrior shining like gold, with a broad chest and dark, curly hair—this is Lakshmana, always watching out for his brother. He’s an expert in politics and war, unbeatable in battle, strong and victorious—he’s basically Rāma’s right hand and would give his life for him. Lakshmana is determined to wipe out all the Rākshasas in this war.

On Rāma’s left is Bibhishana, now king of Lankā, crowned by the most powerful king of kings. He’s burning with anger and coming for you too, surrounded by Rākshasas.

In the middle, like an unshakeable mountain, stands the lord of all monkeys—Sugriva. His power is beyond measure. He’s smarter, stronger, and more famous than any other monkey, just as the Himalayas tower over all other mountains. He and his top monkey leaders live in Kishkindhā, a fortress hidden deep in the forest and hard to reach because of all the trees and rocks. Around his neck is a golden garland of a hundred lotuses, something even gods and humans want, and the goddess Lakshmi herself has blessed it. Rāma killed Vāli and gave Sugriva this garland, his wife Tārā, and the eternal monkey kingdom.

Now, let me explain the numbers: a ‘koti’ is a hundred thousand; a hundred thousand kotis make a ‘Sanku’; a hundred thousand Sankus is a ‘Mahāçanku’; a hundred thousand Mahāçankus is a ‘Vrinda’; a hundred thousand Vrindas is a ‘Mahāvrinda’; a thousand Mahāvrindas is a ‘Padma’; a hundred thousand Padmas is a ‘Mahāpadma’; a hundred thousand Mahāpadmas is a ‘Kharva’; a hundred thousand Khara is a ‘Samudra’; a hundred thousand Samudras is a ‘Mahaugha’. So Sugriva’s army is made up of a thousand kotis, a hundred Sankus, a thousand Mahāçankus, a hundred Vrindas, a thousand Mahāvrindas, a hundred Padmas, a thousand Mahāpadmas, a hundred Kharvas, as many Samudras, and as many Mahaughas. There are even kotis of Mahaughas, as vast as the sea. Sugriva is always surrounded by this massive, unstoppable army and his trusted advisors like Bibhishana. They’re coming for you in battle. Look at this army, glowing like a burning planet. O mighty king, you’d better get ready—fight with everything you’ve got, so you can win and avoid being crushed by your enemies.”
Banyan trees.
The original text has a break here. The descriptions are hard to fit into neat grammar—T.
SECTION XXIX

When Suka pointed out the monkey leaders to him, Ravana saw Lakshmana—famous as Rama’s right-hand man—standing nearby with his brother Vibhishana, as well as Sugriva, the fierce king of the monkeys. He also noticed Angada, the strong grandson of Indra (the thunder-god), the powerful Hanuman, the unbeatable Jambavan, Sushena, Nila, Nala (the top monkey engineer), Gaya, Gavaksha, Sarabha, Mainda, and Dwivida. Ravana felt a flicker of anxiety in his heart, and his anger grew. After the conversation ended, he snapped at Suka and Sarana, scolding them harshly as they stood awkwardly, heads down. His voice shook with rage as he said, “Counselors who live off their king’s wealth should never say anything unpleasant to him, whether they have his favor or not. Without my asking, you both went out of your way to praise our enemy, who’s here to fight us! Clearly, you wasted your time learning from your elders and teachers, because you never really learned the most important lessons in politics. Or maybe you learned them and then forgot. Either way, your ignorance is obvious. It’s only by luck that I’ve held onto my kingdom with counselors as foolish as you. Are you so unafraid of death that you dare to speak to me, your king, like this? Even trees in the forest can survive a fire for a while, but no one who offends the king survives his punishment. If I didn’t remember your past loyalty, I’d kill you both for praising the enemy. Get out of my sight! I won’t kill you now, because I remember your good service—but you're as good as dead to me, you ungrateful traitors.” Embarrassed, Suka and Sarana bowed, murmured “Victory,” and left Ravana’s presence.

Ravana, still furious, turned to Mahodara and told him to bring in some spies. Mahodara quickly sent for them, and they hurried in, bowing and wishing Ravana victory. Ravana addressed the spies—who were brave, loyal, and calm—and ordered, “Go and find out everything you can about Rama’s plans, and about those closest to him. See how he sleeps, how he wakes, what he’s doing every moment. Learn it all, and report back to me. A smart king uses spies to know his enemy, and with just a little effort in battle, he can defeat them.” The spies replied, “Yes, my lord,” and, with Sardula leading them, respectfully circled Ravana before leaving.

After saluting the mighty Ravana, the spies set off toward Rama and Lakshmana. Sneaking up close to the mountain on the beautiful shore (Mount Suvela), they spotted Rama, Lakshmana, Sugriva, and Vibhishana. But when they saw the massive monkey army, they were terrified. While they tried to hide, Vibhishana, the righteous rakshasa lord, spotted them, and the monkeys chased them down. Only the wicked rakshasa Sardula was captured and brought before Rama. But Rama let him go, even though the monkeys wanted revenge. Rama also forgave and released the other spies who had come with Sardula. After being harassed by the swift and powerful monkeys, the spies barely escaped, panting and nearly fainting, and returned to Lanka.

The exhausted but tough spies, who usually stayed hidden outside the city, reported back to Ravana, the ten-headed king. They described the size and strength of Rama’s army, now camped near Mount Suvela.

Indra—the thunder-god.
