SECTION XXX

The spies came to Rāvaṇa with urgent news: Rāma (sometimes called Rāghava) and his massive army had set up camp at Mount Suvela, right outside the city. When Rāvaṇa heard from his spies that Rāma was there with such a powerful force, he looked a bit unsettled. He turned to Sārdula, one of his night-stalking agents, and said, “You don’t look well—your face has lost its color. Did you end up in the hands of our angry enemies?” Shaken and afraid, Sārdula replied, “Those monkeys, my king—they’re incredibly strong and impossible for us to sneak past. We can’t talk to them or even question them. Monkeys, huge as mountains, guard every path. The moment I slipped into their camp to spy, they spotted me. The monkeys dragged me around, hitting me with their fists, teeth, and even their thighs. Furious, they pulled me through the army and finally threw me in front of Rāma, my body battered and bleeding, my head spinning. I begged for mercy, hands folded, and Rāma, merciful as he is, told the monkeys to stop and let me go. 

Now, Rāma has filled up the sea with rocks and boulders to bring his army across. He’s fully armed and waiting at the gates of Lankā. He let me go, and now, surrounded by his army and organized in a Garuda-shaped formation, he’s marching right up to the city walls. So you have two options: either give Sītā back, or prepare to fight him.” 

Hearing all this, Rāvaṇa, king of the Rākshasas, thought for a moment. Then he answered Sārdula, “Even if the gods, Gandharvas, and demons all come against me, I will never give up Sītā—not for fear of anyone.” After saying this, he asked again, “You’ve seen this army. Tell me: who among the monkeys are the real warriors? How strong are they? Which ones are dangerous to face? And who are their families—their fathers and grandfathers? Tell me everything. Once I know their strengths and weaknesses, I’ll decide what to do next. Anyone who wants to win a war has to know these things.” 

Sārdula, the best of spies, answered, “O king, the unbeatable Jāmbavān is famous—he’s the son of Gadgada, king of the bears. Gadgada’s other son is also here, and he once caused terrible trouble for the Rākshasas all by himself. The wise and powerful Sushena is the son of Dharma (righteousness)[82]. The gentle Dadhimukha, king, is the son of Soma (the moon)[83]. Sumukha, Durmukha, and the fierce Vegadarçin—who is like Death itself—were created by the Self-born God in monkey form[84]. Nila is the son of Agni (Fire)[85], and Hanumān, as everyone knows, is the son of the Wind-God. The unstoppable young Angada is Indra’s (Sakra’s) grandson. The strong Mainda and Dvivida are sons of the Ashwini twins. Five others—Gaya, Gavāksha, Gavaya, Sarabha, and Gandhamādana—are the sons of Vaivaswata and are as deadly as Death itself. 

But there are so many more—ten crore heroic monkeys, all sons of gods, all eager for battle. And Rāma himself, son of Daçaratha—he’s young, lion-like, the one who killed Dushana, Khara, and Triçiras. No one on Earth has Rāma’s strength; he’s the one who killed Virādha and Kavandha, monsters like Death. No one can list all Rāma’s virtues—he killed every Rākshasa who attacked Janasthāna. Lakshmana is here too—he’s like a wild elephant. If anyone dares to face his arrows, not even Indra could survive. There’s also Sweta and Jyotirmukha, sons of Vātskara; Hemakuta, son of Varuna; the heroic Nala, best of the monkeys and son of Viçwakarmā; powerful Durdhara, son of Vasu. And let’s not forget your own brother, Bibhishana—he’s joined Rāma and is leading the siege against Lankā. That’s the true strength of the monkey army camped on Suvela. Now it’s up to you to decide what to do.”
Dharma means righteousness.
Soma means the Moon.
In other words, Vegadarçin is Death in monkey form; but I’m using the more common meaning here.
Agni means Fire.
SECTION XXXI

The king’s spies came to him with urgent news: Rama’s army, strong and unshakable, had set up camp on Mount Suvela. When Ravana heard from his spies that Rama’s forces had arrived, he felt a wave of anxiety. He quickly told his ministers, “Gather at once, and be sharp—now is the time for wisdom.” The Rakshasa counselors rushed to him as ordered, and together they held a serious council. After careful discussion, Ravana—feared by all—dismissed his ministers and went back to his private quarters. He brought along Vidyujjibha, a massive, powerful Rakshasa known for his skill with illusions. Ravana gave Vidyujjibha clear instructions: “Use your powers to trick Janaka’s daughter, Sita. Create an illusion of Rama’s severed head and a great bow with an arrow ready, and bring them to me.” Vidyujjibha agreed, saying, “As you wish,” and conjured the illusion Ravana wanted. Pleased with his work and eager to see Sita in the Ashoka grove, Ravana rewarded Vidyujjibha with a fine ornament.

Next, Ravana—the mighty lord of the Rakshasas and younger brother of Kubera, the god of wealth—entered the Ashoka grove. There he found Sita, heartbroken and lost in thought about Rama. She sat on the ground, head bowed in grief, surrounded by terrifying Rakshasis who tried to comfort or threaten her. Approaching Sita, Ravana boasted loudly, trying to break her spirit: “You’ve always counted on your husband, Rama, thinking he would save you. But that slayer of Khara—your Rama—has been killed in battle. You’ve lost everything, and your pride is shattered by me. With him gone, you’ll have no choice but to become my wife. Give up this hopeless dream. What good is a dead man to you? Accept your new life and become the queen of all my wives. Listen, Sita—your cleverness has failed you. Hear the fate of your beloved Rama, just as Vritra was destroyed.

“Rama came with a massive monkey army to the ocean shore, hoping to destroy me. When night fell, Rama’s army camped on the northern shore, exhausted. At midnight, my spies scouted their sleeping camp. Then my powerful warriors, led by Prahasta, attacked. The Rakshasas unleashed a storm of weapons—spears, clubs, swords, and arrows—on the monkey army. In the chaos, while Rama slept, Prahasta used a huge sword and swiftly cut off his head. Vibhishana, who could fly at will, was captured. Lakshmana and the monkey soldiers scattered and disappeared.

“Sita, Sugriva—the monkey king—had his neck broken. Hanuman’s jaw was shattered, and he was killed by my Rakshasas. Jambavan tried to leap up but was struck down, cut by bladed weapons like a tree being chopped down. Mainda and Dwivida, two great monkey warriors, were killed in battle, covered in blood. Panasa (yes, just like the tree) is rolling on the ground. Darimukha, pierced by iron arrows, lies dead in a cave. Kumuda, strong and silent, was shot down with arrows. Angada, hit by a hail of Rakshasa arrows, lies on the ground coughing blood. All over the battlefield, monkeys are crushed by elephants or trapped by chariots, scattered like clouds in a storm. Some monkeys, terrified, ran for their lives—hunted from behind by my Rakshasas, like elephants chased by lions. Some fell into the sea; others tried to escape into the sky. Even the bears climbed trees to hide with the monkeys. On the shore, in the mountains, and in the forests, Rakshasas with monstrous forms have killed countless monkeys.

“So, Sita, your husband is dead—killed by my army along with all his followers. I have his head, still dripping with blood and caked in dust.” With that, Ravana, full of cruel pride, turned to a Rakshasi in Sita’s presence and ordered, “Bring Vidyujjibha here—the one who brought Rama’s head from the battlefield.” Vidyujjibha, carrying the fake head and bow, bowed to Ravana and stood before him. Ravana told him, “Show this head to Sita. Let her see the awful fate that has come to her husband.” Vidyujjibha dropped the fake but realistic head in front of Sita, then vanished. Ravana threw down the great, glowing bow, famous in all three worlds, and said, “This belonged to Rama. This is his bow, with the string fitted. Prahasta killed him last night and brought these here.”
(This refers to the tree named Panasa.)
(Note: The original verse mentioned Angada twice; only one is correct.)
SECTION XXXII

When Sita saw the severed head and the fine bow, and remembered what Hanuman had told her about Rama and Sugriva becoming allies, her heart broke. She recognized Rama by his eyes, his skin tone, the familiar look on his face, his hair and forehead, and the beautiful jewel on his head. Certain this was her husband, Sita was overwhelmed with grief and anger. She cursed Kaikeyi, crying out like a wounded bird, “Are you happy now, Kaikeyi? You got what you wanted. The heir to the royal line is dead, and you’ve wiped out the whole family just because you loved causing trouble. What wrong did Rama ever do to you, Kaikeyi, that you forced him—and me too—into exile, making him wear rags?” With these words, Sita, shaking all over and feeling utterly alone, collapsed to the ground like a cut-down plantain tree. After a while, she slowly came back to her senses. With wide, tear-filled eyes, she placed Rama’s head before her and let her sorrow take over.

“Oh, I’m ruined, my strong-armed husband! You who always followed the hardest vows! Now, with your death, I’ve reached the worst fate—I’m a widow. They say the greatest tragedy for a woman is her husband’s death. You, who always followed the path of righteousness, have gone before me, and I’m left drowning in sorrow. You tried so hard to save me, but you died yourself! And my mother-in-law, Kausalya, who loved you so much—now that you’ve been killed by Rakshasas, she must feel like a cow who’s lost her only calf. Rama, even the astrologers said you’d live a long life, but they were wrong—you died young. Or did your wisdom, as great as it was, fail you? Maybe it’s just fate—everyone has to face the consequences of their actions. But why, when you were so skilled in avoiding danger, did you die like this, without warning? You knew how to keep yourself safe.

It was me—my arrival here, like a deadly omen—that brought you to this. Now you lie here, arms outstretched, holding the earth like you once held me. This golden, perfumed bow you always treasured is all I have left of you. I’m sure your pure soul has reached heaven, joining your father, Dasaratha, and your ancestors. You’re a star in the sky now, rewarded for your greatness. But you’ve left behind your noble family of royal sages. Why won’t you look at me, Rama? Why won’t you answer me—I’m still so young, your wife and your companion! Remember the vow you made when you married me—to walk the path of righteousness with me—don’t forget it now. Take me with you, because I’m lost without you. Why, Rama, have you gone to the next world and left me suffering here? The body I held close, decorated with lucky charms, will now be torn apart by wild animals. You performed so many great sacrifices—why didn’t that protect you? Now, Kausalya will only see one of her sons return—Lakshmana. When she asks him, he’ll have to tell her about your death and the destruction of your allies by the Rakshasas.

When she hears you were killed in your sleep, and that I’m trapped in the Rakshasa’s palace, her heart will break. And all of this happened because of me. Rama, that sinless prince, crossed the ocean to save me, but was killed like a helpless animal. I’ve brought shame to my family—Dasaratha’s son married me without realizing I’d bring him death. Surely, in a past life, I must have done something wrong, refused to give gifts or help others, and that’s why I suffer now, even as your wife. Ravana, just kill me and lay my body beside Rama’s. Reunite me with my husband, bring my head to his head, my body to his. I want to follow my great-souled husband into death.” Sita, burning with grief, kept her gaze fixed on Rama’s head and bow, weeping for him.

While Sita mourned, a Rakshasa guard approached Ravana, bowing low and saying, “Victory to you, my lord!” After paying his respects, he announced that Prahasta, the general, had arrived. “Prahasta is here with all the other commanders. He sent me to let you know he wants to see you. My lord, I’m sure there’s some urgent matter—please go see them.” Hearing this, Ravana, the ten-headed king, left the Ashoka grove and went to meet his advisors. He discussed the situation with his top counselors, fully aware of Rama’s power, and planned his next move. As soon as Ravana left, Rama’s head and bow disappeared. Surrounded by his fierce generals, Ravana made his plans regarding Rama. Then Ravana, who looked as terrifying as doomsday itself, ordered his generals, “Quickly summon the army with the sound of drums, but don’t tell them the reason.” The messengers replied, “As you wish,” and at once called up the massive army. When all the troops had arrived, they reported back to Ravana, who was eager for battle.
Fulfilling your father’s command.—T.
This broken sentence suggests that Ravana, being royal, should forgive this sudden interruption.—T.
SECTION XXXIII

When Sītā was overwhelmed by grief, a Rākshasi named Saramā, who was her closest friend and confidante, quietly approached her. Saramā, speaking gently, tried to comfort Sītā, who was deeply distressed and nearly senseless after being tormented by Rāvaṇa, the king of the Rākshasas. Saramā had become Sītā’s friend while watching over her under Rāvaṇa’s orders, but her loyalty was to Sītā, not her master. Now, seeing Sītā collapsed on the ground and getting up again and again like a tired horse, Saramā tried to soothe her with genuine affection. “I came into this lonely forest to protect you, Sītā,” she said, “and I’m not afraid of Rāvaṇa anymore. I’ve been hiding nearby and overheard everything he’s said to you, and everything you’ve answered. I also know why he suddenly left in such a hurry just now. Rāma can’t be caught off guard, even in his sleep, and I really don’t believe he’s been killed. The monkeys fighting for him, led by Rāghava, are strong and well-defended, just like gods protected by their leader. They can’t be defeated. Rāma himself—long-armed, strong, noble, skilled with a bow, and famous across the earth—is with his brother Lakshmaṇa. He’s a champion in battle, an expert in leadership, and nearly unstoppable. There’s no way he’s dead. Rāvaṇa is just trying to trick you with his magic and lies. Your suffering is almost over—your lucky day is coming. Fortune is on your side. Listen to what I’ve learned: Rāma has crossed the ocean with his army of monkeys and is now camped on the southern shore. I’ve seen him myself, along with Lakshmaṇa and their entire army, all gathered at the edge of the sea, protected by Rāma’s own strength. The Rākshasas who were sent to spy on them have reported back that Rāma has crossed the sea. Now, Rāvaṇa is holding a council with his advisors, trying to figure out what to do.” 

As Saramā was telling Sītā all this, a thunderous roar erupted from the distance, the sound of Rāma’s army shouting with excitement and energy. The air filled with the booming of war drums, beaten so hard the sound shook the ground. Saramā, whose voice was always kind, turned to Sītā and said, “Those drums are the call to battle, Mother. Listen to how they rumble like storm clouds! The war elephants are armored, the horses are harnessed to chariots, and thousands of warriors are mounting up, armed with sharp spears. The streets are filling up with soldiers in shining armor, charging out on all sides, roaring like waves pouring into the sea. See how everything glitters—the weapons, shields, armor, the colorful chariots, horses, and elephants of Rāvaṇa’s army—it’s like a wildfire lighting up a summer forest. Feel the excitement and energy in the air as the Rākshasas get ready for war! Listen to the bells, the clattering of chariot wheels, the neighing of horses, and the pounding drums. The Rākshasas are wild with anticipation, brandishing their weapons—just hearing them could make your hair stand on end. But don’t be afraid—good fortune is coming to you. Rāma, your husband, is about to do what Indra did to the demons: he will defeat Rāvaṇa and set you free. With Lakshmaṇa and his great power, Rāma will fight the Rākshasas just as Vishnu helped Indra defeat their enemies. Soon, Sītā, after the battle is over and the enemy is defeated, I’ll see you reunited with Rāma, lying in his arms just as you’ve dreamed. You’ll cry tears of joy on his chest. And soon, Rāma will finally be able to untie the braid of your hair, which you’ve worn untouched for so many months. When you see his face again, glowing like the full moon, you’ll finally let go of all your pain, like a snake shedding its old skin. Rāma will win, destroy Rāvaṇa, and find happiness with you, his beloved, just like the earth blossoming after rain. Take comfort, Sītā, and trust in Rāma—he will come for you, just as the sun always returns to bring warmth and hope to the world.”
Saramā.—T.
The commentator notes: Like a mare that rolls in the dust to relieve exhaustion.—T.
This line of verse doesn’t fit smoothly with the rest of the passage—it’s a strange interruption.—T.
SECTION XXXIV

Still hurting from Rāvana’s harsh words,[93] Saramā tried to comfort and cheer up Sītā, much like clouds bring relief to the sun-scorched earth. Wanting to help her friend, Saramā—who always knew the right thing to say and started her words with a gentle smile—spoke softly: “Sītā, if you want, I can secretly go to Rāma, tell him your message, and come back without anyone knowing. Even if I travel through the open sky, not even the Wind or Garuda could catch up to me.” Hearing this, Sītā felt a little less sad and replied to Saramā in a gentle voice, “You could even travel to the underworld if you wanted. But please, only do what’s right for you to do for me. If you truly want to help and can stay calm, I want to know what Rāvana is planning since he left. That cunning and evil Rāvana, with all his tricks, overwhelms me like someone drunk off strong wine. He keeps me locked up here forever and always sends terrifying rākshasas to threaten and insult me. I’m constantly anxious and afraid, my mind never at peace. Living here in the Ashoka grove, I’m always on edge. If there’s any talk about rescuing me or keeping me trapped, please tell me what they decide. This is the greatest favor I could ask from you.” As Sītā spoke, wiping tears from her face, gentle Saramā answered, “If that’s what you want, I’ll go, Janaki. Daughter of Mithilā, I’ll find out the enemy’s plans and come back to tell you.” With that, Saramā went straight to the rākshasas and overheard Rāvana’s conversation with his advisors. After listening to Rāvana’s decision, she quickly hurried back to the beautiful Ashoka grove, knowing exactly what was going on. Entering the grove, she found Sītā waiting for her like the goddess Sri separated from her lotus. When Saramā returned, Sītā hugged her warmly and offered her a seat. “Sit down and please tell me everything you learned about what Rāvana, that sneaky and evil man, has decided.” With Sītā trembling in anticipation, Saramā explained everything she’d heard from Rāvana and his advisors. “Vaidehi, Rāvana’s mother and his older counselors spoke to him with real concern for your freedom. They told him, ‘Give Maithili back to the king of men, and show him the respect he deserves. You’ve already seen his strength at Janasthāna—how he crossed the ocean, how Hanumān found Sītā, how so many rākshasas have fallen in battle. Who else could do all this?’ Even after all this advice from his mother and counselors, Rāvana refuses to set you free—just like a greedy man can’t let go of stolen treasure. Maithili, he won’t let you go unless he’s killed in battle. That’s his decision, one he made with his advisors, because they’d rather die than give you up. He won’t free you just out of fear; he’s not afraid of battle or of destroying himself and all the rākshasas. But Sītā, when Rāma kills Rāvana in battle, he’ll take you home to Ayodhyā.” Just then, a massive uproar erupted from the entire army—drums and conch shells thundered, shaking the ground. Hearing the chaos of the monkey army, Rāvana’s servants all over Lankā panicked. They lost their courage and energy, feeling helpless, and saw no hope because of their ruler’s mistakes.
[93] i.e. the words of Rāvana.
SECTION XXXV

Rāma, the mighty warrior who had conquered many enemy cities, was marching toward Lankā. The sound of drums and conch shells filled the air as his army advanced. Hearing this loud commotion, Rāvana, the lord of the Rākshasas, paused to think. He looked at his counselors, then addressed them all. His deep, booming voice echoed through the hall as he mocked Rāma's crossing of the ocean and questioned his strength and courage. Rāvana said, “I've heard everything you’ve said about Rāma’s abilities. I also recognize your own bravery on the battlefield. But if you all know Rāma is so powerful, why are you just sitting here, staring at each other in silence?” 

At that moment, Mālyavān, Rāvana’s wise maternal grandfather, stepped forward to speak. He said, “A king who is skilled in many kinds of knowledge and who follows the rules of good government always becomes wealthy and defeats his enemies. The king who makes peace or goes to war at the right time, who helps his own people, will gain even more success. If a king is weaker than his enemy, he should try for peace; if he is stronger, he can go to war—but he should never ignore a threat. That’s why, Rāvana, I believe you should make peace with Rāma. Give him what he came here for—Sitā. Even the Devarshis and Gandharvas want Rāma to win. Don’t go to war with him; instead, focus on making peace.

The creator god assigned two paths: one for the Asuras and one for the gods—one based on righteousness, the other on unrighteousness. Righteousness is the way of the gods, and unrighteousness is the way of Rākshasas and Asuras. In the Krita Yuga, righteousness is stronger, but in the Kali Yuga, evil overpowers good. While you traveled through the three worlds, you destroyed acts of goodness and collected evil instead. That’s why your enemies are now growing stronger. Because you ignored what is right, evil has taken over, and righteousness now supports the gods against us.

You’ve spent your life chasing pleasures and ignoring your duties. This has angered the holy sages, whose fury burns like fire. The power of these sages, made strong by their fasting and prayers, can’t be resisted—it’s like a wildfire. The twice-born (Brahmins) meditate and chant the Vedas with total focus. Their chanting drives the Rākshasas away, scattering them like clouds in summer. The smoke from the sages’ sacred fires fills the sky, blocking the energy of our people and spreading in all directions. The tough vows and rituals performed by these holy men at sacred places have made life difficult for the Rākshasas.

You received a boon to be safe from gods, Dānavas, and Yakshas. But now men, monkeys, bears, and Golāngulas—creatures with great strength and courage—are here, making war cries. I see many terrifying omens that warn of the Rākshasas’ destruction. Dark, stormy clouds roar and rain blood over Lankā. Chariots and other vehicles seem to cry. The air is thick with dust, and nothing looks bright anymore. Wild animals, jackals, and vultures make horrible sounds, and they gather in bands in Lankā’s gardens.

People are having nightmares—huge, dark women appear outside houses, grabbing at furniture, speaking doom, and laughing with black teeth. In homes, dogs eat sacred offerings. Cows are giving birth to donkeys, mongooses to mice. Cats are mating with leopards, pigs with dogs, and even Kinnaras are pairing with Rākshasas and humans. White pigeons with red feet fly through the sky, as if doomed to destroy the Rākshasas. Female parrots in homes are wounded and killed by other, more violent birds, dropping to the ground with broken cries. All the birds and animals are crying out, facing the sun.

At dusk, a scary, dried-up, yellow-skinned man—bald and looking like Death—peers into people’s homes. Evil signs like these are everywhere. I believe Rāma is actually Vishnu in human form. There’s no way Rāghava could be just a man—he built a bridge over the ocean, something truly amazing. That’s why, Rāvana, you should make peace with Rāma, the king of men. Think carefully and do what’s right.” 

After saying all this to Rāvana, Mālyavān, knowing what Rāvana was planning, stopped talking and watched him in silence.
(Note: The commentator says there are fourteen kinds of learning, but sadly, he doesn’t list them.)
(Note: The Kali Yuga is the age when unrighteousness prevails.)
(Note: While conquering the three worlds, you disrupted sacrifices and other good deeds, going against righteousness.)
SECTION XXXVI

Ravana, the ten-headed king, completely overpowered by his own fate, refused to listen to Mālyavān’s wise advice. Scowling with anger and eyes blazing, he let his rage take over and snapped at Mālyavān, “You think you’re being helpful, but what you just said—assuming the enemy is stronger—no one’s ever dared say that to me before. Why should I be afraid of Rama? He’s just a man. He’s alone, exiled by his own father, and all he has are some monkeys by his side. Why do you act like he could ever defeat me? I’m the king of the Rakshasas, feared even by the gods themselves—how could you see me as weak or powerless? I can’t help but think you’re either jealous of my strength or you’re trying to provoke me on purpose. Who talks like that to someone powerful and high-born, unless they’re just trying to push him? Why should I give up Sita—who’s as beautiful as the goddess Sri without her lotus—just because I should be scared of Rama? Watch: soon, Rama and his army of monkeys, along with Sugriva and Lakshmana, will all be dead. Even the gods can’t stand before me in battle—what makes you think I’d ever be afraid? I’d rather die than bow to anyone. That’s just who I am; people can’t change what’s in their nature. If Rama built a bridge across the ocean, so what? That’s no reason for this sudden panic. And even if he did cross the sea with his monkey army, I promise you—he won’t leave Lanka alive.”  

When Ravana finished, still seething, Mālyavān realized it was pointless to argue further. He simply offered his blessings to the king, asked for permission to leave, and returned to his own home. Ravana, meanwhile, gathered his counselors and strategized how best to defend Lanka. He ordered Prahasta to guard the Eastern gate, and put the formidable Mahaparswa and Mahodara in charge of the Southern gate. For the Western gate, he assigned his son Indrajit—known for his magical powers—along with countless Rakshasas. Suka and Sarana were told to defend the Northern gate, but Ravana added, “I’ll go there myself.” In the center of the fortress, he placed the powerful Virupaksha, supported by an army of Rakshasas, ready for anything. With these defenses in place, Ravana, driven by his own destiny, felt certain he’d done everything right. Confident, he dismissed his ministers, accepted their wishes for victory, and finally headed into his glorious private chambers.
[97] That is, to defend the Northern gate.—T.
SECTION XXXVII

The allied leaders—both human and monkey—gathered together on the edge of enemy territory to plan their next move. Among them were Hanuman (the Wind-god’s son), Jāmbavān (the king of bears), Bibhishana (Ravana’s younger brother), Angada (Vali’s son), Lakshmana (Sumitrā’s son), Sarabha, Sushena with his friends, Kumuda, Nala, and Panasa. They all assembled, looking across at the city of Lanka, ruled by Ravana—a place said to be unconquerable, even by gods, serpents, or celestial musicians. “There’s Lanka,” someone said. “Ravana’s stronghold. We need to figure out how to succeed.” As they spoke, Bibhishana stepped forward to share vital intelligence. “I sent four of my trusted advisors—Anala, Panasa, Sampati, and Pramati—into Lanka. They disguised themselves as birds, slipped past the enemy lines, and came back with news. Listen carefully, Rama. Here’s what they found out about Ravana’s defenses: At the Eastern gate, Prahasta stands guard with his army. The Southern gate is defended by the powerful Mahaparshva and Mahodara. At the Western gate, Ravana’s son Indrajit commands countless Rakshasas, all heavily armed—spears, swords, bows, darts, and maces—surrounded by warrior elites. Ravana himself guards the Northern gate with thousands of his best soldiers and his most trusted advisors; he’s restless and on high alert. In the center of the city, Virupaksha and his force, armed with javelins, clubs, and bows, protect the citadel. My spies saw all of this before returning. The scale of their army is immense—ten thousand elephants, ten thousand chariots, twenty thousand horses, and about a crore (ten million) Rakshasas, all strong and heavily armed. These are Ravana’s favorites, and each of his commanders is backed by a crore of troops in battle.” As Bibhishana finished giving this detailed report, he pointed out the very Rakshasas his spies had seen. Loyal to Rama, Bibhishana did everything he could to keep Rama fully informed about what was happening inside Lanka. “Rama,” he continued, “when Ravana once fought Kuvera, he commanded sixty lakhs (six million) Rakshasas, all nearly as powerful, energetic, and fearless as Ravana himself. I’m not trying to scare you—just to fire you up. You could defeat even the gods if you wanted. So gather your army, arrange the monkeys for battle, and you’ll crush Ravana.” 

When Bibhishana finished, Rama replied, outlining his own battle plan: “Let Nila, the greatest of monkeys, lead a huge force to take on Prahasta at Lanka’s Eastern gate. Angada, Vali’s son, will lead a strong group to fight Mahaparshva and Mahodara at the Southern gate. Hanuman—backed by countless monkeys—will storm the Western gate and try to break through. I myself, determined to end Ravana—whose magical boons have made him arrogant and who has destroyed wise sages and oppressed the world—will lead the assault on the Northern gate, alongside Lakshmana, where Ravana and his main army wait. The monkey king Sugriva, Jāmbavān the bear king, and Bibhishana with his followers will organize and support our troops in the center. The monkeys don’t need to pretend to be human; in fact, let’s keep them in their natural forms so we know who’s who. Only seven of us will fight in human shape: me, my brother Lakshmana, Bibhishana and his group, and our allies.” 

After laying out his plan to Bibhishana, Rama looked at the beautiful Suvela mountain and decided it was the best place to launch their attack. Filled with excitement and surrounded by a massive army, Rama set out for Lanka, determined to destroy the enemy and bring the battle to Ravana’s doorstep.
(The commentator notes: these are the main commanders mentioned above.)
[99] (The commentator explains: “You shouldn’t be angry with me; I’m not trying to scare you, just to stir up your determination against Ravana.”)
SECTION XXXVIII

Rāma, determined to climb Mount Suvela, turned to Lakshmana, Sugriva, and Bibhishana (who was wise and trusted by everyone), and addressed them in a calm but firm voice. “Let’s all go up Suvela, with its gleaming minerals, and spend the night there. From its heights, we’ll look out at the home of that Rākshasa who stole my wife—bringing disaster upon himself. He doesn’t care about what’s right or about honor, and his evil choices have led him to this terrible act.” With his anger at Rāvana burning inside him, Rāma started up Suvela’s colorful slopes. Lakshmana followed right behind. Sugriva, always ready for action, lifted his bow and arrows, and went with Bibhishana and his advisors, climbing after Rāma. Behind them, crowds of mountain-dwelling monkeys, fierce as the wind, hurried up Suvela to where Rāma was waiting.

They reached the top quickly, and from there, everyone could see the city of Lankā, almost as if it were floating in the air. The monkey leaders stared at Lankā, which looked amazing with its grand gates, strong walls, and streets busy with Rākshasas. Dark Rākshasa warriors stood guard everywhere. Some of the monkeys noticed that the guards looked like they formed a second wall above the first. Fired up by the sight of their enemies, the monkeys started letting out wild battle cries, eager for the coming fight, right there in front of Rāma.

As evening came, the setting sun turned the sky red, and the night arrived, lit up by a bright full moon. Rāma, leader of the monkey army, was respectfully greeted and honored by Bibhishana. Together with Lakshmana and the monkey chiefs, he settled in for the night on the slopes of Suvela, feeling ready for what was to come.
SECTION XXXIX

After spending the night in Suvela, the brave monkey leaders explored the woods and forests around Lankā. They gazed at the vast, peaceful, and beautiful landscapes, and couldn’t help but be amazed. The forests were full of champaka, ashoka, vakula, shala, and palm trees; thick with tamala and panasa, surrounded on all sides by even more trees. Around them grew hintala, arjuna, blossoming saptaparna, tilaka, karnikara, and patala trees, all covered in flowers and intertwined with vines. Lankā looked stunning, filled with all these sights, almost like Indra’s heavenly city, Amarāvati. The trees were decorated with colorful flowers and soft pink leaves. There were green lawns and stretches of forest, and the air was full of the scent of sweet blossoms and fruit. It looked as if the trees themselves were people dressed in fancy jewelry. One especially lovely grove, as beautiful as the mythical Chaitraratha or Nandana gardens, seemed to have all the seasons at once, and was alive with buzzing black bees.

Birds called dātyuha and koyasthiva flitted about, and peacocks danced. The coels’ songs echoed near woodland streams. The excited monkeys, who could change their form at will, entered these magical woods, where wild birds sang and huge bees (bhramaras) hummed. The whole place was filled with birdsongs and the calls of ospreys. As the energetic monkeys went deeper, they felt a breeze filled with the scent of flowers—it almost felt like the wind itself gave them life.

Some of the leading monkeys, following Sugriva’s orders, moved ahead toward Lankā, which was crowned with flags. Their shouts scared away birds and animals, and their roars shook the city. As they marched forward with incredible force, they raised clouds of dust. Lions, bears, buffaloes, elephants, deer, and birds, terrified, ran off in all directions.

At the center stood the magnificent summit of Trikuta, tall and shining gold, reaching up toward the sky for one hundred yojanas (an ancient measure), smooth and flat, impossible to climb—even to imagine reaching the top seemed impossible. On the very top stood Lankā, ruled by Rāvana. The city itself was ten yojanas wide and twenty long. Lankā boasted tall, decorated gates that looked like pale clouds, and walls of gold and silver. The city shined with palaces and towers, like the sky filling with clouds at the start of the rainy season. The main palace, with thousands of pillars, seemed to pierce the heavens—like a peak of Mount Kailāsa. It was Rāvana’s residence, the pride of the city, always guarded by hundreds of rakshasas (demons).

Lakshmana’s older brother, Rāma, who was both blessed and powerful, saw this thriving, wealthy city. It looked like a piece of the heavens—made of gold, dotted with mountains, and rich with precious minerals. The air was full of bird calls, and the forests teemed with animals and flowers. Different groups of rakshasas lived throughout the city. Rāma, leading his powerful army, gazed at the palace, packed with gems, lined with rows of buildings, and guarded by massive engines and gates.
Trikuta’s.—T.

Madhyamam Vaishnavam padam—the middle foot of Vishnu. When Vishnu, in his dwarf form, humbled the proud Asura king Vāli, he covered the earth with one step, the sky with another, and heaven with the last.—T.
SECTION XL

Rama, together with the monkey leaders and Sugriva (the monkey king), climbed to the top of Mount Suvela, which was about two yojanas in circumference. They paused there for a while, scanning all directions. From the summit, Rama saw Lanka, beautifully situated on the peak of Trikuta mountain, surrounded by lush groves. At the city’s grand gate stood Ravana, the unbeatable lord of the Rakshasas. Ravana was fanned with white chāmaras and sheltered under a victory umbrella, his body smeared with red sandalwood paste and adorned with red jewelry. He looked like a dark thundercloud, clothed in gold, his chest scarred by the tusks of Airavata, the divine elephant. He wore a crimson cloak like rabbit’s blood, and in the light of the setting sun, appeared as dramatic as storm clouds glowing at dusk.

Spotting Ravana, Sugriva sprang up suddenly in full view of the other monkeys and Rama. Fired up with anger, Sugriva gathered his strength and, leaping from the mountain, landed at the city gate. He paused briefly, stared down the Rakshasa chief without fear, and, dismissing him, shouted harshly, “Hey Rakshasa! I’m Rama’s friend and servant—the king of men. Backed by his power, you’re not getting away today.” With that, Sugriva sprang forward, landed on Ravana, and grabbed his colorful crown, throwing it to the ground.

Seeing Sugriva’s sudden attack, Ravana said, “So you were Sugriva—Good-Neck—when I didn’t know you, but now, near me, you’ll be neckless.” He lunged up and grabbed Sugriva, pulling him down. But Sugriva, quick as a spring, shoved Ravana back with his powerful arms. Both fighters were soon sweating and bloodied, each blocking the other’s moves. They looked like the bright red silk-cotton or kinshuk trees, striking and slapping, exchanging blows with hands and arms.

The two leaders—Ravana and Sugriva—fought fiercely on the gate’s platform, lifting and slamming each other, trying to trip one another with their legs. Locked together, they tumbled between the wall and the moat, finally landing on the ground. After catching their breath for a moment, they grappled again, each wrapping his arms around the other like ropes. Fueled by rage, both showed off their strength and fighting skills, moving like a tiger and a lion with bared fangs, or like young, wild elephants battling head-to-head—pushing and restraining each other until, together, they hit the ground.

They jumped back to their feet and traded insults, circling each other and showing off their strength and technique. Neither seemed to tire quickly. Like giant elephants, they used their arms—the size of elephant trunks—to block and attack, fighting fiercely as they moved fast around the arena. Closing in, each tried to finish the other, like two cats fighting over food.

Ravana and Sugriva, both masters of combat, darted around the arena, displaying an incredible variety of battle techniques—circling, shifting stances, feinting, attacking, retreating, dodging, charging, leaping, twisting, and grabbing in every way possible. (See notes for the specific moves and their meanings.)

In the middle of the fight, Ravana tried to use his magical illusions, but Sugriva noticed and shot up into the sky, avoiding the trick. Now exhausted and out of breath, Ravana was left standing in frustration, his magic useless. Victorious, Sugriva had proven himself in battle by tiring out the king of the Rakshasas. Leaping back from high in the sky, Sugriva—the son of the Sun—returned to Rama and the monkey army. His heart bursting with pride and joy, Sugriva rejoined the other monkeys, boosting their fighting spirit and earning their respect.
The text uses the word “hinagriva”—which means “neckless.” There’s a pun here: Ravana says, “You were Sugriva—Good-Neck—when I didn’t know you, but now, near me, you’ll be hinagriva—neckless.”
This refers to Sugriva.
“Mandala” are types of combat movements: chāri (one leg forward), karana (alternating legs), khanda (special moves added), and mahāmandala (combining two or three khandas).
“Sthāna” are specific fighting stances or step sequences—six main types: Vaishnava, Sampāda, Vaiçākka, Mandala, Pratyālirha, and Anālirha.
“Gomātraka” is a kind of movement that flows like cow’s urine—basically, a smooth, steady motion.
This means advancing quickly to face your opponent.
Moving “like a summer cloud”—swift and drifting.
Standing in front of the enemy after sending others to fight first. Its precise meaning here is unclear.
Turning away from an enemy.
Moving away sideways from the opponent.
Lowering your stance to attack at thigh level.
Jumping in for a kick.
Puffing out your chest to keep your arms free from being grabbed.
Reaching out to grab your opponent’s arms.
SECTION XLI

Seeing all these ominous signs, Rāma, Lakshmana’s older brother, hugged Sugriva and said, “You acted recklessly without telling me what you were planning. Kings should never be so impulsive. By keeping me, this army, and even Bibhishana in suspense, you’ve put yourself in real danger just for the sake of bold action. Please, don’t do this again. If anything happened to you, Sugriva, what would Sita mean to me? Or Bharata? Or my younger brother Lakshmana, or Shatrughna? Or even my own life? Even before you arrived, I had already decided what to do — and I know your strength is equal to Indra or Varuna. My plan is to defeat Rāvana in battle, destroy his sons, armies, chariots — then crown Bibhishana king of Lanka and give Bharata the kingdom before I give up my own life.” After Rāma finished, Sugriva replied, “Knowing my own strength, how could I just stand by and do nothing when Rāvana took your wife, Rāghava?” While Sugriva was explaining himself, Rāma turned to Lakshmana and said, “Let’s camp somewhere with fresh water and fruit trees, split up and organize our troops. I sense a huge threat coming — a disaster that could wipe out the bravest bears, monkeys, and Rakshasas. The wind is wild, the ground shakes, mountain tops tremble, and the rocks roar. The clouds look creepy and violent, pouring down rain mixed with blood. The sky at dusk is terrifying, as red as sandalwood. A burning ring falls from the sun. Weird, scary birds and animals, looking desperate, cry out toward the sun. At night, the moon glows with a black-and-red edge, like the end of the world. The sun’s rim is jagged and red, with a blue spot on its face. The stars don’t move like before. Look, Lakshmana — these are all signs of doom. Crows, hawks, and vultures fall from the sky. Jackals howl with evil cries. The ground will soon be soaked with blood, covered in weapons thrown by Rakshasas and monkeys. Today, we’ll gather our army and march for Lanka as fast as possible.” After saying this, Rāma quickly climbed down the mountain. Once on the ground, the noble Rāghava looked over his tough army, confident they couldn’t be defeated. He ordered the monkey king’s troops to get ready and, with Sugriva, gave the signal for battle at the right moment. Soon, armed with his bow and surrounded by his huge army, Rāma set out to attack Lanka.

Bibhishana, Sugriva, Hanumān, Jāmbavān, Nala, the bear-king Nila, and Lakshmana all followed Rāma. Behind them, an enormous force of bears and monkeys marched, covering the land. The monkeys, as strong as elephants, carried mountain peaks and huge trees by the hundreds. In no time, Rāma and Lakshmana arrived at Rāvana’s city — banners flying, beautiful groves and gardens, colorful gates, tall walls, and strong defenses.

On Rāma’s command, the monkey army surrounded Lanka, making it impossible to enter. Rāma and Lakshmana took position at the northern gate — the main entrance, where Rāvana himself lived. Only Rāma was strong enough to guard this terrifying gate, protected by Rāvana and his weapon-wielding Rakshasas — as hard to break as the ocean guarded by Varuna, or the underworld guarded by demons. Rāma saw piles of weapons and armor stacked nearby.

Nila, the monkey leader, along with Mainda and Dwivida, took up the eastern gate. The mighty Angada, with Rishava, Gavāksha, Gaya, and Gavaya, guarded the southern gate. Hanumān protected the western gate. Sugriva himself, with Prajangha, Tarasa, and other warriors, stayed near the central garrison.

Twenty crores of famous monkey chiefs, as fast and fierce as the wind or Garuda, surrounded Sugriva, sealing off every side. At Rāma’s order, Lakshmana and Bibhishana went from gate to gate, giving instructions to the monkey armies. To Rāma’s west, Jāmbavān and Sushena, with countless troops, were stationed at the main garrison.

The monkeys, fierce as tigers with sharp teeth and claws, wielded trees and mountaintops as weapons. Their tails curled, their bodies were marked with patterns, and their faces were wild and frightening. Some had the strength of ten elephants, some a hundred, some even a thousand or more. The power gathered there was incredible — the monkey army was as thick as a swarm of locusts. The air was full, the ground was covered with monkeys racing toward Lanka and leaping over its walls. Thousands more arrived at the gates, while others poured in from every direction.

The mountain was covered with monkeys. Tens of thousands circled the city. With so many powerful monkeys carrying trees, Lanka was so sealed off that even the wind couldn’t get through. The Rakshasas, overwhelmed by the sheer mass of monkeys — as strong as Indra himself — were shocked and afraid. The noise from the armies rushing around sounded like the crashing of ocean waves. The whole city — walls, gates, mountains, forests — shook from the uproar.

Protected by Rāma, Lakshmana, and Sugriva, the army was now invincible, even to gods or demons. After arranging his forces for the coming battle, Rāghava, skilled in war, consulted with his advisors, carefully considering his next move. Deciding to follow Bibhishana’s advice, he remembered the ethics of kingship: if victory could be achieved through negotiation, punishment should be a last resort.

Then, calling Angada (Vāli’s son), Rāma said, “Go to Rāvana, the Ten-Headed King, and tell him this for me: ‘I crossed the ocean and laid siege to Lanka. I’ve taken away your power, your fortune, and your sense. Blinded by pride and your boon from Brahma, you’ve attacked saints, gods, Gandharvas, Apsaras, Nagas, Yakshas, and kings. Now, that pride is gone — I, suffering from the loss of my wife, am here at Lanka’s gate, ready to punish you. If you stand and fight, you could reach the status of the gods and the greatest sages. Show the same power you used to steal Sita from me with your dark magic. I’ll wipe the Rakshasas from this world with my arrows unless you return Sita and beg for mercy. If you don’t, Bibhishana — righteous and wise — will rule Lanka in peace. You, stubborn and badly advised, are unfit to be king. Stand and fight with all your courage. When my arrows kill you, you’ll finally find peace. Even if you fly as a bird through the three worlds, you can’t escape me. This is your last warning — do what’s best for yourself, see Lanka one last time, because your life is in my hands.’”

After hearing Rāma’s message, Angada shot through the sky like a streak of fire. He arrived at Rāvana’s palace in no time, where the demon king sat calmly with his ministers. Landing nearby like a flaming meteor, Angada — as bright as a golden bracelet — introduced himself and delivered Rāma’s message exactly as it was given, without changing anything: “I am the envoy of the king of Kosala, Rāma — and the son of Vāli. Maybe you’ve heard of me. Rāma, son of Raghu and joy of Kausalya, says: ‘Come out, Rāvana, and fight me if you’re brave. I will destroy you, your ministers, your sons, your friends, and your entire family. When you’re gone, peace will return to the three worlds. Today, I’ll end the enemy of the gods, demons, Yakshas, Gandharvas, Nagas, and Rakshasas — the one who torments the saints. All your wealth will go to Bibhishana, unless you bow to me and return Sita.’”

On hearing Angada’s words, Rāvana was furious. Consumed by rage, he ordered his counselors, “Seize this arrogant fool and kill him now!”

Hearing Rāvana’s order, four fierce Rakshasas grabbed Angada, whose energy burned like fire. Angada let himself be caught, planning to show his true strength in front of the demons. With the Rakshasas clinging to his arms like insects, Angada suddenly leaped up onto a palace rooftop as high as a hill. The Rakshasas, unable to hold on, slipped off and crashed to the ground right in front of Rāvana.

Then, with his powerful legs, Angada smashed the top of Rāvana’s palace, splitting it open like a thunderbolt splitting a mountain. He tore off the rooftop, shouted his name for all to hear, and let out a mighty roar before launching himself into the sky. The Rakshasas were shaken and the monkeys cheered as Angada returned to Rāma’s side.

Rāvana, furious at the destruction of his palace, breathed heavily, sensing his doom. Rāma, in the midst of his excited monkey army, prepared for battle, determined to defeat his enemy. Following Sugriva’s orders, the mighty monkey Sushena, as huge as a mountain peak, led a troop of monkeys who could change their shape at will, patrolling the garrison like the moon among stars.

Seeing the hundreds of thousands of monkeys now stationed all the way to the sea, some Rakshasas were amazed, some terrified, and some felt excitement for the coming fight. The space between the city wall and the moat was jam-packed with monkeys. The Rakshasas, scared by the sight of monkeys everywhere, cried out “Alas!”

“Alas!” The Rakshasas were completely terrified. As the terrifying noise echoed through the city, Rāvana’s soldiers grabbed their weapons and began patrolling the streets, fierce as storm winds at the end of the world.

SECTION XLII

The Rākshasas hurried to Rāvana (the demon king) and told him that Rāma and his monkey army had surrounded the city. Hearing his city was under siege, Rāvana was furious. He learned that Rāma had set up double guards at every gate, so he climbed up to the palace roof. From there, he saw Lankā’s mountains, woods, and forests completely covered by countless monkeys, all ready for battle. The earth seemed to turn golden-brown from the sheer number of them. Rāvana wondered how he could wipe out such a massive force. After thinking for a long time, he calmed himself and stared at Rāma (also called Rāghava) and the monkey leader. Rāma’s forces were closing in on the walls, while Rāvana noticed his city’s defenses packed with Rākshasas (demons) on every side. At the same time, Rāma, son of Daçaratha, saw Lankā decorated with colorful flags and banners, and his heart ached as he thought of Sītā. “Sītā, Janaka’s daughter, with her deer-like eyes, is suffering because of me—she’s lying on the ground somewhere in there,” he thought sadly. Overcome with grief for Vaidehi (another name for Sītā), Rāma quickly ordered the monkeys to attack and destroy their enemies. As soon as Rāma gave the command, the monkeys roared like lions and charged forward with incredible ferocity.

The monkey leaders told themselves, “We’ll break Lankā apart with mountain peaks or with our bare hands.” They stood ready, hoisting huge chunks of mountain and uprooting trees to use as weapons. Determined to please Rāma, the monkey army split into groups and began climbing Lankā’s walls right in front of Rāvana. These copper-faced, golden-furred monkeys, who had dedicated their lives to Rāma, stormed the city with trees and boulders. Smashing countless gates and wall-tops with their makeshift weapons and brute strength, they filled the crystal-clear moats with dust, rocks, straw, and wood. The monkey leaders, commanding thousands and even millions, swarmed the city’s defenses. They smashed golden gates and, breaking down doors that looked like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, leaped forward, roaring wildly. They moved like enormous elephants, charging at Lankā’s walls. “Victory to mighty Rāma! Victory to the powerful Lakshmana! Victory to King Sugriva, protected by Rāghava!” they shouted, shifting shapes at will and filling the air with their thunderous battle cries. Viravāhu, Suvāhu, Nala, and Panaça—monkey leaders—took up positions after breaking through part of the wall, and the army quickly formed battle lines.

Kumuda, supported by ten million monkeys, blocked the Eastern gate. Prasabha and the long-armed Panaça, each with their own groups, backed him up. At the Southern entrance, Satavali, brave and strong, stood with twenty million monkeys. The powerful Sushena, father of Tārā, guarded the Western gate, backed by countless others. At the Northern gate, Rāma himself stood ready, joined by Sumitrā’s son (Lakshmana) and the monkey king, Sugriva. Next to Rāma waited the huge and fearsome Gavāksha, leader of the Golāngulas, along with a million monkeys. Dhumra, the terrifying bear chief, also guarded Rāma’s side, while Bibhishana, Rāvana’s brother—now fully armored and surrounded by his advisors—stood nearby, gripping his mace. Gaya, Gavāksha, Gavaya, Sarabha, and Gandhamadana ranged around to protect the monkey army.

Fired up with anger, Rāvana ordered his entire demon army to charge out. As soon as he spoke, the Rākshasas let out a terrifying war cry. Giant kettle-drums with pale, moon-like faces were beaten with golden sticks, and hundreds of conch shells blared loudly, filled with the breath of fierce Rākshasas. The demons, their blue bodies shining, looked like storm clouds with flashes of lightning as they blew their conchs and got ready for battle. Rāvana’s troops poured out of the city, as unstoppable as a tidal wave at the end of the world. In response, the monkey army’s roar echoed everywhere, shaking the mountains and caves of Malaya. The blaring of conchs and drums, combined with the monkeys’ battle cries, filled the air, land, and sea, mixing with the trumpeting of elephants, neighing of horses, rumbling of chariots, and the pounding of Rākshasas’ feet.

Suddenly, the battle began—monkeys and demons clashed with a violence like the ancient wars between gods and Asuras. The Rākshasas showed off their strength, killing monkeys with maces, spears, and axes. The monkeys fought back, killing demons with trees, rocks, their claws, and their teeth. Both sides shouted their kings’ names: “Victory to King Sugriva!” and “Victory to you, O King!” More Rākshasas stationed on the walls threw spears and darts down at the monkeys. Furious, the monkeys leapt up, dragged the demons down, and beat them with their fists. The battle was brutal and wild, leaving the ground soaked with blood and bodies.
Rākshasas.
SECTION XLIII

As the battle between the mighty monkeys and Rākshasas raged on, their anger only grew stronger at the sight of each other's armies. The Rākshasas stormed forward—riding horses draped in gold, elephants that looked like living fire, and chariots that blazed like little suns. Their armor shone as they charged, making the whole battlefield echo with the noise. The Rākshasas, desperate for victory for Rāvana, fought with terrifying ferocity, while the monkey army, just as eager to win, charged right back. Soon, fighters from both sides started engaging in intense one-on-one duels. Indrajit (Rāvana’s powerful son), full of energy and rage, faced off against Angada, son of Vāli, echoing the legendary battle between Andhaka and the three-eyed god Shiva. Sampati, a tough opponent, clashed with Prajangha. Hanumān squared up against Jambumāli. Bibhishana, Rāvana’s younger brother, burning with anger, fought Satrughna, who was known for his fierce attacks. Nila, another powerful monkey, went up against Nikumbha. Sugriva (king of the monkeys) battled Praghasa, and Lakshmana took on Virupāksha. Meanwhile, Rāma was attacked by Agniketu, Raçmiketu, Mitraghna, and Yajnakopa—four fierce Rākshasas. Vajramushti fought with Mainda, and Açaniprabha faced Dwivida. All across the field, legendary monkeys and terrifying Rākshasas faced off in brutal combat. Pratapana, one of the toughest Rākshasas, fought against the powerful Nala, while Sushena, famed as the son of Righteousness and a mighty monkey, fought Vidyunmāli. Many other monkeys and Rākshasas paired off, and the battlefield became a place of countless, vicious confrontations.

The fighting was so intense and terrifying that it would make anyone’s hair stand on end. Blood from both Rākshasas and monkeys ran like a river, with hair floating along its surface, and the bodies of the dead drifting like logs. In the middle of the chaos, Indrajit, furious, smashed his mace down on Angada, just as Indra would strike with his thunderbolt. Angada, quick and strong, responded by smashing Indrajit’s golden chariot, along with its horses and driver, using his own mace. Sampati was struck by three arrows from Prajangha, but he fought back and killed Prajangha with a blow from an Ashwakarna tree branch. Meanwhile, Jambumāli—riding his chariot and filled with rage—hit Hanumān in the chest with all his might. Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, leapt onto Jambumāli’s chariot and, with a single slap, crushed both the chariot and Jambumāli himself.

Elsewhere, the fierce Rākshasa Pratapana, roaring with fury, rushed at Nala. Pratapana struck Nala with sharp arrows, but Nala fought back, gouged out Pratapana’s eyes, and threw them to the ground. Sugriva, king of the monkeys, grabbed a Saptaparna tree and quickly killed Praghasa, who seemed to be devouring whole squads of monkeys. Lakshmana, showering Virupāksha with arrows, finally killed him with a single, well-aimed shot. The Rākshasas Agniketu, Raçmiketu, Mitraghna, and Yajnakopa shot arrows at Rāma, making him look like he was on fire. Rāma, enraged, took four arrows that looked like tongues of flame and, with precise shots, cut off the heads of all four Rākshasas.

The battle only grew more intense. Mainda killed Vajramushti with a powerful punch, knocking him, his chariot, and his horses to the ground like a collapsing tower. Nikumbha wounded Nila with sharp arrows, piercing his dark blue body like sunlight breaking through clouds. Nikumbha then shot Nila with a hundred more arrows, laughing all the while. But Nila, furious, picked up a wheel from Nikumbha’s own chariot and used it to slice off both Nikumbha’s and his charioteer’s heads, just like Vishnu might in battle.

Dwivida, who was as strong as a thunderbolt, grabbed a mountain peak and hurled it at Açaniprabha in front of the whole Rākshasa army. Açaniprabha, in turn, shot Dwivida with arrows as hard as thunderbolts. Wounded and furious, Dwivida used a huge sāla tree to smash Açaniprabha, destroying his chariot and horses as well.

Vidyunmāli, riding his chariot, attacked Sushena with golden-tipped arrows and shouted taunts at him. Sushena, not intimidated, picked up a massive rock and slammed it into Vidyunmāli’s chariot, crashing it to the ground. Vidyunmāli quickly jumped free, landing on the ground with a mace in hand. Sushena, now enraged, grabbed an even bigger rock and charged at him.

As Sushena approached, Vidyunmāli swung his mace and struck Sushena hard in the chest. But Sushena barely seemed to notice the blow. He brought the giant rock down on Vidyunmāli’s head with all his strength. The impact crushed Vidyunmāli’s chest, killing him instantly and sending him crashing to the earth.

All over the battlefield, the heroic monkeys fought like gods battling demons, throwing the Rākshasa army into confusion. The ground was littered with weapons—darts, clubs, javelins, lances—along with broken chariots, dead horses, and the bodies of monkeys and Rākshasas. Pieces of wheels, axles, yokes, and banners were scattered everywhere. Packs of jackals prowled among the fallen, and horrific headless spirits called Kavandhas began to appear in the chaos, making the scene look like a war between gods and demons. Overwhelmed by the blood and carnage, the surviving Rākshasas, desperate for the sun to set so their powers would return, began preparing themselves for another round of battle as soon as night arrived.

SECTION XLIV

As the battle between the monkeys and the Rākshasas raged on, the sun finally set, and darkness swallowed the battlefield. Night fell, bringing a new layer of danger, and both sides—monkeys and Rākshasas—were desperate to win. In the thick darkness, chaos took over. The monkeys and Rākshasas attacked each other, shouting, “You’re a Rākshasa!” or “You’re a monkey!” All around, you could hear yells: “Kill him!” “Break through!” “Come here!” “Why are you running?” The Rākshasas, their dark bodies covered in golden armor, looked like huge hills shining with glowing medicinal herbs. In this endless blackness, the furious Rākshasas charged forward, moving so fast they seemed to tear through the night, even grabbing and eating monkeys.

Some of the Rākshasas, wild with rage, jumped and used their sharp teeth to rip apart horses dressed in golden gear, and even tore down banners that looked like deadly snakes. The monkeys fought back just as fiercely, throwing the Rākshasas into confusion. Growing angrier, the monkeys bit elephants and their riders, and smashed the chariots decorated with flags and standards. Meanwhile, Rāma and Lakshmana fired arrows like deadly snakes, cutting down the most dangerous Rākshasas—whether they were visible or hidden in the shadows.

The dust kicked up by the fighters and the hooves of horses and chariot wheels filled the air, making it hard to see or breathe. The whole scene was terrifying, with rivers of blood flowing across the battlefield. The clash of kettle-drums, mridangas, and panavas mixed with the blaring of conch shells and the grinding of chariot wheels, creating a wild, deafening noise. Horses neighed, Rākshasas roared, and the monkeys cheered— the sounds were overwhelming.

The ground was littered with dead monkeys, broken weapons, and piles of fallen Rākshasas—some of whom could change their shape at will—lying like mountains. The battlefield was so covered in bodies and weapons that it was almost impossible to tell where anything was; the earth was soaked with blood. The night itself felt as if it wanted to destroy both monkeys and Rākshasas—like the ultimate doomsday that no one could escape.

In this total darkness, the Rākshasas suddenly targeted Rāma, shooting a storm of arrows at him. Their angry shouts sounded like the ocean roaring at the end of the world. In a split second, Rāma fired six flaming arrows and struck down six powerful Rākshasas: Yajnaçatru, who was nearly unstoppable in battle; Mahāpārcwa; Mahodara; the giant Vajradanashtra; and the two warriors Suka and Sārana. Wounded deep in their bodies by Rāma’s arrows, the six barely escaped with their lives, slipping away from the fight.

Then, just as quickly, Rāma, a master of war, shot arrows that lit up the darkness like tongues of fire, clearing the battlefield around him. Any Rākshasa who came near Rāma was destroyed instantly, like an insect drawn to a flame. Gold-tipped arrows scattered everywhere, making the night look like it was lit up with autumn fireflies. With all the noise from the Rākshasas and the pounding drums, the night grew even more terrifying. As the sound grew louder and louder, it felt like the mountain Trikuta itself, with its many caves, was speaking.

Huge Goāngulas—monsters as dark as the night—grabbed Rākshasas in their arms and swallowed them whole. In the middle of the chaos, Angada fought fiercely, determined to take down his enemies. Indrajit, Rāvana’s son, was overwhelmed by Angada—his chariot was wrecked, his horses and driver killed—so he vanished on the spot. The gods, wise sages, Rāma, and Lakshmana all cheered Angada for this amazing feat. Everyone knew how powerful Indrajit was in battle, so seeing him defeated made everyone—especially Sugriva, Bibhishana, and the rest of the monkeys—shout “Awesome!” and “Well done!”

But Indrajit, furious at being beaten by Angada (Vāli’s son), burned with anger. Unable to win in a fair fight, the wicked Indrajit—who had a boon from Brahmā—turned invisible and started firing magical arrows that glowed like lightning bolts. Consumed with rage, he shot arrow after arrow at Rāma and Lakshmana. The arrows, enchanted and shaped like serpents, struck both brothers all over their bodies. Hidden from everyone’s eyes, Indrajit used illusions and trickery, confusing Rāma and Lakshmana and trapping them with his magical arrows.

In full view of the monkeys, the two brothers—famous for their courage—were suddenly overwhelmed by Indrajit’s furious attack. When Indrajit realized he couldn’t beat them face-to-face, he relied on his sorcery to capture Rāma and Lakshmana, binding them tightly with his magic.

SECTION XLV

Eager to figure out which way Indrajit (Ravana’s son) had gone, Rama—strong and determined—called on ten of the monkey leaders. He gave orders to Angada (Vali’s son), Sarabha, Dwivida, Hanuman, the powerful Sanuprastha, Rishabha, and Rishabhaskandha. Without delay, these monkeys, wielding massive tree-trunks, leapt into the sky and sped off in all directions, searching. But Indrajit, master of weapons, blocked their advance with a powerful attack and even stronger weapons. The monkeys, hit and injured by his arrows, caught glimpses of him in the darkness, much like seeing the sun behind thick clouds. Indrajit then turned his attention to Rama and Lakshmana, striking both brothers with his arrows until their bodies were completely covered by shafts that looked like writhing snakes. Blood streamed from their wounds, making them look like red-blossomed kinshuka trees. With his eyes glowing red and his body as dark as crushed charcoal, Indrajit taunted the brothers as he faded from sight: “When I fight invisible, not even Indra, king of the gods, can find or face me—so what chance do you have? Fueled by rage, I’ll rain down my feathered arrows and send the sons of Raghu to the land of the dead.” 

After mocking them, Indrajit pierced Rama and Lakshmana again with razor-sharp arrows and let out a victorious shout. Drawing his huge bow, black as night, he unleashed a terrifying barrage. Every strike hit its mark, and he screamed with excitement as his arrows found their targets. Rama and Lakshmana, held fast by the relentless storm of arrows, found no escape. Their bodies pierced by arrows and spears, they looked like flags torn free from their poles, shaking in the wind—every inch of them bristling with shafts. Overwhelmed by pain, the mighty brothers fell to the ground, blood pouring from their wounds like water from a spring. Their bodies were so covered in arrows there wasn’t a spot the size of a finger untouched. Even their forearms were riddled with wounds. Indrajit, a master of illusions, had struck them down, and blood gushed from them violently.

Rama fell first, mortally wounded by Indrajit’s arrows. Indrajit, the same warrior who had once defeated Indra in anger, now struck Rama with golden-tipped arrows, some swift and straight as wind-blown dust, some half-broken, some shaped like cupped hands, some like calf’s teeth, others like lion’s fangs, some like razors. When Rama’s bow—decorated with gold, curved in three places, and its handle shattered—fell from his grasp, he collapsed like a true hero. Seeing Rama, the greatest of men, lying within reach of enemy arrows, Lakshmana lost hope for his brother’s life. Lakshmana, who always looked up to Rama—the one with lotus-petal eyes, always eager for battle, and a protector to everyone—began to weep as he watched his brother fall. The monkeys, too, were stricken with grief. Tears filled their eyes as they cried out in sorrow for Rama. When both brothers lay bound and wounded as fallen heroes, the monkeys gathered around them, whispering to each other. Led by Hanuman, they were all overcome by heartbreak.
Indrajit.
