SECTION XLVI

The monkey warriors scanned the ground and the sky, searching desperately, until their eyes landed on Rāma and Lakshmana, both lying still and covered in arrows. The demon Indrajit had finished his attack and vanished, just as a storm disappears after a downpour. Soon, Bibhishana arrived with Sugriva. Grieving and in shock, Nila, Dwivida, Mainda, Sushena, Kumuda, and Angada raced to the spot with Hanumān. Rāma and Lakshmana, barely breathing and motionless, were soaked in blood and pierced by a web of arrows. They looked as lifeless as golden statues toppled in battle. The monkey leaders gathered around, tears streaming down their faces, as they gazed at the fallen sons of Raghu.

The monkeys, along with Bibhishana, were overcome with pain at the sight of Rāma and Lakshmana lying still, their bodies blanketed by arrows. They scanned the skies and all directions for Indrajit, but he was completely hidden by his magic. Only Bibhishana, using his own knowledge of illusions, could spot his nephew, Indrajit, standing there invisible to everyone else—a gift he had received from Brahma. Bibhishana saw Indrajit, unmatched in battle, proud of his strength and fame, concealed by divine power.

Indrajit, thrilled with what he’d accomplished, looked at the fallen brothers and boasted loudly to the other Rākshasas, “Rāma and Lakshmana, who killed Khara and Dushana, have now been killed by me! Not even the gods or demons, or even the sages, could save them from my arrows. My father worried and lost sleep because of Rāma. All of Lankā was like a raging river because of him. But now, I’ve finally ended the threat at its source. Just as autumn clouds fade away, the power of Rāma, Lakshmana, and the forest warriors is now useless.”

Indrajit, still speaking to the Rākshasas and threatening the monkey warriors, shot nine arrows at Nila and three each at Mainda and Dwivida. He struck Jambavān in the chest with an arrow, and fired ten more at Hanumān. Then, with blinding speed, he hit Gavāksha and Sarabha with two arrows each, and showered Angada and the king of the Golangulas with countless shafts. Indrajit’s arrows, as fierce as flames, tore into the monkeys, and he let out a triumphant roar on the battlefield.

Indrajit’s savage attack terrified the monkeys and filled them with dread. Laughing cruelly, he declared, “Let the Rākshasas witness these brothers, helpless and bound by my terrible arrows, lying in front of our entire army.” Hearing this, the Rākshasas—who looked as dark and heavy as storm clouds—were amazed by Indrajit’s feat. They cheered with deafening roars. Believing that Rāma was dead, they honored Indrajit, Rāvana’s son. Seeing Rāma and Lakshmana lying motionless, everyone assumed they had been killed. Overjoyed, Indrajit, proud of his victory, returned to Lankā, filling the Rākshasa city with celebration.

Sugriva was gripped by fear when he saw the bodies of Rāma and Lakshmana—every limb pierced and covered in blood. Bibhishana noticed how devastated Sugriva looked—his face streaked with tears, his eyes wild with grief and anger. Bibhishana told him, “Don’t give in to fear, Sugriva. Hold back your tears. This is the way of war—no victory is ever certain. But if fate is on our side, these two great heroes will recover from this. So, pull yourself together and help me now.” Saying this, Bibhishana took some water and gently washed Sugriva’s tear-filled eyes.

Using his knowledge of healing, Bibhishana washed Sugriva’s face and spoke calmly and firmly: “Now isn’t the time to collapse in despair, great monkey-king. Even strong emotions, if uncontrolled, can destroy us at a moment like this. Shake off this daze and think about how you can help Rāma’s army. Or, if you must, stand guard and protect Rāma until he wakes up—when the sons of Kākutstha recover, all our fear will vanish. This is nothing for Rāma; he won’t die now. Fortune (Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity) never abandons someone like him. So, take courage and rally your own troops. I’ll handle the rest of the army. Right now, the monkeys are panicked, eyes wide with terror, whispering to each other in fear. But when they see me, they’ll calm down and drop their fear, like tossing aside an old garland.”

With these words, Bibhishana, lord of the Rākshasas, comforted Sugriva and helped restore order among the fleeing monkey troops. Meanwhile, Indrajit, master of illusions, returned to Lankā with his soldiers and went straight to his father. He bowed to Rāvana and gave him the news that Rāma and Lakshmana had been killed. Overjoyed, Rāvana jumped up in the middle of his people, hugged his son, and kissed his head. Smiling with delight, he asked Indrajit to tell him everything that had happened. Indrajit explained in detail how he had defeated Rāma and Lakshmana, leaving them unconscious and drained by his arrows. Hearing this, Rāvana was filled with relief and happiness—his old fear of Daçaratha’s son vanished, and he showered Indrajit with praise and affection.
Indra.
Rāma and Lakshmana.
The goddess of prosperity.
SECTION XLVII

As soon as Rāvana’s son (Indrajit) returned to Lankā after completing his mission, the top-ranking monkeys quickly formed a protective circle around Rāghava (Rāma). Hanumān, Angada, Nila, Sushena, Kumuda, Nala, Gaya, Gavāksha, Panasa, Samprastha (a powerful monkey), Jāmbavān, Rishava, Sunda, Rambha, Satavali, and Prithu all stood ready, gripping massive tree branches as weapons, eyes darting everywhere—up, down, and all around. The monkeys were so tense that even the rustle of a straw made them think a Rākshasa was attacking. Meanwhile, Rāvana was overjoyed by his apparent victory. He summoned the Rakshasi women who guarded Sitā, including Trijata and the others, and ordered them, “Go tell Vaidehi (Sitā) that Rāma and Lakshmana have been killed in battle by Indrajit. Put her on the Pushpaka (flying chariot), and show her their bodies lying dead on the battlefield. The man she relied on so confidently—her husband—has fallen, along with his brother. With her hope and fear gone, and nothing else to cling to, Sitā, dressed in her finest, will finally turn to me. Today, when she sees Rāma and Lakshmana defeated by fate, she’ll give up resisting and finally accept me. She has no other option.” The Rakshasis, obeying Rāvana, said, “As you wish,” and went to get the Pushpaka. They brought the magical chariot to the Ashoka grove where Sitā was staying. The Rakshasis, with Trijata among them, lifted the heartbroken Sitā onto the Pushpaka. Together, they flew over Lankā, which was decked out with banners and flags for the supposed victory. As they traveled, Rāvana boasted to the people of Lankā, “Rāma and Lakshmana have been killed by Indrajit in battle!” Passing over the battlefield with Trijata, Sitā saw piles of slain monkey warriors. She saw the Rākshasas celebrating, while the monkeys mourned bitterly near the bodies of Rāma and Lakshmana. Sitā then spotted both brothers lying unconscious on the ground, pierced with arrows. Their armor was torn, their bows discarded, and their bodies were bloodied and wounded everywhere. Seeing the two brothers—heroes among men, their eyes like white lotuses, looking almost godlike—lying motionless, Sitā, the daughter of Janaka, was struck by a wave of grief. She began to cry loudly, her tears streaming down her face as she saw them covered in dust. Overcome by sorrow, believing the brothers were dead, she spoke out in anguish.
The phrase “heroes and best of men” is repeated here, so it’s left out to avoid redundancy.
SECTION XLVIII

When Sitā saw her husband Rāma and the powerful Lakshmana lying apparently dead, she was overwhelmed with grief and began to cry bitterly. “The fortune-tellers once said I would have sons and never be a widow. But now that Rāma is gone, it seems even those wise people were wrong. The priests who performed rituals and told me I’d become Rāma’s queen must have been mistaken, too, even though they were supposed to know the truth. Others said I would be honored by the wives of great kings, and by my own husband, but now, with Rāma dead, it all seems like lies, no matter how wise they were. Even the Brahmanas who spoke good omens in my presence—now that Rāma is dead, their words ring false. I have the lotus-marks on my feet that are supposed to mean a woman will become queen alongside her king. But I don’t see any of the marks that are supposed to bring widowhood—yet now, even these good signs seem useless. The marks that are supposed to be unfailing, according to the experts, have failed me, now that Rāma is dead. My hair is fine, even, and blue-black; my eyebrows meet in the middle; my hips are smooth and round, my teeth close together. My temples, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, and thighs are all proportional. My fingers are round and even, with smooth nails. My breasts are firm and full, my navel is deep with raised sides, my chest broad, my skin like precious stones, and my body soft. They said I had twelve lucky signs. The centers of my fingers have wheat-shaped lines; the spaces between my fingers are smooth. My feet have the same even color as the rest of me. My laugh is just a gentle smile. The experts in reading marks on women said I was blessed with all these signs. The Brahmanas skilled in fortune-telling said I would be crowned alongside my husband, but all of that has turned out false. Rāma and Lakshmana cleansed Janasthāna of Rākshasas, found out where I was, and even crossed the Ocean—something no one thought possible—only to die here, in a place where even a cow could walk safely! The sons of Raghu had the weapons of Varuna, Agni, Indra, Vayu, and Brahma. Yet somehow, through some trick, my protectors—Rāma and Lakshmana, both heroes—have been killed. No enemy escapes alive after facing Rāma in battle, not even one as fast as thought. But nothing is too hard for Time, and Death can’t be stopped. Even Rāma and his brother Lakshmana have fallen. But honestly, I don’t mourn so much for Rāma, or for the mighty Lakshmana, or even for myself—as much as I do for my poor mother-in-law. She always hoped for the day when she’d see me and Lakshmana together with Rāma again.”

As Sitā wept, the demoness Trijata spoke gently to her. “Don’t cry, great lady. Your husband is alive. Let me give you some real reasons why I believe Rāma and Lakshmana are still living. When a leader falls in battle, the soldiers either become furious or completely lose hope. But here, the faces of the warriors show neither anger nor despair. And if Rāma and Lakshmana were really dead, this magical chariot—the Pushpaka—wouldn’t even be able to carry you. When an army loses its heroes and chiefs, it becomes like a boat without a captain, drifting and hopeless. But look—these soldiers aren’t panicking or grieving. They’re calmly guarding the princes. I’m telling you this because I care. Take heart, and see for yourself that Rāma and Lakshmana are still alive. I’ve never lied to you before, and I won’t start now, Daughter of Mithilā. You’ve won my affection because of your strength and kindness. Not even the gods and demons led by Indra could defeat those two. That’s why I truly believe they’re alive. And look—this is amazing! They’re lying here, unconscious from the arrows, but their faces don’t look lifeless. Usually the faces of the dead are awful to look at, but these aren’t. So, Janaka’s daughter, don’t let grief and despair take over. Don’t give in to sorrow over Rāma and Lakshmana—you can’t end your life because of this.”

When Sitā, the daughter of Mithilā and beautiful as a goddess, heard Trijata’s words, she folded her hands and said, “I hope you’re right!” Then, turning away, she rode in the Pushpaka chariot—swift as a thought—back into Lankā, with Trijata beside her. Together, they got down from the Pushpaka and, along with the other Rakshasis, entered the Ashoka grove. As she walked into that garden, thick with trees and owned by the demon king, Sitā saw the two princes again, thought of them, and was overcome with a terrible sadness.
The commentator suggests the “ocean” could be symbolic, but that isn’t really necessary.
“And did they not remember this now?” completes the sense.—T.
SECTION XLIX

Rama and Lakshmana, the sons of Dasharatha, lay on the ground, their bodies pierced by arrows and covered in blood. Their breathing was harsh and labored, like wounded snakes. All the leading monkeys, including the powerful Sugriva, stood around them, overwhelmed with grief. Despite being bound by magical arrows, Rama’s strength and resilience helped him regain consciousness. When he saw his brother Lakshmana, wounded, tied down by arrows, and barely conscious, Rama’s heart broke. He began to mourn deeply. “What’s the point of rescuing Sita, or even staying alive, if I have to see my brother defeated and lying here on the battlefield? I might someday meet another woman like Sita, but I’ll never find another brother, comrade, or warrior like Lakshmana. If Sumitra’s beloved son is truly dead, I should give up my own life here in front of the monkeys. What will I say to Kausalya, or to Kaikeyi? How can I face mother Sumitra, waiting anxiously to see her son? If I return without him, how could I comfort her—she’ll be like a cow who’s lost her calf, trembling and heartbroken, like a mourning kurari bird. What will I say to Shatrughna and the noble Bharata—‘He went with me to the forest, but I’ve come back alone’? I can’t bear the thought of mother Sumitra’s anger and grief. So I’ll end my life here; I just can’t go on. Shame on me for being so weak and worthless—for my sake, Lakshmana lies fallen on the battlefield, as if lifeless. Lakshmana, you always comforted me when I was down. But now, you’re gone, and you can’t speak to me in my despair. You, who killed so many Rakshasas in battle, now lie slain yourself, pierced by arrows. Lying here on the field, bleeding and covered in arrows, you look like the sun setting behind the mountains. The shafts piercing your body stop you from speaking, but your face, even silent, shows your pain. Radiant one, just as you followed me into the forest, I’ll follow you now to Yama’s realm. You, who had dear friends and always stood by me, have suffered because of my mistakes. I can’t remember Lakshmana ever speaking harshly, even when he was furious. He could shoot five hundred arrows in a single volley—he was better than Kartavirya at archery. He could match even Indra in battle, yet now that great warrior lies slain on the ground. Rumors and false talk will destroy me for not making Vibhishana king of the Rakshasas. Sugriva, you should leave right now. Because of your loyalty to me, you’re weakened, and Ravana will defeat you. Sugriva, put Angada in charge, gather your troops and supplies, and cross the ocean with Nila and Nala. You’ve accomplished something no one else could have in battle. I’m grateful to the king of bears, the lord of the Golangulas, and Angada, Mainda, and Dwivida have all fought bravely. Kesarin and Sampati have fought fiercely too. Gavaya, Gavaksha, Sarabha, and Gaja—and so many other monkeys—have all fought with a courage few could match, ready to give their lives for me. But Sugriva, no one can fight fate. You, my friend, have done everything you could, out of a sense of duty. And you, noble monkeys, have acted like true friends. With my blessing, you may go wherever you wish.” Hearing Rama’s grief, the monkeys—dark-eyed and others—began to cry as well. At that moment, Vibhishana, carrying a heavy mace, hurried over to Rama to calm the army. But as he approached, looking like a dark storm cloud, the monkeys, mistaking him for Ravana’s son Indrajit, panicked and began to run away.
“Dharma-bhiru,” meaning “fearing righteousness,” usually refers to people who are really afraid of being unrighteous, not of being righteous. It’s an idiom in Sanskrit.—T.
Indrajit. That’s how much fear his terrifying deeds had inspired!—T.
SECTION L

The powerful and energetic king of the monkeys, Sugriva, spoke up: “Why is our army in such chaos, like a boat tossed around by the wind?” When Sugriva said this, Vāli’s son Angada replied, “Don’t you see those two heroes, the sons of Dasaratha—Rama and the mighty Lakshmana—covered in arrows? Look at them, lying on the battlefield, soaked in blood.” Hearing this, Sugriva turned to his son Angada and said, “This isn’t happening for no reason. It must be out of fear. The monkeys all look terrified, running in every direction and leaving their weapons behind. Their eyes are wide with panic. They don’t care what others think, and they don’t look back. They cling to each other, leaping over the fallen as they flee.”

Just then, Bibhishana appeared, holding his mace. He approached Sugriva and Rama, offering blessings for victory. Seeing Bibhishana—who could easily scare the monkeys—Sugriva turned to the king of the bears, Jambavan, and said, “That’s Bibhishana coming this way. The monkeys think he’s Ravana’s son, and they’re panicking because of it. Please calm them down and announce, ‘This is Bibhishana—don’t be afraid.’” Following Sugriva’s orders, Jambavan stopped the fleeing monkeys and reassured them. Once they heard Jambavan and saw Bibhishana, the monkeys calmed down and stopped running.

Bibhishana then saw Rama and Lakshmana, their bodies full of arrows, and was deeply upset. He washed his eyes with water and, overwhelmed with grief, began to cry: “The Rakshasas fought with trickery and have done this to these great heroes—so skilled and strong. My nephew, Ravana’s son, has deceived them with his evil mind. Now, pierced by countless arrows and covered in blood, they lie on the ground like fallen Salyaka trees. I put my hopes in them, but now these great men lie here, having given up their lives. I am left living in misery, my dreams of ruling are gone. Now my enemy Ravana has gotten what he wanted and succeeded.”

While Bibhishana was mourning, Sugriva hugged him and said, “Don’t worry, you know what’s right. You will be king of Lanka—there’s no doubt. Ravana and his sons will fail. Rama and Lakshmana are under Garuda’s protection. They’ll wake up and destroy Ravana and his followers in battle.”

After comforting Bibhishana, Sugriva turned to his father-in-law, Sushena, who was nearby. He said, “When Rama and Lakshmana regain consciousness, take them with some brave monkeys and go back to Kishkindha. I’ll stay here, defeat Ravana and his allies, and rescue Sita—just as Indra recovered the goddess Sri.” Sushena replied, “I once saw the ancient war between the gods and the asuras. The asuras used magic to destroy even the gods, who were skilled fighters. When the gods lost their senses and even their lives, Brihaspati brought them back using mantras and medicines. Let monkeys like Sampati and Panasa hurry to the Milky Ocean to fetch those medicines. The monkeys know about a powerful divine herb, created by the gods themselves, called Vishalya, which can revive the dead. There are mountains named Chandra and Drona, where the gods churned the ocean for nectar; that’s where the best medicine is. Those mountains are hidden in the great ocean. O king, let Hanuman, the son of the Wind-god, go there.”

Meanwhile, a strong wind began to blow, bringing dark clouds and lightning. The wind whipped the waves and shook the mountains. Huge trees on the ocean islands were ripped up and thrown into the salt water by the gale. The snakes living there were terrified, and all the sea creatures dove deep underwater. Suddenly, the monkeys saw Garuda—the son of Vinata—arriving with tremendous strength, blazing like fire. When he appeared, the magical snake-arrows that had bound Rama and Lakshmana tried to slither away.

Garuda (Suparna) landed, bowed to Rama and Lakshmana, and gently touched their faces, which glowed like the moon. As soon as his hands touched them, their wounds healed, their bodies cooled, and their skin glowed with health. They felt a surge of energy, strength, sharper senses, and clearer memories. Then Garuda, powerful as Indra himself, lifted them up and embraced them both with joy.

Rama spoke to Garuda: “Thanks to your help, we survived the disaster caused by Ravana’s son. You’ve made us strong again. My heart is filled with happiness to see you—like seeing my father Dasaratha or my grandfather Aja. Who are you, so beautiful and noble, wearing garlands and perfumes, dressed in spotless clothes and fine jewelry?”

Garuda answered, his eyes sparkling, “Rama of the Kakutstha line, I am your friend—I am Garutman, your life’s guardian, come to help you. Not the mighty asuras, the strongest monkeys, or even the gods and Gandharvas led by Indra, could have freed you from these magical bonds of arrows, created by Indrajit’s illusions. These snakes, born of Kadru, are deadly and venomous; they became arrows through his magic and bound you. Rama, you are truly fortunate—and so is Lakshmana, your loyal brother. When I heard what happened, I rushed here and freed you out of friendship. But you must always be careful. The Rakshasas are naturally tricky fighters, and though you are brave and good-hearted, you rely on your honesty alone. So don’t trust the Rakshasas in battle. Remember how they fooled you this time—they always fight with deception.”

After saying this, the mighty Garuda embraced Rama again and said, “My friend Raghava, even though you’re kind to your enemies, let me go now. Don’t ask about our friendship—you’ll understand everything once you’ve won this war. When you’ve defeated Ravana and his army and taken back Sita, then you’ll know the truth about us.” Then, Garuda, swift as the wind, circled Rama and Lakshmana, embraced them, and soared into the sky, covering it like a cloud.

Seeing Rama and Lakshmana restored, the monkey leaders roared like lions and waved their tails in excitement. Drums and kettle-drums boomed, conch shells blared, and everyone shouted in joy. Some monkeys slapped their arms in challenge. Armed with trees, hundreds and thousands of monkeys got ready for battle. Their thunderous roars scared the Rakshasas, and, eager to fight, the monkeys advanced to the gates of Lanka. The noise they made was like the wildest storm clouds rumbling at midnight at the end of summer.
Note: Angada was Sugriva’s step-son, since Sugriva married Angada’s mother after Rama killed Vali in Kishkindha.
Note: Salyaka is a type of tree.
Note: Refers to Rama and Lakshmana.

[159]  
That is, how their friendship began.
SECTION LI

Ravana heard a wild uproar echoing across the battlefield—the monkeys were roaring along with the Rakshasas, their voices blending into a deep, thunderous noise. The sound filled the air like storm clouds rolling in, and even the ocean seemed disturbed by it. In the middle of his council, Ravana said, "Listen to those roars—so many monkeys, all sounding like thunder. They're definitely celebrating something. But why? Rama and Lakshmana are supposed to be tightly bound by Indrajit’s powerful arrows. This noise is making me uneasy." He turned to the demons (Nairitas) nearby and ordered, "Go quickly and find out why the monkeys are celebrating at a time like this." The Nairitas rushed to the city wall and looked out over Sugriva’s army. There, they saw Rama and Lakshmana—no longer trapped by the magical arrows, but standing free and strong, having broken their bonds. The Nairitas’ faces drained of color and, looking shaken, they hurried back to Ravana to report what they’d seen. With grim expressions, they told him, "Rama and Lakshmana, who were pinned down by Indrajit’s arrows and completely immobilized, are now free. They’re standing in the middle of the battlefield, as strong as ever—like elephants that have snapped their chains." Hearing this, Ravana’s anxiety and anger flared. His face turned pale with worry. He thought, "Indrajit’s arrows—deadly, unstoppable, like venomous snakes and as powerful as the sun—were supposed to keep them down. If my enemies can break out of those bonds, then all my strength means nothing. Those arrows, meant to kill, have failed." Furious, Ravana hissed like an angry serpent and called out to a Rakshasa named Dhumraksha. "Dhumraksha," he said, "take a huge force and go destroy Rama and the monkeys." Dhumraksha accepted the command and left the king’s palace. He hurried out through the city gate and called to the commander of the army, "Move your troops out now! Why wait? Warriors don’t hesitate." At his command, the troops prepared for battle. The Rakshasas—fierce, energetic, and armed with bells on their arms—cheered loudly and gathered around Dhumraksha. They carried all kinds of terrifying weapons: darts, clubs, maces, spears, iron rods, axes, and more. The Rakshasa army poured out of the city, roaring like storm clouds. Many rode in armored chariots, decorated with banners and gold, pulled by mules with strange faces, quick horses, and huge, wild elephants. The Nairitas looked as fierce and unstoppable as tigers. Dhumraksha climbed into his impressive chariot, decorated with gold and shaped with lion and deer faces, its wheels rattling loudly. He led his troops out through the Western Entrance, straight toward Hanuman’s position. As Dhumraksha’s chariot rolled out, ominous signs appeared: birds filled the air, shrieking and blocking his path. A huge, terrifying vulture landed on top of his chariot, and others circled above, dropping down around his banner. Suddenly, a headless corpse crashed to the ground in front of Dhumraksha, and blood rained from the sky as the earth shook. The wind howled like thunder, and darkness swallowed the horizon. Seeing these terrifying omens, Dhumraksha felt dread, and the Rakshasas marching with him were stunned with fear. Still, determined to fight, Dhumraksha led his army out of the city. Ahead of him, he saw the massive monkey army, protected by Rama—their numbers like a vast ocean at the end of the world.
Indra—the one who commands the clouds.
SECTION LII

When the Rākshasa Dhumrāksha, known for his terrifying strength, appeared on the battlefield, the monkeys erupted in loud, excited cheers, eager to fight. What followed was a brutal clash: both sides charged with weapons—trees, spears, maces—anything they could wield. The Rākshasas began to scatter the monkeys, striking them down, but the monkeys hit back, knocking down Rākshasas with huge branches. Enraged, the Rākshasas shot sharp arrows tipped with Kanka feathers at the monkeys. The monkeys, wounded by clubs, darts, daggers, maces, and strange bludgeons, grew even angrier and fought back with incredible bravery. Monkey leaders, their bodies pierced and bleeding from arrows and darts, grabbed trees and boulders as weapons.

The monkeys, full of wild energy, shouted their names as they hurled themselves at the Rākshasa ranks, throwing rocks and trees in every direction. The battle grew even fiercer, with both sides suffering heavy losses. Some Rākshasas, bloodthirsty by nature, coughed up blood as the monkeys attacked. Others were cut along their sides, smashed by trees, crushed under boulders, or bitten in the frenzy. Some Rākshasas were killed by falling standards and swords, and some were trampled by their own war-carts. The battlefield was soon littered with enormous elephants, toppled mountain peaks, dead horses, and their riders—all crushed by the monkeys.

The monkeys, leaping around with wild strength, tore at the Rākshasas with their claws, especially targeting their mouths. Covered in blood and with their hair in disarray, many Rākshasas staggered and fell. Other Rākshasas, burning with anger and gifted with great strength, hit the monkeys with slaps as hard as thunderbolts. The monkeys, just as fierce, knocked down Rākshasas with fists, feet, and teeth, and some Rākshasas were killed by being struck with trees.

When he saw his own troops fleeing, Dhumrāksha—the fiercest of the Rākshasas—became furious and threw himself into the fight, leading a new attack against the monkeys. Some monkeys, badly wounded by sharp spears, started bleeding; others, hit by heavy maces, collapsed. Some were beaten down with clubs, some cut by flying blades, and some lost their lives to deadly darts. The ground became soaked in monkey blood, and some monkeys who tried to run were cut down by the furious Rākshasas. Some lay on their sides with wounds in their chests; others had been stabbed with tridents, their insides spilling out. The battle was a nightmare of violence, fought with every weapon, rock, and tree imaginable.

The chaos of battle was like a wild, disturbing concert: the twang of bowstrings sounded like a musical instrument, the neighing of horses kept the rhythm, and the cries of Mainda elephants were the melody. In the middle of it all, Dhumrāksha, laughing with his bow in hand, chased the monkeys everywhere, sending arrows flying.

Seeing the monkey army in trouble and pushed to their limits by Dhumrāksha, Hanumān—the son of the Wind-god (Vāyu)—became furious. His eyes burning red with rage, he grabbed a massive boulder and charged at Dhumrāksha. Hanumān, as strong as his divine father, hurled the huge rock at Dhumrāksha’s chariot.

Dhumrāksha, seeing the boulder coming, quickly grabbed his mace, jumped down from his chariot, and landed on the ground. The boulder crashed down, smashing the chariot to pieces. Chariot wheels, decorations, and banners flew everywhere, and Dhumrāksha’s bow was left behind. Now weaponless, Dhumrāksha faced Hanumān, who seized trees of all sizes and started mowing down the Rākshasas.

Some Rākshasas had their heads smashed and lay in pools of blood; others, hit with tree branches, fell to the ground. Hanumān, unstoppable, stormed through the Rākshasa army, grabbed a mountain peak, and charged straight at Dhumrāksha. As Hanumān came at him, Dhumrāksha raised his mace, roared, and rushed forward to meet him.

Dhumrāksha, furious, slammed his mace—covered in sharp spikes—down on Hanumān’s head. But Hanumān, filled with the power of the wind, barely noticed the blow. He immediately smashed the mountain peak down on Dhumrāksha’s head. Hit by the massive rock, Dhumrāksha’s entire body was crushed, and he dropped dead to the earth, as if a mountain had collapsed.

When Dhumrāksha was killed, the surviving Rākshasas panicked. They ran back into Lankā, chased by the victorious monkeys. Hanumān, exhausted but triumphant, having caused rivers of blood to flow on the battlefield, was honored and celebrated by the other monkeys for his heroic victory.
The reader will notice that Vālmīki, like Vyāsa in the Mahābhārata, loves to spin out elaborate similes—but the comparisons don’t always line up neatly, as we see here.
The Vinā is a classical Indian stringed instrument, with metal strings and gourds as soundboxes.
Mainda here refers to a type of elephant.
SECTION LIII

When Dhumraksha was killed, Ravana—the king of the Rakshasas (demons)—was consumed by intense rage. He breathed heavily, like an angry snake, his face dark with anger. After fuming for a while, he called for Vajradanshtra (Thunder-Tooth), a fierce and incredibly strong Rakshasa. “Go,” Ravana ordered him, “Take a group of Rakshasas with you. Kill Dasaratha’s son, Rama, and Sugriva, along with their monkey allies.” Vajradanshtra immediately agreed, replying, “As you wish.” Skilled in magic and illusions, he prepared for battle, gathering many Rakshasa army leaders, along with elephants, horses, mules, and camels. His mind was focused and determined, and their troops were decorated with countless bright flags and banners. Under his white umbrella, like the moon, he stands out, wearing a crown and shining earrings, his body as massive as the Vindhya mountains. He’s humbled even Indra and Yama and shines like the sun.”

Rama, the enemy of evil, replied to Vibhishana, “Ravana is incredibly radiant—too bright to look at directly, like the sun. I can’t see him clearly because of his own brilliance. His warriors look like mountains, fighting with boulders and blazing weapons. Surrounded by fearsome spirits with terrifying forms, Ravana appears as imposing as Death itself. At least today that villain has shown himself to me, and now I can finally unleash my anger for what he did to Sita.” Rama, determined and followed by Lakshmana, took up his bow and drew a powerful arrow, ready for battle.

At that moment, Ravana addressed his massive army: “Don’t be afraid—hold your ground at the city gates, crossroads, and buildings in Lanka. If you’ve all left the city with me, the monkeys might take advantage and seize the empty city—don’t let that happen.” After giving these orders, Ravana left his counselors, and as the Rakshasas followed his commands, he plunged into the monkey army like a giant fish diving into stormy waves.

Seeing Ravana, armed with a blazing bow and arrows, charging forward, the monkey king Sugriva ripped a huge mountain peak from the earth and hurled it at the Rakshasa king. The mountain, covered in trees, flew through the air, but Ravana shot it apart with his golden-tipped arrows before it could hit him. The shattered pieces crashed to the ground. Then Ravana picked up an arrow that looked like a giant serpent, glowing with a deadly light, and flung it at Sugriva with all his rage. The arrow struck Sugriva—who was as tough as Indra’s thunderbolt—piercing him deeply. Sugriva, overcome with pain, collapsed to the ground, crying out in agony. The Rakshasas cheered when they saw him fall.

Gavaksha, Gavaya, Sushena, Rishabha, Jyotimukha, and Nala—great monkey warriors—rushed at Ravana, hurling rocks and growing to massive size. But Ravana shot down their attacks with hundreds of razor-sharp arrows. He wounded the leading monkeys with showers of arrows tipped with gold, covering the monkey army in a deadly net of shafts. Overwhelmed and wounded, the monkeys cried out and fled to Rama, seeking his protection.

Rama, the heroic archer, grabbed his bow and rushed forward. Lakshmana came to him and, with hands pressed in respect, said, “Let me take care of that villain, Ravana. Please, let me go and destroy him.” Rama, full of strength and always truthful, replied, “Go ahead, Lakshmana—do your best. Ravana is extremely powerful and his skill in battle is amazing. When he’s angry, no one in all three worlds can resist him. Watch for his weaknesses, just as you’d guard against your own. Always stay alert—protect yourself with both your eyes and your bow.” Hearing Rama’s words, Lakshmana embraced his brother, bowed, and went out to face Ravana.

Lakshmana found Ravana, who had arms like elephant trunks, wielding a fearsome, flaming bow and firing arrows into the monkey ranks. Hanuman, son of the Wind-god, saw Ravana’s barrage and charged at him, deflecting the arrows with his own strength. Hanuman leapt onto Ravana’s chariot, raised his right arm, and shouted, “You can’t be killed by gods, demons, or spirits—but now you’ll know fear, brought to you by monkeys. My hand, with its five fingers, will end your life today.” Ravana, his eyes burning with rage, shouted back, “Come on, monkey! Fight without fear and win your fame. I’ll test your strength and then finish you.” Hanuman replied, “Don’t forget your son Aksha—I killed him, remember?” Enraged, Ravana slapped Hanuman hard. Hanuman staggered but quickly recovered and struck Ravana back with a powerful slap. The ten-headed king shook like a mountain in an earthquake. The gods, saints, and demons watching from above cheered when Hanuman landed his blow.

Regaining his balance, Ravana said, “Well done, monkey. You’re a worthy opponent.” Hanuman replied, “I’m ashamed of my strength, since you’re still standing, Ravana. Come on, hit me again—let’s see who falls first.” Furious, Ravana carefully made a fist and smashed Hanuman in the chest. Hanuman shook from the blow but stood his ground. Seeing Hanuman stunned, Ravana climbed back onto his chariot and attacked Nila, the monkey general, with a rain of arrows that pierced deep like snakes.

Nila, wounded but fierce, grabbed a mountain top with one hand and hurled it at Ravana. Hanuman, having recovered, watched the fight and thought, “It’s not right for me to attack Ravana while he’s fighting Nila.” Ravana, using seven sharp arrows, broke the mountain into pieces before it could hit him. Nila, enraged, attacked with flowering ashvattha trees, sal trees, mango trees, and more. Ravana shot down the flying trees with his arrows and poured another storm of arrows at Nila, the son of the Fire-god.

Hit by a terrifying hail of arrows, Nila shrank himself and leapt onto Ravana’s banner. Ravana was furious at seeing the monkey on his banner, and Nila shouted in defiance. The monkey jumped from the banner to Ravana’s bow, then to the crest of his crown, moving so quickly that Lakshmana, Hanuman, and Rama were amazed. Ravana himself was shocked by Nila’s agility and grabbed a blazing weapon to strike back. The monkeys, seeing Ravana confused, cheered even louder. Ravana, angered by their shouts and agitated, struggled to focus. He finally drew a fiery arrow and aimed it at Nila.

Ravana taunted Nila, “You’re quick because of your magic, but if you can, save yourself now. You may change shapes, but this arrow will end your life.” With that, Ravana fired the arrow at Nila’s chest. Nila, hit and burning with pain, crashed to the ground but, thanks to his father’s power and his own strength, landed on his knees rather than dying.

Seeing Nila stunned, Ravana, eager for battle, rode his thunderous chariot straight at Lakshmana. Ravana stood ready, stretching his bow, blazing with power. Lakshmana called out, “Fight me, Ravana! Leave the monkeys alone and face me!” Hearing Lakshmana’s challenge and the ominous twang of his bowstring, Ravana approached, angry. He said, “You’re lucky, son of Raghu, that fate has brought you here. In a moment, my arrows will send you to the land of the dead.”

Lakshmana, unfazed by Ravana’s power, replied, “True strength doesn’t need loud boasting. I know your power and energy, Ravana, but here I am, bow and arrows ready. Stop bragging and fight me.” Enraged, Ravana fired seven arrows, but Lakshmana split them with his own golden-tipped arrows. As Ravana’s arrows were destroyed like cut snakes, he grew even angrier and shot more sharp weapons. Lakshmana replied with a rain of deadly arrows—razor-sharp, crescent-shaped, and barbed—destroying Ravana’s attacks in midair. Ravana was amazed that his arrows were being stopped so easily and redoubled his efforts, shooting even more powerful arrows.

Lakshmana, like Indra himself, fired a volley of flaming, thunderbolt-like arrows to destroy Ravana. Ravana cut down these arrows and hit Lakshmana in the forehead with a blazing arrow, a weapon given to him by Brahma. Lakshmana staggered from the pain, nearly dropping his bow, but after a moment, he shook off the agony and cut Ravana’s bow in half. Lakshmana then wounded Ravana with three sharp arrows, and the king, hit hard, struggled to stay conscious. Ravana, now bleeding and furious, grabbed a magical dart given by Brahma, his body drenched in blood from the wounds.

Ravana hurled the blazing, terrifying dart at Lakshmana, who tried to stop it with his own arrows. Still, the dart pierced Lakshmana’s broad arm, burning him. Though Lakshmana was incredibly strong, the wound made him glow with pain. Ravana rushed to grab him, but even with all his strength—enough to lift mountains or even the whole world—he couldn’t move Lakshmana. Struck in the chest by Brahma’s dart, Lakshmana remembered that he was truly an aspect of Vishnu. Ravana tried to overpower him, but couldn’t budge him.

Then Hanuman, consumed by rage, charged at Ravana and smashed him in the chest with a punch like a thunderbolt. Ravana dropped to his knees, blood gushing from his mouths, eyes, and arms. He sat dazed on his chariot, not knowing where he was. The gods, saints, and demons cheered to see Ravana—who had terrified even the gods—brought low.

Hanuman gently picked up the wounded Lakshmana and carried him to Rama. Though Lakshmana could not be moved by enemies, he became light as a feather for Hanuman out of friendship and respect. The magical dart withdrew from Lakshmana’s body and returned to Ravana’s chariot.

Ravana, regaining his senses, took up a new sharp bow and arrows. Lakshmana, now fully healed and remembering his divine nature, stood ready for battle again. Seeing his monkey army and heroes battered and wounded, Rama rushed at Ravana.

Hanuman came up to Rama and said, “Climb on my back and take the fight to Ravana, just like Vishnu rides Garuda to battle the enemies of the gods.” Rama agreed, mounted Hanuman, and faced off against Ravana, just as Vishnu once attacked the demon king Virochana’s son. Rama’s bowstring thundered, echoing like a crashing storm, as he called out to Ravana: “Don’t run, Ravana! After all you’ve done to me, where do you think you can escape? Even if you flee to Yama, Indra, the Sun, Brahma, Agni, Shiva, or the farthest corners of the world, you won’t find safety. Lakshmana has been wounded and knocked down, but today death will come for you and your sons and grandsons. I’ve already killed fourteen thousand Rakshasas at Janasthana—are you ready to join them?”

Ravana, burning with rage and remembering his old hatred, shot flaming arrows at Hanuman, who was carrying Rama. But Hanuman’s strength only grew as he was struck, his natural power undiminished. Rama, furious at seeing Hanuman wounded, rushed at Ravana. With razor-sharp arrows, Rama destroyed Ravana’s chariot, wheels, horses, banner, umbrella, streamer, charioteer, and weapons all at once. Then, like Indra splitting a mountain with his thunderbolt, Rama struck Ravana’s chest with a mighty arrow.

Ravana, who had never flinched at the thunderbolt before, now shook and dropped his bow, overwhelmed by Rama’s attack. Rama then took a sharp crescent-shaped arrow and sliced off Ravana’s shining crown. Ravana, suddenly stripped of his glory, looked weak and diminished, like a snake without its venom or the sun hidden by clouds. Rama called out, “You’ve fought bravely and killed many of my best warriors, but now I see you’re exhausted. That’s why I won’t kill you now. Go back to Lanka and rest—get your strength back. Come face me again with your full power, and then you’ll truly see what I can do.” Ravana, his pride shattered, his chariot and bow destroyed, his body wounded, and his crown broken, quickly retreated into Lanka.

As Ravana—the terror of gods and demons alike—returned to his city, Rama healed Lakshmana and the monkey warriors. The gods, spirits, and all creatures celebrated Ravana’s defeat, and even the oceans and animals of earth and water rejoiced.
SECTION LX

Ravana, the king of Lanka, entered his city in fear, his pride shattered by Rama’s arrows. He was deeply troubled, feeling like an elephant defeated by a lion or a serpent crushed by Garuda. The memory of Rama’s arrows—flashing like comets at the end of the world, crackling with lightning—haunted him. Seated on his magnificent golden throne, Ravana looked at the Rakshasas and spoke bitterly: “All my years of strict ascetic practices seem worthless now. Though I once thought myself like mighty Indra, I’ve been beaten by a mere human. I recall what Brahma told me: ‘Your greatest threat will come from a man. You cannot be killed by gods, demons, spirits, giants, or serpents—but you never asked for protection from humans.’ I realize now that Rama, son of Dasaratha, is the one I should have feared all along. I also remember the curse Anaranya of the Ikshwaku line gave me: ‘O worst of Rakshasas, someone from my lineage will destroy you and your family, your army, and your charioteers.’ There was also the curse from Vedavati, whom I once wronged—she may have been reborn as Sita, the noble daughter of Janaka. Other curses, too—those from Uma, Nandishvara, Rambha, and Varuna’s daughter—are now coming true. Given all this, we must fight with everything we have. Post guards at every gate, road, and wall. And wake up Kumbhakarna—the one who humbles gods and demons alike, the one with unmatched strength, though now sleeping under Brahma’s curse.” Now, with his own defeat and the death of Prahasta weighing on him, Ravana gave firm orders to his terrifying troops: “Guard the gates and walls with vigilance. Wake Kumbhakarna—he’s lost in pleasure and oblivious, sleeping soundly. He sometimes sleeps for nine, seven, ten, or eight months at a time. Now, after nine months, the mightiest of all Rakshasas in battle is still slumbering. If he wakes, he’ll slaughter the monkeys and the princes in no time. He is our champion, the pride of the Rakshasas. But he’s always lost in indulgence and heavy sleep. Rama has beaten me in fierce battle, but once Kumbhakarna wakes, my grief will fade. If he won’t help me now, when I need him most—what good is his strength, even if it matches Indra’s?” 

Hearing Ravana’s words, the Rakshasas quickly made their way to Kumbhakarna’s dwelling. Eager to please Ravana, these flesh-eating demons brought perfumes, garlands, and piles of food. They entered Kumbhakarna’s vast and fragrant cave—so large its entrance spanned a yojana. Even Kumbhakarna’s breath was so powerful it nearly blew them back, but they gathered their courage and pressed on inside. The golden and gem-studded floors sparkled as the strong Rakshasas found Kumbhakarna lying there, a mountain of a being, deep in sleep. They tried to wake the sleeping giant, whose body bristled with hair, who lay sprawled like a massive serpent, his breath so strong it could bowl people over. His nose was enormous, his size nearly as big as the underworld itself, his body stretched long, stinking of blood and fat, adorned with golden armlets and a sun-bright crown. There he was: Kumbhakarna, enemy-crusher and the mightiest of Rakshasas.

To wake him, they piled up mountains of animals—deer, buffaloes, boars—hoping to tempt him. They heaped up rice and set out jars of blood and all sorts of foods before him, anointed him with fine sandalwood, and filled the cave with delicious scents and incense smoke. They sang his praises and roared like thunderclouds, blowing their conch shells until the cave echoed. The Rakshasas shouted in unison, slapped their arms, and tugged at him, making a racket that shook the very heavens. Birds dropped from the sky at the noise of conches, drums, and wild shouting. But even all this couldn’t wake Kumbhakarna.

Desperate, the Rakshasas grabbed heavy clubs and mountain-sized maces. They struck his chest with all their might, but even then, his breath was so fierce they could hardly stand near him. Tightening their belts, the Rakshasas played drums and blew conches louder than ever. Ten thousand of them surrounded Kumbhakarna, shouting and hitting him, but he still didn’t stir. Frustrated, they tried even harder: they hit him with horses, camels, mules, snakes, rods, whips, and hooks—anything that came to hand—and banged on all kinds of drums and instruments. They even bashed him with massive logs. Still, he slept on.

Finally, they sounded a thousand kettle-drums with golden sticks, filling all of Lanka with the noise, but the curse kept Kumbhakarna in his deep sleep. Furious, the Rakshasas grew even more determined. Some beat drums and shouted, others cut his hair or bit his ears. Some poured buckets of water into his ears. But Kumbhakarna, under the spell of powerful sleep, didn’t even twitch. Others stabbed him with daggers and clubs, but it was useless—even when they tied sharp weapons to ropes and hit him, he did not wake. At last, a thousand elephants were driven to trample him, and battered by mountain-peaks and trees, Kumbhakarna finally stirred. Yawning and starving after his long sleep, he woke up.

Kumbhakarna looked monstrous as he stretched and yawned, arms as strong as thunderbolts, mouth gaping wide like a cave, his breath roaring like a mountain storm. Sitting up, he looked like the god of destruction at the end of time, ready to devour the world. His eyes blazed like fire and lightning. The Rakshasas pointed out the piles of food—bears, buffaloes, and more—and Kumbhakarna began to eat, gulping down flesh and drinking blood to satisfy his hunger and thirst. Sated, the night-rangers circled him, bowing their heads.

Still drowsy, with red, half-closed eyes, Kumbhakarna looked around and spoke to the Rakshasas: “Why have you woken me up so suddenly? Is the king all right? Is there some grave danger threatening us, or is it something else? Speak honestly—no one wakes me for something trivial. I’ll tear out the root of any threat to the Rakshasa king today. I could even crush mighty Indra, or make Fire itself go cold. Tell me the real reason you woke me.”

A minister named Yupaksha, hands folded, answered the furious giant: “No, Lord, we’re not afraid of gods or demons right now. The danger comes from a human. We’ve never feared gods, demons, or giants as much as we fear this man. Lanka is now surrounded by monkeys as tall as mountains. Rama’s fury—after Sita was taken—burns us all. Already, a single monkey burned our city. Prince Aksha was killed, along with his troops and elephants. Ravana himself, who was more dangerous than any god or demon, was beaten and spared by Rama. What the gods and demons couldn’t do, Rama has done—he brought Ravana to the brink of death.”

Hearing this, and learning of his brother’s defeat, Kumbhakarna’s eyes spun with anger as he thundered, “Today, Yupaksha, I’ll destroy the monkey army in battle, along with Lakshmana and Rama. I’ll feed the Rakshasas with monkey flesh, and drink the blood of Rama and Lakshmana myself.”

As Kumbhakarna boasted, Mahodara, another top Rakshasa soldier, respectfully said, “O mighty one, first listen to Ravana and consider his words before you rush into battle.”

Hearing Mahodara’s advice, Kumbhakarna—fierce and ready for war—prepared to go, surrounded by Rakshasas. Now fully awake, the Rakshasas quickly brought him to Ravana’s palace. There, bowing before the Ten-Headed King, they announced, “Lord, your brother Kumbhakarna is awake. Should he come to you, or do you want him to march straight to battle?” Ravana, delighted, replied, “I want to see him here—welcome him with honor.” The Rakshasas hurried back to Kumbhakarna and said, “The king wishes to see you—go and make your brother happy.” Kumbhakarna, unstoppable and brimming with power, agreed and got up. After washing and bathing, feeling refreshed and in high spirits, he asked the Rakshasas to bring him a strong drink. At Ravana’s command, they brought wine and many different foods. Kumbhakarna drank two thousand vessels of wine, and, now flushed and fired up, looked as terrifying as Yama, the god of death.

With his army behind him, Kumbhakarna marched to Ravana’s palace, shaking the earth with every step. He lit up the streets with his sheer size and brilliance, like the sun itself. As he moved, surrounded by Rakshasas, he looked like Indra going to meet Brahma. The monkeys outside the city, seeing this mountain-sized, crown-wearing giant, were terrified. Some ran to Rama for protection, some fainted, some fled in every direction, and others simply collapsed in fear. Kumbhakarna looked so massive and powerful, as if he could reach up and touch the sun, that the monkey warriors scattered in panic.
Punjikasthala.

Punjikasthala cursed Ravana that he would die if he ever assaulted a woman against her will. Rambha herself didn’t curse Ravana, but Nala Kuvera did, on her behalf: “If you ever force a woman, your head will split into seven.” Uma cursed him that he would die for a woman, when Mount Kailasa shook. Nandishvara cursed him—since Ravana insulted him—that monkeys (his own emanations) would be the cause of his death.—T.
Kumbhakarna represents raw physical power, in contrast to Rama’s spiritual strength.—T.
A type of mace.
Another reading: “then they filled the cave to capacity.”—T.
Brahma’s curse is explained later.—T.
What does this mean?
Literally, “him of a hundred sacrifices”—a title for Indra.—T.
SECTION LXI

Rāma, strong and full of energy, picked up his bow and caught sight of Kumbhakarna—towering, crowned, and massive. The mighty Rākshasa looked like a living mountain, his huge form filling the sky, just as Nārāyana once had. His dark skin was like rain clouds, and his arms were decorated with golden armlets. The sight of him was so terrifying that the entire monkey army panicked and fled in all directions. Rāma, surprised to see his troops scatter and this gigantic Rākshasa growing closer, turned to Bibhishana. “Who is that with tawny eyes and a crown, looking like a living cliff? In Lankā he stands out like a thundercloud lit by lightning, and just his presence sends my army running. Is he a Raksha or an Asura? I’ve never seen anything like him before.” Bibhishana, wise and calm, replied to Rāma, “That’s Kumbhakarna, son of Viçravān. He’s the one who once defeated Yama (the son of Vivasvat) and even Indra himself (Vāsava) in battle. No Rākshasa is his equal in size or strength. He’s brought down Dānavas, Yakshas, Nagas (serpent beings), flesh-eaters, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Pannagas by the thousands. Even the gods, seeing his strength, have compared him to Death itself and failed to defeat him. Kumbhakarna is powerful by nature—other Rākshasas rely on boons, but his strength is his own. When he was just a baby, he devoured thousands of creatures. Terrified, the survivors ran to Indra for help. Indra got furious and struck Kumbhakarna with his thunderbolt, but even that only made Kumbhakarna roar in anger. The sound shook everyone with fear. Then, still raging, Kumbhakarna ripped a tusk off Airāvata, Indra’s elephant, and hurled it at Indra, wounding him. Covered in blood, Indra looked like he was on fire, and all the gods, sages, and Dānavas were shaken. They went to Brahma, the creator, begging him to stop Kumbhakarna before he ate all living things, destroyed holy places, and violated other men’s wives. ‘If he keeps this up, the world will be empty soon,’ they said. Brahma summoned the Rākshasas and brought Kumbhakarna before him. The creator, Prajāpati, was actually afraid when he saw him. Calming Kumbhakarna down, Brahma said, ‘You were born to Paulasta to wreak havoc on the world. From now on, you’ll sleep as if dead.’ Hit by Brahma’s curse, Kumbhakarna collapsed. Ravana, frantic, pleaded, ‘You’re cutting down a golden tree just as it’s about to bear fruit. Please, Lord, don’t curse your own grandson like this. Your words always come true, but at least set a schedule for his sleep and waking.’ Brahma agreed, ‘He’ll sleep for six months, then wake for one day. On that day, driven by hunger, he’ll roam the earth like a raging wildfire, devouring everything in his path.’ Now, with your attack on Lankā, Ravana—scared of your power—has woken Kumbhakarna. Furious and starving, he’s come out of his camp and started eating monkeys. When the monkeys see him, they panic and run. There’s no way they can face him in battle while he’s this angry. Tell them that Kumbhakarna is like a giant weapon—if they understand this, they won’t lose hope.” Rāma listened carefully to Bibhishana’s advice. Then he called out to Nila, the general, “You monkeys—grab your weapons, carry mountain peaks, trees, and rocks. Hold your ground on main roads and bridges!” Following his orders, Nila rallied the monkey troops. Givāksha, Sarabha, Hanumān, and Angada—all as impressive as mountain peaks themselves—picked up boulders and headed for the gate. Energized by Rāma’s words, the monkeys grew bold and charged the enemy, swinging trees like clubs. The monkey army, brandishing huge rocks and tree trunks, looked like a rolling storm of dark clouds moving down the mountainside.
Yama—son of Vivasvat, or the Sun.
Bhujangas: semi-divine serpent beings.
Semi-divine serpents.
By reciting a special mantra.
SECTION LXII
Literally, lord of creatures.
Viçravā.
Meaning, “that is a giant weapon.”
