Kumbhakarna, the fierce and powerful Rākshasa, was still half-asleep as he made his way down the beautiful main road. Surrounded by thousands of Rākshasas, he marched on, while flowers rained down on him from the houses nearby. Soon, he reached the magnificent and elegant palace of the Rākshasa king, shining with golden decorations and as bright as the sun. Entering his brother’s mansion—like the sun disappearing into a thick cloud—he saw his older brother, Rāvana, sitting at a distance, just as Indra might see Brahma sitting in his own brilliance. Kumbhakarna, with a crowd of Rākshasas around him, entered Rāvana’s home so heavily that the ground seemed to shake with each step. Passing through the entrance, he found Rāvana anxiously seated on the Pushpaka chariot. When Rāvana saw Kumbhakarna approaching, the ten-headed king was overjoyed. He got up, greeted his brother warmly, and pulled him close. Kumbhakarna, incredibly strong, bowed at Rāvana’s feet and asked, “What’s going on?” Delighted, Rāvana jumped up and hugged his brother again. After this greeting, Kumbhakarna sat down on a brilliant, luxurious seat set out for him. Looking at Rāvana with eyes still red from sleep and irritation, Kumbhakarna said, “Brother, why did you wake me up with such respect? What’s got you so worried? And who’s supposed to be a ghost?”

At this, Rāvana became angry, his eyes wide with rage, and said to Kumbhakarna, who was sitting in front of him, “You’ve been asleep for a really long time, and because of that, you don’t know about the huge threat I’m facing from Rāma. Rāma, the strong and noble son of Daśaratha, has crossed the ocean with Sugriva, and together they’re destroying our people. Look around: Lankā’s forests are now flooded with an army of monkeys who crossed over easily by building a bridge. Our best Rākshasa fighters have already been killed by these monkeys, but I haven’t seen the monkeys suffer any serious losses. In fact, our Rākshasas have never managed to defeat them in battle. That’s why I’m so afraid. Please, you’re incredibly powerful—help me. Destroy these enemies. That’s why I woke you. Do this for me, your brother, who has nothing left—our treasury is empty, and only the very young and the very old are left in Lankā. Please, use your strength to help your brother now. I’ve never asked you for something like this before. I care about you deeply, and I truly believe you can succeed. You’ve defeated countless gods in battles against the celestials and Asuras, so I know what you’re capable of. Now, summon all your power. There’s no one in the world who can match your strength. You love battle, and you’re always there for your friends—so please, do this for me. Use your incredible power to crush the enemy army, just like a strong wind tears away clouds in autumn.”
Killed by me.
SECTION LXIII

Hearing Ravana’s (the king of the Rakshasas) desperate complaints, Kumbhakarna couldn’t help but laugh. “Brother,” he said, “this disaster is exactly what we warned you about in that council meeting. You ignored what was truly good for you, and now you’re paying the price—just like someone who does wrong and then faces the consequences. At first, mighty king, you didn’t think through your actions. Your pride blinded you to the risks. When someone does things in the wrong order—handling last things first and first things last—it shows a lack of good judgment. Actions taken without considering the right time and place just lead to trouble, like pouring clarified butter into a fire that hasn’t been properly prepared. The wise ruler listens to his advisors and carefully weighs the five factors and the three strategies before acting. A king who acts after thoughtful discussion, who knows how to separate friends from enemies, and who chooses the right time to pursue justice, gain, or pleasure—whether separately or together—truly understands how to rule. But a king or crown prince who hears about these principles but doesn’t understand them has wasted his education. The ruler who controls himself and regularly talks over things with his counselors—discussing generosity, patience, division, strength, as well as duty, profit, and desire—won’t face disaster. When a king can see the likely outcome of his actions and consults wise, insightful advisors, he prospers. But people who don’t really understand the scriptures or the meaning behind things—those who just talk to hear themselves speak—shouldn’t be listened to, even if their advice is relevant. Advisors who recklessly recommend harmful ideas as if they’re helpful are dangerous and should be dismissed. There are also counselors who betray their masters by siding with clever enemies, working against their own king’s interests. During discussions, a wise king should recognize these false friends who have been bought off by the enemy. Just as birds exploit a hole in the mountain Krauncha, enemies easily take advantage of a reckless leader who acts without thinking. Disregarding your enemies and failing to protect yourself always leads to disaster and loss of power. Even your favorite queen, Mandodari, and my younger brother gave advice that would have helped us. Now, do what you think is best.” 

When Ravana heard Kumbhakarna’s words, he frowned, furious. He shot back, “You should treat me with respect, like someone superior. Why waste time with all this talk? Do what needs to be done. There’s no use bringing up what I did in the past—whether it was out of foolishness, pride, or simply being lost. Let’s focus on what’s right for now. If you care about me, if you’re as strong as you say, and if you think my cause matters to you, then use your power to help me recover from this mess I’ve made. True friends help each other when they’re in trouble or have gone astray; that’s what it means to be loyal.” As Ravana spoke in a calm but harsh tone, Kumbhakarna realized his brother was actually pleased and decided to answer more gently.

Kumbhakarna saw how upset Ravana was and tried to comfort him. “Listen to me carefully, my king,” he said. “Let go of your sorrow, put aside your anger, and return to your true self. As long as I’m alive, you shouldn’t let grief take over your heart. I’ll kill the one who’s causing you so much pain. Still, no matter how you’re feeling, I have to tell you what’s best for you. My words come from both friendship and brotherly love. And I’ll do exactly what a true friend should do at a time like this. Watch what I do to our enemies in battle. You’ll see Rāma fall by my hand, along with his brother, and the monkey army will scatter in terror. Today, when I bring you Rāma’s head from the battlefield, you’ll have reason to celebrate, and Sitā will be devastated. The Rakshasas in Lankā who lost family in this war will finally see the sight they long for—Rāma dead in battle. Today, I’ll wipe away the tears of those mourning friends and relatives lost in this fight by defeating our enemies. You’ll see Sugriva, the monkey king—huge as a mountain or a thundercloud—lying dead on the field. 

But tell me, brother, even though so many Rakshasas and I myself are eager to fight for you, why do you still grieve? If Rāma manages to kill me, then maybe he’ll have a chance at you. But honestly, I don’t think Rāma can defeat me. Just give the order, and I’ll go right now. You don’t have to face the enemy yourself—I’ll take care of them. Even if Indra, Yama, Agni, Vāyu, Kubera, and Varuna all join forces against me, I’ll take them on. Even Purandara (Indra) fears me when I appear, towering like a mountain, armed with sharp spears and teeth, roaring into battle. Who could stand against me if I charge in, fighting with just my bare hands? I don’t need weapons—no dart, mace, sword, or arrows. I’ll crush Rāma and even Indra with my arms alone. And if Rāma somehow survives my blows, then my arrows will finish him. Why should you worry while I’m still here? I’m ready right now to go out and destroy your enemies. Don’t be afraid of Rāma—I’ll defeat Rāma, Lakshmana, the mighty Sugriva, and Hanumān, who set Lankā on fire. I’ll devour the entire monkey army in battle. Your fame will be unmatched. If your fear is about Indra or Brahmā, even the gods will fall before me when I’m angry. I’ll conquer Yama and consume the God of Fire. I’ll bring down the very sky. I’ll kill Satakratu (Indra) and even drain the ocean itself. I’ll smash mountains and split the earth. Today, let everyone watch as I show them what Kumbhakarna can do after sleeping so long. Even the heavens wouldn’t satisfy my hunger. I go now to win glory and the joys that come from destroying Daśaratha’s son. After killing Rāma and Lakshmana, I’ll devour all the best of the monkey warriors. Rejoice, my king—drink some Vāruni wine, enjoy yourself, and forget your sorrows. Today, after I send Rāma to the land of the dead, Sitā will finally belong to you for good.”

The five factors are: (1) how to begin an action, (2) the people, resources, and wealth involved, (3) the right timing and location, (4) preparing for setbacks, and (5) achieving success. The three strategies are treaty, war, and so on. The original text is vague here, and even the commentators are not very clear.—T.
The commentator says: Seek virtue in the morning, profit in the afternoon, and pleasure at night.—T.
The passage is full of general statements that are hard to pin down. It’s tough to find real substance behind the abstract words, but as a translator, I have to keep going.—T.
The meaning here is unclear, and the commentator doesn’t help much.—T.
This refers to a hole in the mountain Krauncha, which was made by Skanda, the heavenly general.—T.
“Chapala” means fickle. The commentator suggests it might mean someone who’s easily pleased by whatever sounds good at the moment, but the usual meaning fits.—T.
Mandodari is Ravana’s chief queen.
“Santapam gachchheyam” means “to come by grief.” The commentator says “santapa” here means fear; so the sense is: I have no fear (because of Rāma).—T.
“Abode of Varuna” means the ocean.
SECTION LXIV

After hearing the fierce words of Kumbhakarna, who was massive and strong, Mahodara spoke up. "Kumbhakarna," he said, "you come from a great family, but you’re unbelievably arrogant and honestly, a bit rough around the edges. You don't always see what's the right thing to do. I'm sure the king (Ravana) knows the difference between right and wrong, but you've always acted without respect and love to talk just to hear yourself speak. Ravana, the greatest of the Rakshasas, understands strategy—he knows when and where to act, how to strengthen our side and weaken the enemy. But who ever listens to a plan that’s put forward half-heartedly by someone who’s strong but not wise, and who’s never respected his elders? You don’t really understand what you’re saying about the balance between virtue, personal gain, and desire. Actions bring either happiness or misery, and only those who do things—good or bad—get the results. Virtue and ambition can lead to freedom, heaven, or success, but evil leads only to pain and trouble. People experience the results of their actions, in this life or the next, but the results of desire come quickly. That’s why a king should go after what he wants. We’ve told you this before, honestly. And why is it a bad thing to show your strength against the enemy? Are you really going to go out to fight alone? Let me tell you why that's a terrible idea. How can you alone defeat Rama—the same Rama who already destroyed countless powerful Rakshasas at Janasthana? Don’t you see those same Rakshasas here in the palace now, terrified after losing to him? You want to wake up Rama—son of Dasaratha—knowing he’s like an angry lion or a sleeping snake. Who would want to face him when he’s burning with rage and impossible to approach, as dangerous as Death itself? If you go out to face the enemy, you put our entire army at risk. That’s why, my friend, I can’t support you going into battle alone. Who tries to defeat a powerful enemy while weak and ready to die, as if their opponent was just some nobody? Why do you want to fight a man who has no equal among humans, and who’s as strong as Indra or the sun god, Vivasvat?"

Mahodara, finished talking to the furious Kumbhakarna, turned to Ravana in front of the other Rakshasas. "You already have Sita, so why wait? If you want her, she’ll be yours soon enough. I’ve thought of a way to make her smile at you. Listen, and if you like my plan, do it. Announce that I, Dwijibha, Sanhradi, Kumbhakarna, and Vitardana—the five of us—are marching out to destroy Rama. We’ll go out and fight Rama with everything we’ve got. If we win, then there’s no need for any more tricks to win over Sita. But if Rama survives the battle, and we do too, then I have another plan. We’ll return from the battlefield, covered in blood and wounds from Rama’s arrows, and claim that both Rama and Lakshmana have been eaten by us. We’ll bow at your feet, begging you to reward us. Then, my king, have Gajaskandha spread the word everywhere that Rama and his brother and their army are dead. Act happy—hold a celebration, give food, servants, luxuries, and money to your people. Hand out garlands, clothes, and perfumes to the warriors. Pretend to be pleased—drink and enjoy yourself. After this rumor spreads that Rama and his friends have been killed by Rakshasas, go into the Ashoka grove and find Sita. Comfort her alone, offer her food, riches, and gems. Using this trick, and Sita’s grief, she’ll finally come to you—even if she doesn’t want to. When she loses her beloved husband, she’ll be desperate and vulnerable, and will come under your control. She’s used to happiness, but now she’s suffering. If you make her think she can only be happy with you, she’ll give in. I think this is the best plan. If you see Rama, you’ll only bring disaster on yourself. Stay here. Don’t risk going to fight. By avoiding the battle, you’ll be better off. And, lord of the people, if you defeat your enemy without fighting, you’ll keep your army safe and avoid danger. You’ll win fame, honor, prosperity, and an everlasting reputation."

“Vaktum ashakyam” means incapable of saying. But what does it mean to say, "What man acts according to what is not advanced by one having strength...aged?" I think it means a plan that’s proposed weakly or half-heartedly. — T.
The advice this counselor gives isn’t all consistent. Maybe the text has been changed over time. — T.
"Artha" means sacrifices, gifts, and other things done with wealth. "Sacrifice, gift, and asceticism purify the pious." That’s the Lord’s word. — T.
Dharma, according to Ramanuja, here means contemplation and reciting scriptures, done without caring about gaining happiness from those actions. This is called nishkam dharma—selfless piety. — T.
SECTION LXV

After being spoken to like this, Kumbhakarna turned to Mahodara and scolded him, then addressed his brother, Ravana, the king of the Rakshasas. “Don’t worry. I’ll end your fear by killing Rama, who has brought us so much trouble. Once your enemy is dead, you’ll finally have peace. Some people just brag loudly, like thunderclouds that never actually rain. But real warriors let their actions speak for them on the battlefield. Talking big means nothing; true heroes just do what needs to be done. Mahodara, your advice only appeals to weak and foolish kings who think they know everything. You and the other flatterers have ruined everything for Lanka: the treasury is empty, the army is destroyed, and all that’s left is the king. You pretended to be loyal, but your advice has harmed the kingdom, just like enemies disguised as friends. Now, to fix your mistakes, I’ll go to battle myself and drive out the enemy.” Hearing Kumbhakarna’s words, Ravana, the lord of Rakshasas, laughed and replied, “Clearly Mahodara is terrified of Rama, and that’s why he has no taste for fighting. But there’s no one I trust more than you, Kumbhakarna—no one stronger or more loyal. That’s why I woke you up: to destroy our enemies and make your name famous. The Rakshasas are in real danger now, so go, armed with your spear, like Yama the god of death himself. Devour the monkeys and the two princes, Rama and Lakshmana, who shine with the power of the sun. When the monkeys see you, they’ll run in terror, and even Rama and Lakshmana will be struck down.”

After saying this to his mighty brother, Ravana felt a rush of hope, as if he’d come back to life. He knew what Kumbhakarna could do, and his confidence returned, like the full moon in a clear sky. Kumbhakarna, feeling cheerful, got ready for battle. He picked up a deadly spear: it was razor-sharp, made of black iron, blazing and decorated with gold, as impressive as Indra’s thunderbolt. It was heavy as a mountain, capable of destroying gods, demons, spirits, and serpents, and it was covered in crimson flower garlands, almost spitting fire. With this massive weapon, still stained with the blood of former enemies, Kumbhakarna turned to Ravana and said, “I’ll go alone. Let the rest of the army stay here. Hungry and furious, I’ll devour the monkeys myself today.” But Ravana replied, “No, take the army with you, armed with spears and maces. The monkeys are brave and skilled fighters. If you go alone or let your guard down, they might overwhelm you. So, go with the whole force and crush all our enemies who threaten the Rakshasas.”

Then Ravana stood up and hung a jeweled garland around Kumbhakarna’s neck. He also gave him bracelets, rings, and a chain that shone like the moon. Ravana decorated himself too, with bright and fragrant garlands and set earrings in his ears. Dressed in gold jewelry, Kumbhakarna looked like a fire fueled by offerings at a sacrifice. With his dark, massive belt, he looked like Mount Mandara wrapped by a serpent during the churning of the ocean. When he put on his golden armor, shining like lightning, he looked like a mountain glowing in the sunset. Covered in ornaments and gripping his spear, Kumbhakarna seemed as powerful as Vishnu himself when he strode across the universe. He embraced Ravana, walked around him in respect, bowed his head, and then left. Ravana sent him off with blessings, as war drums and conchs blared and the army, armed to the teeth, followed Kumbhakarna.

Powerful Rakshasa warriors marched behind him, riding elephants, horses, and chariots that rumbled like thunder. Some rode snakes, camels, donkeys, lions, leopards, deer, and even giant birds. All followed the fearsome Kumbhakarna, who was wild with bloodlust. The ground was covered with flowers, and an umbrella shaded him as he marched out, spear in hand, the terror of gods and demons alike. Legions of Rakshasa foot soldiers, armed and fierce, trailed after him. They were huge, with red eyes and dark skin, each carrying weapons—spears, swords, axes, maces, and massive clubs—ready for battle. Kumbhakarna, bursting with strength, transformed himself into a monstrous, terrifying form. Now he was gigantic, with a face like a demon, a hundred bows wide, six hundred bows tall, eyes like chariot wheels, and looked like a burning mountain. He organized the Rakshasa troops and, smiling calmly, said, “Today, like fire burning up moths, I’ll wipe out the monkeys, one group at a time. But really, the monkeys haven’t done anything directly to us—they’re just animals, usually decorating our gardens. The real problem is Rama and Lakshmana. If I kill Rama, the whole invasion will collapse. So I’ll focus on taking him down in battle.”

As he spoke, the Rakshasas cheered so loudly it seemed to shake the sea itself. As Kumbhakarna marched out, bad omens appeared everywhere. Dark clouds flashed with lightning and meteors, looking like wild animals; the earth trembled, and the forests and oceans shook. Jackals howled with fiery mouths, birds circled ominously to the left, a vulture landed on his spear, his left eye twitched, his left arm shook, and a meteor crashed down. The sun grew dim, and the wind stopped blowing, making everything feel unnatural. But Kumbhakarna ignored all these terrifying signs, driven by fate itself. He leapt over the city wall in a single bound and saw the massive monkey army laid out like thunderclouds. When the monkeys saw him—a giant like a living mountain—they scattered in every direction, as if blown away by a storm. The whole monkey army broke ranks and ran, just like clouds splitting apart in the wind, while Kumbhakarna, thrilled, let out a roar louder than thunder. The sound was so terrifying that many monkeys simply collapsed, like trees cut down at the roots. As he advanced with his enormous club, ready to crush his enemies, Kumbhakarna filled the monkeys with absolute terror, like Yama himself at the end of the world.
[219] That is, like autumn clouds that make a lot of noise but produce no rain. —T.
He didn’t actually go out to battle immediately, though. —T.
SECTION LXVI

Kumbhakarna, massive and powerful like a mountain peak, leaped over the city wall and quickly left Lanka. As soon as he was out, he let out a thunderous roar that echoed across the sea, louder than thunder or crashing mountains. When the monkeys saw Kumbhakarna’s fierce eyes and gigantic form—knowing even powerful gods like Indra (Maghavan), Varuna, or Yama couldn't defeat him—they panicked and started to run. Noticing the chaos, Angada, the king’s son, called out to Nala, Nila, Gavaksha, and the strong Kumuda. “Why are you all running away in fear, forgetting your strength and noble lineage? You’re acting like the lowest monkeys! Stop! There’s no point saving yourselves by running. This demon isn’t here just to fight—he’s a terrifying sight meant to scare us. But we can defeat this menace with our own courage. So, stand your ground.” 

The monkeys, heartened by Angada’s words, regrouped. They grabbed trees and moved forward to rejoin the battle. Fired up, they stopped running and started attacking Kumbhakarna, charging at him like enraged elephants. But Kumbhakarna was so strong that when they hit him with huge rocks and flower-covered trees, he barely flinched. The boulders shattered against him, and the trees broke apart and fell to the ground. Driven by rage, Kumbhakarna fought back, tearing through the monkey army like a wildfire burning down a forest. Many brave monkeys were left bloodied and lying on the ground; others, wounded, fell like trees with red flowers. Panicked, the monkeys ran in every direction without looking back or ahead. Some, struck down by Kumbhakarna, fell into the sea or disappeared into the jungle. A few tried to escape the way they had come, across the ocean, while others, pale with fear, rushed into the open fields. Some bears climbed up trees, some hid in the mountains, others dropped down or just ran for their lives. Some monkeys collapsed, while others lay on the ground as if dead.

Seeing his troops falling apart, Angada shouted to the monkeys, “Stop! We have to fight. There’s nowhere on earth you can run where you’ll be safe. Why bother saving your lives? If you run away and abandon your weapons, your wives will mock you—and that’s worse than death for a true warrior. You’re all born into noble families, so why are you acting like cowards? If you give up your courage and run, you become disgraced. What happened to all your talk about honor and loyalty to your king? If you live on after being shamed, you’ll be known as cowards forever. So, stand and fight like true heroes and leave your fear behind. If we die here, we’ll reach Brahma’s realm, which cowards can never enter. Or maybe we’ll win glory by defeating our enemy—and if we die in battle, we’ll enjoy the rewards given to heroes. Kumbhakarna is like a moth drawn to a burning flame—when he faces Rama (Kakutstha), he won’t survive. If we let one demon defeat us all and try to run to save ourselves, we’ll lose all our honor.”

As Angada, shining with his golden armlets, finished speaking, the monkeys—still trying to escape—called back to him, “Kumbhakarna has caused too much destruction. Now isn’t the time to fight. We want to live!” With that, they scattered in all directions as the terrifying, red-eyed demon approached. Even as the best warriors fled, Angada kept trying to rally them, encouraging them with hope and promises of victory. Inspired by the wise son of Vali, all the monkey troops stopped running and waited for his command.
Mahavalāh—plural—probably a misprint for mahavalah—singular.—T.
For fighting, according to the commentator.
Suptāh—means "sleeping," but here it likely means "unconscious."—T.
SECTION LXVII

After hearing Angada’s words, the massive monkey warriors calmed themselves and refocused on the battle. Encouraged by Angada, they gathered their courage and stood ready to fight, determined to face whatever might come. Fired up, the monkeys abandoned all fear for their own lives and charged back into the fray, throwing themselves fiercely at the Rakshasa forces. Grabbing trees and huge boulders, these giant monkeys stormed toward Kumbhakarna.

Enraged, the enormous Kumbhakarna snatched up his mighty mace and smashed it down on his enemies. Wherever he struck, hundreds, then thousands, of monkeys fell dead. Sweeping his massive arms through the crowd, Kumbhakarna grabbed handfuls of monkeys—sixteen, eight, ten, twenty, or even thirty at a time—and devoured them as Garuda devours serpents.

The monkeys rallied, encouraging each other as they regrouped. They grabbed trees and rocks and stood firm at the front lines. Dwivida, one of the strongest monkeys, tore up a huge crag that made him look like a rolling thundercloud, and hurled it at Kumbhakarna, who looked like a mountain peak. But the boulder missed and landed in the midst of the Rakshasa army, crushing horses, elephants, chariots, and elite chargers. Not stopping, Dwivida ripped up another mountain top and threw it at the other Rakshasas. The blow killed Kumbhakarna’s horses and charioteers, turning the battlefield into a bloody chaos.

Rakshasa warriors, firing arrows as deadly as death itself, cut off the heads of the loudest monkey fighters. But the monkeys fought back, uprooting giant trees and destroying chariots, horses, elephants, camels, and Rakshasas alike. Hanuman, fighting from the sky, hurled mountain peaks, rocks, and every kind of tree at Kumbhakarna’s head, but Kumbhakarna shattered them all with his deadly spear, blocking the rain of attacks.

Gripping his sharp spear, Kumbhakarna charged into the thickest part of the monkey army. Hanuman, armed with a mountain peak, stood in his way, furious. Hanuman slammed the crag onto Kumbhakarna, who reeled from the blow, his body now slick with blood and fat.

Just as Guha once struck Krauncha with his spear, Kumbhakarna—towering like a living mountain—drove his own deadly spear into Hanuman’s chest. Hanuman, his chest pierced, coughed up blood and let out a furious roar that sounded like thunder at the world’s end. Seeing Hanuman suffering, the Rakshasas cheered, while the monkeys, terrified and heartbroken, began to flee from Kumbhakarna.

Nila, determined, reorganized his forces and hurled a mountain peak at the cunning Kumbhakarna. As it fell, Kumbhakarna smashed it, shattering the rock into flaming fragments that fell to earth.

Next, five powerful monkeys—Rishabha, Sarabha, Nila, Gavaksha, and Gandhamadana—charged Kumbhakarna together. They battered him with boulders, trees, punches, kicks, and blows, but to Kumbhakarna, their attacks felt as gentle as flower garlands and ointments.

Kumbhakarna grabbed Rishabha and crushed him in a bear hug. Rishabha, suffering terribly, fell to the ground coughing up blood. Then, Kumbhakarna struck Sarabha, hit Nila, and Gavaksha was slapped hard with his thigh. All three fell, bloody and unconscious, like trees cut down.

As these five mighty monkeys collapsed, thousands more rushed at Kumbhakarna. Climbing mountain peaks, these top warriors leapt onto him, biting and clawing. The monkeys swarmed Kumbhakarna with their claws, teeth, fists, and arms, making him look like a mountain covered in trees.

But Kumbhakarna, now raging, snatched up handfuls of monkeys and devoured them, just as Garuda eats snakes. Some monkeys, tossed into his mouth, crawled back out through his nose and ears. He kept eating, crushing the monkey army, growing more furious as he went. The earth became slick with blood and flesh as he rampaged, like a wildfire at the end of the world.

With his deadly spear, Kumbhakarna looked as fearsome as Indra with his thunderbolt or Yama himself. He tore through the monkey army like a fire burns a dry forest in summer. The monkeys, devastated and terrified, screamed in panic as their ranks were destroyed.

With so many monkeys slaughtered, the survivors, desperate and grieving, ran to Raghava (Rama) for protection. Seeing his troops broken and beaten, Angada, son of Vali and grandson of Indra, launched himself at Kumbhakarna.

Angada grabbed a massive boulder, let out a battle cry that shook the Rakshasas, and hurled the rock at Kumbhakarna’s head. The blow enraged Kumbhakarna even more. Roaring, Kumbhakarna charged at Angada, aiming his spear. Angada’s speed saved him, and he dodged the weapon, then landed a solid punch on Kumbhakarna’s chest, stunning the giant.

Kumbhakarna quickly recovered and struck Angada, knocking him unconscious. Now, with Angada down, Kumbhakarna grabbed his spear and went after Sugriva.

Seeing Kumbhakarna coming, Sugriva, the monkey king, leaped up. He tore up a mountain peak and rushed at Kumbhakarna. Kumbhakarna stretched out his arms and confronted Sugriva, his body drenched in monkey blood.

Sugriva, seeing Kumbhakarna’s blood-soaked form, challenged him: “You’ve taken down great heroes and devoured many warriors—your fame is secure. But leave the monkey army now. Why bother with the weak? Face me and take this mountain top instead!”

Kumbhakarna replied, “You talk big because you’re the grandson of Prajapati and son of the king of bears, with all their strength and courage.”

Sugriva didn’t hesitate—he spun the mountain peak and hurled it at Kumbhakarna’s chest. The rock shattered on impact with Kumbhakarna’s broad chest. The monkeys lost heart, while the Rakshasas cheered.

Furious, Kumbhakarna roared and spun his spear, aiming to kill Sugriva. But Hanuman, the Wind-god’s son, leaped in and caught the spear midair, snapping the iron weapon in two with his bare hands. The monkeys cheered wildly at Hanuman’s feat.

With his spear broken, Kumbhakarna felt fear and started to retreat. The monkeys, now overjoyed, filled the air with shouts and thanked Hanuman for saving them.

But Kumbhakarna wasn’t done. He tore a peak from the Malaya mountains and slammed it down on Sugriva, knocking the monkey king unconscious. The Rakshasas roared in triumph.

Kumbhakarna, towering like a mountain, picked up the limp Sugriva and carried him off the battlefield like a gust of wind sweeps away a cloud. As he marched away, the Rakshasas cheered and even the gods looked on in awe at his strength.

Kumbhakarna thought that by capturing Sugriva, he could crush the entire enemy army and defeat Rama in one blow.

Meanwhile, Hanuman, clever son of the Wind-god, saw the monkey army scattered and Sugriva captured. He thought, “What should I do now that our king is taken? Should I turn into a mountain and smash the Rakshasas? Should I kill Kumbhakarna and free Sugriva myself? But Sugriva is strong enough to save himself, even if captured by gods or demons. He must just be stunned by Kumbhakarna’s blow. If I rescue him now, he might lose his reputation. I’ll wait a moment and let him show his own strength—then the monkeys will be inspired. For now, I’ll rally the monkey army.”

Hanuman then began to regroup the monkeys, calming and encouraging them.

As this happened, Kumbhakarna carried Sugriva into Lanka. The city celebrated, showering him with flowers from the rooftops and city gates.

The cool air, scented water, and even fried rice hurled from the balconies revived Sugriva. Slowly regaining consciousness, he realized he was in the arms of the enemy and thought, “How can I strike back now? What can I do to help our army?”

Suddenly, Sugriva attacked. He bit and clawed Kumbhakarna, slicing off the Rakshasa’s ears and nose and digging his heels into his sides. Enraged and bleeding, Kumbhakarna threw Sugriva to the ground and tried to pin him. But Sugriva broke free, shot into the sky like a ball, and rejoined Rama.

Kumbhakarna, now missing his ears and nose and soaked in blood, looked like a mountain covered in streams. Fearsome and massive, black as coal and dripping red, he was a terrifying sight as he prepared to fight again.

Sugriva escaped, and Kumbhakarna, now weaponless, grabbed a huge mace. He stormed from the city, feasting on monkeys as a wildfire devours everything in its path at the end of time.

Hungering for blood, Kumbhakarna tore into the monkey ranks, even swallowing some Rakshasas and ghosts by mistake. He picked up monkeys and Rakshasas alike, tossing them into his mouth—one, two, three, or more at a time—until blood and fat streamed down his body. Despite being battered with mountain peaks, he kept eating. The terrified monkeys fled to Rama for help.

Kumbhakarna, wild with rage, chased after hundreds of monkeys, eating them in handfuls. With blood and guts hanging from his ears and his face smeared with gore, he looked like Death itself unleashed.

At that moment, Lakshmana, son of Sumitra, furious at what he saw, entered the fight. He fired seven arrows at Kumbhakarna’s massive body and followed with more. Kumbhakarna, wounded, broke off the arrows with his own weapon. Lakshmana, even angrier, shot volley after volley, covering Kumbhakarna’s golden armor in arrows like the wind covers clouds.

Kumbhakarna, dark as ink and covered in golden arrows, looked like the sun surrounded by storm clouds. Raging, Kumbhakarna mocked Lakshmana: “You’ve proven your bravery by daring to fight me—I’ve even defeated the Destroyer himself in battle. Even Indra on his elephant, surrounded by all the gods, couldn’t stand against me. But today, young Lakshmana, you’ve impressed me with your courage. Now, let me go fight Rama. If I kill him, the rest will fall easily.”

Lakshmana laughed and replied, “You’re right—your strength is more than even Indra could handle. I’ve seen it for myself today. But there’s Rama, the son of Dasharatha—go face him if you dare.”

Ignoring Lakshmana, Kumbhakarna charged at Rama, making the ground shake. Rama immediately fired a powerful weapon, shooting sharp arrows into Kumbhakarna’s chest. Flames and sparks shot from Kumbhakarna’s mouth as Rama’s arrows struck him, and the furious Rakshasa lunged at Rama, chasing the monkeys as well.

Rama’s arrows, feathered with peacock plumes, hit Kumbhakarna’s chest and knocked the mace from his hand. All his other weapons fell to the ground. Now defenseless, Kumbhakarna started smashing monkeys with his fists.

Bleeding from countless wounds, Kumbhakarna looked like a mountain overflowing with streams. Consumed by rage and pain, he tore into monkeys, Rakshasas, and bears alike, whirling a giant mountain peak and hurling it at Rama. But Rama, quick as ever, shattered the boulder with seven golden-tipped arrows before it could land.

Lakshmana, thinking fast, suggested to Rama, “He can’t tell friend from foe—he’s so crazed by blood he’s eating both Rakshasas and monkeys. Let the strongest monkeys swarm him and weigh him down. If we cover him, he won’t be able to eat anyone else.”

Rama agreed, and the bravest monkeys leaped onto Kumbhakarna. The giant Rakshasa, even more enraged, shook them off like a mad elephant tossing its riders. Rama saw this and, eyes blazing with anger, grabbed his bow, urging his monkey allies to fight on.

Rama, equipped with a golden, snake-like bow and a full quiver of arrows, led the charge with Lakshmana at his side. In the thick of the monkey ranks, he spotted Kumbhakarna—soaked in blood, eyes red, tearing through the army like a maddened elephant, golden armlets glinting, blood dripping from his mouth, smashing everything in his path, and looking like Death itself.

Rama pulled back his bow, filling the air with its thunderous twang. Kumbhakarna, furious at the sound, charged straight at Rama. Rama, arms strong as a serpent, called out, “Come, king of the Rakshasas! Don’t be afraid. Here I am, bow in hand—your destroyer. Today your race ends.”

Kumbhakarna, recognizing Rama, laughed with a horrible, booming voice, then broke into the monkey ranks, terrifying everyone. He taunted Rama, “Don’t mistake me for Viradha, Kavandha, Khara, Vali, or Maricha. I am Kumbhakarna! See my iron mace—it’s brought down gods and demons before. Don’t think cutting off my nose and ears weakens me—I hardly feel it! Watch my power, Rama, and after you’ve shown yours, I’ll devour you.”

Rama fired arrows tipped with iron knobs, but Kumbhakarna barely flinched. Even the arrows that had cut down mighty trees and killed Vali, the greatest monkey of all, had no effect. Kumbhakarna absorbed Rama’s arrows like nothing, then spun his bloodstained mace, frightening gods and demons alike, and drove the monkeys back.

Rama switched tactics, pulling out a mighty wind-weapon. With it, he sliced off Kumbhakarna’s arm holding the mace. The severed arm, still clutching the mace, crashed into the monkey army, causing devastation.

The remaining monkeys, wounded and afraid, stepped aside to watch the titanic duel.

Kumbhakarna, now with only one arm, tore up a tree and charged at Rama. Rama, using another golden-tipped arrow powered by Indra’s weapon, cut off Kumbhakarna’s remaining arm, which crashed down and crushed everything beneath it.

Roaring in pain, Kumbhakarna tried to fight on. Rama then used two crescent-shaped arrows to cut off both of Kumbhakarna’s legs, which landed with thunderous crashes, shaking the earth and everything around.

Now just a limbless torso, Kumbhakarna opened his gigantic mouth and lunged for Rama like a demon swallowing the moon. Rama stuffed his mouth with gold-feathered arrows. Choking and unable to speak, Kumbhakarna tried to roar but only managed a muffled sound before collapsing.

Finally, Rama took an arrow blessed by Indra—blazing and unstoppable, bright as the sun, fatal to any foe—and shot it at Kumbhakarna. The arrow, like a streak of pure fire, sped through the sky and sliced off Kumbhakarna’s head, as Indra once slew the demon Vritra.

Kumbhakarna’s huge head, earrings gone, tumbled to the earth like the moon setting at sunrise, crushing buildings, city gates, and walls along the way. His massive body crashed into the ocean, sinking deep and crushing giant fish and serpents below.

With Kumbhakarna’s death, the earth trembled and mountains shook. The gods, sages, naga-serpents, spirits, Gandharvas, Yakshas, and all celestial beings shouted in joy at Rama’s victory.

The Rakshasas, devastated, cried out in grief over their fallen champion, while the monkeys cheered and celebrated Rama’s strength. Rama stood out among his allies like the sun breaking free of darkness.

The monkeys were filled with happiness, and their faces shone like lotus flowers. They honored Rama, their victorious prince, while Rama himself rejoiced in the same way Indra had after killing the mighty demon Vritra—proud to have finally defeated the unstoppable Kumbhakarna.

SECTION LXVIII

When the Rakshasas saw that the mighty Kumbhakarna had been killed by Rama, they rushed to tell Ravana, their king. They said, “My lord, Kumbhakarna—the one who seemed like Death itself, driven by fate—had torn through the monkey army and devoured so many of them. For a while, he showed his incredible strength, but now he’s been killed by Rama, who fought with all his power. With half his body sunk in the terrible sea, your brother Kumbhakarna lies there, his nose and ears cut off, his body covered in blood, his head and limbs hacked away, and his body exposed. He’s blocking the gates of Lanka like a fallen mountain, looking like a tree burned down in a forest fire.” When Ravana heard that his mighty brother Kumbhakarna had been slain in battle, he was filled with grief, fainted, and collapsed to the ground. Triśiras (Three-heads) and Atikaya, both feared by gods and humans, began to weep when they heard their uncle was dead, overwhelmed by sorrow. Mahodara (Big-belly) and Mahaparswa (Mighty-flank) also broke down in grief after hearing that their uncle had been killed by Rama, who never tires in battle. After a huge effort, Ravana regained consciousness. Still shaken by Kumbhakarna’s death, he began to mourn out loud, his mind clouded by grief: “Oh hero! Oh, the one who humbled our enemies! Mighty Kumbhakarna! Fate has taken you from me, sending you to Yama’s realm. Where are you going, leaving me alone and not finishing off my enemies and yours? It feels like I’ve lost my right arm—without you, I am nothing. With you at my side, I never feared gods or demons. How could a warrior like you, who crushed the pride of gods and demons and looked like the fire at the end of the world, be killed by Rama in battle? Not even thunderbolts could hurt you—how can you now lie dead, struck down by Rama’s arrows? The gods and sages up in the sky are cheering after seeing you fall. Today, the monkeys will be overjoyed and will surely storm all the gates and walls of Lanka. What’s the point of ruling anymore? What use is Sita to me now? Without Kumbhakarna, I don’t even want to live. If I can’t kill Rama—the one who killed my brother—then death would be better than this empty life. Today, I’ll go to wherever my brother is. I can’t go on living without him, even for a moment—otherwise the gods will laugh at me for all the trouble I caused them. But now that you’re gone, Kumbhakarna, how will I ever defeat Indra? Now I see that Vibhishana’s advice was right all along. Because I foolishly ignored what he, Kumbhakarna, and Prahasta tried to tell me, this disaster has fallen on me and brought me shame. By shaming the wise and noble Vibhishana, I brought all this grief upon myself.” After crying and mourning for Kumbhakarna for a long time, Ravana—the Ten-headed one—was completely overwhelmed by sorrow and collapsed again, realizing his brother, Indra’s enemy, had died in battle.
“Three-headed.”—T.
“Huge-bellied.”—T.
“Mighty-flanked.”—T.
SECTION LXIX

As the wicked Rāvana sat overwhelmed by grief, his son Triçiras (Three-Heads) tried to console him. “Father,” he said, “our uncle, who was so powerful, has fallen in battle. But real warriors don’t sink into despair like this. You alone have the strength to conquer all three worlds—so why give in to sorrow? You have Brahmā’s magical dart, your armor, your bow, and your chariot pulled by a thousand donkeys that rumble like thunder. Even gods and demons have been terrified by your might. You should be the one punishing Rāma. But if you’d rather wait, let me go fight! I’ll capture your enemies just like Garuda seizes serpents. I’ll defeat Rāma in battle—just like Indra beat Samvara, or Vishnu conquered Naraka.” Hearing Triçiras' bold words, Rāvana felt as if life had returned to him. Devāntaka, Narāntaka, and Atikāya were also fired up to fight by Triçiras’ speech. These sons of Rāvana, the greatest of the Nairitas (rakshasas of the southwest), were so powerful they could fly, create illusions, and humble even the gods. None had ever been beaten, not even by gods, Gandharvas, or the serpent Kinnaras. They were masters of weapons and warfare, and all had received special boons. Rāvana, surrounded by his sons, looked as glorious as Indra among the gods. He hugged his sons, gave them his blessings, and adorned them with jewels before sending them to the battlefield. He also sent the brothers Yudhyonmatta and Matta to protect his princes in the fight. Bowing to their father and circling him in respect, these huge rakshasas marched out, ready for war, carrying herbs and perfumes to heal wounds. The six warriors—Triçiras, Atikāya, Devāntaka, Narāntaka, Mahodara, and Mahāpārçwa—set off, driven by fate.

Mahodara climbed onto his elephant Sudarçana, a descendant of Airāvata, shining like a dark thundercloud. Armed with every weapon and loaded with quivers, he looked spectacular, like the Sun rising over a mountain. Triçiras took his chariot drawn by fine horses, filled with all sorts of weapons. With his three crowns, he seemed as majestic as the Himalayas with its golden peaks. Atikāya, a giant bowman, rode in the finest chariot, golden and full of weapons—he looked as radiant as Meru Mountain. Narāntaka mounted a huge white horse clad in gold, as fast as the wind, and took up a deadly spear, looking like the war god Skanda on his peacock. Devāntaka, wielding a golden club, resembled Vishnu during the churning of the ocean, while Mahāpārçwa, gripping his mace, looked like the god Kubera himself. With elephants, horses, and chariots making a thunderous noise, these rakshasas marched out like gods leaving Amarāvati. They were followed by a host of powerful rakshasas. Decked in glowing armor and crowns, the princes looked like blazing planets in the sky, and their colorful uniforms seemed like flocks of cranes among autumn clouds. Determined to either die or win, they charged forward, roaring like lions, shaking the earth, and challenging the heavens.

The rakshasas saw the monkey army ready, holding up huge rocks and boulders. The monkeys, in turn, saw the rakshasa horde with elephants, horses, and chariots, all glittering with armor and bells. The rakshasa army looked like storm clouds, surrounded by warriors who burned like fire. As the forces advanced, the monkeys took the chance to lift massive rocks and let out wild shouts. The rakshasas, unable to stand the noise, shouted back. The monkeys replied, and the contest of cries grew louder and fiercer. The monkey leaders dove into the ranks of the rakshasas, swinging stones and trees like living mountains, sometimes leaping into the sky and sometimes landing back on earth. Some monkeys fought with huge tree trunks. The fight between the two armies was brutal—a rain of trees, rocks, and cliffs fell. The monkeys’ attacks were met with volleys of arrows. Both sides roared like lions. Monkeys crushed armored rakshasas with rocks and killed warriors riding elephants, horses, and chariots. Suddenly, monkeys felled many powerful rakshasas. Struck by huge boulders, some rakshasas staggered, fell, or roared in pain.

Meanwhile, rakshasas struck back with sharp darts, clubs, and curved swords, killing many monkeys. Both sides, bloodied, kept attacking each other. Soon the battlefield was littered with rocks, swords, and bodies, soaked in blood. The ground was covered with fallen, mountain-like rakshasas and monkeys. Both sides used fallen corpses as weapons—rakshasas killed monkeys with the bodies of other monkeys, monkeys did the same with rakshasa corpses, and rocks were hurled without mercy. Monkeys even ripped off the arms of their enemies to finish them. The roars kept echoing. Monkeys destroyed chariots with chariots, elephants with elephants, and horses with horses. Rakshasas cut apart trees and rocks thrown by monkeys with sharp arrows. The battlefield became almost impossible to cross, choked with broken weapons, trees, and the dead. Still, the monkeys, full of courage and pride, kept fighting fiercely.

As the savage battle raged, the gods and sages cheered whenever the monkeys gained the upper hand and the rakshasas fell. Then Narāntaka, mounted on a swift horse and armed with a deadly spear, charged into the monkey army like a fish diving into the sea. With his gleaming spear, he killed seven hundred monkeys at once. He tore through the ranks so fast the Vidyādharas and sages watched in awe as his path was marked by piles of bodies and blood. Monkeys tried to fight back, but Narāntaka cut them down with his arrows, burning through their forces like fire through a forest. When the monkeys tried to use trees and giant rocks, he struck them down with his spear, as if splitting mountains with lightning. Narāntaka, spear raised, zipped through the battlefield, hitting everyone whether they jumped, stood, or ran. Monkeys could not withstand the force of his spear, which felt like a thunderbolt. Their cries filled the air as they fell, looking like mountains struck by a thunderclap.

Some monkeys who had survived Kumbhakarna’s earlier rampage were now back with Sugriva. As Sugriva saw his army panicking before Narāntaka, he spotted Narāntaka himself, charging on horseback. The furious monkey king turned to Angada, son of Vāli, and said, “Face that rakshasa on horseback and kill him! He’s slaughtering our troops.” Angada leapt from the ranks like the Sun breaking through clouds, shining with his armbands like a mountain studded with metal. Unarmed except for his claws and teeth, Angada challenged Narāntaka: “Stop! Why attack these lesser monkeys? Throw your thunderbolt-like spear at my heart!” Enraged, Narāntaka bit his lip and charged Angada, hurling his blazing spear. It struck Angada’s chest but shattered, dropping to the ground like a snake cut by Garuda. Angada raised his hand and slapped Narāntaka’s horse on the head, dropping it instantly—its eyes bulged, tongue lolled, and it collapsed like a fallen mountain. Seeing his horse dead, Narāntaka’s fury exploded—he punched Angada in the head with all his might, drawing blood. Angada, dazed for a moment, quickly recovered. He clenched his fist and smashed it into Narāntaka’s chest with a blow like death itself. Narāntaka’s chest split open, and he collapsed, vomiting blood, as if a mountain had been shattered by a lightning bolt.

As Angada killed Narāntaka, cheers erupted from both the monkey army and the gods above. Angada, amazed at his own feat, felt a sudden surge of delight.

Seeing Narāntaka dead, the three mighty Nairitas—Devāntaka, Mahodara, and Triçiras—cried out in anger. Mahodara, still on his elephant, charged at Angada. Devāntaka, furious over his brother’s death, took up a huge club and rushed at Angada. Triçiras rode a golden chariot pulled by splendid horses and joined the attack. Now Angada faced all three at once. He ripped up a huge tree with massive branches and hurled it at Devāntaka as if launching a thunderbolt. Triçiras shot it to pieces with arrows that looked like snakes. Angada, undaunted, sprang forward and began hurling rocks and trees at his enemies. Triçiras cut down the flying projectiles with his arrows, and Mahodara smashed the trees with his club. Then Triçiras shot arrows at Angada, while Mahodara chased him on his elephant and pierced his chest with heavy javelins. Devāntaka battered Angada with his club and quickly retreated.

Despite being attacked by three powerful rakshasas at once, Angada didn’t flinch. He summoned all his strength and slapped Mahodara’s elephant so hard it collapsed and died instantly. Angada then tore out its tusks and used them to strike Devāntaka, who began to gush blood like red lacquer. Devāntaka, encouraged by his allies, spun his club with all his might and hit Angada, knocking him to his knees. But Angada sprang back up. As he rose, Triçiras shot three deadly arrows into his temples. Seeing Angada in trouble, Hanumān and Nila rushed to help.

Nila hurled a mountain peak at Triçiras, but the three-headed rakshasa cut it in half with his arrows, and the broken stone crashed to the ground, sparking with fire. Meanwhile, Devāntaka, grinning, chased Hanumān with his club. Hanumān leapt forward and smashed Devāntaka’s head with a blow like a thunderbolt. The impact crushed Devāntaka’s skull—his teeth and eyes fell out, his tongue lolled, and he dropped dead instantly. As this fierce rakshasa fell, Triçiras, mad with rage, showered Nila with arrows. At the same time, Mahodara, climbing onto another elephant, rained arrows on Nila’s chest. Nila was wounded and dazed but managed to recover, pull up a huge rock with trees still attached, and hurl it at Mahodara’s head. The rock crushed Mahodara, killing him instantly.

Seeing his uncle Mahodara dead, Triçiras grabbed his bow and, burning with anger, shot sharpened arrows at Hanumān. Hanumān, furious, threw a mountain peak at Triçiras, but Triçiras shattered it midair with his arrows. Hanumān then hurled a barrage of trees, but Triçiras cut them all down in the sky and shouted triumphantly. Enraged, Hanumān leapt into the air and, with his claws, ripped apart Triçiras’ horses like a lion tearing an elephant. Triçiras threw a deadly spear at Hanumān, but Hanumān caught it midair, snapped it in two, and roared. The monkeys cheered as Hanumān broke the weapon.

Triçiras, now wielding a sword, slashed at Hanumān’s chest. Hanumān, stunned but still strong, slapped Triçiras on the head with all his might. The blow sent Triçiras’ crowns and ornaments flying, and he collapsed unconscious. Hanumān broke Triçiras’ sword as he fell and let out a terrifying roar that shook the rakshasas. But Triçiras, refusing to give up, sprang back up and struck Hanumān. This only made Hanumān angrier—he smashed Triçiras’ crown, and then, with a sharp sword, cut off all three of his heads, decorated with crowns and earrings, just like Indra once decapitated Tvastri’s son. Triçiras’ heads tumbled to the ground like falling stars, his eyes still glowing like fire.

With Triçiras dead, the monkeys cheered, the earth shook, and the rakshasas fled in panic. Seeing Triçiras, Yudhyonmatta, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka all dead, Rāvana’s brother Matta was filled with rage. He took up a monstrous iron mace, glowing with gold, dripping with blood, and terrifying enough to scare even the mighty elephants Airāvata and Mahāpadma. Burning with fury like the fire at the end of an age, Matta charged at the monkeys.

Rishabha, a mighty monkey hero, leapt forward to meet him. Matta smashed Rishabha’s chest with his mace, and Rishabha reeled, bleeding heavily. After a moment, Rishabha recovered, glared at Matta, and charged in, hitting him in the chest with a punch as hard as a mountain. Matta fell like a tree cut at the roots, covered in blood. Rishabha seized Matta’s own club and roared. Matta, stunned for a moment, sprang up again, looking like a storm cloud, and struck back at Rishabha. Rishabha fell, but quickly recovered, and with a mighty swing, smashed Matta with the mace. The blow cracked Matta’s chest, and blood poured out like minerals from a mountain. Taking the mace, Rishabha swung it wildly, slaughtering Matta’s troops. Finally, broken by his own weapon, Matta fell dead—his teeth and eyes shriveled, his life gone. With Matta dead, the rakshasa army panicked and fled, abandoning their weapons in a desperate rush to escape—like a storm-tossed sea breaking apart.

SECTION LXXI

Atikāya, one of the most powerful Rākshasas and son of Rāvana, was furious when he saw the Rākshasa army in chaos, his mighty brothers—Yudhyonmatta and Matta—defeated, and even his uncles and other relatives falling in battle. Atikāya, massive as a mountain and filled with energy, had earned a special boon from Brahmā that made him nearly invincible in battle. His rage burned as he climbed into a chariot that shone as brightly as a thousand suns. Wearing a jeweled crown and shining earrings, Atikāya pulled back his bow and loudly announced his name to the monkey army, his booming voice and the sound of his bowstring terrifying the monkeys. Seeing his enormous size, many monkeys thought he must be Kumbhakarna returned, and in fear, they huddled together. Atikāya’s form was awe-inspiring, almost godlike, and the monkeys, panicked, scattered in every direction. Some of them, dazed and afraid, ran to take shelter behind Lakshmana’s older brother, Rāma.

From afar, Rāma (also called Kākutstha) spotted Atikāya, looking like a storm cloud ready to burst, mounted on his giant chariot with his bow in hand. Astonished by the sight, Rāma tried to calm the terrified monkeys and asked Bibhishana, “Who is that warrior, mountain-sized, with fierce lion-like eyes, standing on a massive chariot pulled by a thousand horses? He shines with deadly weapons and sharp spears, surrounded by all kinds of arrows and swords, looking almost supernatural. His bows, covered in gold, make his chariot glow like Indra’s rainbow in the sky. Who is this master archer, this Rākshasa who lights up the battlefield, whose arrows fill all directions like sunlight, and whose flag displays Rāhu? His golden-plated bow roars like thunder, and his chariot shakes the ground. I see thirty-eight quivers, terrifying bows, golden bowstrings, and two huge shining swords at his side. He wears red garlands and looks like a walking mountain, his mouth wide and fearsome, arms decorated with golden ornaments, his face both beautiful and intimidating, sparkling like the full moon. Please, Bibhishana, tell me who he is—the Rākshasa who has scared the monkeys so much that they’re fleeing everywhere.”

Rāma’s question was answered by Bibhishana, who said, “That is Atikāya, son of Rāvana and Dhānyamāli. He’s as strong as Rāvana himself, famous, skilled in every art of war, and trusted by all of Lankā. Atikāya has worshipped Brahmā through harsh penance and received powerful weapons and armor as boons. Brahmā made him immune to death at the hands of gods and demons, and gave him this shining chariot and indestructible armor. He has defeated hundreds of gods and demons, protected the Rākshasas, and destroyed Yakshas. He even survived Indra’s thunderbolt and escaped the noose of the sea god Varuna. Atikāya is a terror to his enemies and has slaughtered monkey warriors before. Be careful, Rāma—he’s extremely dangerous.”

Just then, Atikāya stormed into the monkey ranks, stretching his bow and shouting over and over. The bravest monkeys—including Kumuda, Dwivida, Mainda, Nila, and Sabha—rushed him together, swinging trees and mountain rocks. But Atikāya, skilled with weapons, cut down their attacks with golden-tipped arrows. He pierced every monkey in front of him with iron-tipped arrows, leaving them in agony and unable to fight back. The monkeys were terrified, as if a raging lion had charged a herd of deer, but Atikāya didn’t kill anyone who didn’t fight back.

Then Atikāya jumped out in front of Rāma, bow in hand, and shouted arrogantly, “I will only fight someone worthy, not cowards. If there’s anyone here who has real strength and knows how to fight, let him come and face me!”

Hearing this, Lakshmana (Sumitrā’s son) was filled with anger. Refusing to be insulted, he grabbed his bow and stepped forward. His rage building, Lakshmana knocked an arrow, drawing his bow with force in front of Atikāya. The sound of his bowstring echoed through the earth, sky, and ocean, striking fear into all the Rākshasas. Atikāya was surprised by Lakshmana’s boldness and the sound of his bow.

Atikāya, now furious, called out to Lakshmana, “You’re just a boy, Sumitrā’s son. You don’t know what real power is. Go away. Don’t throw your life away fighting me—I am like Death itself. Not the Himalayas, the sky, or the earth could withstand my arrows. You’re waking a sleeping volcano. Drop your bow and go home, or you’ll die. If you’re too proud to leave, then stay—today, you’ll meet your end. Look at my arrows, covered in gold and as deadly as Shiva’s trident. Just as a lion kills an elephant, my arrows will spill your blood.”

With that, Atikāya angrily nocked an arrow, ready to fire. Lakshmana, hearing his arrogant threats, became even more determined. He replied, “Big words don’t make you great. You have to prove yourself in battle. Come on—show me what you’ve got. Today, my golden arrows will drink your blood. Don’t underestimate me just because I’m young. Whether I’m a boy or an old man, you’ll learn what death is today. Remember, Vishnu conquered the universe when he was just a boy.”

Lakshmana’s words, full of logic and pride, were witnessed by Vidyādharas, spirits, gods, demons, great sages, and Guhyakas, who all realized something extraordinary was about to happen.

Atikāya, furious, fired an arrow at Lakshmana that seemed to darken the sky. Lakshmana, quick and deadly, shot a crescent-tipped arrow that cut Atikāya’s missile in two, making it fall harmlessly to the ground. Even angrier, Atikāya grabbed five more arrows and shot them at Lakshmana, but Lakshmana cut them down mid-air with his own sharp arrows. Then Lakshmana selected a powerful arrow and shot it at Atikāya, striking him right in the forehead. Blood flowed from the wound, and the arrow stuck out like a deadly serpent on a mountain.

Stung by the hit, Atikāya recovered quickly and, surprisingly, praised Lakshmana: “Well done! With that shot, you’ve proved yourself a worthy enemy.” Sitting calmly on his chariot, Atikāya began to move around and shoot arrows in patterns—one, three, five, or seven at a time. His gold-feathered arrows, blazing like the sun, lit up the sky. But Lakshmana calmly cut down every single arrow with his own.

Seeing his attacks useless, Atikāya grew even more enraged. He took a sharp arrow, aimed, and shot it straight at Lakshmana’s chest. The shot landed hard, and Lakshmana began to bleed heavily, like a wounded elephant. Lakshmana quickly pulled out the arrow, readied another, and prepared to strike back.

Calling on the power of the Agneya (fire) weapon, Lakshmana’s arrow and bow burst into flames. Atikāya responded by taking up the Raudra weapon, channeling the power of Rudra, and loaded a golden-tipped arrow that gleamed like a serpent. Both warriors then fired their magical weapons at each other; their arrows clashed in mid-air like two angry snakes, canceling each other out and falling to the earth in ashes.

Atikāya, now burning with rage, fired the Aishika arrow dedicated to Tashtri, but Lakshmana countered it with an arrow powered by Indra (Aindra weapon). Atikāya, still not giving up, used a Yamya arrow (channeling Yama, god of death), but Lakshmana blocked it with a Vāyavya weapon (channeling the Wind-god). Furious, Lakshmana then let loose a barrage of arrows like a rainstorm.

But when Lakshmana’s arrows struck Atikāya, they just bounced off his armor, their tips broken. Realizing his normal attacks were useless, Lakshmana fired thousands more arrows, but Atikāya’s armor, blessed by Brahmā, protected him completely.

At this moment, the Wind-god whispered to Lakshmana, “Atikāya has a boon from Brahmā and impenetrable armor. Only a Brāhma weapon can kill him. Nothing else will work.”

Hearing this, Lakshmana picked a fierce arrow and charged it with Brāhma weapon power. As he did, the world seemed to tremble—the sky, planets, sun, moon, and earth all shook with fear. Lakshmana set the deadly arrow to his bow and fired it at Atikāya, who saw it coming, sparkling with diamonds and moving with terrifying speed.

Atikāya tried to stop the arrow with a flood of weapons—darts, spears, maces, and more—but Lakshmana’s arrow cut through everything. The blazing arrow reached Atikāya’s jeweled head and sliced it off, sending it crashing to the ground like a mountain peak falling from the Himalayas.

Seeing Atikāya’s headless body fall, his ornaments scattered, the surviving Rākshasas were overwhelmed with grief. Terrified, they screamed and fled back toward Lankā, abandoning the battlefield. Meanwhile, the victorious monkeys, overjoyed and their faces glowing, surrounded Lakshmana and honored him for saving them all.
SECTION LXIXII

When Ravana heard that Atikaya had been killed by the fearless Lakshmana, he was overwhelmed with anxiety. He said, “Dhumraksha, who was extremely fierce and skilled in all kinds of weapons, as well as Akampana, Prahasta, and Kumbhakarna—all these powerful warriors, great Rakshasas who loved battle, who had always defeated their enemies and never lost a fight—have now been killed by Rama, who never tires. And so many other Rakshasas, massive in size and masters of different weapons—countless brave heroes—have also fallen. Even my son Indrajit, famous for his strength and skill, once captured Rama and Lakshmana with magical arrows granted as boons. I can’t understand what power, magic, or incredible energy helped those brothers—Rama and Lakshmana—escape bonds that not even the gods, the strongest Asuras, or the Yakshas, Gandharvas, or Nagas could break. All the Rakshasa warriors I sent out have been wiped out by these unbelievably strong monkeys. I don’t see anyone left who can kill Rama and Lakshmana now, along with their army and Sugriva and Vibhishana. Rama must truly be powerful—his strength with weapons is unreal. Anyone who goes up against him ends up dead. We need to guard this palace everywhere, with alert soldiers at every post—and also the Ashoka grove where Sita is being kept. We must always know who comes in and goes out. You should stay with your troops wherever there are garrisons. At evening, midnight, and dawn, the Rakshasas should keep watch on the monkeys’ movements. Never underestimate the monkeys. Find out if the enemy is making new moves, advancing, or just staying where they are.” The Rakshasas, all mighty warriors, did exactly as Ravana ordered. After giving these instructions, Ravana—the king of the Rakshasas—still burning with anger, looking defeated and alone, went back to his private chambers. Inside, his rage flared up as he thought about the danger facing his son, and he kept sighing again and again, consumed by worry.

The surviving Rakshasas rushed to Rāvana and told him that all the greatest among the Rakshasas—Devāntaka, Triçiras, Atikāya, and the rest—had been killed. When Rāvana heard this sudden, devastating news, his eyes filled with tears. The loss of his sons and brothers crushed him with grief. Seeing his father broken and drowning in sorrow, Indrajit (Rāvana’s son and a master warrior) spoke up. “Father, you shouldn’t let this grief overwhelm you. As long as Indrajit lives, there’s hope. Rāma and Lakshmana won’t escape me alive. Today, you’ll see Rāma and Lakshmana lying dead on the battlefield, their bodies shredded by my arrows. Listen to my vow, made in the name of my power and divine gifts: today, I will kill Rāma and Lakshmana with arrows that never miss. Let the gods—Indra, Yama (Vaivaçwata), Vishnu, Rudra, the Sādhyas, Vaiçwas, humans, the Sun, and the Moon—all witness my strength, as fierce as Vishnu’s at Vāli’s sacrifice.” After making this promise, Indrajit, glowing with energy, took his father’s permission and climbed into a war chariot as fast as the wind. The chariot was pulled by donkeys and loaded with every kind of weapon. Indrajit looked like a god as he rode out, determined to destroy his enemies. Behind him, countless powerful Rakshasas marched, bows in hand. Some rode elephants, some horses, some bears, predators, lions, and jackals. Some Rakshasas with terrifying power rode crows, swans, or peacocks. They carried spears, clubs, axes, and maces. The air was filled with the blaring of conch shells and the thunder of drums. Indrajit, under a white umbrella like a full moon, looked like the moon in the night sky. Adorned in gold and fanned by a golden fan, he shone like the sun. With Indrajit set out, Lanka looked as dazzling as the sky with the glowing sun.

When Indrajit reached the battlefield, he arranged his troops around his chariot. Then, using secret mantras, he began a fire ritual. He offered fragrant garlands and puffed rice to the fire, using weapons as ritual tools and Bibhitaka fruits as fuel. He had red cloth and an iron ladle. After lighting the fire and making offerings with spears, Indrajit grabbed the neck of a live goat as part of the ceremony. The smokeless fire blazed up, showing signs of victory. Suddenly, the fire god himself appeared, golden and swirling his right tongue, and accepted the offering. With this, Indrajit received the Brahma weapon from the fire god and chanted mantras over his bow and chariot. As the weapon was invoked and the god worshipped, the sky, suns, stars, and planets seemed to tremble in fear. Now blessed with the power of fire and Indra, Indrajit, armed with bows, swords, and spears, vanished into the sky. The Rakshasa army, fired up for battle, charged in with their horses and chariots, banners flying. They unleashed a rain of sharp arrows, spears, and hooks at the monkey army, killing many. Indrajit, furious, encouraged his fellow Rakshasas, “Fight with all your strength and destroy these monkeys!” Roaring for victory, the Rakshasas barraged the monkeys with arrows. Surrounded by Rakshasas, Indrajit himself hurled deadly arrows, maces, and clubs at the monkeys. The monkeys, terrified, responded by hurling trees and boulders at Indrajit. But Indrajit, with incredible energy, shot arrows that pierced the monkeys’ bodies. With a single arrow, he could kill seven or nine monkeys at once. His golden-tipped arrows tore through the monkeys, causing them to collapse in pain, much like demons falling before the gods. Enraged, the surviving monkeys chased after Indrajit, who blazed like the sun and rained down arrows as if they were sunbeams. The monkeys, bleeding and in agony, tried to rally for Rāma and launched more rocks and tree trunks at Indrajit. But Indrajit, unstoppable, blocked the attack and shot arrows like fire or poisonous snakes into the monkey ranks. He hit Gandhamādana with eighteen arrows and wounded Nila from a distance with nine. He struck Mainda with seven arrows that cut deep, Gaja with five, Jāmbavān with ten, and Nila with thirty. Using special arrows granted by boons, he nearly killed Sugriva, Rishabha, Angada, and Dwivida. Indrajit, wild with rage and as destructive as the five elements at world’s end, targeted all the leading monkeys with a storm of arrows. Suddenly, Indrajit vanished from sight—using his magical powers to become invisible. Hidden, he continued to rain deadly arrows on the monkeys, just as black storm clouds unleash torrents of rain. The monkeys, pierced and dying, fell like mountains shattered by Indra’s thunderbolt, their cries echoing across the field. They could only see the deadly arrows flying; Indrajit, thanks to his magic, could not be seen. Indrajit’s arrows, like sunlight, filled the sky and struck down the best of the monkey warriors. He hurled burning weapons—darts, axes, and more—that looked like exploding fireballs, devastating the monkey army. Wounded by Indrajit’s arrows, the monkey leaders looked like blood-red flowers. Some monkeys, shot in the eyes, stared helplessly at the sky before collapsing. Others tried to hide or huddle together, but fell to the ground. Indrajit, with enchanted spears, darts, and arrows, wounded all the great monkeys: Hanumān, Sugriva, Angada, Gandhamādana, Jāmbavān, Sushena, Vegadarçin, Mainda, Dwivida, Nila, Gavāksha, Gavaya, Kesari, Hariloman, Vidyutdanshtra, Suryanāna, Jyotimukha, Dadhimukha, Pāvakāksha, Nala, and Kumuda. After attacking all these leaders with golden maces, Indrajit turned his arrows on Rāma and Lakshmana, bombarding them with arrows like rays of the sun. Rāma, unfazed by the storm of arrows, turned to Lakshmana and said, “Lakshmana, this Rakshasa lord, Indrajit, has gained the Brahma weapon. He’s destroyed the monkey army and now he’s coming for us with magical arrows. He’s invisible because of a boon from the god Brahma. How can we fight someone who is attacking but can’t be seen? The god who gave him this boon is beyond understanding, and the weapon he uses is a part of his power. All we can do is endure this attack together. Let Indrajit fill the sky with his arrows. With our strongest monkeys fallen and us lying unconscious, he’ll think he’s won and leave the battlefield.” As Indrajit trapped them in a web of arrows, Rāma and Lakshmana suffered badly. Indrajit, triumphant, cheered and quickly returned to Lanka, ruled by his ten-headed father. The Rakshasas celebrated him, and Indrajit, full of pride, told his father everything that had happened.
Hutabhoktāram—“eater of sacrificial offerings”—is another name for the fire god.
SECTION LXXIII
[268] This means the deity connected to the weapon was called upon.
Indrajit.
SECTION LXXIV

The battlefield was eerily still—Sugriva, Nila, Angada, Jāmbavān, and the rest of the monkey leaders lay motionless, their army paralyzed by defeat. No one moved. Sensing their despair, Bibhishana, the wise brother of Ravana, tried to lift their spirits. “Warriors of the monkey king,” he said, “don’t let fear overwhelm you. This is not the time for grief. The two sons of Dasharatha—Rama and Lakshmana—may look wounded and helpless after Indrajit’s attack, but they’re actually honoring the Brahma weapon. Brahma himself gave this weapon, and the princes are respecting its power by lying still, as tradition demands. So, don’t lose hope!” Encouraged by Bibhishana’s words, Hanuman replied, “So many of our swift monkey fighters have fallen to this weapon. Let’s go and check on those who are still alive.” Hanuman and Bibhishana, both holding burning torches, wandered the battlefield, seeing the ground covered with monkeys lying like mountains among scattered weapons. Some monkeys had lost tails, hands, thighs, legs, fingers, or even their heads. Blood flowed from the wounded; some were so terrified they lost control of their bladders. Bibhishana and Hanuman found Sugriva, Angada, Nila, Gandhamadana, Jāmbavān, Sushena, Vegadarshin, Mainda, Nala, Jyotimukha, and Dwivida—all barely alive. They saw that sixty-seven crore (670 million) monkeys had been killed by Indrajit in just a fifth of a day. Looking over this devastated army, as wild as a stormy sea, Hanuman and Bibhishana began searching for Jāmbavān.

Eventually, they found Jāmbavān, the ancient bear-king and son of Prajapati, wounded and weakened by age, lying like a dying ember, pierced by hundreds of arrows. Bibhishana called out, “Jāmbavān, are you still alive after being hit by all those sharp arrows?” With great effort, Jāmbavān managed to answer, “Bibhishana, I recognize your voice, mighty rakshasa. I’ve been hit so many times I can’t see you. But tell me—does Hanuman, son of the wind-god, still live? He is the hope of our side.” Bibhishana was surprised. “Why do you ask about Hanuman before Rama or Sugriva?” he asked. “You care more for Hanuman than even the king or Rama himself.”

Jāmbavān replied, “Let me explain. As long as Hanuman lives, there’s hope. If he’s gone, we might as well be dead already, even if we’re still breathing. If that mighty son of the wind-god, as powerful as his father or even fire itself, is alive—then our side still has a chance.” Just then, Hanuman approached Jāmbavān and bowed at his feet. Hearing Hanuman’s voice, Jāmbavān felt his hope and strength return. He told Hanuman, “You’re the only one who can save the monkeys now. This is your moment. No one else can do it. You must cheer up the bears and monkeys and heal the wounded. There’s only one way: leap across the ocean to Mount Himavan, the greatest of mountains. There you’ll find the golden Rishabha peak and the mighty summit of Kailasa. Between them lies a mountain filled with healing herbs. On its top you’ll find four glowing medicinal plants: Mritasanjivani (which brings back the dead), Vishalyakarani (which heals wounds), Suvarnakarani (which restores lost youth), and Sandhani (which joins broken bones). Bring these herbs back quickly, Hanuman, and save us.”

With Jāmbavān’s words fueling his spirit, Hanuman’s energy surged like a stormy ocean. He climbed to the top of Trikuta mountain, stomping so hard the mountain groaned under his feet, looking like a second mountain himself. Trees toppled, the ground shook, and flames flickered from the force of his movements. The peaks crumbled under his steps, and the monkeys who lived there fled as the mountain trembled, its slopes littered with splintered trees and rocks. In Lanka, the city’s giant gates rattled, doors broke, and the whole city seemed to quake in fear, as if dancing in terror. Hanuman, massive as a mountain, shook the earth and seas with his power. He bellowed, his mouth wide as a horse’s, sending out terrifying roars that echoed through the night and scared the rakshasas. He bowed to the ocean, then, thinking of his mission for Rama, Hanuman readied himself to leap. He coiled his tail like a snake, bent his back, pulled back his ears, and opened his mouth wide—then launched himself into the sky.

His leap was so powerful that he pulled along whole tracts of trees, boulders, and even some smaller monkeys, who tumbled into the ocean as they lost momentum. With arms stretched like giant snakes, Hanuman flew toward the Himalayas, shaking the world as he went, roaring so loudly that all directions seemed to tremble. He crossed the raging sea, disturbing the animals below, moving as fast as Vishnu’s discus. As he sped along, Hanuman saw hills, rivers, lakes, cities, and fertile lands flash by. Like his father, the wind-god, he couldn’t be tired, pushing forward with unstoppable force. Remembering Jāmbavān’s instructions, Hanuman soon spotted Mount Himavan, covered in waterfalls, caves, and streams, with golden peaks shining like pale clouds and forests of every kind.

Arriving at the majestic mountain, Hanuman saw sacred hermitages where the greatest sages lived. He saw famous sites like Brahmakoṣa, Rajatālaya, Sakrālaya, Rudracharapramoksha, Hayānana, the blazing Brahmaśiras, and the homes of Yama’s servants. He passed the Fire-god’s abode, the home of Kubera, the brilliant place where the suns meet, Brahma’s own house, Shiva’s bow, and the very navel of the earth. He saw terrifying Kailasa, the stone seat of Shiva, the bull of the mountain, and the golden peaks—all glowing with healing herbs. Seeing the mountain glowing like fire, Hanuman was amazed. He leapt onto the mountain of medicines and began searching for the magical plants Jāmbavān had described. But the herbs, knowing he was coming, turned invisible to test him.

Frustrated and angry, Hanuman’s eyes blazed. He shouted, “Why do you refuse to help Rama, lord of the mountains? You leave me no choice—I’ll tear your summit apart!” With a sudden burst of strength, Hanuman ripped up the mountain’s peak, roots, trees, elephants, and all, its slopes blazing and covered with gold and ore. Uprooting the mighty summit, he leapt into the sky, terrifying the gods and spirits who watched. As he flew, the beings of the air praised him, and with the sunlit mountain in his hands, he looked like another sun flying through the sky. Hanuman and the mountain shone so brightly that he seemed like Vishnu, carrying his blazing discus. The monkeys cheered when they saw him returning, and Hanuman shouted back in excitement. The cheers echoed so loudly in Lanka that the rakshasas tried to shout even louder in reply.

Hanuman landed in the middle of the monkey army, bowing to the leaders and hugging Bibhishana. As soon as the scent of the magical herbs reached Rama, Lakshmana, and the monkeys, their wounds healed instantly. Even those who had been killed stood up, revived—like people waking up at dawn after a deep sleep. Ever since the war began, any rakshasas killed by the monkeys had been thrown into the sea to protect their honor. Now Hanuman, son of the wind-god, sped back to Himavan to return the mountain’s summit, then hurried back to Rama, ready for the final battle.
