SECTION LXXV

Sugriva, the powerful king of the monkeys, turned to Hanuman and said, “Now that Kumbhakarna and the princes have been killed, Ravana can’t defend Lanka any longer. Let the strongest and fastest monkeys grab torches and rush the city.” As the sun set and night took over, the leading monkeys, torches in hand, charged toward Lanka. The Rakshasas guarding the gates—fierce-eyed and ready—panicked and ran when the monkeys attacked with fire. The monkeys cheered and set fire to the gates, upper rooms, wide streets, narrow alleys, and all kinds of buildings. The flames tore through thousands of mansions, and the huge, mountain-like buildings collapsed to the ground. Expensive woods like aguru and sandalwood burned, along with pearls, shining gems, diamonds, and coral. Linen, fine silk, woolen clothes, golden cups, weapons, horse gear, elephant ropes, armor, and chariots—all went up in flames. Swords, bows, arrows, spears, hooks, and darts were destroyed. Blankets, feather fans, tiger-skins, musk, and other valuables burned. Pearls and precious stones melted, and the fire roared through homes everywhere. The flames devoured piles of weapons and the homes of both Rakshasas and regular citizens. The fire raged on, destroying hundreds and thousands of houses—homes filled with gold armor and jewelry, wild-eyed from drink or anger, holding weapons, eating, drinking, or sleeping with their lovers, or running away in terror with their children. Solid, wealthy mansions with countless rooms, decorated with golden moons and crescents, beautiful rooftops, colorful windows, and platforms set with rubies and lapis, all seemed to touch the sun before they fell. The city rang with the cries of cranes, peacocks, and the jingling of jewelry as the buildings burned. The flaming gates looked like storm clouds lit by lightning, or mountain peaks ablaze in a forest fire. Beautiful women, startled from sleep in their tall towers, threw off their jewelry and screamed as the fire reached them. Buildings crumbled like mountaintops struck by lightning. From a distance, the burning city looked like the glowing peaks of the Himalayas. The fire and the bright rooftops made the night in Lanka look like it was full of blooming red flowers. Elephants and horses broke loose and ran wild in the chaos, making Lanka seem like a stormy ocean full of crazed sea monsters. Sometimes, elephants ran from the sight of panicking horses, and sometimes horses froze at the sight of terrified elephants. With the city burning, the sea reflected the red flames, turning the water crimson. In moments, the city set on fire by the monkeys looked like the world ending in flames. The screams of women, choked by smoke and heat, could be heard for miles and miles. Burned and desperate Rakshasas ran from their homes, only to be attacked on the spot by monkeys eager to fight. The battle cries of monkeys and the screams of Rakshasas echoed through the ten directions, across the ocean, and the earth itself.

Meanwhile, Rama and Lakshmana, now healed from their wounds, calmly picked up their powerful bows. Rama strung his legendary bow, and the sound it made was so loud and terrifying that it shook the Rakshasas to their core. Rama, drawing his deadly bow, looked like the furious god Shiva, filled with divine energy. The twang of his bow drowned out the roars of both monkeys and Rakshasas—its sound alone filled the air. Between the cries of the monkeys, the screams of the Rakshasas, and the ringing of Rama’s bow, the whole world seemed to echo with noise. Rama’s arrows smashed the city’s gate—so massive it looked like Mount Kailasa—splintering it to pieces. When the Rakshasas saw Rama’s arrows striking their chariots and homes, they scrambled to prepare for battle. The top Rakshasas, roaring for war, made the night feel like the night of doom. Sugriva ordered the leading monkeys, “Attack the gate! And if any of you tries to run away, take them down by force.” The strongest monkeys gathered at the gate with their torches, and Ravana was filled with a rage as intense as a storm god. As he yawned, the wind from his mouth seemed to fill all directions. Furious, Ravana sent Kumbha and Nikumbha—the sons of Kumbhakarna—alongside countless Rakshasas, to lead the counterattack. At Ravana’s command, warriors like Yupaksha, Sonitaksha, Prajangha, and Kampana joined Kumbhakarna’s sons. Roaring like lions, Ravana ordered, “Go out and fight today!” The Rakshasa heroes, weapons blazing, surged out with deafening roars. Their armor and jewelry shone, lighting up the night sky alongside the fires set by the monkeys. The moon and stars, together with the glitter of armor and the red glare of burning buildings, lit up the battlefield—monkeys and Rakshasas facing off under a surreal glow. The light from burning homes reflected on the waves, making the sea look strangely beautiful. The terrifying Rakshasa army, bristling with banners, swords, strange weapons, fierce horses, chariots, elephants, spears, clubs, scimitars, and bows, charged forward. Their golden armor sparkled, their garlands filled the air with scent, and their battle cries sounded like crashing waves. When the monkeys saw how unbeatable the Rakshasa army looked, they rallied and yelled even louder. The Rakshasas attacked with wild energy, like moths drawn to a flame. Swinging clubs and hammers, they looked fierce and unstoppable. The monkeys, desperate for battle, threw themselves at the Rakshasas with rocks, trees, and their bare fists. Rakshasas, skilled with sharp arrows, sliced off the heads of falling monkeys. All around, Rakshasas fought with torn ears, smashed heads, or crushed limbs from the monkeys’ onslaught. Grim-faced Rakshasas attacked with swords, cutting down monkeys everywhere. Sometimes, someone about to kill another was himself killed first; someone about to knock down an enemy was knocked down instead; and those trading insults or blows found the tables quickly turned. Some challenged, “Come on, then!” and their opponents answered, “I’m coming! Why make it harder? Wait for me.” The chaos was wild and personal. The battle between monkeys and Rakshasas was brutal—arms and armor scattered everywhere, huge spears raised, blows landing, and strange weapons like ploughs used in the fight. Rakshasas killed monkeys in groups, sometimes ten at a time, sometimes seven. But the monkeys surrounded the Rakshasa forces, their clothes torn off and their armor and banners scattered across the battlefield.

SECTION LXXVI

As the brutal and chaotic battle raged on, Angada (Vali’s son), keen for a fight, went straight for the warrior Kampana. Kampana, angry and ready, launched himself at Angada and smashed him with his mace. The blow made Angada stagger, but he quickly regained his footing and hurled a massive mountain peak at his foe. The impact was so powerful that Kampana collapsed to the ground, dead. Watching Kampana fall, Sonitaksha jumped into his chariot and charged fearlessly at Angada. He shot a barrage of razor-sharp arrows—Kshuras (razor-edged), Kshurapras (crescent-tipped), Narachas (iron arrows), Vatsadantas (calf-tooth shaped), Silimkhas (feathered like the Kanka bird), Karnis (double-bladed), Salas (short-leaded), and Vipas (karavira-tipped), along with many other wicked arrows—each arrow cutting into Angada like flames of death.

But Angada, son of Vali, powerful and resilient, though his body was pierced by arrows, smashed Sonitaksha’s chariot, destroyed his weapons, and snapped his fearsome bow. With his car and weapons gone, Sonitaksha quickly grabbed his sword and shield, leaping toward Angada without hesitation. Angada, incredibly fast, grabbed Sonitaksha’s sword from him, shouted out, and, swinging it down at Sonitaksha’s shoulder, sliced him in half diagonally—just like a sacred thread worn across the body. With a triumphant yell, Angada seized the terrifying sword and charged at the next Rakshasa warriors.

Now, the strong and brave Yupaksha, along with Prajangha, drove their chariot furiously toward Angada, determined for revenge. Sonitaksha, having caught his breath, picked up an iron mace decorated with a golden armlet and charged at Angada again. Prajangha, equally fired up, came at Angada with a massive mace, Yupaksha at his side. With Angada between Sonitaksha and Prajangha, he looked like the full Moon nestled between the stars of the Visakha constellation.

Mainda and Dwivida stood by Angada, guarding him and eager to see what would happen in this deadly clash. The giant Rakshasas, full of rage and armed with swords, arrows, and maces, attacked the monkeys. The battle between the three monkey chiefs and the three fearsome Rakshasas was so intense it could make anyone’s hair stand on end.

The monkeys grabbed trees and hurled them at their enemies, but Prajangha slashed them all down with his sword. The monkeys rained rocks and trees onto their foes’ chariots, but the ultra-strong Yupaksha shot them out of the air with arrow after arrow. Sonitaksha, wielding his mace, smashed the trees that Dwivida and Mainda threw. Prajangha, moving quickly, charged at Angada, sword raised—a blade so sharp it could pierce even the heartwood of ancient trees.

Seeing Prajangha coming, Angada, the monkey lord, ripped up an Aswakarna tree and slammed it against Prajangha’s arm, knocking away his sword. When Prajangha’s weapon fell, Angada balled his fist and punched him in the head with a force like lightning. For a moment, Prajangha wavered from the hit, but then Angada, regaining his focus, struck again—this time severing Prajangha’s head from his body with a single mighty blow.

Watching his uncle killed, Yupaksha’s eyes filled with tears. Out of arrows, he jumped down from his chariot and grabbed a sword. Dwivida, angry at the sight, ran at Yupaksha, struck him hard in the chest, and grabbed hold of him. Seeing his brother in trouble, Sonitaksha struck Dwivida hard in the chest. The blow shook Dwivida, but he managed to grab Sonitaksha’s raised mace.

As all this chaos unfolded, Mainda rushed to help Dwivida. Sonitaksha and Yupaksha, determined, tried to drag the two monkeys away by force. But Dwivida slashed Sonitaksha’s face with his sharp nails and slammed him to the ground, pinning him with all his might. Meanwhile, Mainda, burning with anger, wrapped his arms around Yupaksha, crushing him until he dropped dead.

With their greatest warriors dead, the Rakshasa army broke and fled in fear, running to Kumbhakarna’s son, Kumbha, for help. Kumbha, seeing his forces routed by the victorious monkeys, rallied the fleeing Rakshasas and began to show off his own incredible fighting skills.

Kumbha took up his bow and fired arrows that looked like deadly snakes, sharp enough to punch through armor and bone. His bow, shining with gold and lightning, looked like the mighty bow of Indra, king of the gods. Drawing the string back as far as it would go, he struck Dwivida with a feathered, gold-tipped arrow. The hit was so fierce that Dwivida, glowing like the peak of Mount Trikuta, fell to the ground, knocked out cold with his legs sprawled.

Mainda, seeing his brother fall, flew into a rage. He grabbed a huge boulder and hurled it at Kumbha, but Kumbha shot it apart with fire-tipped arrows. Then, firing more sharp arrows like venomous snakes, Kumbha struck Mainda in the chest. Wounded to the core, Mainda collapsed, unconscious.

Watching both his uncles (Mainda and Dwivida) go down, Angada charged at Kumbha, who stood ready with his bow. As Angada closed in, Kumbha fired more arrows, piercing him like spears would pierce an elephant. He kept shooting, each arrow sharp, gold-tipped, and deadly.

Even though Angada was riddled with arrows, he refused to back down, hurling rocks and trees at Kumbha over and over. Kumbha, skilled and calm, sliced every stone and tree out of the air with his arrows. When Angada jumped at him again, Kumbha fired more arrows at him on the ground, the shafts striking like brands of fire—blood poured from Angada’s eyes.

Blinded, Angada covered his eyes with one hand and, with the other, grabbed a huge sala tree nearby. He braced the trunk against his chest, stripped off the branches and leaves, and prepared to use the massive tree as a weapon. In full view of the Rakshasas, he hurled it at Kumbha—like hurling Indra’s own banner. But Kumbha split the tree apart with seven sharp arrows before it could reach him.

The force of seeing his tree destroyed and the pain of his wounds overwhelmed Angada, and he fell unconscious. The monkeys, shocked to see the mighty Angada down, ran to tell Rama (Raghava) what had happened.

Rama, hearing that Vali’s son had fallen in this brutal fight, ordered his top warriors—led by Jambavan—to help. Fired up by Rama’s command, the monkeys charged Kumbha, who stood ready with his bow. Eyes red with fury, they grabbed rocks and trees, determined to protect Angada.

Jambavan, Sushena, and the monkey Vegadarshi rushed at Kumbha in a rage. Kumbha responded by covering them with a rain of arrows so thick it was like a boulder blocking a river. The arrows flew so densely that, just as the ocean can’t see its shores, the monkeys couldn’t even see their own hands.

Watching his warriors suffer, Sugriva, king of the monkeys, picked up his nephew Angada and carried him on his back. Then Sugriva charged at Kumbha like a lion attacking an elephant on a mountainside. He ripped up huge aswakarna trees and other giant trees, flinging them at Kumbha. Kumbha, with lightning-fast arrows, cut every tree from the sky—none could touch him. The shattered trees fell like weapons themselves.

Sugriva, seeing his attacks foiled, wasn’t discouraged. Instead, he pushed through the arrow barrage and grabbed Kumbha’s bow, which gleamed like Indra’s. With a powerful leap, Sugriva pulled off a difficult move, snatching the bow away. Enraged, he spoke to Kumbha (who now looked like a tuskless elephant): “Kumbha, brother of Nikumbha, your strength, your skill, your humility, and your bravery are incredible—just like your father Kumbhakarna and uncle Ravana. You’re as strong as Prahlada, Vali, Indra, Varuna, or Kubera. You’re following in your father’s legendary footsteps. Even the gods would struggle to fight you. Show me what you’re made of, and watch what I can do. Your uncle stands against gods and demons only because of a boon, but your father fought them with his own power. In bowmanship you match Indrajit, in strength you match Ravana, and today you’re the greatest of Rakshasas. Let everyone witness our battle—it will be as epic as Indra versus Samvara. You’ve shown amazing skill, and you’ve brought down heroic monkeys. But I won’t kill you while you’re tired, since people might blame me for striking you at your weakest. Rest up, then see my power!”

Kumbha, fired up by Sugriva’s words, grew even more intense. He grabbed Sugriva by the arms, and the two of them locked together like two wild, rutting elephants. They wrestled, breathing heavily, gripping each other so tightly that steam and sparks seemed to fly from their mouths. Their stomping cracked the earth and made the sea churn with massive waves.

Sugriva suddenly lifted Kumbha completely off the ground and hurled him into the ocean, forcing Kumbha to taste the sea. The splash sent huge waves rolling in every direction, as if mountains had fallen into the water. Kumbha sprang up from the water and yanked Sugriva down, punching him in the chest with all his fury—a blow like a bolt of lightning. Sugriva’s skin broke open, blood pouring out, and the impact snapped his bones. The force of the blow even kindled a fiery blaze at that spot, like a thunderbolt splitting Mount Meru.

But Sugriva, though badly hurt, fought back. He clenched his fingers into a fist shining like the sun and punched Kumbha right in the chest. The blow was so fierce that Kumbha lost consciousness and crashed to the ground, like a fire suddenly extinguished. The Rakshasa fell like the planet Lohitanga (Mars) dropping from the sky, driven by fate.

Kumbha’s body hit the earth with his chest shattered, looking like the sun defeated by the god Rudra. With Kumbha slain by the mightiest of monkeys, the earth itself trembled and fear swept through the Rakshasa army.
SECTION LXXVII

Watching his brother get killed by Sugriva, Nikumbha glared at the king of the monkeys, his eyes burning with rage. Despite his anger, Nikumbha kept his cool and grabbed a massive club wrapped in garlands, with an iron ring as thick as a hand. It gleamed with gold plating and was decorated with diamonds and sapphires, making it look like Yama’s own weapon—fierce and able to strike terror into anyone, even Rakshasas. Nikumbha, powerful and wild, spun this club above his head and let out a roar, his mouth wide open. He looked impressive, his chest covered in gold, fancy armbands (angadas) on his arms, and bright, colorful earrings swinging as he moved. With all his jewelry and that huge club, Nikumbha was like a thundercloud lit up by flashes of lightning and streaked with a rainbow. The head of his club seemed to rip through the sky like a silent, smokeless flame. As Nikumbha swung his weapon, the whole sky seemed to spin, along with the mystical city of the Gandharvas, the planets, stars, and the moon. Nikumbha was almost untouchable, blazing with fury and shining with his weapons and jewels. Everyone—monkeys and Rakshasas alike—froze in fear. But Hanuman, the hero, puffed out his chest and stood his ground.

Just then, Nikumbha, his arms as thick as clubs, hurled his massive weapon straight at Hanuman’s chest. It hit Hanuman hard, but instead of knocking him down, the club shattered into a hundred pieces. The shards scattered across the sky, looking like bursts of fire. Hanuman didn’t even flinch; he stood firm, like a mountain unmoved by an earthquake. Furious, Hanuman, the most powerful of the monkeys, clenched his fist and, moving at lightning speed, punched Nikumbha square in the chest. The blow tore Nikumbha’s armor and blood spurted out. A strange light flashed from Nikumbha’s chest, then vanished as quickly as lightning fading in a cloud.

Staggered by Hanuman’s punch, Nikumbha managed to recover and lunged at Hanuman, grabbing him and lifting him off the ground. The people of Lanka cheered, thinking Hanuman was done for. But Hanuman, humiliated by the Rakshasa, smashed Nikumbha with his iron-hard fist. Breaking free from Nikumbha’s grip, Hanuman landed solidly back on the ground. Furious now, Hanuman knocked Nikumbha down, then leaped up with incredible force and sat on Nikumbha’s chest. With a roar, Hanuman grabbed Nikumbha’s head in both hands and twisted, ripping it off his body.

With Nikumbha dead—killed by the son of the wind god—a brutal battle broke out between Rama’s army and Ravana’s Rakshasa forces, both sides furious. The monkeys shouted in triumph, their cries echoing everywhere. The earth itself shook, and the homes of the gods trembled. The Rakshasas were left terrified by what had happened.
Mahendra is the name of a mountain.
This describes how big the club (parigha) is.
This could also mean Kumbha.
Some say the city is Vitapabati; others call it Alaka.
Literally, arms as thick as clubs.
Some versions say “skin” instead of “armor”—meaning Hanuman’s punch tore Nikumbha’s skin, which shows just how strong Hanuman is.
SECTION LXXVIII

When Rāvana saw that Kumbha and Nikumbha had been killed, his anger flared up like a raging fire. Overwhelmed by both rage and grief, Rāvana (also known as Nairita) turned to Makarāksha, the wide-eyed son of Khara, and ordered, “Go now, take the army, and destroy Rāghava (Rāma) and Lakshmana, along with all the monkeys.” Makarāksha, confident in his own strength, gladly replied to Rāvana, “It will be done.” He bowed and circled Rāvana respectfully before leaving the palace. Makarāksha then called out to the nearby commander, “Bring my chariot here at once, and gather all the soldiers.” At his command, the chief of the night-dwelling Rākshasas quickly brought the army and the chariot forward. Circling the chariot, Makarāksha turned to his driver and said, “Charioteer, get ready—drive the chariot quickly.” 

Makarāksha then addressed his fellow Rākshasas, “All of you, fight up front with me. The mighty Rāvana, our lord, has commanded me to kill Rāma and Lakshmana in battle. Today, with my best arrows, I will destroy Rāma, Lakshmana, Sugriva, and all the other monkeys. Just like fire burning dry wood, I will wipe out the monkey army with my weapons.” Fired up by Makarāksha’s words, the powerful Rākshasas prepared for battle. They armed themselves with various weapons and, using their shape-shifting powers, took on terrifying forms—crooked, with wild hair, sharp fangs, blood-red eyes, and loud roars like elephants. Surrounding Khara’s huge-bodied son, these monstrous Rākshasas marched forward, shaking the ground with their sheer mass. 

Suddenly, a deafening noise erupted all around—the blaring of conches, thousands of bugles, and the clashing of warriors’ arms. But then, bad omens appeared: the charioteer lost his grip on the reins, and the Rākshasas’ flag toppled to the ground. The horses slowed down, hanging their heads, and a violent, dust-filled wind whipped through the air as the evil-hearted Makarāksha marched out to war. Ignoring these ominous signs, the mighty Rākshasas pressed on toward Rāma and Lakshmana. Their skin was as black as storm clouds, elephants, or buffaloes, and they bore scars from swords and maces. All of them were expert fighters, darting across the battlefield and shouting, “I’m going first!”
Nairita is another name for Rāvana.
SECTION LXXIX

When Makarāksha (Makaraksha) came out ready for battle, the leading monkeys suddenly leaped forward, preparing to fight. Immediately, a brutal and terrifying clash broke out between the night-dwelling Rākshasas and the monkeys, like a war between gods and demons. Both sides smashed into each other using trees, spears, clubs, and iron bars. The Rākshasas attacked the monkeys with a storm of weapons—saktis (throwing spikes), swords, maces, spears, javelins, pattiças, Vindipalas (iron spears), arrows, nooses, and clubs. Khara’s son, Makarāksha, fired deadly arrows that struck fear into the monkeys, making them flee in terror. Seeing the monkeys running away, the victorious Rākshasas roared like lions in a frenzy. As the monkeys scattered in all directions, Rāma unleashed a wave of arrows at the Rākshasas. Watching his warriors fall under Rāma's attack, Makarāksha, burning with rage, shouted, “Wait, Rāma, don’t run! Let’s fight one-on-one. I’ll end your life with my sharp arrows. You killed my father in the Dandaka forest. Remembering what you did, and finding you in front of me now, my anger is burning hotter than ever. Rāghava, you evil soul, I’m furious that I couldn’t find you back then in that forest. But today, by good fortune, I finally have you—like a starving lion finding its prey. Soon, my arrows will send you to the world of demons, where you’ll join the heroes you killed before. No need for more talk, Rāma—just listen. Everyone here will witness both our strengths on the battlefield. Use whatever weapon or club you’re best with—come fight me, Rāma!” 

Rāma, son of Dasaratha, listened to Makarāksha’s rant and smiled before replying, “Rākshasa, what’s the point of all this trash talk? No one wins a fight by talking—only by actually fighting. I killed your father, along with fourteen thousand Rākshasas, Triçira, and Dushana, in the Dandaka forest. When I kill you today, vultures, crows, and jackals will feast on your body.” 

Enraged, Makarāksha launched a volley of sharp arrows at Rāma. Rāma shot them down mid-air, splitting the gold-feathered arrows so they fell uselessly to the ground. The fight between Khara’s son and Dasaratha’s son grew even fiercer. The battlefield echoed with the shouts of warriors and the twang of bowstrings, sounding like thunder in the clouds. Gods, demons, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and giant serpents gathered in the sky to watch the incredible duel. Both fighters were wounded by each other's arrows, but their determination only grew stronger. They attacked and countered each other fiercely. Makarāksha shot down Rāma’s arrows, and Rāma did the same to Makarāksha’s. Arrows filled the sky so thickly that nothing on the ground or in the air could be seen.

Anger flaring, Rāghava (Rāma) broke Makarāksha’s bow and pierced his charioteer with eight arrows. Then Rāma smashed the chariot, killed the horses, and brought the whole thing crashing down. Makarāksha was thrown to the ground but quickly jumped back up, holding a massive spear that struck fear into everyone—he looked as terrifying as the god of destruction himself. This huge, shining weapon had been gifted to him by Shiva, and even the gods were afraid of it. Burning with anger, Makarāksha hurled the blazing spear at Rāma. Rāma immediately fired four arrows, shattering the spear in mid-air. The weapon broke into pieces, its golden feathers scattering as it crashed to the earth like a falling fireball. Seeing Rāma destroy the spear, everyone watching from the sky cheered, “Well done! Well done!”

Furious, Makarāksha clenched his fists and shouted at Rāma, “Stay! Don’t run!”

Seeing him charge, Rāma—the descendant of Raghu—smiled and fitted a blazing arrow to his bow. He fired, and the arrow struck Makarāksha, killing him instantly. Makarāksha fell to the ground, his heart pierced, and died. The other Rākshasas, terrified by Rāma’s attack, ran back toward Lanka. Seeing Khara’s son slain by Rāma’s arrows—like a mountain shattered by a bolt of lightning—the gods rejoiced in delight.
A short arrow thrown by hand or shot from a tube.
An iron spear or dart.
Another verse found in some texts says: “And the birds drinking your blood shall fly away in all directions.”
This refers to Shiva’s weapon of destruction—since, in Hindu mythology, Shiva is the god of destruction.
SECTION LXXX

When Rāvana heard that Makarāksha had been killed, his anger burned even hotter. Grinding his teeth in fury, he tried to figure out his next move. Finally, he called his son Indrajit (also called Meghanāda) and ordered him to go to the battlefield. “You are a great warrior, Indrajit,” he said. “Whether you hide in the clouds or face them head-on, kill those two brothers, Rāma and Lakshmana. You once defeated Indra himself—how could you hesitate to kill mere mortals?” Obeying his father, Indrajit first went to a sacrificial altar to perform a ritual for strength. Some female demons with red turbans stood by respectfully as Indrajit made offerings into the fire. For this ritual, he used sara grass as the sacrificial leaves, Beleric myrobalan wood as fuel, red cloth, and iron ladles. He spread fire all around with the sara leaves and spears, and grabbed a live black goat by the neck as a sacrifice. The fire, fed with the offerings, blazed up without any smoke, and good omens appeared, signaling victory. The flames shone like gold and moved south, eagerly receiving clarified butter as an offering. Indrajit offered sacrifices not just to the fire, but also to gods, demons, and other spirits. Then he climbed into his magnificent chariot, which soon vanished from sight. His chariot was pulled by four horses and armed with a huge bow and sharp arrows. It glowed with its own light, decorated with gold, paintings of deer, and a crescent moon. Gold bracelets circled it, and flags made of precious stones fluttered in the wind, making the chariot look like a blazing fire. Indrajit was protected by weapons blessed by Brahmā and shone like the sun, making him nearly impossible to defeat. After finishing the ritual and gaining the power to become invisible, Indrajit, always confident in battle, left the city thinking, “If I kill these two brothers who have wandered into our land, I’ll win victory for my father Rāvana. Once Rāma and Lakshmana are dead and the monkeys are wiped out, my father will be pleased.” With that, he vanished from sight. Rāvana’s terrifying son, now invisible and armed with his bow and deadly arrows, entered the battlefield, ready to carry out his father’s deadly command. He spotted Rāma and Lakshmana fighting fiercely, surrounded by their monkey allies, like a dangerous three-headed serpent among lesser snakes, and prepared to attack.

Indrajit thought, “These must be Rāma and Lakshmana,” and drew his bow, sending a rain of arrows down like a storm cloud. Seated in his chariot high in the sky, invisible to everyone, he began bombarding Rāma and Lakshmana with sharp arrows. The brothers, wounded by his attacks, quickly fired back with their own powerful arrows. But even though they filled the sky with their shots, they couldn’t hit Indrajit at all—he remained hidden, shrouded in smoke and mist. There was no sound of his bow, no rumble of wheels, no hoofbeats—nothing to give away his position. In that thick, unnatural darkness, Indrajit let loose a relentless storm of arrows and nārāchas (special razor-edged darts), like hail pounding down from the clouds. Furious, he managed to wound Rāma with arrows that blazed like the sun, weapons he had received as a gift. Bloodied by the nārāchas, the two brothers fired back with golden-feathered arrows, but when they struck Indrajit in the sky, those arrows, soaked in blood, just fell back to earth. Despite their pain, Rāma and Lakshmana seemed to glow even brighter, fighting off many of the demon’s arrows. They kept aiming at the places where the arrows seemed to come from, trying to find their hidden enemy. Meanwhile, Indrajit, from his chariot, sent arrows flying in every direction and struck the sons of Daçaratha again and again with his deadly weapons. Hit by so many sharp, terrible arrows, Rāma and Lakshmana looked like blossoming red palash (kingsuka) flowers. But the brothers couldn’t see Indrajit at all—his face, his movements, even his weapons were hidden behind clouds, like the sun during a storm. Many monkeys were also struck down by the invisible attack, falling dead to the ground. Angry now, Lakshmana turned to Rāma and said, “Should I use the Brahmā weapon today and end all these demons right now?” But Rāma, marked by his calm wisdom, replied, “No, Lakshmana. It’s not right to destroy all the Rākshasas for the crime of just one. We shouldn’t kill someone who has retreated, is hiding, has surrendered, stands before us with folded hands, has run away, or is confused. We need to focus on Indrajit himself. I’ll use weapons as swift as snakes to find and stop him. Since he’s hiding, it’s up to us to bring him down—if he’d fought openly, our monkey allies might have already finished him. Even if he dives underground or hides in the heavens, my arrows will burn him up and bring him down.” With these words, full of meaning, Rāma—descendant of Raghu and hero among heroes—began to plan, surrounded by monkeys, how to defeat this deadly and wicked Rākshasa.
Sara: a type of reed grass.
Beleric myrobalan: a kind of wood used for fuel.
Sruva: a ladle with two ends, made of wood, used to pour ghee on the sacrificial fire.
SECTION LXXXI

Sensing Rāma’s (sometimes called Rāghava) plan, Indrajit, Rāvana’s powerful son, left the battlefield and returned to the city of Lankā. His mind was burning with rage as he remembered how many of his fellow Rākshasas had been killed. But he didn’t stay inside for long—his anger pushed him back out, ready for revenge. Indrajit, who was descended from the sage Pulasta and hated the gods, marched out of the city from the western gate, surrounded by a huge force of Rākshasas. When he saw Rāma and Lakshmana standing ready to fight, he began using his magic to create illusions. He placed a fake, magical version of Sitā on his chariot, and with his army all around, he set up a scene to make it look like he was about to kill her. Indrajit’s goal was to use his tricks to terrify everyone watching, especially the monkeys. As he moved forward, acting like he was about to kill Sitā, the monkey warriors, furious and eager for battle, grabbed huge rocks and rushed forward. Hanumān, the bravest of the monkeys, led the charge, holding a giant mountain peak in his hands. As he approached, Hanumān spotted Sitā on Indrajit’s chariot. She looked miserable—dirty, exhausted from fasting, wearing just one soiled piece of cloth, and her hair in a single messy braid. Even though she was naturally beautiful, her suffering was obvious. Hanumān hadn’t seen her in a long time, and the sight of her like this broke his heart. He instantly recognized her as Janaka’s daughter, Sitā from Mithilā, and sorrow filled him. He saw her helpless, trapped by Indrajit, and wondered what Indrajit was planning. With his fellow monkey warriors, Hanumān marched toward Rāvana’s son. 

Seeing the monkey army coming, Indrajit lost control of his anger. He drew his sword, Nistrinsha, and grabbed the fake Sitā by her hair. Right in front of all the monkeys, he acted as if he was about to strike her, and the illusion of Sitā began to cry out, “O Rāma! O Rāma!” Watching her being dragged by her hair, Hanumān, son of the wind god Maruta, was overcome with grief and started to cry. Seeing Rāma’s beloved wife—so gentle and lovely—being treated like this, Hanumān shouted furiously at Indrajit, “You’ve just sealed your own doom by touching her hair, you vile creature! You may be descended from the great Brahmā, but you’ve become a monster. You’re cursed for wanting to do something so evil. You’re disgusting—shameless, cruel, and dishonorable. Are you not even embarrassed by this? What has Sitā ever done to you? She’s already lost her home, her kingdom, and been separated from her husband. You deserve death! If you kill Sitā, you won’t live long—you’ll end up in the worst place, where even the most notorious criminals refuse to go.” After these words, Hanumān and the other monkeys, furious and armed with rocks and trees, charged at Indrajit. The Rākshasas, burning with anger, blocked their way. Indrajit shot thousands of arrows at the monkeys, and then shouted at Hanumān, “Today, I’m going to kill Vaidehi (Sitā) right in front of you—the one you, Sugriva, and Rāma came here to rescue. After I kill her, I’ll kill you, Rāma, Lakshmana, Sugriva, and even the traitor Bibhisana. And you talked about not harming women? We Rākshasas always do what hurts our enemies the most.” With that, Indrajit raised his sharp sword and cut down the fake Sitā as she wailed. The illusory Sitā, innocent and beautiful, fell to the ground as if split across the chest, the way a sacred thread lies on someone’s body. After killing her, Indrajit taunted Hanumān, “Look! I’ve just killed Rāma’s beloved right before your eyes. Now all your efforts are pointless.” Proud of his act, Indrajit climbed back onto his chariot, letting out a terrifying roar. The monkeys nearby heard that dreadful sound and watched as he disappeared into his magical castle in the sky. After killing the illusory Sitā, Rāvana’s son was thrilled with himself. But the monkeys, seeing him so pleased, were overwhelmed with grief and fled in despair.

Some versions of the Ramayana include an extra verse here, but many leave it out. In that verse, Indrajit tries to justify himself, arguing that Rāma killed Taraka first, so now he is killing Rāma’s wife in return. Indrajit claims Rāma is just as guilty as he is.
The “castle” mentioned here is a magical fortress Indrajit created in the air using his illusion powers.
The Sitā that was killed was actually an illusion created by Indrajit, not the real Sitā.
SECTION LXXXII

When the monkeys heard that terrifying noise, which sounded as loud as Indra’s thunderbolt, they panicked. Looking around in fear, they started to run away. Hanumān (also known as the son of Maruta, the Wind-god) saw their distress and called out to them, his face full of sorrow and worry: “Why are you all so upset, and why are you running away? Have you given up your desire to fight? Where is your courage? Stay behind me—I’ll lead the charge into battle.” Hearing these words from the wise Hanumān, the monkeys grew angry at the enemy and felt encouraged. They picked up trees and huge rocks, ready to fight. With loud roars, the leading monkeys charged at the Rākshasas, forming a circle around Hanumān on the battlefield. Surrounded by his monkey warriors, Hanumān tore through the enemy ranks like a raging fire. With the monkeys at his side, Hanumān, who looked as fierce as Death itself, began to crush the Rākshasas. Overcome with grief and burning with anger, Hanumān hurled a massive boulder at the chariot of Indrajit, Rāvana’s son. Seeing the giant rock coming down, Indrajit’s charioteer quickly moved the horses, and the chariot darted away. The boulder missed both Indrajit and his driver, landing uselessly on the ground—but it crashed onto many Rākshasas, crushing them. Then, hundreds of giant monkeys, shouting furiously, grabbed more rocks and trees and hurled them at Indrajit. The monkeys, full of wild strength, rained down stones and logs, attacking the enemy with non-stop cries. The grim-faced Rākshasas were battered by this storm of trees and rocks from the furious monkey army. Seeing his troops in trouble, Indrajit, furious, grabbed his spear and advanced, surrounded by his soldiers. He unleashed a storm of deadly arrows at the monkeys. Indrajit killed many monkey leaders with his spears, thunderbolts, swords, axes, and clubs. But the mighty monkeys fought back, smashing his soldiers with rocks, stones, and huge tree trunks. Hanumān alone crushed many fearsome Rākshasas. After holding the Rākshasas back for a while, Hanumān spoke to the monkeys: “Stop fighting for now. The daughter of Janaka (Sītā), for whom we risked our lives and fought to please Rāma, has been killed. Let’s go tell Rāma and Sugriva what happened. We’ll do whatever they decide.” With these words, Hanumān stopped the monkeys from fighting and strode away bravely, undaunted. As Hanumān left for Rāghava (Rāma), Indrajit—wicked and cunning—headed toward the sacred altar at Nikumbhilā to make offerings to Fire. Once there, Indrajit lit the fire and began pouring offerings into the flames. The fire burned brightly as it received offerings of blood and, satisfied, glowed like the setting sun. Indrajit, who knew all the rituals, performed the ceremony properly for the good of the Rākshasas. The Rākshasas stood watching, waiting anxiously to see if the ritual would bring them victory in battle.
This verse is missing in some versions.—T.
SECTION LXXXIII

Hearing the terrifying sounds of battle coming from the Rakshasas and monkeys, Rama (Raghava) turned to Jambavan and said, “My friend, something major is happening—Hanuman must have done something incredible, because I can hear the fierce clash of weapons. Please, lord of the bears, take your troops and quickly go help Hanuman, that greatest of monkeys.”

Jambavan replied, “Of course,” and, surrounded by his bear soldiers, hurried to the Western gate, where Hanuman was fighting. As Jambavan approached, he saw Hanuman returning, surrounded by exhausted monkeys who had just been through a tough fight. Hanuman noticed the approaching bear army, dark and threatening like storm clouds, and signaled for them to stop. Then Hanuman, looking deeply troubled, went straight to Rama and spoke with a heavy heart: “While we were fighting, Ravana’s son Indrajit killed Sita right in front of us as she cried out in pain. I was shocked and overwhelmed—I had to come tell you what happened.”

Hearing this, Rama was crushed by grief. He collapsed to the ground, like a tree whose roots have been cut away. The leading monkeys rushed over and gathered around him. They tried to revive him by sprinkling him with water scented with lotus flowers, hoping to bring him back to himself.

Lakshmana, heartbroken, embraced Rama and tried to reason with him. He said, “Brother, what’s the point of virtue if it can’t protect someone as good and disciplined as you from disaster? People can clearly feel happiness, but virtue is so abstract it’s almost impossible to know if it’s real. If living virtuously always led to happiness, you wouldn’t be suffering and Ravana wouldn’t be thriving. Clearly, sometimes bad people prosper and good people struggle—that’s the opposite of what we’re taught. If evil always brought misery, Ravana would be doomed, and you, who have always done the right thing, wouldn’t be in so much pain.

If people only got what they deserved, then evil would be destroyed by its own consequences. But if fate or destiny is what really decides everything, then what’s the point of worrying about virtue at all? How can virtue, which is invisible and powerless, actually punish the wicked? If virtue mattered, you wouldn’t be suffering like this. But since you are, maybe virtue is just weak—or maybe it depends on strength. If that’s the case, maybe we shouldn’t rely on virtue alone, but on strength, just as much.

And if truthfulness is what matters most, then aren’t you still bound by your father’s promise, the one that cost King Dasharatha his life? And if doing the right thing is always supposed to come first, why did Indra, the king of the gods, kill an ascetic to achieve his goals? Sometimes, even the gods use force to get what they want, and only then worry about virtue.

Brother, I think that true virtue lies in using both goodness and strength to achieve your goals. When you gave up your kingdom, you cut yourself off from the power that makes virtue possible. Everything—good deeds, wishes, and even self-control—comes from having resources. Without wealth or power, even the most righteous acts can vanish, like a dried-up river in summer.

Anyone who gives up wealth but still craves pleasure will eventually be tempted to do wrong just to get it. People respect, befriend, and listen to those who have wealth—it brings intelligence, power, and success. Giving all that up has left us in this terrible position. Wealth brings happiness, energy, pride, and even self-control. When you don’t have it, the world seems empty, even to saints.

You followed your father’s words, left the kingdom, and now your wife—who means everything to you—has been taken by Rakshasas. But Rama, I promise you, I’ll end this suffering that Indrajit has caused. Get up. Rise, my brother, mighty and faithful as you are. Don’t you remember you’re the Supreme Soul? I swear, for Sita’s sake, I’ll destroy Lanka—its chariots, elephants, horses, and Rakshasa warriors—with my arrows, and end this nightmare.”

The whole army is losing hope seeing you like this. Please stay here and pull yourself together. Send Lakshmana with us, along with the best fighters. Lakshmana’s sharp arrows will force Indrajit to stop the ritual, making him vulnerable again. Those powerful arrows, fast and deadly, will taste his blood. If Indrajit completes his sacrifice, he’ll be invisible to both gods and demons, and not even the gods could fight him. We need to act now, before it’s too late.”
(Referring to Indrajit’s blood.)
SECTION LXXXV

When Rāma (also called Rāghava) heard what the Rākshasa had said, he was so overcome with grief that he could barely process the words. Gathering himself, Rāma—the conqueror of enemy cities—turned to Bibhishana, who was sitting near the monkey warriors, and said, “Lord of the Nairitas, I want to hear again what you just said.” Bibhishana, who was skilled at speaking clearly, replied, “Strong-armed Rāma, I’ve arranged the troops just as you ordered. The whole army is positioned all around us, and the leaders are in their proper places. But there’s something else you need to hear. If you truly want to rescue Sītā and defeat the night-dwelling Rākshasas, listen to what I have to say. Send Sumitrā’s son—Lakshmana—out with a powerful force to fight and kill Rāvana’s son, Indrajit, who has gone to Nikumbhilā. Indrajit is performing rituals there, and he’ll be armed with arrows like poisonous snakes, fired from his bow. Because of his intense austerities, Indrajit was granted a boon by Brahmā (the Self-born): he received the Brahmaçiras weapon and swift, magical horses. Right now, he and his army are at Nikumbhilā. If he completes his rituals and rises up, we’re all as good as dead. Brahmā told him, ‘If you are attacked and killed before you reach Nikumbhilā or finish your fire offerings, that will be your end, O enemy of Indra.’ So, Rāma, if you want to defeat Indrajit, you must send a powerful force right away. Once Indrajit is killed, Rāvana and all his followers will fall.” 

When Rāma heard this, he answered, “Bibhishana, you who are always truthful, I know how tricky and dangerous Indrajit is. He’s a master of illusions and the Brahma weapon, and his strength is incredible. In battle, he can even confuse the gods, including Varuna. When he flies through the sky in his chariot, nobody can track him—he’s as impossible to follow as the sun hidden by clouds.” 

Knowing all about Indrajit’s deceptive magic, Rāma turned to Lakshmana and said, “Take the whole army of monkeys with their leaders, especially Hanumān, and Jāmbavān—the king of bears. Hearing Rāma’s words, Lakshmana—who was fiercely brave—took up another fine bow, with Bibhishana at his side. Lakshmana put on his armor, strapped on his sword, grabbed his arrows and bow, and touched Rāma’s feet in respect. Feeling confident, Lakshmana said, “Today, the arrows from my bow will strike down Rāvana’s son and land in Lankā, just like swans land in a pond. Bibhishana came along, and after Rāma had prayed for Lakshmana’s success, they hurried off. Surrounded by thousands of monkeys, Hanumān and Bibhishana, along with Bibhishana’s advisors, quickly followed Lakshmana. 

With the powerful monkey army surrounding him, Lakshmana saw the forces of the bear-king lined up along the way. The enemy’s forces were massive, dazzling with shining weapons and crowded with banners and chariots. The army was so powerful and intimidating, it seemed to fill the battlefield with darkness and energy.

Indrajit’s, that is.

Bibhishana answered Indrajit calmly, “Indrajit, why are you pretending not to know what I stand for? Stop trying to insult me for following what’s right. That said, if a brother turns to evil, it’s right to leave him behind—just like you’d drop a poisonous snake from your hand for your own safety. The wise say anyone who steals from others or violates their wives deserves to be abandoned, just like you’d abandon a burning house. Stealing, abusing women, and scaring your own friends—these are the three worst vices, and they lead to ruin. Or, because of your courage.

Indrajit, master of battle and conqueror of enemies, bent his dreadful bow and unleashed a rain of sharp arrows. Covered in blood but standing tall, Lakshmana looked like a smokeless fire blazing in the dark.

Their fight was like two planets colliding in the sky, or like the legendary battle between Bala and Vrita. These two great souls fought like lions, unleashing endless arrows and showing off their skills. The mighty man and mighty demon kept battling, full of energy, never backing down, both determined to win.

Lakshmana (Rama’s younger brother), burning with anger like a furious serpent, readied his arrows and fired them at Indrajit, the chief of the Rakshasas. The air was filled with the deafening noise of their arrows, sounding like thunderclouds unleashing a storm at the end of the world. Their roars echoed through the field, sharp and thunderous, making anyone who heard them shiver in fear. The noise of their fighting was like deep thunder rolling through the sky. Gold-tipped arrows pierced their bodies, and both warriors, determined to win glory, bled heavily. Many arrows hit their targets, stabbed deep, and then fell to the ground, stained with blood. Around them, the Rakshasas and the monkey warriors darted through the chaos, fiercely loyal and refusing to leave their leaders even for a moment.

Then Indrajit, son of Ravana, tried to boost his fellow Rakshasas’ spirits. Feeling confident himself, he praised them: "It’s so dark out here, we can’t even tell who’s friend or foe. So, my Rakshasas, fight bravely—confuse the monkeys! I’ll join you soon, coming back into the fight with a new chariot. Make sure none of the forest warriors attack me as I return to the city." With that, Indrajit tricked the monkeys and slipped into Lanka to get a fresh chariot.

He soon reappeared, riding a beautifully decorated chariot plated with gold, bristling with swords, spears, and arrows, and pulled by powerful horses. His charioteer was an expert, skilled in the art of war. Mandodari’s son, driven by fate, charged back onto the battlefield, surrounded by the elite Rakshasas. His chariot sped towards Lakshmana and Vibhishana, the monkeys and Vibhishana staring in awe at Indrajit’s speed and skill.

Furious, Indrajit started slaughtering the monkeys by the hundreds, his arrows flying in deadly arcs. The monkeys, terrified by his relentless attack, clustered around Lakshmana for protection like frightened animals seeking shelter from a storm. 

Lakshmana, fired up with righteous anger, quickly cut Indrajit’s bow in half, showing off his own incredible skill. Indrajit grabbed another bow and strung it in a flash, but Lakshmana sliced through that one as well with a pair of arrows. Now weaponless, Indrajit found himself pierced by five of Lakshmana’s arrows, each one as poisonous as a viper. The arrows hit Indrajit hard, and they fell to the ground like deadly red snakes.

Bleeding from the mouth, Indrajit picked up an even stronger bow. He aimed at Lakshmana and unleashed a barrage of arrows as fierce as a monsoon. Lakshmana, calm and focused despite the onslaught, deflected the storm of arrows. He then pushed back, hitting Indrajit with three arrows at once, while Indrajit kept firing back, peppering Lakshmana with countless shafts. But Lakshmana, master of the bow, cut down Indrajit’s arrows mid-air, and then—with a perfectly aimed shot—beheaded Indrajit’s charioteer. The driverless horses began running in circles, which looked almost unreal.

Lakshmana, now furious, shot arrows at Indrajit’s horses, frightening everyone watching. Indrajit, refusing to back down, shot ten arrows at Lakshmana, who seemed nearly impossible to harm—his golden armor stopped every arrow, no matter how sharp or strong.

Realizing that Lakshmana’s armor was virtually indestructible, Indrajit got even angrier. With lightning-fast skill, he shot three heavy arrows that struck Lakshmana in the temples. The sight of Lakshmana standing tall with those arrows in his head made him look like a three-peaked mountain, blood streaming down but still fighting.

Despite being wounded, Lakshmana quickly retaliated, hitting Indrajit with five arrows. Then he shot more, striking Indrajit’s face, the arrows glinting off his fancy earrings. The two warriors—Lakshmana and Indrajit—were both powerful and relentless, wounding each other again and again in a hail of sharp arrows. Soon, both were covered in blood, looking like blooming red flowers, glaring at each other as they traded brutal blows.

The fight grew even more intense as they got closer, each determined to win. Suddenly, Indrajit, overwhelmed by battle rage, shot three arrows into Vibhishana’s handsome face, then struck the monkey leaders with more arrows. Enraged, Vibhishana smashed Indrajit’s horses with his mace, killing them instantly. 

With his chariot destroyed and charioteer dead, Indrajit leapt to the ground and hurled a deadly dart at his uncle Vibhishana. But Lakshmana, quick as ever, shot it out of the air, shattering it into ten pieces before it even landed. Vibhishana, furious, shot five arrows at Indrajit, each one tipped with gold, tearing into Indrajit’s flesh so that blood poured out like red snakes slithering over his body.

Now enraged at his uncle, Indrajit grabbed a legendary arrow given to him by Yama (the god of death)—an arrow feared by all Rakshasas for its power. Seeing this, Lakshmana, not to be outdone, reached for his own magical arrow—one gifted to him by Kuvera (the god of wealth) in a dream, a weapon so powerful that even gods and demons together could barely handle it.

Both warriors drew their bows, their arms bulging with effort, and the arrows began to glow with supernatural energy. As they fired, the arrows blazed through the sky, colliding mid-air with a force that sent sparks and embers flying everywhere. The two arrows shattered into hundreds of pieces and fell to the earth, their power spent.

Shocked and angry that their best shots had canceled each other out, Indrajit and Lakshmana glared at each other, both shamed and furious. Lakshmana, now boiling with rage, chose the Varuna weapon (associated with the water god), while Indrajit responded with the terrifying Raudra weapon (a brutal weapon of destruction). Indrajit’s Raudra weapon countered Lakshmana’s, neutralizing its magic.

Not giving up, Indrajit unleashed the Agneya weapon, blazing with fire, trying to destroy everything in its path. Lakshmana answered with the Solar weapon, which blocked the fire. Realizing his attack had failed, Indrajit fired the Asura arrow, which summoned a storm of daggers, clubs, darts, maces, swords, and axes. But Lakshmana, shining with his own brilliance, countered with the Maheśwara weapon (a weapon of Shiva), breaking Indrajit’s magic again. The battle was so intense that it made the hair on everyone’s arms stand up.

As the two heroes clashed, beings from the sky—gods, sages, spirits—gathered to watch, filling the air with their wonder. All around, the battlefield echoed with the howls of monkeys and Rakshasas, the sky lit up as celestial beings protected Lakshmana. The gods, saints, spirits, Gandharvas (celestial musicians), birds, and snakes, led by Indra himself, shielded Lakshmana as he fought.

Now, Lakshmana prepared his ultimate attack. He set an arrow on his bow that burned with the power of fire, designed to pierce Indrajit’s defenses. This arrow was perfect: feathered, golden, sharp, and deadly—one that even Indra had once used to defeat the demons. Lakshmana, drawing his bow to its full length, invoked its power: “If Rama, son of Dasaratha, is truly righteous and honest and unmatched in strength, then let this arrow end the life of Ravana’s son.”

With those words, Lakshmana let the arrow fly. The weapon shot forward, slicing through the air, and in an instant it cut off Indrajit’s head—armor, earrings, and all—sending it crashing to the ground. Indrajit’s head, golden and blood-soaked, rolled across the battlefield. His body fell, armor still on, his once-mighty bow slipping from his hands.

Instantly, the monkeys and Vibhishana erupted in cheers, just as the gods had cheered when the demon Vritra was defeated. Victorious shouts echoed across the sky from all beings—sages, Gandharvas, and Apsaras (celestial dancers). Seeing Indrajit dead, the Rakshasa army panicked. The monkeys, now wild with excitement, attacked, and the Rakshasas scattered in every direction, dropping their weapons in their rush to escape.

The terrified Rakshasas ran toward Lanka, some into the sea, some into the mountains. Thousands fled as soon as they saw Indrajit’s body on the ground. Just as the sun’s rays disappear at sunset, the Rakshasas vanished across the battlefield, their courage gone.

With Indrajit dead, the world felt as if a curse had been lifted. Even the gods and great sages rejoiced. Drums thundered in the sky as celestial dancers and musicians tossed flowers down in celebration. The dust settled, water ran clear again, and everything seemed brighter, as joy spread among gods and demons alike.

The gods, Gandharvas, and demons gathered, saying, “Now the Brahmanas, free of fear and sin, can finally walk the earth in peace.” The monkey leaders honored Lakshmana, amazed at his achievement. Vibhishana, Hanuman, and Jambavan (the bear king) bowed to Lakshmana, praising his victory. The monkeys cheered, danced, and roared, crowding around Lakshmana, waving their tails and shouting, “Victory to Lakshmana!” Embracing each other, they talked excitedly about Rama’s safety and Lakshmana’s incredible feat. Even the gods were filled with joy at the fall of Indrajit.

SECTION LXLII

After killing Indrajit (also known as Meghanada), Lakshmana—his body covered in blood and marked by victory—felt a rush of happiness. Leaning on Vibhishana and Hanuman for support, the powerful Lakshmana gathered Jambavan, Hanuman, and the rest of the monkeys and hurried to where Sugriva and Rama (Raghava) were waiting. When they arrived, Lakshmana walked around Rama in respect and bowed before his brother, standing before him like Indra’s brother before the king of the gods. Vibhishana, his expression full of meaning, stepped forward and told Rama the full story of Indrajit’s terrifying defeat. Excited, Vibhishana described how Lakshmana had managed to cut off Ravana’s son's head in battle. As soon as he heard that Lakshmana had killed Indrajit, Rama was overwhelmed with joy and said, “Amazing, Lakshmana! I’m so proud of you. You’ve done something truly difficult. With Ravana’s son dead, our victory is certain.”

Rama then pulled the shy, heroic Lakshmana close, kissed his head, and hugged him tightly out of brotherly love. He made Lakshmana sit on his lap, embracing him again and again, gazing at his brother with deep affection. But seeing Lakshmana wounded and pierced by arrows, Rama’s happiness was mixed with grief. He stroked Lakshmana’s body gently and said, “Now that Ravana’s son is dead, I feel as if Ravana himself has already been defeated. That evil enemy is as good as finished. By your bravery, you’ve managed to cut off Ravana’s right arm, his greatest support. Both Vibhishana and Hanuman have done incredible things in battle. In just three days and nights, we’ve brought down our enemy. Now I have no more foes. Ravana, furious over his son’s death, will definitely come out to fight, bringing a huge army with him. When he hears about Indrajit’s death, he won’t stay hidden. When he comes, surrounded by his forces, I’ll destroy him. Lakshmana, with you—my greatest ally—defeating even the conqueror of Indra, I know I can rescue Sita and win this whole world.”

After comforting and embracing his brother, Rama, overjoyed, called Sushena, saying, “Please do whatever you can to heal this wise and loyal son of Sumitra. Treat his wounds right away and help him recover. And also take care of all the wounded heroes among the bears and monkeys—anyone injured in battle.” Following Rama’s orders, the wise monkey-leader Sushena gave Lakshmana a powerful medicine to sniff. As soon as Lakshmana inhaled it, his wounds healed, his pain vanished, and his energy returned. Sushena also treated Vibhishana and the main monkey warriors, just as Rama had asked. Fully healed and re-energized, Lakshmana felt revived and full of life once again. Seeing Lakshmana healthy and back on his feet, Rama, Sugriva, Vibhishana, the bear-king, and all their armies were filled with joy. Rama, son of Dasharatha, praised Lakshmana’s incredible achievement, and Sugriva, hearing that Indrajit—the one who had even beaten Indra—had been defeated, was overjoyed.
[372] That is, Vibhishana’s look said everything about Indrajit’s defeat.
Avapiritam—here meaning wounded or pained. Some say this refers to Lakshmana’s injuries in battle.
SECTION LXLIII
The advisors of Pulastya’s son hurried to tell Ravana—the Ten-necked king—the terrible news that Indrajit had been killed, because he didn’t know yet.

“O great king,” they said, “your brilliant son has been killed right before our eyes by Lakshmana, with Bibhishana’s help. Indrajit fought bravely, but Lakshmana defeated him in single combat. The same hero who once conquered even Indra has now fallen by Lakshmana’s hand. After giving Lakshmana a fierce battle, your son has journeyed to the next world.” When Ravana heard the horrific news of his son Indrajit’s death, he immediately fainted from shock. After a long time, he slowly regained consciousness, but was overwhelmed with grief and confusion. He cried out in agony: “O leader of the Rakshasa army! My mighty son! You defeated even Indra—so how could you fall to Lakshmana today? When you were angry, your arrows could pierce even Death itself, or the peak of Mount Mandara—so how could Lakshmana possibly defeat you? Today, Yama, the god of death, has gained my respect, for he has claimed you despite your strength. But this is the fate of all great warriors and even the gods. Anyone who dies serving his king achieves heaven. Now that Indrajit is dead, the gods, guardians of the world, and holy sages will finally sleep peacefully, free of fear. The whole world, the entire earth and forests, seem empty to me now that Indrajit is gone. Today, I’ll hear the cries of the Rakshasa women in my palace, like the wails of she-elephants in mountain caves. My son, you gave up your claim as heir, your kingdom of Lanka, your people, your mother, me, and your wife—where have you gone, leaving us all behind? I should have died before you, and you should have performed my last rites, but now everything is backwards.” Still grieving, Ravana was suddenly overcome by a raging fury at the loss of his son. His anger burned hotter than ever, like the sun’s rays in summer. As he breathed heavily in his rage, flames and smoke seemed to burst from his mouth, just like from the mouth of the demon Vritra. Consumed by grief and rage, Ravana’s mind turned dark thoughts—he decided he would kill Sita (Vaidehi). His usually red eyes became even bloodier with anger, making his appearance terrifying. His whole form, already fearsome, now looked like an enraged god of destruction. Tears fell from his furious eyes like drops of burning oil from a lamp. As he ground his teeth in fury, the sound was as harsh as the churning of the ocean by the demons. None of the Rakshasas dared approach him as he glared around, looking as frightening as Death itself, ready to destroy anything in his path. Boiling with rage, Ravana addressed his Rakshasas: “I performed harsh penances for thousands of years and pleased the Creator himself. I have nothing to fear from either demons or gods. My armor, a gift from Brahma and shining like the sun, could not be broken even in the great war between gods and demons when struck with thunderbolts. Who dares face me in battle today when I wear it and take up my chariot? Not even Indra himself would. Beat the drums! Bring me my mighty, dreadful bow—the one the Creator gave me in the war of gods and demons. With it, I will destroy Rama and Lakshmana in battle!” Still burning with grief for his son, Ravana’s mind spun with rage and he again resolved to kill Sita. Glaring around with his copper-red eyes, his appearance horrifying, he cried out in a pitiful voice to his Rakshasas: “Through his magic, my dear son tricked the monkey army by killing something else and making them think it was Sita. Now I will do the deed myself—I will kill Vaidehi, the woman devoted to Rama.” After saying this to his counselors, he quickly grabbed a sword—sharp, blue-steel, and deadly—and stormed out, surrounded by his wives and advisors. Out of his mind with grief for his son, Ravana charged toward Sita’s quarters with the sword, blinded by rage. The Rakshasas saw him coming and some let out lion-like roars, while others, alarmed by his fury, hugged each other and said, “Today Rama and Lakshmana will be devastated when they see him like this. This is the one who, in his anger, defeated the four guardians of the world and conquered countless enemies. Ravana has taken treasures from the three worlds—no one on earth matches his strength or power.” As they talked, Ravana—mad with rage—headed straight for Sita, who was staying in the Ashoka grove. His friends, wise and loyal, tried to stop him, but he ignored them and charged at Sita like an angry planet attacking Rohini in the sky. The innocent Sita, protected by Rakshasi guards, saw the furious Ravana approaching, sword in hand. Seeing him coming despite the pleas of his friends, Sita—daughter of Janaka—felt a wave of pain and despair. She wept, thinking, “The way this evil man is charging at me in anger, it looks like he’s determined to kill me, a married woman, as if I were alone in the world. He begged me to be his wife, but I refused him again and again. Now, rejected and desperate, he’s ready to kill me in a fit of rage and lust. Or maybe Rama and Lakshmana have already been killed in battle by this wretched man, and now he’s coming for me. I heard a wild, frightening roar of celebration from the Rakshasas—maybe they were cheering because my beloved Rama and Lakshmana are dead. Or perhaps, after killing them, this sinful demon, mad with grief for his son, is now coming to kill me. I was a fool not to listen to Hanuman when he offered to rescue me. If I had gone with him, riding on his back, I wouldn’t be regretting like this, waiting for Rama’s victory. When Kausalya—Rama’s mother, who has only one son—hears that he’s been killed in battle, her heart will surely break. She’ll remember his birth, his childhood, his good deeds, and his beauty, and then, overcome with grief, she’ll probably end her own life. Shame on the scheming, hunchbacked Manthara, whose evil led to this suffering for Kausalya!” While Sita cried and mourned like Rohini abandoned by the Moon and attacked by a cruel planet, just then Ravana’s noble counselor, Suparshwa, who was wise and brave, stepped forward—even though the other courtiers tried to stop him. He said to Ravana: “Why, O Ten-necked king, brother of Kubera, would you abandon righteousness by killing Vaidehi? Why, after living as a student, learning the Vedas, and performing holy acts, would you now want to kill a woman? Wait, my lord—hold back your anger for now. Save it for Rama. Tonight is the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight—prepare for battle now, and tomorrow, on the new moon, lead your armies to victory. You are a great warrior and swordsman—if you defeat Dasharatha’s powerful son, you will win Sita.” Hearing his friend’s wise words, Ravana finally calmed down and accepted the advice. He returned to his palace, surrounded by his friends, and entered his court.
