SECTION LXLIV

When Rāvana entered his court, he was deeply distressed and overwhelmed with grief. He sat down heavily on the grandest seat, sighing like an angry lion. Mourning the death of his son, the powerful Rāvana folded his hands and spoke to all the brave Rākshasas gathered there: “All of you—go to battle with elephants, horses, and chariots. Surround Rāma alone and attack him with your arrows, just like clouds pouring rain in the monsoon. Kill him if you can. Or, if you only wound him, I will finish him off tomorrow in front of everyone, after you’ve weakened him with your sharp arrows.” Hearing their lord’s orders, the Rākshasas rushed out to battle with a huge army and many chariots.

The Rākshasas hurled deadly weapons at the monkeys—clubs, spears, arrows, daggers, and axes. The monkeys fought back, throwing giant boulders and whole trees at their enemies. As the sun was about to set, a fierce and chaotic battle broke out between the Rākshasas and the monkeys. They smashed into each other with clubs, decorated weapons called chitras, spears, daggers, and axes. The fight raised enormous clouds of dust, but these were quickly washed away by the rivers of blood pouring from the wounded Rākshasas and monkeys.

The battlefield looked like a river of blood: elephants and chariots formed its banks, arrows were the fish, flags looked like trees on the shore, and dead bodies floated like driftwood. The monkeys, injured and under attack, leaped up and tore down the Rākshasas’ flags, armor, chariots, horses, and weapons. With their sharp teeth and claws, they ripped at the Rākshasas’ hair, ears, faces, and noses. Like vultures swarming a fallen tree, hundreds of monkeys would gang up on a single Rākshasa.

In return, the Rākshasas—huge as mountains—struck back at the monkeys with massive clubs, spears, daggers, and axes. Under this assault, the monkey army retreated and took shelter with Rāma, son of Daçaratha, who was the only one they trusted to protect them.

Rāma, glowing with power, picked up his bow and charged into the Rākshasa ranks, unleashing a storm of arrows. As he advanced, the Rākshasas were scorched by his arrows and couldn’t stand against him, like clouds that vanish before the midday sun. Only the night-dwelling Rākshasas could witness the terrifying deeds Rāma performed—acts beyond the power of any ordinary human.

Most of the time, the Rākshasas couldn’t even see Rāma, unless they were leading the army or driving chariots. He moved as invisibly as the wind in a forest. All they could see was their own forces being scattered, wounded, burned with arrows, and broken by weapons—but Rāma himself was nowhere to be found.

It was like trying to see the soul that controls our senses—no one could spot Rāma as he struck them down. “He’s the one destroying the soldiers on elephants, he’s smashing the chariots, and he’s cutting down the cavalry—both horse and rider,” the Rākshasas cried out in panic. Confused and terrified, they even started attacking each other, right there in the battle, while Rāma watched.
SECTION XCV

Their confusion came from the powerful Gandharva weapon Rāma had used, which clouded their senses and made him even harder to see as he wiped out their army. Sometimes, the Rākshasas thought they saw thousands of Rāmas fighting at once, and other times just one. Occasionally, they’d catch a glimpse of the golden tip of his bow, flashing through the chaos like a spinning firebrand—but they never saw Rāma himself.

Rāma appeared almost supernatural, like the wheel of time itself: his torso was the hub, his strength was its energy, arrows were its spokes, his bow was the rim, the twang of his bow was its sound, his power and intelligence were its brightness, and the reach of his weapons was the wheel’s edge.

In just one eighth of a day, Rāma wiped out ten thousand fast chariots, eighteen thousand elephants, fourteen thousand horses and riders, and two million Rākshasa foot soldiers who could change their forms at will—all with arrows blazing like fire.

The Rākshasas who survived, their horses dead and their chariots and flags shattered, fled for their lives back to the city of Lankā. The battlefield, strewn with dead horses, elephants, and soldiers, looked like a place where the furious god Rudra (another name for Shiva) had unleashed his wrath.

The gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and great sages, praised Rāma’s amazing feat. Then Rāma, noble-hearted and powerful as Indra (Sakra), turned to Sugriva, Bibhishana, Hanumān, Jāmbavān, Mainda, and Divida, who stood nearby, and said, “This is the power of my weapons, and also the power of Rudra.” As Rāma, equal to the gods, wiped out Rāvana’s massive army with his arrows and weapons, the gods rejoiced and sang his praises.

Rāma, relentless and focused, unleashed arrows blazing with golden tips, wiping out thousands of elephants, countless horses and their riders, and chariots bearing flaming banners. He slaughtered thousands of fierce Rākshasas—shape-shifters recruited by Rāvana—armed with heavy clubs and iron maces, their golden flags torn down. When the other night-dwelling Rākshasas saw and heard about this, they panicked, confused and wracked with anxiety. The widows and those who’d lost children or family members gathered, overwhelmed by grief, and cried out in despair: “Why did old, grim-faced Surpanakhā—with her sagging belly—have to spot Rāma, so striking and handsome, out in the forest? Seeing him, beautiful and strong, always caring for others, that hideous woman, who deserved nothing but scorn, was filled with lust. Why did she, so ugly and unworthy, even approach Rāma, whose face and character were both beautiful? It’s a tragedy for us Rākshasas that our old she-demon brought such a filthy proposal to him—everyone would find it laughable if it weren’t so disastrous. It was for her sake that Khara, Dushana, and so many others were destroyed—she approached Rāghava (Rāma) with such a vile intention. Because of her, Rāvana became Rāma’s enemy and kidnapped Sītā, daughter of Janaka. But Rāvana couldn’t overpower Sītā, and now this enmity with the mighty Rāghava will never end. Even when Rāvana saw Rāma single-handedly kill the Rākshasa Virādha, he should have realized Rāma’s power was real. Fourteen thousand brutal Rākshasas were killed by him at Janasthāna with arrows like fire. Khara, Dushana, and Triśirā also fell to his arrows, which burned like the sun—how was this not enough proof? Yoyanabāhu and Kavandha, both bloodthirsty, were also killed by Rāma in his rage—again, more proof. He even killed the mighty Vāli, the son of Indra, who was as powerful as a thundercloud—that should have been enough. Rāma restored Sugrīva, who’d been hopeless and exiled at Mount Rishyamukha, to his throne—another sign of Rāma’s strength. But Rāvana, in his arrogance, ignored the wise advice of his brother Bibhīṣaṇa, who only wanted the best for everyone. If Rāvana had just listened to Bibhīṣaṇa, Lankā wouldn’t have become a place of death and ruin. Even after hearing how Rāma killed the mighty Kumbhakarna, how Lakshmana defeated Atikaya, and how his beloved son Indrajit was slain, Rāvana refused to wake up to reality.

All across the homes of the Rākshasas, people are crying out, ‘My son, my brother, my husband has been killed in battle.’ Rāma has wiped out thousands of chariots, horses, elephants, and foot soldiers. Maybe it’s Rudra, Vishnu, Indra, or even Death itself—wearing the form of Rāma—who’s destroying us. Rāma has killed all our heroes. We’re losing hope; we see no end to this terror, and we mourn the loss of our loved ones. Doesn’t Rāvana, the Ten-necked king who once received boons from Brahmā, realize that a disaster is coming for him because of Rāma? No gods, gandharvas, spirits, or even other Rākshasas can save him from Rāma in battle. Rāvana keeps running into disaster after disaster in every fight—clearly, his end is coming at Rāma’s hands. The great creator Brahmā once granted Rāvana a boon—he would fear nothing from gods, demons, or Rākshasas—but Rāvana forgot to ask for protection from humans. Now, it’s certain: a man will destroy Rāvana and the Rākshasas. When the gods suffered under Rāvana’s oppression, they prayed to Brahmā with intense devotion. Brahmā, pleased with their efforts, told them, ‘From now on, Rākshasas and demons will always fear the gods.’ Then the gods, led by Indra, prayed to Shiva, the slayer of Tripura, who rides the bull. Shiva, pleased, said, ‘For your sake, a woman will be born who will bring about the downfall of the Rākshasas.’ Just as hunger, once sent by the gods, destroyed the demons long ago, so too will Sītā be the cause of our extinction along with Rāvana. It’s Rāvana’s own arrogance and wickedness that has brought this destruction upon us, and now we’re drowning in grief. We can’t see anyone who can save us. Rāghava is attacking us like a wildfire. There’s no rescue for us, just as there’s no help for elephants trapped in a burning forest. Bibhīṣaṇa made the right choice at the right time—he found safety with the one person who could truly protect him.” So the Rākshasa women wailed together, holding each other in their fear and grief, their cries echoing through the night.

(Note: Some editors omit one verse here. Translated, it reads: “When Hanumān alone killed Prince Akshaya and burned down the whole city with the fire from his tail, Rāvana should have realized the truth.”)
SECTION LXLVI

All over the city of Lanka, Ravana could hear the cries of grieving demon women, their voices filled with heartbreak. Sighing deeply, he sat in silence for a moment, lost in furious thought. Ravana looked terrifying—his eyes burning red with rage, teeth clenched, and lips bitten in anger. He looked like the very embodiment of destruction itself, too strong for any other Rakshasa to stop. Finally, he glared at his closest generals—Mahodara, Mahaparsha, and Birupaksha—and barked, “Go tell the soldiers to get ready for battle, right now, on my orders.”

The terrified Rakshasa generals did as they were told, racing off to instruct the demon army to prepare immediately. The fearsome Rakshasa warriors responded, “Yes, Lord,” performing rituals for good luck before heading toward the battlefield. The most powerful chariot fighters bowed to Ravana, wishing for his victory, and waited before him with hands pressed together in respect.

Ravana, still boiling with rage, laughed harshly and spoke to Mahodara, Mahaparsha, and Birupaksha: “Today, I will send Rama and Lakshmana straight to the realm of the dead with arrows as bright as the sun at the end of the world. By killing our enemies, I’ll avenge Khara, Kumbhakarna, Prahasta, and Indrajit. The sky, the earth, and all the directions will be hidden by clouds of my arrows. I’ll wipe out every last monkey warrior with my sharpest shafts. Riding my chariot, as fast as the wind, I’ll smash the monkey army with a storm of arrows. Like an angry elephant disturbing a pond, I’ll attack the monkeys, their faces like blooming lotuses, their bodies shining like flower filaments. Their leaders, struck down by my arrows, will fall and cover the ground like lotus flowers torn from their stems. With a single arrow, I’ll slice through hundreds of brave monkeys, even those fighting with tree trunks as weapons. I’ll end the suffering of those who lost brothers or sons by destroying their killer. By the time I’m done, the earth will be buried under the bodies of monkeys, pierced by my arrows, so thick that no one will see the ground. Today, the crows, vultures, and other scavengers will feast on the flesh of my fallen enemies. Prepare my chariot and fetch my bow. Let all the remaining night-demons follow me into battle.”

After Ravana’s orders, Mahaparsha called out to the army leaders nearby, “Get your troops ready!” The commanders ran through every house in Lanka, urging the Rakshasas to get moving. In no time, terrifying Rakshasas poured out—roaring, with monstrous faces, each carrying a deadly weapon: daggers, pikes, maces, clubs, iron plows, razor-sharp spears, nets, rods, spinning discs, axes, vindipalas, sata-ghnis, and plenty of other brutal arms.

At Ravana’s command, the commanders assembled a massive force: a hundred thousand chariots, three hundred thousand elephants, sixty million horses, donkeys, and camels, plus countless foot soldiers. They lined up the army before Ravana, and while they did, his charioteer rolled up with his glittering war chariot—loaded with powerful magical weapons, covered in decorations, stocked with armor, hung with jingling ornaments, crowned with jewels, and topped with a thousand golden jars. The Rakshasas gasped in awe at the sight.

Suddenly, Ravana, lord of the Rakshasas, stood up and climbed into the glowing chariot. It blazed like fire, brighter than a million suns, drawn by eight swift horses, towering and gleaming with power, and driven by his skilled charioteer. Surrounded by hordes of Rakshasas, Ravana looked like he could tear the earth apart with his strength. The air was filled with the blaring of horns and the pounding of drums, conches, and cymbals.

All across Lanka, a cry went up: “Look! The wicked Ravana—the slayer of holy men, the plague of the gods, the one who kidnapped Sita—has come out to fight the greatest of the Raghu clan, with his royal umbrellas and fans!” Ravana’s roar shook the ground, and the monkeys, startled by the sudden noise, scattered in fear. Ravana himself, his arms huge and his body shining, appeared certain of victory as he rode out, his ministers close by.

Following his orders, Mahaparsha, Mahodara, and the unstoppable Birupaksha climbed into the chariot with him. Hungry for victory, they charged out, letting out blood-curdling roars, as if their voices could split the earth.

Now, Ravana—looking like death itself—grabbed his bow and marched to battle, leading his demon army. His chariot, drawn by speeding horses, rolled straight toward the gate that led to Rama and Lakshmana.

As they advanced, the sun dimmed, darkness covered the sky, birds screeched in terror, and the earth trembled. The gods rained down blood, the horses slowed, vultures landed on the banners, and jackals howled bad omens. Ravana’s left eye and arm twitched, his face turned pale, and his voice sounded rough. The Ten-Headed Rakshasa was surrounded by signs pointing to his doom.

A flaming meteor crashed down from the sky with a thunderous sound, and flocks of vultures and crows made haunting cries. But Ravana, ignoring these terrifying warnings—driven by fate—foolishly pressed on, intent on killing his enemies.

As the wheels of the great Rakshasa chariots thundered, the monkey army, shouting to each other, became fired up, eager for revenge, and prepared themselves for a brutal fight.

Then the Ten-Headed Ravana, furious, rained a storm of golden-feathered arrows on the monkey army, causing a massacre. Some brave monkeys were beheaded by Ravana, some had their hearts pierced or their ears cut off. Some were strangled, others killed outright, some had their sides crushed. Some lost their hands, others had their eyes gouged out. Wherever Ravana drove his chariot, eyes blazing with anger, the monkey leaders couldn’t withstand the onslaught of his arrows.
SECTION LXLVII

The ground was littered with monkeys, their bodies torn apart by the arrows of Rāvana, the Ten-necked king. The monkeys were as helpless against Rāvana’s attacks as flies are against blazing fire. Hit by his sharp arrows, they scattered in panic, their cries echoing like elephants fleeing from flames. Rāvana fired arrows at them relentlessly, his attacks swift and unyielding, like chasing storm clouds. As he cut down the monkeys, the king of the Rākshasas quickly made his way toward Rāghava (another name for Rāma) in battle. Seeing his monkey soldiers terrified and under attack, Sugriva put Sushena in charge of a division (gulma) and prepared to fight himself. Sugriva, trusting Sushena’s strength, put him in command and then charged forward, wielding a tree as his weapon. The other monkey leaders followed, armed with huge boulders and different trees. Sugriva let loose a terrifying roar and attacked the Rākshasas and their allies with fury. The massive monkey king smashed through the Rākshasas like a hurricane tearing up trees. He hurled rocks at the Rākshasa army, as if a thunderstorm was pelting birds in the forest with hail. The Rākshasas, struck down by the rocks Sugriva threw, fell like mountains splitting apart. As Sugriva’s onslaught continued and the Rākshasas fell, one fierce Rākshasa, skilled with a bow, named Birupāksha, shouted his name, leapt from his chariot, and climbed onto an elephant. Mounted high, Birupāksha let out a lion-like roar and charged into the monkeys, boosting the confidence of his fellow Rākshasas and easing their fear. He shot deadly arrows at Sugriva and the monkey army. Hit by these sharp arrows, Sugriva roared in anger, determined to destroy Birupāksha. Sugriva ripped a tree from the ground, leapt forward, and struck the elephant right in front of everyone. Injured by Sugriva, the massive elephant stumbled within bow range, roared, and died. Furious over the death of his elephant, Birupāksha, full of rage, rushed at Sugriva. Moving quickly, he grabbed his dagger and armor and advanced. Seeing this, Sugriva picked up a giant boulder, dark as a storm cloud, and hurled it at Birupāksha. The powerful Rākshasa dodged the boulder and struck Sugriva with his dagger. Wounded, Sugriva collapsed, unconscious for a moment. Suddenly, he sprang up, clenched his fist, and punched Birupāksha hard in the chest, knocking him down. Enraged, Birupāksha slashed Sugriva’s armor with his dagger and kicked him to the ground. Sugriva got up again, ready to land a blow as heavy as thunder, but Birupāksha dodged and counterpunched Sugriva in the chest. With his attack blocked and himself struck, Sugriva was filled with rage and waited for a chance to hit back. Then, in a burst of anger, Sugriva struck Birupāksha in the forehead with a crushing punch. The blow landed like the thunderbolt of Indra (Mahendra), and Birupāksha collapsed, blood pouring from his head like water from a fountain. The monkeys saw their enemy, Birupāksha, his eyes wild with anger, his body covered in blood and foam, shaking and crying out in pain. After that, both armies—monkeys and Rākshasas—prepared to clash, their war cries roaring like two oceans breaking their banks. Seeing the mighty Rākshasa with bloodshot eyes killed by the monkey king, both sides fought fiercely, their struggle as turbulent as the rising Ganges.
Gulma: A division of an army; a unit made up of nine platoons, or nine elephants, nine chariots, twenty-seven horses, and forty-five foot soldiers.
SECTION LXLVIII

Both armies had been worn down, like a pond drying out in summer. Seeing his own troops and Birupāksha killed, Rāvana, the lord of the Rākshasas, grew even angrier. He watched as his army was cut down by the brave monkeys, and he noticed bad omens on the battlefield. This made him uneasy and worried. Turning to Mahodara, who stood nearby, he said, “Mahodara, you’re my last hope. I need you to destroy the enemy’s forces and show me your true strength. This is the moment to repay your master. Fight with everything you’ve got.” 

Hearing this, Mahodara replied, “Yes, my lord,” and charged into the enemy army, fearless, like a moth flying into a flame. Fired up by his master’s command and his own power, Mahodara, who was incredibly strong, began attacking the monkeys fiercely. The monkeys, just as determined, grabbed massive boulders and hurled them into the terrifying ranks of Rākshasas, crushing many. Enraged, Mahodara shot arrows tipped with gold, slicing off the monkeys’ hands, feet, and thighs during the intense fight. 

The monkeys, terrified by the Rākshasas, fled in all directions; some ran to Sugriva for protection. Seeing his powerful monkey army getting crushed, Sugriva rushed forward to face Mahodara himself. Sugriva picked up a giant rock, as big as a mountain, and hurled it with all his strength at Mahodara, hoping to kill him. But Mahodara, utterly fearless, shot the rock apart with his arrows before it could hit. The boulder shattered into a thousand pieces and crashed to the ground, like a flock of vultures falling from the sky.

Sugriva, furious at seeing his attack destroyed, ripped a sāla tree from the ground and threw it at Mahodara. But the fierce Rākshasa sliced the tree apart midair with his arrows. Now boiling with rage, Sugriva spotted a heavy iron club (parigha) lying nearby. He picked it up, its surface shining with fire, and struck Mahodara’s excellent horse with it. The horse was killed instantly, so Mahodara leapt into his chariot and, seething with anger, grabbed his own club.

The two warriors—one armed with a club, the other with the parigha—clashed in a furious battle, roaring at each other like two wild bulls or thunderclouds filled with lightning. Mahodara, burning with rage, hurled his blazing club at Sugriva like a shot of sunlight. Sugriva, quick to react, smashed the club in midair with his parigha. The parigha broke apart and fell to the ground. Not missing a beat, Sugriva grabbed a heavy iron mace (musala) decorated with gold from the ground and threw it at Mahodara, who, in return, hurled another club. Both weapons collided and fell to the earth, useless.

Now that their weapons were gone, both warriors—strong, glowing with power, and blazing like fire—prepared to fight hand-to-hand. They roared at each other, trading heavy punches that knocked each other to the ground. Each time they fell, they sprang back up and kept fighting, landing blow after blow with their fists. Neither of them could be stopped, and both were exhausted from the fierce struggle.

Pushed to their limits, they each drew daggers. Shaking with rage, skilled and determined, they circled each other, looking for a chance to strike. Mahodara, proud and determined to win, lunged and stabbed at Sugriva’s armor with his dagger. But as Mahodara tried to pull his weapon free, Sugriva—quick and fierce—used his own dagger to slice off the Rākshasa’s head, helmet and golden earrings (kundalas) and all.

Seeing their leader fall, the Rākshasa troops panicked and ran from the battlefield. The monkey chief, triumphant after killing Mahodara, let out a roar of victory, joined by the other monkeys. Rāvana, the Ten-necked one, exploded with rage, while Rāghava (Rama) was filled with joy. The Rākshasas, hearts broken and faces pale with fear, scattered in every direction.

With Mahodara struck down—like a massive chunk of mountain split and thrown to earth—Sugriva, the son of the Sun, shone with unstoppable power, almost like the sun itself. Victorious, Sugriva was seen by the gods, Siddhas, Yakshas, and all living creatures on earth, all of whom were thrilled by his success.
SECTION LXLIX

After Sugriva killed Mahodara, the fierce Mahāparshwa (let’s call him “Big-Shoulder” for clarity), with eyes blazing with rage, turned his attention toward Sugriva. Mahāparshwa attacked Angada’s army and the leading monkeys with his weapons. He cut off the heads of the monkeys as easily as the wind knocks fruit from the trees. With his arrows, he sliced off some monkeys’ arms and wounded others along their sides. The monkeys were pelted relentlessly with Mahāparshwa’s arrows. Overcome with pain and fear, many of them lost their senses and fell into despair.

Hearing that his troops were in trouble, Angada, who was known for his fierce energy, grabbed his massive iron club, which gleamed like sunlight, and charged forward like a surging tide. Angada confronted Mahāparshwa directly, and with a powerful blow, knocked him and his charioteer unconscious, sending them crashing to the ground.

At this moment, Jāmbavān, the mighty and radiant lord of the bears—his fur the color of red kohl—entered the battlefield with his bear army, dark as storm clouds. Burning with anger, Jāmbavān picked up a huge boulder, like the peak of a mountain, and smashed Mahāparshwa’s horses and destroyed his chariot.

Mahāparshwa quickly regained consciousness and, still formidable, fired a barrage of arrows at Angada. He struck Jāmbavān in the chest with three arrows and shot Gabāksha with several more. Seeing Jāmbavān and Gabāksha overwhelmed by arrows, Angada’s fury grew. Gripping his heavy iron club in both hands, his eyes red with anger, Angada hurled it at Mahāparshwa from a distance, aiming to kill him.

The club, thrown by Angada’s powerful arms, knocked the bow, arrows, and helmet right out of Mahāparshwa’s grasp. Then, Angada rushed in and, with immense strength, punched Mahāparshwa in the ear, right where his shining earrings hung.

Enraged and shining with power, Mahāparshwa picked up a massive battle axe, sharp and gleaming like polished iron, and hurled it at Angada, striking his left shoulder. But Angada managed to block the blow. Then, channeling the strength of his father Vāli, Angada clenched his fist—hard as a thunderbolt—and punched Mahāparshwa square in the chest.

The blow shattered Mahāparshwa’s chest, and he collapsed dead on the battlefield. His soldiers were struck with grief, while Ravana’s fury only grew stronger. The monkeys, overjoyed at their victory, let out a roar so loud it echoed through Lanka’s city walls and towers, sounding like lions and even like the gods themselves with Indra. Hearing this combined uproar from the monkeys and the gods, Ravana, lord of the Rakshasas and enemy of the gods, burned with anger and marched back into battle.
SECTION C

When Rāvana saw Mahodara, Mahāparsha, and the powerful Birupāksha killed in battle, his anger exploded. He ordered his charioteer to drive faster and shouted, “All my top men are dead, and my city is under siege. I’ll end this pain by killing Rāma and Lakshmana. I’ll destroy this Rāma-tree in battle—where Sītā is the flower and the branches are Sugriva, Jāmbavān, Kumuda, Nala, Divida, Mainda, Angada, Gandhamādana, Hanumān, and all the other monkey leaders.” As Rāvana sped toward Rāma, the sound of his chariot roared through all directions, shaking the earth, rivers, mountains, and forests. Wild animals and birds scattered in terror. Rāvana unleashed a terrifying darkness with his weapons, burning monkeys who ran in every direction. Dust filled the air as they scrambled, powerless against this weapon crafted by Brahmā himself. Seeing his own monkey army being sliced apart by Rāvana’s deadly attacks, Rāma charged forward. While Rāvana was cutting down the monkeys, he finally spotted Rāma—still undefeated—standing with his brother Lakshmana. Rāma looked like a god, with a massive bow, eyes like lotus petals, long arms, and a calm, confident presence. Seeing his allies dying and Rāvana closing in, Rāma—joined by Lakshmana—began to ready his arrows, eager for the fight. The sound as Rāma drew his bow was loud enough to feel like it could shatter the earth. The noise of Rāvana’s arrows and the twang of Rāma’s bow echoed across the field, and hundreds of Rākshasas fell. As Rāvana came within range of the two brothers’ arrows, he looked like the shadowy planet Rāhu facing off against the sun and moon. Lakshmana wanted to attack first—he loaded his bow and shot arrows at Rāvana, their tips blazing like fire. But Rāvana, a master archer, shot down every arrow Lakshmana sent, matching him shot for shot: one arrow for one, three for three, ten for ten. Outmatching Lakshmana, Rāvana—the undefeated demon king—then faced Rāma himself on the battlefield, looming like a mountain. Furious, Rāvana’s eyes burned red as he rushed Rāma, sending a hailstorm of arrows. As Rāvana’s arrows rained down, Rāma quickly grabbed a crescent-bladed arrow and began to knock down Rāvana’s flaming shots, which looked like poisonous snakes. The two warriors exchanged a rapid-fire barrage, circling each other on the battlefield. Their arrows tore up the ground, and neither could be stopped. The fight was so fierce, it felt like Death itself had arrived, terrifying everyone watching. The sky was thick with weapons—so many that it looked like storm clouds with lightning. The air was darkened by the constant rain of arrows, like clouds at sunset. The duel between Rāma and Rāvana was brutal—they fought to kill, both masters of their craft, neither revealing the limits of their strength, like Vitra and Vāsava in ancient legends. They kept circling, and wherever they moved, waves of arrows followed, like stormy sea waves whipped up by the wind. Rāvana, never letting up, launched a web of arrows straight at Rāma’s forehead. Rāma, unphased, took the hits on his head—those arrows glittered like blue lotus petals, but they didn’t hurt him. Furious, Rāma muttered a mantra and, burning with anger, grabbed the Raudra weapon, firing off a fresh volley at Rāvana. But Rāvana’s shield of arrows, thick as storm clouds, stopped them cold; still, Rāma felt no pain. Rāma, expert in every weapon, shot another powerful arrow at Rāvana’s chariot. The arrows pierced Rāvana but, blocked by his power, dove into the ground, hissing like five-headed snakes. Rāvana, his anger peaking, pulled out a terrifying Asura weapon. He fired arrows with the faces of lions, tigers, geese, lizards, vultures, hawks, jackals, wolves—each one with gaping jaws, painted red, and five mouths. Next, using his magical powers, Rāvana shot arrows with the faces of mules, bears, dogs, roosters, sea monsters, and venomous snakes—every kind of nightmare. Covered by this monstrous weapon, Rāma—who looked as fierce as fire—responded with a weapon powered by flames. His arrows had faces full of fire, blazing like suns and stars, or like lightning bolts and meteors. Rāma’s weapon destroyed Rāvana’s terrifying arrows in the air, wiping out whole squads of monkeys too. When Rāma’s power broke Rāvana’s weapon, all the monkey warriors—led by Sugriva, who could change shape—cheered and rallied around Rāma. Rāma, the mighty son of Daçaratha, was thrilled to have crushed Rāvana’s attack, and his monkey allies erupted in joyful shouts.
An arrow with a crescent-shaped head.
Koka—a ruddy goose. It can also mean a lizard, chameleon, or wolf.
Makaras are legendary sea monsters—sometimes mixed up with sharks or alligators, but really just mythological creatures.
SECTION CI

When his weapon was blocked, Rāvana, the lord of the Rākshasas (demons), grew even more furious. Blazing with rage, he launched a terrifying Raudra weapon at Rāghava (Rāma), a weapon that Maya had once given him. Instantly, his bow unleashed a storm of deadly weapons—darts, maces, and clubs that glowed like lightning, along with sharp blades, daggers, nooses, and thunderbolts, all raining down like a hurricane at the end of the world. But Rāghava, graceful and shining, used a powerful Gāndharva weapon to counter and neutralize Rāvana’s attack. Seeing his weapon defeated by Rāma’s skill, Rāvana’s eyes burned red with anger as he picked up another weapon—the Solar weapon. From his bow shot out fiery spinning discs, massive and blazing. The sky lit up with their glow, as if the sun, moon, and planets were all falling at once. Rāma, leading his army, fired volley after volley of arrows, slicing apart Rāvana’s flaming weapons and discs before they could strike. Furious at having his attack destroyed, Rāvana shot ten arrows straight into Rāma’s vital points. But though Rāma was pierced by these ten arrows from Rāvana’s powerful bow, he barely flinched. Enraged, Rāma, the master fighter, fired a storm of arrows that pierced Rāvana all over. At the same time, Rāma’s younger brother, Lakshmana, mighty and fierce, grabbed seven sharp arrows. With these, Lakshmana, glowing with energy, cut down Rāvana’s battle standard, which was topped with a human head. Then, with another arrow, Lakshmana killed the charioteer of the demon chief, his earrings flashing in the sunlight. In quick succession, Lakshmana used five more arrows to break Rāvana’s enormous bow, which was as thick as an elephant’s trunk. Meanwhile, Bibhishana (Rāvana’s brother), leaped up and smashed Rāvana’s excellent horses with his mace, horses as large and dark as mountains or thunderclouds. Rāvana, now without horses, jumped from his chariot, burning with rage at Bibhishana. The demon king, using all his strength, hurled a burning dart at Bibhishana, a weapon as deadly as a thunderbolt. But before it could strike, Lakshmana split it mid-air with three arrows. The monkeys on the battlefield roared with excitement as the golden dart fell in three flaming pieces to the ground, like a meteor breaking apart in the sky.

Rāvana picked up another gigantic dart, glowing with its own power—this was a weapon famous for being unstoppable, so powerful not even the god of destruction could withstand it. As Rāvana spun it, the dart blazed with energy. Lakshmana, ever the hero, rushed to stand by Bibhishana, risking his own life to protect him. Determined to save his brother, Lakshmana strung his bow and fired a flurry of arrows at Rāvana, covering him in a rain of shafts. Overwhelmed by Lakshmana’s attack, Rāvana realized he couldn’t reach Bibhishana and decided to let him go for now. Staring at Lakshmana, Rāvana shouted: “So, you think you’re strong? Because you saved Bibhishana, I’ll aim this dart at you instead. It will pass by the other demons and end your life.” With that, Rāvana, more furious than ever, hurled the dart at Lakshmana. It was a weapon crafted by Maya’s magic, decorated with eight ringing bells, impossible to block, designed to kill enemies, and blazing with energy. As he threw it with all his strength, the dart shrieked through the air like a thunderbolt, flashing toward Lakshmana.

As the dart closed in, Rāma called out to it: “Let Lakshmana be safe! Lose your power and fail!” But the weapon, thrown by an enraged Rāvana, shot forward like a venomous serpent and struck Lakshmana hard in the chest. The blazing dart, full of deadly force and shining like a serpent’s tongue, drove deep into Lakshmana’s body. Hit with such power, Lakshmana collapsed to the ground. Rāma, watching his brother fall, was overwhelmed with grief. But he only allowed himself a brief moment of sorrow. Tears filled his eyes, but then his fighting spirit burned even brighter, like a fire at the end of the world. He thought, “This is not the time to give in to grief.” Looking at Lakshmana, Rāma threw himself back into battle, more determined than ever to kill Rāvana.

Rāma saw Lakshmana lying in the bloody mud of the battlefield, his chest torn open by Rāvana’s dart, looking like a hill covered in writhing snakes. The leading monkeys desperately tried to pull out the dart, but it was stuck fast, driven deep by Rāvana’s strength, and all the while Rāvana kept up a relentless barrage of arrows to keep them away. The dart had pierced through Lakshmana and buried itself in the ground. Rāma, seizing the terrible dart with his own hands, yanked it out and snapped it in two with angry strength. While Rāma was pulling out the dart, Rāvana showered him with arrows that cut to the bone, but Rāma ignored them. Hugging Lakshmana, Rāma turned to Hanumān and Sugriva, two of the bravest monkeys, and said, “Stay here and protect Lakshmana. This is the moment I’ve been waiting for. I will destroy this evil Ten-necked demon who lives by breaking all the rules. Just like a bird thirsts for rain after a long summer, I’ve been dying for this chance to face Rāvana. I swear to you, before long, you will see a world without either Rāvana or Rāma. Today I will kill Rāvana, and with his death, I’ll finally be free from every sorrow—the loss of my kingdom, my exile, my wandering in the Dandaka forest, Sītā’s kidnapping, every horror I’ve faced. For Rāvana, I gathered the monkey army, made Sugriva king by defeating Vāli, crossed the ocean, and built a bridge over the sea. Now he’s finally within my reach. And once a deadly serpent is in your sight, it’s doomed—or like a snake that sees Garuda (Vinatā’s son), death is certain. Watch from the mountaintop, you brave monkeys, and witness my battle with Rāvana. Let the whole world—gods, spirits, and sages—see what Rāma can do. Today I’ll do something that everyone, everywhere, will talk about as long as the earth exists.” Finished speaking, Rāma focused all his energy, aiming a storm of sharp, gold-tipped arrows at the Ten-necked demon. Rāvana answered with a barrage of iron arrows and clubs, like a thunderstorm crashing down. The air was filled with the roar of their arrows clashing, each one striking with immense force. Arrows from both heroes collided in midair, their fiery tips falling to the ground. The sound of their bowstrings, loud and terrifying, echoed across the battlefield, making all who heard it tremble. At last, just as storm clouds scatter before the wind, Rāvana, battered and nearly defeated by Rāma’s relentless arrows, lost his nerve and fled the battlefield in fear.
(Commentator’s note: “By stepping in front of the dart, Lakshmana saved Bibhishana.”)
(Commentator’s note: “Rāma addressed the spirit or deity of the weapon.”)

(Commentator’s note: “This dart, after piercing its enemy, always returned to Rāvana. But because Rāma is divine, after he spoke to it, it couldn’t return—he broke it, which no one else could have done.”)
(Gāruda—the eagle god, son of Vinatā.)
(Commentator’s note: “Adbhutadarçana—wonderful to behold—meaning it was a truly awe-inspiring sight.”)
SECTION CII

When Rāma saw his brother Lakshmana struck down by Rāvana’s weapon and lying covered in blood, he fought Rāvana with wild fury, shooting arrow after arrow at him. Then, turning to Sushena, Rāma said, “Lakshmana—my brave brother, who means more to me than my own life—has been brought down by Rāvana. He lies on the ground like a fallen serpent, and my grief only grows. How can I keep fighting when the person I love most is lying here, maybe dying? If he dies, what’s the point of my life, or any happiness? My strength feels pointless, my bow slips from my hand, my arrows fall away, my vision blurs with tears, and my body feels weak, like I’m in a nightmare. My thoughts are in chaos. Honestly, I’d rather die.” Seeing Lakshmana wounded by Rāvana and writhing in pain, Rāma was overwhelmed with grief and lost himself to despair. “Seeing my brother lying wounded in the dirt,” he said, “even winning this war means nothing to me. If the moon disappears, who enjoys the night? What’s the point of fighting, or even living, if Lakshmana is gone? He followed me into exile—now I swear I’ll follow him to the land of the dead. Always loyal, always looking out for me, he’s been hurt by these demons who fight unfairly. You can find wives and friends in many places, but a true brother—one born from the same mother—is impossible to replace. What will I do with a kingdom if Lakshmana is gone? What will I say to mother Sumitrā, who loves him so much? I can’t bear to hear her ask why I came back without her son. What about Kauçalyā, or Kaikeyi? What will I say to Bharata or the powerful Shatrughna? ‘You went to the woods with Lakshmana, so why are you back alone?’ It would be better for me to die here than to face that blame. What crime did I commit in a past life to deserve this—to see my good brother killed in front of me? Oh, my brother! Best of men! Why are you leaving me for the next world? Why won’t you answer me? Please, get up. Why are you lying there? Look at me. In the forest, whenever I was hurting, you always cheered me up, even when I was lost in pain and despair.” As Rāma poured out his grief, Sushena tried to comfort him, saying, “Rāma, don’t let this sorrow cloud your mind—it’s as dangerous as enemy arrows. Lakshmana isn’t dead. Look at his face; it’s still bright and peaceful. His hands are as soft as lotus petals, and his eyes are gentle. No dead man looks like this. Don’t worry—he’s still alive. Look closely: as he lies there, you can see his heart beating and his breath moving.” After reassuring Rāma, Sushena turned to Hanumān and said, “Hanumān, go quickly to Mount Mahodaya—the one Jāmbavān told you about. Bring back the powerful herbs from the top: Viṣalyakaraṇī, Sāvarṇyakaraṇī, Sañjīvanī, and the healing medicine Sandhānī. These will save Lakshmana.” Hanumān rushed to the mountain, but when he got there, he couldn’t tell which herbs were the right ones. Worried, he thought, “I’ll just take the whole mountain top. The herbs must be here, just like Sushena said. If I can’t find Viṣalyakaraṇī, I’ll fail, and if I waste time, Lakshmana could die.” So Hanumān, with his incredible strength, shook the mountain three times and ripped off its peak, which looked like a thundercloud. He carried the whole mountaintop back through the sky. When he landed, he set the peak down, rested for a moment, and said to Sushena, “I couldn’t find the right herb, so I just brought the entire summit.” Sushena praised Hanumān’s effort, then found and picked the right herb. The other monkeys were amazed—none of the gods themselves could have done what Hanumān just did. Sushena crushed the healing plant and let Lakshmana smell it. Instantly, Lakshmana—who had been near death—was cured, and stood up, his wounds gone. The monkeys cheered, shouting, “Awesome! Amazing!” Rāma, eyes full of tears, hugged Lakshmana tightly and said, “I’m so lucky to see you come back from the brink of death. Without you, Lakshmana, my life, Sītā, or even victory would mean nothing. If you had died, what would be left for me?” Hearing this, Lakshmana—upset by Rāma’s hopeless words—replied, “You made a vow, Rāma. Don’t talk like someone weak or uncertain. Great people keep their promises—that’s what defines them. Don’t let my injury make you lose hope. Fulfill your vow—kill Rāvana today. Once he’s within reach of your arrows, he won’t escape—just like an elephant can’t escape a roaring lion. I hope you destroy that evil Rāvana before the sun sets today. If you want to defeat Rāvana and rescue Sītā, then listen to me and act now.”

SECTION CIII

After hearing Lakshmana’s words, Rāma—known as Rāghava, a masterful slayer of enemy warriors—picked up his bow, loaded it with arrows, and fired deadly shots at Rāvana right in the chaos of battle. Rāvana, the lord of the Rākshasas (demons), jumped onto a new chariot and charged at Rāma with the fury of an eclipse swallowing the Sun. Like a thunderstorm unleashing rain on a mountain, the Ten-necked Rāvana hammered Rāma with arrows that struck like lightning. Rāma, focusing all his energy, shot back at Rāvana with golden-tipped arrows that blazed like fire. The gods, Gandharvas (celestial musicians), and Kinnaras (mythical beings) watched in awe, saying they’d never seen a battle like this—Rāma fighting on foot, facing Rāvana atop his chariot.

High above, Indra—the king of gods—heard their words and turned to his charioteer, Mātali. “Take my chariot,” Indra ordered, “go quickly to Rāma of the Raghu line. Welcome him, and help bring victory to the gods.” Mātali bowed low and replied, “At once, Lord Indra. I’ll serve as Rāma’s charioteer too.” Mātali then prepared Indra’s golden chariot—decorated with bells, shining like the sunrise, its pole set with jewels, drawn by horses in golden harness, with white fans and a golden banner—and set out, leaving the heavens behind to find Rāma.

Arriving before Rāma, Mātali took the reins and greeted him with folded hands. “Rāma,” Mātali said, “Indra, the thousand-eyed, sends you this chariot to help you win. Here is Indra’s famous bow, armor blazing like fire, arrows bright as the sun, and a lucky shining spear. Climb aboard, hero. With me as your driver, defeat Rāvana—just as Indra once destroyed the Dānavas (demons).” Rāma walked around the chariot, saluted it, and climbed in, his presence lighting up the world.

The sight of two mighty chariots—Rāma in one, Rāvana in the other—battling was incredible. Rāma, a skilled warrior, countered Rāvana’s Gandharva weapon with one of his own, and matched every divine weapon Rāvana used with his own celestial powers. Enraged, Rāvana unleashed a terrifying Rākshasa weapon. The arrows he shot turned into venomous snakes, gold-plated, that swarmed at Rāma, breathing fire and showing terrible faces with open mouths.

These blazing, deadly snakes, as fierce as Vāsuki (the king of serpents), filled the sky and came down on Rāma from every direction. Seeing this, Rāma called on the Garuda weapon. As he fired, his arrows—gold-feathered and sparkling—transformed into golden birds, natural enemies of serpents, and swept across the battlefield. Rāma’s shape-shifting arrows, now birds, destroyed all the serpent-arrows coming at him.

When his weapon failed, Rāvana grew furious and attacked Rāma with an overwhelming storm of arrows. Rāvana struck Rāma with thousands of shots, and even hit Mātali, the charioteer, with a barrage. With a single arrow, Rāvana broke Rāma’s golden banner, knocking it from the chariot, and wounded Indra’s horses with another wave of arrows.

Watching Rāma struggle, the gods, Gandharvas, Chāranas (celestial bards), Dānavas, Siddhas (perfected beings), holy sages, and the leading monkeys with Vibhishana felt deep sorrow. It was as if the Moon (Rāma) was being swallowed by the shadow of Rāhu (Rāvana), bringing disaster to the world. Budha (Mercury), enemy of creatures, seemed to attack the Rohini star, beloved of the Moon.

The ocean itself raged, sending up smoky, fiery waves that looked like they would touch the Sun. The Sun darkened, its rays dimming, and appeared with a headless body on its lap, joined by a comet. In the sky, the red planet Angaraka (Mars), linked to Indra and Agni, attacked the constellation Viśākhā. Rāvana, with his ten faces and twenty arms, holding his bow, looked like the massive Maināka mountain.

Under attack from the Ten-necked demon, Rāma was pushed to his limit and couldn’t return fire. Then, with his eyes tinged red, Rāma’s rage exploded. His anger seemed to set the Rākshasas on fire. When the creatures saw Rāma’s furious face—so full of intelligence—fear spread everywhere and the earth itself trembled.

Mountains full of lions and tigers shook, trees shivered, and the ocean churned violently. Dark, terrifying clouds thundered across the sky, sending out roars. Stormy clouds rumbled overhead. Seeing Rāma’s anger and all these frightening omens, every living being was terrified, and even Rāvana was shaken.

High in the sky, gods, Gandharvas, great serpents, saints, Dānavas, Daityas, and birds linked to Garuda watched the battle like it was the end of the world, as Rāma and Rāvana fought with dreadful weapons. The gods and the Asuras (demons) both cheered on their favorites: the Asuras called out to Rāvana, “Win!” while the gods kept encouraging Rāma, “Victory to you!”

At that moment, the evil Rāvana, desperate to kill Rāma, grabbed a monstrous weapon powered by the force of thunder. The weapon made a terrible noise, could destroy any enemy, had prongs like mountain peaks, and was terrifying to see—sharp, blazing, impossible to withstand, and frightening beyond belief. Even the god of destruction would fear it. With his anger burning, Rāvana lifted the weapon, surrounded by his bravest Rākshasas.

Rāvana’s massive body, eyes bloodshot, roared as he raised the weapon. His shout made the earth, sky, and all directions shake. The sea churned at the sound of the demon king’s rage, and all living things trembled.

Seething with energy, Rāvana, holding the mighty weapon and letting out thunderous cries, taunted Rāma: “Rāma, in my fury I raise this thunder-weapon. It will end your life, even with your brother by your side. You love fighting—today, I’ll kill you and send you to join the Rakshasas already slain. Stand your ground, Rāghava; I will destroy you with this weapon!”
With that, Rāvana hurled the weapon. It flew from his hand, wrapped in bands of lightning, decorated with eight bells, roaring as it shot up into the sky, shining fiercely.

Seeing the terrifying, blazing weapon coming at him, Rāma drew his bow and fired a barrage of arrows. Rāma’s arrows met the weapon in the air, like Indra’s rain quenching the doomsday fire. But just as flames consume insects, Rāvana’s weapon burned up all of Rāma’s arrows as they flew.

Watching his arrows turn to ash and shatter against Rāvana’s weapon, Rāma’s fury only grew. Now more enraged than ever, Rāma picked up a javelin that Indra himself favored, handed to him by Mātali. As he brandished it, the javelin’s bells rang out and the sky seemed to catch fire like a falling meteor at the end of time.
Rāma hurled the javelin at Rāvana’s monstrous weapon. The weapons collided, and with its power spent, Rāvana’s weapon lost its light, split apart, and crashed to the ground.

Next, Rāma fired arrows straight at Rāvana’s speedy horses, striking them. Then he shot sharp arrows into Rāvana’s chest. Rāma followed up with three feathered arrows to Rāvana’s temples. With arrows piercing every limb and blood streaming down, Rāvana looked like a blooming Ashoka tree—brilliant and red.
Bleeding from Rāma’s attacks, the lord of the Rākshasas, body soaked in blood, was at once deeply shaken and filled with furious wrath right in the midst of his army.
[397] This means each side cheered for the hero they supported out of respect.—T.

SECTION CIV

Rāvana, provoked by Kākutstha's (Rāma's) relentless attacks, was consumed by a furious rage—a kind of anger that made his eyes blaze. Eager for battle, he launched a fierce assault on Rāma. It was like watching a thunderstorm unload torrents of rain on a lake: Rāvana unleashed thousands of arrows, relentlessly firing at Rāma. But even as these arrows poured down, Rāma stood firm—like a mountain that refuses to tremble—completely undaunted by the onslaught. He skillfully blocked the networks of arrows and grabbed his own missiles, bright and deadly as the rays of the Sun. Then, driven by pure anger, Rāvana, swift as night itself, fired a thousand arrows straight at Rāma's chest. Blood soaked Rāma’s body, making him look like a brilliant red Kinçuka tree in the forest. The pain only fueled Rāma's fury. His energy spiked, and he pulled out more arrows—these ones glowing like the Sun at the end of the world. Soon, the air was so thick with arrows from both warriors that neither could see the other in the darkness.

In the midst of this chaos, Rāma, son of Daçaratha, let his anger take over. He laughed harshly and shouted at Rāvana: “You’re the lowest of the Rākshasas. You lost your strength the moment you kidnapped my wife from Janasthāna and forced her under your control. You stole Vaidehi (Sītā) from that vast forest—she was alone, and you think that makes you a hero? Attacking helpless women, doing such cowardly things, and calling yourself brave—what a joke. You’ve lost all honor! You’re shameless and reckless, and your own violence will be your downfall. Sure, you’re a big name—the brother of Kubera, surrounded by armies—but today you’ll face the consequences of your pride and evil deeds. You keep saying you’re a hero, but sneaking off with Sītā like a thief is nothing to brag about. If you’d tried to take Sītā while I was there, my arrows would’ve killed you—then you would have joined your brother Khara. But now, by some stroke of luck, you’re finally within my reach. Today I’ll bring you to the edge of death with my arrows. Vultures will feast on your head, ripped off by my shafts and coated with dust from the battlefield. As you lie dying, vultures will land on your chest and drink the blood pouring from your wounds. Birds will tear at your corpse, just as they do to snakes.” 

With those words, Rāma, destroyer of enemies, launched a fierce barrage of arrows at Rāvana, who stood his ground. Rāma’s power, strength, and determination seemed to double as he focused on destroying his enemy. All the divine Weapons appeared before him—ready to help—and his speed increased as his excitement grew. Seeing all these promising signs, Rāma, the bane of Rākshasas, attacked Rāvana with even more energy.

Meanwhile, the monkeys pelted Rāvana with stones, and Rāma’s arrows rained down on him. The Ten-necked king felt panic twist in his heart. Overwhelmed and confused, Rāvana couldn’t fire his weapons, draw his bow, or fight back. Realizing this, Rāma didn’t keep attacking. The weapons and arrows Rāvana had already fired signaled that his end was near—his final moments had arrived. Seeing his master powerless and defeated, Rāvana’s charioteer quietly turned the chariot away from the battlefield. Noticing the king’s loss of strength, the frightened driver quickly spun the thunderous chariot around and sped away, taking Rāvana out of the fight.
As Rāmānuya comments, Rāma’s words apply “here and in the next world.”
The “Weapons” are the divine beings who preside over each weapon.
According to the commentator, “Vighurnahridayah” means Rāvana’s heart was paralyzed. I prefer the more vivid interpretation: his heart was shaken and thrown into chaos. —T.
SECTION CV

As Rāvana slowly regained his senses, the force of death pushing him on, he exploded in rage. His eyes were bloodshot with fury as he turned to his charioteer and shouted, “You fool! You act like I’m weak and powerless—as if I’m some coward with no strength or skill, as if I’m under some spell or blocked by weapons. You’re making your own decisions, ignoring me and my wishes. Why did you pull my chariot away from battle, right in front of my enemy? Because of you, my hard-earned reputation, strength, and honor are ruined. Right in front of someone famous for his courage, you’ve made me look like a coward when I’m burning to fight. Honestly, with how you’re acting—refusing to drive me back into the fight—I have to wonder if you’ve been bribed by the enemy. What you did wasn’t the act of a loyal friend. Today, you acted like a traitor. If you’re really loyal to me, if you remember everything I’ve done for you, then hurry—turn the chariot back before my enemy leaves!” 

The charioteer, intelligent and humble, replied to Rāvana, “I’m not afraid, I’m not confused, and I haven’t been bribed. I haven’t forgotten your kindness or all you’ve done for me. Out of care for you, I did something you didn’t like, but it was for your own good. My loyalty hasn’t changed, and you shouldn’t accuse me of betraying you. Let me explain why I pulled the chariot away—like a river pulled back from the sea (402). I saw you were exhausted from fighting, and at that moment, your strength didn’t seem greater than the enemy’s (403). The horses were worn out, beaten down, gasping for breath like cows caught in rain. Bad omens kept appearing in front of us, and I sensed things were turning against us. A good charioteer has to understand the timing and place for battle, read the signs, and notice the mood of the fighters—whether they’re tired, excited, or sad. He should know the lay of the land—if it’s rough, flat, or uneven—and recognize when to fight and when to pull back, as well as the enemy’s weaknesses. It’s the charioteer’s job to know when to approach the enemy, when to retreat, when to hold position, and when to turn around. What I did—giving you and the horses a break from that exhausting fight—was the right call. I didn’t turn away of my own will. I acted out of loyalty to you. Just give the order, my lord, and I’ll do whatever you command with all my heart.”

Rāvana, satisfied with his charioteer’s answer and eager for battle, praised him and said, “Charioteer, drive straight toward Rāghava (Rāma). Rāvana doesn’t leave the battlefield without killing his enemy!” As he spoke, Rāvana—lord of the Rākshasas—handed his charioteer a fine hand ornament as a reward. Hearing Rāvana’s words, the charioteer quickly drove the chariot forward. Urged on, the charioteer whipped the horses, and in moments, the powerful chariot of the Rākshasa king was once again in front of Rāma on the battlefield.
On the rising of the Moon.

Both the Rākshasa army and the monkey forces, though armed and ready, were frozen in shock. All around, both Rākshasas and monkeys stared, completely taken aback by the intensity of the fight.
