As ominous signs appeared, Rāghava (Rāma) and Rāvana fought on, steady and fearless, both determined and calm despite their anger. Everyone sensed that Rāma would win and Rāvana would fall, so both fighters pushed themselves to show their full strength. Rāvana, furious, loaded his arrows and fired them at the flag atop Rāma’s chariot. The arrows struck the flagpole but, sensing the chariot’s divine power, dropped harmlessly to the ground. Rāma’s anger flared. He drew his bow and fired back, aiming at Rāvana’s flag. His shining arrow, blazing like a giant snake, hit its mark and shattered Rāvana’s banner, sending it crashing to the earth. Seeing his flag destroyed, Rāvana burned with rage, his fury almost setting the world on fire. Consumed by anger, he unleashed a storm of arrows. Flaming shafts struck Rāma’s divine horses, but they didn’t flinch or slow down—they acted like they’d only been brushed by lotus stems. Rāvana, frustrated by their calm, grew even angrier and began hurling all kinds of weapons—maces, iron clubs, spinning discs, heavy hammers, boulders, trees, spears, axes, and thousands of arrows—using his magical powers. His relentless attack filled the battlefield with chaos, the air echoing with terrifying sounds. Then, turning from Rāma’s chariot, Rāvana attacked the monkey army, filling the sky with a rain of arrows. Even though he risked his own life, the ten-headed demon kept unleashing weapon after weapon. Watching this, Rāma (also called Kākutstha) just smiled and set his own sharp arrows, firing them in hundreds and thousands. Rāvana answered with another cloud of arrows, and soon the sky looked like it was on fire from their attacks. Every arrow found its mark, none missed or failed to clash with another; the spent arrows fell to the ground after colliding in the air. Standing on opposite sides, Rāma and Rāvana kept up a relentless shower of arrows, completely blanketing the sky. As their duel raged, Rāvana killed Rāma’s horses, and Rāma, in turn, killed Rāvana’s. Both infuriated, they battled fiercely, their fight so intense it would make anyone’s hair stand on end. Rāvana, enraged by the loss of his flag and horses, fought Rāma with sharpened arrows, while Rāma—Lakshmana’s elder brother, the leader of the Raghus—met him blow for blow.
The phrase "Lakshmana’s elder brother" refers to Rāma.
SECTION CIX

As Rāma and Rāvana faced off in battle, every animal watched in awe. The two mighty heroes, both furious and determined to kill each other, rushed forward and attacked. Their charioteers showed off their skills, driving the chariots in circles, lines, and all sorts of patterns. Rāma and Rāvana fired arrows at each other, using tricks and illusions as they attacked and defended, moving forward and back—Rāma pressing the attack, Rāvana holding his ground. The two chariots raced around the battlefield like storm clouds pouring rain. After weaving through the chaos, they ended up face to face, the fronts of their chariots and the heads of their horses touching, their flags brushing against each other.

Rāma quickly fired four sharp arrows, pushing Rāvana’s blazing horses away from the fight. Furious at this, Rāvana, the Ten-headed one, shot deadly arrows at Rāma. Despite being hit by Rāvana’s powerful shots, Rāma wasn’t hurt or shaken. He responded by firing arrows that looked like lightning bolts. Rāvana then targeted Rāma’s charioteer, Mātali, with a barrage of sharp arrows that struck hard. But Mātali barely flinched. Seeing his charioteer under attack, Rāma’s anger exploded—he unleashed a torrent of arrows at Rāvana. Rāma’s arrows rained down on Rāvana’s chariot by the dozens, then by hundreds, then by thousands.

Rāvana, furious, struck back with maces and heavy clubs called musalas. The battle became terrifying, enough to make anyone’s hair stand on end. The noise of crashing maces, clubs, iron bars, and golden arrows shook the seven seas. Even the creatures under the oceans—Dānavas and thousands of Pannagas—felt the pain. The earth trembled, mountains, forests, and gardens shaking. The sun lost its shine, and fierce winds howled. Gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, saints, Kinnaras, and serpents all grew anxious.

Watching Rāma and Rāvana’s intense fight, the gods and sages prayed, “Let the Brahmins and cows be safe, let people live in peace, and may Rāghava (Rāma) defeat Rāvana, lord of the Rākshasas.” The Gandharvas and Apsaras, amazed by the battle, remarked, “The ocean looks like the sky, and the sky like the ocean—this epic fight really suits Rāma and Rāvana.”

Now, Rāma—long-armed, the pride of Raghu’s line—was furious. He set an arrow, snake-like and deadly, onto his bow and sliced off one of Rāvana’s heads, bright with shining earrings. Everyone in the three worlds saw Rāvana’s head crash to the ground. But instantly, a new head, just like the last, appeared on Rāvana’s shoulders. Rāma quickly cut it off too. Again, another head grew, and Rāma shot it off, his arrows striking like thunderbolts. He cut off a hundred brilliant heads, but Rāvana just kept coming—death wouldn’t take him.

Rāma, skilled in every weapon and always bringing joy to his mother Kauśalyā, started to wonder: “These are the same arrows I used to kill Māricha, to slay Khara and Dushana, to destroy Viradha in the Krauncha forest, the headless demon in Dandaka, to split even mountains and churn the ocean, and to defeat Vāli. So why aren’t they working on Rāvana?”

Still thinking, Rāma readied himself for battle and fired more arrows straight at Rāvana’s chest. Rāvana, lord of the Rākshasas, sitting in his chariot and burning with rage, answered with a storm of maces and heavy clubs. The fierce, massive battle—enough to make anyone shudder—raged on for seven nights, in full view of gods, Dānavas, Yakshas, ghosts, Uragas, and serpents, whether they were in the sky, on the earth, or on mountaintops. The fight never paused—not by day, not by night, not even for a moment.

As they watched Rāma, son of Daśaratha, fighting the lord of Rākshasas, and saw Rāma gaining the upper hand, the wise charioteer of the king of the gods quickly spoke to Rāma, who was deep in battle.
SECTION CX

At that moment, Mātali leaned over and reminded Rāma, “Why are you hesitating, Rāma? You know what must be done. Don’t be afraid—use the weapon given to you by the great Ancestor (Brahmā). The gods said this is the time for Rāvana’s defeat.” Remembering Mātali’s words, Rāma picked up the blazing arrow that seemed to hiss like a snake. The great sage Agastya had given him this weapon, which was originally created by Brahmā for Indra and passed down to help win great battles. The arrow was legendary: it had wind in its wings, fire and the Sun at its tip, the sky in its shaft, and the weight of the sacred mountains Meru and Mandara. It shined with its own light, was perfectly feathered, decorated with gold, and forged from the essence of all things—bright as sunlight. It was like the fire at the end of the world, wrapped in smoke; like a burning serpent, able to pierce men, snakes, and horses, moving incredibly fast. It could break through gates, iron bars, and mountains. It was soaked in blood, stained with marrow, and terrifying to behold. The arrow was as hard as lightning, made a terrible sound, tore through entire armies, and struck fear into everyone—like a living serpent. On the battlefield, it was as frightening as Death itself and seemed to feed the crows, vultures, cranes, jackals, and even the rakshasas. For the monkey warriors, it brought hope, but for the rakshasas, it brought dread. The arrow looked like a great bird with many colored feathers. Rāma, following the Vedic rituals, consecrated the mighty arrow—the best in the world—on his bow. This weapon would lift the fear from the Ikshvāku dynasty, destroy the enemy’s pride, and bring joy to his own people. As Rāma placed the arrow on his bow, all animals trembled, and the earth itself shook. Burning with anger and completely focused, Rāma held his breath and let the arrow fly straight at Rāvana, striking him in the heart. The weapon, unstoppable like thunder and as deadly as Death, smashed into Rāvana’s chest. The arrow tore into Rāvana’s body, killing him instantly, then, covered in blood, it vanished into the ground. After ending Rāvana’s life, the victorious arrow returned quietly to Rāma’s quiver. Rāvana’s bow and arrows fell from his lifeless hand, dropping to the earth. Then, Rāvana, glowing even in death and moving with the force of a falling star, crashed from his chariot to the ground, his life gone. Seeing their king dead, the remaining rakshasas, terrified and leaderless, ran in all directions. Watching the mighty Rāvana fall and Rāma’s victory, the monkeys cheered, grabbed trees, and chased the fleeing rakshasas. The rakshasas, crying and desperate after losing their king, rushed back to Lanka, terrified. The monkeys, thrilled with victory, shouted Rāma’s name in triumph. In the sky, the gods sounded their trumpets, and a gentle, fragrant wind began to blow. Flowers rained down on Rāma’s chariot, covering it in blossoms. The gods sang Rāma’s praises and celebrated him. With Rāvana, who had terrified the world, finally defeated, the gods and celestial musicians rejoiced. By killing the greatest of the rakshasas, Rāma fulfilled the wishes of Sugriva, Angada, and Bibhishana. The gods found peace again, the directions grew bright, the air cleared, a calm breeze swept the land, and the sun shone at full strength. Sugriva, Bibhishana, and Lakshmana greeted Rāma, celebrating his strength and singing his glory. In the middle of the battlefield, Rāma stood out—true to his promise, surrounded by his army and friends, his enemy defeated—looking as majestic as the king of the gods surrounded by the immortals.
In some versions, it says “did not enter the quiver”—meaning the arrow didn’t return to Rāma’s quiver.
SECTION CXI

Seeing his brother defeated, killed, and lying on the battlefield, Bibhishana (Vibhishan), completely crushed by grief, began to mourn: “O hero, famous for your strength and wisdom, skilled in politics—you once slept on soft beds, so why are you now lying on the bare ground, your long lifeless arms spread out, no longer moving, still wearing your Angadas (armlets) but without your sun-bright helmet? You’ve ended up exactly as I feared, even though you wouldn’t listen—blinded by your own delusions. Prahasta, Indrajit, Kumbhakarna, Atikāya, Atiratha, Narāntaka, you, and the others—none of you bothered to listen to my warnings, blinded by pride, and now what I warned has come to pass. Oh! The bridge of righteousness has collapsed; the very image of virtue is ruined; the protector of the strong is gone, and you have joined the ranks of fallen heroes. It’s as if the sun has crashed to earth, the moon has lost its glow, the fire has been put out, and virtue has stopped acting—now that this great warrior, the best among weapon-masters, lies defeated. O greatest of the Rakshasas, lying still in the dust of battle as if asleep—who else among the Rakshasas will now be drained of their power and energy? The great tree that was the lord of the Rakshasas—with patience as its leaves, speed as its flowers, ascetic power and courage as its roots—has been uprooted by Raghava (Rama), like a powerful wind. Ravana, like a wild elephant—his strength as tusks, royal blood as backbone, anger as legs, joy as his trunk—has been brought down by the lion of the Ikshvaku line. The mighty Rakshasa fire, with rays of power and energy, angry breath as smoke, strength as its burning force, has been put out in battle by Rama, like a great raincloud. The bull among Rakshasas, always besting others and strong as the wind, with Rakshasas as its tail, hump, and horns, and restlessness as its ears and eyes, has today been killed by Rama, the tiger.” 

Hearing Bibhishana’s words, full of logic and reason, and seeing how deeply grief had shaken him, Rama spoke: “This lord of the Rakshasas, so fearsome and powerful, was not killed because he was weak. He was always strong, energetic, and not afraid of death.[462] True Kshatriya warriors, who die in battle to earn glory, should not be mourned when they fall. Now is not the time to grieve for him, even though he’s been taken by death—he once struck such fear into Indra and all the three worlds by his intellect. Besides, victory in battle is never permanent; either you kill your enemy, or you’re killed yourself. This is the code of the Kshatriyas, passed down from the old teachers—a Kshatriya slain in battle should not be mourned. Accept this truth, calm your mind, and free yourself from your sorrow. Now, think about what needs to be done next.” 

Still overwhelmed by grief, Bibhishana answered Rama, speaking with care for his brother’s honor: “You have defeated him, like the ocean breaking through its banks—someone even the gods like Basava (Shiva) could never conquer before. He gave generously to those who asked, enjoyed every luxury, took care of many servants, shared wealth with friends, and destroyed his enemies. He honored the sacred fire, performed great penances, was learned in the Vedas, and made many sacrifices. Please, show me how to perform his funeral rites properly—I want to honor him as he deserves.” 

Hearing Bibhishana’s heartfelt words, Rama—the great son of King Dasharatha, full of energy and compassion—told him to go ahead with the funeral and said, “Now that he is dead, our enmity is over and our goal is achieved. He is as dear to me as he is to you. Go ahead—perform his last rites.”
[462] In other words, he met death not by weakness or chance, but as a warrior.
SECTION CXII

When Rāvana was killed by the noble Rāghava, the female demons (Rākshasees) of Lanka, devastated by grief, rushed out from the palace’s inner chambers. Their hair was messy and they ignored all attempts to calm them, collapsing in the dust like cows mourning their lost calves. Along with some male Rākshasas, they exited through the northern gate and entered the blood-soaked battlefield, desperately searching for their fallen lord. The she-demons cried out in heartbroken voices, “O lord, O husband, O our everything,” as they wandered through the field littered with headless bodies. Tears filled their eyes as they mourned, moving like female elephants lost without their leader. 

They soon found Rāvana’s giant, powerful body lying on the ground, shining even in death, like a smear of vivid red kohl against the earth. Seeing their king lying there, the women threw themselves onto his corpse, clinging to him with the desperation of vines ripped from their tree. Some hugged him tightly, others clutched his feet, and some wrapped themselves around his neck. A few took his hand and rolled in the dust, while others were nearly mad with grief at the sight of his lifeless face. One lay her head on his lap, weeping and bathing his face in tears, like a lotus flower covered in heavy rain. Seeing their husband dead on the battlefield, the women’s sorrow was overwhelming—they sobbed and wailed uncontrollably.

They remembered how Rāvana had once defeated King Vaisrabana and taken his magical chariot, how he had terrified Gandharvas, sages, and even gods in battle, and had never feared Asuras, gods, or serpent-people (Pannagas). Now, he had been killed by a mere human. The gods, demons (Dānavas), and other Rākshasas couldn’t destroy him, but a mortal man on foot had ended his life. The one who was supposed to be invincible to gods, Yakshas, and demons had died like any ordinary man. 

As they grieved, the she-demons cried out, “You ignored the advice of your friends, who always wanted what was best for you, and you brought Sitā here—this led to your destruction and the doom of the Rākshasas. Your brother Bibhishana warned you with wise words, but you got angry and pushed him away, and now you see what happened. If only you had returned Sitā, the daughter of Mithilā’s king, to Rāma, all this horror—this disaster that destroyed everything—would never have happened. Rāma’s wishes would have been fulfilled, his side would have won with Bibhishana’s help, we would still have our husbands, and our enemies would not have succeeded. By keeping Sitā here against her will, you doomed yourself, the Rākshasas, and us. O greatest of Rākshasas, maybe this wasn’t just your fault—maybe it was fate itself that brings everything together and tears everything apart. The destruction of the monkeys, the Rākshasas, and even you was caused by fate. When fate decides something—wealth, desire, power, or rule—nothing can stop it.” 

So the wives of the Rākshasa lord cried out in anguish, like a herd of mourning elephants—broken, devastated, and with tears streaming down their faces.
SECTION CXIII

Mandodari, the chief wife of the Rakshasa king, wept bitterly, her eyes fixed hopelessly on her husband’s lifeless body. Seeing Ravana—her Ten-necked husband—killed by Rama, whose deeds seemed impossible for any mortal, Mandodari cried out in grief: “Oh mighty-armed one! Oh brother of Kubera! Even Indra himself feared to fight you when you were angry. Great sages, famous Gandharvas, and Charanas all fled at your approach. How could Rama, just a man, defeat you in battle? Aren’t you ashamed, my king, my lord of the Rakshasas? You conquered the three worlds and earned your fame, and yet a man living in the forest has killed you. You, who could change your form at will, were killed by Rama right here in Lanka, a city no human could even approach. I can’t believe this is really Rama’s doing—you, who always succeeded, brought down by a mere human force. It must have been Death itself, disguised as Rama, using illusions to destroy you, my strong lord. Or maybe it was Indra—but what power would he have against you, who possessed such strength and energy and opposed the gods? No, it’s clear now: Vishnu, the eternal spirit, greater than the greatest, the Preserver, the one with the conch, discus, and club, marked by the Shrivatsa on his chest, beautiful and invincible, must have become a man—surrounded by gods in monkey forms—to defeat you, the terrifying enemy of the gods, along with your family and Rakshasas, all for the good of mankind. You controlled your desires and conquered the three worlds, but now, those same worlds have overpowered you, remembering old grudges. Rama isn’t just a man—he killed your brother Khara at Janasthana, despite Khara being guarded by many Rakshasas. We were terrified when Hanuman entered Lanka by his own power, a city even gods couldn’t reach. I tried to stop you from becoming Rama’s enemy, but you ignored me, and now this is the result. Oh greatest of Rakshasas, you, blinded by desire, ruined your wealth, yourself, and your relatives by falling for Sita—who was even more virtuous than Arundhati or Rohini. You did a terrible thing by tormenting the blameless and devoted Sita, the very embodiment of patience and fortune herself. By tricking her from the lonely forest and bringing her here, you sealed your family’s fate. You never got what you wanted with Sita. But now, my lord, it’s her devotion to her husband that has destroyed you. You weren’t destroyed when you captured the woman who even Indra and Agni feared. My husband, when the right time comes, everyone faces the results of their actions—there’s no doubt. Good deeds bring good results, and evil deeds bring destruction. Vibhishana is now happy, and you have met your end. There are women in your harem far more beautiful than Sita, but blinded by desire, you couldn’t see it. I’m neither Sita’s equal nor her better in birth, beauty, or accomplishments, but you didn’t see that. Death doesn’t come without a reason—Sita is the cause of your end. Death, through Sita, has taken you away. Now she, free from sorrow, will live with Rama, while I, less virtuous, am drowning in grief.

I remember riding with you in our beautiful chariot across Mount Kailasa, Mandara, Maru, visiting the Chaitraratha garden and other heavenly groves, seeing many lands, wearing colorful clothes and garlands. Now, with your death, all joy and pleasure have left me—I am a widow. Oh, how quickly fortune changes! My king, your face shone like the sun, your grace was like the moon, your beauty like a lotus. You had magnificent brows, flawless skin, a proud nose, and your face was crowned with jewels and earrings. How handsome you looked, adorned with garlands, your eyes sparkling with drink, your smile charming in the palace. But now, your face is ruined—cut by Rama’s arrows, drenched in blood, your spine and head shattered, covered in dust from the chariot wheels. Alas! My fate has made me a widow, something I never imagined. My father is king of the Danavas, my husband was lord of the Rakshasas, my son defeated Indra. I was so proud, always sure my protectors were fearless and renowned for their strength. How could mere men bring such terror to all you Rakshasas who were so mighty?

Your body is cool and green like an emerald, tall as a mountain, decorated with armbands, bracelets, jewels, and flower garlands. It was splendid in moments of pleasure and terrifying in battle. You shone with your ornaments like thunderclouds lit by lightning. Now your body is pierced with arrows; it’s no longer mine to embrace, covered with wounds that go to the bone. Your green skin is now red with blood, lying on the ground like a mountain struck by lightning. The idea that Rama could kill you once seemed like a dream, but now it’s come true! You were like death itself to even Death—how did you end up conquered by him? You owned the wealth of three worlds, made the gods tremble, threatened even Shiva, humbled the arrogant, and your power was legendary. You crushed your enemies, killed many holy men, and boasted proudly in battle. You took care of your kin and servants, destroyed thousands of gods, demons, and yakshas, defeated the Nivata Kavachas, stopped many sacrifices, protected your relatives, disrupted the righteous, created illusions in battle, and kidnapped the daughters of gods, demons, and men. You made your enemies’ wives weep, led your people, protected Lanka, and gave us so much pleasure—you were the greatest warrior of all. Now, seeing you killed by Rama, I am still alive, even though my heart should have broken. Oh lord of Rakshasas, you once slept on luxurious beds; why are you lying on the dusty ground now? When my son Indrajit was killed by Lakshmana, I was heartbroken—but today, with you gone, I am destroyed. Alone, deprived of friends, relatives, and all pleasure, I will mourn you forever.

You’ve taken the long, difficult road of death—take me with you, for I cannot live without you. Why are you leaving me behind, so lost and alone? Why don’t you reach out for me, your grieving wife? Why aren’t you angry, seeing me unveiled, walking on foot through the city gates? Oh beloved, look at your wives—we have thrown off our veils. Why aren’t you upset seeing us all out here? I was your companion in joy, my lord; I yearn for you—why won’t you comfort me now? King, you were cursed by those devoted wives you made into widows, women who were pious and served their husbands—now their curse has come true. It’s said that the tears of faithful wives never fall in vain, and now I see it’s true. You conquered the worlds, but how could you stoop to stealing other men’s wives? You took Rama and Lakshmana from their forest home with a fake deer, just to steal Rama’s wife. I never heard you cry out in battle before—surely, your downfall began the day you brought Sita here, just as Vibhishana, your brother, warned you. All this destruction of the Rakshasa leaders came from your anger and lust. Because of your actions, all our good fortune is lost, and our entire race is destroyed. You’ve left all the Rakshasa families without their leaders. You were known for your strength and courage—I shouldn’t even be mourning you, but my heart is weak and full of sorrow. You’ve reached your destiny through both good and bad deeds—I mourn only for myself, left alone in my grief.

Oh Ten-necked one, you ignored the advice of friends and brothers who spoke from love. You wouldn’t listen to Vibhishana’s wise, gentle words meant for your own good. You ignored the warnings of Maricha, Kumbhakarna, and even my father, blinded by your own pride—and this is what came of it. Oh, you who shone like red clouds, dressed in yellow and adorned with fine jewelry, why are you now lying in blood? Why don’t you rise and comfort me, your grieving wife? I am the granddaughter of the mighty Rakshasa Sumali, who never fled a battle—why don’t you greet me now? Get up! Rise! Why are you lying here in defeat? Now the sunlight enters Lanka without fear. The mighty mace you used in battle, your favorite weapon, feared by all and decorated with gold, lies shattered by arrows. Why are you lying on the battlefield, holding it like a lover? Why don’t you welcome me, your beloved? My heart must be made of stone, not breaking from the pain of losing you!”

As Mandodari wept and sobbed, her tears flowing, she finally collapsed, overcome with emotion. She threw herself on Ravana’s chest, looking like lightning against a red sunset cloud. The other wives, also grieving, lifted her up and tried to comfort her: “Don’t you know, dear queen, that life is uncertain, and even royal fortune can disappear in hard times?” Comforted a little, Mandodari cried out again, soaking her chest and beautiful face with tears.

Meanwhile, Rama said to Vibhishana, “You should perform your brother’s funeral rites and comfort his wives.” Vibhishana, wise and thoughtful, replied, “I don’t think I should cremate someone who abandoned good deeds, was cruel, a liar, and who took other men’s wives. He was my enemy in the form of a brother, always doing harm. Ravana doesn’t deserve my respect, even if he was my elder brother. O Rama, maybe people will call me cruel, but when they hear of his crimes, they’ll understand my actions.”

Hearing this, Rama—always righteous and skilled with words—answered Vibhishana with a smile: “I want what’s best for you, since you helped me win this victory. Listen to my advice, lord of Rakshasas. Although Ravana did many evil things, he was powerful, brave, and strong in battle. I’ve heard that even the gods led by Indra couldn’t defeat him. Enmity ends with death—there’s no point holding onto it now. Perform his funeral rites—he was your brother as much as he was my enemy. You should carry out his rites quickly and properly, and people will praise you for it.”

Hearing Rama’s words, Vibhishana immediately began preparing for Ravana’s cremation. He went into Lanka and brought out Ravana’s sacred fire vessel, carts, brass pots, fire, priests, sandalwood, fragrant woods and essences, precious stones, pearls, and coral. With the Rakshasas and Malyavan by his side, Vibhishana began the funeral.

The priests, weeping, covered Ravana’s body with silk and placed it on a golden, beautifully decorated litter. With the sounds of horns and chants of praise, they carried the litter, along with firewood, toward the southern cremation ground. Brahmins versed in the Yajur Veda, carrying burning fire, led the way, followed by attendants. The palace women, not used to walking, hurried after them, leaping along. At the cremation ground, they laid Ravana on the pyre made of sandalwood, padmaka, usira, and other fragrant woods, covered him with an antelope skin, and performed the proper rites for the dead. They built an altar in the southeast corner and placed the fire there. They poured yogurt and clarified butter over Ravana’s shoulders, put a mortar on his legs, a wooden pestle on his thighs, and set other ritual items in their places, completing the ceremonies.

Following the scriptures, the Rakshasas sacrificed animals and used their marrow and clarified butter in the rituals, placing the mixture on Ravana’s face. They decorated him with flowers and fine clothes, and Vibhishana’s friends, hearts heavy with grief, scattered dry rice over his body. Vibhishana, following the proper rites, lit the funeral pyre. After bathing and putting on clean clothes, he offered linseed and grass mixed with water, and tried to comfort Ravana’s wives, asking them to return home. The women went back into the city. After they entered, Vibhishana approached Rama, standing quietly at his side.

Rama, with his army, Sugriva, and Lakshmana, felt great relief and joy after defeating his enemy—like Indra after slaying Vritra. He put down his bow and arrows, set aside his armor, and let go of his anger now that Ravana was dead, showing a calm and gentle side once more.
The Shrivatsa is a special mark, often described as a curl of hair, on Vishnu’s chest. It’s the emblem of the tenth Jina, or the mark commonly attributed to Vishnu or Krishna.
The Earth is a symbol of patience, but Sita is considered even more patient than the Earth itself.
Shri is the goddess of wealth and fortune, but Sita is said to be more fortunate than fortune herself.
[466] In other words, the fact that you weren’t destroyed instantly when you took Sita only shows her greatness of character.
Agni—the god of fire.
