SECTION CXIV

When Rāvana was finally defeated, the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas got back into their own vehicles and left, singing about what had just happened. As they traveled, they chatted excitedly about Rāvana’s terrifying fall, Rāma’s (Rāghava’s) incredible courage, the bravery of the monkeys, Sugriva’s smart advice, Hanumān’s (the Wind-God’s son) loyalty and strength, Lakshmana’s dedication, and Sītā’s devotion to her husband. Pleased and amazed, they all headed home. Meanwhile, Rāma—with his strong, long arms—told Mātali, the charioteer sent by Indra, that he could take the magical chariot back. He thanked and honored Mātali before sending him off. Mātali, following Rāma’s orders, took the shining chariot up into the sky and disappeared. Feeling happy and relieved, Rāma hugged Sugriva. As Lakshmana bowed to him and the monkeys celebrated, Rāma, respected by all, led them back to their camp.

Rāma then turned to Lakshmana (the son of Sumitrā), who always had good fortune, and said, “Lakshmana, please take Bibhishana—who’s always been loyal and helped us so much—to Lankā. I really want to see Bibhishana, Rāvana’s younger brother, crowned as king of Lankā.” Lakshmana, thrilled by Rāma’s words, replied, “Of course,” and quickly fetched a golden jar. He gave the jar to Sugriva, the monkey king, and instructed the monkeys to fill it with water from the ocean. The monkeys rushed to the shore and returned with the seawater. Lakshmana then set up a beautiful seat for Bibhishana (Saumitri), and with everyone watching—Rākshasas, monkeys, and counselors—he poured the sacred water over Bibhishana, crowning him king of Lankā, just as the Vedas prescribe. Surrounded by friends and followers, Lakshmana completed the ceremony properly. The Rākshasas, now devoted to Bibhishana, his advisors, and all the monkeys, cheered and sang praises to Rāma.

Seeing Bibhishana made king of the Rākshasas, Rāma and Lakshmana both felt overjoyed. Bibhishana comforted his new subjects, then went to meet Rāma. The monkey citizens, celebrating, brought him gifts like curd, roasted grains, sweets, popped rice, and flowers—symbols of good luck. Bibhishana, full of energy, offered all these gifts to Rāma and Lakshmana. Rāma, pleased to see Bibhishana’s success, accepted the gifts with gratitude.

Then Rāma turned to Hanumān—the heroic monkey who stood before him with hands respectfully folded, looking strong as a mountain—and said, “Hanumān, after you get Bibhishana’s permission, go into Lankā and check on Sītā (Maithili). Let her know that Rāvana has been defeated and tell her that Lakshmana, Sugriva, and I are all safe and well. Please come back quickly with news of how she’s doing, and share this good news with her.”
SECTION CXV

Following his orders, Hanumān (also called Anjaneya), son of the Wind God, respected even among the rakshasas (night-demons), entered the city of Lankā. With Bibishana’s (sometimes called Vibhishana) permission, Hanumān made his way to the Briksha Vatika—the royal grove. Once inside, he saw Sitā, who already knew him. Sitā looked unkempt, sitting at the base of a tree, sorrowful and surrounded by terrifying demonesses. It was as if she were the moon (Rohini) eclipsed by the shadow of Rāhu. Hanumān approached her quietly, bowed, and stood still, showing respect. At first, Sitā just stared at him in silence, not recognizing him right away. But soon, realizing it was Hanumān, her face lit up in joy. Seeing her gentle expression, Hanumān, the bravest of monkeys, shared Rāma’s message with her: “Vaidehi, Rāma, Sugriva, and Lakshmana are all safe. Rāma sends his love and says he has defeated his enemies. The powerful Rāvana has been killed by Rāma, with help from Bibishana, the monkeys, and Lakshmana. I’ve come to bring you this wonderful news: victory is ours, thanks to your faith and virtue, Sitā. Please don’t worry anymore—the enemy is gone, and Lankā is under control. Rāma himself built a bridge over the sea to reach you, staying awake for days to keep his promise. Don’t be afraid of living here anymore—Rāma has given Bibishana the throne of Lankā, so you can feel as safe as if you were home. Bibishana will come soon to bring you to Rāma.”  

Hearing this, Sitā, her face glowing like the moon, was so overwhelmed she couldn’t speak. Seeing her unable to reply, Hanumān asked softly, “What’s on your mind, Lady Sitā? Aren’t you happy to see me?” Wiping tears of joy, Sitā—always loyal and wise—finally answered, her voice trembling with emotion: “I’m so overjoyed at the news of my husband’s victory that I’m speechless. Hanumān, I don’t have anything to give you to match the happiness you’ve brought me. There’s nothing on earth—no gold, silver, jewels, or even the rule of the three worlds—that could repay you for this news.”  

Hanumān folded his hands and replied, smiling, “Your words mean more to me than any treasure, jewels, or even ruling the heavens. Just seeing Rāma victorious and at peace is enough reward for me.” Sitā, daughter of King Janaka, then said to Hanumān, “You are truly gifted, Hanumān. Your words are wise and kind, showing the depth of your knowledge. You are the praiseworthy son of the Wind God and possess so many virtues: strength, courage, heroism, learning, nobility, energy, forgiveness, patience, endurance, humility, and so much more.”  

Unmoved by praise, Hanumān stood humbly before her and said, “If you allow me, I’d like to punish these demonesses who tormented you here in the Ashoka grove, following Rāvana’s cruel orders. I’ve heard how they used harsh words and distressed you. If you wish, let me punish them—strike them, pull their hair, cut off their ears and noses, whatever you wish—so they pay for what they did to you.”  

Sitā, always compassionate, thought for a moment and answered, “Why be angry at these demonesses? They only followed their master’s orders. My suffering is the result of my own fate, maybe even from a past life. Please, Hanumān, don’t speak of revenge. This is just how fate works. I forgive these women out of pity. Now that Rāvana is gone, they won’t harm me anymore. Listen, Hanumān, to a verse from an old legend—a boar once told a tiger: ‘No one else carries the burden of another’s sins. The truly good should act with compassion, even to those who do wrong. Who among us hasn’t done something wrong? Even those who love violence deserve some mercy.’”  

Hanumān, skilled in words, replied, “You are truly Rāma’s worthy wife, with all your virtues. May I now go and tell Rāghava (Rāma) what you have said?” Sitā answered, “Yes, I want to see my husband, who cherishes those who are loyal to him.” Hanumān, delighted, reassured her: “You will soon see Rāma, whose face shines like the full moon, together with Lakshmana and his friends, surrounded by victory, just as Sachi sees Indra, king of the gods.”  

After saying this to Sitā, who seemed as radiant as the goddess Lakshmi herself, Hanumān returned to Rāma. He respectfully told Rāghava everything that Janaka’s daughter had said.
(474: The Briksha Vatika is a garden in the city of Lankā.)
SECTION CXVI

After bowing to Rama, the greatest archer with eyes like lotus petals, the wise monkey Hanuman spoke up. “Rama, it’s time for you to see Maithilee (Sita), the woman for whom you started all of this. Because of her, you faced so many dangers, and now you’ve finally achieved your goal. When Sita heard about your victory, she was still overwhelmed by grief, tears streaming down her face, and she told me she wanted to see you. With complete trust and through sobs, she said, ‘I want to see my husband.’” Hearing Hanuman’s words, Rama—the most righteous man—was moved to tears and immediately fell into deep thought. He let out a heavy sigh, looked down at the ground, and then turned to Bibhishana (Vibhishana), who stood nearby, dark and imposing like a storm cloud. Rama said, “Please, quickly bring Sita here—the daughter of the king of Mithila. Make sure she’s bathed, sprinkled with heavenly perfume, and dressed in divine ornaments.”

As soon as Rama spoke, Bibhishana hurried off. He went into the women’s quarters and sent word to Sita through her attendants. Seeing Sita, Bibhishana—the graceful lord of the Rakshasas—bowed with his hands folded above his head and spoke humbly, “Vaidehi (Sita), may only good come to you. Please bathe, dress in these divine clothes and ornaments, and get on this chariot. Your husband wants to see you.” Sita replied, “Lord of Rakshasas, I want to see my husband right away, even without bathing.” Bibhishana answered, “You should do as Rama has asked.” Out of devotion, and always seeing her husband as her god, Sita agreed: “So be it.”

So they bathed Sita, performed the proper rituals, dressed her in fine clothes, and adorned her with jewelry. They set her in a palanquin carried by several strong Rakshasas and brought her to Rama. As Bibhishana approached, Rama—who had been deep in thought—was told that Sita had arrived. Hearing that Sita, who had spent so long in the Rakshasa’s captivity, was finally here, Rama felt a mix of anger, happiness, and sadness all at once. Looking at the palanquin, where Sita sat overwhelmed by grief, Rama—his heart stirred—spoke to Bibhishana: “Lord of Rakshasas, my friend, you’ve always helped me. Please, bring Vaidehi closer to me right away.”

Bibhishana, always respectful of what’s right, quickly began clearing the area. Guards with armor, helmets, sticks, and drums moved through the crowd, pushing everyone back. The bears, monkeys, and Rakshasas hurried away in all directions. The noise of the crowd being moved sounded almost like the roar of the ocean during a storm. Seeing his monkey allies being forced back and distressed, Rama was filled with both anger and compassion. He stopped Bibhishana and, with eyes blazing, said sharply, “Why are you treating my people this way? They’re my friends—don’t make them anxious. No wall, house, dress, or formal reception should hide a woman from her own family. There’s no sin in seeing a woman during times of danger, difficulty, war, or at a svayamvara [475] or marriage. Sita is in distress; there’s nothing wrong with seeing her now, especially here with me. So leave the palanquin and let her walk here on foot. Let the monkeys see Vaidehi with me.”

Feeling regretful, Bibhishana did as Rama asked and gently brought Sita to him. Hearing Rama’s words, Lakshmana, Sugriva, and Hanuman all felt deeply sad. Sita, shy and embarrassed, followed Bibhishana toward her husband. With a gentle face and treating Rama as her god, she looked at him with wonder, happiness, and love. Staring at her beloved husband’s kind face—so much like the full moon—Sita felt her pain disappear. Her face shone with the beauty and calm of a clear, bright moon.
A svayamvara is a kind of marriage ceremony where the bride chooses her own husband.
SECTION CXVII

Seeing Maithili (Sita) standing quietly by his side, Rama finally let his emotions show. “Sita,” he said, “I have destroyed all our enemies in battle and defeated the one who wronged you. I’ve done everything a man could do. My anger has run its course—I’ve erased the shame of having my wife taken, and at the same time, I’ve ended both my humiliation and my enemy. Today, my strength has been proven, my efforts have paid off, and I’ve kept my promise through my own actions. The terrible fate that led to your kidnapping by that impulsive Rakshasa, while I was gone, has been overcome by me, a mortal man. What’s the point of strength if a man can’t erase the insult done to him? No matter how great he is, he’d still be small. Hanuman’s brave deeds—crossing the ocean and destroying Lanka—have finally achieved their goal. Sugriva and his army fought bravely and gave me wise advice, and today, all their hard work has succeeded. Even Vibhishana’s (Bibhishana’s) choice to leave his own brother, who had lost all goodness, and join me, has finally paid off.” As Rama spoke, Sita looked at him sadly, her eyes shining with tears, like a frightened deer. Seeing his beloved wife so close, but fearing what people would say, Rama’s heart felt torn in two. Then, in front of the monkeys and Rakshasas, he spoke to Sita—so beautiful, with eyes like lotus petals and long, dark hair—saying, “Just as the great sage Agastya conquered the distant south, I have killed Ravana for you, to restore my honor, as a man should. May you be well. Know that all my efforts in battle, with the help of my friends, were for your sake. I did all this to protect the reputation of my family, erase the shame of your abduction, and restore my own honor. But I’ve doubted your purity; now, standing before me, you trouble me like a lamp to someone with sore eyes. So, daughter of King Janaka, go wherever you wish, to any of the ten directions. I give you permission, Sita. I have nothing more to do with you. What strong man from a noble family would take back his wife, just out of desire, after she’s lived in another man’s house? Ravana took you into his arms, looked at you with evil intent—how could I bring disgrace to my family by taking you back? The goal for which I rescued you is done. I have no attachment left—go wherever you want, Sita. I say this because I believe it’s my duty. If you want, you may stay with Lakshmana, Bharata, Shatrughna, Sugriva, or even Vibhishana the Rakshasa. Choose wherever you’ll be happy, Sita. I can’t believe Ravana, with you in his house and you so beautiful, would have left you untouched.” Hearing these harsh words from the man she loved—words she’d never heard from him before—Sita, always sensitive, began trembling like a vine torn by an elephant’s trunk, and broke down in tears.
SECTION CXVIII

After hearing these words from Rāma (Rāghava), Sitā was devastated. The harshness of his accusations in front of everyone cut deep, and she felt humiliated and ashamed. It was as if she wanted to disappear from the shame, and Rāma’s words hit her like arrows. Tears streamed down her face, but she wiped them away and gathered herself. With a trembling voice full of pain, she spoke to her husband, “Why are you talking to me like I’m just any woman, using such cruel words? I swear by my own character, I am not the person you think I am. Just because you’ve seen other women act wrongly, you’re judging all of us. Let go of your suspicion—you’ve already tested me. Yes, my body was touched by someone else, but I had no control over that; it wasn’t by my choice. Circumstances forced it. My heart is still mine, and it belongs to you. I couldn’t control what happened to my body when I was Ravana’s prisoner. O giver of honor, we’ve lived together for so long, our love grew from that, and if even then you can’t trust me, I am truly lost. When you sent Hanumān to Lankā to find me, why didn’t you abandon me then? If you’d sent a message with him telling me you doubted me, I would have taken my own life right there, and you wouldn’t have had to risk your life or trouble your friends. O king, you’re so angry that you only see me as a woman and nothing more, like any ordinary man would. Even though I have a father, I was literally born of the earth. And yet, you still doubt my character, even though you know people so well. Are you just going to ignore the fact that we married when we were young, and all the loyalty I’ve shown you?” Overcome with tears, Sitā turned to Lakshmana (Saumitri), who was deep in thought. “Lakshmana, please build a funeral pyre for me. It’s the only way out of this shame. My own husband has rejected me in front of everyone, and I can’t live with this stain on my name. The only proper thing is for me to step into the fire.”

Hearing Vaidehi (Sitā) say this, Lakshmana, usually calm but now furious, glared at Rāma. But seeing Rāma’s silent signal, Lakshmana understood what he wanted and, though angry, started preparing the pyre. No one dared question or even look at Rāma—he seemed as untouchable as Death itself.

Sitā, head bowed, walked around Rāma, then approached the burning pyre. She bowed to the gods and the Brāhmanas, folded her hands, and spoke to the fire: “If my heart has always been true to Rāghava, then, O fire—witness to all—protect me. If I am pure, even though Rāghava doubts me, may this fire keep me safe from harm.” With steady resolve, she circled the fire and then stepped into the flames.

Everyone in the assembly, young and old, watched in shock and sorrow as Maithili (Sitā) entered the fire. She glowed like molten gold as she walked into the flames before everyone’s eyes. People stared as Sitā, with her wide, beautiful eyes, moved into the fire like a golden altar. The sages, gods, and Gandharvas saw her enter the flames like a sacred offering in a great ritual. Seeing her fall into the fire, sanctified by her truthfulness, all the women began to weep.

The three worlds—gods, Gandharvas, and demons—watched as Sitā fell into the flames, like a goddess cast down from heaven. As she entered the fire, cries of grief erupted from every side, from both the Rākshasas and the monkeys, unlike anything anyone had ever heard before.
SECTION CXIX

Hearing the cries and mourning of the Rakshasas (demons) and monkeys, Rama — who was noble-hearted — felt overwhelmed with sadness; his eyes filled with tears as he sat and thought deeply. Suddenly, the gods themselves arrived at Lanka in their radiant chariots. There was King Vaisravana, Yama with his ancestors, Indra the thousand-eyed king of gods, Varuna the lord of the waters, the three-eyed Shiva (Mahadeva) riding his bull, Brahma the creator, and others wise in the knowledge of Brahma. These powerful gods came before Rama, raised their decorated hands in greeting, and spoke reverently to him: “Lord, you protect every world and are the wisest among us. Why do you ignore Sita entering the fire? Don’t you realize your true nature — that you are the greatest of the gods? In your previous birth, you were Kratadhama, the eldest of the Vasus. You are the creator of the three worlds. You are the eighth Rudra and the fifth Sadhya; the Ashwini twins are your ears, and the sun and moon are your eyes. You exist at the beginning and end of creation. So why do you treat Sita (Vaidehi) like any ordinary man would?” After hearing these words from the guardians of the universe, Rama, leader of men and the most righteous, replied to the gods: “I know myself only as a man — Rama, the son of Dasaratha. Please, Great Father, tell me who I really am and where I come from.” Then Brahma, who was most knowledgeable, answered Rama: “Listen closely to the truth, you who are true in strength. You are the brilliant and mighty Narayana, wielder of discus and mace. You are the one-tusked boar; you have conquered past, present, and future; you never age or end, Rama. You are the source of all virtue and the one who sets the laws. You are four-armed, the master of time itself, the conqueror of your senses, the supreme being whom sin cannot touch. You are Vishnu, the dagger-holder, Krishna, and you alone have unmatched strength. You are the army and the commander; you are the universe itself — wisdom, forgiveness, and self-control. You are both creation and destruction, Upendra and the one who defeated the demon Madhu. You created Indra and are Mahendra. Your navel is like a lotus, and you are the destroyer of your enemies. The gods and holy sages see you as the refuge for all who seek help. You are the heart of the Vedas and all their branches and rules. You yourself created the three worlds. You are the shelter of the Siddhas and Sadhyas, the one who existed before creation, the sacrifice, the holy chant, the sacred ‘Om,’ and the greatest of all. No one knows your beginning or end — you exist in all living things, in cows and Brahmins, in all directions, in the sky, the mountains, and rivers. You have a thousand legs, a thousand heads, and a thousand eyes. You support all beings, the earth, and the mountains. Beneath the earth, you are like the great serpent in the waters. Rama, you sustain the three kinds of beings — the gods, Gandharvas, and Danavas. I am your heart, Saraswati (the goddess of learning) is your tongue, and all the other gods created by Brahma are the hairs on your body. When you close your eyes, it is night; when you open them, it is day. The Vedas are formed from your will and your control; nothing exists separately from you. The whole universe is your body; the earth is your patience; fire is your anger; the sun and moon are your joy. You have the mark of Srivatsa (a special curl of hair), and you once crossed the three worlds in three steps. You bound the terrifying Bali and made Mahendra king. Sita is Lakshmi, and you are Krishna and Vishnu, the protector of people. To destroy Ravana, you took on human form. You have completed our task, most righteous Rama. Ravana is dead. Go now to heaven, joyful. Your divine power is real, and your strength is never wasted. Rama, your gaze and your praise are never without effect. On earth, those who are devoted to you will always succeed. Those who are loyal to you, united with the Purana and the Supreme Spirit, will have all their wishes fulfilled in this world and the next. Those who chant this story — full of deep knowledge and ancient history — will never fail, here or hereafter.
The Vasus are a class of demigods, usually counted as eight.
Rudras are demigods — lesser forms of Shiva; there are eleven in total.
Sadhyas are a group of minor deities, twelve in number.
Siddhas are saints who have achieved spiritual perfection.
“Purvaja” means one who existed before creation.
“Vashatkar” refers to offerings in sacred fire rituals.
“Om” is the sacred sound at the start of Hindu prayers, believed to be supremely holy.
“Paratpara” means the greatest among the great.
The Puranas are ancient sacred Hindu texts.
“Purusha” means the supreme spirit — the eternal being inside all living things.
SECTION CXX

When the great creator spoke those words, Bibhābasu (the god of fire, Agni) rose up from the funeral pyre with Sita (Vaidehi) on his lap, shaking the flames aside. Sita, the daughter of King Janaka, appeared radiant, dressed in a red sari that glowed like the rising sun and adorned with shining gold jewelry. Her hair was thick and curly, her clothes fresh and new. Holding her gently, Bibhābasu handed Sita over to Rama. Then Agni, the god of fire and a witness to human actions, spoke to Rama: "Rama, here is your Sita. She is completely innocent. She has not sinned against you—not in her words, not in her thoughts, not in her understanding, not even with her eyes. Sita is good and beautiful, and has never strayed from you, her heroic and virtuous husband. She was alone and helpless in the forest when Ravana, the powerful rakshasa, kidnapped her. Even when locked away and guarded by terrifying demonesses, Sita always kept her heart with you. No matter how much Ravana tempted or threatened her, she never gave him a single thought. Her heart is pure, untouched by sin. Take Maithili back—she belongs with you. Don’t say otherwise; I command you." Hearing these words, Rama, skilled and wise, was filled with joy and took a moment to think. Then, the brilliant and steadfast Rama replied to Agni: "Sita lived in Ravana’s inner chambers for a long time, so she needed to be purified in front of everyone. If I took King Janaka’s daughter back without this test, people might say Rama, son of Dasaratha, is blinded by desire and doesn’t care about honor. But I know Sita—she has always been true to me and never even thought of anyone else. Just as the ocean never leaves its shores, Ravana could never touch Sita, whose virtue protected her like a shield. Even in his mind, Ravana could not reach Maithili—she was always out of his grasp, like a burning flame. Her heart never wavered, even while trapped in his palace. Sita is mine, just as sunlight belongs to the sun. Now, in front of the whole world, Maithili has proved her purity. I could never abandon her, just as a self-respecting person cannot give up their own honor. I must listen to your wise and loving advice, all of you who care for me." Saying this, Rama—victorious, powerful, and widely respected—reunited with his wife and finally found happiness again.
The god of fire, Agni.
Another name for the fire god.
SECTION CXXI

After Rāma (also called Rāghava) spoke those wise words, Maheswara—also known as Siva—replied with even more powerful ones. “Rāma, with your lotus-shaped eyes, strong arms, and broad chest, you are truly a destroyer of your enemies and a leader among the virtuous. It is a great blessing that you have done this. Thanks to you, Rāma, the terrifying darkness that was Rāvana—a fearsome threat to everyone—has been ended. Now, comfort poor Bharata and the famous Kausalyā, see Kaikeyi and Sumitrā (Lakshmana’s mother), reclaim the throne of Ayodhyā, make your friends happy, restore your family’s honor, and use your strength to perform horse-sacrifices. Earn lasting glory, reward the Brahmins, and then, after all this, ascend to heaven. There—look—your father, King Daçaratha, is waiting for you on his chariot. He was your elder and master here on earth, O Kaķutstha. After having you as his son, that noble king went to Indra’s realm. Bow to him now, with your brother Lakshmana.” 

Hearing Siva’s words, Rāma and Lakshmana respectfully bowed to their father, who was seated at the top of his shining chariot, dressed in spotless clothes and surrounded by a bright aura. Seeing his sons—especially Rāma, whom he loved more than his own life—Daçaratha was filled with joy. He pulled Rāma into his lap, hugged him tightly, and, seated high up in his chariot, spoke: “I may be in heaven now, equal to the gods, but without you, Rāma, it doesn’t feel right—I swear that’s the truth. I still remember the words Kaikeyi said when she sent you into exile. Now, seeing you safe and holding you and Lakshmana in my arms, my sorrow is gone, like the sun when its shadows disappear. My soul is finally at peace because of you—my good and noble son—just as the virtuous Brahmin Kapāla was freed by Asthabakra. Gentle Rāma, I have heard from the gods themselves that you are the supreme Purusha, disguised as a man, sent to destroy Rāvana. Kausalyā is truly blessed—she will be so happy to see you return from the forest, victorious over your enemies. The people who see you crowned king in Ayodhyā are blessed too. I wish to see you reunited with Bharata, devoted, strong, pure, and living by dharma. You spent fourteen years in exile with Sitā and Lakshmana, and your time is now over—you kept your promise. By defeating Rāvana, you have pleased the gods. You have done something amazing and achieved great fame—so now, as king, live a long life with your brothers.”

When the king finished speaking, Rāma folded his hands and replied, “Father, you know what’s right—please forgive Bharata and Kaikeyi. You once cursed Kaikeyi and her son, saying ‘I renounce you both’—please, let that terrible curse not fall on them.” 

Daçaratha answered Rāma’s request, saying “So be it,” and hugged Lakshmana. Then he said, “Lakshmana, you are wise and famous on this earth. You will also reach heaven and a great state there. You bring joy to your mother, Sumitrā—stay close to Rāma and keep doing good. Rāma always cares for everyone’s well-being. All the gods, led by Indra, along with Siddhas and great sages, bow to Rāma, this supreme being. Rāma, the conqueror of enemies, is the eternal, indescribable sound ‘Brahma’ described in the Vedas as the heart and secret of the gods. Because you have served alongside Sitā, the daughter of the king of Videha, you have earned religious merit and fame.”

Turning to Sitā, Daçaratha spoke to her as she stood with folded hands. “Vaidehi, don’t be angry at Rāma for sending you away; he only did it to prove your purity, always wanting the best for you. What you have done to defend your honor is incredibly hard. Your example will inspire all women. You don’t need advice on how to treat your husband, but remember—he is your greatest protector.”

After giving these words of wisdom to his two sons and Sitā, Daçaratha got back into his chariot and departed for Indra’s realm. Glowing with happiness and light, the great king left for the world of the gods, his spirit at peace after advising his sons and daughter-in-law.
SECTION CXXII

After Daçaratha arrived, Indra (Mahendra), feeling very pleased, spoke to Rāma, who stood respectfully with his hands folded. “Rāma,” he said, “you are the best among men. Since we are all gathered here, let’s not let this moment go to waste. I am pleased with you—ask for any boon you want.”

Rāma, delighted by Indra’s offer, replied sincerely, “O King of the Gods, if you are truly pleased with me, I would like to ask for a favor. Please bring back to life all these mighty monkeys who died for my sake. I want to see these brave monkeys, who left behind their families because of me, alive and happy again. O Purandara, please revive all these heroic, powerful monkeys who risked everything for me and never feared death. This is the boon I ask for—let all those who were loyal to me and gave their lives get a second chance. I wish to see all the monkeys, Golangulas, and bears, even those who are wounded or weakened, fully healed and as strong as they were before. Also, wherever these monkeys live, let them always have flowers, fruits, and roots available—even out of season—and let the rivers there always be full of clean water.”

Hearing Rāma’s heartfelt wish, Indra replied with genuine happiness, “Dear Rāma, greatest of the Raghu dynasty, you have asked for a wonderful boon. My promises never fail, so your wish will be granted. Let all the bears and Golangulas who were killed by Rākshasas, whose heads and arms were severed, rise again. Let all the monkeys regain their original strength and health, waking as if from a deep sleep, their wounds healed. May they be reunited with their friends and families and experience great joy. And wherever they live, may the trees always be full of flowers and fruit and the rivers always flow with water, no matter the season.”

Suddenly, all the leading monkeys who had been wounded or killed began to rise, completely healed, as if they had only been sleeping. The monkeys looked around in amazement, wondering what had happened. Seeing Rāma and Lakshmana, the gods and celestials, filled with joy, praised them, saying, “Rāma, return to Ayodhyā now. Send the monkeys home. Comfort Sītā (Maithilee), who has always been devoted to you. See your brother Bharata, who has been living like an ascetic out of grief for you, as well as the noble Satrughna and all your mothers. Then, take your rightful place as king and bring happiness to your people.”

After blessing Rāma and Lakshmana, Indra, the thousand-eyed god, happily departed with the other celestials in their radiant chariots. Rāma, after respectfully bidding farewell to the gods, turned to Lakshmana and gave the order to break camp. The vast monkey army, now happy and healthy under Rāma and Lakshmana’s protection, looked glorious on every side—like a night lit brilliantly by the rays of the moon.
SECTION CXXIII

After spending the night in comfort, Rāma woke up early the next morning. Bibhishana (Vibhishan), proudly celebrating their victory, approached Rāma with folded hands and said, “Here are everything you need for bathing—fragrant pastes, fresh clothes, ornaments, sandalwood, and beautiful garlands. There are also women with lotus-like eyes, skilled in helping you get ready. Let them do their work, O Rāghava.” Rāma replied, “Invite all the monkeys, led by Sugriva, to bathe first. My brother Bharata, who’s always enjoyed comfort and has strong arms, is suffering because of me. Until I see Bharata, the son of Kaikeyi, who’s always performing good deeds, I don’t care about bathing, new clothes, or fancy ornaments. Please, arrange things so we can go to Ayodhyā as soon as possible. The road to Ayodhyā is difficult and I don’t want any delays.” Hearing this, Bibhishana answered, “O son of King Daśaratha, don’t worry, I’ll get you to Ayodhyā soon. The Pushpaka chariot, which looks as bright as the sun, originally belonged to Kuvera, my brother. Rāvana took it by force, but since his defeat, it’s yours now. This magical flying chariot is in Lanka and will take you to Ayodhyā without trouble. But, if you’re willing, if you still consider me a friend and value what I’ve done, please stay a little while—let me worship you here, with Lakshmana and Sītā by your side, before you leave. I’ll do this with happiness and I ask you, with all respect and love, to accept my hospitality. I’m your servant—I can’t order you, but I ask for your permission.” Rāma replied, in front of all the Rākshasas and monkeys, “Bibhishana, you’ve already honored me with your good advice, your hard work, and your friendship. Don’t think I’m refusing your request—I just can’t wait any longer to see my brother Bharata, who came all the way to Chitrakuta to bring me home, who placed his crown at my feet, and whose wishes I didn’t grant. I want to see Kauśalyā, Sumitrā, Kaikeyi, my friends, and everyone in Ayodhyā. Please, Bibhishana, think of me as already worshipped. Don’t be upset, my friend—I mean no offense. Please bring the chariot quickly, O lord of Rākshasas—my mission here is finished, and I can’t stay in Lanka any longer.” After Rāma finished speaking, Bibhishana quickly went to fetch the Pushpaka chariot, shining like the sun.

Soon, the chariot arrived. It was decorated all over with gold designs, its altars sparkling with Baidurja (cat’s eye) jewels. There were upper rooms, everything covered in silver, and white flags and flagpoles flying high. Gilded lotuses, golden houses, and delicate gold chains hung everywhere. The windows were made of pearls and gems, and a net of little bells surrounded the whole thing, ringing out in sweet, musical tones. The chariot looked like the peak of Mount Meru. It was built by Viśwakarmā, the gods’ architect, and had massive apartments decorated with silver and pearls. The base was set with crystal, and there were luxury seats made from Baidurja gems, expensive fabrics, and heaps of treasure. It was unbreakable and could fly wherever you wanted. Bibhishana announced to Rāma that the chariot was ready and waited nearby. When Rāma and Lakshmana (Saumitri) saw the magnificent, mountain-like Pushpaka chariot, their amazement was obvious.
SECTION CXXIV

After bringing the Pushpaka chariot, which was decorated with flowers, Bibhishana (Vibhishan), the lord of the Rakshasas, stood at a respectful distance. Urged to hurry, he approached Rama with folded hands and asked humbly, “What would you like me to do, Raghava?” Hearing this, mighty Rama, standing beside Lakshmana, spoke affectionately: “All these monkeys and bears have helped me achieve my goal with great dedication. Bibhishana, please reward them with jewels and wealth. With your help and theirs, I was able to conquer Lanka, lord of Rakshasas. They all fought bravely and never left the battlefield, even risking their lives. Show your gratitude by giving them gifts of riches and jewels, as a reward for their hard work. Once honored and happy, the leading monkeys will return to their homes. If you act generously, fairly, and with compassion, your people will remain loyal to you. I tell you this because soldiers turn away from a king who lacks these qualities or needlessly kills his own men.” After Rama spoke, Bibhishana honored all the monkeys by distributing jewels and riches among them.

Seeing the leading monkeys rewarded with treasures, Rama climbed into the splendid chariot, taking the shy and noble Sita (Vaidehi) onto his lap. Lakshmana, his skilled and powerful brother, joined them. Standing on the chariot, Rama honored all the monkeys, Sugriva, and Bibhishana, and said, “Foremost of monkeys, you have shown true friendship—I truly appreciate it. Please return to your homes as you wish. Sugriva, you have always acted rightly and done everything a loyal friend should. Take your army and head back to Kishkindha. Bibhishana, you should rule your kingdom of Lanka, which I have given you. Not even the gods, led by Indra, will be able to harm you now. I wish to return to Ayodhya, my father’s city. I ask for your permission before I go, which is why I have called you all here.”

After Rama spoke, all the leading monkeys, bears, and Bibhishana folded their hands and replied, “We all want to go to Ayodhya with you. Please take us along. We would love to explore the forests and gardens together. Once we see you crowned and bow to Kausalya, we’ll happily return to our own homes, O greatest of kings.” Hearing this from the monkeys and Bibhishana, Rama replied to them, as well as to Sugriva and Bibhishana: “I will be happier than ever when I return to my city with all of you, my friends and loved ones. Sugriva, please come aboard the chariot with your monkeys. Bibhishana, you and your courtiers should join us too.”

So, Sugriva, filled with joy, boarded the magical Pushpaka chariot with his monkeys, and Bibhishana joined with his courtiers. Once everyone was on board, the incredible chariot of Kubera, at Rama’s command, lifted into the sky. The chariot, which could travel anywhere and was pulled by glowing swan-like birds, made Rama look like Kubera himself. Inside, all the monkeys, bears, and powerful Rakshasas rode the heavenly chariot with ease and excitement, completely free to enjoy the journey.
SECTION CXXV

At Rāma’s command, the magnificent flying chariot, drawn by giant swan-like birds, took off with a thunderous roar, soaring high into the sky. As they rose, Rāma, descendant of the Raghu dynasty, turned to Sitā (also called Vaidehi), the daughter of the King of Mithilā, her face as radiant as the full moon. He said, “Look, Sitā, there’s Lankā, sitting on top of Mount Chitrakuta. It’s like a second Kailāsa, and was built by the divine architect Viśwakarmā. See that bloody battlefield below, where so many monkeys and Rākshasas lost their lives. There lies Rāvana, king of the Rākshasas, who oppressed so many, now dead because of you. Kumbhakarna was killed there too, along with Prahasta, another fearsome night-stalker, and Dumrāksha—Hanumān took them down. Sushena defeated Bidyutmāli there, and Indrajit, Rāvana’s powerful son, was killed by Lakshmana. Angada killed Bikata, and others like Birupāksha (who was terrifying to behold), Mahāparsha, and Mahodara also died. Akampana, a fierce warrior, was slain there as well as Trishirā, Alikāya, Devāntaka, and Narantaka. The two mighty sons of Kumbhakarna, Nikumbha and Kumbha, along with Bajradanstra, Danstra, and several more Rākshasas were destroyed. I myself killed the unstoppable Makarāksha in battle. Sonitāksha was killed, along with Yupāksha and Prajangha in that great war. Viddutsjmha, who always looked grim, was killed there, as well as Yajnāsatru and the powerful Suptaghna. Suryāsatru and Brahmasatru also fell. There, Rāvana’s wife Mandodari mourned him, surrounded by a thousand other wives. Look, Sitā, there’s the place by the ocean where I rested for a night after crossing the sea to rescue you. For your sake, I built that impossible bridge across the ocean, with Nala’s help. See the calm, endless sea below—the home of Varuna, echoing with the sound of conches and full of pearls and oysters. There’s the golden mountain that rose out of the sea for Hanumān to rest on. That’s where I camped with my army. Here, Lord Shiva himself was worshipped with me. You should see the sacred spot called Setubandha, where the ocean meets the land—a place honored by the entire world, believed to wash away even the worst sins. That’s where Bibhishana, now king of the Rākshasas, first came to join me. Over there is Kishkindhā, a beautiful city ruled by Sugriva, full of gardens, where I killed Vāli.” As Sitā saw Kishkindhā, the city Vāli once ruled, she turned to Rāma and said, her voice full of longing, “My king, I’d love to return to your city, Ayodhyā, with you, and to travel with Tārā, Sugriva’s wife, and the wives of the other leading monkeys.” Rāma replied to Vaidehi (Sitā):

“Of course—let’s do that,” he said. As they reached Kishkindhā, he stopped the flying chariot and turned to Sugriva. “Sugriva, tell all the leading monkeys they should come to Ayodhyā with their wives. They can all travel together with Sitā. Please hurry them up. We’ll leave soon, lord of monkeys.” At Rāma’s request, Sugriva, still surrounded by his followers, quickly went into his palace. He found Tārā and said, “Dear, Rāghava (Rāma) wants you to come, and Sitā wishes for your company. Please gather the wives of all the great monkeys and join us. We’ll see Ayodhyā and meet the wives of Daśaratha.” Hearing this, Tārā, beautiful and gracious, gathered all the monkeys’ wives and told them, “Sugriva has asked us to go to Ayodhyā with the monkeys, which I’m excited for too. I want to see Rāma enter the city, welcomed by its people, and meet the wives of Daśaratha.” Following Tārā’s instructions, the monkey wives put on their best jewelry, walked around her in respect, and boarded the chariot, eager to meet Sitā. As the chariot lifted off with everyone aboard, Rāma turned to Sitā near Mount Rishyamuka and said, “Look, Sitā, that’s the great Rishyamuka mountain, rich in gold and ores, shining like storm clouds with lightning. That’s where I first met Sugriva. There, we made our pact to defeat Vāli. That’s Lake Pampā, full of lilies and surrounded by a beautiful forest—where, when we were separated, I mourned for you. On its shore I met the wise Savari, and there I killed Kavandha and Yoyanavāhu. Over there is Janasthāna and the beautiful tree where, for your sake, the powerful bird Jatāyu was killed by Rāvana. See our old hermitage and the leaf hut from where you were taken by force by Rāvana. There’s the sacred Godāveri river with its clear water, and the hermitage of Agastya, surrounded by banana trees. See the great hermitage of Sarabhanga, where Indra, lord of a thousand eyes, once came. Among all those sages is Atri, the head of our family, shining like fire or the sun. I killed the giant Virādha there. You met Atri’s wife there too, always dedicated to her rituals. Now you can see the king of mountains, Chitrakuta, where Lakshmana, son of Sumitrā, came to support me. There’s the beautiful Yamunā river, with its forests and the pleasant hermitage of Bharadwāja. There’s the sacred Ganges, splitting into three branches. Over there is Sringabera, where I became friends with Guha. Finally, look, Sitā, that’s my father’s capital city. Bow to Ayodhyā, Vaidehi.” At this, all the monkeys and Rākshasas, along with Bibhishana, rose up in excitement and gazed at the city. The monkeys and Rākshasas saw Ayodhyā shining with white houses, full of elephants and horses, looking as beautiful as Amarāvati, the city of Indra.

Today, the remains of this ancient bridge (Setubandha) can still be seen near Rāmeswar, a famous pilgrimage site. Pilgrims usually travel there via Madurai, in South India. The Raja of Ramnad, whose estate includes this area, is called Setupati.
SECTION CXXVI

After completing their fourteen years of exile, Rama—the calm and disciplined older brother of Lakshmana—arrived at the hermitage of Bharadwaja (let’s call him “the sage”) on the fifth day of their return journey. Rama bowed respectfully to the sage and asked, “O wise one, have you heard any news about my city? Is Bharata still taking care of the people? Are my mothers doing well?” Bharadwaja, pleased and smiling, replied to Rama, “Bharata, following your wishes and dressed in matted hair and simple clothes, is waiting for you. He honors your sandals every day, and everyone in your house is well. To be honest, I was really sad when I saw you, Lakshmana, and Sita heading into the deep forest, dressed in bark, stripped of your kingdom just for the sake of doing what’s right, walking barefoot, giving up everything to obey your father, losing all comfort—almost like a god cast out of heaven by Kaikeyi’s words, surviving on wild fruits and roots. But now, seeing you safely back with your friends after defeating your enemies, I couldn’t be happier. I know all about the hardships and joys you faced while living in Janasthana. I heard how your innocent wife Sita was secretly kidnapped by Ravana while you were busy helping the Brahmanas and protecting the sages. I know about your encounter with Maricha, Sita’s abduction, the headless demon you met, your journey to Lake Pampa, your friendship with Sugriva—where you killed Vali—the search for Sita led by Hanuman (the wind god’s son), the bridge built by Nala once you found out where Sita was, Hanuman setting Lanka on fire with help from the monkeys, and finally, the defeat of Ravana—who was so proud of his strength—together with his sons, friends, courtiers, army, and horses. I even know how the gods arrived after Ravana’s death and granted you boons. I’ve learned all these things through my spiritual powers, Rama. My disciples have also brought back news from the city. Now, I’d like to offer you a boon. Please accept my arghya (a respectful offering—see note [1212]) and set out for Ayodhya tomorrow.” Respectfully agreeing, Rama asked for his boon: “O wise one, as I travel to Ayodhya, please let all the trees along the way bear fruit and honey—even out of season—so that the path is filled with sweet, heavenly fruit.” The sage promised, “It shall be as you wish.” Instantly, the trees became like those in paradise. Trees that hadn’t borne fruit were suddenly full, leafless trees burst into fresh leaves, and all the trees dripped with honey. For three yojanas (about 24 miles) on the way to Ayodhya, the path was lined with these magical trees. Thousands of monkeys living with Rama were overjoyed, feasting on the delicious fruit as if they’d arrived in heaven.
[489] That is: you, Lakshmana, and Sita.
An arghya is a respectful offering to gods or respected people, usually consisting of rice, sacred grass, flowers, and water presented in a small boat-shaped vessel.
SECTION CXXVII

When Rāma finally saw Ayodhyā on the horizon, he was full of energy and eager to bring happiness to others. He wanted to make sure everyone was prepared for his return. With this in mind, the clever and radiant Rāma turned to the group of monkeys and spoke directly to Hanumān. “Hanumān,” he said, “you’re the best among the monkeys. Please hurry to Ayodhyā and find out how everyone in the palace is doing. On your way, stop at Sringavera and tell Guha—the Nishadha king who rules the forests—that I am safe and well. Guha is as close to me as my own self, and hearing I’m safe will make him happy. Guha will also show you the way to Ayodhyā and let you know how Bharata is doing.

When you see Bharata, ask after his wellbeing in my name, and tell him that I’m returning with Lakshmana and my wife Sītā, having fulfilled my father’s wishes. Tell him everything: how Rāvana kidnapped Sītā, how I became friends with Sugrīva and defeated Vāli, how you searched for Sītā by crossing the vast ocean, how we all reached the ocean’s shore and built a bridge, how Rāvana was defeated, and how I received blessings from Indra, Brahmā, and Varuna. Also tell him about my meeting with my father’s spirit, thanks to Shiva’s grace. Be sure to let Bharata know that I have arrived at Ayodhyā’s gates, together with the king of the monkeys and the leader of the Rākshasas, after defeating my enemies and gaining great fame.

Watch closely how Bharata reacts—look for signs of happiness or sadness. From his face, eyes, and words, you’ll be able to tell what he truly feels about me returning. After all, who wouldn’t be tempted by an ancestral kingdom filled with wealth, elephants, horses, and chariots? If Bharata, son of Raghu, wants the kingdom for himself, he’s free to keep ruling. That’s why, Hanumān, you must return quickly and tell me what Bharata’s intentions are before we proceed.” 

Given these instructions, Hanumān, the son of the wind-god, transformed himself into a human and sped toward Ayodhyā. He shot through the sky as swiftly as Garuda swooping down upon a massive serpent. Passing over the sky-paths, flocks of birds, and the wild meeting point of the Ganges and Yamunā rivers, Hanumān reached Sringavera and found Guha. Overjoyed, Hanumān greeted Guha, saying, “Your friend Rāma, of the Kākutstha line, who is as true as he is brave, sends his regards to you, Guha. He is with Sītā and Lakshmana (the son of Sumitrā). After spending five nights here, and getting permission from the sage Varadwāja, he will leave tomorrow.” 

After delivering this message, the energetic monkey, ignoring any tiredness from his journey, leapt up again, his fur bristling with excitement. Flying over the holy Parasurāma river, over the Bālukini, Baruthi, and Gomati rivers, and through vast forests of Sāla trees, Hanumān sped across many lands crowded with thousands of people. Soon he arrived at the outskirts of Nandigrām, where the trees looked as beautiful as those in Indra’s own heavenly gardens—full of women and children picking flowers and wearing sparkling jewelry.

From a distance of just one krosha (about two miles) from Ayodhyā, Hanumān saw Bharata. Bharata wore deer-skin clothes, looked thin and weak, and lived simply in a hermitage. His hair was matted, his body covered in dust, and he looked worn down from grief for his brother. He survived on roots and fruit, followed strict vows, and lived like a true ascetic, always keeping Rāma’s sandals before him as a symbol of Rāma’s rule. He protected his people, who also avoided fine clothing out of respect for Bharata’s simple life. Surrounding him were wise priests, loyal ministers, and soldiers, all dressed in red.

Hanumān, son of the wind-god, approached Bharata with folded hands and spoke respectfully to this virtuous prince, saying, “Rāma, for whom you grieve—the one who lived in the Dandaka forest wearing bark and matted hair—sends you his greetings. Please tell me how you’re doing, and let go of your deep sorrow. You’ll be reunited with your brother Rāma very soon. He has defeated Rāvana, rescued Sītā, and fulfilled his mission. Rāma is here now, along with the heroic Lakshmana and the famous Sītā, who is safe with him, just as Sachi is safe with Indra.”

Hearing Hanumān’s words, Bharata, son of Kaikeyi, was so overwhelmed that he fainted from joy. He quickly regained consciousness, warmly welcomed Hanumān, and expressed his happiness with tears—not from sadness but pure joy. Bharata embraced Hanumān and said, “Are you a man or a god to bring me such amazing news? I want to reward you, who gave me this wonderful message, with hundreds and thousands of cows, hundreds of prosperous villages, and sixteen young wives—noble, beautiful women adorned with gold, with bright faces and lovely features, all from good families.”

After hearing about Rāma’s miraculous return from Hanumān, Bharata was both thrilled and impatient to see his brother. Still filled with excitement, he spoke again joyfully to Hanumān.
(Note: Guha is a low-caste, forest-dwelling Hindu, somewhat like the Chandālas. The Raja of Ramnad in South India claims descent from Guha.)
(Note: After completing fourteen years of exile, Rāma spent five more nights at the hermitage of Varadwāja, and will leave tomorrow.)
(Note: Nandigrām is the country of Bharata’s maternal uncle.)
SECTION CXXVIII

“I’ve just heard amazing news about my brother, who’s been living out in the wild for so many years. It makes me think that the old saying is true: as long as someone is alive, there’s always hope for happiness, even after a hundred years. Please, tell me honestly—how and where did Rāghava (Rāma) join forces with the monkeys?” After the prince asked this, Hanumān, who was sitting on some kusa grass, began to recount Rāma’s story in the forest. “First, Rāma was exiled. Your mother received two boons that led to this, and King Daçaratha died from the grief of losing his son. Messengers were sent to bring you, my lord, from your uncle’s house. When you arrived in Ayodhyā, you didn’t want the kingdom, and instead, you urged your brother—the one who always defeats his enemies—to take the throne. Following the path of righteousness, you went to Mount Chitrakuta, and your brother gave up the throne to honor your father’s word. You returned after taking your revered brother’s sandals—all these events, long-armed prince, you already know. Now I’ll tell you what happened after you returned. When you left, the birds and animals were terrified, and the forest itself seemed upset. Then Rāma entered the deep, wild, and dangerous Dandaka forest, full of elephants, lions, tigers, and deer.

As they made their way through the dense woods, a powerful demon named Virādha (kind of like a monster boss fight) appeared, making a terrifying noise. Rāma grabbed him, lifted him up, and threw him face-first into a pit, ending the threat. With that challenge handled, Rāma and Lakshmana reached the peaceful hermitage of Sarabhanga by evening. After Sarabhanga rose up to heaven, Rāma—who’s known for his honesty—paid respects to the other sages and set off for Janasthāna. There, the mighty Rāghava killed fourteen thousand of Janasthāna’s inhabitants. With only Lakshmana by his side and in just a quarter of a day, Rāma wiped out all the fierce and strong demons that had been tormenting the forest’s ascetics. Rāghava slaughtered every Rākshasa in his way. Khara was killed in battle, then Dushana, and after that, Trishirā.

Next, a demoness named Surpanakhā showed up and came after Rāma. On Rāma’s orders, Lakshmana jumped up suddenly and, with his dagger, cut off her ears and nose. Humiliated, she ran straight to Rāvana. Then, Rāvana’s henchman, a terrifying Rākshasa named Māricha, turned himself into a magical, jewel-covered deer to lure Sītā (Vaidehi). When Sītā saw it, she said to Rāma, “Can you catch it? If we have it, our home here will look even better.” Rāma chased after the deer with his bow and killed it with a single arrow. While Rāghava was out hunting and Lakshmana had also left the hermitage, the ten-headed demon Rāvana snuck in. He grabbed Sītā, just like the planet snatches Rohini in the sky. On his way out, Rāvana killed the vulture Jatāyu, who tried to rescue her, then rushed off to his city with Sītā.

Meanwhile, a group of monkeys, huge as mountains and standing on a mountaintop, saw Rāvana flying by with Sītā. Rāvana, with Sītā beside him, sped away in the Pushpaka chariot, which could go anywhere he wished, and arrived in Lankā, his golden city. Inside his magnificent palace, Rāvana tried to comfort Sītā with all kinds of words, but she ignored him, treating him and his words like they were nothing. Sītā was then imprisoned in the Ashoka grove. Afterward, Rāma came back from hunting the deer. When he returned and saw Jatāyu—who was dearer to him than his own father—dead, Rāma, the descendant of Kākutstha, was heartbroken. Searching for Sītā, Rāma and Lakshmana wandered along the banks of the Godāveri river and through flower-filled forests. In those deep woods, they met a demon called Kabandha.

Following Kabandha’s advice, Rāma, true to his word, traveled to Mount Rishyamuka and met Sugriva. Even before they really knew each other, they felt a strong bond. Sugriva had been exiled by his furious brother, Vāli. As they got to know each other’s stories, their friendship grew even deeper. Then, Rāma used his own strength to kill the powerful Vāli in a fierce fight, restoring Sugriva’s kingdom. Once he was king again, Sugriva, with all the monkeys, promised Rāma that they’d search for the princess Sītā. When Sugriva, the wise monkey king, gave the order, ten crore (kotis) of monkeys spread out in all directions to look for her. Some of us got lost in a cave in the Vindhya mountains and were terrified, which caused a big delay. Eventually, the powerful Sampāti, brother of the vulture king, told us where Sītā was being held in Rāvana’s palace.

To comfort my worried friends and relying on my own strength, I (Hanumān) leaped a hundred yojanas across the sea and found Sītā in the Ashoka grove. She wore a red dress, looked pale and joyless, and was keeping strict vows. When I got close and saw how blameless she was, I gave her a sign—a ring with Rāma’s name engraved on it. In return, she gave me a precious jewel as a sign for Rāma. With my mission done, I returned and handed Rāma the brilliant gem from Sītā. When Rāma heard the news about Sītā, he was revived—like someone near death coming back to life after tasting nectar. Fired up, he urged his army to get ready, determined to destroy Lankā like a raging fire. When they reached the ocean, Nala built a bridge so the army of monkey heroes could cross.

On the battlefield, Nala killed Prahasta, Rāghava defeated Kumbhakarna, Lakshmana took down Rāvana’s son, and Rāma himself killed Rāvana. Then, gods like Indra (Sakra), Yama, Varuna, Shiva, Brahmā, and Daçaratha appeared to him. The noble Rāma, the great warrior from the Kākutstha dynasty, received special blessings from them and the assembled sages—gifts both heavenly and earthly. Overjoyed, Rāma reunited with the monkeys and returned to Kishkindhā in the Pushpaka chariot. Back at the Ganges, he’s now living with the hermit. You’ll be able to see him tomorrow under the Pushya constellation, with nothing standing in your way.” Delighted by Hanumān’s words, Bharata folded his hands and replied joyfully, “After so long, my wish has finally come true.”
A demon by that name.
The Pushya constellation—a group of three stars, one of which is in Cancer.
SECTION CXXIX

Hearing these joyful words, Bharata—known for his truthfulness and skill in battle—happily gave Satrughna some instructions: “Have everyone purify themselves and then worship the city’s gods and altars with fresh garlands and all kinds of music. Gather the bards who know our family’s history, the singers, musicians, dancers, queens, courtiers, soldiers with their wives, Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, and everyone else. Let them all go out to see Rama’s face, which is as lovely as the moon.” Satrughna, always ready for action, divided up the work among the servants: “Level the road from Nandigram to Ayodhya. Water it thoroughly. Sprinkle flowers and dry rice over everything, hoist up flags, and decorate every house before nightfall with garlands, jewels, gold flowers, and bright colors. Post guards along every major street.” As soon as Satrughna gave the order, Dhristi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddartha, Arthasadhaka, Asoka, Mantrapala, and Sumantra rushed out excitedly to organize things. Soon, people on horseback and in chariots rode out, along with thousands of elephants dressed with banners, and female elephants carrying golden seats. Some warriors marched surrounded by a thousand top-notch horses and soldiers carrying spears, maces, banners, and thousands of footmen. Then Sumitra and the other wives of Dasaratha, with Kausalya in the lead, rode in beautiful carriages. Hearing that his brother was returning, Bharata—who was thin from fasting, dressed in bark and deerskin, and always followed dharma—set out to welcome Rama. He was surrounded by his advisors, priests, people from every caste, his family, garland-bearers, and folks carrying modaka (a kind of sweet). Bards praised him, the arrival was announced with conch shells and bugles, and Bharata carried Rama’s sandals on his head, along with a white umbrella, golden fans, and other royal symbols. The noise from the horses, chariots, conches, and bugles made the ground tremble, and the entire city went out to Nandigram. When he saw Hanuman, Bharata asked, “Did you give in to the monkey’s usual playfulness? We can’t see Rama, the great hero from the Kakutstha line who defeats his enemies. Nor do we see the monkeys who can change their shapes at will.” Hanuman replied honestly, “The monkeys are in the trees, thanks to Varadwaja’s blessing. They’re eating fruit and honey, making a buzzing noise like crazy bees. Rama received this boon from Indra. Varadwaja is treating him and his army with great respect. Listen to the wild noise the monkeys are making—they must have crossed the Gomati river by now. Look at that huge dust cloud near the Sala forest. The monkeys are stirring things up over there. And see that chariot shining like the sun in the distance? It’s the Pushpaka, a flying chariot created by Brahma’s mind that Rama gained after defeating Ravana. This chariot moves wherever it wants and was given to Rama by Kubera, the god of wealth. Inside are Rama, his brother Lakshmana, Sita (Vaidehi), the shining Sugriva, and the rakshasa Vibhishana.” At the rumor that “Rama is here!”, women, children, and people of all ages cheered so loudly it seemed to reach the heavens. People climbed down from chariots, elephants, and horses to see Rama standing in the chariot, glowing like the moon in the sky. Bharata, overjoyed, greeted Rama respectfully with water for his feet and other welcoming gifts. Rama, his eyes wide and bright like Indra’s, stood in the chariot built by Brahma’s own mind. Bharata bowed low before Rama, who sat high above like the sun on Mount Meru. At Rama’s command, the magical Pushpaka chariot landed on the ground. Bharata climbed aboard, thrilled to see Rama again, and bowed to him. Rama, filled with happiness, hugged Bharata tightly and lifted him onto his lap. Bharata then paid respects to Sita and greeted Lakshmana warmly. The son of Kaikeyi (Bharata) then embraced Sugriva, Jambavan, Angada, Mainda, Dwivida, Nila, and Rishava. Next, he hugged Sushena, Nala, Gabaksha, Gandhamadana, Sarabha, and Panasa. The monkeys, now in human form, happily asked Bharata how he was doing. Bharata embraced Sugriva and said, “Sugriva, you’re like our fifth brother. Friendship comes from brotherhood; hurting each other is the sign of an enemy.” Bharata then turned to Vibhishana and said kindly, “We’re lucky that, with your help, Rama was able to accomplish this nearly impossible task.” Satrughna then bowed to Rama and Lakshmana and greeted Sita respectfully. Rama, approaching his mother—who looked pale and tired from grief—humbly touched her feet, making her incredibly happy. He then greeted Sumitra, Kaikeyi, and all his mothers, and approached the priests. All the citizens welcomed Rama with folded hands, saying, “Welcome, long-armed hero! You bring joy to Kausalya!” Rama saw the sea of folded hands, looking like a field of lotuses. Bharata, ever dutiful, took Rama’s sandals and placed them at his brother’s feet. Bharata then said to Rama, “Here is your entire kingdom, which you left in my care—I return it to you now. I feel blessed and fulfilled today, seeing you return as king to Ayodhya. Please inspect your wealth, treasury, palace, and army—all of which I’ve increased tenfold thanks to your guidance.” Hearing Bharata’s words and seeing his devotion, the monkeys and Vibhishana were moved to tears. Rama, overjoyed, sat Bharata on his lap and, with the whole army, headed toward Bharata’s palace in the chariot. When they arrived, Rama and everyone got down to the ground. Rama turned to the Pushpaka chariot and said, “You can go back to Kubera now—I release you.” At his command, Pushpaka sped north to Kubera’s home. This chariot, once stolen by Ravana, now returned to its rightful owner at Rama’s word. Rama then touched the feet of his priest and sat on a special seat, shining like Indra beside his teacher Brihaspati.
A kind of sweet.
SECTION CXXX

With his hands pressed together on his head, Bharata (sometimes called "Bharat"), who had brought happiness to his mother Kaikeyi, spoke to his older brother Rama, who was known for his honesty and strength. He said, “You gave me this kingdom because of my mother’s wishes, but now I want to return it to you. I can’t handle the huge responsibility of ruling, just as a calf can’t carry the heavy load that only a strong bull could. Running this kingdom is like trying to rebuild a bridge swept away by a raging river—it’s full of dangers and too hard for me. An ass can’t keep up with a horse, and a crow can’t fly like a swan. That’s how I feel compared to you, great hero and destroyer of enemies—I just can’t follow in your footsteps. If a tree is planted in the inner courtyard, and it grows big and leafy but dries up before it ever bears fruit, then it fails the person who planted it. This is what will happen to us if you, our master, don’t rule over us, lord of men. Let the world see you crowned today, shining fiercely like the midday sun. You should wake and sleep to the sound of music, the jingling of women’s jewelry, and beautiful songs. Rule the people for as long as the sun rises and as far as the earth stretches.” Hearing Bharata’s words, Rama, the conqueror of enemy cities, said, “So be it,” and sat down on a fine seat.

Then, at Satrughna’s command, skilled and quick barbers gathered around Rama. First, Bharata, the strong Lakshmana, Sugriva—the monkey king—and Vibhishana—the king of the Rakshasas—all bathed. After Rama’s matted hair was cut and he had bathed, he was dressed in fine clothes, wore beautiful garlands, and looked radiant. Satrughna, graceful and proud of his heritage, personally prepared the clothes for Rama and Lakshmana. The noble wives of Dasaratha (Kausalya, Sumitra, and Kaikeyi) themselves decorated Sita with lovely jewelry. Kausalya, happy and loving, also carefully adorned the wives of the monkeys.

At Satrughna’s word, Sumantra the charioteer prepared a beautiful chariot. When Rama saw the magnificent chariot, glowing like fire, waiting for him, he climbed aboard. Sugriva and Hanuman, dressed in heavenly clothes and shining earrings, also bathed and got ready to see the city. Sita and the wives of Sugriva, all adorned with jewels, eagerly prepared to see the city as well.

Meanwhile, all of King Dasaratha’s ministers in Ayodhya respectfully consulted with the royal priest. Asoka, Vijaya, and Siddhartha discussed how to best serve both Rama and the city. They ordered the servants: “Gather everything we’ll need for Rama’s auspicious coronation.”

Once the priest and ministers gave their orders, everyone hurried out of the city to greet Rama. Like Indra, the thousand-eyed king of gods, arriving in his horse-drawn chariot, Rama rode toward the city. Bharata took the reins, Satrughna held the royal umbrella, and Lakshmana fanned Rama’s head with a chowrie (a whisk). Vibhishana, king of the Rakshasas, stood at Rama’s side, holding another white chowrie, bright as a second moon.

From above, ascetics, gods, and wind spirits sang Rama’s praises. Sugriva, dazzling among monkeys, rode atop a huge elephant named Satrunyaya, as grand as a mountain. Nine thousand monkeys, transformed to look like humans and decked out in jewelry, followed on elephants. With the sound of conch shells and horns, Rama, the greatest of men, entered the city filled with houses.

The people of Ayodhya watched Rama ride into the city, looking majestic in his chariot, and bowed to him. Rama greeted them all, and they joined the procession around him and his brothers. With his court, priests, and people surrounding him, Rama looked as beautiful as the moon surrounded by stars.

Musicians playing stringed instruments, people clapping and making music with karatalas and sustikas, and singers performing joyful songs led the way. People carrying rice, gold, cows, girls, priests, and sweets (modaka) walked ahead of Rama. Soon, in front of the ministers, Rama began to tell the story of his friendship with Sugriva, Hanuman’s amazing bravery, and the heroic deeds of the monkeys.

When the people of Ayodhya heard about the monkeys’ feats and the power of the Rakshasas, they were amazed. After telling these stories, Rama, surrounded by monkeys and his friends, entered Ayodhya, a city full of happy and well-fed people.

The citizens raised flags on every house, celebrating as Rama returned to his ancestors’ grand home, the palace of the Ikshwaku dynasty. On entering, he bowed to Kausalya, Sumitra, and Kaikeyi, showing his respect. Then, the noble prince, who brought joy to the Raghu family, turned to Bharata and said warmly, “Set aside my grand palace, rich with pearls and gems, for Sugriva.”

Bharata, always true to his word, took Sugriva by the hand and led him to the palace. Following Satrughna’s orders, servants quickly filled the palace with lamps, beds, and bedding. Next, Satrughna, Rama’s shining younger brother, said to Sugriva, “Lord, please have someone bring water for Rama’s coronation.”

Sugriva gave four leading monkeys four golden jars decorated with jewels and said, “Go, my friends, and bring water from the four oceans by dawn.” The monkeys, strong as elephants, leapt into the sky like speedy vultures. Jambavan, Hanuman, Vegadarshi, and Rishabha brought jars filled with water from five hundred rivers. Sushena, known for his strength, brought a gem-studded jar filled with water from the Eastern Ocean. Rishabha brought water from the Southern Ocean. Gavaya filled a golden jar with sweet-smelling water from the great Western Ocean. Hanuman, son of the wind-god, with the power of both Garuda and the wind, quickly brought water from the Northern Ocean in a jeweled jar.

Seeing the jars brought by the monkeys for Rama’s coronation, Satrughna and his ministers informed the chief priests and their friends. Then, the wise and elderly Vasishtha, along with other Brahmanas, seated Rama and Sita on a jeweled throne. Vasishtha, Vijaya, Javali, Katyayana, Gautama, and Vamadeva sprinkled Rama with clear, fragrant water, just as the gods once crowned Indra.

After that, the royal priests, Brahmanas, young women, ministers, soldiers, and merchants all joyfully sprinkled Rama with holy water. Then, the gods in the sky, the guardians of the four directions, and all the other deities sprinkled Rama with the juice of sacred herbs.

Seated on a throne decorated with gold, gems, and rich ornaments, Rama received the jeweled crown created by Brahma himself—the same crown used to crown Manu and other kings from his family in ancient times. After Vasishtha placed the crown on Rama, the priests dressed him in divine clothes. Satrughna held the white umbrella, Sugriva held the white chowrie, and Vibhishana held another chowrie that shone like the moon.

The wind, under Indra’s command, brought Rama a garland of a hundred golden lotuses, glowing with their own light. The wind, under Sakra’s command, also brought a jeweled garland decorated with many different gems.

Once Rama, wise and deserving, was crowned, the gods and Gandharvas (heavenly musicians) sang, and the Apsaras (celestial dancers) performed. The earth was full of crops, trees were heavy with fruit, and flowers scented the air on the day Rama was crowned. Rama gave a million horses, a hundred thousand cows, and a hundred thousand bulls to the Brahmanas. He also gave them thirty crores (three hundred million) gold coins, as well as countless precious jewels and clothes.

Rama gave Sugriva a heavenly garland shining like the sun, covered in gold and gems. To Angada, Vali’s son, he gave two armlets (called “angadas”), bright as moonbeams and made from special gems. Rama also gave Sita a beautiful pearl necklace, fine clothes, and many lovely ornaments. Sita, remembering Hanuman’s help, took off the necklace and gave it to him, glancing again and again at Rama and the monkeys.

Rama noticed Sita’s gesture and said, “My dear, you should give this necklace to whoever you’re most pleased with.” So Sita, her eyes like lotus petals, gave it to Hanuman. Hanuman, known for his endless energy, patience, fame, skill, courage, humility, cleverness, and intelligence, wore the necklace and looked like a mountain shining with moonlight and clouds.

All the other elder and leading monkeys were honored with clothes and jewelry. With plenty of gifts and jewels from Rama, Vibhishana, Sugriva, Hanuman, Jambavan, and the other leading monkeys happily returned home. The lord of the earth, Rama, also gave everything Dwivida, Mainda, and Nila wanted.

After seeing Rama crowned, the noble monkeys said their goodbyes and returned to Kishkindha. Sugriva, too, honored by Rama, went back to his city. Vibhishana, now king of Lanka, returned to his home with all the Rakshasas.

Having defeated his enemies, Rama ruled the earth generously and with great happiness. He said to Lakshmana, “My brother, help me rule this kingdom, just as our ancestors did. Be my partner on the throne, as they once were.” But Lakshmana, son of Sumitra, refused the title of heir apparent, even though Rama asked again and again. So Rama gave that honor to Bharata.

Bharata went on to perform many great sacrifices, like the Paundarika, Ashwamedha, and Bajimedha. Rama ruled for ten thousand years, performing ten horse sacrifices with excellent horses and generous gifts. He was a powerful ruler, with long arms reaching his knees and a broad chest, and Lakshmana always by his side.

With his sons, brothers, and friends, Rama performed many more sacrifices. Under his rule, widows did not suffer, there was no fear of wild animals or disease, and people were safe from thieves and all other troubles. No parent had to grieve for a lost child; everyone was happy and devoted to doing good. People looked at Rama and felt no jealousy toward each other. Under his reign, people lived for a thousand years, had a thousand children, and were free from sickness and sorrow. The trees always bore fruit and flowers, rain fell when needed, and the wind was always pleasant. People enjoyed their work, told the truth, and practiced good deeds, blessed with every sign of happiness. Rama ruled for ten thousand years.

This sacred epic, the first of its kind, brings piety, fame, and long life, and tells the story of kings’ victories. It was written long ago by Valmiki. Anyone who hears this story will have their sins washed away. If you wish for children, you will have them; if you wish for wealth, you will get it. Hearing about Rama’s coronation will help you achieve your desires, conquer your enemies, or bring you home if you’re far away. Just as Kausalya gave birth to Rama, Sumitra to Lakshmana, and Kaikeyi to Bharata, women who hear this story will have sons. Hearing about Rama’s triumphs brings long life. Anyone who listens to this epic with devotion and self-control will overcome all troubles. If you live far from home, hearing this story will help you return and be happy with your loved ones. Hearing this brings all your wishes to Rama, and the gods will be pleased. Keeping this book in your house protects you from evil spirits. Kings who hear this story can conquer the world, and people far from home will do well. Women who listen during their monthly cycle will have excellent sons. Reading or hearing this ancient story frees you from sin and brings a long life. Kshatriyas should bow their heads and listen to Brahmanas read it daily. Anyone who reads or hears the whole Ramayana will gain sons and wealth, with Rama always pleased. Rama is the eternal Vishnu—the first god, the mighty Hari, Narayana, and Lord. This ancient story brings blessings. May you all be well. Spread the word so that Vishnu’s glory grows. The gods will rejoice to hear this story, and your ancestors will be pleased. Anyone who writes down this story first told by Valmiki will reach Brahma’s realm. Hearing this, you’ll gain friends, wealth, crops, beautiful wives, happiness, and all your desires. You’ll live long, be healthy, famous, smart, brave, and have good brothers. That’s why everyone who wants a good life should hear this story again and again.

SECTION I

After the Rākshasas were defeated, all the sages came to congratulate Rāma, who had just regained his kingdom. Among them were Kauśika, Yavakrita, Gārgya, Gālava, and Kanva (son of Mādhālithi), who lived in the east. From the south came the respected Swastyāstreya, Namuchi, Pramuchi, Agastya, Atri, Sumukha, and Vimukha—Agastya led this group. From the west, Nrishadgu, Kahashi, Dhaumya, and the powerful sage Kauśeya arrived with their students. From the north came Vasishtha, Kaśyapa, Atri, Viśwamitra, Gautama, Jamadagni, Bharadwaja, and also the seven great sages. When they reached Rāma’s home, these wise men, glowing like fire, stopped at the entrance and asked the guard to announce their arrival. The renowned sage Agastya, an expert in many fields and the Vedas, spoke to the gatekeeper: “Please tell Daśaratha’s son that we, the sages, have come.” Hearing Agastya’s message, the gatekeeper quickly went to Rāma, who was radiant like the full moon, and told him that Agastya and the other sages had arrived. Rāma, hearing that these brilliant ascetics had come, replied, “Please bring them in and make sure they are comfortable.” When the sages entered, Rāma greeted them with folded hands, washed their feet as a sign of respect, and gave each a consecrated cow. He then had seats prepared for them. The sages sat down according to their rank on beautiful seats made of sacred grass or golden-embroidered deer-skins. Once everyone was settled and their well-being had been asked after, the sages spoke to Rāma: “O Rāma, son of Raghu, we are well. We are lucky to see you victorious, with all your enemies gone. It’s fortunate that you defeated Rāvana, the destroyer of beings. Honestly, for you, defeating Rāvana and his sons and grandsons was not difficult—you could destroy the three worlds if you wanted. We’re glad to see you with Sītā and your loyal brother Lakshmana. We’re happy to see you reunited with your mothers and brothers. We’re thankful that the powerful night-dwellers—Prahasta, Vikata, Virupāksha, Mahodara, and the unbeatable Akampana—are all gone because of you. It’s also fortunate that Kumbhakarna, whose size was unmatched on earth, was brought down by you. We’re lucky that you defeated the mighty night-rangers Triśiras, Atikāya, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka. You even faced Rāvana, who couldn’t be killed even by the gods, and still won. While defeating Rāvana was a big deal, it’s especially lucky that you defeated his son in battle. We’re thankful that you escaped from the enemy whose power was like Time itself, and that you were victorious. When we heard Indrajit was dead, we were amazed—he was said to be impossible to kill and a master of illusions. Now that you have freed us from fear, Rāma, your victories will only grow.” Hearing these words, Rāma, full of wonder, respectfully asked, “Respected sages, why do you praise Rāvana’s son so much, even more than the powerful Kumbhakarna and Rāvana himself? Why do you speak so highly of him instead of Mahodara, Prahasta, Virupāksha, Matta, Unmatta, Devāntaka, or Narāntaka, all of whom were great warriors? Why do you focus on Rāvana’s son instead of Atikāya, Triśiras, or Dhumrāksha, who were all extremely strong? What made him so impressive? How was he even greater than Rāvana? If you’re willing, please tell me. I’m not demanding, but I’d like to know if it’s okay to share. How did he defeat Indra (Sakra), and how did he get his special powers? How did Rāvana’s son manage to defeat Indra, and what made him stronger than even his father? Please, greatest of sages, explain all this to me today.”
The name Agastya had already been mentioned among those arriving—but that’s how it appears in the original text.

“Turnam” means mental quickness, while “drutam” means physical speed, according to the commentator. However, Sanskrit authors rarely make this distinction.
