SECTION II

After hearing these words, the powerful Kumbhayoni said, “Given Indrajit’s strength and power, I’ll tell you the story of his family. This will help you understand why Ravana’s son was able to defeat his enemies, but couldn’t be killed by them. Raghava, I’ll explain how Ravana was born, who his ancestors were, and the special boon he was granted.

“A long time ago, during the Krita age, there was a great sage, a Brahmarshi, who was a son of Prajapati—the lord of all living things. He was so virtuous and wise that it’s hard to describe just how extraordinary he was. Because he was Prajapati’s son, the gods adored him, and thanks to his perfect character, all living beings loved him too. This remarkable sage went on a spiritual journey to the hermitage of Trinavindu, near the great Mount Meru, and decided to live there. He dedicated himself to studying the Vedas, focusing all his senses on his spiritual practice. But his meditation was interrupted by a group of young women—the daughters of sages, Pannagas (serpent beings), royal sages, and even Apsaras (celestial dancers)—who often came to that beautiful spot to play, sing, and dance. The area was always pleasant, and the scenery was gorgeous, so they loved to visit. Their singing and dancing disturbed the sage’s rituals and concentration. Finally, the powerful ascetic became angry and declared, ‘Any girl who comes near me will become pregnant.’ The girls, terrified by the possibility of a Brahmin’s curse, stopped visiting. However, Trinavindu’s daughter hadn’t heard about the curse. She wandered into the hermitage alone, searching for her friends, without realizing the danger. At that moment, Prajapati’s son, now pure through his intense meditation, was deep in Vedic study. She heard his chanting and saw his aura of ascetic power. Suddenly, her body began to change—she grew pale and showed signs of pregnancy, which made her anxious. Confused, she wondered, ‘What’s happening to me?’ and returned to her father’s hermitage. When Trinavindu saw her changed appearance, he asked, ‘Why do you look so different?’ With her hands folded and looking distressed, she said, ‘Father, I don’t know why I look like this. I went alone to Maharshi Pulastya’s hermitage, searching for my friends, but found no one there. Now, seeing what’s happened to me, I came here out of fear.’ Trinavindu, glowing with spiritual energy, meditated and realized what had happened—she had been affected by the sage’s curse. Understanding this, he took his daughter to Pulastya and said, ‘Great sage, please accept my daughter, who has come to you on her own, as a gift. She will serve you wholeheartedly and live a life of spiritual discipline.’ The sage agreed, saying, ‘Very well.’ After giving his daughter to Pulastya, Trinavindu returned to his own hermitage. The girl stayed with Pulastya, taking care of him and living a virtuous life. Pulastya was pleased with her character, and, happy with her, he said, ‘You are truly remarkable. Because of your goodness, I will grant you a son who will continue both your family lines, and he will be famous as a Paulastya. Since you heard me reciting the Vedas, your son will be named Visrava.’ The girl was overjoyed, and soon she gave birth to Visrava, who became famous throughout the three worlds for his virtue and knowledge. Visrava was a true ascetic, just like his father.”

SECTION III

Pulastya’s son, Viçravā (let’s call him Viçravā), quickly followed in his father’s footsteps as a great ascetic. Like Pulastya, he was honest, disciplined, and focused on spiritual study, especially the Vedas. He avoided indulgence in worldly pleasures and was deeply religious. Seeing Viçravā’s character, the powerful sage Bharadwāja gave his own daughter, Devavarnini, to Viçravā in marriage. Viçravā married Devavarnini according to sacred rites, and felt incredible happiness as he began to think about his future children and their well-being. Viçravā, who truly understood right and wrong, had a remarkable son with Devavarnini—a child full of energy and blessed with all the qualities valued by Brahmā. When the boy was born, his grandfather was overjoyed. Noticing the boy’s sharp mind, he predicted the child would one day become the lord of wealth. Pleased, Pulastya and the divine seers (Devarshis) agreed: “Since this is Viçravā’s son and he looks just like him, he should be known as Vaiçravana.” 

Soon, Vaiçravana grew stronger as he practiced meditation and self-discipline in the forest, his power increasing steadily, like a fire fed with fuel. While living in the hermitage, Vaiçravana decided, “I will follow the highest path of virtue. True goodness is the best way to live.” He spent a thousand years practicing severe austerities in that vast forest, keeping strict vows the whole time. Each stage of his penance brought new challenges: for a while he lived only on water, then only on air, and finally, he gave up food entirely. The thousand years seemed to pass in no time. At the end of his penance, the powerful god Brahmā, along with Indra and other gods, came to his hermitage and spoke to Vaiçravana: “My child, I am pleased with your dedication and your excellent vows. Ask me for any blessing you want—you have earned it.”

Vaiçravana replied to Brahmā, “Respected one, I would like the power to protect and support people.”

Brahmā and the other gods, clearly happy, said, “Very well! I am about to create a fourth protector of the world, alongside Yama, Indra, and Varuna. You shall have the position you seek. Become the lord of wealth, the fourth among the great protectors. Take this chariot, Pushpaka, as your vehicle—it shines like the sun. With it, you will be equal to the gods. Good luck! Now, we must return to where we came from. Our duty is done, and you have received your boons.” With that, Brahmā and the gods left for their own realms.

After they left, the self-controlled lord of wealth, Vaiçravana, respectfully approached his father and said, “Father, I have received the blessing I wanted from Brahmā. But the creator hasn’t given me a place to live. Please, can you find me a home where I’ll be safe from all harm?”

Viçravā, the wise sage, replied, “Listen, my son. On the southern sea coast stands Mount Trikuta. At its peak is a beautiful, wide city built by Viçwakarmā, called Lankā. It’s as grand as Indra’s own city, built for the Rākshasas—a real masterpiece, like Amaravati itself. Lankā is surrounded by golden walls and a moat, armed with defenses and weapons, with gates made of gold and precious stones. Long ago, the Rākshasas abandoned it out of fear of Vishnu and fled to the underworld, leaving Lankā empty and unruled. Now, Lankā stands vacant—no one is in charge there. Go there, my son. You’ll have peace, and nothing will disturb you in that place.”

Taking his father’s wise advice, Vaiçravana moved to Lankā, accompanied by thousands of happy and excited Rākshasas. Soon, under his rule, Lankā became wealthy and prosperous. As the righteous son of Viçravā, Vaiçravana, lord of the Nairitas, happily ruled Lankā, protected by the ocean. Sometimes, riding the Pushpaka chariot, Vaiçravana would visit his parents, always showing them respect. Praised by gods and Gandharvas, his palace filled with the dancing of Apsarās and shining like the sun, the lord of wealth would return to see his father.
(These are qualities like self-control, spiritual discipline, purity, and so on.)
SECTION IV

After hearing Agastya’s words, Rāma found himself genuinely puzzled about how the Rākshasas originally appeared in Lankā. Shaking his head in disbelief, he glanced at Agastya, who looked almost like a living flame, and asked, “Respected sage, your story about Lankā once belonging to the flesh-eating Rākshasas has really surprised me. I always thought the Rākshasas came from the family of Pulastya. But now you’re saying they have a different origin. Were those earlier Rākshasas stronger than Rāvana, Kumbhakarna, Prahasta, Vikata, or even Rāvana’s sons? Who created them, and what was the name of their most powerful ancestor? And what wrong did they do that made Vishnu drive them out? Please, holy one, tell me everything in detail and satisfy my curiosity, just like the sun drives away the darkness.”

Agastya was impressed by Rāma’s thoughtful and well-spoken questions. He replied, “The lord of all beings, who came from water, first created water itself. Then, from a lotus, he created living creatures to protect that water. These new beings came to the creator and said, ‘What should we do? We’re suffering from hunger and thirst.’ The creator laughed and said, ‘You humans, your job is to carefully guard this water.’ Some of them answered, ‘Rakshāma’—which means, ‘we will protect.’ Others said, ‘Yakshāma’—meaning, ‘we will worship.’ Because of this, the creator declared, ‘Those of you who said ‘Rakshāma’ will be Rākshasas. Those who said ‘Yakshāma’ will be Yakshas.’  

From these groups came two brothers—Heti and Praheti—who were powerful leaders of the Rākshasas, as fierce as the demons Madhu and Kaitava. Praheti, who was righteous, left for a life of meditation in the forest. Heti, on the other hand, was determined to find a wife. He married Bhaya (whose name means ‘Fear’), the terrifying sister of Kāla (Time). Together, they had a son named Vidyutkeça. Vidyutkeça grew up with dazzling energy, shining like the sun, just as a lotus flourishes in water.  

When Vidyutkeça was old enough, Heti started searching for a wife for him. He eventually arranged for Vidyutkeça to marry the daughter of Sandhyā (the evening twilight, wife of the Sun), who was as powerful as her mother. Sandhyā agreed to give her daughter in marriage, and Vidyutkeça began to enjoy life with his new wife, just as Indra enjoys being with the daughter of Pulomā.  

After some time, Vidyutkeça’s wife, Sāla Katankatā, became pregnant, just as clouds fill with water from the ocean. She went to Mandara and gave birth to a child who glowed like a storm cloud, much like how Gangā once bore a child by the fire-god Shiva (Maheçwara). But after giving birth, she wanted to return to her husband and left her newborn behind. The baby, whose cries sounded like thunder, was abandoned by both parents. Alone and shining like the autumn sun, the baby put his fist in his mouth and started crying softly.  

At that moment, Shiva (riding his bull and traveling with Pārvati) heard the baby’s cries from the sky. Pārvati was touched with compassion and asked Shiva to help the child. To please her, Shiva made the Rākshasa baby instantly grow to adulthood and granted him immortality. For Pārvati’s happiness, Shiva also gave him the power to fly. Pārvati added her own blessing: from then on, Rākshasi women would conceive, give birth, and have their children reach adulthood all in a single day.  

That’s how the great and proud Sukeça, filled with confidence from these blessings, roamed everywhere, just like Indra did after he gained control of heaven.”

SECTION V

When Sukeça, now righteous and blessed with a divine boon, had come into his own, a respected Gandharva named Grāmani—shining as bright as fire—chose to give his daughter Devavati to Sukeça. Devavati was as beautiful and famous as the goddess Sri herself, her beauty and youth known across the three worlds. Giving her to Sukeça was like granting him the goddess of fortune among the Rakshasas. Devavati, thrilled by her good fortune—like a poor person suddenly becoming rich—was overjoyed to marry Sukeça, who was now powerful thanks to his boon. Sukeça looked proud and noble with Devavati at his side, much like a mighty elephant (from Anjana) walking alongside a graceful mate.

In time, Sukeça and Devavati had three sons, each strong and radiant like the three sacred Fires. Sukeça’s sons—Malyavān, Sumāli, and the powerful Māli—were like his three eyes, each one strong and commanding. They stood out among Rakshasas as the three worlds do among all creation; they were fierce like the three sacred fires, and as threatening as the three major diseases caused by Air, Bile, and Phlegm (the ancient system of the humors). Like an illness that’s ignored and allowed to grow, Sukeça’s sons increased in power.

Learning that their father’s strength came from asceticism and the boon he’d received, the three brothers made up their minds to gain power the same way. They traveled to Mount Meru to practice harsh penances, taking on strict vows and terrifying rituals that would frighten even the bravest beings. Their intense practices, marked by truthfulness, self-control, and honesty, started to disturb the entire universe—gods, demons (Asuras), and humans alike.

At last, the four-faced Brahmā himself appeared before Sukeça’s sons, arriving in his splendid chariot. He announced, “I am here to grant you boons.” Seeing Brahmā, surrounded by Indra and other gods, ready to bless them, the brothers stood trembling—like trees shaking in the wind—but joined their hands respectfully and made their request: “O god, honored by our penance, if you truly wish to grant us a boon, make us invincible, able to defeat our enemies, immortal, powerful, and always loyal to each other.” Brahmā agreed, saying, “So be it,” and then returned to his own realm, always caring for the Brahmins with affection.

With their wish granted, the three Rakshasa brothers—now fearless—began to terrorize the gods and demons. The gods, celestial singers (Charanas), and sages suffered under their attacks and felt as hopeless as people condemned to hell—no one could save them.

Soon, the Rakshasas gathered and approached Viśwakarmā, the legendary architect of the gods. They said, “You, Viśwakarmā, are the master builder of the gods, strong and full of energy. Build us a city near Himavān, Meru, or Mandara—something magnificent, a palace as great as Shiva’s own.” Viśwakarmā, powerful and skilled, replied, “There is a mountain called Trikuta on the southern sea, and another nearby called Suvela. On the highest peak—so tall even birds can’t reach it—the four directions are marked with bones. If you wish, I can build your city, Lankā, there. It will cover thirty yojanas, be a hundred yojanas long, surrounded by golden walls and gates. Live there, mighty Rakshasas, just as the gods live in Amarāvati with Indra. In Lankā, with countless Rakshasas to support you, you will be safe from enemies and able to defeat them.”

Delighted by Viśwakarmā’s proposal, the three Rakshasa brothers and thousands of their followers moved into the new city. Lankā, with its strong walls, deep moat, and hundreds of golden buildings, became their proud home. Overjoyed, the night-stalking Rakshasas settled into their new city.

At the same time, a Gandharvi named Narmadā lived freely in Lankā. She had three daughters, each as radiant as Sri, Hri, and Kirti. Though Narmadā wasn’t a Rakshasi herself, she happily married her daughters—each with a face like the full moon—to the three Rakshasa brothers, starting with the oldest. Under the influence of the star Bhagadaivata, Narmadā’s three daughters went to the three Rakshasa brothers in order.

Once married, Sukeça’s sons enjoyed their new lives, living with their wives like gods among the Apsaras. Malyavān’s wife, Sundari, was beautiful, and together they had several children: Vajramusthi, Virupāksha, Burmukha, Suptaghna, Yajnakopa, Matta, Unmatta, and a lovely daughter named Analā.

Sumāli’s wife, Ketumati—whose face glowed like the full moon—was dearer to him than life itself. Their children included Prahasta, Kampana, Vikata, Kālikāmukha, Dhumrāksha, Danda, Supārcwa (the fierce), Sanhrādi, Praghasa, Bhāsakarna, Rākā, Pashpotkatā, Kaikasi (with her radiant smile), and Kumbhinasi.

Māli married a graceful Gandharvi whose eyes looked like lotus petals. She was as beautiful as any Yakshi. Māli and his wife had three sons: Anala, Nila, and Sampāti. These three would become close advisors to Bibhisana.

The three Rakshasa brothers, now surrounded by hundreds of children and followers, grew proud of their overwhelming power. They began to torment sages, serpents, Yakshas, and even the gods with Indra at their head. No one could face them in battle—these Rakshasas were as deadly as Death itself, roaming the world like the wind and constantly disrupting the sacrifices of the wise.
This refers to a type of elephant.

Ancient Hindu medicine believed that diseases came from imbalances in three bodily “humors”: Air, Bile, and Phlegm. While this might sound strange today, Hindu doctors were skilled in diagnosing illnesses using this method. They could tell a lot just by feeling a patient’s pulse and could often predict the outcome of an illness with surprising accuracy. This system may seem outdated, but it worked well in its time.
The word “tanka” can also mean a hatchet or a sword.
SECTION VI

Terrified and desperate, the gods, sages, and ascetics sought out Maheçwara (also known as Shiva), the god of gods—creator and destroyer of the universe, eternal and unseen, the protector of all beings, and the greatest teacher. They approached Shiva, the enemy of Kāma (the god of love) and destroyer of Tripurā, the three-eyed deity, and spoke to him with trembling voices and joined hands: “Lord, the creatures created by the Lord of Creation are being tormented by the sons of Sukeça. These sons, empowered by a boon from the great-father, have become arrogant and are constantly harassing us. Our sacred places, meant to be our refuge, no longer protect us. The sons of Sukeça have driven us out of the heavens and now rule there as if they were gods themselves. They boast, ‘I am Vishnu! I am Rudra! I am the king of the gods! I am Yama! I am Varuna! I am the Moon! I am the Sun!’ Māli, Sumāli, and the Rakshasa Malyavān, along with their followers, act like they own the place, filled with pride and thirst for battle. Lord, we beg you—save us from this torment. Please take your most terrifying form and destroy these enemies of the gods.” Hearing their plea, Shiva (also called Kaparddi, with his matted hair and reddish-blue skin) thought it would be wrong to personally destroy Sukeça, so he told the gods, “I cannot kill them. They are beyond my reach. But I can tell you how they will be defeated. Go now, great sages, and seek the help of Vishnu. He will destroy them.” The gods bowed to Shiva, shouting “Victory!” and, still frightened by the Rakshasas, went to Vishnu. They bowed to Vishnu, who holds the conch, discus, and mace, and told him, “Because of a powerful boon, Sukeça’s three sons have driven us from our home, just like fire consumes all it touches. Their city, Lankā, sits atop Trikuta mountain and is nearly impossible to enter. From there, these Rakshasas attack us constantly. Please, slayer of Madhu, destroy them for us. We have no one else to turn to, and we are terrified. Cut off their heads with your discus and offer them to Yama. Please, destroy the arrogant Rakshasas and their armies—wipe away our fear as the sun dries morning dew.” Vishnu, god of gods and the terror of his enemies, comforted the gods: “I know Sukeça and his sons, with Malyavān as the eldest, have grown arrogant from the boon given by Īśāna (Shiva). These worst of Rakshasas have disrespected you, but I will destroy them in my anger. Don’t be afraid.” Cheered by Vishnu’s promise, the gods returned to their homes, praising Janārdana (Vishnu).

When Malyavān heard that the gods were seeking help, he spoke to his brothers: “The gods and sages went to Shiva, begging for our destruction. They complained that the powerful sons of Sukeça are bullying them at every turn. They said, ‘We’ve been overpowered by the Rakshasas and can’t even stay in our own homes. Please, three-eyed lord, destroy them for us.’ But Shiva told them, shaking his head and hands, ‘I cannot kill Sukeça’s sons, but I will tell you who can. Seek help from Janārdana, Hari, the one who holds the discus and mace and wears yellow robes—go to Vishnu.’ So the gods went to Vishnu and told him everything. Vishnu promised, ‘I will kill your enemies. Have no fear.’ Brothers, Hari (Vishnu) has promised the frightened gods that he’ll destroy us. We need to think carefully about our next move. Hiranyakaçipu, Namuchi, Kālanemi, Sanhrāda, Rādheya, Vahumāyi, Lokapāla, Yāmala, Arjuna, Hārdikya, Sumbha, Niçumbhaka—all these mighty Asuras and Dānavas, skilled in magic, wise, and feared by their enemies—have been killed by Nārāyana (Vishnu), even though they were never defeated before. We need to decide what’s best for all of us. Beating Nārāyana is nearly impossible if he wants to destroy us.” Sumāli and Māli replied to Malyavān, “We’ve learned, given to charity, gained wealth, lived long and healthy lives, and followed true righteousness. We’ve fought the best of the gods and won, so we have no fear of death. Even Nārāyana (Vishnu), Rudra (Shiva), Indra, and Yama hesitate to stand against us in battle. Vishnu’s anger towards us is only because the gods tricked him. So we should take our revenge on the gods who are behind this.” With that, the brothers gathered their forces. They ordered preparations for battle, and all the powerful Rakshasas set out for war—riding chariots, elephants, horses as strong as elephants, mules, cattle, camels, dolphins, snakes, crocodiles, tortoises, fish, birds like Garuda, lions, tigers, boars, Srimaras, and Chāmaras. Swollen with pride, the Rakshasas left Lankā and headed for the heavens to do battle with the gods. The gods living in Lankā saw disaster coming and were terrified. The Rakshasas, in their hundreds and thousands, climbed into their best chariots and raced toward the celestial realms, their minds focused on war. The gods followed their path. As fate would have it, ominous signs began to appear on earth and in the sky, warning of the Rakshasa chiefs’ destruction. Clouds rained down bones and hot blood. The seas flooded their shores, and mountains trembled. Horrible jackals with voices like thunder laughed and howled. Creatures dropped dead one after another, and flocks of vultures with flaming mouths circled over the Rakshasas like Death itself. Blood-soaked pigeons and shrieking Sārikās darted about. Crows and two-legged cats cried out loudly. But the Rakshasas, trapped by destiny, ignored these signs and pressed on, led by the powerful Malyavān and Sumāli, blazing with strength at the front. Just as gods look to their creator for protection, the Rakshasas followed Malyavān, as immovable as a mountain, and Māli led their roaring army toward the heavens, hungry for victory. Hearing from a messenger about the Rakshasa army, Nārāyana (Vishnu) prepared for battle. He armed himself and climbed onto Garuda (his eagle mount, Vinata’s son). Wearing armor shining like a thousand suns, with his quivers full, sword at his waist, and carrying his conch, discus, mace, Sārnga (his bow), and other weapons, the lotus-eyed god set off to destroy the Rakshasas. Seated on Garuda, dressed in yellow, Vishnu looked like a storm cloud on a golden mountain, lit by lightning. Praised by Siddhas, gods, sages, great serpents, Gandharvas, and Yakshas, Vishnu—enemy of Asuras—arrived holding his weapons. The Rakshasa army, battered by the winds from Garuda’s wings, shook like mountain peaks in a storm, their banners and weapons tossed about. Then the Rakshasas surrounded Mādhava (another name for Vishnu) and attacked him with thousands of sharp, blood-stained weapons, as fierce as the fire at the end of the world.
Kāma is the Hindu god of love—Shiva once burned him to ashes when Kāma tried to interrupt his meditation. (The poet Kālidāsa’s epic “Kumāra Sambhava” is based on this story.)
The text mentions dolphins (purpoises) as war animals, though it’s unclear if “Siçumāra” might mean something else.
“Srimara” could mean a type of animal or a young deer.
“Chāmara” refers to the yak.
“Overleapt their continents” means the seas flooded the land, as in Shakespeare’s sense.
“Sārikā” is a kind of bird, sometimes compared to a harlot.
Garuda, Vishnu’s eagle mount.
Sārnga is the name of Vishnu’s bow.
“Suparna” means “fair-feathered”—another name for Garuda.
Mādhava is another name for Vishnu.
SECTION VII

The battle erupted like a storm hitting a mountain. The Rakshasas, loud as thunder, charged at Narayana (Vishnu), who stood firm like a mountain. Vishnu, his skin glowing with a deep blue-brown color, was surrounded by Rakshasas with dark faces, making him look like Mount Anjana under storm clouds. The arrows from the Rakshasas came thick as locusts in a field, or gnats around a flame, or bees at a pot of honey, or sea monsters in the ocean. Their arrows, fast as thought and as powerful as lightning, struck Hari (Vishnu) as if this was the end of the world. Warriors attacked in every way—those in chariots charged with their chariots, elephant riders with their elephants, horsemen with their horses, and foot soldiers even attacked from the sky. The strongest Rakshasas, massive as mountains, hurled spears, javelins, and heavy axes at Vishnu, making it hard for him to breathe, just like when a yogi holds his breath in deep meditation. (See [67]) Pushed hard by these night-dwelling demons, as the ocean is churned by fish, the unstoppable Vishnu grabbed his bow, Sarnga, and fired a rain of arrows into the Rakshasa army.

With arrows sharp as thunderbolts and fast as the wind, Vishnu shot down hundreds, then thousands of Rakshasas. His arrow storm scattered their ranks like a powerful wind scattering rain. Then, Vishnu—the greatest of gods—blew his mighty conch, Panchajanya, with all his strength. The sound was so loud and fearsome, it seemed to shake the three worlds. The blast of his conch terrified the Rakshasas, just as a lion’s roar scares wild elephants in a jungle. Horses panicked, elephants lost their energy and courage, and warriors tumbled from their chariots at the sound. Arrows from the Sarnga, feathered and razor-sharp, crashed through the Rakshasas like thunderbolts, driving them into the ground. Rakshasas struck by Narayana’s arrows fell like mountains split by lightning. The wounds from Vishnu’s spinning discus poured streams of blood, looking like red rivers running down mountains. The blaring of the conch and the snapping of the Sarnga, mixed with Vishnu’s own roars, drowned out the cries of the Rakshasas. With his arrows, Hari chopped off their heads, arms, banners, bows, chariots, flags, and quivers, scattering them everywhere.

Vishnu’s arrows streamed through the Rakshasa ranks like sunlight piercing clouds, or waterfalls tumbling from a cliff, or elephants thundering down a slope, or rain pouring from the sky. He hunted the Rakshasas relentlessly—chasing them like an elephant chases a tiger, a tiger hunts a wolf, a wolf chases a dog, a dog a cat, a cat a snake, or a snake a rat. Many Rakshasas fell, sprawled across the earth. After wiping out thousands, the killer of Madhu (another name for Vishnu) blew his conch again, filling the air like Indra, king of gods, filling clouds with rain. Stunned by Narayana’s arrows and the deafening conch, what remained of the Rakshasa army panicked and fled toward Lanka.

With their forces in chaos, the Rakshasa leader Sumali tried to stand his ground, firing a shower of arrows at Hari and covering him like a heavy mist hides the sun. Fired up by their leader, the Rakshasas regained their courage for a moment. Sumali, full of rage and pride in his strength, let out a massive roar and charged at Vishnu, trying to rally his army. Swinging his ornamented arm like an elephant waves its trunk, Sumali roared with delight, glowing like thunderclouds lit by lightning. Vishnu aimed and cut off the head of Sumali’s charioteer, whose earrings sparkled as it fell. Without their driver, Sumali’s horses ran wild, dragging the chariot all over the battlefield. Disoriented, Sumali was helpless, like someone who’s lost control of his senses.

With Sumali’s chariot out of control, another Rakshasa, Mali, grabbed his bow and charged at Vishnu’s chariot as it landed on the field. Mali’s golden-tipped arrows flew like birds into Vishnu’s body, but Vishnu stayed calm, completely in control, even as thousands of arrows rained down on him. Then, Vishnu—the creator of all beings, also known as Gadadhara (the Mace-Bearer)—pulled back his bowstring and shot a storm of arrows at Mali. The arrows, shining like lightning, tore into Mali and drank his blood as if they were snakes drinking nectar. Vishnu smashed Mali’s crown, banner, bow, and horses, knocking him from his chariot. Stranded, the night-dwelling Mali grabbed his mace and leapt at Vishnu like a lion leaping from a hilltop.

Mali swung his mace at Garuda, the king of birds and Vishnu’s mount, slamming it into Garuda’s forehead—like Yama once struck Rudra, or Indra smashes a mountain with his thunderbolt. (See [73]) Garuda, reeling in pain, carried Vishnu away from the fight. The Rakshasas cheered loudly when they saw Vishnu and Garuda withdraw. Enraged by the shouts, Vishnu, still seated awkwardly on Garuda, hurled his discus at Mali, desperate to kill him. The spinning disc, bright as the sun and as deadly as the Wheel of Time (Kala), filled the sky with light as it cut off Mali’s head and sent it crashing to earth. The gruesome head, dripping blood, landed before the Rakshasas just like the head of Rahu once fell from the sky.

The gods shouted in joy, roaring “Well done, O God!” when Mali was slain. Stricken with grief, Sumali and Malyavan grabbed their troops and raced back toward Lanka. Cheered on, Garuda turned around, furious, and scattered the Rakshasas with the wind from his wings. Rakshasas fell from the sky into the ocean—some with their faces sliced by the discus, some with chests crushed by the mace, some with necks broken by the plough, some with their heads split by clubs, others hacked by swords, and many more pierced by arrows.

Vishnu’s arrows, like thunderbolts and lightning, tore through the Rakshasas, their hair flying wildly in the wind. Their umbrellas were shredded, arms cut off, fine clothes torn, guts spilling out, and eyes rolling—leaving them unable to tell friend from foe. The noise and fury of the Rakshasas and their elephants, attacked by the Primal Lion (Vishnu in his man-lion form), matched the wild roars of fighting jungle beasts. Driven by Vishnu’s endless arrows, the Rakshasas—dark as storm clouds at the end of days—fired back but were swept away like clouds in a hurricane. Top Rakshasas, chopped in half by swords, fell like mountains crashing down. The earth was littered with the bodies of night-dwellers, their dark skin, jeweled necklaces, and earrings making them look like black mountains fallen from the sky.
This is a breathing technique called pranayama, where yogis control and even suspend their breath. It’s believed to give them great power.
Anjana is the name of a mountain.
Gadadhara means “the holder of the mace,” another name for Vishnu.
There was once a battle between Rudra (Shiva) and Yama in the Sweta forest to protect Markandeya and a certain king. In that fight, Yama struck Rudra. This story is told in the Puranas.
The Wheel of Time (Kala) symbolizes the relentless passage of time—days, months, years, centuries, and ages.
The “Primal Lion” refers to Vishnu’s earlier form as Narasimha, the man-lion who killed the asura king Hiranyakashipu to save his devotee Prahlada.
SECTION VIII

As Padmanābha (Vishnu) attacked the rear of the Rākshasa army, Mālyavān turned back, just like the ocean stops when it meets the shore. His eyes burning with anger, this night-stalker shook his head and shouted at Padmanābha, the great warrior, “Nārāyana, you don’t know the honorable ways of Kshatriyas. That’s why you attack us when we’ve stopped fighting, acting like a coward. O lord of the gods, anyone who kills someone who isn’t fighting can never reach the heavens, no matter how many good deeds they’ve done. If you really want to fight, holder of the conch, discus, and mace, then I’ll stand my ground right here—show me what you’ve got.” Seeing Mālyavān, who looked as massive as a mountain, the powerful younger brother of the king of the gods (Vishnu) answered, “I promised the gods, who were scared of you, that I’d wipe out the Rākshasas completely. That’s what I’m doing now. I’d gladly give my life for the gods, and I’ll defeat you even if you run to the deepest underworld.” 

As Vishnu—the god with lotus-red eyes—spoke, Mālyavān, furious, hurled a dart at his chest. The dart, decorated with bells, struck Hari’s (Vishnu’s) chest and shone like a flash of lightning in a cloud. Vishnu pulled the dart out and, aiming carefully at Mālyavān, threw it back at him. The weapon, launched with all the power of Govinda (Vishnu), looked like a shooting star streaking toward the Anjana mountains, and smashed into Mālyavān’s broad chest, which was covered in heavy chains, just like thunder hitting a mountaintop.

The blow shattered Mālyavān’s armor and knocked him senseless, but after a short pause, he stood up again, unmovable as a mountain. He grabbed a black iron javelin with sharp spikes and struck Vishnu hard in the chest. Then, thrilled by the fight, Mālyavān also punched Vishnu’s younger brother Vāsava and retreated about a bow’s length away.

A huge cheer erupted in the sky: “Excellent! Excellent!” After hitting Vishnu, Mālyavān also attacked Garuda. Angry, Vinatā’s son (Garuda) created a hurricane with his wings, blowing the Rākshasas around like dry leaves in a storm. Seeing his older brother being driven back by Garuda’s wind, Sumāli gathered his troops and headed for Lankā. Mālyavān, humiliated and battered by Garuda’s wings, returned to Lankā with his forces, full of shame.

So, Rāma, lotus-eyed hero, the Rākshasas had countless warriors defeated and their greatest leaders killed. Even though they were proud and powerful, they couldn’t stand against Vishnu. They abandoned Lankā and hid in the underworld with their wives. These legendary Rākshasas, from the family of Sālakantankatā and led by Sumāli, were even stronger than Rāvana. Only Nārāyana—the god with the conch, discus, and mace—could defeat these Rākshasas, who were the gods’ mortal enemies. And you, Rāma, are that eternal four-armed Nārāyana—unbeatable, undying, born to destroy the Rākshasas. The creator of all beings, who always protects those who seek him, appears on earth when evil is at its worst, to wipe out the wicked and restore order. 

So, lord of men, I’ve told you in detail the origin of the Rākshasas. Now, greatest of the Raghus, get ready to hear the incredible story of Rāvana and his sons—their births and their strength. The mighty Rākshasa Sumāli, terrified of Vishnu, wandered the underworld for a long time with his sons and grandsons, while the lord of riches ruled in Lankā.
“Padmanābha” means “lotus-naveled”—another name for Vishnu.
“Wielder of the Dart” is a title for Kārtikeya, the god of war.
This is similar to the idea in the Bible that great leaders appear to reform religion when people have strayed furthest from the right path, as before the birth of Christ.
SECTION IX

After some time, a Rakshasa named Sumali (Sumāli) emerged from the underworld and started wandering across the earth. He looked like a dark storm cloud, with gold earrings shining on his ears. Taking his daughter, who was as beautiful as the goddess Sri (Lakshmi) but without her lotus, he roamed the land. One day, Sumali saw the god of wealth, Kubera (the lord of riches), flying by in his Pushpaka chariot on his way to visit his father, Visrava (Viçrava), the son of Pulastya. Sumali was stunned by the sight of Kubera, who looked almost godlike, glowing like fire. Shocked, Sumali quickly slipped back into the underworld. There, he started thinking hard: “How can I help the Rakshasas grow stronger and ensure their success?” He kept pondering, searching for a plan.

After a while, Sumali turned to his daughter, Kaikasi. “My daughter,” he said, “the time has come for you to marry. You’re no longer young, and because I was afraid you might be rejected, I haven’t arranged a marriage until now. But for the sake of our family’s future, we must act. You are perfect in every way, like the goddess Sri herself. Having a daughter is a heavy worry for any honorable father; we never know who will come to ask for her hand. No matter where she marries, she creates uncertainty for the three families she’s connected to—her father’s, mother’s, and husband’s.” (see note [89]) “So, my daughter, go to Visrava, the greatest sage in the line of Prajapati, son of Pulastya, and choose him as your husband. If you do, you will have sons as radiant as the Sun.” Hearing this, Kaikasi, wanting to honor her father’s wishes, went to find Visrava, who was deep in meditation.

At that time, Visrava was performing sacred fire rituals (Agnihotra), glowing with spiritual energy, almost like a living flame. Even though it was a frightening time of day, Kaikasi stood before him, head bowed respectfully, nervously shuffling the earth with her foot. Visrava noticed her—she was beautiful, with a face like the full moon and graceful hips. He asked gently, “Young woman, whose daughter are you? Where have you come from, and why are you here? What do you want of me? Please, tell me honestly.” With her hands joined in respect, Kaikasi replied, “Great sage, you already have the power to know what I wish. But to be clear: I am here because my father asked me to come. My name is Kaikasi. The rest you surely already understand.”

Visrava closed his eyes and meditated for a moment. When he opened them, he spoke: “I know what you want, Kaikasi. You deeply desire children. But since you have come to me at such an ominous hour, listen carefully—your children will be terrifying Rakshasas, fierce, cruel, and fond of frightening company.” Kaikasi bowed, saying, “Respected sage, I do not wish for such dreadful sons from you, who follow the Vedas. Please, have mercy on me.” Moved by her plea, Visrava replied, “Beautiful Kaikasi, your youngest son will be different. He will be righteous and uphold the honor of my family line.” (Like the full Moon speaking to Rohini—see note [91].)

After this, Kaikasi eventually gave birth to a monstrous child, a Rakshasa with ten necks, huge teeth, and a body as dark as coal. He had copper-colored lips, twenty muscular arms, fierce faces, and fiery hair. As soon as he was born, jackals with flaming mouths and wild beasts howled on the left side—a bad omen. Blood rained from the sky; thunder rumbled; the sun lost its light; meteors streaked down; the ground shook; strong winds blew; and the calm ocean churned wildly. Seeing him, his father named him “Dasagriva” (the Ten-necked), who would later be known as Ravana.

Next, Kaikasi gave birth to Kumbhakarna, a giant with unmatched strength and size. Then came Surpanakha, a sister with a terrifying face. Last was Vibhishana, the youngest, who would be known for his virtue. When Vibhishana was born, flowers rained down from the sky and the gods played their drums in celebration. The heavens echoed with shouts of “Wonderful! Excellent!” In the great forest, the powerful Kumbhakarna and the Ten-necked Ravana grew up, quickly becoming a menace to everyone.

Kumbhakarna, wild and insatiable, wandered the worlds, eating even the greatest sages devoted to their faith. But Vibhishana, always righteous, stayed at home, studying the Vedas, eating little, and controlling his senses.

After many years, Kubera (Vaishravana), the god of wealth, came to visit his father Visrava, traveling in his Pushpaka chariot. Seeing this, Kaikasi, glowing with energy, went to Ravana and said, “My son, look at your brother Kubera—radiant and powerful! He is your half-brother, and yet you are not his equal in glory. Ravana, with your incredible power, you should strive to be like Kubera.”

Hearing his mother’s words, the Ten-necked Ravana was filled with anger and jealousy. He made a vow: “Mother, I swear I will become equal to my brother—or even surpass him. Don’t be sad anymore.” Driven by this burning ambition, Ravana and his younger brother began harsh austerities, focusing their minds on gaining power.

Determined to get what he wanted through intense meditation, Ravana went to the sacred hermitage of Gokarna with his brother. There, the two Rakshasas performed severe penances, hoping to please the creator god, Brahma (the great-father). When Brahma was satisfied with their dedication, he granted them powerful boons that would make them nearly invincible.
SECTION X

Then Rāma turned to the sage and asked, “O Brāhmana, how did those incredibly powerful brothers perform their austerities in the forest? What kinds of penances did they undergo?” Agastya, pleased with Rāma’s curiosity, replied, “Each brother followed the path of morality suited to him. Kumbhakarna put in his greatest effort and stayed dedicated to righteousness. During summer, he sat surrounded by five blazing fires; in the rainy season, he would sit heroically, drenched by the downpour. In winter, he stayed submerged in cold water. This went on for ten thousand years—he was relentless in his pursuit of religious duty and honesty. Bibhishana, always focused on virtue and pure at heart, stood on one leg for five thousand years. When he finished that penance, Apsarās appeared and danced, flowers rained down, and the gods sang his praises. For the next five thousand years, he worshipped the Sun, standing with his head and hands raised, his mind fully focused on the Vedas. In this way, Bibhishana spent ten thousand years, living under strict vows like a god in paradise. As for Rāvaṇa, the Ten-necked one, he went ten thousand years without eating. Every thousand years, he cut off one of his own heads and offered it as a sacrifice in fire. After nine thousand years, nine of his heads had been burned away. When he was about to cut off his tenth head in the last year, Brahmā, the Great-father, appeared before him.

The Great-father, pleased and accompanied by the gods, said, ‘O Ten-necked one, I am very pleased with you. Ask for any boon you wish. Your hard work shouldn’t be for nothing.’ Bowing low, Rāvaṇa replied, his voice trembling with excitement, ‘O revered one, the greatest fear for all living beings is death—nothing is a bigger enemy. So, I wish for immortality.’ Brahmā answered, ‘I can’t grant immortality. Ask for something else.’ Rāvaṇa, standing with hands folded, said, ‘O lord of all beings, then make it so that I can’t be killed by birds, snakes, Yakshas, Daityas, Dānavas, Rākshasas, or the gods. I have no fear of any other creatures—humans and such are nothing to me.’ Brahmā, righteous and just, said, ‘So be it, O greatest of Rākshasas. Your wish will be granted.’ Pleased, Brahmā added, ‘And because I am so satisfied, I will give you another boon. The heads you sacrificed, which were burned in the fire, will be restored to you. Also, you will be able to change your form to whatever you desire, instantly.’ As soon as Brahmā said this, Rāvaṇa’s sacrificed heads reappeared.

Then, turning to Bibhishana, Brahmā said, ‘O Bibhishana, I am pleased with you because you have always chosen righteousness. Ask for the boon you desire, O virtuous one.’ Bibhishana, folding his hands, replied, ‘Since you, the spiritual master of all beings, are pleased with me, I feel as complete as the moon surrounded by its rays. If you wish to grant me a boon, let it be this: May my mind always be devoted to righteousness, even in the greatest danger. May I gain knowledge of Brahmā without needing a teacher. And may all my senses, which I’ve disciplined through my way of life, remain in harmony with virtue, so I can practice righteousness no matter what path I follow. This is the best boon for me, since those who are devoted to righteousness can achieve anything.’ Brahmā, delighted, replied, ‘Because you are virtuous, all of this will come true for you. And since, even though you were born a Rākshasa, your mind is free from evil, I grant you immortality.’

After this, Brahmā prepared to grant a boon to Kumbhakarna. But the gods, worried, pleaded with him, ‘Please don’t grant any boon to Kumbhakarna. You know how much he frightens everyone. He has already eaten seven Apsarās in Nandana, ten of Indra’s attendants, as well as sages and humans. If he gets a boon now, he’ll devour the three worlds. Instead, pretend to give him a boon, but actually grant him confusion and sleep. That way, people will be safe, and Kumbhakarna’s honor will still be preserved.’ Brahmā, the Lotus-born, thought about this, and Saraswati, the goddess of wisdom, standing by his side, grew anxious as well. Saraswati asked, ‘O lord, I am here. How can I help?’ Brahmā replied, ‘O Vāni (Saraswati), become the goddess of speech for Kumbhakarna—make him speak in a way that benefits the gods.’ Saraswati agreed, saying, ‘So be it,’ and entered Kumbhakarna’s throat.

Then Prajāpati said, ‘O Kumbhakarna, mighty one, what boon do you wish for?’ Under Saraswati’s influence, Kumbhakarna replied, ‘O lord of lords, I wish to sleep for many years.’ Brahmā said, ‘So be it,’ and then left with the gods. Saraswati also left Kumbhakarna. When Brahmā and the gods returned to heaven, Saraswati left him, and Kumbhakarna regained his senses. He thought sadly, ‘What did I just say? It seems the gods must have confused me.’

So, having received their respective boons, the three brothers—filled with incredible power—went to live peacefully together in the Sleshmātaka forest.
Hindu Yogis practice various postures that help them control their breathing.—T.
Literally “word”; a name for Saraswati.
[40] That is, become the presiding goddess over Kumbhakarna’s speech while he asks for his boon, and make him ask for something that will benefit the gods.—T.
SECTION XI

When Sumāli and his followers heard that these night-dwelling rakshasas had gained powerful boons, they gathered their courage and rose up from the underworld. Furious, Sumāli’s advisors—Māricha, Prahasta, Virupāksha, and Mahodara—also emerged, burning with anger. With his top advisors around him, Sumāli went to Rāvana (the Ten-necked one), hugged him, and said, “We’re so lucky, my child. Thanks to you, our deepest wish has come true—you’ve received the greatest boon from the mightiest being in all the three worlds. The terrible fear of Vishnu, which once drove us out of Lankā and deep underground, is finally gone. Many times, that fear forced us to abandon our homes and flee into the depths with everyone close to us. Lankā used to be our city, home of the rakshasas. Now, your brother—the wise god of wealth—lives there instead. If you can take it back, whether through self-control, generosity, or by showing your strength, it will be a huge achievement. Then, without a doubt, you’ll be the lord of Lankā, and you’ll raise up the rakshasa race, which has fallen so far. With your incredible strength, you’ll rule over all.” 

Rāvana replied to his grandfather, “The lord of wealth is our elder, so you shouldn’t say things like that.” Because of Rāvana’s respectful answer, Sumāli recognized his intent and stayed quiet. 

After Rāvana had spent some time there, Prahasta spoke to him respectfully: “Ten-necked one, mighty hero, you shouldn’t talk that way. Heroes don’t let brotherly love get in the way of ambition. Listen to me! Long ago, there were two sisters, Aditi and Diti. They were very close and both married Kaçyapa, the lord of creatures. Aditi gave birth to the gods, who now rule the three worlds. Diti gave birth to the Daityas, also children of Kaçyapa. Once, the earth—wrapped in oceans and mountains—belonged to the Daityas, and they became very powerful. But then the gods took over the entire undivided world. So you aren’t the only one who’d ever go against his brother; even the gods and demons have fought each other before. That’s why you should listen to my advice.”

Encouraged by Prahasta, Rāvana felt happy and, after thinking it over, agreed. Excited, Rāvana set out that very day into the forest with his fellow rakshasas. When they reached Trikuta mountain, Rāvana, ever the skilled speaker, sent Prahasta as his messenger: “Prahasta, go to the lord of wealth and say this gently in my name: ‘King, this city of Lankā has always belonged to the powerful rakshasas, but now you live here. That’s not right. So, if you’re willing to hand it back, I’ll be deeply grateful—and you’ll also be doing the right thing.’”

Prahasta traveled to Lankā, now well-guarded by Kubera, the god of wealth, and delivered Rāvana’s message: “O lord of wealth, I come from your brother, the Ten-necked one. You, wise and learned, please listen to what he asks: ‘This beautiful city, once ruled by rakshasas led by Sumāli, belongs to us by tradition. So, son of Viçrava, he asks you to give it back, as he humbly requests.’”

Kubera, the god of wealth (also called Vaiçravana), listened and replied politely, “My father gave me this city after it was emptied of the night-dwellers. I’ve lived here, practicing generosity, honor, and virtue. Go tell the Ten-necked one that this city and kingdom are as much his as they are mine. Enjoy this realm without worry or rivalry. May our kingdom and wealth never be divided while you are here!”

After saying this, Kubera went to his father Viçrava, bowed respectfully, and explained Rāvana’s request: “Father, the Ten-necked one sent me a messenger asking me to give back Lankā, which was once the rakshasas’ home. Please tell me what I should do.”

Viçrava, the great sage, answered his son Kubera: “Listen, my son. Rāvana once said something similar in front of me. I scolded him harshly for it, telling him he was ignoring what’s right and honorable. I warned him many times, but because of the boon he was granted, his judgment is clouded, and he can’t tell who deserves respect and who doesn’t. Plus, because of my curse, he’s become fierce by nature. So, my advice is to go to Mount Kailāsa with your family, counselors, chariots, and wealth. There, you’ll find the Mandākini river, its waters shining with golden lotuses like little suns, as well as lilies, blue lotuses, and many fragrant flowers. Gods, Gandharvas, Apsarās, serpents, and Kinnaras often visit and play there. Lord of wealth, don’t get into a fight with Rāvana—you know how powerful a boon he’s been granted.”

Listening to his father, Kubera respected his advice. He left Lankā for Kailāsa, taking his family, counselors, vehicles, and wealth with him. Prahasta hurried back and happily told Rāvana, who was with his counselors and brothers, “Lankā is empty now. The god of wealth has moved out. Let’s go in and rule it, following our own way.”

Following Prahasta’s words, Rāvana—the mighty Ten-necked one—entered Lankā with his brothers, his army, and his followers. Just as the king of the gods ascends to heaven, Rāvana, enemy of the immortals, took over the well-planned city that Kubera had abandoned. Once crowned, Rāvana ruled Lankā, filling the city with rakshasas as dark as storm clouds. Meanwhile, Kubera, out of respect for his father, lived in a splendid palace atop a mountain shining like moonlight, surrounded by beautiful, decorated buildings—just as Indra resides in Amaravati.
SECTION XII

The ruler of the Rakshasas, Ravana, was officially crowned as king along with his brothers. After that, he started thinking about arranging the marriage of his demon sister. So, Ravana decided to give his sister, the Rakshasi Surpanakha, in marriage to Vidyujjibha, the powerful king of the Kalakas and leader of the Danavas. After this, Ravana went out hunting in the forest. While roaming, he happened to come across Maya, the son of Diti. Maya wasn’t alone—his daughter was with him. Seeing them, Ravana, known as the Ten-necked one, asked, “Who are you, wandering alone in these empty woods where there aren’t even any animals? And who is this girl with you, with eyes like a young deer?”

Maya replied, “Listen, I’ll explain everything. You might have heard of an Apsara named Hema. The gods gave her to me, just like they gave Paulomi to Indra. I spent a thousand years with her, completely devoted. But it’s now been thirteen—no, fourteen—years since she left on business for the gods. While she was gone, I built a golden palace decorated with diamonds and lapis lazuli, using my special skills. I lived there, sad and missing her. Eventually, I left the palace with my daughter and came to this forest. This is my daughter, born from Hema. I’ve brought her here to find her a husband. Honestly, being a father to a daughter can be tough for anyone who cares about their family’s honor. A daughter always seems to belong halfway to her father’s family and halfway to the one she’ll marry. Besides her, I also have two sons with my wife Hema—Māyāvi and Dundubhi. So that’s the whole story. But now, tell me—who are you?”

Ravana replied respectfully, “I’m called the Ten-necked one, the son of the sage Paulastya, who himself was Brahma’s third son.”

When Maya, leader of the Danavas, learned that Ravana was the son of the great sage Paulastya, he decided he wanted Ravana to marry his daughter. Smiling, Maya took his daughter’s hand and said, “This is my daughter, Mandodari, born from the Apsara Hema. Please accept her as your wife, O king.” Ravana agreed right away. He lit a sacred fire and took Mandodari’s hand in marriage. Maya, aware of an old curse from a sage about Ravana’s birth, still gave his daughter to Ravana, because Ravana’s family line was honorable. As a wedding gift, Maya also gave Ravana a powerful magical dart that he had earned through intense meditation—this was the very weapon Ravana would later use to wound Lakshmana.

After the wedding, Ravana returned to Lanka and arranged marriages for his brothers as well. Ravana married Kumbhakarna to Vajrajwala, the granddaughter of Virochana on their mother’s side. Vibhishana married Saramā, a good-hearted woman who was the daughter of Shailusha, king of the Gandharvas. Saramā was born on the shores of Lake Manasa. When the lake overflowed during the rains, her mother, hearing the baby’s cries, called out affectionately, “Saromavarddhata—O lake, don’t swell!” Because of this, the girl was named Saramā.

Once they were all married, the Rakshasas and their wives enjoyed themselves, much like the Gandharvas do in the gardens of Nandana. Soon after, Mandodari gave birth to a son named Meghanada. You might know him by his other name, Indrajit. As soon as he was born, Meghanada let out a cry so loud it sounded like thunder, startling everyone in Lanka. Because of that, Ravana himself named him Meghanada. Hidden away like a fire buried under wood, Ravana’s son grew up in his father’s grand palace, bringing joy to both his parents.

The “two lines” refer to the family lines of her father and her mother. In modern Hindu society, once a girl is married, she leaves her father’s family line and joins her husband’s. But in ancient times, it seems this wasn’t always clear-cut. This raises some interesting questions about old social customs.
This curse is related to Ravana’s birth.
SECTION XIII

Once, Sleep herself—sent by the creator god—overwhelmed Kumbhakarna in her true form. Kumbhakarna, feeling the force of drowsiness, turned to his brother, who was sitting nearby, and said, “Brother, I can’t fight off this sleep. Please have a mansion built for me.” At his request, skilled architects—who looked like Viśvakarma, the divine builder—constructed a stunning palace. It stretched a yojana diagonally and two yojanas in area, with smooth floors and no walls blocking its beauty. The grand building sparkled with gold and crystal pillars, had staircases made of lapis lazuli, was lined with strings of tiny bells, boasted ivory gates, and featured platforms studded with diamonds and crystal. The whole place was impressive and built to last—almost like a magical cave from the desert of Maru. Inside, Kumbhakarna, overwhelmed by sleep, lay down and didn’t wake up for thousands of years.

While Kumbhakarna slept, his brother Daśānana (Rāvana, also called Ten-necked), went on a rampage. With nothing holding him back, Rāvana attacked and killed divine sages, Yakshas, and Gandharvas. He invaded their beautiful gardens—places like Nandana—and destroyed them mercilessly. His destructive power was like an elephant churning a river, a wind tearing down trees, or a lightning bolt shattering mountain peaks.

News of Rāvana’s violence spread. Remembering both his brother’s nature and his family’s reputation, Vaiśravaṇa (the god of wealth, also known as Kubera), decided to act out of brotherly concern. He sent a messenger to Lanka to look out for Rāvana’s wellbeing. The messenger arrived in the city and went straight to Bibhīṣaṇa, Rāvana’s other brother. Bibhīṣaṇa welcomed him politely and asked why he had come. After checking on the health of the king and his family, Bibhīṣaṇa brought the messenger to Rāvana, who was sitting in his court.

Seeing the king glowing with power, the messenger bowed and greeted him with “Jaya!” (meaning “victory!”). Then, standing before Rāvana, who lounged on a luxurious couch, the envoy delivered his message: “King, I bring words from your brother, words that respect your family’s honor. Enough with the wrongdoing—it’s time to change your ways. If you can, return to a righteous path. I saw for myself how Nandana was destroyed, and I’ve heard about the sages you’ve killed. The gods are preparing to act against you. Even though you haven’t listened to me, remember—when someone makes a mistake, even a child, their friends should still protect them.

“I have always controlled my desires and followed strict vows. I once traveled to the Himalayas to pursue righteousness. There, I saw the lord of the gods (Shiva) with Umā (Pārvatī). Out of curiosity, I glanced at the goddess with my left eye, just to understand who she was—nothing more. At that moment, thanks to her divine power, my left eye was burned; it became dusty and changed color to tawny. I then went to another mountain peak to continue my silent vows. When my vow was complete, Lord Shiva, pleased with my dedication, said, ‘You have impressed me with your penance. I too followed this vow, and now you have done the same. There’s no third person who has achieved this. It’s a difficult vow—one that I started. So let’s be friends. You’ve earned my respect. Your left eye was burned by the goddess’s energy and turned tawny from seeing her beauty; from now on you’ll be called Ekākshipingali (One-Tawny-Eyed).’

“By Shiva’s blessing, I gained his friendship. But now, hearing of your evil plans, I beg you—stop this path of sin that stains our family. The gods and sages are planning how to bring about your end.”

Rāvana, the Ten-necked, grew furious. His eyes turned red, he ground his teeth, and rubbed his hands together. He snapped, “Messenger, I’ve heard what you said. Neither you nor my brother who sent you will survive this. The keeper of riches (Kubera) isn’t offering me good advice. And now he brags about being friends with Shiva! I can’t forgive these words. Until now, I’ve held back because he’s my older brother, and it wouldn’t be right to kill him. But after hearing this, I’ve made up my mind. Relying on my own strength, I’ll conquer all three worlds. And because of him, I’ll send the four guardians of the directions (Lokapālas) straight to the land of the dead.”

Rāvana finished speaking, then killed the messenger with his sword and handed his body over to the demons to be eaten. After performing a ritual to bring luck (Swastyāyana), Rāvana climbed into his chariot and set out to challenge the lord of riches, determined to conquer the three worlds.
From here on, we’ll use this important nickname for Rāvana, which means “Ten-faced.”
Ten-necked.
“Jaya” can mean (1) victory and (2) all the deities in the Hindu pantheon.
Swastyāyana: a religious ceremony to please a deity or a star and protect against disaster or to bring good luck—still common in Hindu society today.
SECTION XIV

Ravana (sometimes called Dasagriva or the Ten-necked one), confident in his power, set out with his six trusted advisors—Mahodara, Prahasta, Maricha, Suka, Sarana, and the fierce Dhumraksha—ready for battle. His anger was so intense it felt like he could destroy everything in his way. Leaving behind cities, rivers, mountains, forests, and groves, Ravana quickly reached Mount Kailasa. When the Yakshas heard that Ravana, the notorious and arrogant king of the Rakshasas, had arrived with his entourage, they were terrified; knowing he was the brother of their own king, Kubera (the lord of riches), they went straight to him and reported everything Ravana was doing. With Kubera’s permission, the Yakshas prepared for war. Soon, Ravana’s army created chaos at the foot of Kailasa, making the whole mountain seem to shake with their movements, like a stormy sea.

The battle between the Yakshas and Rakshasas began, and Ravana’s advisors fought hard but were hit fiercely by the Yakshas. Seeing his team in trouble, Ravana shouted and, burning with anger, rallied his forces. Each of Ravana’s counselors fought against a thousand Yakshas at once. The fight was brutal—clubs, maces, swords, darts, and spears flew everywhere. Ravana himself plunged into the thick of the battle, but the onslaught of weapons was so intense it almost paralyzed him, like being caught in a flood of arrows. Even as blood poured from his wounds, streaming over him like rain over a mountain, Ravana showed no pain, thanks to his supernatural toughness.

Roaring with rage, Ravana raised his massive mace, which looked like the staff of Death itself, and smashed his way through the Yaksha army, sending many to their deaths. Like fire tearing through dry grass, he destroyed the Yaksha forces. Ravana’s advisors—Mahodara, Suka, and the rest—scattered the survivors, just as wind scatters clouds. The Yaksha army was left in ruins: some wounded, some dead on the ground, others collapsing from exhaustion, even embracing each other before falling, like riverbanks crumbling away. The sky itself seemed packed with the souls of fallen sages and warriors, who, having died in battle, ascended to the heavens.

Seeing his strongest Yakshas being pushed back, Kubera sent more troops into the fight. Meanwhile, a Yaksha named Sanyodhakantaka, backed by a huge force and many chariots, charged into battle. Sanyodhakantaka hit Maricha with his discus, knocking him off the mountain—almost as if Vishnu himself had struck him—like a star falling from the sky after losing its power. Maricha quickly recovered and rejoined the fight, but after being beaten by Sanyodhakantaka, he fled.

Ravana pushed forward, breaking through the palace gates, which were decorated with gold, lapis lazuli, and silver. But as he tried to enter, the gatekeeper Yaksha named Suryabhanu blocked his way. Ravana ignored the warning and forced his way in. Suryabhanu fought back, using the massive gate as a weapon and smashing it into Ravana. Blood streamed from Ravana, making him look like a mountain streaked with red minerals. Still, because he had a special blessing from Brahma (the Self-born), Ravana wasn’t hurt by the blow, even though the gate was as massive as a mountain peak. The same gate, when swung at Suryabhanu, burned him to ashes in an instant.

When the Yakshas saw Ravana’s overwhelming power, they panicked and ran for their lives. Terrified and exhausted, their faces pale, they threw down their weapons and took refuge in rivers and caves, desperate to escape.
The author’s point here is: "The sky was crowded with both sages and warriors. As warriors died in battle, they joined the ranks of the sages in the heavens."—T.
That is, it was the Yaksha who fled.
SECTION XV

When the Yakshas—mighty supernatural beings—saw their best warriors panicking by the thousands, their leader, Kubera (the lord of riches), turned to a powerful Yaksha named Manichara. “Manichara,” he commanded, “you are our champion. Kill the evil Ravana—he’s become a real threat. The other Yakshas are depending on you for protection.” Manibhadra, a mighty and undefeated Yaksha, rallied four thousand Yakshas and charged into battle. The Yakshas attacked the Rakshasas with maces, clubs, spiked darts, and heavy bludgeons, fighting fiercely and spinning around like hawks in flight. The chaos of battle was intense—some Yakshas shouted, “Come fight me!” while others hesitated or demanded to join the fight. The gods, Gandharvas (celestial musicians), and Vedic sages watching the battle were stunned by the ferocity on display.

Prahasta, one of Ravana’s commanders, killed a thousand Yakshas, and Mahodara took down another thousand skilled warriors. Then Maricha, furious and hungry for a fight, swiftly killed two thousand more Yakshas in a flash. The Yakshas fought openly, but the Rakshasas used their magical powers, which gave them an advantage. In the heat of the fight, Dhumraksha confronted Manibhadra and struck him in the chest with a heavy club—but Manibhadra stood his ground. In response, Manibhadra smashed Dhumraksha on the head with his mace, knocking him out cold and leaving him drenched in blood.

Seeing Dhumraksha defeated and bleeding, Ravana (the “Ten-necked one”) charged at Manibhadra in a rage. Manibhadra met him head-on and hit Ravana with three darts. Ravana retaliated, smashing Manibhadra’s head so hard that his crown dented deeply on one side. From that day on, Manibhadra’s head was permanently caved in on one side. When the noble Manibhadra was finally overwhelmed, chaos erupted across the mountain.

At a distance, Kubera—wielding his mace and accompanied by his allies Sukra, Praushthapada, Padma, and Sanka—spotted Ravana on the battlefield. Kubera saw his brother’s brilliance dimmed by an old curse. He spoke solemnly, honoring his family’s tradition: “Ravana, you refuse to listen to me and keep walking down this dark path. Soon enough, you’ll pay for your actions and find yourself in hell. People who stubbornly ignore warnings and recklessly drink poison eventually face the consequences of their choices. The gods have turned against you because of something you did, and you don’t even realize the trouble you’re in. If you disrespect your father, mother, or teacher, you eventually answer to the lord of the dead. Life is unpredictable. Anyone who doesn’t seek wisdom or self-control ends up exactly where they deserve. A twisted mind rarely turns to good, and you will reap what you sow. In this world, good fortune, beauty, strength, children, wealth, and bravery come from good deeds. But with your evil ways, you’re headed straight for hell. I won’t waste my words on you any longer. Decent people should be cautious when dealing with the wicked.”

After Kubera’s rebuke, Ravana’s advisors—led by Maricha—were so shaken by Kubera’s attack that they ran for their lives. But Ravana himself, even after being struck on the head by Kubera’s mace, held his ground. The Yaksha and Rakshasa leaders kept hitting each other with everything they had, but neither seemed tired or confused. Then Kubera unleashed a fiery magical weapon, but Ravana blocked it with a water-based Varuna weapon. Ravana then tapped into his illusion magic, transforming his appearance again and again to defeat Kubera. He became a tiger, a boar, a cloud, a mountain, the ocean, a tree, a Yaksha, and a Daitya—changing forms so quickly that he was no longer recognizable.

Finally, Ravana grabbed a massive weapon and, spinning it around, smashed Kubera on the head with his powerful mace. Kubera, defeated and bleeding, collapsed to the ground, like a tree chopped at the roots. Padma and the other Nidhi (treasure guardian) deities rushed to Kubera’s side, helped him up, and carried him to the Nandana forest to recover.

With Kubera beaten, Ravana, now thrilled with his victory, claimed Kubera’s magical flying chariot, the Pushpaka, as his prize. This incredible vehicle had golden pillars, gates set with precious stones, pearl-encrusted canopies, magical fruit trees, and could travel anywhere at the speed of thought. It could change shape, fly through the sky, and had golden stairs, jeweled platforms, and dazzling artwork designed to inspire awe. Created by Brahma, it was filled with every luxury, comfortable in any season, and beautiful beyond compare.

Ravana, wearing a shining crown and necklace, climbed aboard the Pushpaka—now his by right of conquest. Bursting with pride, he considered himself the new master of the three worlds. Victorious, he left Mount Kailasa. Now, with his new power, Ravana sat in his court, glowing with triumph, looking as radiant as fire itself.
Unless someone serves their parents, their heart won’t naturally turn toward goodness.
SECTION XVI

“Rāma, after defeating his brother—the god of wealth—the king of the Rākshasas, Rāvana, headed to the vast forest of reeds where Mahāsena had been born. The Ten-headed Rāvana saw this massive golden forest, shining with sunlight and almost looking like a second sun itself. As he climbed up the mountain to explore the heart of the woods, Pushpaka—the magical flying chariot—suddenly stopped moving. Rāvana couldn’t understand why his chariot, which always followed his will, suddenly wouldn’t budge. Confused, he discussed it with his advisors: ‘Why won’t Pushpaka fly as I want it to over this mountain? Who’s behind this?’ 

Māricha, the smartest among them, spoke up: ‘There must be a reason Pushpaka won’t fly, my lord. Maybe it’s because Pushpaka was only ever meant to carry the god of wealth, and now that he’s not riding it, it refuses to go further.’ 

While they were talking, a strange figure appeared—Nandi, the fierce attendant of Shiva (also known as Bhava). Nandi was small, sturdy, yellowish-black, with a shaved head and short arms. He walked up to them and, without fear, addressed Rāvana: ‘Stop, Ten-headed one. Shiva is playing in this mountain right now. At this moment, no one—bird, snake, Yaksha, god, Gandharva, or Rākshasa—can approach him.’

Hearing Nandi’s warning, Rāvana grew furious. His eyes turned red, his earrings shook as he jumped down from Pushpaka. ‘Who even is this Shiva?’ he shouted, landing at the foot of the mountain. There, he saw Nandi standing guard by Shiva’s side, holding a blazing spear, looking almost like a smaller version of Shiva himself. 

Seeing Nandi’s monkey-like face, Rāvana mocked him and burst out laughing, his voice booming like thunder. This made Nandi angry. Channeling Shiva’s power, Nandi addressed Rāvana, ‘Listen, Daśānana (Ten-heads): since you’re laughing at my monkey face with a thunderous roar, someday monkeys with my strength and energy will be born to destroy your entire race. They’ll be fierce, fast as thought, strong, wild in battle, and as tough as moving mountains. They’ll tear down your pride, your power, and defeat your sons and advisors. I could destroy you right now, but I won’t—your own actions have already sealed your fate.’

As Nandi finished speaking, divine drums echoed from the sky and flowers rained down. But Rāvana ignored Nandi’s words. Full of pride and anger, he marched up to the mountain and shouted, ‘So this is the mountain that stopped Pushpaka. I’ll just rip it out of the ground! I need to see what power Shiva has here, acting like a king. Does he not realize he’s in danger?’

With that, Rāvana grabbed the mountain with his massive arms and tried to lift it. The whole mountain shook violently. The spirits and attendants living on it were terrified and trembled. Even Parvati, Shiva’s wife, was so scared she clung to Shiva. But Shiva, amused, simply pressed down on the mountain with his big toe. The force was so great that Rāvana’s arms, as strong as stone, felt shattered. Rāvana’s advisors were shocked. In agony and rage, Rāvana let out a scream so loud it shook the three worlds. His counselors thought it was the sound of universal destruction.

The gods, led by Indra, were shaken as they traveled. The oceans churned and other mountains shook. Yakshas, Vidyadharas, and Siddhas all asked, ‘What’s happening?’ They pleaded with Rāvana, ‘Bow down and pray to Shiva, the blue-throated god, Uma’s husband. Only he can help you now, Daśānana. Go, seek his forgiveness and protection. If you do, he might be merciful.’

Taking their advice, Rāvana bowed to Shiva, the god with the bull banner, and began to sing hymns in his praise. He spent a thousand years in pain and prayer. Finally, pleased by his devotion, Shiva released Rāvana’s trapped hands and spoke to him: ‘Daśānana, your devotion and prayers have pleased me. Because your arms were hurt by the mountain and you let out such a terrifying scream that shook the three worlds, from now on you’ll be known as Rāvana—the one who makes the world tremble. Gods, humans, Yakshas, and everyone else will call you Rāvana, terror of all beings. Now, Paulastya (descendant of Pulastya), you are free to go wherever you wish, with my permission.’

Grateful, Rāvana replied, ‘If you are pleased with me, please grant me a boon. I already have one: I can’t be killed by gods, Gandharvas, Dānavas, Rākshasas, Guyhakas, Nagas, or any other superhuman beings. I didn’t even bother asking for protection from humans—they seem too weak. Brahmā has also given me a long life. Now, I just want to live the rest of my days in peace—and I’d like a weapon from you.’

Shiva agreed and gave Rāvana a brilliant sword called Chandrahasa. He also granted him peace for the rest of his life, warning, ‘Never disrespect this sword. If you do, it will return to me immediately.’ 

Receiving his new name and the sword from Shiva, Rāvana saluted him and climbed back onto Pushpaka. After that, Rāvana traveled all over the world. Whenever strong Kshatriya warriors refused to submit to him, he defeated and destroyed them and their followers. The wise, who knew that Rāvana was invincible, simply told him, ‘We surrender.’”

Marutta grabbed his bow and arrows and prepared to fight, but Samvartta stopped him. The sage spoke kindly: “Please listen to me. Besides, victory is never certain, and Rāvana is extremely hard to defeat.” Taking his teacher’s advice, Marutta put down his bow, gave up the fight, and focused on finishing the sacrifice.

Seeing this, Suka announced to everyone that Marutta had been defeated, and shouted, “Victory to Rāvana!” Rāvana, thrilled, killed and devoured the great sages at the sacrifice, quenching his thirst with their blood before returning to roam the earth. Next, the god of righteousness addressed the crow sitting near the sacrificial hall: “I’m grateful to you, bird. Because of this, you and your kind will be free from most illnesses that plague birds.
