These Daityas were strong, skilled warriors, armed to the teeth and filled with confidence, making them nearly unbeatable in war.

A vicious battle broke out between the Dānavas and Rākshasas, with both sides hurling darts, tridents, axes, and other weapons at each other, their rage boiling over. The fight raged for an entire year, but neither side could claim victory or defeat. Then, the great creator god, known as the Great-father (Brahmā), suddenly appeared, riding his magnificent chariot. He commanded the Nivatakavachas to stop fighting and said clearly, “Not even the gods or the demons can defeat Rāvana in battle; and you Dānavas cannot be destroyed by anyone, even if the gods helped. So make peace with the Rākshasas—friends share each other's strengths.” 

Rāvana and the Nivatakavachas swore friendship before the sacred fire and celebrated together. Rāvana was honored by his new allies and spent a year there, enjoying himself so much it felt like home. While staying, he learned a hundred different kinds of magical illusions. Then, Rāvana set off again, this time for Rasatala, searching for the city of the lord of the waters.

He visited the city of Açma, ruled by the fierce Kalakayas, and killed the Kalakayas—demons of great strength. There, he also killed his own brother-in-law, Vidyutjibha, who was married to his sister Surpanakhā. Vidyutjibha was a terrifying Rākshasa who, in the middle of the fight, was actually licking the bodies of Rāvana’s fallen warriors. After defeating him, Rāvana wiped out four hundred Daityas in a flash.

Next, Rāvana saw the magnificent home of Varuna, shining like a bank of white clouds and as brilliant as Mount Kailāsa. He also saw Surabhi, the magical cow whose milk formed the legendary ocean of Kshiroda (the sea of milk). Rāvana admired Surabhi, the mother of cows and the greatest of bulls—the very source of the moon, from whom both holy sages and ascetics living only on milk froth drew nourishment. Surabhi was also the origin of ambrosia and the offerings used by the ancestors, and she traveled among humans as the sacred cow.

After circling Surabhi in respect, Rāvana entered Varuna’s fearsome palace, which was heavily guarded. He marveled at the splendid mansion, with its hundreds of streams and cloud-like beauty, always glowing with happiness. Rāvana fought his way past the guards, killing all who stood against him, then addressed the remaining warriors: “Go tell your king that Rāvana is here to challenge him. Either come out and fight, or surrender and admit defeat—if you do, you have nothing to fear.”

While this was happening, Varuna’s sons and grandsons, along with the sons of Pushkara, arrived with their armies. They brought bright chariots that moved as quickly as they wanted, shining like the rising sun. What followed was a battle so intense it would make anyone’s hair stand on end: Varuna’s sons and Rāvana’s warriors fought fiercely. In a short time, Rāvana’s own powerful advisor, Mahodara, managed to crush Varuna’s entire army.

Seeing their troops overwhelmed, Varuna’s sons launched into the sky in their speedy chariots, matching Rāvana, who was flying in Pushpaka. Now, the battle moved to the skies, as fierce as any war between gods and demons. Using arrows that looked like fire, Varuna’s sons forced Rāvana back and shouted in triumph.

Watching his king struggle, Mahodara became furious. He shook off all fear and charged, determined to fight. With his massive mace, Mahodara struck Varuna’s sons—who were as swift as the wind—knocking them out of the sky. After killing them and their horses, Mahodara cheered loudly. The battlefield was littered with the destroyed chariots and horses of Varuna’s sons.

Even after losing their chariots, Varuna’s sons, because of their divine origin, floated in the sky unharmed. Drawing their bows, they fired arrows at Mahodara and, now seriously angry, tried to stop Rāvana together. Their arrows struck like thunder, battering Rāvana as if storm clouds were smashing into a mountain. But Rāvana, burning with rage like a fire at the end of the world, fired back with deadly arrows, wounding them deeply. From above, he rained down maces, clubs, pikes, and spiked weapons, trying to crush his enemies.

The soldiers were exhausted under this relentless attack, like young elephants stuck in the mud. Seeing Varuna’s sons so beaten and desperate, Rāvana let out a roar of victory, sounding like thunder. Then, with a storm of arrows, he destroyed the last of Varuna’s sons. The survivors fell dead to the ground, and the rest ran for their lives back to their homes.

Rāvana ordered, “Tell Varuna what’s happened.” His advisor, Prahasta, replied, “Great King, Varuna’s sons are dead, and the lord of the waters you challenged is away in Brahmā’s realm, listening to music. There’s no point in waiting—Varuna isn’t here, and all his brave sons have already been defeated.”

Hearing this, Rāvana was pleased to have spread his fame and left Varuna’s realm in high spirits. He returned the way he came, flying through the sky towards Lankā.
"Cyalā" means a wife's brother, but Vidyutjibha was actually Rāvana’s sister’s husband.
This is the commentator’s explanation.
Literally, the sea of milk.
Some Hindu ascetics were so devoted they’d only eat the foam from milk, after the calf had drunk—so they wouldn’t take food meant for the calf.
The ancestors who receive offerings through rituals.
Earlier, Rāvana was fighting from Pushpaka in the sky, while Varuna’s sons fought from the ground.
Because they were divine, Varuna’s sons felt no pain.
A special arrow with a crescent-shaped head.
SECTION XXIV

Rāvana and his followers continued their journey through the city of Açma, a place known for its fierce warriors. There, the ten-headed demon spotted an incredibly beautiful mansion. The house was decorated with pearl lattices, had gates topped with precious Vaidurja stones, golden pillars, and elegant floors. The staircase, sparkling like it was made of crystal, was wrapped with golden bands and reminded Rāvana of the palace of Indra (Mahendra). Staring at this stunning mansion, Rāvana wondered, “Who owns this amazing place? It looks like the peak of Mount Meru.” He turned to Prahasta and said, “Go find out whose house this is.” Obeying the order, Prahasta went inside. He checked one room, found no one, then searched through seven rooms in total, until he finally saw a blazing fire. Inside the flames, he saw a man laughing loudly and ominously. The sound sent chills through Prahasta. Next to the laughing man was another figure, draped in a garland of golden lotuses, who glowed so intensely he was hard to look at—like the sun itself—and he looked as fearsome as Yama, the god of death. Terrified, Prahasta quickly left the mansion and reported back to Rāvana.

Hearing this, Rāvana stepped off the Pushpaka chariot and entered the house himself. Standing in the doorway was a massive, terrifying figure—his whole look was intense: flaming tongue, red eyes, sharp teeth, lips as red as bimba fruit, a strong and handsome frame, a nose that looked dangerous, a shell-like neck marked with three lines, wide jaws, thick beard, and huge teeth—everything about him screamed danger. He held a giant iron mace and blocked the entrance. Seeing him, Rāvana’s hair stood on end and his heart raced. Noticing these bad omens, Rāvana hesitated, but the man at the door called out, “What are you thinking about, demon? Tell me honestly. I’ll give you a proper welcome—with a fight, if you want, night-walker.” Then he asked, “Are you here to challenge Bali, or do you have something else in mind?”

Rāvana was shaken, but tried to stay calm. He replied, “You seem to know how to talk. Who lives in this house? I want to fight him. Just tell me.” The doorkeeper answered, “This is the home of the great Danava (demon) king, Bali. He’s generous, brave, and values truth above all. He has many talents, shines like Yama with his mace, or like the rising sun, and is unbeatable in battle. He’s powerful, victorious, unstoppable—a true master of many skills, kind to those who depend on him, respectful to teachers and Brahmins, always waiting for the right moment to act, highly intelligent, and extremely handsome. He’s a hero, a student of the Vedas. Sometimes he walks the earth as fast as the wind, glows like fire, and radiates heat like the sun. He travels with gods, spirits, snakes, and birds. He has no fear. Are you sure you want to fight Bali? If you do, Rākshasa-lord, then step inside and face him.”

Rāvana accepted the challenge and went in to meet Bali. Bali, the lord of the Danavas, looked fierce and blinding, like a raging fire or the sun at midday. He saw Rāvana, laughed, and pulled him onto his lap, saying, “Ten-headed lord of Rākshasas, with your long arms—what brings you here? Tell me what you want, and I’ll see what I can do for you.”

Rāvana answered, “I’ve heard that you were once bound by Vishnu. I believe I have the power to set you free.”

Bali laughed and replied, “Listen, I’ll explain. The red-faced man who always stands at the door—he’s the one who conquered all the top Danavas and other powerful beings. He even bound me. He’s as unbeatable as Death itself. Who in this world could defy him? The one at the door is the destroyer, creator, and protector of the three worlds. Neither you nor I truly know him. He’s the past, present, and future all in one. He is Kali, he is Time, the destroyer of all living things. He creates and destroys the worlds—the moving and unmoving alike—and he brings the universe back again when it ends. He rules over sacrifices and offerings. He created and preserves the universe—nobody in the three worlds is more amazing. Son of Pulastya, he’s controlled the ancient Danavas, me, and even you, as if we were animals tied with ropes.

There have been many powerful beings—Vritra, Danu, Suka, Sambhu, Nishumbha, Sumbha, Kalanemi, Prahlada, Kuta, Vairochana, Mridu, Jamala, Arjuna, Kansa, Kaitabha, and Madhu. They shone like the sun, moved like the wind, and brought rain like Indra. All of them performed great sacrifices, did intense meditation, and mastered yoga. With their wealth, they enjoyed luxuries, gave generously, ruled wisely, and protected their people. They fought bravely—no one could match them in battle. They were learned, came from noble families, and were unbeatable fighters. They defeated thousands of gods and conquered many realms. They often did things the gods hated, but always took care of their own. They were proud, bright as the rising sun, and full of themselves. But only Vishnu (Hari) knows how to defeat those who constantly challenge the gods. He creates and destroys them, and at the end of time, he remains. All these mighty Danava leaders, who could change their forms at will, have been destroyed by the great God’s power. Even the most famous and invincible warriors have been defeated by the amazing power of Kritānta—Death itself.”

After this, Bali continued, “If you truly want to know the way to eternal freedom, take that glowing discus you see over there and bring it to me. Afterward, I’ll explain the secrets of liberation. Go on, Rāvana. Don’t waste time.” 

Laughing confidently, Rāvana walked up to the celestial earring (kundala). He grabbed it easily, but no matter how hard he tried, he couldn’t move it. Embarrassed, he tried again. As soon as he lifted it, he collapsed to the ground, covered in blood, like a tree yanked from the earth.

Just then, a loud noise echoed from the Pushpaka chariot, and Rāvana’s advisors shouted in alarm. He came to his senses after a moment, stood up, and bowed his head in shame. Bali told him, “Come here, Rākshasa king, and listen. The jeweled earring you tried to lift belonged to one of my ancestors. It fell here, and another was thrown on a mountaintop. His crown also fell to the ground during a battle, right in front of the altar. My ancestor, Hiranyakashipu, had no enemies—no one could kill him, not time, death, or any sickness. He couldn’t die by day or night, evening or morning, or be killed by any weapon. But he ended up making a deadly enemy of Prahlada. During their fight, a terrifying man-lion appeared—a nightmare to everyone. When that being looked around, all the worlds trembled in fear.

“That man-lion grabbed Hiranyakashipu and destroyed him with his claws. The being now standing at the door is that supreme Vasudeva—calm and beyond desire. I’ll share with you the words of that ultimate God, so listen if you’re open to spiritual wisdom. The one at the door has subdued, over thousands of years, a thousand Indras, tens of thousands of gods, and hundreds of great sages.”

Rāvana replied, “I’ve seen Kritānta, the lord of spirits—Death himself, with hair that stands on end. His hair is made of snakes and scorpions, his tongue is as hard as lightning, his teeth are terrifying, his eyes are red, he moves incredibly fast, and everyone fears him. You can’t even look at him—he’s as blinding as the sun, unbeatable in battle, and punishes the wicked. I even defeated him once in a fight. I felt no fear or pain then, lord of the Danavas. But I don’t know this doorkeeper. You need to explain who he is.”

Bali answered, “He is Hari—Nārāyana—the protector of the three worlds. He is Ananta (the Endless), Kapila (the Sage), Jishnu (the Victorious), and the mighty Man-lion (Narasimha). He is Kratudhama (Protector of Sacrifices), Sudhāma, and wields a deadly mace. He is like the twelve Adityas, the ancient Purusha, and the best of gods. His form is red like the clouds at sunset. He is surrounded by flames, a devoted lover of his followers, the creator and preserver of everything. He is incredibly strong and destroys as Time itself. Hari, holding his discus, is the sacrifice and is worshipped in all sacrifices. He is one with all gods and all beings, the entire universe and all knowledge. He is all forms, the greatest form, Baladeva, with long arms, the slayer of heroes, with heroic eyes, indestructible, and the teacher of the three worlds. All the sages seeking liberation meditate on him. Whoever understands this Supreme Being is untouched by sin. By remembering, hearing about, and worshipping him, you can get anything you desire.”

After hearing Bali’s words, Rāvana, filled with rage, drew his weapon and stormed out. Seeing him so furious, Hari (Vishnu), holding his club, thought, “I won’t kill this sinner out of respect for Brahmā,” and vanished, returning to his true form. When Rāvana saw that the Supreme Person was gone, he left the realm of Varuna, yelling in triumph, and returned the way he had come.
Ananta: meaning “eternal” or “endless,” a name for Vishnu.
Kapila: a famous sage, founder of the Sankhya philosophy, regarded as an incarnation of Vishnu.
Jishnu: means “victorious,” another name for Vishnu.
Narasimha: the man-lion form of Vishnu, who appeared to save Prahlada and killed Hiranyakashipu.
Kratudhama: “protector of sacrifices,” a name for Vishnu.
Sudhāma: here, another name for Vishnu. In some texts, Sudhāma is a guardian of the east.
SECTION XXV

After thinking for a while, Rāvana (the lord of Lankā) set out toward the realm of the sun. He spent the night on the beautiful peak of Mount Meru. Then, he climbed aboard his flying chariot Pushpaka, which could move as fast as the sun’s own horses. Taking different routes, he traveled until he came face to face with the magnificent sun god—brilliant and radiant, shining with golden armlets and jewel-encrusted robes. The sun’s handsome face was decorated with excellent earrings, and his body was adorned with armlets, necklaces, and garlands made from red lotuses. He wore red sandalwood paste and glowed with a thousand rays of light. Seeing this supreme god—the sun, the ancient and endless deity, who rides the divine horse Uchaisravas, the witness of all things and ruler of the universe—Rāvana, dazzled by the intense light, turned to his minister Prahasta and said, “Minister, go over and deliver my message: ‘Rāvana is here to challenge you to a fight. Either face me or admit defeat. Pick one—there’s no middle ground.’” 

Prahasta obeyed and approached the sun’s palace, where he met two guards named Pingala and Dandi. Prahasta told them Rāvana’s challenge and waited quietly, almost blinded by the sun’s rays. Dandi went up to the sun and reported everything. The wise sun god, upon hearing Rāvana’s demand, replied, “Go on, Dandi. You can either defeat Rāvana or tell him that I have been defeated. Do as you wish.” Dandi returned to Rāvana and relayed the sun’s message. Hearing this, the lord of the Rākshasas declared his own victory and moved on.
SECTION XXVI

After spending the night on the stunning peak of Mount Meru, Rāvana (the lord of Lankā) spent some time thinking before heading toward the realm of the moon. On his way, he saw someone traveling in a chariot, covered in heavenly perfumes and surrounded by beautiful Apsarās. The man looked exhausted but content, while Apsarās showered him with affection. Curious, Rāvana turned to a nearby Rishi and asked, “Welcome, celestial sage. You’ve come at just the right moment. Who is this shameless guy riding in a chariot and pampered by Apsarās? Doesn’t he see anything to fear?” The Rishi, Parvata, replied, “My child, you’re wise—let me explain. This man has conquered all the worlds and has won Brahmā’s favor. He’s now headed to a blissful realm, seeking final liberation. Just as you, lord of Rākshasas, have conquered many worlds with your asceticism, so has he, through good deeds and drinking Soma. You’re brave and honest, and the truly powerful never resent the virtuous.” Then Rāvana noticed another grand, radiant chariot, glowing with music and song. He asked, “Great Rishi, who is that person shining so brightly, surrounded by singers, dancers, and Kinnaras?” Parvata answered, “He’s a true hero and a great warrior—he never lost a battle. He performed countless heroic acts, defeated many enemies, and died fighting for his master. After destroying many on the battlefield, he was finally killed by his foes and is now headed to Indra’s realm or somewhere similar. Now, he’s being entertained by these expert musicians and dancers.”

Rāvana pressed further: “Who is that one, glowing like the sun?” Parvata explained, “The person you see, radiant as the full moon and decked out in jewelry and fine clothes, riding in a golden chariot full of Apsarās, is someone who gave away much gold. He shines with a special light and is now moving swiftly onward.” Rāvana asked, “Tell me, great Rishi, which of these kings would grant me the honor of a battle if I challenged them? You’re like a father to me—please point out someone who would fight.” Parvata replied, “All these kings desire heaven, not battle. But I’ll tell you of someone who won’t back down: Māndhāta, the powerful king and lord of the seven islands. He’ll accept your challenge.” Rāvana asked, “Tell me, devoted sage, where does this king live? I want to go meet this great man.” Parvata answered, “Māndhāta, son of Yuvanaswha, has conquered the world of seven islands, starting at the sea. He’s just about to meet you.” Rāvana, confident in the boons he’d received and his power over the three worlds, soon saw Māndhāta—the heroic king of Ayodhyā and ruler of the seven islands. Māndhāta rode in a golden, beautifully decorated chariot that shone like Mahendra’s and was covered in heavenly perfumes. Rāvana, the Ten-necked demon, called out, “Fight me!” Māndhāta laughed and replied, “If you don’t value your life, Rākshasa, then fight me.” Rāvana shot back, “I, Rāvana, have never been troubled by Varuna, Kuvera, or Yama. Why should I be afraid of you—a mere human?” Furious, Rāvana ordered his Rākshasas to attack.

Rāvana’s ministers, skilled and savage in battle, unleashed a hail of arrows. But Māndhāta, the powerful king, fought back with razor-sharp arrows, targeting Prahasta, Suka, Sārana, Mahodara, Birupaksha, Akampana, and other top warriors. Prahasta tried to overwhelm Māndhāta with arrows, but Māndhāta shattered them mid-air. Like a wildfire burning dry grass, Māndhāta tore through the ranks of Rākshasas with hundreds of Bhushundis, Vallas, Vindipālās, and Tomaras. Just as Kartikeya, son of fire, split Mount Krauncha with his arrows, Māndhāta, enraged, pierced Prahasta with five lightning-fast Tomaras. Then, swinging his mace like Yama’s own, he smashed Rāvana’s chariot. The mace hit with the force of a thunderbolt, flipping Rāvana’s chariot as if it were a flag in a storm. Māndhāta’s strength and joy surged, just like the ocean rising at the full moon.

The Rākshasa army, roaring fiercely, surrounded Rāvana on all sides. Regaining his senses quickly, Rāvana—now furious—attacked Māndhāta with all his might. The night-dwelling demons cheered loudly as Māndhāta was knocked unconscious. But Māndhāta soon woke up and saw Rāvana being celebrated by his followers. Enraged, Māndhāta’s body shone like the sun and moon as he unleashed a storm of arrows, tearing into the Rākshasa army. The arrows and noise overwhelmed the demons like a raging sea. A brutal battle erupted between men and demons. Both Māndhāta and Rāvana, fierce and determined, sat on their war chariots, bows and daggers in hand, firing arrows at each other. Both were wounded in the fight.

Rāvana nocked the terrifying Raudra arrow and fired, but Māndhāta countered with his own flaming arrows. Rāvana then used the Gandharva weapon, while Māndhāta unleashed the Brahmā-weapon, filling everyone with dread. Rāvana went even further, summoning the terrible Pāsupata weapon, which he had earned from Rudra through intense penance. Its power made every creature, moving or still, tremble. The whole universe shook with fear—gods and serpents froze in terror.

Sensing the danger, two great sages, Pulastya and Gālava, realized what was happening through meditation. They intervened, pleading with Māndhāta and Rāvana to stop. After their words, both man and demon made peace and returned to their own lands the way they had come.
SECTION XXVII

After the two brahmans left, Rāvana, king of the Rākshasas (demons), set out on his journey. First, he traveled ten thousand leagues through the sky. He reached the upper aerial region, home to skilled ganders (swan-like birds) who live there forever. This region also spans ten thousand leagues and is filled with three types of clouds: Agneya, Pakshaja, and Brahma. Next, Rāvana continued to the third aerial region, where the wise Siddhas and Charanas dwell, again stretching ten thousand leagues. Then, moving quickly, he entered the fourth region, populated by goblins and Vinayakas. After that, he reached the fifth aerial region—another ten thousand yojanas wide—where the sacred Ganga flows and the elephants led by Kumuda play in her waters, pouring down the holy river’s water. The Ganga’s waters are dried by the sun and softened by the wind before falling as rain and dew, O Rāghava. Rāvana then traveled to the sixth region, which is also ten thousand yojanas across, where the mighty Garuda lives, honored by his kin and friends. He continued to the seventh region, ten thousand leagues higher, where the seven Rishis reside. Ascending another ten thousand leagues, he came to the eighth region, where the celestial Ganga—known as the Ganges of the sky—roars loudly as she flows along the sun’s path, suspended by the wind. Beyond this, I’ll describe the area where the moon lives, eighty thousand leagues above. Here, the moon is surrounded by stars and planets, sending out thousands of rays that light up the worlds and bring joy to all creatures. But when the Ten-necked Rāvana arrived, the moon seemed to burn him with its freezing, fiery light. Rāvana’s followers couldn’t bear the cold, and Prahasta cried out in defeat, “My king, we can’t survive this cold—we have to leave! The moon’s rays scare the Rākshasas, and these cold beams seem to burn like fire.”  

Rāvana, furious, grabbed his bow and fired arrows at the moon. At that moment, Brahmā appeared in the moon’s region and said, “O Ten-necked Rāvana, son of Visravas, mighty one, leave this place—don’t attack the moon. This radiant king of the twice-born (the moon) only seeks the well-being of all. Let me teach you a sacred mantra: if you remember it at the moment of death, it will protect you.” Rāvana folded his hands and replied, “If you’re pleased with me, O Lord of the Worlds, please teach me this incantation. With it, may I be free from the fear of the gods. Grant me your favor, Lord of the celestials, so I’ll be unbeatable by Asuras, Dānavas, and even birds.”  

Brahmā answered, “O king of the Rākshasas, recite this mantra only at the time of death—not every day. Take a string of prayer beads and chant this holy incantation. As long as you do so, you will be invincible. If you don’t, you won’t succeed. Listen, I’ll teach you the mantra. Reciting it will help you win in battle:

‘Salutations to you, O god, Lord of gods, honored by gods and Asuras, you who exist in past and future, great god with red eyes. You are a child, yet you can take the form of an old man; you wear tiger skin. You are worthy of worship, lord of the three worlds, called Hara, Haritanemi, Yugantadahaka, and Valadeva. You are Ganesha, Loka-Sambhu, Lokapala, mighty-armed and great, holder of a huge spear, with dreadful teeth, the greatest of gods. You are time itself and strength, with a blue neck and a large belly. You are the destroyer of gods, greatest ascetic, lord of all beings. You hold a spear, have the bull as your symbol, are a leader, protector, destroyer, and preserver. You have matted hair, are called Mundi, Sikhandi, wear a crown, and shine with great light. You are lord of spirits and goblins, the soul and protector of all, all-knowing, destroyer, creator, and eternal teacher. You hold a kamandalu (water pot), wield the Pinaka (trident), are called Dhurjati, worthy of worship, the great OM, the first singer of Sāman, the bringer of death, the substance of death, Parijātra, and keeper of penances.  

You are an ascetic, live in caves, carry a Vinā (stringed instrument), a Panava (drum), and a quiver; you are immortal and shine like the rising sun. You dwell in cremation grounds, are the glorious lord of Umā, free from all flaws. You tore out Vagadeva’s eyes and Pushā’s teeth. You destroy fever, wield a mace, and represent dissolution and time. You have a fiery mouth, fire as your emblem, are brilliant and lord of men. You are mad, make people tremble, called the fourth, most honored of men; you are a dwarf, Vāmanadeva, and the dwarf circling the east. You are a beggar, seem like a beggar, naturally tricky; you once struck Indra’s hands and the Vasus. You are the seasons and creator of seasons, time, honey-eyed, a fruit-bearing tree, arrows as your seat, worshipped by all. You protect and create the universe, are the Purusha, eternal, definite; lord of all faiths, Virupāksha, embodying the three gunas, protector of all. You have three eyes, take many forms, shine like a million suns; you are lord of the gods, supreme deity, with beard and moon on your hair, one with Brahman, worthy of devotion, identical with all beings. You blow all bugles, break all bonds, enchant and bind everyone, always bringing death. Your teeth are like flowers, you are division itself, the greatest, destroyer of all; you have a fearsome beard, hold a bow, are terrifying and immensely strong.’

These eight hundred holy names I’ve given you will remove all sins, bring holiness, and protect those who seek them. If you recite them, O Ten-necked Rāvana, you will be able to defeat your enemies.”
The three types of clouds are: (1) Agnija, created from fire; (2) Pakshaja, formed in a fortnight; and (3) Brāhma, created by Brahma.
A kamandalu is a water pot made out of clay or wood, used by ascetics and religious students.
Pinaka is Shiva’s bow—a trident or three-pronged spear.
Dhurjati is a name for Shiva, meaning he who bears the burden of the three worlds.
Parijātra is the name of a mountain, apparently the central or western part of the Vindhya range.
A Vinā is a type of stringed musical instrument.
Panava is a kind of small drum or tabor.
SECTION XXVIII

After receiving his boon from Brahmā (the “father, sprung from lotus”), Rāvana didn’t waste any time. Brahmā quickly returned to his own realm, and Rāvana headed back too. Not long after, Rāvana, who was feared by everyone, arrived at the western shore of the ocean, bringing his advisors with him. There, on an island, Rāvana spotted a dazzling figure named Mahajambunada, sitting alone. This person looked terrifying, blazing like fire at the end of the world. To Rāvana, he seemed as impressive as Indra among the gods, the moon among planets, a lion among legendary beasts, Airāvata among elephants, Meru among mountains, and the Pārijāta among trees. Rāvana, the ten-headed demon, challenged him: “Fight me!” The man’s eyes flashed dangerously, and when his teeth clenched, it sounded like thunder. Rāvana and his advisors roared back, and hurled a barrage of weapons—darts, spears, and more—at this radiant giant with long arms, a fierce face, huge teeth, a conch-shaped neck, broad chest, a belly like a frog’s, a lion-like face, legs like Mount Kailasa, red hands, and an immense body surrounded by flames and adorned with lotus garlands. He was covered in gold, and moved with the speed of the wind and mind. But just like a lion ignores a wolf’s attack, or a mountain stays unmoved by a river, this great being wasn’t bothered at all. He told Rāvana, “You evil-minded night-stalker, I’ll soon make you regret wanting a fight.” Rāma, the power of this being was a thousand times greater than Rāvana’s, who terrified the whole world. In this being’s body, piety and asceticism were his thighs, love was his manhood, the Viswadevas at his waist, the Maruts near his bladder, the Vasus in his midsection, the oceans in his belly, the directions at his sides, the Maruts in his joints, the ancestors on his back, and Brahmā himself in his heart. Good deeds and gifts were his body hair; the Himalayas, Hemkuta, Mandara, and Meru mountains were his bones; his palms were like thunderbolts, his body was the sky, clouds wrapped his neck, and gods and celestial beings rested on his arms. Poisonous snakes curled under his fingernails, ready to strike. Fire was in his mouth, the Rudras on his shoulders, the months and seasons on his teeth, and the phases of the moon in his nostrils. Air moved through his pores. Saraswati was in his throat, the twin Aswins in his ears, the sun and moon his eyes. All the Vedas, rituals, stars, and energy filled his body in human form. Then, this cosmic being casually struck Rāvana with hands hard as thunder. Rāvana was knocked to the ground. After seeing Rāvana fall, this massive, mountain-like being, glowing and decked with lotus garlands, disappeared beneath the earth. Rāvana asked his advisors, “Prahasta, Sukasārana, and the rest—where did that guy go?” The night-wandering demons replied, “He, who crushes the pride of gods and demons, has gone below.”

Like Garuda swooping down on a snake, Rāvana rushed to the mouth of the cave where the being vanished, and, without hesitation, entered. Inside, he saw a crowd of men, each glowing red like vermilion, wearing armlets (“keyuras”), looking heroic, draped in red garlands, smeared with red sandalwood, and covered in gold jewelry and gems. There were three million of these fearless, pure, radiant men, dancing wildly in celebration. Rāvana, even with his terrifying power, wasn’t scared at all; he just watched them dance from the entrance. Each one looked just like the first being he’d fought: same color, same clothes, same physique, all with four arms and incredible energy. Still, Rāvana’s hair stood on end, despite Brahmā’s protection, and he quickly left the place. Outside, he saw another gigantic figure lying on a bed. Everything—the house, the seat, the bed—was dazzling white and precious. This being slept, surrounded by fire. At his side sat the goddess Lakshmi, the most beautiful in all three worlds, looking like she belonged in a divine painting—chaste, adorned with celestial garlands, scented with fine sandalwood, glittering with jewelry, and dressed in luxurious fabric, fanning herself with a lotus. Rāvana, alone and overtaken by desire, tried to grab her hand, like a doomed man reaching for a sleeping snake. The sleeping god, wrapped in flames, understood Rāvana’s intentions and laughed loudly. Suddenly, Rāvana was burned by the being’s energy and collapsed to the ground like a tree struck by lightning. The deity looked at the fallen Rākshasa and spoke: “Rise, Rākshasa chief. You won’t die today. You’re protected by Brahmā’s boon, so leave here safely, Rāvana—you’re not meant to die just yet.” Rāvana instantly recovered, but was shaken with fear. He asked the glowing deity, “Who are you, with such power, burning like the fire that ends the world? Tell me your name and where you come from.” The god, smiling, answered in a voice deep as thunder: “What will you do with my name, O ten-headed one? You’re not fated to die at my hands—at least not today.” Rāvana, palms pressed together, said, “Brahmā declared I can’t die—I’m unmatched by any god or mortal, and no one can undo his words. No force in the universe can break his promise. I see no one in the three worlds who could cancel my boon. O great god, I am immortal, and I do not fear you. But if I must die, let it be by your hand—that would be an honor.” Then, Rāvana saw the entire universe—gods, spirits, ancestors, Yama, Kubera, oceans, mountains, rivers, the Vedas and all forms of knowledge, fire, planets, stars, space, sages, Garuda, serpents, gods, yakshas, demons, and more—all reflected, incorporeal, within that cosmic being’s body as he lay there. At this point, Rāma asked Agastya, “Who was that man on the island? Who are those three million men? And who is the being who destroys the pride of demons?” Agastya replied, “Listen, O Rāma, eternal one, god of gods—I’ll explain. The being on the island is the great sage Kapila. The dancers are deities equal to Kapila in power and wisdom. Rāvana, evil as he was, wasn’t destroyed because Kapila didn’t look at him in anger—otherwise, Rāvana would have been reduced to ashes on the spot. That mountain-like being struck Rāvana, wounding him, and he fell. With sharp words, he humbled Rāvana, piercing him deep. After some time, Rāvana regained his senses and returned to his advisors.”
Sarabha: a legendary creature, said to have eight legs.
Keyura: a type of arm ornament.
SECTION XXIX

As Rāvana (let’s call him “Ravana” for ease), with his cruel heart, rode back in delight, he secretly kidnapped the daughters of royal sages, gods, and demons along his route. Any beautiful woman he saw—married or single—Ravana would capture, ruthlessly killing any friends or family who tried to protect her. His chariot soon filled with women from many races: Nagas, Rakshasas, Asuras, Yakshas, Dānavas, and humans. Terrified and grieving, these women cried hot, burning tears. Their fear and sorrow filled the chariot with a flood of tears, just as rivers fill the ocean. Hundreds of women wept—Nagas, Gandharvas, daughters of powerful ascetics, Daityas, and Dānavas. These women had long hair, graceful bodies, faces like full moons, high chests, waists as slim as black bees, and backs as straight as chariot poles. They shone with youthful beauty, like goddesses or glowing gold, but now they were overwhelmed by grief, fear, and sadness. The chariot seemed to glow from all sides with their sighs, and Pushpaka looked almost like a furnace where fire burns constantly. The faces and eyes of these beautiful captives, now at the mercy of the ten-headed demon, were full of sorrow—like deer that had just been attacked by a lion. Some wondered, “Will he eat me?” while others, stricken with fear, asked themselves, “Is he going to kill me?” All of them, thinking of their mothers, fathers, husbands, and brothers, cried out in grief: “What will happen to my son now that I’m gone? What kind of pain is my mother or brother suffering? What will my husband do without me? Death, please take me and end my misery. What terrible thing did I do in a past life to deserve this suffering? We’re drowning in an ocean of sorrow, and I can’t see any end to this pain. Humanity is cursed—no one is weaker than mankind. Just as stars vanish when the sun rises, our husbands were destroyed by the powerful Ravana. This Rakshasa is obsessed with destruction. Even though he knows that taking another man’s wife is a great sin, this wicked demon still enjoys what isn’t his. He’s as strong as he is evil, and for these crimes, he’ll be destroyed by his own actions.” As soon as these faithful women spoke their curses, bugles sounded in the heavens and flowers rained down to earth. Because of the curses of these loyal wives, Ravana lost his strength and radiance—he seemed almost out of his mind. Hearing their laments and cheered by the other demons, Ravana, the most powerful of Rakshasas, entered his city of Lanka.

At that moment, Ravana’s sister—a terrifying, grim-looking demoness—suddenly collapsed to the ground. Ravana quickly picked her up and tried to comfort her. “Tell me, dear sister, what’s wrong? What do you want to say?” he asked her. With bloodshot eyes full of tears, she replied, “Brother, you, of all people, have made me a widow, even though you’re so powerful. Fourteen thousand demons known as the Kalakeyas were killed by you in battle, including my husband—who was dearer to me than my own life. You killed him, my own brother—my enemy in disguise. Because of you, I’m condemned to be called ‘widow’ forever. You should have protected my husband in battle, but it was you who killed him. Aren’t you ashamed?”

Hearing his sister’s heartbreaking words, the ten-headed Ravana consoled her gently: “Don’t waste your tears, sister. You don’t have to fear any of your relatives. I’ll make it up to you with gifts, honors, and favors. In the heat of battle, obsessed with winning, I was firing arrows everywhere and honestly couldn’t tell friends from enemies—your husband died by my hand without me knowing. I’m truly sorry. I’ll do whatever I can to help you now. Go and live with our wealthy brother Khara. He’ll lead fourteen thousand Rakshasas. Khara will provide food and clothes to all the Rakshasas and will always obey your commands—he’s your cousin and a powerful night-stalker. Let him go now to protect the Dandaka forest, with the mighty Dushana as his general. Khara will always do as you ask and command the Rakshasas who can change their forms at will.”

After saying this, the ten-headed demon ordered his army of fourteen thousand powerful Rakshasas to follow Khara. Surrounded by these fierce Rakshasas, Khara fearlessly set off for the Dandaka forest, where he ruled firmly. Surpanakha, too, went to live in the Dandaka forest.
The original literally means: for you, I will forever be known as a widow.
The word in the text is “Jāmata,” which literally means “son-in-law”—but here it likely means “husband,” since she was Ravana’s sister.
SECTION XXX

After giving command of his massive and terrifying army to Khara and comforting his sister, the ten-headed demon Rāvana finally felt satisfied and relieved of worry. Then, this powerful ruler of the Rākshasas, along with his followers, went into a beautiful garden in Lanka called Nikumbhilā. There, he saw the place filled with hundreds of sacrificial posts and altars, glowing with the fire and energy of an elaborate ritual. He also saw his intimidating son, Meghnāda (also called Indrajit), dressed in an antelope skin, with his hair tied in a topknot and holding a water vessel. Seeing Meghnāda, Rāvana hugged him tightly and asked, "What are you doing here, my son? Tell me the truth." At that moment, the respected sage Usanas (also known as Shukra), who was performing strict penances and wanted the sacrifice to succeed, spoke to Rāvana, the Rākshasa king: "Listen, I’ll explain everything, O King. Your son has gained the rewards of many important sacrifices—Agnistoma, Ashvamedha, Bahusuvarna, Rajasuya, Gomedha, and Vaishnava. Now, while carrying out this Maheshvara sacrifice—which normal humans can’t even attempt—your son has received a boon from Pashupati himself."

"He has also gained special magical powers—abilities that can create darkness and confusion—like flying through the sky, never dying, riding a chariot that moves wherever he wishes, and even making darkness appear at will. O king of Rākshasas, if your son uses these powers in battle, not even the gods or demons will be able to follow his movements. On top of that, he’s received a quiver with endless arrows, a rare and powerful bow, and a terrifying weapon perfect for destroying enemies in war. After being granted these boons, your son and I have been waiting here, since the sacrifice is over, to see you." Rāvana answered, "You shouldn’t have worshipped my enemies—Indra and the others—with all those offerings. But what’s done is done; there’s still some good in this, I suppose. Come, let’s go home." So, with his son and Vibhishana, Rāvana returned and released all the captive women—goddesses, Dānavas, and Rākshasas—who had been taken from the gods and demons. Seeing Rāvana’s obvious lust for these women, the righteous Vibhishana said, "You keep doing whatever you want, even when you know your actions hurt others and destroy your own goodness, wealth, and reputation. You killed their families and dragged these women here, but while you weren’t looking, Madhu ran off with Kumbhanashi." Rāvana demanded, "I don’t understand. Who is this Madhu you’re talking about?" Furious, Vibhishana replied, "Listen, the consequences of your evil actions have finally caught up with you. There was a wise old Rākshasa named Malyavān—our maternal grandfather’s elder brother. His granddaughter is Kumbhanashi—she’s the daughter of our aunt Analā, so she’s basically our sister. While your son was busy with the sacrifice and I was underwater, the powerful Rākshasa Madhu kidnapped her. Kumbhakarna was asleep at the time. Madhu killed all the guards and counselors, and snatched her from your own palace. When we heard, we let it go—after all, an unmarried girl should be given to her husband by her brothers, but that didn’t happen. This is just the result of your bad deeds, and it’s happened to you immediately, as people say." Hearing Vibhishana’s words, Rāvana was shaken—his guilt and rage built up like a stormy sea as he remembered his own crimes. With eyes red from anger, he shouted, "Get my chariot ready, and prepare all our warriors! Kumbhakarna and the rest of our top fighters must mount their vehicles, armed for battle. Today, I’ll kill Madhu, who dares not fear me! Surrounded by my allies, I’ll march to the gods’ realm for war." 

At his command, four thousand Akshauhini (huge army units) of Rākshasas, armed with all kinds of weapons, set out for battle. Indrajit led at the front, Rāvana stayed in the center, and Kumbhakarna brought up the rear. Righteous Vibhishana stayed in Lanka to continue his religious duties. The rest of the Rākshasa leaders headed for Madhu’s city. The Rākshasas filled the sky, riding animals like donkeys, camels, horses, fast dolphins, and giant snakes. Seeing Rāvana on the move, hundreds of Daityas—enemies of the gods—joined him. When they reached Madhu’s city, Rāvana couldn’t find Madhu, but he saw his own sister instead. Afraid, Kumbhanashi bowed at his feet, her hands folded. Rāvana lifted her up gently and said, "Don’t be afraid. What can I do for you?" She replied, "O King, if you care for me, please don’t kill my husband today. For a woman of high birth, there’s no fear greater than losing her husband. Please, keep your promise—look at me, I’m begging you. You’ve just said, ‘No fear.’" Rāvana answered, "Then tell me quickly, where is your husband? I want him to join me in conquering the gods’ realm. Out of love for you, I’ll spare Madhu." Relieved, Kumbhanashi woke her sleeping husband and said, "Here’s my brother, Daçagriva (another name for Rāvana). He wants to conquer the gods and asks for your help. You should help him, since he’s asking out of affection for me." Madhu replied, "Alright, I will." He then greeted Rāvana respectfully, and Rāvana spent a night at Madhu’s house before preparing to leave. Then, Rāvana led his army to Mount Kailāsa, home of Vaiśravaṇa, ready to face the gods.
Another name for Shukra. Indrajit had taken a vow of silence, so he didn’t want to disturb him.
A sacred fire ritual lasting five days, performed in spring.

SECTION XXXI

After sunset, the powerful Rāvana (Ravana) set up camp for his army. The bright, clear moon rose above the mountains as the massive army, carrying all kinds of weapons, drifted off to sleep. Rāvana lay on the top of the mountain, looking over the caves glowing under the moonlight and surrounded by trees. The forest below was full of shining Karnikar groves, Kadamba and Vakula trees, blooming lotuses, the waters of the Mandākini river, and other trees like Champaka, Asoka, Punnaga, Mandāra, mango, Pātala, Lodra, Pryangu, Arjuna, Ketaka, Tagara, coconut, Pyāla, jackfruit, and many more. Kinnaras—magical beings with beautiful voices—sang love songs that filled the air with happiness. The Vidyadharas, another group of celestial beings, danced and partied with their lovers, their eyes red from drinking. In the home of Kubera, the lord of wealth, the sweet music of Apsarās (celestial nymphs) rang out like bells. The wind shook the trees, their nectar-scented flowers showering the hilltop and filling it with fragrance. The breeze, rich with the scent of honey and flower pollen, blew through the camp, making Rāvana’s desire even stronger. Surrounded by the songs, the abundance of flowers, the cool night air, the beauty of the hills, and the rising moon, Rāvana felt restless and kept glancing up at the moon with deep sighs.

Just then, Rambhā, the most beautiful Apsarā, passed by. She was dressed in stunning jewelry and her face glowed like the full moon. She wore the best sandalwood paste, her hair was decorated with Mandāra flowers, and her body was covered in other blossoms, moving in a way that drew attention. Her eyes were captivating and her waist, wrapped with a Mekhala (a jeweled belt), seemed like the very embodiment of Rati—the goddess of love. Her forehead and face were painted with red sandalwood marks and flower ornaments that bloom in all six seasons. Rambhā looked like a second Sree (goddess of beauty), her grace and beauty both natural and enhanced. She wore green clothes like rain clouds, her face shone like the moon, her eyebrows were shaped like perfect bows, her thighs were as sturdy as elephant trunks, and her hands were as soft as fresh leaves.

Rāvana saw Rambhā walking among the soldiers. He got up, overcome by lust, grabbed her by the hand even as she shrank back in embarrassment, and smiled as he spoke: "Where are you going, beautiful? Who are you hurrying to please? Whose lucky day is it that you’re about to enjoy with him? Who will taste the nectar of your lips, scented like lotus flowers? Whose chest will your lovely, golden, upturned breasts touch? Who could possibly be as handsome as me—Indra, Vishnu, or the Ashvins—that you’d pass me by? Come, rest with me on this rock, beautiful one. There’s no other lord in all three worlds but me. I, Daçānana (Ten-Heads), lord of all lords, am begging you, hands folded. Please choose me."

Rambhā, trembling, put her hands together and pleaded, "Please, show some mercy. You are my superior; you shouldn’t speak to me this way. If anyone else tried to hurt me, you should protect me. I’m basically your daughter-in-law. I’m telling you the truth."

But Rāvana, looking at her standing with her head down and hair standing on end in fear, replied, "If you were my son’s wife, then you would be my daughter-in-law."

Rambhā answered, "It’s true! By virtue, I am your son’s wife, O greatest of Rākshasas. Your brother Vaisravana has a son, Nalakuvara, who is loved throughout the three worlds. He is as virtuous as a Brahmin, as strong as a Kshatriya, fierce when angry, and patient like the earth. I belong to him, and I’ve dressed up for him tonight. I’m not interested in anyone else. He is waiting for me right now. Please, O king and slayer of enemies, don’t get in the way. Let me go, O greatest of Rākshasas, and do what is right. You deserve my respect, and I am under your protection."

Rāvana answered her, "You say you’re my daughter-in-law, but that only applies to those who have one husband. The law of the gods is that Apsarās never truly have a husband—they can’t belong to just one man." With that, he ignored her pleas and raped her.

Afterwards, Rambhā was released, stripped of her jewelry and garlands, looking broken and defeated, like a river churned up by rampaging elephants. Her hair was a mess, her hands shook, and she trembled like a flowering vine in a storm. Shaken, ashamed, and still trembling, she hurried to Nalakuvara and collapsed at his feet.

Seeing her like this, Nalakuvara, son of Vaisravana, asked, "What happened, beautiful one? Why have you thrown yourself at my feet?"

Sighing and shaking, Rambhā told him everything, from start to finish. "My lord," she said, "as Rāvana was heading to heaven, he stopped here with his army for the night. While I was on my way to you, he saw me. He grabbed me and asked where I was going. I told him the truth, but he wouldn’t listen—he was overcome by lust. I begged him again, reminding him I was your wife, but he ignored me and forced himself on me. Please, forgive me for what happened. You know a woman’s strength can never match a man’s."

Nalakuvara was furious when he heard what had happened. He closed his eyes and meditated for a moment to find out the truth. Then, eyes blazing with anger, he scooped water into his hands, rinsed his mouth as part of a ritual, and cast a terrible curse on Rāvana: "Because Rāvana forced himself on you against your will, he will never be able to touch an unwilling woman again. If he ever tries to assault a woman who resists him, his head will split into seven pieces."

As soon as Nalakuvara spoke this curse, a sound like celestial trumpets filled the air and flowers rained down from the sky. The gods, including Brahmā, were overjoyed, knowing Rāvana had been punished and that his end was inevitable because of his actions. When Rāvana heard about Nalakuvara’s curse, he was so shaken that he never again tried to force himself on a woman who resisted him. All the women he kept captive, hearing of the curse, felt a surge of hope and relief.
A kind of ornament worn around the waist.
Wife of Kama, the Hindu god of love.
SECTION XXXII

After crossing Mount Kailāsa, the powerful Ten-necked demon Rāvana (sometimes called “Dashānana”), along with his army, reached Indra’s realm. The arrival of the Rākshasa army sent a roar through the heavens, loud as a stormy ocean. Hearing that Rāvana had come, Indra trembled on his throne. He turned to the gathered gods—Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and Maruts—and said, “Get ready to fight Rāvana, who is full of evil intentions.” At Indra’s (also called Śakra) command, the gods—his equals in battle and strong in their own right—armed themselves for war. But Indra, afraid of Rāvana’s power, went to Vishnu and pleaded, “How am I supposed to stand against this Rākshasa Rāvana? He’s only this strong because of a boon he was given, not for any other reason. Brahmā’s words must be kept true. Just as I relied on your strength to defeat Namuchi, Yitra, Bali, Nānrin, and Samvara, I ask for your help again. There’s no better protector in all the worlds—living or non-living—than you, O Lord, O God of gods, O destroyer of Madhu. You are the gracious, eternal Nārāyana, with the lotus at your navel. By your power the worlds were created, including myself and the other gods. You made the three worlds, with everything that lives or does not live, and at the end of time, all will return to you. Please, tell me honestly: should I go and fight myself, or will you use your sword and discus to defeat Rāvana?” 

Hearing this, Nārāyana replied, “Don’t be afraid; listen to me. Because of his boon, Rāvana can’t be defeated—not even by the gods or the Asuras. Thanks to his power, he and his son are going to achieve something huge. Even if you ask me, I won’t fight Rāvana directly. Vishnu never turns back in battle without destroying his enemies, but Rāvana is protected by a boon that makes that almost impossible. Still, I promise you, King of the gods, performer of a hundred sacrifices, I will become the cause of Rāvana’s death in time. I will destroy him and his family soon, and the gods will rejoice. After that, the Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, Maruts, and Ashvins—all well-armed and armored—came out to face the Rākshasas. Around the end of the night, the sounds of Rāvana’s army fighting could be heard everywhere. The powerful Rākshasas woke up, looked at each other, and eagerly prepared for battle. But when the gods saw the size of the Rākshasa army at the start of the fight, they lost heart. 

A fierce battle broke out, echoing with the clash of weapons, as Rākshasas and gods fought fiercely. Rāvana’s counselors—grim-faced and heroic—joined the fight: the likes of Māricha, Prahasta, Mahāparswa, Mahodara, Akampana, Nikumbha, Suka, Sārana, Sanghrāda, Dhumaketu, Mahādangstra, Gathodara, Jāmbumāli, Mahāhrada, Virupāksha, Suptaghna, Yajnakopa, Durmukha, Khara, Trisirā, Karaveerāksha, Suryyasatru, Mahākāya, Atikāya, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka. Leading them was Sumālin, Rāvana’s maternal grandfather, who was extremely powerful. Sumālin, furious, attacked the gods’ army with many sharp weapons, scattering them like storm winds scatter clouds.

Assaulted by the night-dwelling demons, the gods’ forces scattered in all directions, like deer fleeing a lion. At that moment, the heroic Sāvitra, the eighth Vasu, entered the battlefield, surrounded by his troops and striking fear into his enemies. Two powerful Adityas, Tushthā and Pushā, joined together, unafraid, and entered the fray. A terrible clash broke out between the Rākshasas and gods, neither side willing to let their reputation be tarnished. The Rākshasas rained down thousands of terrifying weapons on the gods. The gods fought back, sending many powerful and fearsome Rākshasas to their deaths with flawless weapons.

In the chaos, Rāma, a furious Rākshasa named Sumālin began to tear through the gods’ army with all kinds of weapons. Like a furious wind splitting apart clouds, Sumālin, driven by rage, tore through the gods with his sharpened weapons. The gods, battered by a hail of arrows, maces, prāsas, and all sorts of deadly weapons, couldn’t hold their ground. Seeing the gods struggling under Sumālin’s attack, the eighth Vasu, Sāvitra, stood his ground, burning with anger. Surrounded by his fellow charioteers, this mighty Vasu used his strength to push back the attacking night-dwellers.

A brutal showdown began between Sumālin and Sāvitra, so intense it would make anyone’s hair stand on end. Sāvitra destroyed Sumālin’s serpent-drawn chariot with a barrage of arrows. After that, he picked up a deadly mace, its head burning like the rod of Death itself. Sāvitra struck Sumālin on the head with the mace. The blow made the mace flash like a ball of fire, as if Indra had hurled his thunderbolt onto a mountaintop. The impact was so powerful that Sumālin’s body was reduced to ashes—no bones, no flesh, nothing left on the battlefield.

Seeing their leader killed, the other Rākshasas cried out in grief and ran in all directions. Overwhelmed by Sāvitra’s might, they could not stand their ground in the battle any longer.
SECTION XXXIII

When Sumālin was killed and burned to ashes by Vasu, and the gods attacked, the Rākshasa army broke apart and scattered in every direction. But Meghanāda (also called Indrajit), the powerful son of Rāvana, gathered the remaining Rākshasas, furious at what had happened. Like a raging wildfire racing into a forest, this mighty warrior rode into battle on his magical chariot.
