During the chaos, a powerful Daitya chief named Pulomā, who was Jayanta’s grandfather (since Sachi, Jayanta’s mother, was Pulomā’s daughter), grabbed Jayanta and vanished. Pulomā carried his grandson into the ocean for safety. Believing Jayanta was dead, the gods were filled with grief and fear and scattered in all directions. Furious, Meghanāda and his loyal Rākshasa warriors chased after the fleeing gods, shouting loudly. When Indra realized his son was missing and saw the gods running away, he ordered Mātali, “Bring my chariot!” Mātali quickly brought out the gods’ enormous, terrifying, and fast-moving chariot, ready for battle.

As Indra climbed aboard, storm clouds filled with lightning gathered and thunder rumbled ahead of his chariot. The Gandharvas played music, and the Apsarās danced as he prepared for war. Armed with his weapons, Indra set off for battle, joined by the Rudras, Vasus, Adityas, the twin Aswins, and Maruts. As they marched out, the wind howled, the sun lost its brightness, and giant firebrands sent up flames.

Meanwhile, Rāvana (also called Daśagrīva, meaning “Ten Heads”) climbed onto the gods’ own chariot, which had been built by their divine architect. He was surrounded by colossal serpents, so powerful they could topple anything upright, and their breath set the battlefield ablaze. With his demon and night-stalker followers around him, Rāvana faced Mahendra (another name for Indra) in battle. He called his son back from fighting and took his place on the front line. Meghanāda withdrew from the field and stood silently aside.

Now the gods and the Rākshasas clashed directly, unleashing a storm of weapons thick as a monsoon. Kumbhakarna, Rāvana’s monstrous brother, arrived armed with countless weapons—but he had no idea who he was fighting, since he’d just woken up (he slept for months at a time). In his fury, Kumbhakarna attacked the gods using his teeth, feet, arms, hands, as well as weapons like spears, axes, and clubs—basically anything he could get his hands on. He fought fiercely with the powerful Rudras, but they wounded him again and again. The Rākshasa army fought the Maruts and were battered by a barrage of weapons. Some Rākshasas fell dead or torn apart, others collapsed unconscious on their mounts.

All around, the battlefield was chaos: warriors stood dazed, clinging to chariots, elephants, donkeys, camels, snakes, horses, porpoises, boars, and even demon-mouthed beasts. Some embraced serpents (Pannagas) in confusion. Other night-stalkers were cut down by the gods and died where they fell. The bodies of Rākshasas littered the ground, making the scene look almost surreal, like a painting come to life. Rivers of blood flowed between weapons, their silent streams crowded with crows and vultures.

Seeing his army slaughtered by the gods, the enraged Daśānana (another name for Rāvana) plunged into the heart of the gods’ forces, killing gods as he fought his way to Indra. Indra grabbed his massive bow, whose twang echoed across all ten directions. He let loose arrows that flashed like fire and sunlight, striking Rāvana on the head. Rāvana, with his ten arms, fired back with hundreds of arrows from his own bow. As these two mighty leaders exchanged deadly volleys, darkness fell over the battlefield, making it impossible for anyone to see what was happening.
Kumbhakarna had been asleep until now, so he didn’t know anything about what had been happening in the war. He usually slept for six months at a stretch.
SECTION XXXIV

As night fell, the gods and Rakshasas—both groups filled with wild strength—began fighting fiercely, crushing each other in the darkness. But in the chaos, three figures stood out, untouched by confusion: Indra, Ravana, and Meghanada (also called Indrajit, Ravana’s son). Seeing his entire army slaughtered almost instantly, Ravana was consumed with furious rage and let out terrible, echoing roars. Burning with anger, the unstoppable Ravana shouted at his charioteer, who stood ready at his side: “Drive me to the far end of the enemy ranks. I’ll cut down these gods with my weapons and send them straight to the land of the dead. I’ll kill Indra, Kubera, Varuna, and Yama—no one can stop me. I’ll destroy all the gods and claim their place for myself. Don’t worry—just drive! I’ve told you twice now: take me to the edge of their army. We’re waiting near the Nandana grove—head for the hill where the sun rises.” Hearing this, the charioteer urged the horses forward, racing right through the enemy’s lines.

Meanwhile, realizing what Ravana intended, Indra—the king of the gods—spoke to his fellow deities right there on the battlefield: “Listen, everyone. We need to defeat this Ten-necked demon now, while he’s still alive. Riding his chariot as fast as the wind, he’s charging through our army like a stormy ocean during a monsoon. We can’t kill him right now because of the boon he has, but we can capture him if we act together. Remember how we captured Bali and took control of the three worlds? We should stop this evil soul the same way.” After saying this, Indra left Ravana and moved to another part of the battlefield, fighting so fiercely that he terrified the Rakshasas. Ravana, who could not be stopped, entered the gods’ army from the north, while Indra attacked from the south.

Ravana pushed deep into the enemy forces—nearly a hundred leagues in—and overwhelmed the celestial army with a storm of arrows. Seeing his own side falling apart, Indra returned without fear and confronted Ravana directly. In the chaos, as Ravana was being restrained by Indra, the demons and Rakshasas cried out in panic, “We’re doomed!”

At that moment, Ravana’s son Meghanada, wild with rage, leapt onto his chariot and entered the most dangerous part of the battle. Using the magical powers he’d been given long ago by Pasupati (a form of Shiva), he slipped into the gods’ camp and started attacking them fiercely. Ignoring the other deities, he went straight for Indra. Indra, also called Mahendra, quickly noticed that Meghanada was after him. Despite being attacked by powerful gods, Meghanada—now without his armor—showed no fear. He took down Indra’s charioteer with a barrage of arrows and then showered Indra himself with missiles.

Forced to abandon his chariot and charioteer, Indra climbed onto his elephant Airavat and searched the battlefield for Meghanada. But using his magic, Meghanada made himself invisible in the sky, and, catching Indra off guard, struck him with hundreds of arrows. When Meghanada realized that Indra was exhausted, he used his illusions to bind Indra and dragged him away toward the Rakshasa army.

Seeing mighty Indra being taken away by force, the gods were shocked and confused, thinking, “What just happened?” The one who had overpowered Sakra (another name for Indra), and who could defeat even the most skilled in magic, had disappeared, and no one could see how Indra had been captured. While this was happening, the gods, furious, attacked Ravana with a storm of arrows, battering him from all sides. Exhausted from fighting the Adityas and Vasus (groups of gods), Ravana couldn’t keep up the battle any longer.

Watching his father struggle and get battered in the fight, Meghanada—still invisible—called out, “Come on, Father, our job here is done. We’ve won! Don’t worry, and stop suffering. With my magic, I’ve captured Mahendra, lord of the three worlds and leader of the gods, crushing their pride. You’ve beaten your enemies with your own strength, so enjoy ruling the three worlds however you want. There’s no need to keep fighting.”

Hearing these words from Ravana’s son, the gods realized they had been defeated. They withdrew from the battlefield, leaving without Indra. Hearing his son’s comforting words, Ravana—the great enemy of the gods, famous for his strength—stopped fighting and said warmly, “You’ve brought honor to our family by showing such power. You’ve defeated the gods and their mighty king. Take Indra back to our city in your chariot, with our soldiers all around you. I’ll follow you soon, pleased, along with my advisors.”

So, with his army and chariots, and with Indra as his captive, Ravana’s powerful son Meghanada returned home. He dismissed his victorious warriors as they celebrated their incredible win.
SECTION XXXV

After Mahendra (another name for Indra) was defeated by Rāvana’s son, all the gods, led by Brahmā, went together to Lankā. They found Rāvana, surrounded by his sons and brothers. Brahmā, hovering calmly in the sky, spoke, “Rāvana, I’m impressed by your son’s performance in battle. His strength is incredible—maybe even greater than yours. You’ve kept your promise and conquered the three worlds through your own power. I’m truly pleased with both of you, father and son. Your son is immensely powerful, and he will be famous everywhere as ‘Indrajit’—the one who defeated Indra. This Rākshasa will be unstoppable, and thanks to him, the gods are now under your control. Now, Rāvana, release Mahendra, the punisher of Pāka (another name for Indra), and tell us what you want in exchange from the gods.” Then, Indrajit (whose real name is Meghanāda), replied, “If you’re offering, O god, I want immortality.” But Brahmā said to Meghanāda, “No living being—bird, beast, or anything else—is truly immortal.” Meghanāda listened and responded, “Then hear my wish for releasing Indra: whenever I perform a sacrifice before battle, let a chariot with horses rise from the fire, and let me be immortal as long as I’m on that chariot. That’s my request. But if I ever fight without finishing my sacrifice, let me be destroyed. Others gain immortality through penance, but I’ll earn it through my own strength.” Brahmā agreed, saying, “So be it.” With that, Meghanāda released Indra, and the gods returned home. But, Rāma, Indra was left weakened, his divine glow gone, anxious and troubled. Seeing him like this, Brahmā asked, “O you who performed a hundred sacrifices, why did you commit such a terrible deed in the past? Listen, King of the gods: When I first created beings, I made them all the same—same color, speech, and form. There were no differences. Then, I thought deeply and decided to create someone unique. I gathered the best qualities from all my creations and made a woman named Ahalyā. ‘Hal’ means ugliness, and ‘Ahalyā’ means one without flaw. I gave her that name. After creating her, I wondered who she should be with. You, Indra, thought of her as your own because of your pride. But I entrusted her to the sage Gautama, who cared for her for many years. Impressed by Gautama’s patience and asceticism, I married her to him. He enjoyed her company, and the other gods were disappointed. But driven by lust and anger, you went to Gautama’s hermitage, saw her shining like fire, and forced yourself on her. The sage caught you and, furious, cursed you with these words:

“Indra, because you dared to take my wife without fear, you will suffer a reversal of fortune. You will be defeated and captured by your enemies in battle. And the desire that drove you to this crime will spread among mortals. Anyone who commits this sin will be half responsible, and the other half of the guilt will fall on you. Your position among the gods will never be secure. Whoever becomes king of the gods will never have lasting security. That is my curse.” Then, Gautama turned to his wife and said, “Because of your fickle mind and beauty, your looks will fade here at the hermitage. You are young and beautiful, but you will no longer be the only beautiful woman in the world. Your beauty will be shared by all living beings because your unmatched beauty caused all this trouble.” From then on, all beings had beauty. Ahalyā pleaded with Gautama: “O twice-born sage, Indra tricked me by taking your form. I didn’t do this willingly. Please forgive me.” Gautama replied, “One day, a mighty warrior will be born in the Ikshvāku dynasty—Rāma, who is actually Vishnu in human form. When he comes to the forest to perform sacrifices, he will purify you of your sin. Welcome him as a guest, and after you meet him, you can return to me and live with me again.” Saying this, Gautama left. From then on, Ahalyā lived alone, devoted to her penance, chanting holy verses. Indra suffered all this because of the sage’s curse. So, Indra, remember your past mistake. That’s why you’re now under your enemies’ power. Control yourself, perform a sacrifice to Vishnu, and you’ll be purified and return to heaven. Don’t worry—your son wasn’t killed in battle; his grandfather took him into the ocean for safety.” Indra listened, performed the sacrifice for Vishnu, and returned to his throne among the gods. Now, Rāma, I’ve told you how powerful Indrajit is. Not only did he defeat many heroes, he even conquered Indra, king of the gods.” 

Hearing Agastya’s words, Rāma, Lakshmana, the Vānaras (monkey warriors), and the Rākshasas all marveled, saying, “That’s incredible!” Bibhishana, standing beside Rāma, added, “These old memories have just come back to me.” Rāma then said to Agastya, “Everything you say is true.” Agastya replied, “Rāma, it was after this that Rāvana, with his growing power, along with his son, defeated Indra, king of the gods.”
SECTION XXXVI

After bowing respectfully to Agastya, the greatest of sages, the brilliant Rama spoke again, sounding surprised: “O holy one, O best of the twice-born, when that ruthless Ravana traveled across the earth, was the world empty of people? Was there no king or prince anywhere who could punish him? Were all the kings at that time weak and powerless? I’ve also heard that Ravana defeated many kings and drove them out using all sorts of powerful weapons.”

When Rama finished speaking, Agastya, who was wise and wealthy in virtue, laughed gently—almost like Brahma talking to Rudra—and replied: “Rama, lord of the earth, as Ravana wandered across the world, he eventually came to the city of Mahismati, which looked as splendid as a city of the gods. The fire deity lived there eternally. The king of that city was named Arjuna, who shone like a flame kept safe in a hidden well. One day, Arjuna, king of the Haihayas, went to the river Nerbuda with his wives to have some fun. On that very same day, Ravana, lord of the Rakshasas, arrived and asked his advisors, ‘Where is King Arjuna? Tell me right away—I am Ravana and I’ve come to challenge your king. Go and let him know I’m here.’

Ravana’s advisors explained that King Arjuna wasn’t in the city at the moment. Hearing this, Ravana, the son of Visravas, left Mahismati and headed toward the Vindhya mountains, which looked as grand as the Himalayas. The mountains stretched across the sky like a mass of clouds, towering so high they seemed to split the earth and block out the heavens. With a thousand peaks, the mountains were home to lions in their caves and had hundreds of waterfalls streaming down from above. The mountain seemed to laugh out loud, while gods, Gandharvas, Apsaras, and Kinnaras played with their partners there, making it look like a heavenly realm. Crystal-clear rivers ran through it, looking like a thousand snakes with flickering tongues.

Ravana admired the Vindhya mountain, with its massive caves and Himalaya-like presence, and then made his way to the Nerbuda river. This sacred river rushed towards the western ocean. Its waters churned with buffaloes, deer, tigers, lions, bears, and elephants all cooling off from the heat. The river was crowded with chakrabakas, karandavas, swans, watercocks, and sarasa birds, all singing loudly. The beautiful Nerbuda looked almost like a woman—her ornaments were blossoming trees, her chest was the flocks of chakrabakas, her waist was the wide forest, the line of swans was like a jeweled belt, flower filaments were her scented paste, foamy water was her white silk dress, the thrill of entering her waters brought pleasure like a loving touch, and blooming lotuses were her bright eyes.

Ravana got down from his chariot, bathed in the Nerbuda—who looked as lovely as a beautiful woman—and then sat with his counselors on the riverbank, a place where many sages lived. He was charmed by the river’s beauty and praised Nerbuda, comparing her to the Ganges. Then, using gestures, he spoke to his advisors Suka and Sarana: ‘Look, the sun is up in the sky, bleaching the earth with its burning rays. But now that I’m sitting here, even the sun’s heat feels cool, like moonlight. Even the wind seems to blow carefully out of fear of me, now cool and fragrant from the river, easing our exhaustion. This wonderful Nerbuda, full of crocodiles, fish, and birds, is flowing so calmly, it’s as if she’s a woman terrified in my presence. You all have blood on you from so many battles with kings. Just as mighty elephants cool off in the Ganges, you should step into the Nerbuda’s waters. It will bring you good fortune and health. Bathing here will wash away your sins. I’ll stay on the bank, like the autumn moon’s rays, and respectfully worship Mahadeva (Shiva), who holds the Pinaka bow.’

When Ravana finished, Prahasta, Suka, Sarana, Mahodara, Dhrumakshya, and the other advisors stepped into the Nerbuda. The river was stirred up by these huge, elephant-like Rakshasa chiefs, just as the Ganges is churned when mighty elephants like Vamana, Anjana, and Padma enter it. After bathing, the powerful Rakshasas gathered flowers for Ravana’s offerings. In no time, they piled up heaps of flowers along the picturesque riverbank, which looked like patches of white clouds.

With the flowers collected, Ravana, king of the Rakshasas, stepped into the Nerbuda and bathed like a giant elephant entering the Ganges. After his bath, he chanted sacred mantras, changed out of his wet clothes, and put on a fresh white garment. Looking for a place to worship, he walked with folded hands along the bank, followed by the Rakshasas, who looked like moving mountains. Wherever Ravana went, his golden Shiva Linga was carried along. Ravana placed the Linga on a mound of sand and began the worship, offering fragrant flowers and sandalwood paste.

When his worship of Shiva—the god with the crescent moon in his hair, the giver of blessings and reliever of suffering—was finished, Ravana began to dance with his arms raised, singing in front of the Linga.
SECTION XXXVII

Not far from where Ravana, the terrifying lord of the Rakshasas, was gathering flowers on the banks of the river Narmada, Arjuna, the King of Mahishmati, was enjoying himself in the water with his wives. Surrounded by his many queens, King Arjuna looked like a massive elephant in the middle of a thousand female elephants. Wanting to show off his strength, Arjuna, ruler of the Haihayas, blocked the flow of the Narmada with his thousand arms. Because of this, the river’s pure waters overflowed the banks and even started flowing backwards. The currents rose high, just like during the monsoon, carrying fish and crocodiles. The river, almost like it was being forced back at Ravana by Arjuna, carried away all the flowers Ravana had collected. Ravana, frustrated that he had to abandon his half-finished worship, looked at the Narmada, which now seemed wild and unwilling. He saw the river’s currents rushing from west to east, while further away, the waters were calm and peaceful, with birds sitting quietly on the banks.

Wondering what had caused the river to rise like this, Ravana signaled to Suka and Sarana with a gesture of his right finger. Obeying his command, the two Rakshasa brothers, Suka and Sarana—both brave warriors—immediately set off westward through the air. After traveling half a league, they spotted a man in the water surrounded by women. He was gigantic, as tall as a sala tree, with his hair floating on the water. Clearly drunk, his eyes were red. Like Mount Sumeru supporting the earth with a thousand feet, he was stopping the river’s flow with his thousand arms. All around him were a thousand beautiful women—he looked just like an elephant among a herd of females.

Seeing this incredible sight, Suka and Sarana hurried back to Ravana and reported what they had seen. “O Lord of Rakshasas, there’s a huge man, as tall as a sala tree, playing in the water with women and blocking the Narmada like a dam. The river keeps throwing up huge waves because of his thousand arms.”

When Ravana heard this, he said, “That must be Arjuna,” and immediately decided to confront him. As Ravana set out to fight Kartavirya Arjuna, the wind picked up, swirling dust everywhere and making a deafening noise. Clouds rumbled and rain started pouring down. Ravana, the Rakshasa lord, marched toward Arjuna with his generals: Mahodara, Mahaparswa, Dhrumakshya, Suka, and Sarana. In no time, the fierce Rakshasa—strong as the elephant named Arjuna—reached the Narmada’s bank and saw Arjuna in the water, surrounded by women like an elephant with his herd.

Just seeing this made Ravana’s eyes burn red with pride and anger. He turned to Arjuna’s counselors and said, “Go tell the King of the Haihayas that Ravana, Lord of the Rakshasas, is here to challenge him.”

Hearing Ravana’s words, Arjuna’s ministers stood up with weapons and replied, “Ravana, you know the right time and place for battle. Right now, our king is drunk and playing in the water with his wives. Is this really the moment you want to fight him? If you’re set on a duel, wait until morning—or if you’re impatient, you’ll have to kill us all first before you can face the king.”

But Ravana’s hungry counselors didn’t wait; they attacked, killing some of Arjuna’s ministers and eating others. A terrible battle broke out on the riverbank between Ravana’s and Arjuna’s followers. Arjuna’s warriors fought back fiercely, shooting hundreds of arrows, prashas (long spears), darts, tomaras (javelins), thunderbolts, and karpanas (swords). They roared with fury, sounding like a stormy sea filled with crocodiles and other monsters. Suka, Sarana, and the rest of Ravana’s generals, angered and eager to prove their strength, began slaughtering Arjuna’s soldiers.

Terrified, some of the survivors ran to Arjuna and told him what was happening. Hearing the news, Arjuna reassured his wives, “Don’t be afraid,” and rose from the water like a mighty elephant. His eyes, burning with rage, made him look like a raging fire. Grabbing his golden club, he charged after the Rakshasas, moving as swiftly as Garuda, the great bird.

Arjuna held his massive club high and hurled it forward with all his strength. Suddenly, one of Ravana’s ministers, equally furious, blocked his path, armed with a mace and standing as immovable as the Vindhya mountains before the sun. Roaring like the god Yama, he threw his iron mace, its tip glowing like asoka flowers in bloom. But Arjuna didn’t flinch—instead, he deflected the mace with his club.

Then, lifting his huge club—five hundred hands long—Arjuna went after Prahasta. In a flash, Arjuna struck Prahasta down with a blow so powerful that the Rakshasa fell to the ground like a mountain peak struck by Indra’s thunderbolt. Seeing Prahasta fall, Maricha, Suka, Sarana, Mahodara, and Dhrumakshya fled the battlefield.

With all his commanders gone and Prahasta dead, Ravana rushed at Arjuna himself. The two mighty kings—thousand-armed Arjuna and twenty-armed Ravana—clashed in a fight so intense it would send shivers down anyone’s spine. Each grabbed a club, and they battled with the sound of thunder, like two raging bulls fighting for a mate, two colliding oceans, two moving mountains, two blazing suns, two wildfires, two proud elephants, or like Rudra and Kala themselves.

Just as mountains withstand countless strikes of lightning, they exchanged blow after blow. The crash of their clubs echoed in all directions like thunder. When Arjuna’s club smashed into Ravana’s chest, the sky flashed golden, as if lit by lightning. When Ravana’s club struck Arjuna, it blazed like a burning log. Neither one showed any sign of tiring, and their duel was as fierce as the legendary battle between Bala and Indra.

Back and forth, Arjuna and Ravana battered each other, like two bulls locking horns or two elephants clashing tusks. Finally, Arjuna, furious, struck Ravana’s chest with all his strength. But Ravana was protected by a divine boon, so the club shattered in two as if thrown by someone weak. Still, Ravana was wounded by Arjuna’s blows and, tears streaming from his eyes, he staggered back about four feet and sat down.

Seeing Ravana overwhelmed, Arjuna leapt forward and grabbed him, just as Garuda seizes a serpent or Vishnu bound the demon Bali. With Ravana bound, the Siddhas, Charanas, and gods shouted, “Well done! Well done!” and showered Arjuna with flowers. The king roared in triumph, like a tiger celebrating after catching its prey.

After coming to his senses, Prahasta saw Ravana captured and attacked Arjuna in fury. The Rakshasa army surged like a stormy ocean. They shouted, “Let him go! Let him go! Wait! Wait!” and hurled hundreds of maces and darts at Arjuna. But the king, unmoved, withstood all their attacks. Using his own powerful weapons, Arjuna fought back, scattering the Rakshasas like the wind blows away clouds.

Having terrified the night-dwelling demons, Arjuna, surrounded by his men, returned to his city with Ravana bound, just like Indra carrying the captive Bali. As he entered the city, Brahmins and townspeople showered him with flowers and fried rice, celebrating his victory.
SECTION XXXVIII

Pulastya heard from the gods that Rāvana had been captured—a feat as unbelievable as trying to catch the wind. Moved by love for his son, the powerful and radiant sage immediately set out to see the king of Mahishmati. Traveling through the sky with incredible speed—almost as fast as thought—Pulastya arrived at the city. He entered Mahishmati just as Brahmā might enter Indra's city of Amaravati; the place was vibrant, beautiful, and full of happy, well-fed people. When the guards saw the fearsome sage approaching—glowing like the sun itself—they hurried to inform King Arjuna. Realizing from their words that Pulastya was on his way, Arjuna, king of the Haihayas, put his hands together in respect and went out to greet him. The royal priests led the way, carrying gifts like Maduparka (a ceremonial offering) and water for washing Pulastya’s feet, just as Vrihaspati would lead the way for Indra. As soon as Pulastya—shining like the sunrise—arrived, King Arjuna bowed deeply, showing respect like Indra himself greeting Mahadeva. Arjuna then offered the sage the traditional gifts—Maduparka, a cow, and water for washing his feet. Overwhelmed with joy, Arjuna spoke, his voice trembling: "Honored Sir, your visit is incredibly rare. With your arrival, my city Mahishmati feels as blessed as Amaravati itself. Today is my luckiest day; my religious practices and my birth feel truly worthwhile, and my prayers have been answered because I can bow to your feet, which even the gods have honored. My kingdom, my family—everything I have—is yours. Please tell me what you wish." After asking Arjuna about his religious duties, his offerings, and his family's well-being, Pulastya spoke: "O great king, with eyes like lotus petals and a face as bright as the full moon! You have defeated Rāvana; your strength is unmatched in all three worlds. You managed to bind my son, who is so powerful that even the wind and ocean fear him. He happily released the king of the Rakshasas, honored him with divine ornaments and garlands, and made peace with Rāvana in a ceremony before the sacred fire. Then Arjuna bowed to Pulastya and returned to his own house. Freed thanks to Pulastya, the mighty Rāvana accepted Arjuna’s hospitality and, after being embraced by him, went home—embarrassed by his defeat. Once Daśagriva (another name for Rāvana) was released, Pulastya—the son of Brahma and greatest of sages—returned to the heavens. So, Rāma, this is how the powerful Rāvana was beaten by Arjuna and then freed by Pulastya. Remember, descendant of Raghu, that there is always someone stronger than the strongest; for your own good, never underestimate others. After making peace with the thousand-armed Arjuna, Rāvana—the king of the Rakshasas—once again roamed the world, causing trouble for kings everywhere.
Just as it’s impossible to trap the wind, it should have been impossible to capture Rāvana and lead him away as a prisoner.
SECTION XXXIX

After being released by Arjuna, Rāvana, king of the Rākshasas (demons), wandered the earth once again, completely unashamed. Whenever Rāvana heard about a powerful Rākshasa or human, he would go to them and challenge them to a fight. Eventually, he arrived at the city of Kishkindhā, which had been built by Vāli, and challenged Vāli—who wore a golden garland—to battle. But Tāra, her father Sushena, and Prince Sugriva told the demon king, "O lord of the Rākshasas, there’s no one here who can stand up to you. What other monkey could possibly face you? But Rāvana, Vāli will be back soon after finishing his Sandhyā rituals at the meeting point of the four oceans. Wait here just a while. Take a look, O Daçānana (Ten-headed One), at the bones scattered here—those are the remains of all who came before to challenge the mighty monkey king. Rāvana, even if you’ve drunk amrita (nectar of immortality), your life will end the moment you face Vāli. O Vaisravana (Rāvana), look around and enjoy the world now—after a moment, you won’t have any life left to enjoy. If you really want to die, just go down to the southern ocean, and there you’ll find Vāli, blazing like wildfire on earth." Hearing this, Rāvana, who had conquered the three worlds, argued with Tāra. Then he got back into his magical Pushpaka chariot and flew to the southern ocean, where he spotted Vāli, whose face glowed red like the rising sun, deep in meditation for his Sandhyā rites.

Rāvana quietly got out of his Pushpaka chariot and sneaked up on Vāli, hoping to catch him off guard. But Vāli, even though he noticed Rāvana’s intentions, stayed calm. He didn’t worry at all, just like a lion doesn’t care about a hare, or Garuda isn’t bothered by a snake. Vāli thought to himself, "This evil-hearted Rāvana is trying to catch me. Instead, I’ll grab him under my arm and fly over the three great oceans. Everyone will see Rāvana, my enemy, stuck under my arm like a snake caught by Garuda, his clothes and limbs flailing." The jewels that were gathered for me—I now give them to my two daughters.” After Janaka, the wise king, left, Rāma turned to his uncle, Kaikeya (Yudhājit), and said humbly, “This kingdom, myself, Bharata, and Lakshmana—we are all at your service. The old king must have missed you during your long absence. It would be good for you to return home now. Lakshmana will go with you, bringing gifts and treasures.” Yudhājit agreed, saying, “Rāghava, may you always have endless wealth and prosperity.” Rāma then bowed and circled him out of respect, and Yudhājit, with Lakshmana, left for his kingdom—like Indra returning home with Vishnu after the defeat of the demon Vitra. After saying goodbye to his uncle, Rāma embraced his friend Pratardana, the brave king of Kashi, and said, “You’ve shown your friendship by helping with my coronation alongside Bharata. Now, please return to your beautiful and well-defended city, Baranushi.” With that, Rāma stood and warmly embraced him. Pratardana, after taking leave of Rāma and bringing joy to Kausalya, left fearlessly for his city with his entourage. Next, Rāma, smiling and speaking kindly, addressed the three hundred assembled kings: “You have all shown incredible loyalty and strength in protecting your kingdoms and in supporting me. Through your virtue, honesty, wisdom, and power, the evil Rāvana was defeated. I was simply the instrument—he fell because of your strength. When Bharata heard that Sītā, Janaka’s daughter, had been kidnapped, he brought you here—but thankfully, you didn’t have to suffer. You were ready and willing to help, and you’ve been here a long time. Now, I think it’s best for you to return to your homes.” The kings, very pleased, replied:

“Rāma, we are so glad that you have been victorious and crowned king, and that Sītā has been safely returned while your enemy Daçānana has been defeated. Seeing you happy and free from enemies is our greatest reward. The praise you give us just shows your true nature—you always make others feel valued. You deserve every honor, but we hardly know how to express our admiration for you. With your permission, we’ll return to our own kingdoms, but you will always remain in our hearts. May your affection for us last forever, so that we will always have a place in your thoughts.” Rāma replied, “So be it.” With that, the delighted kings said farewell to Rāma with folded hands, received his blessings, and headed home to their own lands.
SECTION XLIX

After shaking the earth with their huge armies of elephants and horses, the kings headed back to their own lands. Many Akshauhini divisions with their horses remained in Ayodhya, ready to support Rama, as Bharata had ordered. The kings—proud and strong—talked among themselves: “We never even got to face Ravana, Rama’s enemy. Bharata called us here after Ravana was already defeated. If they’d summoned us sooner, we could have taken him down ourselves. Imagine fighting on the other side of the ocean, protected by Rama and Lakshmana’s strength—we would have fought as we pleased, without a care.” Pleased with these thoughts, the princes returned to their kingdoms, chatting about this and other things. When they reached their famous cities, unharmed and welcomed by joyful people, surrounded by wealth, crops, and jewels, they sent Rama gifts of precious gems to honor him. On top of that, they sent him countless horses, chariots, fierce elephants, sandalwood, fine jewelry, pearls, coral, beautiful female attendants, and all kinds of vehicles. Bharata, Lakshmana, and Satrughna gathered up these treasures and brought them back to Ayodhya. Once home in the beautiful city, the three brothers presented the jewels and gifts to Rama. Rama accepted them happily, but then shared them with Sugriva, Vibhishana, and the other Rakshasas and monkeys who had helped him win. The powerful monkeys and night-dwellers proudly wore the jewels Rama gave them on their heads and arms. Then Rama sat Angada and Hanuman in his lap—both strong and loyal—and spoke to Sugriva.

“Angada is your good son, and Hanuman is your wise advisor,” Rama said to Sugriva. “Both of them have always looked out for me and given me good advice. Because of you, King of the Monkeys, I want to honor them in every way I can.” With that, Rama took off his own valuable ornaments and put them on Angada and Hanuman. Then he welcomed the leading monkeys—Neela, Kesarin, Kumuda, Gandhamadana, Sushena, Panasa, Mainda, Dwivida, Jambavan, Gabaksha, Dhumra, Baleemukha, Prajaghna, Saunada, Dareemukha, Dadbimuka, Indrajanu, and the rest—greeting each with kindness and affection. He told them warmly, “You’re all my true friends—like my own brothers and limbs. You forest dwellers saved me from disaster. Sugriva is truly blessed to have friends like you.” Rama then gave out fine clothes and ornaments to them all and hugged each one. The monkeys enjoyed their days feasting on sweet honey, perfectly cooked meat, and all kinds of fruits and roots. They spent more than a month this way, but because of their devotion to Rama, it felt like only a moment. Rama, too, enjoyed spending time with the shape-shifting monkeys, the powerful Rakshasas, and the mighty bears. That’s how the joyful monkeys and Rakshasas spent the second month of winter, living happily in Ayodhya, always working for Rama’s happiness.
SECTION XLX

While in Ayodhya, the monkeys, bears, and Rakshasas spent their days together. Then, Rama, shining with energy and a descendant of Raghu, spoke to Sugriva: “My friend, go back to your city, Kishkindha, which even gods and demons find hard to reach. Rule there peacefully, surrounded by your advisors. Always look out for Angada—care for him like family. And Sugriva, protect Hanuman, Nala, your father-in-law Sushena, the powerful Tara, the unstoppable Kumada, Neela, the brave Satabali, Mainda, Dwivida, Gaya, Gavaksha, Gavaya, Sarava, the mighty bear king Jamvaban, Gandhamadana, the brave Rishava, Supatala, Keshan, Sarabha, Sumbha, and all the other heroic monkeys who risked everything for me. Never do anything that would upset them.” After saying this and hugging Sugriva again and again, Rama turned to Bibhishana and spoke kindly. “I know you understand dharma. The people of Lanka, your advisors, and your brother Kuvera all love you. Go now and rule Lanka with justice, O king. Never give in to anything evil. Good kings always prosper. My only wish is that you remember me and Sugriva with love. Go now, and don’t be sad.” Hearing Rama’s words, the bears, monkeys, and Rakshasas all shouted praises for Rama, saying, “Rama, your wisdom is like Brahma’s, your strength is incredible, and your beauty is unmatched!” 

After everyone finished speaking, Hanuman bowed and said to Rama, “May I always love and respect you, O king. May my devotion never waver, and may I never care for anything else more than you. May my life last as long as your stories are told on earth. Let nothing change that. O greatest of men, descendant of Raghu, may the Apsaras always let me hear tales about you. Just like the wind scatters clouds, listening to your stories will clear away my worries.” 

After Hanuman finished, Rama stood up from his throne and embraced him warmly, saying, “Bravest of monkeys, everything you’ve wished for will come true. As long as my story is told on earth, your fame and your life will endure. My story will be told as long as the world exists. I could never repay even one of the many things you’ve done for me, Hanuman—not even if I gave my own life. I’ll always be in your debt, especially for your last great help. But perhaps, just as people help each other in times of danger, the debt can wear away over time.” 

Then Rama took off a sapphire necklace, shining like moonlight, and placed it around Hanuman’s neck. With the necklace on his chest, Hanuman looked as magnificent as the golden Sumeru mountain lit by the rising moon. Hearing everything Rama had said, the powerful monkeys came forward one by one, bowed to Rama, touched his feet, and left. Sugriva and noble Bibhishana hugged Rama, and the three of them were so overcome with emotion that they wept. The other monkeys and Rakshasas were also moved to tears as they said goodbye to Rama. Having received Rama’s kindness, the monkeys returned to their homes, like souls leaving their bodies. Then the Rakshasas, bears, and monkeys—eyes full of tears at their separation from Rama, the pride of the Raghu family—bowed to him and went back to their own lands.
SECTION LI

After saying goodbye to the bears, monkeys, and Rakshasas, Rama—known for his long arms—started living happily with his brothers. Then, suddenly, they heard a sweet voice from above: "Gentle Rama, look at me with happiness. I am Pushpaka, the flying chariot from Kuvera’s home. At your command, I once went to serve Kuvera. But he told me, 'Rama, the great hero who defeated the unstoppable Ravana in battle, has now conquered you, Pushpaka. I am truly pleased that Ravana and his evil family and friends have been destroyed. Rama defeated you in Lanka; I now allow you to serve him. You are the perfect vehicle for traveling anywhere. My wish is for you to carry Rama, the descendant of Raghu. So, go to him, and do your duty.' After hearing Kuvera’s command, I have come to you, Rama. Please accept me without fear. I am above being conquered by anyone in the world. On Kuvera’s order, I will bravely travel anywhere you ask." 

Hearing Pushpaka’s words, Rama—powerful as ever—spoke to the returning chariot floating in the sky: "Pushpaka, if this is the case, come here. Since the lord of wealth, Kuvera, has ordered it, I can’t be blamed for accepting you." Rama then honored the chariot with dried rice, sweet-smelling flowers, and incense. He said, "Pushpaka, go for now, and return whenever I call you. Don’t feel sad when we’re apart, and don’t let anything get in your way as you travel the world." 

After Rama’s worship, Pushpaka said, "So be it," and disappeared in the direction it wished to go. With the sacred chariot gone, Bharata folded his hands and said to Rama, the pride of the Raghu family: "Brother, while you’ve ruled, we’ve seen many amazing things—animals and objects talking like humans. Since your coronation, no one has gotten sick, not even once. Even the oldest animals haven’t died. Every woman gives birth safely, and everyone is healthy and happy. People in the city are more joyful than ever, Rama. Indra sends us gentle, life-giving rain at the perfect times. The wind is always pleasant. People everywhere say, ‘May we always have a king like Rama!’" 

Hearing Bharata’s kind words, Rama—the greatest of kings—felt truly happy.
SECTION LII

After sending away the golden Pushpaka chariot, Rama, strong and full of energy, entered the Asoka forest. This forest was alive with sandalwood, aguru, mango, dark sandal, and devadaru trees. All around were champaka, aguru, naga, kesara, madhuka, panasa, sarja, parijata trees—each glowing like a smokeless fire—along with sodhra, neepa, arjuna, naga, saptaparna, muktaka, mandara, kadalee, and a tangle of vines. The place was rich with priyanga, kadamba, vakula, jambu, pomegranate, and banana trees, all bursting with flowers and fruit. The air was thick with sweet scents, fresh leaves, and the colors of countless other trees. Some trees were golden, others burned as bright as fire, and some glowed like red eye paint. Bees, drunk on nectar, swarmed the thick flowers, making the whole place hum as if it had been designed by master builders. Cuckoos sang from the mango trees, and flocks of birds flashed every color. Ponds with clear water dotted the land. Their banks were lined with coral steps, crystal floors, and were filled with lotuses and lilies. Chakrabaka birds glided across the water, while the banks bloomed with even more vibrant trees and flowers. Stone walls protected the forest, and inside, rare Sārdula birds, shining like gems, made their homes. Flowers covered every tree and even blanketed the rocks, making them look like the night sky scattered with stars. Rama’s Asoka forest was as beautiful as Indra’s Nandana garden or Kuvera’s Chitraratha, both said to be crafted by Brahma himself. Inside this lush paradise, filled with places to sit, rest, and wander, Rama found a comfortable seat covered with a stunning cloth. Like the god Purandara with his wife Sachi, Rama took Sita’s hand, helped her sit beside him, and together they drank wine from the region of Mira. Servants quickly brought well-cooked meat and platters of fresh fruit. As they relaxed, lovely apsaras—celestial dancers—skilled in music and dance, performed before Rama, joined by the Kinnaris. Rama, always generous and thoughtful, made sure the beautiful women, adorned in shining jewelry, felt welcomed and happy. With Sita beside him, Rama shone like the sage Vasishtha sitting with his wife Arundhati. Every day, Rama, filled with joy, made Sita—who was as beautiful as a goddess—feel loved and cherished. Together, Rama and Sita spent their days in happiness, and the winter passed with every pleasure imaginable. Enjoying everything the world had to offer, Rama and Sita lived this way for ten thousand years.

One day, after performing all the morning rituals, Rama decided to spend the evening in his private quarters. Sita, after finishing her own prayers, first went to attend to her mothers-in-law. Then, dressed in vibrant clothes and sparkling with jewelry, Sita came to Rama, looking like Sachi meeting the king of the gods in heaven. Rama noticed the first signs of pregnancy in Sita and was overcome with happiness. He said to her, “Vaidehi, I can see you’re pregnant. Is there anything you want or desire? Tell me, and I’ll make it happen.” Sita smiled shyly and replied, “Raghava, I want to visit the holy hermitages. I wish to greet the great rishis who live simply on fruit and roots along the banks of the Ganges. More than anything, I want to spend just one night in their hermitage.” Rama, always eager to please, answered, “Of course. Believe me, Vaidehi, you’ll go there tomorrow.” After promising Sita this wish, Rama, the descendant of Kakutstha, left the inner rooms and went to the central hall, where his friends were gathered.
SECTION LIII

After Rāma sat down, his trusted advisors gathered around him and started sharing funny and entertaining stories. Bijoya, Madhumatta, Kasyapa, Mangala, Kula, Surajni, Kalya, Vadra Dantavakta, and Sumagadha all tried to amuse Rāma with lighthearted conversations. In the middle of this, Rāma turned to them and said, “Hey Vadra, what are people in the city and countryside saying about Sita, Bharata, Lakshmana, Shatrughna, and mother Kaikeyi? You know how kings get criticized when they act unfairly—not just in people’s homes, but even out in the forests.” After Rāma spoke, Vadra, with his hands folded respectfully, replied, “My lord, the people say many good things about you; they talk a lot about your victory over the Ten-necked demon.” 

Hearing Vadra’s words, Rāma said, “Don’t hold anything back. Tell me everything you’ve heard, both good and bad, from the beginning. I want to hear people’s honest opinions so I can avoid doing wrong and focus on doing what’s right. If people are criticizing me for anything, whether in the city or the provinces, I want you to tell me about it openly, without fear.”

Hearing Rāma’s gentle request, Vadra, calm and with his hands still folded, answered, “Listen, my lord. I’ll tell you all the unpleasant things people discuss in their courtyards, markets, streets, woods, and gardens. People say that what you accomplished was incredible—no one, not even the gods or demons, ever built a bridge across the ocean. You defeated the unstoppable Rāvana, brought monkeys, bears, and Rakshasas to your side, and rescued Sita. But people also say that even though Rāvana forced Sita onto his lap, you didn’t seem angry about it and brought her back to your city. They wonder how you can really be happy with her after everything she went through with Rāvana. Sita was held captive by Rākshasis in the Asoka forest, under Rāvana’s power, and still, you don’t seem to hold it against her. Now, people say, should we also accept whatever our wives do, just because our king does? People tend to follow their king’s example, after all. So, in the cities and provinces, people are talking about all of this.”

When Rāma heard Vadra’s words, he felt deeply troubled and asked his friends, “Is this really what people are saying about me?” The advisors lowered their heads, paid their respects, and replied to Rāma, whose spirits were low, “Yes, this is what people are saying.” After hearing all this, Rāma, who defeated his enemies, dismissed his friends.
SECTION LIV

After sending away his other friends and making up his mind, Rama (the pride of the Raghu dynasty) called over the guard sitting nearby. He said, “Go quickly and bring Lakshmana, son of Sumitra, who’s marked by good fortune, as well as Bharata and the unstoppable Shatrughna.” The guard listened, bowed with his hands pressed together, and hurried to Lakshmana’s house, walking in without delay. Bowing, he told the noble Lakshmana, “The king wants to see you—please come right away.” Lakshmana, understanding Rama’s order, replied, “All right,” got into his chariot, and rushed to Rama’s home. Once Lakshmana had left, the guard respectfully went to Bharata and bowed, saying, “The king wishes to see you.” As soon as Bharata heard that Rama wanted him, he immediately stood up and walked out, not waiting for a ride. Watching Bharata go, the guard hurried to Shatrughna and, after respectfully greeting him, said, “Come, great prince—the king wants to see you.” Shatrughna nodded, bowed his head, and quickly headed for Rama. After that, the guard went back to Rama, folding his hands, and told him that his brothers had arrived. Meanwhile, Rama sat in deep, troubled thought, his head bowed low. As soon as he heard his brothers were there, he gave the guard another order.

“Bring my brothers in right away. My life depends on them—they mean everything to me.” Following Rama’s instructions, the three brothers, dressed in white, entered quietly, hands folded in respect and minds calm. As they entered, they noticed that Rama’s face had lost its glow—it looked pale and sad, like the moon during an eclipse, the sun at sunset, or a wilted lotus. His eyes brimmed with tears. The brothers hurried to him, bowed at his feet, and sat down anxiously. Rama wiped his tears away, hugged them tightly, helped them up, and urged them to sit beside him. He told them, “You are my world, my very life. I’m only ruling this kingdom because of you. You are all wise, good, and intelligent. Please, follow the duties I lay out for you.” After Rama, the descendant of Kakutstha, said this, the three brothers sat in silence, waiting anxiously and attentively for his next instructions.
SECTION LV

The princes sat together, hearts heavy with worry, when Rāma, his face drawn and tired, spoke to them. “Listen to me, and please don’t go against my wishes. I want you to hear what the people of the city—and even those from the countryside—have been saying about me and Sitā. They’re talking badly about us; their words have cut me deeply. I was born into the great family of the Ikshwākus, and Sitā comes from the noble line of King Janaka. Lakshmana, you know how, in the lonely forests of Dandaka, Rāvana kidnapped Sitā, and how I fought and killed him to rescue her. Even then, I worried about bringing her back, since she had lived in the home of the Rākshasas. To prove herself, Sitā entered the fire in front of you all. At that moment, the fire god Agni and the wind carried word to the heavens, declaring Sitā’s innocence. In front of all the sages and gods, even the Sun and Moon spoke up to confirm that Janaka’s daughter was pure. Indra, king of the gods, placed chaste Sitā back into my hands on the island of Lanka. I have always believed in Sitā’s purity. That’s why I brought her back to Ayodhyā with me. But now, the harsh words of the people have wounded me deeply. If someone is infamous, that reputation sticks with them and they are treated with contempt. Even the gods look down on those with a bad name, while everyone wants to be respected. That’s why great people work so hard to earn a good reputation. Honestly, I would give up even my own life—or you, my brothers—if it meant avoiding disgrace. See now what a deep pit of sorrow and shame I’ve fallen into. I’ve never felt grief like this before. So, Lakshmana, tomorrow morning, take Sumantra’s chariot and bring Sitā away to another land. There’s a beautiful hermitage belonging to the wise sage Vālmiki, on the banks of the Tamasā River, across from the Ganges. Go there, and after leaving Sitā in that peaceful place, come back quickly. Please do exactly as I say. Don’t tell Sitā why she’s being sent away, Saumitri; if you try to talk me out of this, it will only make things worse for me. For the sake of my life and my rule, don’t try to change my mind—you would only hurt me, and I’d have to see you as my enemies. If you want to honor me, follow my orders now. Take Sitā away from here. She once mentioned wanting to visit the hermitages of the sages along the Ganges—let that wish be granted now.” As he spoke, tears filled Rāma’s eyes. He sighed heavily, like an elephant in pain, and, heartbroken, left for his own quarters with his brothers.
SECTION LVI

When the night ended, Lakshmana (also called Saumitri) woke feeling heavy-hearted and his face looked tired. He spoke to Sumantra, the royal charioteer: “Sumantra, please quickly hitch the fastest horses to a fine chariot. Make sure there’s a comfortable seat for Sita. The King has ordered that I take Sita to the hermitage where the sages live and practice their rituals. Bring the chariot right away.” Sumantra obeyed and soon arrived with a beautiful, sacred chariot pulled by excellent horses and fitted with plush seats. He said to Lakshmana, “My lord, the chariot is ready. Please do as you wish.” After hearing this, Lakshmana went to Sita’s quarters and told her, “Queen Sita, you had asked the King to let you see the hermitage, and he promised you could go. Now he’s ordered me to take you there. Please come with me—by the King’s command, I will escort you to the forest where the sages live.” Lakshmana’s words filled Sita (also called Janaki) with excitement and eagerness to leave. She gathered jewels and expensive clothes and said to Lakshmana before departing, “I want to give these ornaments, fine clothes, and treasures to the women ascetics.” Lakshmana replied, “Of course, we’ll do that,” then helped Sita into the chariot. Remembering Rama’s instructions, he set off, the chariot racing forward.

As they traveled, Sita spoke to Lakshmana, who always brought prosperity to his family: “Descendant of Raghu, I’m seeing bad omens. My right eye and my whole body are twitching. My mind feels troubled and anxious, and I can’t calm down. Everything feels empty and joyless. Lakshmana, is your brother Rama in trouble? Are my mothers-in-law and all the people in the city okay?” With these words, Sita folded her hands and prayed to the gods. Lakshmana, hearing her, bowed low and touched the ground with his forehead to show respect, and though he was deeply upset, he forced a cheerful voice and replied, “Everything’s fine.”

They reached the hermitage on the banks of the river Gomati and spent the night there. When dawn arrived, Lakshmana got up and told the charioteer to get the chariot ready, saying, “Like Lord Shiva, we’ll carry the waters of the Bhagirathi on our heads.” Sumantra quickly harnessed the horses, who ran as fast as thought, and told Sita, “Please get in the chariot.” Sita, with Lakshmana, entered the fine vehicle. In no time, Sita—whose eyes were large and bright—arrived at the banks of the Ganges, the holy river that washes away all sins. They reached the waters of the Bhagirathi before noon, and as Lakshmana saw the river, he suddenly cried out in distress. 

Seeing him so upset, Sita—who understood the ways of righteousness—grew worried and asked, “Why are you crying, Lakshmana? I’ve finally made it to the banks of the Ganges, a place I’ve longed to visit. This should be a moment of happiness, not sorrow. You spend every day and night with Rama, and you’ve only been apart for two days—are you sad about that? Rama is even dearer to me than my own life, but I’m not overwhelmed with sadness. Please don’t let grief take over. Bring me across the Ganges so I can meet the ascetics and give them these clothes and ornaments. After we pay our respects and spend a night with them, we’ll go back to the city. I’m eager to see Rama again, with his lotus-like eyes, broad chest, and lion-like strength.” 

Hearing Sita’s gentle words, Lakshmana wiped his tears and called for the boatmen. They arrived quickly and said, “The boat is ready.” Lakshmana, calm again, led Sita into the boat, and together they crossed the sacred river Ganges.
SECTION LVII

First, Lakshmana led Sita to a large, well-decorated boat manned by fishermen. He climbed aboard with her. Then he told Sumantra to stay behind with the chariot, and, overcome with grief, he ordered the boatmen to set off. After crossing the Bhagirathi river, Lakshmana, speaking softly and with his hands pressed together, said to Sita, "O daughter of the king of Videha, this hurts me deeply—like a spear to my heart. My brother has made me the instrument of this action, and now I’ll be blamed by everyone. Death and its pain would be better than doing what I’m about to do. Please, don’t be angry with me, and don’t hold me responsible for this, beautiful lady." Saying this, humble Lakshmana began to cry and wished for death. Seeing him so overwhelmed, Sita asked, "Lakshmana, what’s wrong? I don’t understand any of this. Please tell me the truth, plainly. You look completely distraught—is everything all right in the kingdom? I beg you, in the name of the king, tell me why you are so sad." After Sita spoke, Lakshmana, with a heavy heart and a quiet voice, replied, "My honored queen, I’ve kept in my heart the words the king spoke before he went into his palace, upset after hearing in the court the rumors and accusations about you, daughter of King Janaka. Those words are too painful to repeat, so I won’t. I’ll just say this: afraid of what the people are saying, he has abandoned you, even though I’ve seen your innocence proven. Don’t blame yourself for this. Rama has ordered me to leave you near the hermitage, pretending it’s to fulfill your wish, since you’re pregnant. Please don’t grieve any more. There is a sacred hermitage of saints on the banks of the Jahnavi (Ganga) river. Valmiki, the greatest of sages and a close friend of our father Dasaratha, lives there. O daughter of Janaka, go to that noble sage and live peacefully, keeping Rama always in your heart. Please the gods, pure lady—doing so will bring you blessings."
SECTION LVIII

When Lakshmana’s harsh words hit her, Sita, the daughter of Janaka, was so heartbroken that she collapsed onto the ground. She lay there unconscious for a while, then, with tears streaming down her face, she spoke to Lakshmana: “Truly, Lakshmana, fate must have created me just to suffer. All my pain is out in the open today. I must have done something terrible in a past life—maybe I broke up a husband and wife—because now Rama is abandoning me, even though I am innocent and faithful. Before, living in the forest felt almost pleasant because I could serve Rama. But now, how am I supposed to survive in the hermitage, cut off from everyone I love? Who can I turn to with my pain? What will I say to the sages when they ask, ‘Why did Rama, the noble one, abandon you? What did you do wrong?’ Lakshmana, should I just end my life in the river Ganga (Jāhnavi)? But I stop myself, because that would mean ending Rama’s family line. Please, Lakshmana, do what you have been told. By leaving me behind, you’ll fulfill the king’s command. But listen to me. Bow to my mothers-in-law for me, and ask how the kingdom is doing. Then, when you see the righteous King Rama, tell him from me: ‘You know that Sita is pure, devoted to you, and always wishes you well. She understands you’ve sent her away because you fear gossip and blame. Her duty is to protect your reputation, because you are her greatest refuge.’ Also, tell Rama to treat his people like his own brothers, and to gain virtue by protecting them, because that’s what makes a ruler truly great. Say that I don’t care about my own suffering—what hurts me most is that the people have slandered me. A husband is a woman’s god, her friend, her guide. So it’s right for me to do whatever I can for Rama’s sake, even if it costs me my life. Tell Rama this, Lakshmana, in short. Now go—my pregnancy is starting to show.” After Sita finished speaking, Lakshmana, his mind spinning, bowed and touched his head to the ground before her. He was too choked up to speak. Crying out loud, he circled her in respect, then paused for a moment and said, “Why are you saying this to me, respected lady? I’ve never even looked at any part of you except your feet. We’re alone in this forest, and Rama isn’t here—how could I look at you now?” After saying this, Lakshmana called for a boat again and got in, telling the boatmen to row. Once they reached the other side, overwhelmed with grief, Lakshmana quickly got into the chariot. As he left, he kept looking back, seeing Sita wandering helplessly on the far bank of the Ganges. Sita watched Lakshmana and the chariot until they vanished from sight, and then, crushed by sorrow and anxiety over losing Rama, she broke down in tears. Alone in the forest, surrounded by the calls of peacocks, the devoted Sita wept loudly, overcome by her pain.
SECTION LIX

Seeing Sitā crying out in distress, the young sons of the Rishis quickly went to the great sage Vālmiki, who was deep in his spiritual practice. Bowing before him, they told him about Sitā’s desperate cries. “Respected Sir,” they said, “we don’t know who this beautiful woman is—she looks like a goddess, as lovely as Lakshmi herself, and we’ve never seen her before. She’s crying out all alone by the riverbank, completely heartbroken, as if she has no one in the world to care for her. Someone like her shouldn’t be left in such a state. Honestly, she didn’t even seem like an ordinary woman to us. Please, you should go and see her for yourself. She’s near the hermitage, probably looking for your help, and she clearly needs someone to protect her, Sir. Please look after her.”

Vālmiki, thanks to his spiritual insight, understood everything. Using his deep wisdom, he realized that what the boys had said was true, so he quickly made his way toward Sitā. His students followed him as he walked. Carrying water for a welcoming ritual (Arghya), the wise Vālmiki reached the riverbank and saw Sitā, Rāghava’s wife, crying helplessly. With his calming presence, he soothed her a little, then spoke gently to her.

“Dear lady,” Vālmiki said, “you are the daughter-in-law of Daçaratha, beloved wife of Rāma, and daughter of Janaka; your arrival here is a blessing. Through my meditation and spiritual power, I know why you have come. I also know for certain that you are pure and completely innocent. In fact, I am aware of everything that happens in all three worlds. By my spiritual vision, O daughter of Janaka, I see your innocence. You have come to me for shelter, Vaidehi—please be comforted. All the sages around my hermitage are good people; they’ll treat you like their own daughter. Accept this Arghya from me, and trust that you can let go of your grief. Don’t be sad anymore; think of this as your own home now.”

Hearing these wonderful words, Sitā bowed humbly at Vālmiki’s feet and said, “Your wish will be fulfilled.” With her hands folded, she followed him.

When the wives of the Rishis saw Vālmiki and Sitā coming, they were delighted. They hurried over and said, “Welcome, honored sage! It’s been so long since you visited us. We all bow to you—please tell us what you need us to do.”

Vālmiki replied in a kind but firm voice: “This is Sitā, wife of the wise Rāma, daughter-in-law of Daçaratha, and daughter of Janaka. She has now come to our hermitage. Though she is completely innocent and pure, her husband has abandoned her. So, it’s our duty to protect her. She deserves your respect—especially since I, your teacher, request this. Please, all of you, care for her with great affection.”

After placing Sitā in the care of the women ascetics, the great sage Vālmiki, followed by his students, quickly returned to his holy hermitage.
SECTION LX

Seeing the great sage Vālmiki lead Sitā into his hermitage, Lakshmana was overwhelmed with sorrow and confusion. He turned to the skilled charioteer, Sumantra, and said, “Can you see how much pain Rāma is in after being separated from Sitā? She’s the daughter of Janaka and completely innocent. What could be worse than Rāma having to live alone, forced to abandon her? I really believe, Sumantra, that this painful separation is the work of fate—there’s no way to escape what destiny has planned. Rāma, who could destroy gods, Gandharvas, Asuras, and Rākshasas if he was angry, is now bowing to destiny. He already suffered for fourteen years in the Dandaka forest because his father told him to. But this exile of Sitā is far more cruel and heartless. The opinions of the people aren’t even fair, so what’s the point of doing something so terrible just for public approval, like sending Sitā away?” Hearing Lakshmana’s words, the wise Sumantra answered with respect, “Don’t be so upset about Sitā, Saumitri. Long ago, in front of your father, the Brahmins told the story of Sitā’s exile. They said Rāma would lose all happiness and be separated from his beloved wife; and even more, the noble Rāma—with his long arms—would, because of fate, have to let go of you, Sitā, Satrughna, and Bharata, too. When King Daçaratha asked the sage Durbasa about your futures, Durbasa replied in exactly this way. I’m telling you what I heard. Don’t tell Satrughna, Bharata, or anyone else. Durbasa told this to Daçaratha in front of me, Vasishtha, and other great men. After hearing the sage’s words, Daçaratha told me, ‘Charioteer, do not share this secret with anyone.’ It’s very important not to break the promise I made to King Daçaratha. I will always be careful to follow his orders. I really shouldn’t tell you this secret, but I see how much you want to know. Even though Daçaratha told me to keep it quiet, I’m telling you so you won’t be overwhelmed by grief—because fate can’t be avoided. That’s why you’re dealing with this sadness now. But please, don’t tell Satrughna or Bharata.” After hearing these serious words from Sumantra, Lakshmana told him to go on with the story.
SECTION LXI
After Lakshmana (younger brother of Rama) asked him to explain the secret behind Durvasa’s story, Sumantra began to reveal what he knew.

“A long time ago,” Sumantra started, “the great sage Durvasa, son of Atri, spent a year living at the sacred hermitage of Vasishtha. Around that same time, your father, the famous and powerful Dasaratha, decided to visit his wise priest, Vasishtha. When Dasaratha arrived, he saw Durvasa sitting beside Vasishtha, shining with an almost blinding light, like the sun. Dasaratha greeted both ascetics respectfully, bowing to them. The two sages welcomed Dasaratha warmly, offering him a seat, water to wash his feet, a traditional gift, and some fruits and roots to eat. So, Dasaratha stayed with the sages for a while.

At noon, the group of ascetics sat together and talked about pleasant things. During a pause, Dasaratha folded his hands and, raising his arms, addressed Durvasa, the strict and powerful son of Atri. ‘Great sage,’ he asked, ‘how long will my family line last? What about the lifespan of Rama and my other sons? How long will Rama’s descendants live, and how will my family’s story end? Please, tell me everything.’

After Dasaratha finished speaking, Durvasa, glowing with spiritual power, replied, ‘Listen closely to the ancient story, O King. Long ago, during the war between the gods and demons, the demons sought protection from the wife of Bhrigu, who was your priest. Bhrigu’s wife agreed to help them, and so the demons stayed with her without fear. When the gods saw this, Indra (also called Hari), the king of the gods, became furious and killed Bhrigu’s wife with his spinning discus. Devastated and enraged by his wife’s death, Bhrigu cursed Vishnu (another name for Hari), saying, “You lost control and killed my wife, who did not deserve to die. For this, O Janardana (Vishnu), you will be born among humans, and you will be separated from your wife for many years.” After casting this curse, Bhrigu was heartbroken. But when Vishnu prayed and honored him, Bhrigu softened, and Vishnu promised, “After killing Ravana and others, for the sake of humanity, I will accept this curse.”

O best of kings, Vishnu, long ago cursed by Bhrigu, has now been born as your son in this life, and is known as Rama. Rama will surely face the results of Bhrigu’s curse. He will rule Ayodhya for a long time, and his people will live in happiness and prosperity. After reigning for eleven thousand years, Rama will travel to Brahma’s world. No one will be able to defeat him. He will perform many horse sacrifices, giving away great gifts, and will establish several royal families. He will have two sons with Sita.’

After telling Dasaratha about the fate of his family, past and future, the brilliant sage Durvasa became silent. Once Durvasa stopped speaking, King Dasaratha respectfully bowed to both sages and returned to Ayodhya. I was present and heard everything that Durvasa said. I have remembered those words ever since. The words of great sages never fail. According to Durvasa, Rama will install Sita’s two sons as rulers in Ayodhya—nowhere else. So, Lakshmana, don’t be sad about Sita or Rama; be patient, for their sake.”

After hearing these amazing words from Sumantra, Lakshmana felt great happiness and praised him again and again. As they talked together on their way back, the sun set. That night, they camped on the banks of the Kesini River.
SECTION LXII

After spending the night on the banks of the Kesini river, the powerful warrior Lakshmana woke up early and set out again for home. By noon, he reached the city of Ayodhya, which was full of sparkling jewels and happy, well-fed citizens. But even as he arrived, Lakshmana felt a heavy sadness, worried about what he would have to tell Rama when he saw him. Lost in thought, he approached Rama’s beautiful palace, which shone like moonlight. Getting down from his chariot at the palace gate, Lakshmana—usually so confident—walked in with his head lowered, heart weighed down by guilt. He entered the palace without anyone stopping him. Inside, he saw his older brother Rama sitting on a grand seat, looking defeated, his eyes brimming with tears. The sight pained Lakshmana deeply. He bowed and touched Rama’s feet, then stood with his hands pressed together and said, "My lord, I have done as you asked. I left Janaka’s daughter, Sita, at the sacred hermitage of Valmiki, near the banks of the Ganges. After leaving that noble and pure woman at the edge of the hermitage, I have come back to serve you. Please don’t grieve, great one—this is the way of the world. People as wise as you aren’t overcome by sadness. Where there is growth, there will eventually be decay; where there is fortune, there will be loss; and where there is birth, death will come. So, getting attached to wives, children, friends, or wealth isn’t wise, because separation from them is unavoidable. You have always had control over yourself and your mind—shouldn’t you be able to handle this small pain of separation? Strong men like you are never defeated by sorrow. Raghava, people will talk and blame you again. To avoid their criticism, you let go of Maithili (Sita). If you keep grieving for her, the rumors and criticism will only get worse in the kingdom. So, please, be patient and don’t let this break you. Let go of this weakness and don’t be sad." When Lakshmana, Sumitra’s wise son, finished speaking, Rama—descendant of Kakutstha and someone who truly valued his friends—looked up with relief and replied, "You’ve spoken the truth, Lakshmana, greatest among men. I’m truly grateful for how faithfully you carried out my orders. Gentle Saumitri (Lakshmana), your comforting words have lifted my sadness and eased my grief."
SECTION LXIII

When Lakshmana finished speaking, Rama’s face lit up with happiness. He said, “Lakshmana (Saumitri), you always know the right thing to say. You’re clever and thoughtful, and a friend like you is hard to find, especially in times like these. But, my dear Saumitri, now that you know what I have in mind, please listen to what I’m asking. Gentle Lakshmana, son of Sumitra, I’ve been neglecting my royal duties for four days now, and it’s really weighing on me. So, please, call in anyone who’s come with matters for the king—men or women, priests or counselors. It’s said that a king who ignores the affairs of his kingdom ends up in a hell so dreadful that not even the wind blows there. 

I once heard a story, Lakshmana, about a great and noble king named Nriga—a man of truth and pure mind, always devoted to the Brahmanas. At the holy pilgrimage spot of Pushpaka, King Nriga once donated a crore of cows, all with calves and golden ornaments, to the Brahmanas. But by accident, he gave away a cow and calf belonging to a poor Brahmana who lived on very little. That Brahmana, desperate and hungry, wandered for a long time searching for his lost cow. Eventually, he reached Kanakhal and spotted his own cow in another Brahmana’s home. The cow was well cared for and her calf had grown up. The Brahmana called out, using her name, ‘Savala, come.’ The cow recognized his voice and followed him. He led her away, determined to get his cow back.

But the Brahmana who had been keeping the cow chased after him and said, ‘That cow is mine—King Nriga gave her to me.’ So, the two Brahmanas started arguing fiercely. Still fighting, they both went to see King Nriga, the one who had given the cow away. But even after waiting a long time at the palace gates, they weren’t allowed inside. Angry, they cursed the king: ‘Because you refused to see us, you’ll become invisible—a lizard living in a dark hole for thousands of years. When Vishnu is born as a human in the Vasudeva family of the Yadavas, he’ll finally free you from this curse. Just before the Kali Yuga begins, the sage Nara Narayana, full of power, will also come down to earth to help her.’

After placing this curse on the king, the Brahmanas fell silent. Since the cow was now old and weak, they agreed to give her to another Brahmana. But King Nriga is still suffering because of that terrible curse. Lakshmana, this is what happens when a king fails in his duty—the quarrels and confusion among his people show it. So please, quickly bring everyone who’s come with any business before me. Only a fair king can truly benefit his people. Go yourself, Lakshmana, and see who’s here to speak with me.”
SECTION LXIV

After listening to Rāma’s story, Lakshmana, who was wise and thoughtful, folded his hands and asked, “O Kākutstha (Rāma), was it really for such a small mistake that the two Brāhmanas cursed King Nriga? Their curse was as harsh as Yama’s own punishment. I’m curious—what did King Nriga say to the Brahmans when they cursed him?” Rāma replied, “Listen, Lakshmana. I’ll tell you exactly what King Nriga said after the curse. When he heard that the Brahmanas had left, the king called for his priest, his ministers, and all the citizens. He was deeply upset, and he addressed them all: ‘Listen carefully to what I have to say. The great sage Nārada and the ascetic Parvata, after placing a terrible curse on me, have already left swiftly for Brahmā’s realm. So today, you must put Prince Vasu on the throne in my place. Also, I want the architects to build a comfortable underground den for me where I can wait out this curse. Let them dig one shelter to keep me safe from the rain, another for the cold of winter, and one more for the heat of summer. I want these dens to be surrounded by beautiful trees—branches heavy with fruit and flowers. As long as fate doesn’t change, I’ll live happily in this den. Plant flowering trees for half a league around my shelter.’ 

Once these arrangements were made and Vasu was crowned king, Nriga said to him, ‘My son, always follow the path of virtue and rule the people as a true Kshatriya should. You’ve seen for yourself how the Brahmanas cursed me for such a minor mistake. Don’t waste your energy on regret for my sake. Happiness and sorrow are controlled by time, and it’s only because of fate that I’m in this situation. Everyone must face what destiny has in store for them, go where fate leads, and receive whatever is meant for them. Our past actions are behind everything, so don’t be upset, my son.’ After giving this advice, the noble King Nriga went to live in his sweet-smelling underground den. Surrounded by jewels inside his shelter, the high-minded king began to patiently endure the curse given by the two Brahmanas.”
SECTION LXV

“So that’s the story of the curse on Nriga. If you want to hear about something else, just let me know.” When Rama finished, Lakshmana said, “Honestly, I could listen to these amazing stories all day, my king. I’m not bored at all.” Hearing Lakshmana’s reply, Rama, who was a descendant of Ikshwāku, began another story about morals and fate: “There was once a very pious and powerful king named Nimi. He was the twelfth son of Ikshwāku. Nimi built a beautiful city, almost as stunning as those of the gods, near the hermitage of Gautama. The city was called Vaijayanta, and this wise royal sage made his home there.

After creating this gorgeous city, Nimi decided to honor the gods and his father by performing a massive sacrifice. He invited his father, Ikshwāku, who was Manu’s son, and began by welcoming the sage Vashishtha. Then Nimi also welcomed the other great sages: Atri, Angiras, and Bhrigu, all known for their spiritual power.

But Vashishtha told Nimi, ‘Indra has already asked me to help with his sacrifice. You’ll have to wait until I’m done there.’ After Vashishtha left, the sage Gautama took over Vashishtha’s responsibilities for the sacrifice. While Vashishtha performed Indra’s sacrifice, King Nimi gathered all the Brahmins and began his own gigantic sacrifice near the Himalayas, not far from his city. This ceremony lasted five thousand years.

When Indra’s sacrifice finished, Vashishtha—famous for his virtue—came to visit King Nimi. But he found Gautama busy in his place and got extremely angry. He waited a while to see the king. That day, Nimi was deeply asleep. Not finding the king, the great sage Vashishtha grew furious and said, ‘Since you, O King, chose someone else over me and ignored me, your body will become senseless.’

When Nimi woke up and heard about Vashishtha’s curse, he was stunned and furious. ‘I was asleep and didn’t even know you were here, yet in your anger you cursed me as if you were Yama himself! Well, in return, your own body will lose its senses for a long time,’ Nimi said.
Overcome by anger, both the king and the sage cursed each other, and instantly, both lost their bodies.”
SECTION LXVI

After listening to Rama’s explanation, Lakshmana (sometimes called Lakshman), who was always ready to fight evil, spoke respectfully with his hands together. “How did that Brahmin, so respected by the gods, and the king, get their bodies back after they had died?” he asked. In response, Rama, the great descendant of the Ikshwaku dynasty and leader among men, answered: “After giving up their bodies, both Nimi and the virtuous Vasishtha—who valued spiritual power above all—were transformed into air. When Vasishtha, now bodiless and full of spiritual energy, found himself in this state, he went to Brahma, the Creator, hoping to get a new body.

Vasishtha, now merged with the air, bowed to Brahma—his father—and spoke, ‘O mighty lord of the gods, O you who were born from the lotus! Because of Nimi’s curse, I have lost my body and become just air. Being without a body is extremely painful and makes it impossible for me to do anything. Please, out of your kindness, grant me a new body.’

Brahma, powerful and self-born, replied, ‘Great sage, enter the vital energies of Mitra and Varuna. Still, you will not be born from a woman. Because of your deep spirituality, you will become a patriarch among sages.’ After hearing this, Vasishtha bowed, circled Brahma in respect, and traveled to Varuna’s realm.

At that time, Mitra and Varuna were ruling together over Varuna’s kingdom, honored by all the gods. Just then, the famous apsara (celestial nymph) Urvasi arrived, surrounded by her friends. When Varuna saw the playful and stunning Urvasi, he was overwhelmed with desire and wanted to be with her. But Urvasi, bowing respectfully, said, ‘Lord of the gods, Mitra has already invited me for the same reason.’
