Still longing for her, Varuna told Urvasi, ‘If you will not be with me, I will release my vital energy into this pot.’ Hearing these gentle words, Urvasi smiled and replied, ‘Do as you said. Right now, my body belongs to Mitra, but my heart is drawn to you, and you feel the same for me.’ With that, Varuna released his energy into the pot.

Afterward, Urvasi went to Mitra, but he was furious. He said, ‘I asked you first! Why did you ignore me and go to another? For this betrayal, I curse you: you will spend time among mortals on earth. Go to King Pururava of Kasi, the son of Budha. He will be your husband.’ Because of this curse, Urvasi was sent to Pururava.

Pururava, son of Budha, ruled the grand city of Pratishthana. With Urvasi, he had a strong and handsome son named Ayu. Ayu’s son was Nahusha, who was as powerful as Indra. When Indra, king of the gods, was struck by the demon Vritra’s thunderbolt, Nahusha took over as king of heaven for one hundred thousand years.

In this way, Urvasi—famous for her beautiful teeth, eyes, and eyebrows—lived on earth for many years. Once her time under the curse ended, she returned to Indra’s heavenly realm.”
SECTION LXVII

Hearing this amazing and almost otherworldly story, Lakshmana was deeply impressed. He turned to Rama and asked, “Hey Kākutstha (Rama), how did that twice-born sage, who was honored by both the gods and King Nimi, get his body back after becoming bodiless?” Rama, always truthful and wise, began to tell Lakshmana the story of Vasishtha. “Listen, greatest of the Raghu lineage. Two of the most respected Brahmin sages were born from the spiritual energy of the powerful Mitra and Varuna. They placed this energy into a pot. First, the famous sage Agastya emerged from the pot and, saying ‘I am not your son,’ left Mitra behind. Before Varuna put his energy into the pot, Mitra had already released his own, inspired by Urvasi. That led to Agastya’s birth. After that, Varuna also placed his energy into the same pot, mixing both their energies together. Sometime later, from the combined energy of Mitra and Varuna, the radiant Vasishtha was born—he would become the priest of the Ikshwāku dynasty. As soon as Vasishtha was born, Ikshwāku, who was himself full of light and wisdom, chose this faultless sage as our family’s priest. That’s how Vasishtha came into the world with such a unique origin. Now, listen to what happened to King Nimi.

When King Nimi lost his body, the wise rishi performed the proper rituals to begin the sacrifice, even though the king was just a spirit. The respected Brahmins, along with the people and servants, tried to preserve Nimi’s body by covering it with oils, flowers, and clothes. At the end of the sacrifice, Bhrigu said, ‘King, I am pleased with you. I will bring you back to your senses.’ The gods, happy with Nimi, spoke to his wandering spirit: ‘Great King, ask for a blessing—where do you want your consciousness to go?’ Nimi’s spirit replied, ‘Let me live in the eyes of the gods.’ The gods agreed: ‘Okay, ruler of the earth, your consciousness will move through their eyes in an instant. Any tiredness the gods feel in their eyes, caused by you moving like the wind, will disappear right away.’ After this, the gods returned to their realms. The wise rishis took Nimi’s body to the sacrificial site, dedicated it as an offering, and began to churn it with powerful mantras to create a new heir.

While they were churning, hoping to get a son for Nimi, a boy was born, full of spiritual strength. He was called Mithi because he came from ‘Manthana’ (churning). He was also named Janma because he was born from ‘Janan’ (birth), and Vaideha because he came from ‘Videha’ (the bodiless one). This way, Janaka, the first king of the Videha dynasty, was born. He was also called Mithi, and his descendants became known as the Maithilas. Lakshmana, I’ve now told you the amazing stories of how, because of a curse, the great sage Vasishtha and the noble King Nimi were reborn in such extraordinary ways.”
SECTION LXVIII

After Rama finished speaking, Lakshmana—always fierce in battle—responded, his eyes shining: “My brother, this story of the sage Vasishtha and King Nimi is honestly amazing and strange. But Nimi was a Kshatriya, a warrior king—he was brave. Still, even though he’d taken vows, he couldn’t forgive the great sage Vasishtha.” 

Rama, the chief among Kshatriyas, turned to his brilliant brother and said, “Lakshmana, not everyone is capable of forgiveness. Listen closely, and I’ll tell you about King Yayati, who once faced overwhelming anger but chose to forgive, thanks to his good nature. Yayati, who made his cities prosper, was the son of Nahusha. He had two beautiful wives. One was Sarmishtha, granddaughter of Aditi and daughter of Brishaparva. He loved her the most. His other wife was Devayani, granddaughter of Usanas, but he cared for her less. Each wife had a son—both boys were good-looking and attentive. Sarmishtha’s son was Puru; Devayani’s son was Yadu. Because of both his love for Sarmishtha and Puru’s own qualities, Puru became Yayati’s favorite. 

Yadu, feeling rejected, spoke sadly to his mother: ‘Mother, you come from the great Bhrigu line, famous for its tireless deeds, yet you’re suffering insults and pain. Let’s end this by stepping into fire together. Let the king spend his nights with Sarmishtha, the demon’s daughter. Maybe you can handle these insults, but I can’t. Please, let me give up my life.’ Tears in his eyes, Yadu said this in deep distress.

Hearing her son’s words, Devayani was furious. She thought immediately of her father. Instantly, Bhrigu (also called Vargava) appeared, and saw his daughter pale and joyless. ‘Daughter, what’s happened?’ he asked, worried. He kept asking, but Devayani, burning with anger, replied: ‘Great sage, I’ll walk into fire or water, or drink poison—but I refuse to go on living. You don’t see the pain and humiliation I’ve suffered. When a tree is ignored, everyone who depends on it suffers too. The king has ignored me, so you’ve been disrespected as well.’

Bhrigu listened, and his anger flared. He cursed King Yayati: ‘You, son of Nahusha, are wicked. You have insulted me, so now you’ll grow old and weak while you’re still young!’ After casting this curse and comforting his heartbroken daughter, the radiant sage Bhrigu returned to his own home. Having comforted his daughter, the great sage—shining like the sun—left that place.
SECTION LXIX

When Yayāti, the son of Nahusha, heard that his teacher, Sukra, was furious with him, he became deeply troubled. Because of Sukra’s curse, Yayāti instantly became old and weak. Desperate to enjoy life again, he went to his son Yadu and said, “Yadu, you understand what’s right and wrong. Please, take this old age from me for a while, so I can enjoy life’s pleasures a bit longer. I promise, after I’ve had my fill, I’ll take my old age back.” 

Hearing this, Yadu replied, “Why don’t you ask your favorite son, Puru, to take your old age instead? You’ve taken everything from me and don’t even let me near you. Let Puru, the one you eat and live with, do this for you.” 

After hearing Yadu’s response, Yayāti turned to Puru and said, “Puru, my strong-armed son, will you take my old age for me?” Puru respectfully folded his hands and answered, “I’m always ready to do as you ask, Father. I’m honored by your request.” 

Yayāti was thrilled by Puru’s loyalty and happily transferred his old age to him. Regaining his youth, Yayāti ruled the kingdom for thousands of years and performed countless rituals and sacrifices. 

After a long time, Yayāti said to Puru, “My son, it’s time to give me back the old age I left with you. Don’t feel bad—I only borrowed your youth for a while. I’m grateful for your obedience, and now I’ll reward you by making you king.” 

After telling Puru this, Yayāti turned angrily to Yadu and said, “You wicked one! Are you really my son, or some demon in a Kshatriya’s body? Why did you refuse to obey me? Because of this, you will never be king. I am your father and teacher, but you ignored me. Your descendants will become fierce demons, and your family will be kicked out of the lunar dynasty. Your children will be just as stubborn as you.” 

After cursing Yadu, Yayāti honored Puru by making him king, and then retired to the forest. Eventually, Yayāti died and went to the realm of the gods. The wise and famous Puru ruled the great city of Prathishtan with justice. Meanwhile, Yadu had thousands of demon children and, after being banished from the royal family, ruled in the distant and hard-to-reach city of Kraunchavana. 

So, according to Kshatriya tradition, Yayāti accepted Sukra’s curse, but the teacher never forgave him. I’ve told you the whole story. Let’s learn from these great men’s examples, so we don’t end up disgraced like King Nriga.” 

As Rama, with his glowing, moon-like face, finished speaking, the stars faded from the sky and the first rays of sunlight made the eastern horizon look like a woman dressed in flowery colors.
SECTION LXX

Early in the morning, after finishing his daily rituals, the lotus-eyed Rāma sat on his royal throne. He was surrounded by Brāhmanas, citizens, and his advisors, all gathered to discuss matters of the state. The assembly included his priest Vasishtha, the sage Kashyapa, ministers skilled in politics, other religious teachers, moral philosophers, council members, and visiting kings. Rāma’s court, always energetic and active, seemed as grand as the courts of Indra, Yama, or Varuna themselves. Turning to his brother, Rāma said, “Lakshmana (Saumitri), with your strong arms and good fortune, please go to the city gate and see if anyone has come with business for us.” Following Rāma’s instructions, Lakshmana went to the gate and called out to anyone who might have a request or grievance. But no one stepped forward—there was no one in need. In Rāma’s kingdom, there was neither sickness nor poverty. The land was rich with crops and resources. Children, young adults, and the middle-aged all lived long, healthy lives. The kingdom was ruled justly, so there were no problems or complaints. In Rāma’s reign, no one came seeking justice for a wrong. Lakshmana returned to Rāma, bowed respectfully, and said,

“No one has come with any business.” Rāma, clearly pleased, replied, “Go again, Saumitri, and check if anyone has arrived. When a king’s policies are fair, wrongdoing can’t survive. People protect each other because of respect for the king. Even though my laws are protecting everyone like arrows, you must always stay alert and continue ruling wisely.” Lakshmana left the palace again and noticed a dog waiting at the gate, looking around nervously and barking repeatedly. Seeing this, Lakshmana asked kindly, “What brings you here, friend? Tell me your business in confidence.” The dog replied, “I wish to speak to Rāma himself—he protects all creatures and promises safety to everyone.” Hearing this, Lakshmana went back inside the beautiful palace and told Rāma about the dog. After informing him, Lakshmana returned to the dog and said, “If you have something true to say, come and tell the king.” But the dog answered, “We dogs cannot enter the homes of gods, kings, or Brāhmanas, nor places with fire, Indra, the sun, or the wind. We are considered low-born, so I can’t go in. The king is the symbol of virtue, and especially Rāma, who is truthful, skilled in battle, and always cares for everyone. He knows exactly how to use the six qualities of leadership—he’s a master of morality, wise, watchful, and truly noble. He is like the moon, death, Yama, Kuvera (the god of wealth), fire, Indra, the sun, and Varuna all at once. Saumitri, please go and tell the king—who protects his people—that I do not wish to enter without his permission.” So, the radiant and noble Lakshmana returned to Rāma and said, “With your permission, I will explain everything, my brother, the joy of Kausalyā. The dog is waiting at the gate like a beggar, seeking your orders.” Rāma replied, “Bring in whoever is waiting at the gate for an audience—bring him here immediately.”
SECTION LXXI

After hearing Rāma’s words, Lakshmana (sometimes called Laks) quickly sent for the dog and told Rāma when it arrived. Seeing the dog brought before him, Rāma said, “Don’t be afraid. Tell me what you want.” The dog, its head bowed low, spoke up: “O King, you are the protector and ruler of all creatures. You stay awake to guard us while your people sleep. By upholding the law, you ensure righteousness (Dharma) is preserved. Without your protection, your subjects would be destroyed. The king is like the father and lord of the whole world—he represents time itself, the ages, and all of creation, living and non-living. He is called Dharma because he supports everything. It is virtue (Dharma) that holds society together and preserves the three worlds. Virtue defeats enemies and ensures people are governed fairly. That’s why virtue is called ‘the holder.’ Protecting others is the highest virtue, and it brings rewards even after death. Nothing in this world is harder to earn than real virtue. Charity, kindness, respect for the good, and innocence—these are the highest qualities, and they lead to happiness in this life and the next. O Rāghava, you are the best example of these virtues. You understand the ways of the good. You are like an ocean where all virtues find refuge. O greatest of kings, I may have spoken too much out of ignorance. With my head lowered, I ask your forgiveness. Please don’t be angry with me.”

Hearing the dog’s wise words, Rāma replied, “What can I do for you? Tell me honestly.” The dog answered, “A king must rule by virtue—he protects people through righteousness, becomes a safe haven for everyone, and helps them overcome fear. With this in mind, please listen, Rāma. There’s a beggar called Sarvarthasiddha (which means ‘one whose desires are all fulfilled’) living in a Brahmin’s house. Even though I did nothing wrong, he hurt me for no reason.”

When Rāma heard this, he sent a messenger to bring Sarvarthasiddha, the well-known beggar. When Sarvarthasiddha arrived at the assembly, he greeted Rāma respectfully and said, “O flawless Rāma, what do you want from me?” Rāma replied, “You hurt this dog. What did it do to deserve being beaten with a stick? Anger is a dangerous enemy that can destroy a person’s life. It pretends to be your friend but is actually your worst enemy, like a sharp dagger. Anger can steal everything you gain from good deeds, sacrifices, and charity. That’s why everyone should do their best to overcome anger. Our desires can run wild like untamed horses, but it’s better to control them with patience. Through your mind, actions, words, and even your eyes, you should try to help others. Don’t harm anyone, and don’t be addicted to anything. An uncontrolled mind can do worse than any weapon, snake, or angry enemy. Even someone who seems humble can’t always be trusted—often, a person’s true nature is revealed in time.”

After Rāma finished speaking, Sarvarthasiddha, the Brahmin, replied, “All day I’d been begging for food and was exhausted and angry. I saw this dog sitting in the way and asked it to move, again and again. It finally moved, but hesitated and stood fearfully by the side of the road. O descendant of Raghu, I was starving and hit the dog because I was angry at its behavior. O king, I know I was wrong, and I accept whatever punishment you decide. Please punish me so I can be free from the fear of hell.”

Rāma then asked his ministers, “What should we do? How should we punish him? We can only protect our people if we punish fairly, according to the crime.” Vrigu, Angiras, Kutsa, Vasishtha, Kashya, and other sages—along with the ministers, citizens, and experts in law—spoke up: “A Brahmin should never be sentenced to death.” After the law experts had their say, the ascetics turned to Rāma and said, “O Rāghava, as king you rule over everyone—especially you, since you are the eternal Vishnu, the protector of all three worlds.”

When they had finished, the dog spoke: “You promised to grant my request, Rāma. If you really wish to reward me, then make this Brahmin the head of a family estate.” So, honored and pleased, Sarvarthasiddha climbed onto an elephant and went to take up his new position.

Rāma’s counselors were shocked. “O great king, you haven’t punished him at all! In fact, you’ve given him a reward.” Rāma replied, “You don’t understand the real reason. The dog knows the truth.”

When Rāma turned to the dog, it explained: “I used to be the head of the Kālanjava estate. After worshipping the gods and Brahmins, and feeding the male and female servants, I would eat my own meal. I always divided things fairly and never let myself be tempted by wrongdoing. I carefully guarded the property of the household gods, was humble and kind, and worked for the good of all creatures. And yet, look at me now—I’ve ended up in this miserable state. This Brahmin is naturally angry, impious, hurts others, is impatient and cruel, speaks harshly, and is ignorant. He will disgrace seven generations of his family, past and future. He will never be able to handle the responsibilities of running a family estate. If you want to drag someone down to hell, along with their children, animals, and friends, make them serve Brahmins and cows. Anyone who steals the wealth of a Brahmin, a god, a woman, a child, or takes back a gift they’ve given is doomed, no matter what good they’ve done. O Rāghava, someone who steals from a Brahmin or a god ends up in the hell called Vichi. Even those who only think about stealing it are sent to hell again and again.”

Hearing this, Rāma’s eyes widened in surprise. The dog left, returning to where it had come from. In its previous life, the dog had been noble, but now it was cursed to be reborn in a lower state. In the end, the dog went to Vārānasi and took a vow to fast.
SECTION LXXII

For a long time, a vulture and an owl lived on a mountain that stretched along a riverbank. The area was alive with the songs of cuckoos and crowded with lions, tigers, and many kinds of birds. It was a beautiful forest full of trees, not far from the city of Ayodhyā. One day, the vulture—who was known to be rather mean—claimed the owl’s nest as his own and started a fight. Finally, both said, “Rāma (let’s call him Ram for short) is king over all. Let’s go to him—he’ll decide who owns the nest.” So, still angry and arguing, the vulture and the owl went to Rāma and bowed before him.

Seeing Rāma, the vulture spoke up first: “O protector of people, you are the greatest among gods and demons. You shine with intelligence and learning beyond even Vrihaspati and Sukrachārya. You know what is good and bad for everyone. You’re as beautiful as the moon, as unstoppable as the sun. Your glory is like the Himalayas, your seriousness like the ocean, your strength like the first ancestor, your patience like the earth, and your speed like the wind. Rāghava, you are the teacher of everything that moves or stands still, rich in every way, famous, forgiving, invincible, always victorious, and master of all knowledge and law. Please listen to my request. I built a nest for myself, but now this owl is living there as if it’s his own. So, great king, please help me.”

After the vulture finished, the owl began: “It’s true, O king, Rāma has qualities of the moon, Indra, the sun, Kuvera, and Yama, but he is also partly human. Still, you are truly the god Nārāyana, present everywhere. You judge everyone fairly, so you show real kindness, which is why people see you as connected to the moon. In anger, punishment, rewards, and fear, you’re our giver, destroyer, and protector—just like Indra. Your energy is like fire: intense and unstoppable, and your light touches all beings, just like the sun. You’re the lord of wealth, even greater than Kuvera, and fortune (Sri) is always with you. Because you give us wealth like Kuvera, you’re called the giver. Rāghava, you treat everyone—friend or enemy—the same way and protect your people fairly. Death comes for anyone you’re angry with, which is why people call you the mighty Yama. O greatest of kings, because you forgive everyone and are a kind ruler, people praise you as the best of men. A king is the strength of the weak, the eyes of the blind, and shelter for those who have none. You are our king too, so listen to me. This vulture has moved into my nest and is making my life miserable. Only you, Rāghava, can bring justice.”

After hearing both sides, Rāma called for his advisors. The ministers who served both Daçaratha and Rāma—Vrishthi, Yayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, Rāshtravarddhana, Asoka, Darmapāla, the powerful Sumantra, and others—were all experts in law, wise, well-educated, and came from respected families. Rāma gathered them all and, riding in his Pushpaka (a magical flying chariot), went to the spot in question. Once there, he asked the vulture, “How long have you lived in this nest? Tell me if you remember.” The vulture answered, “I’ve lived here since humans first appeared and spread across the world.” The owl replied, “This nest was built for me when trees first grew on earth.”

After hearing this, Rāma spoke to his advisors: “A real council isn’t one without friends, and old men aren’t wise if they never talk about religion. Religion isn’t real without truth, and truth isn’t truth if it’s mixed with lies. Advisors who don’t answer questions they’re qualified to answer are dishonest. Anyone who answers while driven by passion, anger, or fear traps himself in a thousand chains of Varuna, and only loses one chain each year.”

The ministers replied, “Wise Rāma, what the owl said is true—the vulture is lying. You’re the proof of this, because the king is everyone’s last refuge, the root of justice, and the foundation of what’s right. Someone who is punished by the king isn’t doomed, but actually saved from fear and will reach a better state.”

Rāma answered, “Listen to what the Puranas say. Long ago, the sun, moon, sky, stars, earth, mountains, forests, all three worlds, everything living and non-living—were all covered by water. At that time, only Nārāyana existed, like a second Sumeru mountain. Inside Nārāyana’s belly was the earth, with Lakshmi. When everything was destroyed, Vishnu (who is the soul of all creatures) slept in the water for ages. Seeing Vishnu sleeping and the universe destroyed, Brahmā, the great sage, entered his stomach. Then a golden lotus grew out of Vishnu’s navel, from which Brahmā was born. He performed tough meditation to create the earth, air, mountains, trees, people, reptiles, and all creatures born from eggs or wombs. At that time, two powerful demons, Madhu and Kaitabha, came from Nārāyana’s ears. They got furious when they saw Brahmā and chased him. Brahmā cried out in fear, which woke Nārāyana. Vishnu then fought Madhu and Kaitabha and killed them with his discus. Their blood flooded the earth. Afterward, Vishnu purified the earth and covered it with trees and plants. The earth got called Medini because it was filled with the fat (medas) of Madhu and Kaitabha. That’s why, ministers, I believe this nest belongs to the owl, not the vulture. The vulture should be punished for stealing someone else’s home and making life difficult for the owl.”

Suddenly, a voice echoed from the sky and revealed the truth: “Rāma, don’t kill the vulture. He’s already been burned to ashes by Gautama’s powerful curse. In his first birth, this vulture was a brave and honest king named Brahmadatta. Once, a Brahmana named Gautama, the very image of death himself, came to Brahmadatta’s house for food and said, ‘O king, I’ll eat at your house for more than a hundred years.’ Brahmadatta welcomed Gautama, washed his feet, and prepared his meal. But accidentally, some meat got into Gautama’s food. Furious, Gautama cursed the king, saying, ‘Become a vulture!’ The king pleaded, ‘Please have mercy! I made a mistake out of ignorance. Please let the curse end someday!’ Seeing that the king’s mistake was unintentional, Gautama said, ‘A king named Rāma will be born in the Ikshwāku dynasty. When he touches you, you’ll be freed from this curse.’”

After the voice finished, Rāma touched Brahmadatta. Instantly, the vulture shed his bird form and took on a beautiful, heavenly body, smelling of divine perfumes. He praised Rāma, saying, “O wise one, your kindness has saved me from a terrible fate—my curse ends here.”
SECTION LXXIII

While Rāma and Lakshmana were wrapped up in their daily conversations, a spring night arrived—pleasant, neither too warm nor too cold. The next morning, after finishing his morning rituals, Rāma (also called Kākutstha), who understood the mood of his people, felt an urge to go somewhere he could observe the citizens. Just then, Sumantra came in and said, “O king, there are some ascetics waiting at the gate—great sages, led by Bhārgava and Chyavana. These holy men live by the Yamunā river, and they’re eager to see you. They’ve sent me to let you know, mighty king.” Rāma, ever righteous, replied, “Let the honored sages come in.” Obeying the royal command, the doorkeeper respectfully brought in the ascetics, who were not easy to approach due to their spiritual power. There were more than a hundred of them, glowing with their own inner light, as they entered the palace.

The sages offered Rāma a variety of fruits and vessels filled with holy water collected from sacred places. Rāma accepted these gifts—the holy water and the fruits—and then addressed the great ascetics: “Please, take these seats in a way that suits your traditions.” Hearing Rāma’s words, all the Maharshis sat down on the beautiful golden chairs provided for them. Seeing the saints settled, Rāma, conqueror of enemy cities, stood with hands pressed together and asked, “What brings you here? What can I do for you? I am at your service and will fulfill any request you have, without hesitation. My entire kingdom, and even my life, are dedicated to those who seek knowledge and truth. I swear this to you.”

The sages, famous for their intense spiritual practices and who lived along the Yamunā, applauded Rāma’s words. Overjoyed, they replied, “O greatest of men, only you could say something like this. Many powerful kings have come before you, but, afraid of the difficulty involved, they wouldn’t promise anything without knowing what was being asked. But you have pledged yourself to help, just for the honor of the Brāhmanas, without even knowing the task. We have no doubt that you will succeed—and now, we ask you to save the sages from a terrible fear.”
SECTION LXXXV

After the sages finished speaking, Kakutstha (another name for Rama) replied, "Respected ascetics, tell me exactly what you need me to do. I promise, whatever is frightening you, I will take care of it." As Rama spoke, Bhargava stepped forward and began, "O king, let me explain the origin of the threat that endangers our land. Long ago, during the Krita age, there was a great asura named Madhu, the eldest son of Lotā and a descendant of Diti. Although he was an asura, Madhu was generous, intelligent, and especially kind to Brahmanas and anyone who sought his protection. Even the gods admired his generosity. To honor him, Rudra (Shiva) granted Madhu an extraordinary boon. Rudra took a powerful, glowing dart from his own arsenal and, pleased with Madhu’s devotion, gave it to him. Rudra said, 'Because you have lived with unmatched righteousness, I am giving you this special weapon. As long as you do not use it against the gods or holy sages, it will remain yours. But if you ever attack them, the weapon will lose its power. This dart will destroy anyone who dares to fight you, then return to your hand.'

Having received this gift, Madhu bowed again to Shiva and asked, 'Great lord, please let this dart stay in my family forever.' Shiva replied, 'That cannot be. However, so your wish is not wasted, I will grant that one of your sons may wield this dart, and as long as he holds it, no one will be able to defeat him.' With this powerful blessing, Madhu—the chief among asuras—built a magnificent city. His wife, the noble Kumbhinasi, was the daughter of Viçwavasu and Analā. Their son, Lavana, was strong, vicious, and wild from childhood. Despite Madhu’s grief over his son’s evil ways, he said nothing. Eventually, Madhu left this world for Varuna’s realm, entrusting both the dart and the story of the boon to Lavana.

Now, with the power of this weapon, Lavana oppresses everyone, especially the sages and holy men. That’s why Lavana is so dangerous—because of this dart. Rama, we believe you are the only one who can save us. Many kings have already been asked by the sages to defeat Lavana, but none have succeeded. When we heard that you destroyed Ravana and his armies, we realized no other king on earth could help us. So we ask you, Rama: please free us from the terror of Lavana. Now you know the cause of our fear. We trust in your strength—please, do what is needed."
SECTION LXXVI

After hearing the sages, Rāma folded his hands respectfully and asked them, “What does Lavana eat? How does he live? And where is his home?” The sages explained how Lavana (sometimes called Lavana-asura) gained his strength. “He eats all living things, especially ascetics,” they said. “His life is ruled by violence, and he lives in Madhuvana. Every day, he kills thousands of lions, tigers, deer, birds, and even people, eating their flesh for food. Like the god of destruction during the end of the world, Lavana—who is incredibly strong—devours every creature he can.” 

Hearing this, Rāma turned to the powerful ascetics and said, “I will kill this demon. You don’t need to be afraid anymore.” With that promise, Rāma, together with his brothers, said, “Who among us should defeat Lavana? You decide—should Bharata do it, or should Satrughna be the one?” Bharata spoke up, replying, “I’ll do it. Let me take on this task.” 

Inspired by Bharata’s courage, Satrughna rose from his golden seat, saluted the king, and said, “Bharata, the mighty son of Raghu, has already accomplished something great. He once ruled Ayodhyā when you were gone, carrying the pain of your absence in his heart. He endured incredible hardships—sleeping on the ground, eating only fruits and roots, wearing rough clothes. After all he’s suffered, Rāma, you shouldn’t ask him to face more trouble now, especially while I’m here to serve you.” 

Rāma listened and replied, “Very well. Do as I ask, Satrughna. I’ll make you the king of Madhu’s beautiful city. Or, if you prefer, you can let Bharata take this task. You are strong and capable—you could even build a city on the Yamunā River and rule over prosperous lands. Anyone who rules a people but leaves them without a king will be condemned. If you accept what I’m saying, then after you defeat Lavana, Madhu’s evil son, rule the kingdom justly. Tell me what you think. But remember, a younger brother should always respect the wishes of his elder brother. Accept the kingship I offer you, along with the sacred rituals led by the priests and Vasishtha.”
Rāma.

When Rāma spoke to him, Satrughna (Shatru), who was full of energy, turned red with embarrassment and answered slowly, “My lord, this doesn’t feel right. How can you make a younger brother king while the elder brother is still alive? Still, I have to do as you command; I could never disobey you. I’ve learned from you and from the Scriptures about what’s right and wrong. Since my older brother had already promised to kill Lavana, I shouldn’t have said what I did before. When I said, ‘I’ll slay the terrible Lavana in battle,’ I spoke out of turn, and that was wrong. Because of that mistake, I now have to go through this strange situation. Even if this path isn’t right and could lead me to trouble, if it’s your wish, I can’t argue. And I won’t say anything else about it; I don’t want to make things worse by objecting a second time. So, I’ll do exactly what you want, but please, Rāma, arrange it so I won’t be blamed for simply following your order.” 

Hearing Satrughna’s words, Rāma smiled with relief and told Bharata and Lakshmana, “Get everything ready for the coronation—today I will make Satrughna, the best among men, king. And go summon the priests, the citizens, the royal advisors, and the councilors.” 

Bharata and Lakshmana did exactly as they were told. Soon, warriors, priests, and nobles all came to the palace, bringing everything needed for the ceremony. The auspicious water-sprinkling began, marking Satrughna’s coronation and bringing joy to everyone in Rāma’s household. After being crowned, Satrughna shone like the sun—he was like Skanda (Kartikeya) when the gods led by Indra made him their leader. With Satrughna crowned by Rāma, the people and the learned Brāhmanas were thrilled. Kausalyā, Sumitra, Kaikeyi, and the other royal ladies celebrated loudly in the palace. Even the wise sages living along the Yamuna River believed that Lavana must have already been defeated now that Satrughna had become king. Then, Rāma, proud of Satrughna’s abilities, took him onto his lap and spoke to him gently and with praise:
SECTION LXXVII

“O conqueror of enemy cities, this magical arrow, which never misses its target, is now yours. With it, Satrughna, you’ll defeat Lavana. This arrow was created long ago, when gods and demons couldn’t be seen, by the self-born, undefeatable god as he rested on the cosmic ocean. At that time, the world was being threatened by Madhu and Kaitabha and other demons. In his anger and with the intent to create the three worlds, he made this unbeatable arrow to destroy evil, and used it to defeat those monsters in battle. After killing Madhu and Kaitabha with this very arrow, the gods were able to create the worlds in peace. 

When I was preparing to fight Rāvana, I didn’t use this arrow because I knew that, if released, it would cause too much destruction to innocent creatures. Lavana, on the other hand, keeps with him a powerful weapon that was given to Madhu by the great Tryamvaka (Shiva), using it to destroy his enemies. He constantly worships this weapon and becomes invincible when he has it, burning anyone who challenges him to ashes. That’s why, Satrughna, you must wait at the city gate and challenge him before he enters—before he can arm himself. When he’s unarmed, call him out for battle, and only then will you have a chance to defeat him. There’s no other way to kill him. If you do this, you will succeed. My son, now you know how to counter his deadly weapon. Remember, no one can easily overcome the power of the mighty Nilkantha (Shiva).”

(Note: This reference means “of being installed as a king during the life of my elder brother.”)
SECTION LIXVIII

After speaking to Satrughna (Shatrughna), Rama praised him again and said, “You’re one of the best among men. Take four thousand horses, two thousand chariots, and a hundred excellent elephants with you. Bring all the supplies you need—plenty of shops with different goods, singers and musicians for entertainment, and enough gold and silver coins for expenses. Make sure your soldiers have everything they need to be comfortable, well-fed, and happy—don’t give them any reason to be upset with you. Use kind words with them; remember, when soldiers go to battle, they leave their families and friends behind, so what really matters to them is good food and rewards. Satrughna, send a large, well-supplied army ahead of you, then follow them to Madhuvana. Make sure you travel in secret so that Lavana, Madhu’s son, doesn’t find out you’re coming to challenge him. He can’t be defeated by any other method than the one I told you about. If Lavana finds out someone is coming for him, he’ll definitely destroy that enemy. Wait until the rainy season begins, after this summer ends—that’s the right time to kill him, because he’ll be moving around carelessly, thinking nobody would attack during the rains and leaving his deadly dart behind. For now, send the soldiers ahead with the sages leading the way; the summer isn’t over yet, so it’s easy for them to cross the Ganges now. Once you’ve set up camp with your army on the far side of the Ganges, go forward alone and quickly, carrying your bow.” Hearing Rama’s instructions, Satrughna gathered his strongest warriors and told them,

“All of you, go ahead and camp at places you already know well. Don’t trouble anyone along the way.” After giving these orders, Satrughna respectfully bowed to Kausalya, Sumitra, and Kaikeyi. He walked in a circle around Rama, Lakshmana, and Bharata with folded hands as a sign of respect, then bowed to the priests. With Rama’s permission, and after circling him, the powerful Satrughna set out. He sent the massive army—filled with the best elephants and horses—ahead of him, then said goodbye to Rama. Everyone gave him a proper farewell.
SECTION LXXVIII

After sending off his army and spending a month in Ayodhya, Satrughna (Shatrughna), known for defeating his enemies, set out on his own. He traveled for two days and nights until he reached the peaceful and beautiful hermitage of the sage Valmiki. Bowing respectfully to Valmiki, Satrughna greeted him with folded hands and said, “Respected Sir, I’d like to stay here tonight. I’m here on some business for our master, Rama. I’ll continue westward tomorrow morning.” Hearing this, Valmiki, the renowned sage, replied, “Satrughna, you’re welcome here—please, stay as long as you need. This hermitage belongs to the descendants of the Raghu dynasty, so you have nothing to worry about. Make yourself comfortable—sit down and have some water to wash your feet.” Satrughna washed up, ate some fruits and roots, and felt very content.

Next, he asked Valmiki, “Great sage, who do all those sacrificial items near the hermitage belong to?” Valmiki answered, “Listen, Satrughna, and I’ll tell you whose sacrificial ground this was long ago. There was a king named Saudasa, one of your ancestors. His son was Virjashaha, a powerful and virtuous king. Saudasa himself loved hunting since he was young. One day, during a hunt, he spotted two Rakshasas in the forest. He’d heard about them before—they looked like tigers, were terrifying, and had eaten thousands of deer but still weren’t satisfied. Saudasa saw these two Rakshasas and noticed the forest was empty of other animals. Angry, he killed one of them. Afterward, as he watched the dead Rakshasa, the other one, stricken with grief, said, ‘You have killed my companion for no reason. I’ll make sure you pay for this.’ With that, the Rakshasa vanished.

Time passed, and soon Virjashaha became king. Saudasa decided to perform a grand horse sacrifice near this very hermitage, with Vasishtha acting as the chief priest. The sacrifice lasted for many thousands of years, and the amount of treasure involved made it seem almost divine. As the ritual was nearing completion, the surviving Rakshasa, still holding a grudge, disguised himself as Vasishtha and came to King Saudasa, saying, ‘King, the sacrifice ends today. Please, quickly serve me some meat.’ Believing the request came from Vasishtha, Saudasa told his best cooks, ‘Prepare a meat dish that will satisfy my guru Vasishtha.’ The cooks left to prepare the meal, but the Rakshasa, taking on their form, brought the food to the king. The king and his queen offered this food to Vasishtha, but when he tasted it, Vasishtha realized it was human flesh. Furious, he cursed, ‘King, since you have served me this, let this be your own food from now on. My words will not fail.’

Enraged by the curse, Saudasa scooped up water in his hands, ready to curse Vasishtha back, but his queen stopped him, saying, ‘Husband, Vasishtha is our guru and priest. You must not curse him.’ Listening to her, Saudasa poured the water on his own feet, which immediately turned dark. From then on, he was also called Kalasampada. Afterwards, Saudasa and his wife bowed to Vasishtha and explained what the Rakshasa had done, pretending to be a Brahmin. Vasishtha, realizing what had happened, said, ‘King, my curse will not go unfulfilled, but I grant you this: after twelve years, you will be free from it. And, by my blessing, you won’t remember anything about your condition during those years.’ After suffering through the curse, Saudasa eventually regained his kingdom and ruled his people once again. So, Satrughna, the sacrificial ground you asked about belonged to King Saudasa.”

After hearing this grim story about Saudasa, Satrughna thanked Valmiki and went inside a thatched cottage for the night.
SECTION LXXIX

That same night, while Satrughna was staying in a simple thatched hut, Sitā gave birth to twin sons. Around midnight, some young students of the ashram came to Vālmiki and told him the good news: "Respected sir, Rāma’s wife has given birth to two sons. Please make sure they’re protected from evil spirits." Hearing this, the wise and radiant Vālmiki hurried over and was overjoyed to see the newborn boys, who glowed like the rising sun and looked almost divine. Vālmiki immediately made arrangements to keep away ghosts and evil spirits. He took kusa grass (the upper part) and lava grass (the lower part), and prepared rituals for protection. Thanks to Indra’s energy, Khshupa brought the earth under his command; with Varuna’s energy, he strengthened his body; with Kuvera’s, he gave wealth to his people; and with Yama’s, he ruled them fairly. So, Rāma, because you carry a portion of Indra’s energy, you can accept this ornament and, by doing so, grant me spiritual liberation.”

After hearing Agastya’s explanation, Rāma accepted the glowing celestial ornament, bright as the sun. Then, curious, Rāma asked the great sage Kumbhayoni: “Where did you get this extraordinary ornament? Who gave it to you? Brahmin, I ask because I’m genuinely curious—you are a source of so many wonders.”

Agastya answered, “Listen, Rāma, and I will tell you how I received this ornament during the Tretā age.”
SECTION XC

“Hey Rama, back in the Treta Yuga, there was this massive forest that stretched for a hundred yojanas. It was completely empty—no people, no animals. That’s where I used to do my tough penance. One day, I decided to wander through the whole forest, wanting to explore every bit of it. The place was beautiful in a way that’s hard to describe. Everywhere I looked, there were trees loaded with sweet fruits and roots. Right in the middle of the forest, I found a huge pond that was about a yojana wide. The water was deep, calm, and crystal clear—no moss at all. The pond was covered with lotuses and lilies, and birds like swans, karandavas, chakravakas, and all sorts of waterfowl were playing there. Not far from the pond, I came across an old, sacred hermitage, but strangely, there were no animals or people around. Since it was summer, I decided to spend the night in that hermitage.

The next morning, I got up and walked to the pond. That’s when I noticed a large, dead body floating in the water. It looked fresh—none of its limbs were pale, and it hadn’t lost its beauty. I stood there on the bank, staring at it, lost in thought. I wondered, ‘What is this?’ Suddenly, I saw a beautiful chariot, fast as thought, pulled by giant white birds—ganders. Riding in the chariot was a radiant, celestial figure. He was surrounded by Apsaras—heavenly women with stunning jewelry and lotus-shaped eyes. Some were singing, some dancing, some playing instruments like the mridanga and vina, while others waved golden fans that sparkled like moonlight, cooling his face.

Rama, as I watched, that divine being—who looked as majestic as the moon leaving the peak of Mount Sumeru—stepped down from his chariot and began eating flesh from the dead body. Once he’d had enough, he walked into the water and carefully washed himself. After that, he started to get back into his chariot. Seeing this, I couldn’t hold back and called out to him: ‘Who are you? You look like a celestial, so why are you eating something so disgusting? Someone as revered as you shouldn’t have to eat like this. I’m really curious and want to understand. Honestly, seeing you eat a corpse just doesn’t sit right with me.’

O King, I asked him these questions directly, just because I had to know. And when he heard me, the celestial being told me everything.”
SECTION CXI

"Rāma, listen to what happened next," Agastya began, his voice calm but serious. He had two queens, and each had a son—my name is Sweta, and my younger brother was Suratha. When our father died, the people made me king, and I ruled them fairly and carefully for a thousand years. At some point, I learned when my life would end. When I realized my time was almost up, I decided to become a hermit. I put Suratha on the throne and retreated into a dense forest near this very pond, a place empty of people and animals, to devote myself to spiritual practice.

I spent a long time doing intense meditation and self-denial by this pond. After three thousand years of this, I finally reached Brahmā’s realm. But even there, I was tormented by hunger and thirst. It wore me down over time. Finally, I went to Brahmā, lord of the three worlds, and asked, "O Brahmā, this is supposed to be a place free of hunger and thirst—so why am I still suffering here? Is this a punishment? What did I do to deserve this? What can I survive on now?" Brahmā answered, “Sweta, son of Sudeva, you should eat delicious meat each day. You focused only on growing your spiritual power during your penance, but you never practiced charity. Nothing grows if nothing is planted; you did the work of an ascetic, but you never gave to others. That’s why, even in heaven, hunger and thirst torment you. Now, you must survive by eating your own dead body, which was nourished by all sorts of food in your life. Only when the great sage Agastya, who can even give salvation to the gods, comes to this forest, will you be freed from this curse. He will end your suffering.’

I get some relief from this, but I still suffer. Now that I see you, I realize you must be the legendary Agastya—no one else could have reached this place. Please, save me from this torment. Take this precious ornament as a gift. I beg you, have mercy on me. I offer you gold, wealth, fine clothes, food, beautiful jewelry, and all sorts of treasures. O wise one, please, out of compassion, help me.’

That, O Kākutstha, is how this amazing, celestial ornament came into my hands—given to me by Sweta, the royal sage who was as mighty as Indra.”
SECTION CXII

SECTION XCIII

After telling this story to Rāma, the great sage Agastya continued: “O Kākutstha (Rāma), King Danda, who had mastered his desires, ruled peacefully for many years. Arajās cried out in the forest, not far from the hermitage, and waited for her father to return from his visit to the gods.”
SECTION XCIV

After hearing from a student about everything that happened to Arajās, the teacher (Sukra, also called Usanās), surrounded by his disciples, went back to his own ashram. Listening to the sage and teacher Sukra, Arajās answered her father sadly, “I will do as you say.” Then Sukracharjya left and lived somewhere else. Just as he had predicted, Danda’s entire kingdom—his servants, army, and vehicles—was destroyed within seven nights. 

Rāma, back in the golden age, the land between the Vindhya and Saivala mountains, which was ruled by Danda, was cursed by the Brahmin sage because of Danda’s evil deed, and it turned into a desert. From then on, it was called the Dandaka forest. It’s also known as Janasthāna, because many hermits used to do their spiritual practices there. 

Rāghava (Rāma), I have now told you everything you wanted to know. Now it’s time for the evening rituals. Look, the great sages everywhere are bathing and worshipping the sun with water jars. The sun god, Aditya, is about to set, having been praised by Brahmins chanting Vedic hymns. So, Rāma, it’s time for you to perform the ceremony too.”
SECTION XCV

He dismissed the magical chariot, saying, “Thank you—may good fortune go with you.” Then Rama turned to a palace guard and said, “Go quickly and tell Lakshmana and Bharata that I’ve arrived, and bring them here.”
SECTION CXVI
