You yourself took shelter from the storm and fell asleep in the hermitage. There’s nothing to fear now. So relax, brave one, and try to be happy here by living off fruits and roots.’ 

But even with these comforting words, King Ila—heartbroken over losing his people—answered sadly, ‘O Brahman, I’ll give up my kingdom. I can’t live without my servants, not even for a moment. Please let me do this. My oldest son, the noble and devout Sasabindu, should rule in my place. I can’t stay here after losing my servants and the wives of my country. So, please, don’t make me stay here—it’s too painful.’ 

Budha listened to these heartfelt words from King Ila and reassured him, saying, ‘Stay here. Don’t grieve, powerful son of Kardama. If you stay here for a year, I promise things will get better for you.’ 

After hearing Budha’s words, King Ila agreed to stay. The next month, he turned back into a man and started practicing ascetic rituals. In the ninth month, Ila—now with a beautiful figure—gave birth to a radiant son named Pururava, who took after his father Budha in both looks and power. She handed her strong son over to Budha. When the year was over and Ila returned to his male form, Budha used kind words to bring him happiness once again.
SECTION CIII

After Rāma finished telling the story of Pururava’s strange birth, Bharata and Lakshmana—curious as ever—asked him, “Rāma, what happened to Ila after spending a year with Soma’s son? What did he do next?” Rāma listened to their eager questions and continued the story of Kardama’s son: “When heroic Ila’s year was up and he became a man again, Budha—the wise and brilliant son of Soma—decided to help. Budha, who knew all about the mysteries of birth and was a gifted speaker, called upon his generous friend Sangbarta, Chyavana (the son of Vrigu), the powerful sage Aristhanemi, the famous Durvasa, who could bring happiness to anyone, and some other patient friends. Budha said, ‘You all know the strange situation Ila, the son of Kardama, is in.’ While they discussed what to do, the radiant Kardama himself arrived at the hermitage. With him came Pulastya, Kratu, Vashatkar, and the bright Omkāra. Everyone was happy to see these great sages, and each of them shared ideas about how to help the king of Vālhakee.

Kardama, caring deeply for his son, said: ‘Listen, wise ones. Here’s how we might help King Ila. For this bizarre condition, I can’t think of a better cure than turning to Lord Umā’s husband—Shiva (Mahādeva). And no ritual pleases him more than the Ashvamedha—the horse sacrifice. So let’s perform this challenging sacrifice for the king’s sake.’ 

Sambarta’s student, the royal sage Marutha (who had conquered many cities), gathered all the things they’d need for the ritual. Right near Budha’s hermitage, they held this great sacrifice. Lord Rudra (Shiva) was pleased by their devotion. He appeared before the wise ones and Ila, and said, ‘Great sages, I’m truly pleased by your offering and your faith. What can I do for King Ila?’ 

The Brahmanas, overjoyed, respectfully asked Mahādeva to restore Ila’s manhood. Shiva, satisfied, granted Ila his wish and then vanished. When the sacrifice was finished and Shiva had disappeared, all the wise sages went back to their own hermitages.

Ila then made his oldest son, Sasavindu, ruler of Vālheeka, and went on to build a new city in the heart of the land. Eventually, Ila reached the highest spiritual state—the realm of Brahmā. His son, Pururāva, became king of Pratishthāna. So you see, Bharata and Lakshmana, the horse sacrifice is so powerful that it let Ila, who’d been changed into a woman, become a man again.”
SECTION CIV

After speaking to both his brothers, Rama (descendant of Kakutstha, and famous for his unmatched strength) turned to Lakshmana with words full of moral wisdom: “Lakshmana, invite Vasishtha—the greatest of the brahmins—who knows every detail of the Ashwamedha sacrifice. Also invite Vamadeva, Javali, and Kashyapa. Once we’ve consulted with them, I’ll release the sacred horse with all its auspicious marks.” Lakshmana, always ready and strong, immediately invited all these respected brahmins and returned to Rama. When Rama saw them, he greeted them by touching their feet in respect. The brahmins, recognizing Rama’s divine presence, blessed him warmly. With his hands folded, Rama then asked these wise men about every part of the Ashwamedha (horse sacrifice) ritual. Hearing his questions, the brahmins—after offering prayers to Rudra—began to praise the greatness of the horse sacrifice. As they told him about many virtues of the Ashwamedha that he had never heard before, Rama felt truly happy.

Following their advice, Rama said to Lakshmana, “Brother, send a messenger quickly to Sugriva. Tell him: ‘Come join us for the festival, and bring all your powerful monkeys and bears. Good things await you.’ Also, make sure Vibhishana—the unmatched king of the rakshasas—comes with his followers. Invite all the great kings who wish me well, and their retinues, to the sacrifice. And don’t forget to invite other pious foreign kings who are my friends, along with rishis known for their spiritual strength, and brahmins from every province. Be sure to invite actors and singers as well. Order that a huge sacrificial ground be prepared on the banks of the Gomati River, in the Naimisha forest. That place is perfect and sacred. Arrange for peace-invoking ceremonies everywhere. Invite hundreds of my people so they can all come to Naimisha, watch the ceremony, and return home happy and honored. Lakshmana, let Bharata go ahead with a million animals carrying rice, sesame seeds, kidney beans, chickpeas, pulses, masha beans, salt, oil, clarified butter, and a hundred crore silver and gold coins. Merchants should set up shops along the way, and actors, dancers, cooks, and many young women should accompany Bharata. Soldiers should march before him. Bharata must lead the way with children, elders, brahmins, citizens, servants, officials, mothers, wives, and the golden statue of my wife, who will be symbolically present for the ritual.”

Following Rama’s orders, Bharata and Shatrughna arranged for the best lodgings, food, drinks, and clothes. Sugriva’s powerful monkeys and the brahmins helped distribute everything. Vibhishana, surrounded by rakshasas and women, devoted himself to serving the wise rishis engaged in deep meditation and penance.
SECTION CV

After sending ahead all the necessary items for the sacrifice, Rama, Bharata’s older brother, released a black horse marked with all the traditional signs of sacrifice. He put Lakshmana, along with the chief priests (the Rittwigas), in charge of watching over it. Then Rama, strong and determined, traveled with his army to the Naimisha forest. When he saw the incredible site prepared for the sacrifice, he was overjoyed and said, “This place is truly beautiful.” While Rama stayed in the Naimisha forest, kings from many lands sent him gifts, and Rama sent gifts in return. When the kings arrived, they were welcomed with plenty of food, drinks, and clothes. Bharata and Shatrughna focused on taking care of the visiting kings. Sugriva and the other monkeys, disciplined and self-controlled, made sure the Brahmanas were looked after. Vibhishana and a group of Rakshasas, calm and focused, served the Rishis, who valued their spiritual power above all else. Rama, always thoughtful, set aside fine houses for the kings to stay in. With everything organized, the horse-sacrifice began.

Lakshmana kept a close eye on the sacrificial horse. In this way, Rama, the greatest of kings, began his Ashwamedha ritual. During the sacrifice, gifts were handed out to everyone until nobody wanted more. The only sound anyone could hear was people saying, “Give! Give!” At Rama’s horse-sacrifice, sweets and other treats were freely distributed until everyone was satisfied. In fact, before the beggars could even ask for anything, the monkeys and Rakshasas had already given them what they wanted. The ascetics, who lived only for their spiritual practices, said they had never seen a sacrifice with so many gifts—not even one held by Indra, Soma, Yama, or Varuna. The Rakshasas and Vanaras went everywhere, handing out wealth and clothing even to people who hadn’t asked for anything. Despite the year-long sacrifice, which had every traditional sign and requirement, Rama’s treasury never ran out; instead, it actually grew.
SECTION CVI

The grand sacrifice, greater than any that had come before, had begun. Vālmiki, the famous sage, arrived with his students to witness it. Seeing this incredible event—so magnificent it looked like something out of the heavens—Vālmiki’s followers, the Rishis, set up beautiful little cottages for themselves a little ways off, in a quiet corner. Inside Vālmiki’s own lovely hut, they placed his decorated cart, loaded with fruits and roots.

Then Vālmiki spoke to his students, Lava and Kusa: “I want you both to sing the entire Ramayana, with care and joy, in all the sacred hermitages of the Rishis, in the homes where Brahmanas maintain the eternal fire, in the streets and palaces, at the gates of Rama’s house, in the sacrificial arena, and in front of all the priests. Before you perform, eat the delicious fruits that grow on the mountaintop near our hermitage—if you do, you won’t get tired while singing, and you won’t feel hungry. If Rama, the king, asks you to sing the Ramayana, you should do it confidently and respectfully in front of all the gathered sages. Each day, sing twenty sections from the many I’ve composed in the Ramayana, which is made up of countless verses. Don’t wish for wealth—what use is money to ascetics who live on fruits and roots? If Rama asks about your father, just say, ‘We are disciples of the great Vālmiki.’ Kusa and Lava, sing the Ramayana in the right mood, with beautiful melodies and the sweet sounds of the vina. Before you start singing, show respect to the king by bowing to him—after all, the king is like a father to everyone. So, every morning, sing the Ramayana with joy, concentration, and music.” After giving these instructions, Vālmiki, the generous and wise son of Pracheta, fell silent.

Following the sage’s orders, Sita’s sons, Lava and Kusa—both brave and noble—set out from the cottage, saying, “We’ll do as you say.” Like the twin Ashwins, who always follow their teacher’s advice, the two brothers kept Vālmiki’s words in their hearts and spent the night, their minds full of curiosity and anticipation about what was to come.
SECTION CVII

As the night ended, Lava and Kusa woke up, bathed, and performed the morning fire ritual. Following their teacher Valmiki’s instructions, they began to sing. The song, composed by Valmiki—their first and greatest teacher—was unlike anything anyone had heard before. It used sounds from six different places, included every poetic meter, offered many kinds of reasoning and evidence, and was played with a stringed instrument. Hearing the boys sing, Rama’s curiosity was instantly piqued. He put aside his royal duties for a while and invited Valmiki, along with kings, scholars, experts in logic, Puranas, and language, elders, Brahmins, musicians, palmistry experts, Gandharvas (celestial musicians), townsfolk, masters of grammar and word-play, prosody experts, musicologists, astronomers, ritual specialists, businessmen, famous logicians, debaters, poets, historians, Vedic Brahmins, painters, and singers. Rama requested Lava and Kusa, with affection, to perform the song before this grand assembly. As everyone settled down and chatted among themselves, the two young sages began their song, bringing joy to everyone present. The song was so beautiful and mesmerizing that no one could get enough of it. The ascetics and kings, thoroughly delighted, kept stealing glances at the boys as if they couldn’t look away. They whispered to each other, “They look just like Rama—almost as if they were his mirror image! If not for their forest clothes and matted hair, you couldn’t tell them apart from him.” As the crowd murmured, Kusa and Lava sang the first twenty sections of the epic, as indicated by Narada.

After hearing up to the twentieth section, Rama, who was fond of his brothers, said to Lakshmana that afternoon, “Hey Kakutstha, give these two remarkable boys eighteen thousand gold coins each, plus anything else they want.” Lakshmana quickly began to fetch the coins, but Kusa and Lava, refusing the offer, replied in surprise, “We live in the forest, surviving on roots and fruit—what would we do with gold coins? Living in the woods, gold is useless to us.” Hearing this, both Rama and the entire audience were amazed and even more curious about the boys and the song.

Eager to know more about the origins of this epic, Rama asked the boys, “What proof do you have for this story? Who is the composer, and how famous is he? Which great sage wrote this incredible poem?” In response, Lava and Kusa replied, “The illustrious Valmiki is the author of this epic. He has described your endless story in this poem. He has recently come to your sacrifice, and this poem—containing a hundred stories and twenty-four thousand verses—was composed by him. Valmiki is our teacher. He’s written about all your deeds in six books, the first of which has five hundred sections. Every good thing you’ve done since birth is recorded here, O mighty king. If you wish to hear the entire story, you can listen to it with your brothers whenever you like.” Rama agreed, saying, “So be it,” and dismissed them. The boys left, happy, to return to Valmiki, their great teacher.

After hearing this beautiful song along with the ascetics and kings, Rama returned to his royal duties. He couldn’t forget the way Kusa and Lava sang the Ramayana—filled with musical skill, poetic sections, vowels, consonants, and played with the music of a stringed instrument.
SECTION CVIII

For many days, Rāma listened to the sacred story in the company of ascetics, kings, and Vanaras. As he heard the tale, he realized that Kusa and Lava were the sons of Jānaki (another name for Sitā). Bringing up her name before everyone, Rāma said, “Send a trustworthy messenger to the great sage Vālmiki. Have him tell the ascetics that if Jānaki has truly lived a pure and blameless life in the forest, she should prove her innocence—with Vālmiki’s permission. The messengers should also find out what Vālmiki thinks about this, and whether Sitā is willing to provide proof. To protect both her reputation and mine, let Maithili, the daughter of King Jānaka, swear an oath in front of everyone here.” The messengers quickly left for Vālmiki. Bowing respectfully to the radiant sage, they delivered Rāma’s message in gentle words. After hearing them and understanding Rāma’s wishes, Vālmiki replied, “What Rāma asks will be done. Good luck to you. For women, their husband is the greatest god, so Sitā will follow his wishes.” When the sage had finished, the messengers hurried back to Rāma and told him everything Vālmiki had said. Rāma was deeply pleased by Vālmiki’s response. Turning to the gathered Rishis and kings, he announced, “All Rishis and their students, all kings with their followers, and anyone else who wishes may witness Sitā’s oath here.” After hearing Rāma’s words, the Rishis praised him, saying, “O best of men, only you could act with such honor.” It was then decided that Sitā would take her oath the next day. Rāma, destroyer of his enemies, dismissed everyone. After making sure everything was ready for Sitā’s trial, the noble and generous King Rāma said farewell to all the kings and Rishis.
SECTION CIX

The next morning, Rāma arrived at the sacrificial ground. He sent invitations to the Rishis: Vasishtha, Vamadeva, Javali, Kashyapa, Viswamitra—who had all practiced deep meditation for years—Durvasa, Pulastya the ascetic, Salastri, Vargava, the long-lived Markandaya, the renowned Madgalya, Gargya, Chyavana, Satananda who understood religion deeply, the radiant Varadwāyā, Vasuprava (son of Agni), Nārada, Parvata, the great Gautama, and many more ascetics known for their discipline. Powerful Rākshasas (demons) and monkeys also showed up, curious about what would happen. Thousands of Kshatriyas, Vaisyas, Shudras, and Brahmans—many of them dedicated to spiritual practices—gathered from all over to witness Sitā’s trial. When everyone arrived, they sat quietly, as still as mountains.

Soon, Vālmiki—the greatest of the ascetics—entered quickly, bringing Sitā with him. Sitā followed him, head bowed, palms pressed together, her eyes full of tears, silently focusing her thoughts on Rāma. The crowd erupted with praise when they saw Sitā walking behind Vālmiki, just as the sacred texts are said to follow Brahmā. But sadness swept through the crowd, and people began to murmur emotionally. Some praised Rāma, some praised Sitā, and others honored both of them together.

Once Vālmiki and Sitā had entered the huge assembly, Vālmiki spoke to Rāma: “Son of Daçaratha, you abandoned Sitā near my hermitage because you feared people’s gossip, even though Sitā is pure and always lives by moral principles. Rāma, you are afraid of public criticism. Sitā is ready to prove her innocence and clear her name—please, show her some kindness and allow her to do this. I’m telling you the truth, Rāma: these twin boys are your sons, descendent of Raghu. I am the tenth son of Pracheta, and I never lie—not even in my thoughts. So I know for certain that these twins are yours. I have performed intense penances for thousands of years; I swear now, in front of you, that if Sitā is guilty of any sin, may I lose all the spiritual merit I’ve gained over all these years. I have never committed a crime—in thought, word, or deed. If Maithili (Sitā) is found blameless, then let me enjoy the fruits of my spiritual practice. Descendant of Raghu, I found Sitā pure in mind and body when I took her to the spring in the forest. Today, this pure-hearted, sinless Sitā, who always sees her husband as a god, wants to prove her innocence. You were afraid of public slander, and that’s why you sent away this Sitā, who is truly pure and devoted. I know this because of my ability to see the truth.”
SECTION CX

After the great sage Vālmiki finished speaking, Rāma saw Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, standing in the middle of the assembly. She looked almost divine. With his hands pressed together, Rāma said, “Great sage, you know all about righteousness. Your words, so pure and honest, have convinced me of Jānaki’s innocence. Still, Brahmin, I will do as you ask: let Sītā prove her purity in front of everyone. Back in Lanka, Vaidehi (Sītā) already faced a trial before the gods, which is why I brought her home. But public opinion is powerful. Even though I know Jānaki has done nothing wrong, I still sent her away. Please forgive me. I also know that these twins, Kusa and Lava, are my sons. But if Jānaki herself gives proof of her innocence here, in front of everyone, I will be truly satisfied.” 

News of Rāma’s plan for Sītā’s trial spread, and the gods gathered to witness it. The Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viswadevas, Maruts, Sadhyas, Siddhas, Nagas, and Rishis—led by Brahmā—arrived together. Seeing all the gods and sages gathered, Rāma turned again to Vālmiki and said, “Great sage, the words of the holy Rishis are pure, so I would trust Sītā’s innocence on your word alone. But now that everyone has come, eager to see her trial, I would be very pleased if Jānaki gave her own testimony in front of them.” 

As soon as Rāma finished speaking, a sweet, fragrant, and cool breeze began to blow—gentle and refreshing, as if nature itself was watching and judging what would happen. People from many lands had gathered, all completely focused on this shocking, incredible moment. In the golden age, only the gods felt such a breeze, but now, in the Treta Yuga, everyone felt it, and it amazed them all.

With everyone watching, Sītā, dressed in a red sari, stood with her head bowed and her hands pressed together. She said, “I have never thought of any man except Rāma, not even in my mind. Because of the strength of this truth, let the goddess Earth (Vasundharā) take me in. With my mind, body, and words, I have always wished only for Rāma’s happiness. Because of this, let the goddess Earth give me a place in her embrace.”

As soon as Sītā swore this, something incredible happened. The ground opened, and a beautiful, glowing throne rose from the earth. It was carried by powerful Nāgas—serpent beings—adorned with divine jewels and ornaments. The goddess Earth herself reached out her arms, welcomed Sītā, and seated her on the throne. As Sītā sat on the throne and began to sink into the earth, showers of heavenly flowers rained down on her.

The gods praised her, saying, “Oh Sītā, your actions are truly admirable.” From the sky, the celestials kept praising her as they watched her disappear into the earth. The sages, kings, and all the important people there were amazed by what they saw. With Sītā’s honor restored, every creature—living or not, on earth or in the sky—felt joy. Some cried out in happiness, some stood silent, and others stared at Rāma or Sītā, motionless. Seeing Sītā enter the earth, the ascetics felt deep joy. For a moment, as everyone shared the same feeling, it was as if the whole universe was united in peace.
SECTION CXI

After Sitā disappeared into Rasātala (the underworld), all the monkeys and Rishis (sages) praised her in front of Rāma. Overwhelmed by sadness and grief, Rāma lowered his head, his eyes full of tears and his face turned downward. He sat there, looking defeated. For a while, he sat quietly, crying from a mix of sorrow and anger. Then he spoke: “I’ve never felt pain like this before. Right in front of me, beautiful Jānaki (Sitā), who was like the goddess Lakshmi herself, has vanished. Before, when I was gone, Jānaki was kidnapped and taken across the ocean to Lankā, and I rescued her. So why shouldn’t I be able to get her back from Patāla (the underworld)? Goddess Vasudha (Earth), bring Sitā back to me now, or I’ll make you pay for your neglect. You’re my mother-in-law, since the sage-king Janaka found Sitā in your soil while he was plowing. So please, return my Sitā to me—or at least give me a place among the gods, because I can’t bear to be without her. I’m desperate for her—bring her back. If you don’t, Vasudha, I’ll flood the whole earth, destroying everything—your mountains, your forests—until nothing remains.” Rāma’s words were harsh, fueled by his grief and anger.

As Rāma finished speaking, the god Brahmā, with the agreement of the other gods, addressed him: “Rāma, you are strong and true to your word. You shouldn’t grieve like this. Remember who you really are: you are an avatar of Vishnu. I wouldn’t remind you of this secret if it weren’t necessary now. Remember your divine origin as Vishnu. Sitā is pure, loyal, and always devoted to you. Her deep devotion has led her to the realm of the Nāgas (serpent spirits). You will see her again in heaven. Now, listen to what I have to say in front of everyone. You’ll learn everything by hearing this great poem that tells your story. Vālmiki has described all your joys and sorrows, from your birth to what will happen after Sitā’s descent into Patāla, and even into the future. This is the first epic, the Rāmāyana, and it tells of your deeds. No one but you deserves the fame of this story. Rāghava (Rāma), you and the other sages should listen to the Uttarakānda, the final part of the poem. Only the greatest of kings and sages are worthy of hearing it.”

After saying this, Brahmā, lord of the three worlds, left with the other gods for the realm of immortals. The wise and radiant sages who lived in Brahmā’s domain stayed, with his permission, eager to hear what would happen next to Rāma in the Uttarakānda. Hearing Brahmā’s words, Rāma, shining with divine light, turned to Vālmiki and said, “Venerable sir, the sages from Brahmā’s world want to hear the rest of my story. Let’s begin it tomorrow morning.” Having arranged this, Rāma gathered Kusa and Lava (his sons), dismissed the crowd, and went back to his palace, where he spent the night mourning for Sitā.
SECTION CXII

When morning came, Rāma gathered the leading sages together and asked his sons to sing the poem without fear. As the respected Rishis took their seats, Kusa and Lava began to recite the final part of the Uttarakānda. After Sitā (Jānaki) vanished into the earth by the power of her vow and the great sacrifice was completed, Rāma fell into deep sadness. Without Sitā, the whole world felt empty to him. He was overwhelmed by grief and couldn’t find peace of mind. After giving generous gifts to kings, Rakshasas (demons), monkeys, and respected Brahmanas, Rāma sent them home, then entered Ayodhyā, always thinking of Sitā’s absence. From the moment Sitā went into the earth, Rāma never married again. Instead, he had a golden statue of Sitā made, and he used it as her stand-in during many rituals and sacrifices.

For a thousand years, Rāma performed countless Horse-sacrifices, Bajpeya rituals with lavish gold, Agnisomas, Atirātras, endless Gomedhas, and many other complicated ceremonies. While he ruled the kingdom and performed these sacred rites, a long time passed peacefully. Under his leadership, the bears, monkeys, Rakshasas, and kings were always loyal and happy to serve him. Because the rains fell at the right times, there was plenty of food. The land was clean and beautiful. People in the cities and villages were healthy and content. No one died young or before their time. In fact, during Rāma’s reign, all disasters and misfortunes disappeared.

After many years, Rāma’s famous mother, Kausalya, surrounded by her sons and grandsons, peacefully passed away. Kakeyi followed her, performing many sacred rites, and found peace in the realm of the immortals. These noble women were reunited with King Dasaratha in heaven, where they were filled with joy and gained every virtue. Later, when performing his father’s Srāddha ceremony, Rāma honored the gods and ancestors, gave away many jewels, and carried out an extremely difficult sacrifice. In this way, after carrying out many rituals and good deeds, Rāma spent thousands of years living in happiness.
SECTION CXIII

Once, Yudhajit, the king of Kekaya, sent a message to Rama. He chose Gargya, the son of his own teacher Angeras, to deliver it—a Brahmin sage known for his great power. Along with Gargya, Yudhajit sent gifts to show his affection: ten thousand horses, countless blankets, all kinds of jewels, different clothes, and perfectly clean coverlets. When Rama heard that the respected sage Gargya had arrived with these valuable gifts from his uncle Yudhajit, he and his brothers went about a krosa (roughly two miles) out of the city to greet him. Rama welcomed Gargya with the same respect that Indra gives to his teacher Brihaspati. After honoring the great sage and accepting the gifts from his maternal uncle, Rama asked Gargya about his health and well-being in every way. Once Gargya was seated, Rama said, “You’re one of the best speakers I’ve ever met—like the gods’ own teacher. Since you’ve come all this way yourself, my uncle must have sent you with an important message.” Gargya nodded and said, “Rama, if you’re willing, listen to the words your uncle Yudhajit has sent. There’s a beautiful land on the banks of the Sindhu river, full of fruits and roots, but guarded by the Gandharvas. These Gandharvas, armed and skilled in war, are the sons of Sailuska. They’re incredibly powerful, and there are thirty million of them. If you raise your flag and conquer their stunning city, you can add that kingdom to your own. No one else can get in there. Rama, I’m not asking you to do anything dangerous, but I hope you’ll come to love that amazing country.” Hearing these words, Rama was pleased. He said, “What you ask will be done.” Then he looked at Bharata and, with a smile and folded hands, told Gargya, “Great sage, these two young princes are Bharata’s sons, Taksha and Pushkala. Protected by their uncle Yudhajit and led by Bharata with his army, they will defeat the Gandharvas and split the kingdom between them. Bharata will set up two new kingdoms for his sons, and then, as the pious man he is, he’ll return to me.”

After telling this to the sage, Rama ordered Bharata to carry out the plan and welcomed the two princes warmly. When the stars were right, with Gargya leading the way, Bharata set out from Ayodhya with Taksha, Pushkala, and the army. Rama’s army was so strong that even the gods wouldn’t want to fight them. For a month, they marched out of the city like a divine force under Indra’s command. Along the way, wild animals that eat flesh and huge Rakshasas (demons) who craved blood followed Bharata’s forces. Thousands of birds soared overhead, and lions, tigers, and boars ran ahead of the army. After traveling for half a month, the happy and healthy army finally reached the Kekaya kingdom in great shape.
SECTION ICXIV

When Gargya and Yudhajit—the king of the Kekayas—heard that Bharata had arrived with his army, they were overjoyed. Gathering their own forces, they quickly marched out to fight the Gandharvas. Bharata (Rama’s younger brother) and Yudhajit, leading their troops and followers, soon reached the city of the Gandharvas. Hearing that Bharata was coming, the powerful Gandharvas assembled together and let out fierce, roaring battle cries.

A brutal battle began, intense enough to make anyone’s hair stand on end, and it lasted for a whole week. Neither side could claim victory or defeat. Blood flowed everywhere, turning the ground into rivers where bodies floated. Weapons like daggers, spears, and bows lay piled up like riverbanks. Furious, Bharata unleashed a terrifying arrow called Sangharata, which burned with the fire of destruction, against the Gandharvas. The arrow bound the Gandharvas in the grip of death and destroyed them all, sending every last one to the realm of the dead. The gods themselves couldn’t remember seeing such a terrible battle before. In just a moment, the massive Gandharva army was wiped out.

After defeating the Gandharvas, Bharata, son of Kaikeyi, founded two great, prosperous cities in the Gandharva region. He made Taksha the ruler of Takshasila and Pushkala the ruler of Pushkalabati. Both cities quickly became rich, glittering with jewels and filled with gardens. They seemed to compete with each other in wealth and beautiful ornaments. Thanks to fair trade and the good conduct of their people, the cities became truly charming places. Both were filled with gardens, carriages, and neat rows of shops lining the streets. The cities boasted fancy goods, attractive houses, magnificent palaces, and were shaded by tall, beautiful trees like Tala, Tamala, Tilaka, and Vakula.

Within five years, Bharata, the strong-armed son of Kaikeyi and Rama’s younger brother, had built up these two cities. After that, he returned to Ayodhya. Just like the god Indra greeting Brahma, Bharata respectfully saluted the noble Raghava (Rama), who was the very model of virtue, and told him in detail about the defeat of the Gandharvas and the founding of the two cities. Hearing Bharata’s story, Rama was filled with overwhelming joy.
SECTION CXV

When Rāma and Lakshmana heard Bharata’s thoughtful words, both of them were genuinely pleased. Rāma then turned to Lakshmana and said, “Saumitri (Lakshmana), your two sons, Angada and Chandraketu, are both wise in matters of religion and skilled at ruling. They’re also strong and capable. I think it’s time to make them kings. Please help me find regions where these two talented archers can rule freely—places where their new kingdoms won’t upset the peace or happiness of other kings.” Once Rāma finished, Bharata responded, “The land of Karupada is beautiful and peaceful, with no problems. Let’s establish a city there for Angada. And for Chandraketu, let’s give him the lovely country of Chandradyuti.” Rāma agreed with Bharata’s suggestion and soon brought Karupada under his control, giving it to Angada. Rāma had a strong and beautiful city built for Angada there. For Chandraketu, he created a city called Chandrakānti in the land of Mallya—it was stunning, almost like a city of the gods.

Afterward, Rāma, always unstoppable in battle, along with Lakshmana and Bharata, happily completed the royal ceremony to crown both princes and sent them off to their new cities. Angada set out to the West, and Chandraketu went North. Lakshmana (Sumitra’s son) traveled with Angada, while Bharata accompanied Chandraketu. Lakshmana stayed with Angada in his city for a year, making sure his son was settled as king, before returning to Ayodhyā. Bharata, on the other hand, spent more than a year in Chandrakānti with Chandraketu before coming back to Ayodhyā and respectfully greeting Rāma.

Lakshmana and Bharata, both deeply devoted to Rāma, never felt troubled by being apart from their sons, even while living elsewhere. With such virtue and unity, Rāma—the most righteous of all—alongside Bharata and Lakshmana, ruled their people wisely for ten thousand years. Living in Ayodhyā, the city of goodness, the three brothers flourished, much like a sacred fire glowing during a great sacrifice, and eventually found true happiness when the time was right.
SECTION CXVI

After spending some time in Kāla disguised as a wandering monk, the noble Rāma finally arrived at the palace gates. There, he saw his brother Lakshmana (sometimes called Saumitri), standing guard. Rāma, still disguised as an ascetic, said to him, “Please let Rāma know that I’m here on important business. I am a messenger from the great sage Atibala, who is famous for his brilliance. I have to speak with Rāma about a particular matter.”

Lakshmana listened carefully to the ascetic’s words. Without delay, he went inside to see Rāma (also called Rāghava) and announced, “O radiant one, may you achieve victory in this world and the next for following your kingly duties. There’s an ambassador outside, shining almost like the sun from his spiritual power, who’s come to see you.”

Hearing this, Rāma told Lakshmana, “Bring the ascetic in here as quickly as you can. He has an important message.” Lakshmana replied, “Yes, of course,” and led the glowing ascetic into Rāma’s private chambers. When the ascetic—his energy almost burning to the touch—approached Rāma, he greeted the king warmly, saying, “May you be blessed, great king.”

Rāma welcomed him with the traditional offerings of water and Argya, then asked how he was doing. The ascetic, a master of words, sat down on a golden seat after Rāma’s greeting. Then Rāma said, “Please, tell me the message from the one who sent you.”

The ascetic replied, “If you truly want to help the gods, I’d like us to speak in private. And if you respect the words of Atibala, the great sage who sent me, you must promise that anyone who sees or hears us during our conversation will be put to death.”

Rāma agreed and told Lakshmana, “Brother, send the guards away and wait at the door. I will speak with this ascetic in private, and I swear that anyone who spies on us will be killed by my hand.”

Once Lakshmana was standing guard outside, Rāma turned to the ascetic and said, “Great sage, please share the message you’ve been sent to deliver. Who sent you, and what do you want to tell me? I’m eager to hear everything you have to say—don’t be afraid.”
SECTION CXVII

The great sage spoke: “Listen, O king, you who are full of strength, and know why I am here. The great Creator himself has sent me to you. I am your son. In your earliest existence, you created me with Māyā—I am Kāla, the destroyer of all things. Lord Brahmā, the father of all living beings, reminded you of your promise to protect the three worlds. Long ago, after you destroyed all living creatures through your Māyā and slept in the endless ocean, I was born. After that, you created the mighty Ananta, who rules as the king of serpents in the waters. Then you created two powerful asuras, Madhu and Kaithabha. When their bones were scattered everywhere, the earth, with its many mountains, was called Medini. You brought me into being from the lotus at your navel, shining with divine brilliance, and gave me the task of creating life. I took on that responsibility and created humans. But, not knowing how to protect them, I prayed to you, the lord of the universe, and said: ‘Father, you are my creator and the source of my strength. Only you can protect these beings.’ Because of this, you left your unstoppable original form and took on the form of Vishnu. You were born as the son of Aditi’s powerful child and brought joy to my brothers. You always protected the gods whenever disaster struck. That’s why, to stop the destruction of creatures, you were born on earth to defeat the demon with ten heads. At that time, you promised to live among humans for eleven thousand years. So you took on a human body to fulfill that vow. Now, that time has come, and I’m here to let you know. Great king, if you want to rule over people a bit longer, you can stay here in the mortal world. But if you wish to return to the realm of the immortals, become lord of the gods again in your Vishnu form, and relieve their fears. O hero, the Creator wanted you to know this.” 

Hearing these unmatched words from Kāla, the destroyer, who spoke on behalf of the Creator, Rāma smiled and replied, “I’m truly pleased and grateful that you’ve come, my son. I came to earth for the good of the three worlds. May you be blessed. Now I will return to the place I came from. I was already thinking about this when you arrived, so I have no doubts. O lord of destruction, the immortals depend on me, so I will be with them in all things. The Creator has spoken the truth.”
SECTION CXVIII.

While Rāma and Kāla (Time) were deep in conversation, the famous ascetic Durvāsā arrived at the palace gates, wanting to see Rāma. He went straight to Lakshmana (also called Saumitri) and said, “Saumitri, take me to Rāma immediately. My time is short, so I need to see him first.” Hearing this, Lakshmana, who always respected holy men, bowed to Durvāsā’s feet and replied, “Respected sir, please tell me your purpose. What do you need? Please let me know what you want me to do. Rāma is busy right now, so could you wait here for a little while?” 

Durvāsā, known for his quick temper, became furious. His eyes burning red, he snapped, “Saumitri, if you don’t go right now and tell Rāma I’m here, I’ll curse you, Rāma, Bharata, Satrughna, as well as your sons and grandsons. I’ll also curse your kingdom and your cities. My anger is growing and I can’t hold it back much longer.” Hearing these terrifying words, Lakshmana thought to himself, “It’s better for me alone to be destroyed than for everyone to suffer.” Making up his mind, Lakshmana went straight to Rāma and told him what had happened.

When he heard Lakshmana’s message, Rāma ended his conversation with Kāla and came out quickly to meet Durvāsā, the son of Atri. Rāma greeted the powerful ascetic respectfully, folding his hands, and asked, “What brings you here?” Durvāsā, who was one of the greatest sages, answered, “Listen, Rāma. For a thousand years I’ve been fasting, and today my vow ends. Please give me as much food as I need.”

Rāma was overjoyed to hear this and made sure to serve Durvāsā the best food possible. Durvāsā ate the delicious, almost magical meal, thanked Rāma, and then returned to his hermitage. But after this, Rāma remembered what Kāla had told him and felt a deep sadness. The weight of those dark words left him silent and full of grief, his head bowed. For a while, he just sat there in distress. But thinking about Kāla’s prophecy, Rāma finally pulled himself together, realizing that disaster was coming and bracing himself for what lay ahead.
SECTION CXIX

Seeing Rāma (Ram) sitting with his head bowed, looking broken and lost—like the moon eclipsed by Rāhu—Lakshmana (Laksh) spoke up in a gentle, reassuring voice, trying to lift his brother’s spirits. “Don’t feel so troubled because of me, mighty brother,” he said. “This is just the way fate works; everything that happens to us is shaped by our past actions, whether good or bad. Please, keep your promise to Durvāsā and kill me if you must. You know, Ram, people who break their promises end up in hell. If you really care about me, you should fulfill your word—even if it means killing me. Don’t hesitate.”

Hearing Lakshmana’s words, Rāma was deeply shaken. He called his priests and ministers together and told them about the promise he had made and the arrival of Durvāsā. The group fell silent, unsure what to say. Then Vasishtha, wise and radiant, spoke up: “Rāma, I foresaw this moment, this tragedy, and your parting from Lakshmana, through my spiritual insight. Time is powerful, and we cannot go against it. Don’t break your promise. If you don’t keep your word, you’ll destroy your virtue—and once virtue is lost, it threatens the balance of the entire universe, including gods, sages, all living things, and even things that don’t move. So, for the good of everyone, you must let Lakshmana go.”

The other priests and ministers agreed with Vasishtha. Listening to this advice, Rāma turned to Lakshmana in front of everyone and said, “Lakshmana, I can’t go against what’s right. So, I’m banishing you. According to the wise, banishment and death are the same.”

After Rāma said this, Lakshmana didn’t return home. Tears filled his eyes as he quietly left. He went to the banks of the Sarayu river, washed his mouth, and stood there with his hands folded in prayer. He stopped breathing, closing off all his senses and passages, focusing completely on meditation. As Lakshmana, Rāma’s younger brother, gave up his life in this way, Apsarās (celestial dancers), Indra, other gods, and sages appeared in the sky and showered him with flowers.

Soon, invisible to humans, Indra—the king of the gods—took Lakshmana’s powerful soul into his own form and brought him to his divine city. When the gods saw Lakshmana, who was actually a fourth part of Vishnu, arrive in heaven, they were filled with joy and honored him with worship.
SECTION CXX

After leaving Lakshmana behind, Rama was overwhelmed with sadness. He turned to his citizens and ministers and said, “Today, I will put the noble and brave Bharata on the throne of Ayodhya, and then I’ll go into the forest. Please, gather everything needed for Bharata’s coronation right away. I’m going to walk the same path that Lakshmana took.” When Rama said this, everyone—his people—hung their heads and stood perfectly still, as if they were lifeless. Bharata was just as shocked. He spoke bitterly about ruling, saying, “My king, I swear on truth itself—I don’t want the kingdom. In fact, I wouldn’t even want to live in heaven if you weren’t there. Please, Rama, let Kusi rule Kosala and Lava rule North Kosala. Also, send messengers quickly to Satrughna to tell him what’s happening.” 

Seeing Bharata’s reaction and the grief of the people, Vasishtha spoke up: “Look, Rama, the people are lying on the ground in despair. Please, understand what they want and grant their wish.” Following Vasishtha’s advice, Rama helped the people up and asked them, “What can I do for you?” The people replied, “King, wherever you go, we want to follow. If you care for us at all, please let us come with our wives and children and walk the same path as you. Lord, as long as you don’t abandon us, we’ll go wherever you go—be it forest, wilderness, river, or ocean. That would be the greatest happiness for us. This is all we ask. Our joy is simply to be with you.”

Rama saw how loyal his people were, and he agreed to their request. After making his decision, he officially crowned Kusi as king of Kosala and Lava as king of North Kosala. He gave each of them a thousand chariots, countless elephants, countless horses, and many kinds of jewels and treasures—making sure both brothers ruled their new kingdoms well. Once he had settled everything with the princes, Rama sent a messenger to Satrughna with all the news.
SECTION CXXI

After being sent by Rama, the fast-moving messengers quickly reached Mathura. They traveled non-stop for three days and nights before finally arriving and delivering the news to Satrughna. They told him about Lakshmana’s departure, Rama’s vow, and how the people of Ayodhya were following their king. They said, “The wise Rama has built a grand city called Kusavati at the foot of the Vindhya mountains for Kusi. For Lava, he has constructed the city of Sravanti. Now, with Ayodhya left empty, Rama and Bharata—both great warriors—are preparing to leave this world and ascend to heaven.” After quickly sharing all this, the messengers rested. Then they urged Satrughna to leave as soon as possible. Seeing the terrible end of his family line approaching, Satrughna gathered his people and priests and explained everything to them—including that he and his brothers would soon be gone. Satrughna then decided to make his two sons rulers in his place. He crowned Suvahu as king of Mathura and made Satrughati the king of Vidisha. After settling his sons on their thrones, Satrughna, the brave hero, got into his chariot and left for Ayodhya.

When he arrived, he saw Rama—dressed in fine silk and shining like fire—standing among the ascetics. Remembering his duty, Satrughna bowed to Rama, folded his hands, and said, “I have put my two sons on the throne. Now I am ready to follow you, my king. Please don’t tell me otherwise. I only ask that I never disobey your command.” Seeing how determined Satrughna was, Rama, descendant of Raghu, agreed to his request.

As soon as Rama gave his blessing, monkeys who could change their shape, along with bears and Rakshasas, began to gather there. When they heard that Rama was preparing to leave the world, monkeys born from the gods, sages, and Gandharvas brought Sugriva with them to see Rama. They all said, “Rama, greatest among men, if you go to heaven and leave us behind, it will be like a death sentence for us.”

Sugriva, full of strength, also bowed to Rama and said, “Lord, after making Angada king, I have come here. I am ready to follow you, my king.” Hearing the words of the monkeys, Rama told them he would grant their wish.

Then Rama turned to Bibhishana, king of the Rakshasas, and said, “Bibhishana, as long as people live and breathe, you must remain in your body and rule Lanka. As long as the sun, moon, and earth exist—and as long as my story is remembered—your kingdom will too. You have always been a loyal friend and followed my wishes. Rule your people with goodness. I have nothing more to add, except this, powerful king of Rakshasas: worship Jagannath, the lord of the world, the guiding god of the Ikshwaku dynasty.”

After speaking to the ever-loyal Bibhishana, Rama (also called Kakutstha) turned to Hanuman. He said, “It is decided—you will live forever. So now, keep your promise. As long as my story is told on earth, live here happily and carry out my wishes.” Hearing this, the noble Hanuman was overjoyed and replied, “As long as your sacred tale is known in this world, I will stay here and obey you.” 

Then Rama addressed Jambhavan (son of Brahma), Mainda, Dwivida, and five others with them: “You all must remain alive as long as the Kali Yuga lasts.” After speaking to them, Rama (Kakutstha) said to all the bears and monkeys, “Come with me, all of you.”
SECTION CXXII

When night ended, the legendary Rāma—broad-chested and with eyes like lotus petals—spoke to the priest. “Let the shining umbrellas of Agnihotra and Bājapeya go first, along with the Brāhmanas. They’ll look impressive on the main road.” Vasishtha, glowing with wisdom, took charge and organized all the rituals needed for departing to the next world. Wearing a simple cloth, holding kusa grass between his fingers, and chanting Vedic hymns, Vasishtha led the way to the banks of the Saraju River. Rāma gave up all worldly actions and, despite the discomfort of walking, left the city in silence, as radiant as the blazing sun.

On Rāma’s right walked the goddess Sree (Lakshmi, goddess of fortune, sometimes called Sri), whose hands were as soft as lotus petals. On his left was the goddess Earth. Leading the way before him was the personification of destruction. Weapons—arrows, enormous bows, and daggers—took on living forms and followed him. The four Vedas, embodied by the Brāhmanas, walked with him, as did the sacred Gayatri mantra, Omkāra, and Vasatkāra. Great sages and even mighty Asuras (demons) followed Rāma as he headed toward the open gates of heaven.

All the palace women, both young and old, and the maidens of the royal chambers—along with their attendants, including eunuchs—joined the procession. Bharata and Lakshmana, each with their wives, walked with him, carrying Agnihotra. All these noble souls, gathered together with their families and the sacred fire, followed Rāma. Ministers and servants, along with their children, animals, and friends, happily joined Rāma’s journey.

The people of Ayodhyā, healthy and joyful, followed Rāma, drawn to his virtues and feeling purified of their sins. Men and women alike, with their animals and birds and friends, followed Rāma in high spirits. The monkeys, all bathed and happy, marched behind Rāma, filling the air with cheerful noise. There was no one poor, sad, or suffering—everyone looked wonderfully content and excited.

As Rāma left the city, anyone who came out just to see him soon found themselves swept up in the journey, eager to follow him to heaven. Bears, monkeys, Rākshasas (demons), and all the townspeople followed him with deep devotion and focused minds. Even the animals that usually stayed hidden in the city came out to follow Rāma on his heavenly path. Every living thing, moving or still, that saw Rāma (Kākuthstha) wanted to go with him. Every creature in Ayodhyā, no matter how small or invisible, joined Rāma as he walked on.
SECTION CXXIII

After traveling for more than half a Yojana, Rama (also called Kakutstha, descendant of Raghu) spotted the holy river Sarayu, which flowed westward. He crossed the river, riding its rising waves, along with his followers. They arrived at the very spot where Rama was meant to leave his mortal body. Just then, Brahma—the grandfather of all beings—appeared, surrounded by all the great gods and accompanied by hundreds of millions of celestial chariots. They came to the place where Rama was preparing to ascend to heaven. The sky itself was already shining, but the brilliance of the gods made it even more radiant. The air was filled with sweet, fragrant breezes, and divine flowers rained down from the gods’ hands. The sound of hundreds of trumpets, played by Gandharvas and Apsaras, echoed all around. Rama then got ready to step into the waters of the Sarayu.

At that moment, Brahma spoke from the sky: “Come, Vishnu! We are blessed that you are returning to us. Rama, hero of the Raghu line, listen—come here with your brothers, all of you shining like gods, in whatever form you wish—either as you are now or in your true form as Vishnu. You are the refuge of all beings; nobody truly knows you. You are beyond comprehension—eternal, immortal, imperishable. Only Maya, your first wife with wide eyes, truly knows you. Enter here, taking whatever brilliant form you desire.”

Hearing Brahma’s words and understanding everything, Rama took his true form as Vishnu and entered the waters, together with his brothers. Immediately, all the gods, including Sadhyas, Maruts, Indra, and Agni, worshipped Vishnu. Celestial sages, Gandharvas, Apsaras, Suparnas, Nagas, Yakshas, demons, Danavas, and Rakshasas all paid their respects as well. The gods praised Vishnu, saying, “Our world is now free from sin. Everyone here is overjoyed, and all our wishes have been fulfilled.”

Then the radiant Vishnu turned to Brahma and said, “Brahma, please assign these people their proper places in heaven. They have followed me out of love and devotion. They deserve my respect for giving up their lives for me.” Brahma replied, “All who have come here will go to the region called Santanaka. Even those born into the lowest states can reach this place if they see all things as Vishnu. There’s no doubt that those who followed you and gave up their lives out of devotion will attain this region. Santanaka has all the qualities of Brahma’s own realm and is just next to it. The monkeys and bears will take their true celestial forms. Each will merge with the god they originally came from. Sugriva will enter the region of the Sun. They will all regain their forms as the divine fathers among the gods assembled here.”

After Brahma finished speaking, everyone present at the sacred site of Gopratra stepped into the Sarayu’s waters, their eyes filled with joyful tears. They bathed, let go of their lives willingly, and left behind their human bodies, ascending into the waiting celestial chariots. Hundreds of birds, born in sacred lineages, also attained immortality, regaining their original divine forms. In these forms, they shone like the gods themselves. All creatures, living and non-living, who bathed in the Sarayu, also reached the best celestial realms. The bears, monkeys, and Rakshasas who gave up their bodies there were welcomed into the worlds of the gods. Having reached heaven, everyone who had gathered there—together with Brahma and the gods—rejoiced and happily entered the highest realm.
SECTION CXXIV

This story concludes with the Uttara Kanda. It is deeply respected by Brahma and was written by Valmiki, who is considered the greatest among poets. The epic is known as the Ramayana and is honored above all other stories. After its conclusion, Vishnu—who encompasses all the worlds and everything in them, living or not—returned to his divine realm, just as before. In heaven, the gods, Gandharvas, and great Rishis would listen to the Ramayana every day with joy. During the Śrāddha ceremony, the wise are encouraged to recite the Ramayana, as it is as sacred as the Vedas, believed to wash away sins and bring long life and prosperity. Even reading a single verse of this epic is said to bless a childless person with children, or grant wealth to someone in need. It is also believed to free people from their daily sins. Anyone who recites this poem should be given gifts like clothes, cows, or gold, because pleasing the reciter pleases all the gods. Whoever reads the Ramayana, which brings long life, will be respected in this world along with their children and grandchildren, and even in the afterlife. No matter if someone reads the Ramayana in the morning, at noon, or in the evening, they will never get tired of it. The beautiful city of Ayodhya was empty for many years, but became lively again during the rule of King Rishava, who was the son of Pracheta. Valmiki wrote this poem, which grants long life, and included the future story of the god and the Uttara Kanda. Even Brahma praised this work.
